text:
Dendritic Morphology in Coarsened Microstructures

By Erhan Altinoglu

Abstract

This study addresses the quantification of dendritic evolution in coarsened microstructures. Such measurements stem from the computational assessment of a microstructure's interfacial orientations and curvatures. Samples of aluminum with 26% copper by weight (Al-26wt%-Cu) were coarsened for either 10 minutes or 5 days. Serial sectioning techniques were utilized in imaging and reconstructing the microstructures into three-dimensional arrays. Interactive Data Language (IDL) software was then employed to calculate the orientation and curvature from the triangulated three-dimensional surfaces. The data was finally displayed in Mean vs. Gaussian curvature and stereographically projected orientation probability density plots. Assessment of these distributions quantitatively illustrates a dendritic morphology toward a greater density of solid tubular shapes of low principle radii during coarsening.

I. Motivation

One of the basic principles of materials science states that the overall behavior of a system is governed by the properties of its constituent parts. In this regard, the mechanical properties of metals are dictated by the microstructures formed during their solidification. A particular interest to a system's mechanical response is the substructure's component grain size and dendrite arm spacing. It has been experimentally demonstrated that as these parameters increase, the ultimate tensile strength and the percent elongation at fracture of the solidified metal decrease.¹ For this reason, grain size has been the traditional tool used to characterize a metal's mechanical properties. Flemings, however, has discovered that dendrite arm spacing yields a greater correlation to the mechanical responses.¹ Under this premise, it is proposed that understanding the evolution of these dendrites may be a significant step in quantifying the underlying processing-property relationship of solidified metals.

Fig. 1 Schematic of secondary arm spacing λ₂, in dendritic structures ²

The progression of dendritic solid-liquid mixtures is conventionally registered through analyses of the secondary arms spacing, λ₂, which is identified in Figure 1. This arm spacing is altered during solidification through a coarsening, or Ostwald ripening, process. Under isothermal conditions, interfacial liquid phase composition prompts coarsening, which, as expressed by the Gibbs-Thompson equation for a binary alloy (Eqn.1), is a function of the mean curvature, H, of the solid-liquid interface:

C = C∞ + lc H (Eqn.1)

where C is the composition in the liquid at the solid-liquid interface, C∞ is the equilibrium composition of the liquid at a flat interface, lc is the capillary length that is a function of the solid-liquid interfacial energy, and H is the mean curvature, as expressed below (Eqn.2):²

H = (1/R₁ + 1/R₂)/2 (Eqn.2)

where R₁ and R₂ are the principle radii of curvature. The above equations demonstrate that different compositions at the solid-liquid interface are a result of interfacial areas of differing curvature. In turn, these composition gradients lead to fluxes of solute through the dendrite, generating the morphological evolution of the solid-liquid mixture. A comprehension of the coarsening process will shed light on the morphology of the secondary arm spacing, which in turn divulges the morphological evolution of the entire dendritic microstructure. This morphology can be recounted by two basic assessments: the time evolution of interfacial orientations and surface curvatures. For such a detailed characterization, however, traditional two-dimensional microstructural information via metallographic cross-sections is insufficient. Instead, a three-dimensional analysis must be undertaken, and is described herein.

II. Computational Background

It is our objective to quantify the dendritic evolution in coarsened microstructures by generating three-dimensional reconstructions of dendritic microstructures. These digital reconstructions will then be analyzed for interfacial directionality and surface curvature variations. A range of coarsening times will be used to illustrate the evolution of the microstructure and to relate the subsequent microstructural array to the time-dependent coarsening process.

An automated serial sectioning technique is used to create the three-dimensional reconstructions. Serial sections are taken at 4.75 μm intervals. A digital image is recorded of each section and the exact position of the sample is noted. The groups of images are then cleaned, the threshold adjusted to clearly distinguish the liquid-eutectic interface, and layered in sequence. Using the positioning data, an area common to all images in the sequence is then selected to account for any misalignment during the image capturing procedure. The resized images are finally stacked and aligned before being run through Interactive Data Language (IDL) software for the three-dimensional reconstruction.

Once the dendritic microstructure is reconstructed, the proposed analyses are undertaken. To quantitatively determine the presence of any preferential directionality or symmetry of the interfacial orientations, surface normal vectors are utilized in a stereographic projection of the microstructure. A stereographic projection is a graphical technique that converts three-dimensional angular information into two two-dimensional images. First, the interface of the reconstruction is triangulated into millions of patches, each with a unique normal vector, n. Now, considering the reconstruction completely enclosed by a theoretical reference sphere (Fig. 2), normal vectors from each triangulated patch can be projected out from the structure until it intersects the surface of the sphere at a set of points called poles. A projection plane tangent to the reference sphere and perpendicular to the growth direction (z-axis) illustrates the intersection of each pole on a hemisphere. Two complimentary hemispheres together comprise the entire three-dimensional reference sphere. Plotting the frequency at which poles of equal orientation intersect the projection plane transforms the stereographic projection into a probability distribution plot. By observing trends in these orientation distributions, the directionality of the microstructural interfaces can be visualized. Consequently, any symmetry will be resolved through this process.

Fig. 2 Schematic of stereographic projections Each hemisphere is a projection about the growth direction (z-axis)

Due to the morphological variation present during coarsening, a morphology independent measure of the microstructure, interfacial curvature, is required for sufficient assessment and comparison of dendritic evolution. Interfacial curvature may be gauged through the analysis of two parameters, the mean curvature, H, and the Gaussian curvature, K:

H = 1/2 (1/R₁+1/R₂) (Eqn.3)

K=(1/R₁)(1/R₂) (Eqn.4)

As discussed in the MOTIVATION, the mean curvature, H, determines the solute concentration at the interface under the Gibbs-Thompson equation (Eqn.1). As material concentration changes, so will the mean curvature. The time derivative of mean and Gaussian curvatures are proportional, thus it is applied as an additional measure.³ The importance of the Gaussian curvature is also illustrated by a saddle-shaped surface in which the principle radii of a surface (identified in Fig. 3) are exact opposites, R₁ = -R₂. In this case, Eqn. 3 yields H = 0, thus making the interfacial solute concentration equal to that of a planar interface, despite the interface not resembling such a physical orientation. Therefore, it is necessary to measure both the mean and Gaussian curvatures in order to characterize the true interfacial orientation.²

Fig. 3 Principle radii of curvatures, R₁ and R₂ of surface patch

Fig. 4 Parallel surface patch method employed in mean and Gaussian curvature calculations²

The three-dimensional mean and Gaussian curvature information can be obtained using a method employed by Jinnai, et al.⁴ This involves triangulating the interface and constructing a parallel patch by displacing each surface point by a distance d normal to the interface, as shown in Figure 4. The area of the parallel interfaces, A(d,p), is related to the area of the original interface patch, A(0,p) by:

A(d,p) = A(0,p)[1+2H(p)d+K(p)d²] (Eqn.5)

By constructing a parallel interface, there become two equations with two unknowns. Solving these equations reveals H and K at a point p, thus completely characterizing the surface shape at that point.²

IV. Reconstructions

Two samples of a directionally solidified Al-26wt%Cu were coarsened at 5°C above the aluminum liquidus temperature (553°C) for duration of 10 minutes and 5 days (Fig. 5, Fig. 6). The samples were then serial sectioned at 4.75 μm intervals to a total of 100 sections and digitally reconstructed. The phase pictured represents solid Al, while the encompassing eutectic liquid phase has been set to total transparence for viewing ease. The solid phase accounts for a 40% volume fraction of the sample.

Fig. 5 Three-dimensional reconstruction of a 10 minute coarsened sample of Al-26wt%Cu from 100 serial sections at 4.75μm increments

Fig. 6 Three-dimensional reconstruction of a 5 day coarsened sample of Al-26wt%Cu from 100 serial sections at 4.75μm increments

On initial inspection, it is clear that the sample coarsened for 10 minutes is extremely interconnected, complex and dense in the solid Al orientation (Fig. 5). Such a configuration would be expected to yield surface orientations and curvatures across the entire spectrum. For instance, it is clear that surface normals placed randomly throughout the sample would be positioned in almost every possible direction. Furthermore, the visibly diverse range of dendritic shapes is expected to yield a wide range of curvature measures. On the other hand, the sample coarsened for 5 days (Fig. 6) is much less dense in solid packing, and the dendritic shapes have undergone a visually evident change in length scale. A more limited distribution of normal vectors and surface curvatures would be expected for this microstructure.

V. Interfacial Orientation

Figure 7 shows the stereographically projected, orientation density plots for the 10 minute sample created through IDL. The figure presents the two hemispheres of the reference sphere projected around both the positive z-axis (the growth direction) and the negative z-axis (refer to Fig. 2). Most clearly illustrated by the plot is the broad range of surface orientations present throughout the microstructure, which is seen in Figure 5. Furthermore, there are clearly four localized density regions projected about the z-axis. This observation signifies that there is in fact a general directionality present in the system with respect to the growth direction. The projection planes of a microstructure with limited or no directionality, such as the sphere in Figure 9, would yield a uniform density of poles throughout both hemispheres. Moreover, the particular arrangement of orientation density peaks illustrates almost perfect four-fold symmetry. Such symmetry is expected in an unvaryingly complex and interconnected microstructure of limited or no coarsening.

Fig. 7 Stereographically projected distribution plots of interfacial orientations in the 10 minute sample about the (left) positive growth direction and (right) negative growth direction

Coarsening to 5 days has a marked influence on interfacial orientation, as seen in Figure 8 (left). Perhaps most evident is the narrower distribution of orientations, which would be expected for a more regular arrangement of solid dendrites. There remains a significant density of theta angles along the Θ = π/2 direction. In this case, however, these theta angles are distributed less uniformly along the phi direction. The theta peaks in Figure 8 (left) are separated by a measure of π along phi. In this respect, it can be visualized that for each vector of Θ = π/2, there exists a complimentary angle of equal theta 180 degrees away in the phi direction. Such an orientation proposes a shape of high relative uniformity in the growth direction (z-axis) with respect to the x- and y-axes, limiting phi angles toward specific directions, such as the planar shape in Figure 7.

Fig. 8 Stereographically projected distribution plots of interfacial orientations in the 5 day sample about the (left) positive growth direction and (right) negative growth direction

Coarsening to 5 days has a marked influence on interfacial orientation, as seen in Figure 8. Perhaps most evident in this figure is the narrower distribution of orientations, which would be expected for a more regular arrangement of solid dendrites. There remain two significant density peaks parallel to the x-y plane. However, these normals are distributed less uniformly after the lengthened coarsening process. The two peaks in Figure 8 are separated by a measure of π about the growth direction. In this respect, it can be visualized that for each normal vector projected from an interfacial patch, there exists a complimentary vector, 180° away in almost perfect two-fold symmetry. Such an orientation proposes an elevated density of shapes exhibiting high relative uniformity in the growth direction (z-axis) with respect to the x- and y-axes. This stereographic projection is typical of the planar shape in Figure 9, where each surface yields its distinct peak complemented by another peak from the parallel surface in the opposite direction.

(a) sphere uniform density of projections in all possible orientations

(b) cylinder uniform projection of normals parallel to the x-y plane

(c) plane distinct regions of normal peaks projected by each face

Fig. 9 Normal vector orientations with respect to common shapes and their respective theoretical stereographic projection peaks

VI. Surface Curvature

In addition to directionality assessment, computational analysis using IDL software can determine curvature distributions and mode interfacial shapes. Alkemper and Voorhees have previously generated plots that display H and K distributions independently, illustrating the distribution of the curvatures within the microstructure.⁵ Additionally, Mendoza's previous curvature analysis has identified key parameters of curvature that dictate the morphology of the interface. If H is positive, the interface has a solid spherical shape, while a negative H represents a liquid spherical shape.² Moreover, Mendoza's analysis determined that if a point on the interface has a positive Gaussian curvature, the concavity of the interface is determined by the sign of H. If H is positive, the interface is concave towards the solid, while if H is negative, it is convex towards the solid. Additionally, an interface with K=0 has a cylindrical interface composed of solid (if H is positive) or liquid (if H is negative). Interestingly, saddle-shaped interfaces are characterized by negative Gaussian curvatures.² Thus, the sign of the mean curvature determines the dominant principle curvature. Figure 10 graphically illustrates these curvature criteria.

Fig. 10 Theoretical map of local interfacial shapes for the H-K contour plots²

Figure 11 is another theoretical curvature map generated by Mendoza. The criteria for this map are dictated by K₁-K₂ relationships and do not involve mean curvature. Nonetheless, these criteria serve similar purposes and may be used as an alternative means of visualizing the surface curvature distributions.

Fig. 11 Theoretical map of local interfacial shapes for the K₁-K₂ contour plots²

Probability density plots of the mean and Gaussian curvature created from the data arrays of the three-dimensional reconstruction can be used, along with Mendoza's criteria, to identify the most probable interfacial shapes present within the microstructure. These plots for the two coarsened times are included below (Fig. 12, Fig. 13). It is clear from Figure 12 that the microstructural curvatures of the 10 minute coarsening comprise a high density of interfaces concave toward the solid, which is observed by the complex and interconnected dendritic microstructure of Figure 5. It is interesting to note that the distribution of curvature shapes encompass a wide range of curvatures (both high and low principle radii), indicating that the interfaces are homogenously short in their length scale but diverse in their curvature orientations.

Fig. 12 (left) H vs. K and (right) K₁ vs. K₂ probability density plot for the 10 minute sample

The significance of these plots, however, lies in the curvature comparison over additional coarsening durations. The plots generated for the 5 day coarsened sample (Fig. 13) show a marked change in distribution range. However, such figures must be scaled by surface area per volume in order to account for the drastic changes in length scale between the two microstructures. The scaled K₁ vs. K₂ plots for the two samples are shown in Figure 14.

Fig. 13 (left) H vs. K and (right) K₁ vs. K₂ probability density plot for the 5 day sample

A comparison between the scaled curvature probability distribution plots illustrates curvature evolution with respect to the coarsening time. Most evident is the shift in peak density around the solid cylinder axis from 10 minutes to 5 days of coarsening. Furthermore, an increase in coarsening time appears to promote a more uniform concentration of curvatures around the peak density, as seen by the more regular spread of distributions in the 5 day sample. This uniformity around the solid cylinder peak results in an almost equal distribution on either side of the K₁ axis. An overlay of the two scaled distributions reveals that the density peak of the 5 day sample has also shifted slightly to a region of higher K curvature (smaller principle radii). Such a transition depicts a unique path of dendritic morphology toward more cylindrically shaped interfaces, which can be visually verified by the more simplistic, tubular structures present in Figure 6.

Fig. 13 SV-scaled K₁ vs. K₂ curvature distribution plots for a (top) 10 minute and (bottom) 5 day coarsened sample

VII. Conclusion

An increase in coarsening time from 10 minutes to 5 days for an Al-26wt%-Cu alloy has a significant morphological effect on the underlying microstructure. It is clear that the dendritic structures evolve into larger, less densely packed solid configurations in efforts to reduce interfacial curvatures. However, the aforementioned analyses have now quantified this morphological evolution through probability density calculations.

The distribution of interfacial orientations is shown to contract and orient normal to the growth direction. Vectors normal to the surface have also shown a significant transition toward complimenting directions separated by an angle of 180°, which is characteristic of a tubular structure. Furthermore, interfacial curvatures were directly identified to undergo a similar evolution. A 5 day coarsening duration for this system transformed the microstructure from a complex mixture of interfaces concave toward the solid phase to a more uniform distribution of solid cylinders. Interfaces concave toward the liquid phase were almost entirely eliminated. Such a distribution shift quantifies the expected process by which high curvature dendritic arms coarsen into larger, lower curvature structures. Furthermore, the probability density distribution of curvatures shifted slightly to higher values, illustrating morphology specifically toward solid cylinders.

This curvature analysis has provided the computational evidence that confirms the notion that dendritic morphology stems from an effort to reduce surface curvature. This was displayed by both the interfacial orientation and curvature shape distributions. Furthermore, this quantitative analysis illustrates a unique direction of dendritic morphology under coarsening. Seen by this Al-26wt%-Cu eutectic system, coarsening has driven the interfacial evolution of component dendrites toward solid cylindrical structures.

References

¹M.C. Flemings. Solidification Processing 1974; McGraw-Hill Book Company.

²R. Mendoza. “The Morphological Evolution of Dendritic Microstructures During Coarsening,” Research Proposal 2002; Northwestern University.

³D.A. Drew. “Evolution of Geometric Statistics,” SIAM Journal of Applied Math 1990; 50(3):649-666.

⁴H. Jinnai, T. Koga, Y. Nishikawa, T. Hashimoto, S. Hyde. “Curvature determination of Spinodal Interface in a Condensed Matter System,” Physical Review Letters 1997; 78(11):2248-2251.

⁵J. Alkemper, P.W. Voorhees. “Quantitative Serial Sectioning Analysis,” Journal of Microscopy 2001; 201:388-394.

title: Snail Kite Rostrhamus sociabilis Accipitridae size and color selectivity of Apple Snail Pomacea flagellata Ampullaridae
notes: Field study in Palo Verde National Park, Costa Rica. Advisor named on the contents page ("Advisor: J. Mauricio Garcia-C., Duke University"); the acknowledgements add the Organization for Tropical Studies in Costa Rica.
text:
Snail Kite Rostrhamus sociabilis Accipitridae size and color selectivity of Apple Snail Pomacea flagellata Ampullaridae

By Alissa Genthon and Natalia Corrales

Abstract

In Costa Rica's Palo Verde National Park, the specialist predator Rostrhamus sociabilis (Snail Kite) inhabits a freshwater marsh where it specifically hunts for Pomacea flagellata (Apple Snails). It is thought that the Snail Kite is selective for specific size ranges of the Apple Snail. In this study, Apple Snail size selectivity was explored by comparing sizes of prey to a representation of the available Apple Snail population in order to exploit Snail Kite bias toward size extremity within the population. Snail Kites in this study were selective for larger, more rare snails, indicating that not only does the Kite specialize in type of prey, but also in size of prey. In addition, color selectivity was observed and determined to be unrelated to selection of the snails. Finally, the study evaluated any existing snail selectivity for specific plant species to determine the complexity of the system in which the Snail Kite must hunt. Apple Snails were found to have a higher density among Bladderwort (Utricularia gibba), but this density was also shown to vary with other factors such as surface temperature, vegetative thickness, and presence of emergent vegetation. In any case, Snail density and size distribution, which are ultimately dependent on the health of the habitat, limits the success of the Snail Kite population.

I. Introduction

Evolutionarily, specialization has become an important mechanism for the success of many species. As a specific example, the Snail Kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis Accipitridae) has an almost exclusive predator-prey relationship with the Apple Snail³,⁴,⁵ (Pomacea flagellata Ampullariidae). Snail Kites are more common in freshwater marshes and sloughs, and their population ranges from southern Florida and southeastern Mexico to Ecuador and northern Argentina.⁷ In Costa Rica, they are found in the Tempisque basin and Rio Frio-Cano but are rare in the lowlands of these regions.⁷ Seasonal movement is normal for Snail Kites as they must respond to changing water levels from wet to dry seasonal variations, which affects availability of prey.⁷ The Snail Kite depends primarily on the Apple Snail that inhabits tropical and neotropical freshwaters and consumes local aquatic plants or floating vegetation.⁵

Although the Apple Snail is consumed by several predators (crocodiles, turtles, fish, other bird species, and young alligators), each specialist predator has a separate foraging method which clearly distinguishes their distinct niches.⁵ The Snail Kite, a medium sized raptor, utilizes two different foraging techniques to capture its prey: the course-hunting technique and still-hunting technique.³ In the first, the Snail Kite will fly low over the marsh using its visual acuity to locate snails up to 16 centimeters below the marsh surface.⁴ It then carries its prey to a designated perch and uses its curved beak to remove the operculum of the snail, permitting the Kite full access to the snail meat.³ With the second technique, the Snail Kite will remain at its perch until it locates a snail. The prey in each case is carried back to a specific perch where it is consumed, and the shell is then discarded into a pile below the perch. According to Collett (1977), although Apple Snails reach a range of sizes during a lifetime, Snail Kites normally consume snails of a “large” size because they hunt by sight. Also, Snyder and Kale (1983) attribute the failure of Snail Kites to consume smaller snails to the fact that extraction is more difficult with a smaller snail, as there is a smaller opening to remove the operculum. It has also been shown by Bourne (1985) that Snail Kites forage in order to maximize caloric return per energy expenditure which would imply a tendency toward snails of larger size.

Both the predator and the prey in this situation depend on the presence of emergent vegetation for survival. Apple Snails are found in freshwater marshes, lakes, rivers, and springs, which all must include emergent vegetation in order to provide breathing and egg laying surfaces. Apple Snails also depend on the aquatic plants within the marsh habitat as a food source.⁵ The Snail Kite also requires emergent vegetation or perches in order to successfully locate and consume its prey. In effect, there is a certain degree of association between wetland plants and the Snail Kite-Apple Snail relationship. Because of this, the health of the wetland habitat becomes a limiting factor to the success of the Snail Kite. This has recently become an important issue since the Snail Kite is now endangered in Costa Rica (Wildlife Conservation Law 7317).

This study aims to explore the applicable selectivity of size and color of the Apple Snails by the Snail Kite. Also, possible specific plant-snail association is examined. It was expected that the Snail Kite would be selective for larger and lighter colored snails because they are more easily located and provide maximum caloric return. Furthermore, it was predicted that the Apple Snail would in fact show a specific plant association.

II. Methods

The study was conducted at the Palo Verde National Park between October 11 and October 14 of 2003 (wet season) in the freshwater marsh, where Pomacea flagellata are frequently preyed upon by Rostrhamus sociabilis. Palo Verde National Park lies in the Rio Tempisque lowlands in a tropical dry forest, covering an area of 13, 058 hectares.⁵ In this area, there is a defined dry season, January through March, as well as a wet season, June through December.

To evaluate size, a comparison was made between snail size and color by examining consumed snails and the live snail population. We identified nine perches of Snail Kites and gathered 400 snail shells from beneath these perches. The shells were collected by hand when floating or by using a net when they were on the marsh floor. These shells were then measured for shell length, shell width, operculum length, operculum width with Vernier calipers (precision ± 0.001m), and shade (light or dark using a color chart). To compare the general population of snails available to the Snail Kite, the live population of snails was sampled by gathering snails from randomly placed transects in the vicinity of the identified perches. Randomization was achieved by using a stopwatch to determine number of paces out from the shore that a transect should begin in the area of a known perch. One transect was 50m by 2m and nine transects were 25m by 2m because we found it to be more time efficient (the 50m by 2m transect is excluded in analysis due to disproportion). Only the live snails on the surface were collected, where surface is defined as all floating vegetation and open areas of water. Snails collected in the transects were then measured just as those collected from beneath the perches. To evaluate plant-snail associations, the dominant plant species in terms of highest percent coverage was recorded for every 10m² in each of the transects sampled for live snails.

Since the distribution of snail shell sizes between the transects was not normal, a Wilcoxon/Kruskal Wallis test was used to compare mean shell size collected between transects and perches (it is important to note that operculum length and width were used in shell size comparisons because it was established as a more stable measurement for snail size). Then, a Chi Square analysis was done to determine Snail Kite preference for color of snail shell, where color is defined as light or dark. In addition, one way ANOVA analysis was performed on operculum size (operculum length by width) between perches to determine foraging differences between individuals within the Snail Kite population itself. Finally, the relation between operculum size and shell size was evaluated using regression analysis. In our second objective, we assessed the possibility of specific plant-snail association. As the transects were completed for the primary objective, the dominant vegetation for every 5 meters was observed and recorded as well as the number of snails collected. After establishing that there was a statistically significant difference in the number of snails collected between transects by using a Chi Square analysis, these observations of dominant vegetation were employed to relate snail density to vegetation type, thereby reflecting any specific plant-snail association. This analysis and all others were completed using the JMP 3.2 statistical analysis program (SAS Institute 1997).

III. Results

The 400 snail shells collected from the perches were compared to the 313 live snails collected in the transects. Snail Kites were highly selective for larger snails present in the nine perches (Fig. 1), but were shown to have no preference for color of snail shell (Fig. 2). Also, snails in the live population showed no bias toward lighter or darker shell color (Fig. 2). Snail shell sizes differed significantly between perches (Figure 3), indicating distinct ownership of each perch. After the regression analysis (Fig. 4), operculum size (operculum length by width) was shown to be highly correlated with shell size (shell size by width). Finally, since there was a significant difference in the number of live snails collected in each transect (Fig. 5), these differences indicate discrepancies in the aquatic plant distribution in each transect, suggesting the existence of specific plant-snail relationships.

Fig. 1 Mean operculum sizes (+1 sd) of Pomacea flagellata between transects and perches at Palo Verde National Park. (X² = 365.69, d.f. = 1, p<0.0001)

Fig. 2 Number of individuals of different shell colors between perches (n=400) and transects (n=313) at Palo Verde National Park (X² = .6, d.f. = 1, p<0.4387)

Fig. 3 Mean Operculum sizes (+1 sd) of Pomacea flagellata between perches of Snail Kites at Palo Verde National Park (one way ANOVA, F=13.015, p<0.0001)

Fig. 4 Regression analysis for operculum size versus shell size of Pomacea flagellata (n=713) at Palo Verde National Park. (simple linear regression, R² = 0.8675, p<0.05)

Fig. 5 Number of Pomacea flagellata individuals collected between transects of 25 m by 2 m (n=313) at Palo Verde National Park (X² = 844.84, d.f. = 5, p<0.05).

IV. Discussion

As hypothesized, the Snail Kites in the Palo Verde National Park marsh were shown to be highly selective for snail size, as is illustrated by Figure 1, with mean operculum size in perches significantly higher than mean operculum size for transects. These findings are concurrent with past studies and with the general biology of the Snail Kite itself. Because the Snail Kite hunts by sight, it is conceivable that it can locate a larger snail more easily. Also, a larger snail has a larger opening to the operculum, which is more easily removed by using the Kite's long, curved bill.⁴ Furthermore, the Snail Kite captures its prey using its talons, so a larger snail is more easily grasped by the talons of the Kite. This further promotes the theory that by selecting for larger prey, the Kite is most efficient in energy usage. The Kite receives a greater caloric intake to compensate for energy expended in the capturing process by selecting for larger snails.¹ One study notes that a breeding Snail Kite couple will select increasingly larger snails as the distance from the nest increases, again showing the most efficient use of energy.¹ The significantly lower mean size of the snails in the live population of this study suggests that larger snails are more rare in the habitat, which can be problematic for the Kite who is selective for these larger size snails. However, Janzen and Reed (1999) suggest that larger snails spend more time near the surface and are therefore more easily captured. Our study indicates that while it may be true that larger snails spend more time on the surface, they are more rare within the snail population and therefore less easily captured. It would be useful to take measurements of surface durations for different size snails to more clearly address whether larger snails actually spend more time at the surface. Also, a study with a larger sampling pool could reveal greater certainty as to whether larger snails are in fact more rare in the population.

Although Snail Kites were selective for snail size in this study, they had no preference for snail shell color, with nearly equal amounts of light and dark shells found in both transects and perches. Because Snail Kites hunt by site, it was expected that a lighter color shell would be more visible to the Kite and therefore captured more often. Janzen and Reed (1999) propose that lighter color snails are taken more often by Snail Kites because of their observation of directional selection against lighter color in the snail population. However, this was not the case in this study, indicating that the Kite can locate a dark shell just as easily as it can locate a lighter one. This would imply the presence of more important visual cues than contrast in color on the surface of the habitat. During our study, we observed that snails floating on the surface of the marsh were generally floating operculum side up, which would also support the fact that color of the shell provides no consistent visual cue for the Snail Kite. Perhaps, the reflection of light off of the operculum serves as a better visual cue for the Snail Kite than shell color. It is possible that the Kite in fact easily distinguishes between lighter and darker shells, but a directional selection against lighter colored shells does exist (as Janzen and Reed (1999) propose) because of some physical property rendering it more beneficial for capture (e.g. easier to break). In that case, the Kite may capture lighter colored snails preferentially, but supplement with darker snails, therefore appearing to have equal color preference.

Within the Snail Kite population, differences in selection of prey were found between individuals, with some perches containing shell sizes of a broader range as opposed to snails of strictly larger size. The differences may lie between adults and juveniles, with the less experienced juveniles choosing snails of a broader range, making less efficient use of energy.¹ More experienced adults may be more equipped to make the distinction of the energy advantage in larger size snails.¹ During our study, we observed two active perches (Perch 1 and Perch 8) that were occupied by juveniles. These active perches were also shown to have the lowest mean shell sizes, further suggesting these juvenile's inexperience. Another possibility is that the other perches with piles found to contain more variability in shell size came from a breeding Snail Kite couple. A breeding pair will select larger snails to bring back to the nest, while consuming smaller snails themselves and leaving those smaller shells beneath the perch.¹ Since the discarded shells at the perches were collected from both on the surface and below the surface, it is possible that shells were accumulated from different individuals at different points in time. In this case, the snail shell sizes can reveal which individuals may have inhabited a specific perch at one time (for example smaller shells indicate possible presence of juvenile or breeding couple). However, it was observed that all of the active perches with lower mean snail size were inhabited by juveniles.

Another interesting comparison between operculum size and snail size that was conducted reflects a strongly positive relationship between the two. Although the relationship is fairly strong, the lack of a definitive ratio suggests a specific purpose behind these disproportionate characteristics. In one study, it is suggested that this variation is due to a defensive advantage in the shape of the shell.² An odd and unpredictable shape of snail shell will be more difficult for a predator to identify, capture, and consume. In general however, it is thought that freshwater snails have less selective pressure to evolve such elaborate defense mechanisms because there are generally fewer predators in freshwater than in oceans.² However, although the Apple Snails are freshwater snails, they have many natural predators, including two specialist predators – the Limpkin and Snail Kite.⁷ Therefore, there may be more selectional pressure than usual for a freshwater snail to evolve defensive mechanisms through shell shape and size. Yet another reason for this variability can be revealed through observations made during this study. It was observed throughout the course of the study that many snails had their operculums set farther back into the shell (where the shell is more narrow) while others did not. This would account for the lack of a constant ratio between operculum size and snail shell size, while also suggesting a defensive mechanism. If the operculum is set farther back within the shell, it becomes difficult for the kite to remove the operculum in order to gain access to the snail meat. Therefore, it is beneficial for a snail possessing an extended shell opening. The lack of a direct relationship between operculum size and shell size in this situation cannot be attributed to any one theory with certainty without further investigation.

In order to investigate the presence of any specific plant associations with the Apple Snails, it had to be established that differences existed between the number of live snails collected in each transect. After a Chi Square statistical analysis, it was shown that there were in fact significant differences in the amount collected depending on the location of the transect. Observations of dominant vegetation made in each transect show that transects most abundant in available live snails coincided with the partial or complete dominance of Bladderwort (Utricularia gibba) within the transect. However, it was also determined from these observations that the presence of the Bladderwort was necessary but not sufficient to support a more abundant snail population in a given area (Table 1). Other variables seem to affect the distribution of the snails that were not addressed by the methodology. For example, transects having a thicker layer of floating vegetation generally had a lower abundance of snails. A thicker vegetation layer would limit the amount of oxygen and light available to the snails, so naturally they would avoid these area.¹ Areas with a higher surface temperature also demonstrated a lower abundance than those areas with a more mild surface temperature. In addition, higher snail abundances were found to be in areas of emergent vegetation, especially in areas with higher Thalia geniculata (an emergent aquatic plant) density. Thalia seemed to compose a major egg laying site for Apple Snails at Palo Verde, which may support the fact that a higher abundance of snails were found near areas of higher Thalia density. The apparent relationship in this study between Bladderwort and snail density is

These results would also be enhanced by further investigation of other factors observed in this study that affect the distribution of snails since the Snail Kites tend to concentrate foraging efforts in areas of high prey abundance.¹ A more rigorous methodology including more quantitative measurements of these observed factors will improve available information on this subject since it is relatively unaddressed in available literature. It is a possibility that Snail Kites recognize limiting factors in Snail distribution (like vegetative thickness, heat, and plant associations). According to Bourne (1985), Kites generally avoid areas dense in floating vegetation and the majority of the time select the most profitable and efficient foraging site. From the suggestive plant-snail association in this study, it can be proposed that the snails themselves are selective within the habitat which puts even more foraging pressure on the specialist Kite, which is then amplified by habitat destruction that removes plants important to the snail population.

Ultimately, the selection of type and size of prey by the Snail Kite limits its diet, which may be secondarily limited by snail dependence on specific plant species. Therefore, the future success of the endangered Snail Kite will depend on the health of its habitat. Efforts to improve the management and conservation of wetland habitats should be further considered as one solution to the critical state of the Snail Kite.

Advisor named on the contents page ("Advisor: James Colgate, Northwestern University") and in the acknowledgements. text:
Electro-Active Polymer Research for LIMS Applications

By Raphael Anstey

Abstract

The information presented in this paper is the result of a quarter of research for the Laboratory for Intelligent Mechanical Systems (LIMS) in the field of Electro-active Polymers (EAPs).

I. Motivation

LIMS is a research laboratory of the Mechanical Engineering Department of Northwestern University in Illinois that concerns itself with robotics and other applications that use the integration of electromechanical systems and computer controls to achieve various goals. Recently, the Office of Naval Research has approached this laboratory with the ambitious project of investigating fish propulsion systems. Though many watercraft employ fish-inspired stream-lined hull geometries and smoothed surfaces, boat builders have avoided the imitation of tail fins because of the tail's large movements. It has been determined, however, that specialized fish driven by their pectoral fins as well as those who utilize a “ribbon fin” on their underbelly for propulsion have the potential to be mechanically imitated. The end goal of this endeavor would be to utilize the efficiencies obtained through millions of years of evolution to improve on current propeller driven remotely operated vehicles (ROV) and submersibles.

Another advantage that these fish have is exceptional maneuverability. The ribbon fin of the knife fish and pectoral fins of the wrasse are of interest. The wrasse's fins allow flight-like motion through the water as the pectoral fins are manipulated to create lift. The knife fish's “ribbon” allows for complete reversal of direction literally on a dime, even at top speed. If proven effective as intelligent mechanical systems, fish inspired propulsion methods could even make their way to large-scale war submarines in the future.

Current technologies dictate that the standard in actuating any fin apparatus that might be built is electromagnetic motors. These motors can be electrically controlled and therefore mesh very well with software control systems. Unfortunately, these motors are only standard as linear or angular actuators. Consequently, any motions that do not have a circular or linear path will require sometimes-complicated apparatuses on top of the motors themselves. Additionally, motors are very difficult to scale down to the centimeter range. In fish fins, the wrasse's pectoral fin is driven by a stiff leading edge. With some work, this fin could be imitated by a combination of motors and mechanisms. The ribbon fin, however, has proven more difficult to imitate with motors, (as seen by Professor Maciver's mechanical fin in Figure 1). Although functional for researching fluid forces generated by movement in water, the mechanism would not be ideal in a fully emerged submersible-like application due to its large size and weight.

Fig. 1 Prof. Maciver's Motor Driven Ribbon Fin Illustrates the size Limitations Associated with Electromagnetic Motors (approx. 1m long).¹

II. Introduction to Electroactive Polymers

In light of the end goal of creating a large-scale In light of the end goal of creating a large-scale mechanical pectoral or ribbon fin, LIMS has sought to investigate the emerging field of Electro-active polymers (EAPs) as actuators. EAPs are essentially polymers that have been manipulated in such a way that they transform electrical input (in this case voltage) into mechanical output (displacement). Due to the discovery of particular plastics and the novel use of compliant electrodes, researchers have demonstrated fast response times (<1ms), high efficiencies (80-90%), high area actuation strain (215%), and energy densities up to .15 J/g.² These claims along with the light weight of polymers have made EAPs very promising as actuators for eventual fin systems. EAPs come in two varieties; ionic and electronic.

Ionic EAPs use mechanisms of electro-chemistry, namely the movement of charged ions in the molecules of advanced materials. These materials include ionomeric polymer-metal composites, conductive polymers and even carbon nanotubes.³ Conventional batteries may be used with these EAPs, as voltages as low as 1V will activate movement. These Ionic EAPs however require significant knowledge of advanced material fabrication, finances, and equipment. In essence, the LIMS lab is not equipped to produce polymer-metal composites and nanotubes, and contracting the Material Sciences Department would complicate the project beyond practical limitations.

Electronic EAPs offer a much more robust and practical alternative. Powered by electric fields that attract compliant electrodes (usually conductive carbon grease) stenciled onto each side of a flat polymer, these assemblies expand as the electrodes squeeze in and cause significant Maxwell stresses. Until now, Maxwell stress has generally been regarded as a side effect in polymers, generally not strong enough to offer practical actuation.⁴ However, the identification of soft polymer thin films with high dielectric breakdown strengths has led to exceptionally high performance in dielectric elastomers. Dielectric elastomers are simply the polymer with compliant electrodes stenciled on each side. The only draw back to this method is the high voltages needed (over 1 kV).

III. Mechanisms of Actuation

The operation of electronic EAPs is based on the aforementioned dielectric polymer “sandwich” where high voltage squeezes down on the polymer to create an expansion in area. Such elastomers have coupled squeezing and stretching stresses that are consolidated into an effective compressive stress, p, given by Equation1:⁵ p = ε εₒ E² = ε εₒ (V/z)² (Eqn. 1)

In this equation, εₒ is the permittivity of free space (8.85 X 10⁻¹² F/m), ε is the relative dielectric constant (Capacitance of our selected polymer/ Capacitance of Air). E represents the applied electric field, V is the applied voltage, and z is the thickness of our polymer film. The importance of super high voltages becomes evident when viewing this equation, as the pressure of squeeze is directly related to the square of the voltage. Thus, the most effective way to increase the pressure and thereby the actuation strength is to increase the voltage applied. This equation also reveals the importance of a high relative dielectric constant. This constant basically describes a specific material's resistance to electric flow. In this case, the constant refers to current flow through the polymer between the oppositely charged electrodes. Since the squeezing effect is achieved by trapping electrons in the electrodes and harnessing their attraction to the other side's opposite charge, any flow or “leakage” through the polymer would effectively reduce the strain and subsequent strength of actuation. Thusly, any material that has a high ε while still delivering flexibility, relatively low density, and the other advantages associated with polymers will be a winner.

Through a trial and error process of material selection, researchers at SRI International have discovered that a cheap and common acrylic polymer manufactured by 3M that can deliver the needed compressive stresses for effective actuation. This polymer has been identified as VHB 4910. A further enticing study is one done by SRI researchers that determined that pre-straining the material actually increases performance by increasing the compressive stress. What is actually happening in this process is an increase in ε through the pre-strain. This phenomenon is not currently explained, but some SRI personnel have proposed an intriguing mechanism. They believe the stretching of VHB 4910 orients the molecular polymer chains along the axis of stretch, and this orderly arrangement seems to close molecular holes through which electrons could have previously penetrate.³ Thus the material's resistance to current increases.

In embarking upon the creation of an EAP actuator for LIMS, it is known that the following will be needed: A High Voltage source, conductive carbon grease for electrodes, VHB 4910, and an apparatus that can pre-strain the material yet still provide free range of motion in the direction normal to this pre-strain.

IV. Proposed Apparatus Design

The entire device can be divided into two main components. One aspect of the device regulates and delivers High Voltage in a controlled manner. The other part fulfills the mechanical requirements of pre-strain while allowing free movement.

High Voltage and Safety Concerns

Literature calls for 980V when dealing with acrylic polymers.⁶ While LIMS does have variable 0-12 volt DC power supplies as well as variacs that are good up to 120V AC, such a high voltage would essentially require its own apparatus to be successfully delivered. This seemed daunting at first due to some confusion over budget limitations. While the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory's website on EAPs did point directly to EMCO's patented Voltage source as a convenient solution, this first-time researcher thought that the roughly $100 price tag deemed the device a non-possibility. As a result, help was sought from Norm

Flasch, an electronics specialist. Mr. Flasch used a variac and heavy-duty transformer run through a full-wave rectifier and capacitive filters to deliver up to 1300 V of DC power. However, upon further investigation by Prof. Peshkin, the source proved extremely dangerous. Criteria for “dangerous” are as follows.

Due to the use of capacitive filters, the worst-case scenario involves a full discharge of the capacitors into the researcher. Using the capacitive energy formula, the variac driven source would discharge 750 Joules. Prof. Peshkin uses the rule of thumb that 25 joules will kill a person. Thus, the original set-up, if discharged directly into a person, would kill them 30 times over. Obviously, this High Voltage source was scrapped.

Emco sources were decided upon instead. The selected E20 series provides a proportional output of 0 – 2000V DC from an input of 0-12 V DC. The source is safe since it only uses four 0.845 μF capacitors for filtering and therefore can only discharge (.5)(.845*4*10⁻⁶ F)(1000² V) = 1.7 Joules. While 1.7 Joules is not fatal, it could potentially cause injury. In order to achieve the safest source possible, plans for a box to contain the source and all associated circuitry were realized.

The following schematic shows the output loop:

Fig. 2 High –Voltage Circuit

In this circuit, a voltage divider composed of two 10 MΩ resistors and one 200 KΩ is used to create lower voltages in order to prevent the overload of the digital voltmeter that would be used for monitoring. One must simply multiply the voltmeter reading by 100 to obtain the voltage being exerted on the EAP. The two 100 KΩ resistors provide another degree of safety, as they act as fuses that would disintegrate from the sudden current surge that a high voltage discharge would create. All these components, along with appropriate input wiring and interconnects were successfully assembled into a metal box. The high voltage source did test properly and delivered high voltages while the voltmeter reading was in fact 100 times lower.

Mechanical Apparatus Description

The mechanical aspect of the fixture stretches the polymer in the horizontal direction (pre-strain) while allowing it freedom to actuate in the vertical direction. This tapestry-like hanging was accomplished using a simple Lexan base and stand. Aluminum was then employed for its malleable properties to provide the top and bottom bracket supports. Specifically, tapped holes were put into the front face of each of these principal brackets. Screws were then run into these holes to provide the squeezing force necessary to secure the elastic material. The screws were a horizontal distance of 3 inches away from each other. This provides 300% pre-strain for a one inch width of tape. Though effective, the top and bottom brackets can only pre-strain the material directly at the top and bottom of the sheet, thus causing the intermediate polymer to shrink back on itself. To counter act this behavior, a series of copper welding rods were cut to size and glued as ribs to the surface of the VHB as it was completely pre-strained in a rigid frame. Once the frame was cut away, the VHB retained its pre-strain throughout and achieved the original aim of pre-strain with freedom of movement in the direction normal to the pre-strain.

V. Evolution of Apparatus

Problems Encountered with Proposed Design

Initially, the complex mechanical apparatus was hooked up to the 2kV high voltage source. Unfortunately, all observers present perceived no movement upon application of 2kV. This failure could have been caused by various factors. First, the mechanical set-up is exceedingly complicated. As mentioned above, the device pre-strained the 1 in wide tape 300% to 3 in and used glued copper welding rods for support. This glue becomes very stiff when set and effectively became a stiff overcoat on the VHB that could have constricted any motion. Additional aspects of the complex design most likely contributed to the failure, but the “glue” hypothesis seems to be the biggest factor. In any case, this first design was scrapped.

In order to avoid the repetition of the above mistakes associated with complexity, Professor Colgate suggested simplifying the apparatus to something akin to Figure 3. This configuration essentially simplifies the EAP to its fundamental structure, two compliant electrodes that impose Maxwell stresses (through application of voltage) on an intermediary polymer (VHB 4910). Here the pre-strain is achieved by simply stretching the VHB uniformly over a rigid frame, thus creating a “drum” like set-up.

Apparatus Number Two

To create the frame for such a device, square metal pipes with roughly 8 cm sides were cut into cross-sections about 1 cm thick. The VHB was then stretched over this frame to create pre-strain in square geometry. Building off the apparatus suggested by Prof. Colgate, conductive carbon grease from MG Chemicals was used to create the compliant electrodes needed to transport the high voltage and not oppose any resulting motion. A square paper stencil with a roughly 1 cm² hole ensured that the grease would be slathered in an orderly fashion consistent with frame geometry. This stencil was applied to both sides of the VHB to create the active area that would hopefully expand and contract. Thin lines of grease that would not be active (as they would be applied to only one side of the VHB) were extended beyond the active area in order to connect with copper strips that carried the high voltage. Figure 3 shows this set-up from a birds-eye-view.

Fig. 3 Mechanical Apparatus in “Drum” configuration

The active area is clearly seen in the center of the frame with intermediate grease lines supplying voltage from the copper strips. The grayish bands inside the metal frame are simply pieces of duct tape used to secure the stretched polymer and insulate the metal frame from the bottom copper strip.

The next logical step would be to apply voltage. Though the expectation was for some sort of motion, initial observations saw no movement of the active region. A closer look through a magnifying device indicated that there actually was some movement on a sub-millimeter scale. A step forward had been achieved, but the literature had to be consulted to facilitate real results.

Upon review, we learned that the field strength (Voltage/ Thickness of VHB) used was over 30 times smaller than that used in literature.⁶ Contributing to this difference is the fact that Pelrine used voltages that “were typically 4 to 6kV” in addition to smaller thicknesses achieved in the polymer by pre-strain.⁶

This knowledge compelled the ordering of a thinner version of the acrylic polymer known as VHB 3905, which is the exact same material as VHB 3910, except the 3905 is 0.02 inches thick as opposed to the 3910 which is 0.04 inches thick.

Subsequent testing with the thinner polymer in hand caused significant motion, as can be seen in the photos of the initial crude apparatus in Figure 4.

Voltage = 0 Voltage = 2,000

Fig. 4 2,000 Volts causes the EAP to expand in the active regions (black greased centers)

Numerically, the film thickness after pre-strain shrank to a 2.1 thousandths of an inch (53.34 microns). If 2,000 volts is applied and electric field as in Equation 2:

E = V/t (Eqn. 2)

Where E is the field, V is voltage and t is thickness, then it follows that a field of 2,000/53.34 = 37.50 V/μm acted on the polymer. This field, in turn created a 15% average linear expansion of the active region as well as a 23.2% increase in area. These percentages were calculated by roughly estimating the active region to be a rectangle.

Although the thinner VHB provided evident progress, it also proved incredibly fragile as the material would very frequently tear under pre-strain or the stress of activation. As a result, a more durable solution was sought.

Final Apparatus Considerations

In order to return to the thicker, more reliable VHB 3910 and still get results, an increase in voltage would be necessary. To accomplish this, a new high voltage source was purchased from EMCO High Voltage Company. This new model, the E70, is capable of 0 to ± 7,000 volts and actually uses less capacitive filtering than the E20. As discussed earlier, capacitance directly correlates with danger to the researcher, and the E70 does indeed meet safety specifications.

The output circuit underwent other changes due to the 100K Ohm resistors failure to act as burn-out fuses in the event of a short circuit. In practice, these resistors serve no effective purpose at all and were accordingly removed from the output circuitry. The read-out proportion was also changed in order to achieve a 1000/1 voltage to voltmeter proportion. Specifically, the voltage divider used two 30 M Ohm resistors and one 60 K Ohm resistor to divide the voltage as seen in Figure 5:

Fig. 5 Revised High Voltage Out-Put Circuitry

Equipped with higher voltages, we can return to using trusty VHB 3910 and still create movement on a usable scale.

VI. Current Apparatuses

Two final set-ups of EAPs have been built. The first set-up follows the “drum” design as seen in Figures 3 and 4, while the other set-up has a vertical configuration in order to facilitate the addition of load.

The load-bearing EAP apparatus is comprised of a series of 0.4 inch spaced vertically drilled holes in an aluminum base. Two aluminum dowels are then inserted into these holes to create two vertical poles. One of these dowels is fixed in its hole at one end of the base while the other dowel remains unattached to the base (free to rotate or be moved to other holes). VHB 3910 is then stretched between the plates and fixed by wrapping the adhesive polymer around the dowels and back onto itself. Greased active areas, trails, and copper ribbon are also added in the same way as the “drum” set-up. The only missing part now becomes the application of load. After much thought as to how to incorporate such a feature without damaging the EAP, the final result involved a washer tied to a fine string that is attached just below the active area of the VHB using “plastix” glue (Fig. 6). The washer serves as a 1.5 gram load and can also be used to affix larger loads by incorporating a nut and bolt for example. Video of actuated EAPs can be found at othello.mech.nwu.edu/~peshkin/eap.⁷

VII. Quantitative Results

Measurements were taken to achieve some rough numerical understanding of these EAPs. Specifically, the dielectric constant, ε, of the VHB material was of particular interest as its value most likely holds the

Fig. 6 Vertical EAP Set-up with Washer Hanging key behind high-voltage EAPs. As already mentioned, Pelrine has identified the effective compressive stress, p, as shown in Eqation 1.

In addition, Pelrine adds that this compressive stress “is twice the stress normally calculated for two rigid, charged capacitor plates”. The stress described for charged capacitor plates can be derived from two equations (Eqn. 3⁸ and Eqn. 4⁸):

Fz(z) = -δW/δz (Eqn. 3)

Pelectrostatic = Fz / A (Eqn. 4)

Where Pelectrostatic is the stress across two capacitive plates, Fz is the force applied through the thickness of the dielectric, W is work, z is thickness and A is the area of the plates themselves. Here we must simply find the change in work over the change in thickness before and after activation, substitute into Pelrine's equations and solve for ε. However, this presents a problem in the case of measuring thickness during activation. Since optical devices are not available, only a highly conductive steel micrometer could achieve reliable results. During measurements, the device would have to come within millimeters of the active high voltage region and the researcher would undoubtedly receive an electrical shock.

Thus to avoid such a hazard and achieve simplicity, the widely known equation for capacitance (Eqn. 5) was instead used to calculate ε:

C = (ε εₒA) / z (Eqn. 5)

Where C is the capacitance measured with a capacitance meter provided by Mr. Flasch.

Upon rearrangement, we achieve:

ε = (C z) / (εₒA) (Eqn. 6)

We are now allowed to measure the pertinent dimensions of the inactive 0 volt EAP without fearing shock. The following results were obtained for the final “drum” set-up at zero volts as seen in Figure 3.

Since we know εₒ = 8.85 X 10-12 F/m, Equation 6 yields ε = [(12*10⁻¹² F)*(.0000762 m)] / [(8.85 * 10⁻¹² F/m)*(.00009m²)] = 1.148.

Thus, with ε now seen to be a very reasonable and normal value instead of much larger number as originally thought, we wonder if any measurements contained errors. The biggest concern here involves the Capacitance reading, as the “12 pF” was not a direct observation, but rather an interpretation by an instrument. The ECE department uses the capacitance meter in question to sort through various wayward capacitors in order to classify them and reuse them in subsequent teaching laboratories. Due to the facts that these laboratories continue to operate with minimal problems and that seasoned technicians such as Mr. Flasch continue to utilize this device on a regular basis, I would conclude that the capacitance reading is accurate.

The following photos were taken of the EAP at 0 volts and 7,000 volts:

VIII. Other Results and Observations

Pertinent measurements were also taken of the vertical set-up in Figure 6. They are summarized in Table 3.

% Area increase | 50%

Unfortunately, the VHB used in the vertical set-up did not last more than a week and split in half before a capacitance reading could be taken. As a result, no dielectric constant can be deduced at this time.

Also of interest is the fact that only 5.13 kV was applied to the vertical EAP. The fragility of the VHB contributed to low voltage because higher voltages would cut through the material and cause the previously strained polymer to snap back to its un-strained arrangement. The exact “safe” voltage was determined rather crudely by slowly increasing the voltage until the VHB broke and observing any changes present before the failure. During the testing, I noticed certain sputtering sounds and fluctuations in the grease patterns that could have been voltage seeping out of the grease and into the polymer or air. The EAP was then rebuilt with careful efforts made during the actuation process to reduce the voltage at the onset of any of the above indicators.

The following photos illustrate this final set-up and show expansion at a lower voltage than that described in Table 3:

Fig. 8 Vertical EAP Expansion from 0 (left) -3,100 Volts (right)

Vertical EAP With Load

In order to utilize the vertical set-up as a true actuator, the electrical energy from the volt source would have to somehow be transferred into mechanical energy beyond the simple expansion of the VHB itself. To this end, a load was glued to the VHB as previously described. Also, the permanent load as seen in the video is a 1.5 gram washer. In this configuration, the washer was raised 1.4 millimeters. When a 7.35 nut and bolt combination were integrated into the washer, the load was still lowered. The exact same distance was raised with this total 8.85 gram weight. Unfortunately, the rupturing of the VHB as seen above ended this load investigation before even more weight could be added. It is my inclination that much more weight could have been added without a decrease in distance traveled. This assertion comes simply from observing how the EAP did not seem to struggle or lose its structure at all under the 8.85 gram nut-washer-bolt combination. If energy for gravitational potential follows the form in Equation 8:

PEgravitational = mgh (Eqn. 8)

Where m is mass (kg), g is gravitational acceleration (~9.8 m/s²), and h is height (m), our larger load, while being lifted, would required: (.00885 Kg)*(9.8 m/s2)*(.0014 m) = 116.62 μJ.

Thus, electrical energy was converted to mechanical and the EAP did perform as an actuator. The true energy potential of this set-up would require more weight to be realized.

IX. Conclusions and the Road Ahead

As you can see, many aspects of high voltage Electrically Actuated Polymers have been explored. Personal highlights include the breakthrough achieved in Figure 4 and the successful application of load to the EAP as seen in the video link. Other significant findings include the calculation of the dielectric constant. Knowing that ε is a very normal value does however raise many questions. For instance, if ε is in fact slightly more than 1, how can the voltage on either side of the EAP stay insulated from each other? This is a valid question that deserves further investigation into the validity of the calculation of ε itself, as well as the physical and electrical properties of the VHB 4910 and the conductive carbon grease.

With more progress, more actuation properties can be quantified. Hopefully, the problem of how to integrate into the actual fin project can then be addressed. Even if electrical EAPs prove ineffective in water due to HV, their future significance cannot be overlooked. As one of the most promising breakthroughs in years in the fields of actuation, all projects in the LIMS lab could potentially benefit greatly from the future use of EAPs. Thus, the knowledge obtained through this project will surely pay-off down the road of innovation.

title: Phasefield Simulations and Visualizations in 3D
