text:
Phasefield Simulations and Visualizations in 3D

By Daniel A. Cogswell

Abstract

In this multi-disciplinary project a three-dimensional phase-field simulation was developed to study quantum dot growth kinetics and analyze the effects of anisotropic interfacial energy. The code was developed from a two-dimensional simulation written by J.J. Eggleston. Quantum dot kinetics with isotropic interfacial energy were analyzed and preliminary results of anisotropic interfacial energy are compared with their two-dimensional counterparts and are shown to be qualitatively similar. The three-dimensional implementation of anisotropic interfacial energy necessitated finding a regularized interfacial energy in three dimensions that enforces equilibrium at the corners of the facets and allows for cusp formation. In addition hardware-accelerated rendering software was developed to visualize three-dimensional simulation results, as well as models such as dendrite reconstructions. The software performs efficient curvature, surface normal, and lighting calculations and is optimized to handle multiple-frame progressions of a simulation, rendering real-time results in a virtual 3D environment.

I. Introduction

Quantum dots are nano-scale structures which form from thin films deposited on a substrate by heteroepitaxy. It has been found that dots form to balance elastic strain energy due to lattice misfit between the film and the substrate and the increase in free energy associated with increasing surface area as the film forms dots. There is hope to use quantum dots in the upcoming shift from microelectronics to nanoelectronics because of their unique electrical, optical, and magnetic properties. When electrons are confined within a quantum dot they begin to take on discrete energy levels and act as quantum wells, making single-electron transistors possible.¹ The dots, which are on the order of about 100nm, may eventually be used as nano-scale switches in electronics because, like there microelectronic counterparts, they can connected (for example with carbon nanotubes) to form electronic circuits. Quantum dots play an important role in the study of spintronics where they can be used to make single-electron transistors, allowing for the design of devices at the quantum level.² Quantum computing has been proposed an may one day become a reality.³ It has been suggested that lattices of quantum dots and nanowires may be superconductive at high transition temperatures.⁴ Arrays of quantum dots have been used to produce lasers,⁵ and metal quantum dots can hold distinct but recognizably unique magnetic domain patterns which make them good candidates for high-density computer memory.⁶

It is important to understand the shape and growth kinetics of quantum dots so they can be engineered to a specified size and placed in regularly repeating patterns for use in electronics. Current research is focusing on how to engineer large arrays of dots of a relatively uniform size and spatial distribution and to understand what factors control growth kinetics.

The aim of this project has been to develop and accurate model of interfaces for studying the growth kinetics of quantum dots forming from a thin film deposited on a substrate and determining the stress-free equilibrium shape of an isolated particle in a two-phase mixture in which there are preferred surface orientations due to surface energy anisotropy. The work is a continuation of a thesis written by J.J. Eggleston in 2001, in which he modeled 2D quantum-dot kinetics with both isotropic and anisotropic interfacial energy using a phase-field approach.⁷

II. Phasefield Simulations

The phase-field computational model is ideal for simulating quantum dots. The phase-field model, due to the fact that it models diffuse rather than explicit interfaces, avoids the complication of having to calculate surface integrals over the particle to calculate its total interfacial energy. Additionally, no explicit tracking of boundaries is necessary because the model uses chemical potential gradients and Cahn-Hilliard evolution to evolve the system.

In the phase-field model a variable φ from one phase to another. Because the transition occurs over a distance, the interface is a region with a finite width where φ changes rapidly – hence the phase-field method is based on a diffuse interface model. The diffuse interface model is an approximation for interfaces which has been adopted as a computational method for modeling solid surfaces. When the interfacial thickness is taken to be sufficiently small the diffuse interface description agrees with the classical description of an interface. We take the interface thickness to be small enough to assure accurate results. Phase-field modeling has also been used to study processes such as solid-to-solid transformations and solidification.

Phase-filed modeling is performed assuming a double-well free energy function with a minimum at φ = 0 and φ = 1 and a maximum at φ = ½.⁸ To determine how φ evolves to equilibrium, the code solves the Cahn-Hilliard equation:

dφ/dt = ∇·(M(φ)∇ dF/dφ) (Eqn.1)

M is the mobility and F is called the free-energy functional. The free energy functional needed to solve the Cahn-Hilliard equation (Eqn. 1) is:

F = ∫Ω [f(φ) + 1/2 ε² |∇φ|² + We] dΩ (Eqn. 2)

and the variational derivative of the free energy functional with elastic strain energy now becomes:

∂F/∂φ = ∂f/∂φ + ∂We/∂φ - ε²∇²φ (Eqn. 3)

where Ω is a volume of space, the function f(φ) is the double well potential, and ε is called the gradient energy coefficient (discussed in Section IV). The interfacial energy γ is proportional to ε. We is the elastic strain energy density which occurs due to a lattice misfit between the substrate and the film. Equation 1 can now be solved using an explicit finite difference method and applied across a three dimensional grid of points. It is necessary that the grip point spacing is small enough for accuracy and that the timestep is small so that the numerical method is stable.

If Equation 1 is solved analytically in 1D, one of the steady-state solutions, besides φ = 0, φ = ½, and φ = 1, is a tangent function. Thus it is possible for the two phase system to reach a stable equilibrium with diffuse interfaces separating the phases. The value of φ changes smoothly from 0 to 1 over the finite width of these diffuse interfaces. In order to produce pictures of the evolution for analysis, the system is contoured at φ = ½ , the value of φ that occurs at the middle of an interface.

To evolve the system, a forward Euler difference method is used. Although not as fast as other techniques because it requires a very small time step to maintain stability, the method is simple to implement and only the current state needs to be known in order to calculate states in the future (hence a “forward” method). The basic assumption of the Euler method is that all the terms beyond the 1st in the Taylor expansion of the function can be ignored over small time increments.

The forward Euler differencing equation is thus:

dφ(t)/dt ≈ (φ(t +Δt) - φ(t))/Δt (Eqn. 4)

III. Quantum Dot Simulations with Isotropic Interfacial Energy

The three-dimensional growth simulation developed in the project is a modified version of a two-dimensional simulation that was written by J.J. Eggleston.⁹ To simulate isotropic quantum dot growth, the free-energy functional F (Eqn. 1) can be rewritten by defining the free energy density of the material as a function of φ. Upon making the substitution for f(φ), Equation 1 can be rewritten as:

dφ/dt = ∇·[M∇{1/2 W (2φ³ - 3φ² + φ) - ε²∇²φ + ∂We/∂φ}] (Eqn. 5)

Thus an Euler method with a small enough time step can be used to calculate the phase value at each point in the future from the current phase values. The forward Euler method approximation (Eqn. 4) is combined with Equation 5 to produce an equation which can be solved on a computer using finite time steps to find φ:

(φ(t +Δt) - φ(t))/Δt = ∇·[M∇{1/2 W (2φ³ - 3φ² + φ) - ε²∇²φ + ∂We/∂φ}]|t (Eqn. 6)

Although the basic Equations which control the evolution of φ still apply in three dimensions, several changes had to be made to the two-dimensional code. First, two dimensional variables were give a third dimension. Initial boundary conditions had to be set in the new z-dimension, and the initial phasefield configuration had to be adapted to the new axis so that initial starting conditions could be configured. Laplacians and divergences had to be recalculated as follows, which requires the additional calculation of the derivative of φ in the z- direction, φz:

∇·φ = (φi+1,j,k - φi-1,j,k)/h + (φi,j+1,k - φi,j-1,k)/h + (φi,j,k+1 - φi,j,k-1)/h (Eqn. 7)

(∇²φ)i,j,k = (φi+1,j,k + φi-1,j,k + φi,j+1,k + φi,j-1,k + φi,j,k+1 + φi,j,k-1 - 6φi,j,k)/h² (Eqn. 8)

The simulation accounts for the elastic energy caused by atomic misfit between the film and the substrate.

To migrate to three dimensions, the elastic energy equations had to be recalculated. This involved calculating two extra send derivatives not necessary in two dimensions, φxz, and φyz. Additional displacement fields U1,3, U3,1, U2,3 and U3,2 had to be calculated as well.

The partial Derivative of the elastic energy term was changed to the following for three dimensions:

∂We/∂φ = 1/2 (λ' + 2μ'){(U1,1 - εᶠ)² + (U2,2 - εᶠ)² + (U3,3 - εᶠ)²} + λ' {(U1,1 - εᶠ) (U2,2 - εᶠ) + (U1,1 - εᶠ) (U3,3 - εᶠ) + (U2,2 - εᶠ) (U3,3 - εᶠ)} + 1/2 μ'{(U1,2 + U2,1)² + (U1,3 + U3,1)² + (U2,3 + U3,2)²} -2εᶠ′ (3λ + 2μ) (U1,1 + U2,2 + U3,3 - 3εᶠ) (Eqn. 9)

IV. Isotropic Quantum Dot Results

Although the main focus of this project was to develop a computational model for simulation, preliminary simulations have produced some promising results. Isotropic quantum dot growth results are presented in Figures 1-3. Figure 1 (a)-(c) show the evolution of stable quantum dots from a randomly perturbed this film. The coloring denotes the height of the film at each frame – red represents the highest points and purple the lowest. The simulation shows that dots form at random positions and at a variety of sizes.

Quantum dots have a characteristic spacing λ at which they prefer to grow. When perturbations were put in a film at even multiples of λ, a regular array of dots was produced (Fig. 2). The array of dots looks qualitatively similar to the self-assembled arrays of dots produced experimentally by depositing a SiGe film on a patterned Si(001) substrate.¹⁰ However, when perturbations were placed halfway between multiples of λ, a situation occurred where the growth of separate dots interfered with each other.

(a) Early stage of evolution

(b) Quantum dots are beginning to form

(c) quantum dots grew at random locations on the surface

Fig. 1 Isotropic quantum dot growth from a randomly perturbed or rough surface.

(a) Four pits were placed in the film surface a distance of λ apart from each other

(b) The initial simulation conditions self-assembled into an ordered array of dots

(c) An AFM image of an ordered array of SiGe islands grown on a SiGe/Si superlattice¹⁰

Fig. 2 Ordered arrays of dots were simulated and appear qualitatively similar to ordered arrays of dots grown experimentally

An interesting phenomenon discovered through the simulation and documented experimentally is the formation of a quantum ring structure (Fig. 3). Simulation of a small mound on a smooth surface produced a quantum ring (Fig. 3(b)) which has been observed by AFM in a CdTe/ZnTe system (Fig. 3(a)). Unlike the simulation in which interfacial energy is completely isotropic, the CdTe/ZnTe system has interfacial anisotropy present which produces some slight facets in the structure and causes the shape to differ slightly from the simulation.

V. Regularization of Anisotropic Interfacial Energy

Anisotropic interfacial energy was introduced into the phase-field model because some degree of interfacial energy anisotropy is found in may material systems. The interfaces arrange so that they minimize surface energy, possibly resulting in the formation of facets or cusps when interfacial anisotropy is present. Anisotropic crystal equilibrium shapes are found by generating an interfacial energy description in 3D and solving for the Wulff construction. The interfacial energy model does not correspond to any particular crystal structure (i.e. FCC, BCC, HCP), although it has been constrained to be four-fold symmetric. The anisotropic interfacial energy used in the 3D numerical simulation is defined by the following equation:

γ = ε/6 √(W/2) (Eqn. 10)

ε = ε₀ (1 + ε₄(Nx⁴ + Ny⁴ + Nz⁴ - 6(Nx²Ny² + Ny²Nz² + Nz²Nx²))) (Eqn. 11)

where γ is the interfacial energy, Nx, Ny, Nz are surface normals, ε₀ is a constant, and ε₄ is the degree of anisotropy. The interfacial energy can be converted from the surface normals description to a spherical coordinates and plotted, as shown in Figure 4. The solution for the equilibrium particle shape is the Wulff construction, the shape described by the inner envelope of planes normal to the plot of interfacial energy.¹¹ The degree of anisotropy is controlled by the ε₄ parameter – changing its value (Eqn. 11) changes the shape of the interfacial energy plot. Once ε₄ has been set, the interfacial energy description can be used in Cahn-Hilliard dynamics (Eqn. 1).

(a) Quantum ring photographed with AFM in a CdTe/ZnTe system

(b) simulation of a mound at the center of a smooth film produced a quantum ring.

Fig. 3 A quantum ring was observed experimentally (a) and simulated (b) by placing a mound in the middle of a smooth thin film and allowing the system to evolve

Fig. 4 Interfacial energy ε, for ε₄ = 0.20

Unfortunately for values of ε₄ > 1/15, the plot of 1/ε becomes non-convex at certain points, creating an instability in the evolution equation then requires regularization of the interfacial energy. A common tangent construction is performed on the 1/ε to eliminate the concave regions, providing an interfacial energy that yields accurate particle shapes.⁹

The focus of the work in three-dimensional anisotropic simulations is to develop a regularized interfacial energy that produces a numerically stable solution. Fiero et al.¹² produced a stable anisotropic interfacial energy through a process of convexification of the polar plot of 1/ε. Convexified interfacial energy in two dimensions solution was developed by Eggleston, McFadden, and Voorhees.⁷ Tangent lines are drawn on each side of the 1/ε plot, and regions where the plot is concave are replaced with the tangent lines. 2D and 3D regularized shapes are shown in Figure 5. Although the approach to regularize the 3D shape is the same as in 2D, the 3D regularization is much more complicated since the edges of the shape are concave in addition to the faces. Tangent planes are drawn on each face and around the edges of the 1/ε plot, as illustrated in Figure 6 (b-c). The shape is then “inflated” within the bounds imposed by the tangent planes. The resulting convexified interfacial energy is shown in Figure 6 (d). Unlike the solution for 2D which is relatively simple, the 3D regularization solution is a 7-way piecewise function which was calculated using Maple, a symbolic manipulation software package. The mathematical solution is long and will not be presented in this paper.

VI. Anisotropic particle Equilibrium Shapes

Stress-free anisotropic particle equilibrium shape results are shown in Figure 7 and compared with results from Eggleston’s 2D code. The 2D and 3D code produce qualitatively similar results. The initial conditions in 2D were a circular particle and in 3D a spherical particle was used. The case where ε₄ = 0 is the isotropic interfacial energy case, and, as expected, the equilibrium shape is a circle or sphere. As ε₄ is increased, flat faceted faces and cusps are observed to develop.

(a) Polar plot showing 2D regularization of ε (ε₄ = 0.20)⁷

(b) spherical plot of regularized ε (ε₄ = 0.20) in 3D.

Fig. 5 Comparison of the 2D regularized ε plot to the 3D regularized plot

(a) Convexifying the polar plot of 1/ ε (ε₄ = 0.20) in 2D

(b) Convexifying the faces of the 1/ ε with tangent planes

(c) Convexifying the edges of the 1/ ε with tangent planes

(d) Convexified 3D 1/ ε

Fig. 6 Moving from 2D to 3D convexification to obtain a regularized model. Convexifying the 3D plot involves convexifying faces and edges of the 1/ ε plot in spherical coordinates (ε₄ = 0.30)

VII. Visualization with SimulationView

Creating accurate and informative visual displays from three-dimensional data is a challenging problem. Two dimensional simulation data can be plotted using a wide variety of plotting packages. However, with a third dimension the amount of data that must be analyzed drastically increases, making two-dimensional plots ineffective for visual displays. To convey three-dimensional results, sophisticated techniques in computer graphics must be used. Advanced rendering software was written to address the specific problem of 3D model visualization. The software, named SimulationView, makes OpenGL graphics calls to allow 3D models to be rendered and evolved through time. The software was designed to be cross-platform compatible, and can be compiled and run in Windows, MacOS, and Linux. This makes it an effective solution for scientific analysis, producing animations, and real-time model exploration.

OpenGL is the standard language used in computer graphics to issue drawing commands on a computer’s graphics card. OpenGL translates statements into rendering commands which can be processed by the GPU (Graphical Processing Unit), which is designed to be extremely efficient at rasterizing images. Today’s fastest graphics cards are highly specialized and parallelized for processing graphics commands. These graphics cards can perform upwards of 1.25 trillion operations per second, which is significantly faster than the CPU of most computers. OpenGL is the graphics library of choice for writing most of the fastest and most graphics-intensive computer and video games on the market such as Doom III, Unreal Tournament, and John Madden Football.¹⁴

OpenGL renders scenes by drawing large numbers of

(a) ε₄ = 0.00

(b) ε₄ = 0.05

(c) ε₄ = 0.20

(d) ε₄ = 0.50

(e) ε₄ = 0.00

(f) ε₄ = 0.06

(g) ε₄ = 0.13

(h) ε₄ = 0.30

Fig. 7 Comparison of 2D equilibrium shapes to 3D equilibrium shapes for various degrees of anisotropy. Note that the 3D results were obtained without one-sided derivatives and are thus not finalized results.

two-dimensional convex polygons. Polygons are defined in OpenGL by their 3D vertices, and are mapped to two-dimensional polygons with the use of transformation and perspective projections. The OpenGL framework can be used to define specific properties at each vertex such as texture, color, and surface orientation. It is the job of the graphics card to interpolate these properties across each polygon. OpenGL does the work of defining and applying the viewport transformations that map the 3D world to a 2D screen by eliminating hidden or overlapping polygons, applying translate, rotate, and scale transformations to vertices, and managing texturing, and lighting operations.

Visual appeal and contrast have been added to the rendering by implementing lighting and perspective calculation. Three controllable lights have been placed around the origin in SimulationView so as to illuminate the scene and crate shadows. Lighting helps to create contrast and bring out the 3D shape of the interface.¹⁵ In order to shade the model, surface normals must be provided for each vertex. The amount of light (and thus the brightness) of each vertex is related to the angle between the surface normal and the vector at which the light source hits the pixel. OpenGL has a smooth shading mode which interpolates the value of the normal at each vertex to each pixel when it is rendered, and thus presented produces a very realistic looking lighting effect. In order to create a realistic looking lighting for models, the surface normal vector at each vertex should be a weighted average by surface area of normals of all the polygons which contain the vertex. That is, if a small polygon and a large polygon share a vertex, the surface normal at the vertex should be mostly determined by the larger polygon. This refinement in the vertex normals is applied by the viewer program, which calculates normals from the polygon and vertex data supplied in the input file.

SimulationView is optimized for visualization. Whereas most commercial graphical analysis packages use interpreted languages that often translate programs inefficiently into system calls, SimulationView has been written directly in C/C++ to make the OpenGL calls and interact directly with the graphics card. The result is impressive performance – SimulationView is small enough to fit on a floppy disk, yet multiple models can be loaded at once and rendered fluidly in real-time using the keyboard and mouse to interact with the model.

The most unique feature of SimulationView, when compared with commercial graphics packages, is that it allows multiple frames of a simulation to be viewed in sequence, producing an animation. The ability to view sequential frames gives the user a very visual idea of where, when, and how quickly structures form and grow. Without the ability to view time evolution, one would have to draw each frame separately and attempt to infer information about when and at what rate growth events took place. The model can be manipulated and rotated as it evolves, effectively providing four dimensions for exploration. The camera can be pointed, for instance, at a particular point or feature of interest in the model, and that feature can then be moved forward and backward through time.

VIII. Modeling of Dendrite Reconstructions

Although SimulationView was written specifically for viewing 3D phase-field simulation results, it was easily adapted to dramatically improve the modeling of three-dimensional dendrite reconstructions. 3D dendrite reconstructions are performed by coarsening a two-phase sample (Sn-Pb is commonly used), and using a high-precision milling machine to mill off micron-thin layers of material. After a layer of material is removed by the milling machine, a digital picture of the microstructure is taken through a microscope and the process is repeated. The pictures that are generated can then be “stacked” on top of each other with a computer to reconstruct the dendrite model.

Unfortunately, the detail involved in 3D reconstruction can produce models with upwards of 2 million polygons. Today’s fastest commercial graphics cards are designed to render on the order of 100,000 polygons per second fluidly, so the size of the dendrite model surpasses the rendering capabilities of the graphics card by about an order of magnitude. Thus large dendrite files are extremely slow to load, and manipulation of the dendrites is choppy and sluggish. Polygon simplification algorithms developed by Michael Garland were used to reduce the number of polygons used to represent the reconstructions.¹⁶ The results of simplification are shown in Figure 8.

An effect of performing polygon simplification was a dramatic decrease in the size of the dendrite reconstruction files. The files can now be put on a disk or sent via email and rendered with SimulationView. Additionally, Gaussian and mean curvature calculations, which took on the order of a day for large reconstructions, can be performed virtually instantaneously in SimulationView using curvature approximation algorithms developed by Fialkowski, Aksimentiev, and Holyst.¹⁷ Mean and Gaussian curvatures are two important parameters which are used to characterize dendritic systems. Figure

9 shows a polygon-reduced dendrite reconstruction rendered in SimulationView, which has been colored by Gaussian curvature. The curvature calculations on the simplified models agree closely with the values calculated on the large models.

(a) 125,000 polygons

(b) 50,000 polygons

(c) 10,000 polygons

(d) 5,000 polygons

(e) 1,000 polygons

Fig. 8 Polygon reduction of a directionally cooled Sn-Pb dendrite reconstruction rendered in SimulationView

Fig. 9 Dendrite colored by Gaussian curvature. Blue areas denote areas of high negative curvature, red areas denote areas of high positive curvature.

IX. Conclusion

With recent advances in computing power, the impact of computation and simulation is increasing rapidly. Simulations that predict phenomenon and can be used to guide physical experimentation in the laboratory are invaluable because simulations are generally quick and inexpensive to develop and apply. The 3D extensions made to J.J. Eggleston’s 2D quantum dots simulation add yet another degree of realism to the simulation and open the door for more research and investigation of quantum dot growth. Simulation in three-dimensions showed the self-assembly of quantum dots during annealing of thin films. Randomly perturbed thin films were observed to self-assemble into random arrangements of dots of varying sizes. Initial conditions which yielded ordered arrays of dots were found and shown to produce dots which look qualitatively similar to those observed experimentally. An interesting phenomenon, the formation of a quantum ring that has been observed experimentally, was independently simulated. Anisotropic interfacial energy was implemented in three-dimensions and preliminary results show qualitative agreement with Eggleston’s 2D simulations.

As computer processing power increases and three-dimensional simulations become more and more common, effective visualization of results will become almost as important as developing the simulations themselves. SimulationView was written specifically to address this problem. It is small, efficient, and cross platform compatible code that produces dramatic, interactive 3D visualizations which are effective at conveying evolution of 3D morphologies. SimulationView is easily extensible to perform advanced perspective, lighting, surface normals, and curvature calculations.

Killary and Steven T. Lott, University of Texas M.D. Anderson") and in the acknowledgements (University of Texas M.D. Anderson Cancer Center). Figure captions jump from Fig. 5 to Fig. 7 as printed.
text:
The Characterization of CAR-1 Protein

By Katrina Chuang

Abstract

Recently a novel gene on human chromosome 1, Cancer Associated Ring-1 (CAR-1) of the RBCC subfamily, was identified as a candidate tumor suppressor gene. Members of the RBCC family have been observed to form macromolecular structures that may be crucial for the normal function of these proteins. In this study, the CAR-1 protein was characterized through Western blots, immunocytochemistry, and immunohistochemistry on normal and tumor samples. The Western blot indicated that CAR-1 is a 64 kD protein. Immunocytochemistry analysis of normal tissues yielded a diffuse background staining for the CAR-1 protein that included speckling, similar to the macromolecular structures of BRCA1 and other RING finger proteins. In contrast, in tumors, CAR-1 displayed a distinct spider-like network of staining but without the numerous speckles found in the normal cells. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed CAR-1 staining in only very specific cells, particularly around the ductal structures as seen in breast, uterus, and kidney tissue samples.

I. Introduction

The advent of cancer and the metastasis thereof is a convoluted pathway involving a spectrum of changes to the genome of a normal cell that include of point mutations, gene amplification, recombination, gene deletion, reduced or overexpression, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH). Many of these targeted genes have been singled out as oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.¹ Tumor suppressor genes code for proteins that function in the cell cycle to suppress or inhibit the growth of tumor cells by inhibiting cell proliferation. Without their normal and active presence, the genesis of tumors or the preclusion of apoptosis can occur. In cancer cells, tumor suppressor genes can be deleted, mutated, methylated, or their expression downregulated.¹,²

The isolation of a particular tumor suppressor gene involves a series of steps, narrowing the region of location and discovering the extent and mechanism of its inactivation in cancer. Mapping of genomic loss of heterozygosity (LOH) should show sites of LOH of alleles on a chromosome that suggest the inactivation of a tumor suppressor gene at that site for a specific tumor.³ Evidence must also prove that the suspected tumor suppressor gene has suffered loss of expression or is considerably downregulated in the same cancer form where LOH was detected. Mutational screenings and methylation tests further establish tumor suppressor gene inactivation. Gene expression is determined through functional studies involving the tumor suppressor gene protein that will suggest the function and localization of that protein. Cells transfected with the candidate tumor suppressor gene are injected into mice with malignancies. The results will confirm whether or not introduction of the gene into a malignancy that contains the inactive gene significantly suppresses the tumor.

The Ring-B-box-Coiled-coil domain (RBCC) proteins, a subfamily of the RING finger protein family, are suspected interactors in tumorigenesis through gene expression regulation, cellular proliferation, oncogenesis, apoptosis, and ubiquitination.⁴⁻⁸ Through a functional genetic approach with suppression subtractive hybridization cloning, a novel member of the RBCC subfamily has been identified as CAR-1 (Cancer Associated Ring-1) and its full-length cDNA isolated. The proposed structure of the CAR-1 protein consists of an RBCC domain followed by an rfp domain, which has been shown to function as a transcriptional repressor and to be a protein that interacts in cellular epigenetic silencing mechanisms (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1 Schematic showing the genomic architecture of the CAR-1 gene. Expected Splice product and the resultant proteins are also depicted.

CAR-1 has been mapped to a chromosomal region where high frequency loss of heterozygosity has been shown in breast, colon, and brain cancers. This region also shares proximity with a translocation breakpoint region in a renal carcinoma cell line. Cytogenetic aberrations as well as high frequency LOH have been observed within the short arm of human chromosome 1.⁹⁻¹⁴ Previous expression studies of CAR-1 tentatively suggest that it is expressed ubiquitously in all normal tissues analyzed; however, its expression is absent or significantly down-regulated in a number of cell lines and tumors derived from breast, colon, and kidney.

CAR-1 has also been found to sustain putative mutations, particularly in breast cancer, and methylation in colon cancer. Previous molecular analysis conducted on breast carcinoma cell lines has shown both heterozygous missense and intronic mutations in exon 2. Mutational analyses of exon 4 in breast tumor samples also show mutations, indicating a possible loss, decrease, or change of protein function.

Many RING finger proteins of the RBCC family form oncogenic fusion proteins linked to oncogenesis by functioning in either epigenetic silencing mechanisms or transcriptional repression. RING finger family proteins such as Breast Cancer 1 (BRCA-1), promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML), and Enhance of Polycomb (EPC) have been shown to form multi-protein complexes in cells. For instance, in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), the RBCC protein PML was seen as discrete, nuclear localized PML oncogenic domains (PODs). Since formation of PODs relies on fully functional RING domains, the RING may be important in protein-protein interactions. Such macromolecular complexes vary in size from the larger entities of PML to the smaller complexes of BRCA1. Evidence also indicates involvement of the RBCC domain in homo-oligomerization, which may function in the physical interaction of the various RING finger proteins.¹,²

Affinity-purified CAR-1 anti-peptide antibodies, targeted to the amino and carboxyl terminal regions of CAR-1, have been isolated. These antibodies will be utilized in immunocytochemistry and immunohistochemistry.

As part of a functional study of CAR-1 as a tumor suppressor, protein function and localization will be analyzed to characterize the normal function of CAR-1. Western blots, immunocytochemistry, and immunohistochemistry will be used to examine the role of specific CAR-1 domains in subcellular localization and the formation of macromolecular complexes. The results may substantiate CAR-1 as a tumor suppressor gene for histologically diverse cancers.

II. Materials and Methods

Western Blot

Transfectant protein from tumor samples, 21MT (FL-C)J6 (3.51 mg/ml) and 21 MT(S-C)B9 (6.70 mg /ml), underwent electrophoresis. Each sample was mixed with loading buffer (125 mM Tris-HCl (pH 6.8), 4% SDS.

50% glycerol, and 0.02% beta-mercapethanol) and water. The samples, Kaleidoscope prestained standard marker (BioRad, Hercules, CA), and ECL protein molecular weight marker was loaded into a PAGEr Gold precast gel (12% with 12 lanes) (Cambex, Rockland, ME) and mounted in a EC120 mini vertical gel system with Tris-Glycine electrode buffer (125 mM Tris Base, 960 mM glycine, 0.5% SDS, and water).

Following electrophoresis, the gel soaked in transfer buffer (3.03 g Trizma Base, 14.4 g glycine, 200 ml methanol, water). A sheet of Hybond-P protein transfer membrane (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ) was prewet in 100% methanol, washed in distilled water, and equilibrated in transfer buffer. The gel and Hybond-P was set up in an electroblot system for protein transfer, which ran for 1.5 h. The protein blot was blocked overnight with 10 ml TBST and 5% Amersham blocking reagent at 4°C.

The membrane was washed with TBST and then incubated for one hour with rotation with primary antibody, CAR-1 Rb anti-7b5-Coil peptide (C-terminal peptide) (Bethyl Laboratories, Montgomery, TX) at 1:20,000. The membrane was then incubated with secondary antibody, goatarabbit HRP at 1:5000 and Streptavadin-HRP (Amersham) at 1:25,000 for one hour with rotation. The membrane was washed with the same series of TBST washes as before.

The membrane was then treated with an ECL plus Western Blotting Detection System and exposed to Hyperfilm ECL (Amersham).

Fluorescent Immunocytochemistry

One normal (HFS) and one tumor cell (21MT) line were split and plated onto chamber slides. Upon harvest, the cells were washed with PBS and then incubated with 2% paraformaldehyde + PBS (4 g paraformaldehyde, 200 ml PBS, 12 ml 10 M NaOH) at pH 7.4. Cells were then washed with PBS and then with 1 ml 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS.

Cells were incubated with blocking buffer (10% Goat Serum in PBS + 0.1% NP-40). The blocking buffer was aspirated and the cells incubated in 500 ml primary antibody, a-CAR-1 N peptide, diluted to 1:100 in blocking buffer, for one hour with gentle rocking. The slides were then washed with PBS + 0.1% NP-40, and incubated with 500 ml secondary antibody, diluted to 1:100 in blocking buffer, for one hour with gentle rocking. After incubation, the slides were washed with PBS + 0.1% NP-40, which contained counterstain (propidium iodide or DAPI at 200 ng/ml). Vectashield was added to the center of each slide and a coverslip applied.

The slides were examined using a Zeiss fluorescent microscope.

Immunohistochemistry

Various tissue samples were used, including breast, spleen, colon, kidney, uterus, lung, and heart. The sample slides were rehydrated in a series of washes: xylene, 100% ethanol, 95% ethanol, diH20, and PBS.

Immunohistochemistry was performed using a Super Sensitive Detection System kit (Biogenex, San Ramon, CA). The slides were treated with 3% H202 and Power Block. Incubation for one hour with CAR-1 antibody at 1:100 followed. The slides were then incubated with Superblock for 20 min, treated with Poly-HRP, and treated with AEC substrate until the slides were sufficiently stained, between 5-40 min. After rinsing with PBS, they were treated with Hematoxylin, rinsed with tap water, and dipped in 10% ammonium water for, rinsed with tap water, and finally Supermounted.

III. Results

From the Western blot probed with the CAR-1 C-terminal antibody, the size of CAR-1 was determined to be approximately 64 kD (Fig. 2).

Fig. 2 CAR-1 Western blot; at 1:20,000; size 64kD

The immunocytochemistry slides were stained with DAPI to visualize DNA and CAR-1 protein was visualized as a CAR-1-GFP fusion. For all samples, CAR-1-GFP fluorescence occurred outside the nucleus, in the cytoplasm, indicating cytoplasmic localization of CAR-1. The normal HFS cells exhibited diffuse CAR-1-GFP fluorescence (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3 HFS Cells (left) and tumor cells from 21MT (right)

More importantly, numerous bright green speckles were seen in almost all the cells. These speckles are purported to be the formation of macromolecular structures, similar to those seen associated with BRCA-1.¹,² In contrast, the tumor cell (21MT) slides produced a distinct network of GFP fluorescence with a spidery texture and very few speckles could be found in the cells (Fig. 3).

The immunohistochemistry slides contained a blue nuclear staining and a brick red CAR-1 protein staining. The results of the normal tissues indicated distinct CAR-1 staining predominantly targeted around ductal structures, suggesting CAR-1 localization specific for ductal tissue. Lung, heart, and uterus (Fig. 4) samples appeared to exhibit CAR-1 staining concentrated at specific structures. Spleen samples showed weak and diffuse CAR-1 staining throughout (Fig. 4).

Fig. 4 (Clockwise from top left) Lung, heart, uterus and spleen samples

In normal breast tissue, CAR-1 staining was very distinct, targeting the epithelial cells lining the ductal structures (Fig. 5).

Fig. 5 Staining in normal breast tissue (left) and breast fiboradenoma tissue (right)

Though the ductal structures in breast fibroadenoma tissue are compressed, staining was still specific (Fig. 5). Staining in the uterus and kidney (Fig. 7), both ductal tissues, were especially concentrated around ductal structures.

Fig. 7 Kidney Tissue

IV. Discussion

RBCC proteins are crucial to normal cellular functions. The normal as well as disrupted function, which may contribute to neoplasia, of CAR-1 can be better understood with the characterization of the role of particular protein domains in localization and complex formation.

With the immunocytochemistry results in consideration, we can begin to reason whether the complex formation is unique or linked with other characterized RING finger and RBCC family proteins such as BRCA-1 or PML. Further study with coimmunoprecipitation experiments could identify specific binding partners of CAR-1 found in macromolecular structures.

Results from the immunohistochemistry, showing a concentration of CAR-1 staining around ductal structures, are particularly significant because the majority of breast cancers primarily originate in ductal epithelial cells. These data suggest that mutations disrupt the normal function of CAR-1 protein in these ductal regions, suggesting the role of CAR-1 in tumorigenesis.

Further studies involving CAR-1 gene transfection and targeted gene knockouts in mice will hopefully provide more evidence to determine if CAR-1 is a tumor suppressor gene.

In light of theories such as the “two-hit” model of tumorigenesis that proposes that tumor suppressor genes generate a tumorigenic effect when both alleles become inactivated by mutation or chromosomal deletion, it is of supreme importance to isolate tumor suppressor genes.³ By pinpointing possible causation of tumorigenesis, further investigation into the development and progression of human cancer can be performed, and, optimistically, mechanisms of cancer will be understood to engender a better understanding of cancer.

title: GaN Based p-i-n Personal Ultraviolet Photodetection Device
notes: Advisor named on the contents page ("Advisor: Manijeh Razeghi, Northwestern University") and in the acknowledgements.
text:
GaN Based p-i-n Personal Ultraviolet Photodetection Device

By Derek Shiell, Ryan McClintock, and Alireza Yasan

Abstract

An ultraviolet UV detection system based on a gallium nitride (GaN) p-i-n ultraviolet (UV) photodetector has been developed to monitor a user’s UV radiation exposure and warn the user before s/he receives a potentially harmful dose of UV radiation. The entire device is portable and consists of a three-stage amplifying circuit, a peripheral interface controller (PIC), a liquid crystal display (LCD), and a GaN based p-i-n UV photodetector. Two buttons allow for user input. The accumulated UV exposure, instantaneous UV exposure, total UV exposure time, skin type, and sun protection factor (SPF) are displayed on an LCD module. It appears possible that this technology could be commercialized, thereby providing a means to reliably prevent UV overexposure and consequently to reduce the incidence of skin cancer among the general population.

I. Background

Since the 1970’s, the incidence of skin cancer has increased by approximately 3 percent per year.¹ Currently, the number of cases of skin cancer annually is nearly equivalent to all other cases of cancer combined. It is believed that skin cancer is almost exclusively the result of prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.² The human body has no way to sense UV radiation directly. Furthermore, excessive exposure results in burning, but by the time burning occurs, the skin has already been damaged. The sun emits an extremely broad spectrum of electromagnetic radiation much of which is absorbed within the ozone layer located in the earth’s upper atmosphere; however, the ozone layer transmits radiation at wavelengths ranging from ~280 nm into the visible region allowing light of these wavelengths to reach the earth’s surface.

Fig. 1 Seasonal irradiance and erythemal weighting function⁹

The light reaching the surface is called the solar irradiance and is about ten times more intense during the summer than during the winter (see Fig. 1). However, the ability of UV radiation to damage the skin is dependent on the wavelength. This leads to an erythemal weighting function, also shown in Figure 1, which can be used to account for the skin’s sensitivity to different wavelengths of light.³ Long exposure to these wavelengths can be harmful to human skin due to the skin’s high sensitivity to UV radiation. Weighting the solar UV irradiance with the erythemal weighting function shows that the greatest potential threat to human skin by UV radiation lies in the region from 280 nm and declines out to 330 nm (Fig. 2).

Fig. 2 Erythemally weighted UV irradiance⁹

II. Overview

We have developed a small portable instrument for estimating an individual’s exposure to UV radiation for extended periods of time using a gallium nitride (GaN) based p-i-n UV photodetector. Figure 3 shows the detector structure with the p-type, intrinsic, and n-type layers. The device accounts for the user-specified skin type and sunscreen to warn the user when his/her accumulated exposure to UV radiation reaches potentially harmful levels. The GaN p-i-n photodetector that we have developed for this device detects potentially harmful UV radiation from about 220 nm out to 365 nm, but shows virtually no response outside this range, making it ideal for this application. In addition, the associated electronics and software provide a user-friendly means of operation. It should be noted that numerous other applications exist for UV detectors which cover a wide range of military and industrial uses including: early missile threat detection and interception, chemical and biological threat detection, UV flame monitoring, and industrial UV environmental monitoring.⁴,⁵

Fig. 3 GaN based detector structure used for the device

III. Details of the Photodector Fabrication and Characterization

This GaN based UV photodetector was grown on a sapphire substrate using a horizontal flow low-pressure metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) reactor at a growth pressure of 10 ~ 100 mbar and temperature of ~1000 °C. A p-i-n configuration was used for the detector structure where silicon was used for the n- type dopant and magnesium for the p- type dopant. Metal contacts were achieved using a Ti/Au bilayer for the n- type ohmic contact and a Ni/Au bilayer for the p- type ohmic contact. The overall detector structure is shown in Figure 3. A technique known as lateral epitaxial overgrowth was used to dramatically reduce the number of defects in the template used as the foundation for the growth of the GaN p-i-n detector. This was accomplished by first growing up from the substrate through etched SiO₂ channels then growing horizontally due to the preferential GaN crystal formation on the horizontal plane⁶,⁷ (Fig. 4).

Fig. 4 General structure for a material grown by lateral epitaxial overgrowth (LEO)

The measured peak responsivity of the detector was 200 mA/W at 362 nm. This corresponds to an external quantum efficiency of 69% (Fig. 5); and taking into account surface absorption and scattering, an estimated internal quantum efficiency of ~86%. Figure 5 shows that the responsivity of the GaN detector decreases by approximately 5 orders-of-magnitude for wavelengths greater than ~365 nm. This means there is virtually no detection of electromagnetic radiation from about 365 nm up into the visible light region making the detector visible blind. The response of the detector does not perfectly follow the erythemal weighting function at longer wavelengths (greater than ~365 nm). At these wavelengths, the GaN detector shows a flat response whereas the erythemal weighting function shows a declining response. Incorporating aluminum into the GaN photodetector structure would allow one to design an active region which would more closely follow the erythemal weighting function. The feasibility of this approach has already been demonstrated.⁸

Fig. 5 Responsivity and External Quantum Efficiency vs Wavelength for GaN p-i-n photodetector showing a peak responsivity of 200mA/W at 362 nm with a corresponding external quantum efficiency of 69%

IV. Details of the Associated Electronics and Software

The portable UV detection device consists primarily of the GaN detector, a multi-stage operational amplifier (op-amp) circuit, a microcontroller circuit, and a liquid-crystal display (LCD) module (Fig. 6). The photocurrent generated by the detector is fed through the multi-stage transimpedance amplifier to boost the signal into the millivolt range (Fig. 7). High-precision OPA277 op-amps were used for the gain circuit. The first stage of the amplifier circuit converts the current signal to a voltage signal, while the second and third stages provide dynamic gain. The dynamic gain is exponentially varied over four orders-of-magnitude using a digital potentiometer controlled by the 16F873 peripheral interface controller (PIC). For simplicity, the gain is divided into powers of two to allow the PIC microcontroller to continually adjust the gain in order to keep at least 6 bits of resolution in the internal analog to digital converter (ADC).

The 16F873 PIC microcontroller used in this device runs at 19.66 MHz with an instruction time of only 200 ns. The code for this controller is 1,200 lines, which compiles to approximately 500 14-bit instruction words. The code is divided into a main loop, which handles detector sampling and the user interface, and an interrupt driven routine used to keep accurate time. With a 200 ns instruction time, this allows the controller to sample the UV exposure several times per second. High-resolution sampling is carried out using the 16F873 microcontroller’s internal 10-bit ADC. In addition, there are 3 I/O ports, which are used to handle user input, drive the digital potentiometer, and drive the LCD module.

Fig. 6 Internal layout of device showing the power supply, the 16F873 microcontroller, the three-stage amplifying circuit, and the LCD display module

Fig. 7 Three-stage Op-Amp gain circuit. Stage 1 acts as a buffer amplifier. Stages 2 and 3 are variable gain stages

The user interface for this device consists of a select button, a set button, and an LCD module. The select and set buttons are used to choose skin type and sun protection factor (SPF) from a pre-set list and allow resetting of the device. The LCD module simultaneously displays the instantaneous UV exposure, the accumulated UV dosage, the total UV exposure time, the selected skin type, and the selected SPF. The device is designed to use the selected skin type and SPF to calculate the user’s personal UV exposure. This provides the user with continuous feedback of his/her UV exposure. It also alerts the user when the accumulated UV exposure begins to reach potentially harmful levels.

V. Discussion

While our prototype GaN UV detector functions according to our initial specifications, it could still benefit from further improvement. Specifically, by incorporating aluminum into the GaN photodetector structure, it is theoretically possible to grow a UV photodetector which has a much higher correlation with the erythemal weighting function. In addition, the options for skin type and SPF in our prototype are extremely limited; the skin’s sensitivity to UV radiation needs to be more accurately modeled to take into consideration variances based on a wider number of skin types and SPF’s. Finally, the device must have reduced size, weight, and power consumption to be feasible for commercial use. At present, the whole unit measures ~15 x 10 x 3 cm; ideally the device could be made small enough to fit in a watch or cellphone.

VI. Summary and Conclusion

Steadily increasing rates of skin cancer due to prolonged exposure to solar UV radiation indicate the need for personal UV exposure monitoring. In this paper, we have reported the development of a compact prototype GaN based p-i-n UV photodetector unit which provides a convenient way to monitor personal UV exposure. Our research has covered all aspects of this device from the fabrication of the semiconductor photodetector to the accompanying electronics and associated software. It appears possible that our technology could be commercialized, thereby providing a means to reliably prevent UV overexposure and consequently to reduce the incidence of skin cancer among the general population.

title: Fabricating a sensor to measure the material flow in sheet metal forming process and characterizing its behavior in a simulated lab setup
notes: Advisors named on the contents page ("Advisors: Jian Cao and Michael Peshkin, Northwestern University") and in the acknowledgements, which spell the author "Numpoon Mahayotsanun". Includes three appendices of figures (previous prototype results, current setup results, circuit diagram). Two section headings are both numbered III as printed.
text:
Fabricating a sensor to measure the material flow in sheet metal forming process and characterizing its behavior in a simulated lab setup

By Numpon Mahayotsanun

Abstract

One of the major processes in automobile manufacturing is sheet metal forming. This process is broadly used due to its high degree of design flexibility and low cost. In the sheet metal forming process, draw-in (deformation of punched sheet metal) frequently occurs and lessens the effectiveness of the process. Currently, monitoring and controlling draw-in during each stamping operation is unfeasible, time-consuming, and used only in laboratory settings. However, one of our previous prototypes was developed to monitor draw-in by using Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) and produced elaborate results. Our goal is to design a draw-in sensor that will provide high sensitivity in monitoring; ease of setup, measurement and controlling; and eventually be implemented in industry. Based on our previous prototype, we consider physical factors that affect the relationship of the results and examine what dimension of the transducer provides the highest sensitivity. The results show good linearity and insensitivity to pulling speed and starting position of a sheet metal. One major finding of the results was the effect of material type to sensitivity since the draw-in sensor provides high sensitivity to aluminum but low sensitivity to steel. In addition, the induction of the transducer can be affected by the movement of the blank holder. The invention, implementation, and integration of the draw-in sensor will have an enormous impact on revolutionizing the stamping process and provide solid ground for process variation and uncertainty studies.

I. Introduction

Sheet metal forming is one of the predominant processes in the manufacture of automobiles, and widely employed in the manufacture of aircraft, appliances, beverage cans and many other products. Integrating the recent advances micro-sensing and IT technologies to sheet metal forming process will make the stamping tool a smart one; for instance, one that can sense the material movement inside the forming press and make intelligent adjustment to maximize material’s potentials. In order to reach the aspiration, we aim to develop a novel draw-in sensor which can accurately measure material flow in the clamped area in real-time process. The results can be used to exactly quantify process variations in sheet metal stamping and further used for process control to reduce product disparities. Additionally, new product and process designs can be created based on the quantified and referenced variations.

II. Background

Draw in

Typically, draw-in occurs in the sheet metal forming process: This process is performed by placing a sheet-metal blank over a die cavity and then pushing the metal into the opening with a punch, as seen in Figure 1.

Fig. 1 A cross-section schematic of sheet metal forming process

Fig. 2 The original and final blank shapes in an irregular blank forming A, B, C, and D show the four corners

Figure 2 illustrates uneven draw-in distribution. “Draw-in” is the amount of blank edge movement. Commonly, the occurrence of tearing or wrinkling, and the draw-in is caused by the blank holder force.²⁻⁴

Linear Variable Differential Transformer

One of the MEMS technologies that we use is Linear Variable Differential Transformer (LVDT). This machine is commonly used for translating the displacement into an AC voltage that is a linear function of displacement. Basically, the LVDT consists of primary and secondary coils wound on an air core, and a moveable armature that controls the electrical coupling between them.

Fig. 3 : The standard LVDT winding configuration incorporates a center primary winding flanked by two individual secondary windings (A). A special winding configuration positions the primary winding directly under the two secondary windings (B).⁵

Figure 3 shows the basic winding configuration of a 3- and 4- coil winding type. When the armature is displaced from the null position (output voltage approaches zero), an electromagnetic imbalance occurs. This imbalance generates a differential AC output voltage across the secondary coils, which is linearly proportional to the direction and magnitude of the displacement.

Fig. 4 : With the core positioned at null, the output signal approaches zero. Displacements moving the core to the left result in a negative opposite phase signal output. Displacements moving the core to the right result in a positive in-phase signal output. Note: P is primary and S is secondary.⁶

As shown in Figure 4, when the magnetic core is moved from the null position, the induced voltage in the secondary coil, toward the core is moved, increases while the induced voltage in the opposite secondary coil decreases. LVDT provides good sensitivity of micro-order linear movement over several millimeters in the fields of instrumentation and measurement.⁷

III. Prior Research Accomplishments

To address the need of an affordable and accurate draw-in sensor, we experimented with a prototype printed on a conventional printed circuit board, and based on electromagnetic detection. The sensor consists of an inexpensive and possibly disposable sensor element and an electronic circuit remote from it as shown in Figure 5.

Fig. 5 Preliminary Sensor Prototype Setup

The circuit reads data from the sensor and gives the data to a computer, which can control aspects of the forming operation. Note that the sensor element is inherently rugged and lends itself to embedding in the mold surface. It consists of only conductive traces on a substrate. The sensor has a novel geometric layout: two long rectangular coils interspersed or otherwise near each other with mutual inductance. Figure 6 shows a sketch of a typical pair of coils.

Fig. 6 A schematic of the sensor element

This inductance causes the excitation current flowing in one coil induces a signal (voltage or current) in the other coil. The presence of metal (ferrous or non-ferrous) near the coils affects the magnetic field lines, changing the degree of mutual inductance (magnetic coupling) from one coil to the other. Thus the response signal reflects how much of the coil is covered up. Figure 7 shows a schematic of the edge of a plate being formed (rectangular one), which retreats to the right as it slips through the binders.

Fig. 7 Preliminary result – Theory

Fig. 8 Output voltages as length of uncovered sensor length with various sheet materials sliding through the sensor in the setup shown in Fig. 5. ‘t’ here stands for thickness, in mm.

Figure 8 plots the resulting voltages as sheets slide through the sensor for a variety of sheet materials. As shown, this type of sensor is very promising in reaching the objectives we set. The responses show linear relationships between displacement and output voltage, which can be amplified. It can be seen that the output voltage depends on the material type (aluminum [Al] vs. steels), coating type (electro-galvanized [EGCR] vs. plain steel sheet [1018]). However, it is not significantly sensitive to the sheet thickness. All of the experimented results can be found in Appendix A.

III. Experimental Setup

According to the good linear results of the previous prototype, the single-transducer prototype is to determine the factors that affect the relationship of the results. These factors are input voltage, sheet metal type, position of sheet metal over the covered area of a transducer, pulling speed of a sheet metal, blank holder size, and vertical movement of the blank holder. 5-inches and 8-inches of the transducers are considered to determine which dimensions provide the highest sensitivity. The primary results show that the 8-inches transducers provide poor sensitivity. Thus, in this experiment, we focus on testing the 5-inches long transducers as shown in Figure 9.

Fig. 9 Transducers (0.06 thick)

The setup for the single-transducer prototype is very similar to that of the preliminary prototype as shown in Figure 10 and Figure 11.

Fig. 10 Die block with transducer slide under epoxy

Fig. 11 Actual setup with sheet metal attached to the position sensor and a blank holder on top

The transducer is placed in the slot of the simulated die block and a thin sheet of epoxy is placed on top of the transducer to protect it from scratch. Another advantage of using epoxy is that there is no interference to the magnetic fields during testing. A flat sheet metal is placed on top of the die block and attached to the linear position sensor. The simulated blank holder block is located on the top of the sheet metal to exert pressure. During testing, the sheet metal is pulled horizontally to the left and the voltage readings from the draw-in sensor and the linear position sensor are sent to the computer for later analysis.

IV. Results

Fig. 12 Repeatability check testing 0.030-in aluminum by using 0.05x5 in transducer and a small block on top

From Figure 12, the setup gives a linear result with good repeatability.

Fig. 13 Results of various starting positions of a sheet metal over the covered area of the transducer

According to the linear throughout property of the transducers as shown in Figure 13, it shows that there is no effect of starting position of the sheet.

Fig. 14 Results of the effect of pulling speed of a sheet metal

Figure 14 demonstrates that the pulling speed does not affect the linearity of the results.

Fig. 15 Results of the effect of blank holder size (the dimensions shown are the thickness of the block)

In Figure 15, the blank holder blocks with different sizes give the same slope. However, if the block is removed, the slope will change.

Fig. 16 Result of the effect of the vertical movement of the blank holder over a stationary sheet metal

Fig. 17 Result of the effect of the vertical movement of the blank holder over a moving sheet metal

Figure 16 and Figure 17 show moving blank holder causes a change in the output voltage. However, the change does not affect the linearity of the results.

The factor of the input voltage is also considered and it was determined that the range of the sensor’s output voltage varies with input voltages. Each transducer has different input voltage providing maximum output voltage. Moreover, the transducer’s dimension has an affect on the sensor’s sensitivity. The transducer that has 0.65-in wide gives the highest sensitivity on both 0.030-in and 0.065-in Al. In addition, sheet metal type also has an effect on the sensitivity of the transducers because all transducers work well with aluminum but less sensitive with steel. Thus, the sensor is sensitive to the amount of irons in the material (aluminum is non-ferrous but steel is ferrous). In order to obtain a better result from testing steel, the input voltage has to be reduced to a certain value. The graphical comparisons of each transducer while testing with different materials can be found in Appendix B.

V. Further Work

IIn the actual stamping process, sheet metal can become wrinkled when it is stamped. Thus, experimenting with wrinkled sheet metal will determine the effectiveness of the draw-in sensor. However, using only a single-transducer prototype will not yield a linear result because the shape of wrinkled sheet metal creates inconsistent gaps between the transducer and the sheet metal. The solution to this problem is to create double-transducer prototype that places one transducer on top and the other under a wrinkled sheet metal. Consequently, the sum of the readings from each transducer will generate linear results.

Since the ultimate goal is to incorporate the draw-in sensor in the real manufacturing environment, the implementation of draw-in sensor into existing and new tooling will be studied. In addition, the development of advanced closed-loop control strategies with the draw-in sensor will be explored. The traditional proportional and integral (PI) control may not work well as it requires fine tuning for the parameters. The Auto-Regressive Moving-Average model (ARMA)⁷⁻¹⁰ that can automatically generate control parameters based on previous performance and has shown more robust than a PI controller in a machining process will be used.

VI. Conclusion

The draw-in sensor produces good linear results and insensitivity to pulling speed and starting position. Since material type affects the sensitivity of the transducer, the draw-in sensor’s input voltage is adjustable to obtain the highest maximum output voltage. Although the movement of the blank holder block causes a change in the output voltage, the change does not affect the linearity of the results. With these capabilities, the draw-in sensor is effective and ready to be implemented in the discussed further work. The implementation and integration of the draw-in sensor will make the stamping tool sense the material movement inside the forming press and make intelligent process adjustment to maximize material’s potentials. Furthermore, the lead-time for introducing new light-weight materials into mass production can be dramatically decreased and the consistency of stamping products will be increased.

title: Quantum Dot Infrared Photodetectors grown by low pressure metalorganic chemical vapor deposition
notes: Advisor named on the contents page ("Advisor: Manijeh Razeghi, Northwestern University") and in the acknowledgements.
text:
Quantum Dot Infrared Photodetectors grown by low pressure metalorganic chemical vapor deposition

By Tom Sills

Abstract

We report the fabrication and testing of InGaAs/InGaP quantum dot infrared photodetectors (QDIPs). Self-assembled InGaAs quantum dots were grown on an InGaP matrix using low pressure metalorganic vapor deposition (LP MOCVD). The dot size and uniformity, as well as material quality were optimized by changing the temperature, flow rate, and growth rates throughout the device. Both a high detectivity of 3.6×10¹⁰cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W and low dark current were observed. In addition, a photoresponse with a peak wavelength of 4.7 μm was observed above 200K, varying slightly with changes in temperature. These measurements correlate well with previously predicted advantages of quantum dot photdetector technology over quantum well photodetectors.

I. Introduction

Quantum dot (QD) photodetectors have received significant attention within solid-state research due to their potential advantages over quantum well (QW) photodetectors.¹⁻³ QW photodetectors have carriers confined in only one dimension. For example, if the carriers are confined in the z-direction, then they are free to move within the x-y plane. As temperature rises, the energy levels utilized for intersubband transitions are broadened due to the free electron movement within the x-y plane. This, in turn, broadens the detector’s response curve, meaning there is less photocurrent for the detector’s response at a specific wavelength. Due to this chain of events, QW photodetectors must be cooled to increase the photocurrent, increasing their cost and size. In addition, the lack of confinement in the x-y plane means that a QW photodetector cannot respond to normal incident light due to the polarization characteristics of light.

In contrast, quantum dots allow for the three-dimensional confinement of carriers. As a result, a photodetector with quantum dots should not be sensitive to the polarization of incoming light (Fig.1). This feature should reduce the cost and complexity relative to QW photodetectors, which must use Bragg gratings to improve their ability to capture normal incident light waves.

Three-dimensional confinement also eliminates the effect of energy level broadening at higher temperatures because it requires carriers to have quantized energy levels in all directions. In addition, quantum dots have a Dirac-delta function like density of states at specific energies, allowing very precise wavelength selectivity (Fig. 2). This characteristic could be utilized to construct a multicolor QD photodetector if different sized dots are used within the same photodetector. Phonon scattering rates are also reduced inside quantum dots. The scattering rate between two energy levels is proportional to the overlap of the density of state for those two energy levels⁴ and is also related to the energy difference between the levels. Because the density of states of quantum dots has no overlap between energy levels, the phonon scattering rate is significantly reduced relative to that of quantum wells, provided that the energy difference between the levels is not equal to the phonon energy. This phenomenon is known as “phonon bottleneck,”⁵ and could improve device performance by allowing for a longer carrier lifetime.

Fig. 1 Polarization independent absorption

Fig. 2 2D density of states (for QW) compared to 0D density of states (for QD)

In addition, the overlap of the Fermi-Dirac distribution function with the 0D density of states illustrates the temperature independence of quantum dots. As the temperature increases, the overlap area of the 0D density of states changes less than that of the 2D density of states for quantum wells. Thus, quantum dot photodetectors should experience fewer changes in carriers available for excitation, allowing their performance to be stable throughout a larger range of temperatures. A lower dark current is also expected due to the small area overlap of the Fermi distribution function and the 0D density of states, allowing for higher operating temperatures than QW photodetectors.

II. Overview of present research

The research reported here is part of an extensive investigation of quantum dot infrared photodetectors (QDIPs), conducted at the Center for Qunatum Devices (CQD).⁶ The overall goal of the group is to improve the performance of QDIP devices made at CQD, including increasing their detectivity and lowering their dark current. Two teams were formed, each working with their own low-pressure metalorganic vapor deposition (LP MOCVD) reactors. These teams subdivided into more focused areas, including theory, III/V semiconductor material properties, and device processing. After completing extensive background research on the work of other research groups investigating quantum dots, a material system was chosen to start each segment of the research. Next, quantum dots were grown and optimized with the chosen material system for a device structure. After device processing, each sample was tested and compared to previous results.

III. QDIP device structure

The material system chosen for QDIP research is an InGaAs/InGaP structure on a semi-insulating InP substrate, grown by a LP MOCVD reactor (see Fig3). A 0.5μm GaAs contact layer doped to n = 1×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ was first grown on the GaAs substrate, followed by a 0.1μm InGaP barrier layer. Next, 10 layers of n-type doped GaInAs quantum dots were grown, with an InGaP barrier layer between each quantum dot layer. Multiple layers were grown in order to increase the overall efficiency of the device by providing more area for photon absorption. This structure is completed with a .5μm GaAs top contact layer doped to n = 1×10¹⁸ cm⁻³.

Before this device structure was grown, the optimal growth condition for the quantum dots was found by changing the reactor’s growth parameters such as growth rate, V/III ratio, and growth temperature. The quantum dots were grown through a self-assembly epitaxial growth technique known as the Stranski-Krastanow growth mode.⁷,⁸ This method utilizes the strain produced between two materials of different lattice parameters to grow small islands of strained material, or quantum dots. The optimal growth rate, V/III ratio, and temperature for the InGaAs quantum dots grown on InGaP were found to be 0.68 ML/s, 480, and 440°C, respectively. A typical AFM scan of quantum dots is shown in Fig.4.

Fig. 3 QDIP photodetector structure

Fig. 4 AFM scan of InGaAs quantum dots

IV. Device results

The InGaAs/InGaP QDIP structure described above was tested using a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer, which gave a peak photoresponse at 4.7μm with a cutoff wavelength of 5.2μm. This response peak did not change considerably with a change in temperature form T = 30K to T = 140K, showing the predicted insensitivity of quantum dots with varying temperature. The device had a very high responsivity of 3.1 A/W at T=95K and a bias voltage of –5V, as shown in Figure 5. A low dark current was observed in the QDIP device, which was 0.98 pA at T = 120K at a bias of 0.1V (Fig.6). This observation shows the predicted low dark current for quantum dot devices. In addition, a high detectivity of 3.62×10¹⁰cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W at a bias of –1.4V at T = 95K was observed in the device. This is comparable to the performance of most QWIP devices around 100K.⁹,¹⁰

Fig. 5 Responsivity as a function of bias voltage at T = 77K and T = 95K

Fig. 6 Dark current as a function of bias voltage for several temperatures.

V. Discussion

Several important parameters of the device were given in the above measurements, including responsivity, detectivity, and dark current. The measured responsivity of the QDIP device reflects the amount of photocurrent, Iph, produced by optically excited electrons for a given incident input power, Pin, on the photodetector. The input power of the photodetector can be defined as:

Pin = AΦph hν (Eqn. 1)

where A is the area of the photodetector, Φph is the incident photon flux, h is Plank’s constant, and ν is the frequency of light. Using the above expression, the responsivity is given by Equation 2.⁴

R = Iph/Pin = Iph/(AΦph hν) (A/W) (Eqn. 2)

The responsivity is a good measurement parameter to determine how much gain will be needed for a circuit to read out a signal from the detector. However, once a signal is amplified, more noise will be present, which must be taken into account to determine the overall performance of the detector. For this reason, another parameter called the specific detectivity, D*, is needed to compare the performance of two different detectors. The specific detectivity is defined as:⁴

D* = (A Δf )^1/2 / PNEP (cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W) (Eqn. 3)

where A is the area of the photodetector, Δf is the frequency bandwidth of the photodetector, and PNEP is the noise equivalent power. This parameter provides a way to compare the sensitivity of different detectors by normalizing the size, frequency bandwidth, and noise characteristics of each detector.

The dark current of a detector is the current running through a device in the absence of photons from illumination. This current can be due to thermally excited electrons, and must be added to the photocurrent to get the total current flowing across the detector. If the dark current is too large, small changes in the photocurrent will not be distinguishable from the dark current. Thus, a low dark current is desirable in photodetectors.

The detectivity of the InGaAs/InGaP QDIP studied in this report was 3.62 x 10¹⁰ cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W, which is comparable to most QWIP devices at 100K.⁹,¹⁰ However, theory has predicted that QDIP devices should surpass QWIP technology.¹⁻³ Our goal at CQD is to fabricate a detector that surpasses QWIP sensitivity, possibly with a detectivity in the range of ~10¹² cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W. In order to achieve this goal, many areas of theory and experiment must be studied. Electron transport theory is important for lowering the dark current while studying the optical properties of quantum dots will allow a better understanding of absorption within quantum dots. Experimentally, different material systems of III/V semiconductors can be utilized to form new detector structures. Here, the quantum dots size and uniformity may also be optimized to improve the detector’s performance.

VI. Summary and Conclusion

In this paper, we reviewed several aspects of theoretical and experimental research performed at CQD on InGaAs/InGaP quantum dot infrared photodetectors. We have found that such devices can be fabricated to have a high detectivity, low dark current, and be insensitive to temperature changes. We conclude that quantum dot photodetectors are a promising technology that may eventually surpass quantum well photodetectors, possibly even offering room-temperature operation for solid-state photodetector devices.

²David M. -T. Kuo, Angbo Fang and Y. C. Chang. “Theoretical modeling of dark current and photoresponse for quantum well and quantum dot infrared detectors.” 2001; 42:433-442.

³J. Phillips. “Evaluation of the fundamental properties of quantum dot infrared detectors.” J. Appl. Phys. 2002; 91:4590-4594.

⁴Manijeh Razeghi. Fundamentals of Solid State Engineering. Massachusetts: Kluwer Academic Publishers, 2002; 539-540, 549-556.

from the editor

FROM THE EDITOR

To the Northwestern Research Community:

It gives me great pleasure to present to you the second annual edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal. NURJ is part of an increasing effort to involve and recognize undergraduates in cutting-edge research . Here at Northwestern, the willingness of professors to teach undergraduates in their laboratories has created unprecedented opportunities for students. In the scientific and engineering disciplines, research is a critical part of a Northwestern education. This experience allows students to apply the theoretical knowledge learned in the classroom to practical problems.

Moreover, the journal seeks to improve communication within disciplines. Problems we are now facing in the scientific community, such as the treatment of cancer, require complex solutions based on interdisciplinary work. As a result, the ability to express the purpose, results, and conclusions of research becomes an important skill for students.

The submissions to the journal were evaluated based on the clarity, purpose, and scientific merit of the research. After a student review board had expressed their opinions on these criteria, a faculty review board assessed the research. Students were then allowed to improve their papers based on our cumulative suggestions. The submissions included in this year’s journal reflect the high-quality research being performed by Northwestern undergraduates.

This year, in addition to research articles from undergraduates, we have also included three profiles on professors who have inspired our staff: Professors Guillermo Ameer, Robert Lamb, and Richard Silverman. I hope that you enjoy reading the articles.

Sincerely,

Laura Hughes Editor
