monitored in real-time using the Portapres™ finger plethysmograph (Figure 4).  The transcranial Doppler, Portapres™, monitoring hardware, and a data acquisition laptop were housed in the base of the rotating chair (Figure 5).

The combined facility of the rotating chair and instrumentation was named the Biomedical Angled Restrained Rotating Facility (BARRF) (Figure 6).

Protocol

After completion of our OVAR chair, we began a randomized, blinded, and counterbalanced protocol with control, where the 6 subjects susceptible to motion sickness underwent OVAR.  Subjects were briefed on the experimental protocol and refrained from caffeine, medications (prescription and non-prescription), and strenuous exercise 24 hours prior to testing.  Subjects were familiarized with the 5-level subjective symptom scale used to quantify motion sickness for this experiment (Table

Table 2.  Symptom Level Scale

Symptom Level | Description

1 | No Symptoms

2 | Minor sensations: no discomfort. (Able to continue critical tasks.)

3 | Mild nausea: mild discomfort, not distracting. (Able to continue critical tasks.)

4 | Moderate nausea: discomforting and distracting. (Affects performance on critical tasks.)

5 | Severe nausea:  Intense discomfort, symptoms not tolerable for a prolonged period. (Critical tasks are compromised.)

Figure 5.  Data acquisition hardware in the BARRF base.

2). In this experiment, the use of a symptom scale for each minute as an addition to “time on OVAR” was used to quantify the motion sickness symptoms in an effort to better differentiate between levels of motion sickness.  Previous studies have used only “time sustained on OVAR” as the quantifying variable for motion sickness, however this quantification did not differentiate between subjects whose “time on OVAR” were similar though experienced at different symptoms levels (i.e. under previous methods 15 minutes on OVAR with mild/moderate symptoms would be considered quantifiably identical to 15 minutes with no symptoms).³

Figure 6.  Subject on BARRF.

Each subject completed two sessions of OVAR with either the active ITD (−7 cm H₂O inspiratory resistance) or SHAM (0 cm H₂O resistance).  A minimum of 7 days passed between sessions to minimize habituation to OVAR.

Subjects experienced the following protocol: 5 minutes to collect baseline data with no rotation, 15 minutes of OVAR (15 revolutions per minute at 15 degree tilt), followed by an additional 5 minutes of baseline with no rotation.  At 15 seconds before rotation, the subjects began breathing through either an active ITD or a control SHAM device.  A nose-clip was used to insure that subjects breathed through the device.  During rotation, subjects were asked to indicate their subjective symptoms according to the 5-level scale at minute intervals with their free hand.  The subjects were informed to terminate rotation once symptoms reached those of intense motion sickness (symptom level 5).  For subjects who had terminated rotation before the 15 minutes, a symptom level of 5 was recorded for the subsequent minute symptoms.  After each session, subjects completed a survey detailing their experienced symptoms.

Analysis

Data was collected on the housed laptop using Windaq data acquisition software. A representative graph of mean CBFV is presented in Chart 1.  The diastolic and systolic points of the CBFV waveform and the minute symptoms were recorded and statistically analyzed using t-tests on Microsoft Excel.  For CBFV reductions, we used a one-tailed t-test to compare the significance of the difference between the mean baseline CBFV and the mean rotation CBFV with each device (i.e. how much lower is the mean CBFV for rotation than the mean CBFV for baseline on each device).  Since this change was defined to be directional—a reduction from baseline to rotation CBFV—we found the one-tailed t-test to be well-suited for statistical analysis of CBFV.³  For the analysis of non-directional subjective symptoms we used two-tailed t-tests comparing the means of the symptoms between the subjects using the ITD and SHAM.  A p-value of 0.05 was used to establish significance for statistical tests.

PRELIMINARY RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The ITD prevented a significant reduction in mean CBFV (Chart 2).

The results are displayed in Chart 2. The bars indicate the standard error.  Mean CBFV was calculated using the equation: CBFVmean = CBFVdias + 0.4(CBFVsys − CBFVdias).⁴  The subjects using the SHAM showed a significant decrease (p = 0.040) between baseline and rotation mean CBFV, while the subjects on the ITD did not have a significant decrease (p = 0.231).  We would expect the difference for the active ITD not to be significant as this shows that there was not a significant reduction in mean CBFV between baseline and rotation when on the ITD. This indicates the ITD prevented a significant reduction

Chart 2.  Reductions between baseline and rotation CBFV and their corresponding p-values. Subjects using the ITD maintained mean CBFV between baseline and rotation, while there was a significant decrease (p = 0.040) in mean CBFV between baseline and rotation for subjects using the SHAM.

Chart 3.  Minute Symptoms.

in mean CBFV.  The results match this expectation and confirm the results of previous work.²  The difference between the baselines of the ITD and SHAM was not significant, which shows that before rotation and use of the device, the mean CBFV is not different for both devices. This also matches expectations.

The ITD does not appear to mitigate motion sickness symptoms (Charts 3, 4).

Mean minute symptoms are presented in Chart 3. The data shows there is no statistically significant difference (average p = 0.273) in the minute motion sickness symptoms for any minute between symptomatic subjects when on the ITD or SHAM.  Total mean motion sickness symptoms were calculated through the integration of the minute symptom curve and are presented in Chart 4.  Total symptoms also show no statistically significant difference between symptoms for the ITD and SHAM (p = 0.397). This indicates that though the ITD prevented a significant reduction in mean CBFV, motion sickness symptoms were not significantly alleviated.

Chart 4.  Total Symptoms.

CONCLUSION

The mitigation of motion sickness carries a direct application for symptomatic astronauts, aviators, and sailors.  The causes and physiological variables involved with motion sickness are still under study and the successful expansion of our understanding of the physiology of motion sickness is vital for its prevention.  The data from this experiment suggest that while inspiratory resistance through the ITD is successful in maintaining cerebral bloodflow during motion sickness, it does not prevent the onset of its symptoms. This indicates that cerebral hypoperfusion, though related to the onset of its symptoms, may not be an underlying physiological cause of motion sickness.  However, from our preliminary data we cannot yet conclude the level of efficacy of the ITD in mitigating the symptoms of motion sickness and continued study is warranted.  The development of our protocol and construction of our OVAR chair will permit us to test the role of changes in cardiovascular parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, and cerebral blood flow) in the development and maintenance of motion sickness during OVAR and provide a better understanding of the physiology and possible preventive measures for motion sickness.

Hydroquinine-based Chiral Ionic Liquids

Claire M. Schmerberg DEPARTMENT OF CHEMISTRY

Sonbinh T. Nguyen FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF CHEMISTRY, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Green chemistry and asymmetric catalysis are two very active fields of current research. Green chemistry is a field in which chemists attempt to conduct chemical reactions with the highest efficiency and lowest waste possible.  In a similar vein, researchers in asymmetric catalysis focus on the synthesis of highly valuable chirally pure compounds from achiral starting materials, thus reducing the production of an unwanted—and subsequently discarded—enantiomer.  In this paper, concepts from these two fields were combined in the synthesis of four compounds that may be useful in asymmetric catalysis as reusable chiral solvent media.  These compounds belong to the family of chiral ionic liquids (CILs) and are synthesized from naturally occurring hydroquinine via amine quarternization and anion exchange reactions with good yield.

In recent years, the chemical industry has been increasingly concerned with the “greening” of chemical manufacturing by minimizing energy consumption and waste production.¹  One way to increase efficiency in chemical synthesis is catalysis, where a catalyst is added to a particular reaction to decrease both the reaction time as well as its energy requirement.  Catalysis may also provide selective transformations, producing only the most desirable product, either as a pure chemical compound or as a single isomer from a mixture of possible isomers. This increases efficiency and reduces waste by eliminating purification steps that would otherwise be necessary to remove byproducts.

Supported catalysis as a solution to the separation/recycling problem.

Although catalysis can be a successful strategy in green chemistry, catalysts are often difficult and/or expensive to synthesize, and hence their recycling is essential for the “greening” of a catalytic process.  To this end, many catalysts have been modified and immobilized on solid materials.  This allows the catalysts to be easily recovered, either by filtration or centrifugation, and reused after a simple washing step.²

Recently, new strategies in which catalysts are immobilized in a liquid phase have received a great deal of attention.³  In these strategies, the reactants and products are dissolved in a solvent phase and the catalyst is dissolved in a second support phase that is also a liquid but can be made immiscible with the solvent.  After the reaction, the catalyst can be separated from the product-containing phase for subsequent reuse via a simple phase-separation. The use of a liquid support phase for the catalyst lends a number of advantages over traditional solid supports. The catalyst support phase can be made more miscible with the reactant phase during the reaction by controlling the temperature or agitating the mixture vigorously, thereby increasing the reaction rate via better diffusion. In addition, the polarity and ionic strength of the support phase can be readily tuned to allow for different modes of reactivity that are not commonly available in traditional reaction media (water, gases, organic solvents).

Ionic liquids (ILs) comprise one of the catalyst support systems that possess both of the aforementioned advantages.  An IL is a salt that melts at low temperature (below 100°C), allowing it to exist as a liquid under easily attainable laboratory conditions.  It consists of two parts: a positively charged ion, which usually is derived from an amine-, sulfur-, or phosphorous-containing organic compound, and a negatively-charged ion, which is often a bulky anion such as triflate ([OSO₂CF₃]⁻), tetrafluoroborate (BF₄⁻) or hexafluorophosphate (PF₆⁻) (Figure 1).⁴  ILs readily dissolve polar compounds but are immiscible with non-polar organic solvents due to their ionic character.  As such, they can selectively dissolve a polar catalyst for use with non-polar reaction mixtures, thereby extending the range of reactivity and allowing for catalyst recycling by phase separation.  Another attractive feature of ILs is their low vapor pressure⁵—as salts, ILs produce negligible vapor when compared to traditional organic solvents and can be handled with little loss due to evaporation.

Figure 1.  Imidazolium and phosphonium based ionic liquids.

Figure 2.  Hydroquinine, a naturally occurring chiral alkaloid and the starting material for the CILs synthesized in this manuscript.

The importance of chirality and the challenge of obtaining a single enantiomer

Chiral⁶⁻⁷ compounds are very important in living systems; all organisms are created from chiral building blocks and many biological processes only occur with a specific enantiomer of a molecule.  For example, the nucleosides in DNA—the fundamental genetic materials—and the amino acids that make up the proteins in our body are all chiral. Hence, a majority of modern medicines must be enantiomerically pure to work correctly without causing adverse side effects.  While the proportion of drugs that are active only as chiral compounds is increasing each year, these compounds are not easy to obtain.  Often, a chiral resolution process must be performed on a racemic mixture to isolate one isomer, or expensive chiral building blocks and/or chiral catalysts (i.e., asymmetric catalysis) must be used in the manufacture of a chirally pure compounds, which can result in higher costs for consumers.⁸

A novel solution to the aforementioned problem is to carry out syntheses in recyclable chiral solvents, where the chirality of the solvent may influence the chirality of the products due to their close proximity during the reaction.  For this application, chiral ionic liquids (CILs), ionic liquids made from chirally pure precursors,⁹ are ideal candidates.  As such, several reports have appeared in recent years on the syntheses and applications of CILs, and promising success has been achieved for asymmetric catalysis in a CIL phase.¹⁰  For instance, Malhotra and Wang described a CIL based on α-pinene and demonstrated that the achiral catalyst Cu(OSO₂CF₃)₂ dissolved in this CIL can afford enantiomeric excess (ee) of up to 76% in the diethylzinc addition to enones.¹¹

Herein, we report several new CILs and proto-CILs (i.e., organic salts that can be modified slightly to obtain CILs) that are derived from hydroquinine, a naturally occurring chiral alkaloid.  We chose hydroquinine as a precursor because it is readily available and its stereospecific structure can be effective when used for asymmetric catalysis upon modification to a CIL.  In addition, the hydroquinine structure can be modified at several sites to give a wide range of different CILs for use as asymmetry-inducing solvents in catalytic systems.

CILs 1-4 were designed to evaluate the effects of alkyl chain length and anions on their physical properties (Figure 3).  In IL development, these effects are often examined to fine-tune the physical properties (e.g. melting

Figure 3.  Chiral ionic liquids 1-4 derived from hydroquinine.

Scheme 1.  Alkylation of hydroquinine with (a) n-butyl bromide and (b) n-octyl iodide.

point, miscibility, and viscosity) of ILs.  We have therefore prepared chiral ionic liquids with two different alkyl chains, butyl and octyl, and four anions, bromide, triflate, L-(+)-lactate, and iodide.  Synthetic steps utilized in the present work can be applied to the syntheses of other CILs for the generation of a vast library.

Results and Discussion

Alkylation of Hydroquinine

Alkylation of hydroquinine to the alkylammonium salt was accomplished by a simple quarternization of the tertiary amine with alkyl halides (Scheme 1).  Two different alkyl halides, n-butyl bromide and n-octyl iodide, were employed to yield compounds 1 and 4 respectively.  To drive these syntheses to completion, they were carried out under reflux in toluene.  As our initial attempt to use n-octyl bromide was not successful, the more reactive alkyl iodide was used and a longer reaction time was applied. The products were isolated by either a simple filtration (for the butyl salt) or evaporation of the solvent (for the octyl salt) and were characterized by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectrometry.

Ion Exchange

To produce compounds 2 and 3, we carried out ion exchange reactions on compound 1 using silver triflate and silver (L)-lactate, respectively (Scheme 2).  We choose L-(+)-lactate to evaluate possible chiral reinforcement between it and the hydroquinine cation.  As triflate is a non-coordinating anion, its use in ILs designed for catalysis can help ascertain the effect of potentially coordinating anions such as halides and carboxylates.  Silver salts are employed in our anion-exchange reactions because they form highly insoluble silver halide salts, which drive the

Scheme 2.  Ion-exchange reaction with silver salts.

Scheme 3.  Possible modifications of the hydroxyl group reaction forward.  In our hands, the less expensive sodium lactate did not readily exchange with the bromide anion in 1.

The anion exchange reactions were carried out in the dark and under a N₂ atmosphere to prevent potential decomposition of the silver salts.  These reactions occurred over different time periods, depending on the silver salt used.  While the reaction with silver triflate went to completion in just a few hours, the reaction with silver lactate took days.  Products 2 and 3 were isolated from the reaction mixture by filtering out the silver salt and evaporating the solvent.  Their ¹H NMR spectra in the relatively non-polar CDCl₃ solvent show quite distinctive resonances for the chiral CH(OH) groups.  Compound 3—with the lactate anion—exhibits the biggest chemical shift differences between the methine and hydroxyl protons (1.9 ppm), consistent with the expectation that the lactate anion can most readily form hydrogen bonds to the hydroxyl group.  Compound 2 also has a relatively large differences between the methine and hydroxyl chemical shifts (0.6 ppm) compared to that in the parent compound 1 (0.1 ppm), suggesting a degree of hydrogen bonding to the hydroxyl proton that is intermediate between that in 3 and 1.

Attempted alkylation at the hydroxyl group

The hydroxyl group in hydroquinine is located at a chiral center and its modification into an ether group can potentially lead to new CILs with variable chiral environments, depending on the ether substituents.  To this end, we hypothesized that deprotonation of the hydroxyl group on hydroquinine may generate an alkoxide that can compete effectively with the more bulky tertiary nitrogen center of the quinuclidine moiety in an SN2 reaction with an alkyl halide such as dibromobutane (Scheme 3).  Subsequent intramolecular reaction of the remaining bromide functionality with either the quinuclidine nitrogen or an external N-butyl imidiazolium bromide would yield ether-modified hydroquinines that could be used as the cationic components in CILs.  Unfortunately, neither of these reaction sequences proceeded to completion in our hands, and we were unable to isolate a single major product after numerous tries.  Monitoring the reaction using TLC reveals several reaction byproducts that could arise from either competitive reaction of the alkyl halide with the quinuclidine or dimerization through the dibromobutane linkage.  Although unverified, it is also possible that elimination products also formed.  Attempts to separate the reaction mixture using chromatography were unsuccessful due to strong column absorption. Although other separation techniques, such as reverse phase chromatography, might be useful in this separation, they were not available to us.  Efforts devoted to isolating the ether-monohalide intermediate prior to the second alkylation also met with failure due to the instability of this species.

Melting points

Modifying the quinuclidine nitrogen with different substituents and exchanging the resulting cations with different anions afforded compounds with a wide range of melting points.  Table 1 shows that compound 4 has a lower melting point than the similar compound 1, probably due to the larger steric size of the iodide anion and the longer tail on the quaternary ammonium center. The degree of hydrogen bonding and the surface-area-to-charge ratio can be used to explain the melting points in the homologous series 1-3.  Compound 3, with the best hydrogen-bonding potential and the largest surface-area-to-charge ratio for the anion has the lowest melting point. By the same argument, compound 1 should have the highest melting point, which is indeed observed.

It is important to note that not all of the compounds synthesized here are ILs in the strictest definition of the term.  Because some (1, 2) melt above 100°C, they can only be considered as “proto-CILs”, compounds that can serve as the building blocks from which different CILs can be synthesized by further anion exchange or covalent modification to the hydroquinine cation.  Our data thus far illustrates an inherent difficulty in the syntheses of ILs:  while there are general trends to help guide the choice

Compound | Melting point (°C)

1 | 188-189

2 | 120-121

3 | <20

4 | 94-97

of constituent ions and alkyl modifiers, there is no exact formula that can be used to determine if a particular organic salt will melt below 100°C.  This complication makes rational design of ILs difficult, and any theories suggesting what types of ILs to synthesize must be backed up with experimental proof that the compound will in fact have the desired melting point.

Conclusion and Future Work

We reported the successful syntheses of several CILs and proto-CILs from hydroquinine via amine quarternization and anion exchange reactions.  To the best of our knowledge, our work constituted the first attempt to systematically modify the hydroquinine framework for potential use in CILs.  Even though some of our compounds melt above 100°C and thus are not strictly ILs, they can be readily converted into ILs with a different anion.

We also attempted to modify the hydroxyl group at the chiral center of hydroquinine, which would expand the variety of cations that could be made from this natural precursor.  Unfortunately, our efforts did not reliably produce a single identifiable product.  Further work can be devoted to developing reaction conditions that will allow for selective and complete modification of this functional group.  In addition, our CILs should be tested with several catalytic systems to assess their potential as asymmetry-inducing solvents.

Experimental

All reactions were conducted under ambient laboratory conditions unless otherwise noted.  For anhydrous syntheses, HPLC-grade toluene, methylene chloride, and chloroform were obtained from Fisher Scientific and dried over neutral alumina via the Dow-Grubbs solvent system installed by Glass Contours (Laguna Beach, CA).¹²  The solvents were collected under argon, degassed under vacuum, and stored under nitrogen in Straus flasks prior to use.  For bench-top syntheses, HPLC-grade toluene was obtained from Aldrich and used without further purifications.  Deuterated solvents (Aldrich Chemicals and Cambridge Isotope Laboratories) and n-butyl bromide (Avocado Organics) were purchased from commercial sources and used as received.  All other reagents were purchased from Aldrich Chemicals and used without further purification.

In a N₂-filled dry box, silver triflate (0.278 g, 1.08 mmol), 1 (0.500 g, 1.08 mmol), and CH₂Cl₂ (10 mL) were placed in a 25-mL round-bottom flask equipped with a magnetic stir bar. text:
Role of Supra-Segmental Information in Attribution of Meaning

Alison Moy DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATION SCIENCES & DISORDERS

Viorica Marian FACULTY CO-AUTHOR, DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATION SCIENCES AND DISORDERS, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Unlike English, Mandarin is a tonal language, meaning it relies on tone distinctions to tell the difference between different words with the same phonemic pronunciation. The present study examined how knowing Mandarin tones influenced English word recognition in Mandarin-English bilinguals, which would suggest that tonal knowledge carries over from Mandarin into English and influences word perception in a non-tonal language.  For this experiment, homophones were presented in different tones, and the word chosen, along with three reaction times, were recorded.  We found that bilinguals did not appear to identify and choose words differently than monolinguals based on the corresponding tone.  However, we did find an apparent processing difference between bilinguals and monolinguals in our reaction time data, which provides support for an interactive account of bilingual spoken language processing.

Background and Introduction

The number of bilingual people in the world is increasing, and many have suggested that the population of bilinguals and multilinguals outnumbers that of monolinguals.  In just the United States, according to the most recent United States Census, approximately 18% of the population (47 million out of 262.4 million people) speaks a language other than English at home.  Among those 47 million, two million speak Mandarin, which is the third most-spoken language in the United States after English and Spanish.¹  In spite of this large population of bilinguals, there is still much more to discover about the complex influence of multiple languages on bilingual language processing.  Previous studies have examined the extent to which multiple languages are processed together or separately and have found that there is parallel activation of lexical items within and between languages.²  However, there has been limited research on the influence of learning a tonal language, such as Mandarin, on perception of a non-tonal language, such as English.

In Mandarin, one of the most important concepts to grasp is that of the four tones—high level, rising, dipping, and falling.  If the wrong tone is used, the meaning changes and a word is likely to be misunderstood.  Therefore, in order to understand Mandarin, one must be trained to distinguish between tones for both production and perception.  It has been suggested that all speakers of Chinese “feel unconsciously that a tone is such an integral part of the word that a syllable of the same consonantal and vocalic makeup but spoken in a different tone sounds like a totally different word.”³  With just a few exceptions, English does not differentiate between tones and stress for meaning (for example, address, as in “a location”, and address, “to speak to”, or produce, the noun, and produce, the verb), so there is usually no confusion regarding word inflection and semantic meaning.  Research on perception of tones has found that tone perception is related to linguistic experience and background; in other words, learning a tonal language influences how well one perceives tones.⁴,⁵  This suggests that Mandarin-English bilinguals may be more likely to recognize and perceive the necessary tones than English monolinguals, who have limited experience with these tones.  Additional studies have been done to test the processing interactions between segmental and supra-segmental information in native English and Mandarin speakers with the idea that “native Chinese listeners may incorporate both segmental and supra-segmental information in their lexical representations, whereas native English listeners may represent primarily segmental information.”⁶ Segmental information involves consonants and vowels in speech, which are key aspects of the English language. Supra-segmental information, on the other hand, involves things such as intonation contours or stress patterns, which extend over more than one segment.⁷  Lee and Nusbaum’s study found that Mandarin listeners showed mutual and symmetric integrality between supra-segmental and segmental information when performing a speeded classification task (i.e., response times were affected by the addition of tones to the stimuli).  English speakers, on the other hand, showed asymmetric integrality, consistent with the fact that supra-segmentals are not lexically important in English.

The current study observed this interaction between tones and reaction times, while also going beyond this and taking into account another dimension, word meaning. Though in English there is no dependence on tone in determining semantic meaning to cause confusion, there are other aspects of the language which can still create problems with understanding, such as homophones, words which are pronounced the same but have different meanings.  For monolingual speakers of English, homophones can generally be distinguished only by context within a sentence or situation.  The objective of this study was to observe whether Mandarin-English bilinguals take the skill acquired in Mandarin of relying on tones to differentiate meaning in words and automatically apply it to their interpretation of English words.  It was hypothesized that Mandarin-English bilinguals would choose a homophone that is presented in a tone which matches the tone of the Mandarin translation of the word.  English monolinguals, on the other hand, were expected to choose either version of the English homophone at random.  Gaining information about how individuals process language, particularly how bilinguals do this, provides insight into how bilinguals manage their languages and to what extent each language influences processing and comprehension in the other.  It also has implications for how tonal-language bilinguals learn and perceive other languages that do not have a tonal aspect.

Methods

Design

The study followed a 2×2 factorial design, with two between-subject independent factors, group and tone. Group has two levels: 1) monolingual English; and 2) bilingual Mandarin-English.  Tone also has two levels: 1) the Mandarin tone of one translation of the homophone; and 2) the Mandarin tone of the other translation of the homophone.  The four dependent variables are 1) word choice, 2) first reaction time, 3) second reaction time, and 4) third reaction time.  The first, second, and third reaction times measure 1) the time required for auditory recognition of the word, 2) written production of the word, and 3) oral production of a simple sentence containing the word, respectively.

Participants

Participants in this experiment included 20 balanced (equally proficient in both languages) Mandarin-English bilinguals (eight males and 12 females; mean age = 21.550, SD = 5.300) and 20 English monolinguals (nine males and 11 females; mean age = 19.800, SD = 1.200).  All Mandarin-English participants were native Mandarin speakers who learned Mandarin either prior to, or concurrently with, English and were highly proficient in both languages; proficiencies in speaking, listening, and reading were assessed through self-reports using the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q).⁸  All monolingual participants were also given the LEAP-Q to assess their self-rated proficiencies in English, as well as to exclude any participants who might have any prior exposure to or knowledge of Mandarin or other tonal languages.  See Tables 1 and 2 for participant information.

Stimuli

The stimuli used in the experiment were 20 single-syllable English homophones which had single syllable Mandarin translations with different tones for both homophone definitions.  These homophones were checked for word frequency using the CELEX lexical database.⁹  Homophone pairs that showed too great a difference in frequency within the pair were discarded, since the effect of word frequency could possibly confound the results, with high frequency words being chosen preferentially over low-frequency words due to familiarity rather than supra-segmental influences.  These homophones, along with 55 non-homophone filler words, were recorded by an English monolingual speaker with no accent or speech disorder.  These words were manipulated using Praat computer software in order to superimpose the appropriate Mandarin tone, using guidelines established in a previous research study.¹⁰ Duration and amplitude were also normalized using Praat.  Each homophone was presented in a Mandarin tone that corresponded to the tone of one of the translations of the homophone, and the filler words were presented in random tones balanced between the four possible tones.  The stimuli were presented in one tone for half the participants (Block 1) and the other tone for the other half of the participants (Block 2) in a random order, using Superlab computer software.

After running the experiment on all forty participants, a by-items analysis was conducted to determine if any stimuli should be removed from the experiment.  Pairs were excluded if, among all the participants, one word out

Procedure

Prior to the experiment, participants were asked to complete the LEAP-Q¹¹ as a pre-screening process for participant selection.  This was to ensure that participants had the desired proficiency levels in Mandarin and English (for bilinguals) or no prior exposure to Mandarin or tonal languages (for monolinguals).  After providing written consent, participants were placed in a quiet room in front of a computer and microphone and were provided with a blank numbered sheet of paper and a pen.  Instructions given to participants prior to the experiment were to listen to the word, press a button to indicate that they understood the word, write down the word that they heard, press a button to indicate that they were finished writing, think of and record a simple sentence using the word in context, and press a button to indicate they were ready to move to the next word.

Coding and Analysis

The results were coded as correct or incorrect for all the stimuli, homophones and fillers, based on whether the word written by the participant was the word presented.  A homophone was coded as correct if it was a correct spelling of either homophone, so that there were two possible correct responses for each homophone.  Filler words

Words coded as incorrect included misspelled words and correctly spelled words that sounded similar to the stimulus word but were different.  Correct homophones, but not filler words, were further coded as a match or mismatch.  A match indicated that the participant wrote the homophone which was presented in the Mandarin tone of the translation of that word.  For example, if the sound “|meɪl|” was presented in the fourth tone, a match response would be “mail,” since the Mandarin translation of “mail” is in the fourth tone. On the other hand, if the participant’s response to that same fourth tone stimulus was “male,” it would be coded as correct but a mismatch, since it does not match the correct translation tone (the translation of “male” is in the second tone).  The participants’ responses were analyzed by computing the number of times each homophone matched its tone, recorded across all items, for each subject.  A match percentage for word choice was computed as the number of matches relative to the number of correct responses.

There were three reaction times recorded in the experiment using Superlab computer software.  The first reaction time was the time for auditory word recognition, the second reaction time was the time for written word production, and the third reaction time was the time for oral production of a simple sentence containing the word. Outliers for each subject were removed if they were 2.5 SD above or below the mean of the reaction times for all the subject’s correct items, whether they were a match or mismatch.  For each subject, reaction times for the experimental stimuli were analyzed and categorized as a match, mismatch, or incorrect, in accordance with the coding described above.

Results

Word Choice

Analyses of variance were performed to examine if there was a difference in how monolinguals and bilinguals matched or mismatched items.  On average, bilinguals chose 11 items correctly, while monolinguals chose 11.65 items correctly out of a total of 12 items.  Of these, bilinguals matched 5.3 items out of 11 correct (percent match = .483, SD = .135), while monolinguals matched 5.95 items out of 11.65 correct (percent match = .511, SD = .151).  See Tables 4 and 5 for word choice matching data.  To test for a difference in word choice matching, an independent samples t-test was performed, which found no significant differences between monolinguals and bilinguals, t(38) = .609, p = .546.

Reaction Times

To test differences between bilingual and monolingual performance across reaction times, we ran a 2×3×2 ANOVA examining the interaction between match and mismatch, the three reaction times, and group.  A significant three-way interaction was found, F(1,38) = 6.176, p = 0.017. This indicates that there was a significant reaction time difference between bilinguals’ and monolinguals’ match and mismatch reaction times between the first, second, and third reaction times.  In addition, there was a marginally significant effect of group, with bilinguals performing slower than monolinguals across all three reaction times, F(1,38) = 3.546, p = .067.

In addition, 2×3 ANOVAs were run, one for bilinguals and one for monolinguals, with within-subjects factors of match and mismatch reaction times and the three reaction times to further examine the three-way interaction.  A significant interaction was found in bilinguals between the match and mismatch conditions across reaction times, F(1,19) = 9.589, p = .006.  Follow-up paired t-tests were then run to look at reaction time differences between the match and mismatch conditions for the first, second, and third reaction times.  A graph of bilingual reaction times is shown in Figure 1.  For the first reaction time, bilinguals performed slower for the match (M = 2322.613, SE = 240.889) than for the mismatch condition (M = 2022.074, SE = 163.983), but this did not reach significance, t(19) = 1.600, p = .126 (two-tailed). No significant differences were revealed between match and mismatch conditions for the second reaction time, t(19) = .821, p = .422 (two-tailed). Prior to the experiment, participants were given the LEAP-Q to assess their language history and background, including current exposure to languages in different contexts.  One that was of particular interest in bilinguals was current exposure to Mandarin radio and music, which is one of the only passive, auditory receptive (not productive) factors, since the basis of the task was an auditory receptive one.  Participants’ self-rated exposure to Mandarin radio and music scores were factored into a 2×3×2 ANCOVA parallel to the ANOVA previously run.  From this, a significant interaction was found, F(1,37) = 8.910, p = .005, as well as a main effect of group, F(1,37) = 6.292, p = .017, with bilinguals performing slower than monolinguals across all tasks. Discussion

In the present research, the effect on a word recognition task of a supra-segmental feature, tone, was examined. More specifically, we examined whether the superimposition of Mandarin tones on English words affected how Mandarin-English bilinguals perceived those words.  Data analyses of word choice suggested that Mandarin-English bilingual speakers did not perform differently than monolingual English speakers in word choice when a Mandarin tone was superimposed on the word.  This was not consistent with our hypothesis, which predicted that the Mandarin tone would affect the word choice and lead to a greater number of word choices where the superimposed tone matched the tone of the homophone’s Mandarin translation.  This could be due to different reasons, including word frequency and current exposure to English and Mandarin.  Stimulus words were chosen to not differ in English word frequency between the two members of a homophone pair by checking frequencies on the CELEX lexical database.¹²  However, we were not able to control for Mandarin word frequency, which may have played an important role in how readily participants recalled the Mandarin translation of the English words.  The factor of current exposure to Mandarin and English, measured using the LEAP-Q,¹³  revealed that the bilingual participants, though balanced, were currently and on average exposed to English 72.6% of the time, while only exposed to Mandarin 24.6% of the time.  This greater exposure to English, along with the fact that the entire experiment was conducted in English, may have led to Mandarin being less active than English while the bilinguals were participating in the experiment.  This could be an explanation as to why bilinguals appeared to perform similarly to monolinguals at this lexical level of the experiment.

Though ultimate word choice did not appear to be affected by tone in bilinguals, there did appear to be an effect of superimposed tone on how bilinguals processed the English words, as evidenced by the reaction time data.  For monolingual participants’ reaction times, no significant differences were found between the time it took to recognize, write, and orally produce words that matched or mismatched the Mandarin tone presented. Bilinguals, on the other hand, showed differences in the time it took for them to match and to mismatch in all three reaction times, though only the third reaction time, oral sentence production, reached significance.  For the auditory recognition task (first reaction time) and written production task (second reaction time), bilinguals matched slower than they mismatched.  Results for the first reaction time did not reach significance, though Power Analyses suggest that with a slightly larger sample size, a significant result could be achieved.  The second reaction time showed no significant difference, which is most likely due to the large variability in different participants’ writing speed.  In contrast to the first and second reaction times, for the oral production task (third reaction time) in the experiment, bilinguals matched significantly more quickly than they mismatched.  These seemingly contradictory patterns might be explained by activation of similar and competing information across languages.  Previous studies have found that words with large phonological neighborhoods, that is, words which have many phonetically similar “neighbors”

Monolinguals, not familiar with tones or even recognizing that there are tones superimposed, performed similarly on every word, whether they matched or mismatched.  No differences were found in either recognition or production, suggesting that the supra-segmental aspect of tone does not act as competing information in monolinguals as it does in bilinguals.

The results regarding current exposure to Mandarin radio and music seem to suggest that more current exposure to listening in Mandarin might make one more aware of the importance of tones in listening for meaning.  There may be a few reasons for this; it may be the case that the increased exposure to passive Mandarin listening, either in the form of talk radio or music, increases the sensitivity to Mandarin tones, thus leading to a greater effect on processing.  In addition, those who listen to Mandarin radio and music may identify more with their Chinese culture and thus keep Mandarin more active all the time, even when performing an English task.  This interaction between listening and tone perception in language is an area which could be looked at more in depth in future studies.

From the results of our study, we seem to have preliminary evidence that even if bilinguals’ word choice is not ultimately affected by the superimposition of tone, their processing does seem to be affected in some way, which makes them different from monolinguals.  This provides support for previous studies which suggested that Chinese listeners incorporate both segmental and supra-segmental information into their lexical representations, whereas English listeners do not take this supra-segmental information into account.¹⁷  Future studies might further explore this relationship by measuring reaction times in a more objective, non-subject regulated method, by monitoring electrical activity in areas of the brain using electrodes, as physical evidence of when brain activity starts and stops.  We did not find the expected difference in word choice between bilinguals and monolinguals, perhaps due to methodological issues, which leaves possibilities open for future studies in this area.  One possibility includes attempts to increase the strength of Mandarin activation during the study, either by choosing participants who are more proficient in Mandarin than English (therefore they would choose to activate their more proficient language) or by activating Mandarin through the experimental procedure and communication, while keeping the actual English experiment intact.

Taking the results of this study in conjunction with previous studies, we have evidence suggesting that Mandarin-English bilinguals process English differently than English monolinguals due to the presence of supra-segmental information.  Even if we did not find evidence supporting the hypothesis that word choice would be affected, findings that processing differences appeared in the reaction time data suggest that there is some effect of supra-segmental information taken from Mandarin when processing English.

text:
Nabokov’s Memory and the Creation of Fictive Authority

Nicholas Anderman DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH

Kevin Bell FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH, NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Charles Kinbote, the narrator of Vladimir Nabokov’s 1962 novel Pale Fire, creates fictive authority through the deployment of a selective memory.  The implications of Kinbote’s establishment of power through narrative voice are serious and wide reaching, and ultimately suggest a cultural re-evaluation of the importance of fiction itself.

Introduction

Pale Fire (1962), like much of Russian/American novelist Vladimir Nabokov’s work, brims over with thinly veiled allusion to memories of his own life and other writing.  The novel features Charles Kinbote, a Slavic émigré college professor as narrator, a cameo by Professor Pnin (the subject of Nabokov’s 1957 novel Pnin), and Zembla, a purportedly made-up locale that suggests the Russian arctic island Nova Zembla, where there is a Nabokov River named after the author’s great-grandfather. Nabokov, as a young Russian exile (he fled the country during the Revolution of 1917, when he was 18 years old), understood on a very literal level that those who possess the authority to narrate the past (in the name of an ideological agenda, for example) possess great power indeed.  As his personal and artistic history suggests, Nabokov is very much concerned with the effects of historical representation (and misrepresentation) of the past in the present day.

Scholarly interest in Pale Fire has been and continues to be intense, as the book is rightly considered one of Nabokov’s best and most complex.  Existing Pale Fire scholarship falls into two categories.  There are those like Brian Boyd, major Nabokov scholar and definitive biographer, who view the novel as a puzzle to be solved, citing as motivation for this view Nabokov’s well-known obsession with chess problems.  Others disregard the ‘puzzle’ aspects of the novel in favor of a more inclusive approach, most clearly delineated by Michael Wood, who writes, “what matters is not what happens but what might happen…this is one of the more attractive meanings of ‘fiction.’”ⁱ  Wood hints at the importance of fiction in Pale Fire, but does not go any further.

This paper will argue that in Pale Fire memory, or in Kinbote’s case the calculated distortion of narrative representations of the past, has the effect of drawing attention to the creation of fictive authority itself.  When taken seriously, the idea of memory as a mechanism for composing reality has the potential to challenge the greater epistemological question of how texts possess credibility in the first place.  Pale Fire is an unusually vivid study of a text in the process of dealing with its own authority – a topic vital not only to the study of Nabokov’s entire canon, but also to our collective understanding of history, culture, aesthetics, and politics.

Background

Pale Fire consists of two sections: a nine hundred and ninety-nine line poem called “Pale Fire” by the fairly well-known poet John Shade (“born July 5, 1898, died July 21, 1959”ⁱⁱ), and the commentary on that poem by Dr. Charles Kinbote, a colleague of Shade’s in the English department at Wordsmith College.  Shade’s poem, in five cantos, describes his life and various related themes in rather dated heroic couplets.  The poet’s description of himself as “one oozy footstep”ⁱⁱⁱ behind Robert Frost is apt – much of “Pale Fire” is spent faux-philosophizing on nature, art, death, and the possibility of life after death. Notably, the poem also depicts the death, probably by suicide, of Shade’s only daughter, Hazel.  “Pale Fire” is adorned with a Foreword, extensive commentary, and index, all of which are attributed to the aforementioned Dr. Charles Kinbote.  In addition to their professional link via Wordsmith College, we learn that Kinbote and Shade were neighbors in the Appalachian town of New Wye before Shade’s death.  Kinbote claims to have obtained the rights to the original (and only) copy of “Pale Fire” from Sybil Shade, John’s wife, directly after the poet was gunned to death in Kinbote’s front yard.

Kinbote describes himself as Shade’s best friend, intellectual equal, and ideal editor – identities quickly problematized by Kinbote himself.  From the first page of Pale Fire, it is clear that Kinbote is not a very reliable commentator.  In the Foreword, we learn that he gained the rights to the poem “Pale Fire” under extremely questionable circumstances, and that his coworkers in the English department have serious (and well-founded) doubts about his abilities as an editor.  We learn, alarmingly, that during the “few months”ⁱᵛ he actually knew Shade he often spied on the poet and his wife through the windows of their house.  It is clear from the Foreword that Kinbote’s relationship with Shade was creepy, to put it mildly.  It is also clear that Kinbote himself is an interesting and multi-faceted character.  He informs us that he is a strict vegetarian, drives a “powerful red car,”ᵛ is probably a homosexual, and most perplexingly, believes himself to be the deposed king of a far-away nation called Zembla.

The absurdity of Kinbote’s self-centered Foreword is only expanded upon in his 228 pages of commentary to Shade’s poem.  Each of his comments is attached to a line of “Pale Fire,” but often they do not relate to the subject matter of the poem at all.  Instead, Kinbote uses the comments to narrate what we eventually understand to be the primary plot of Nabokov’s novel:  Kinbote, i.e. King Charles the Beloved, is the recently overthrown king of Zembla, a “distant northern land”ᵛⁱ somewhere in the vicinity of Russia.  He describes in great detail his idyllic royal childhood, his daring escape from Communist-controlled Zembla in 1958, and his ensuing undercover life as a mild-mannered, if eccentric, professor of literature at Wordsmith College in New Wye, Appalachia.  His admiration for Shade’s poetry originated in his youth, and seems to be genuine, albeit misguided.  With this royal framework in place, Kinbote claims that Shade was accidentally shot by the Zemblan assassin Jakob Gradus, whose actual target was the disguised King.  The other explanation for Shade’s murder, seen clearly only after the careful reader pieces together seemingly random facts found throughout Pale Fire, is that Gradus was actually Jack Grey, an escaped convict seeking revenge upon the judge that sentenced him to life in prison.  Shade, we learn, greatly resembles Judge Goldsworth, whose house Kinbote is renting while the judge is on sabbatical in England.  Kinbote, who claims to have visited and talked to Gradus/Grey in prison after the murder, vehemently denies this second explanation, though by the end of the novel Kinbote’s narrative voice has been brought into question too many times to count.

Pale Fire is a confusing read, to say the least. Kinbote’s narration is so obviously flawed as to be hilariously funny at times, and quite unnerving all the time. Ultimately, it is up to the individual reader to decide what to believe.  Zembla, we learn from Kinbote’s coworkers (including Shade himself), is a real place in the world of the book.  This paper works from the position that Kinbote’s explanation of Shade’s murder (and indeed Kinbote’s self-identification as King Charles) is a function of Kinbote’s flawed memory, and so is false.  More importantly, the identification of some concrete “reality” in Pale Fire is not the most fruitful of tasks, as we will eventually see here.  The fact of the matter is, Kinbote’s narration is imperfect, but it is the only narration we have. King Charles the Beloved himself best describes his own treatment of Shade’s poem, when he writes, “…for better or worse, it is the commentator who has the last word.”ᵛⁱⁱ Whether we like it or not, Kinbote’s interpretation of “Pale Fire” is the one we have in front of us, and so must be treated with some modicum of respect.

Memory and Narrative

Kinbote’s flaws as a narrator can be traced to his seriously inconsistent memory.  The term “memory” is used broadly here.  Importantly, the word does not imply anything about the question of intentionality in Kinbote’s professed memories.  Whether or not his misrepresentations of his own history are deliberate – that is, whether or not he is lying to us – is irrelevant.  The fact of the matter is, Kinbote actively and often distorts the past, and it is impossible to know his precise motives.  In this paper, then, the term “memory” is used to refer to any and all of Kinbote’s narrative distortions.  This admittedly broad view of the narration of Pale Fire is possible only because the book is a flashback, related by Kinbote after the fact, and so all the events of the novel have been necessarily filtered through Kinbote’s memory.

On page 78, Nabokov (as Kinbote) introduces Gradus into the plot.  He writes:

We shall accompany Gradus in constant thought, as he makes his way from distant dim Zembla to green Appalachia, through the entire length of [Shade’s] poem, following the road of its rhythm, riding past in a rhyme, skidding around the corner of a run-on, breathing with the caesura, swinging down to the foot of the page from line to line as from branch to branch, hiding between two words (see note to line 596), reappearing on the horizon of a new canto, steadily marching nearer in iambic motion, crossing streets, moving up with his valise on the escalator of the pentameter, stepping off, boarding a new train of thought, entering the hall of a hotel, putting out the bedlight, while Shade blots out a word, and falling asleep as the poet lays down his pen for the night.ᵛⁱⁱⁱ

Nabokov keeps this promise.  Throughout the rest of the commentary, Gradus’s journey from Zembla to Kinbote’s front yard – via Copenhagen, Paris, Geneva, Nice, Paris again, and finally New York – runs parallel to Shade’s composition of “Pale Fire.”  In his comment upon the very first line of the poem, which was begun “a few minutes after midnight July 1,” Kinbote admits that he is tempted “to synchronize a certain fateful fact, the departure from Zembla of the would-be regicide Gradus, with that date.”  In reality, we learn, the assassin left Zembla on July 5.ⁱˣ  Kinbote generally succumbs to the temptation of synchronization, and is rarely so forthright when it comes to his deployment of such wordplay.  A bit later in the book, for example, he describes Gradus approaching New Wye: “the force propelling him is the magic action of Shade’s poem itself, the very mechanism and sweep of verse, the powerful iambic motor.”ˣ Kinbote eventually admits that the synchronization of Gradus’s approach with the composition of Shade’s poem is just a literary device (and an overused one, at that), but the damage has already been done – our narrator has a problem delineating style from content.

Kinbote is a limited narrator that pretends to be omniscient.  His description of Gradus’s gradual approach is only one aspect of this trait.  We quickly learn that he has no problem filling the holes in his memory (of which there are many) with other, invented histories.  He obviously does not have extensive knowledge of Shade’s family history (he admits he has only known the poet for a few months, after all), but implies that he does through the invention of extended scenes set in and around Shade’s home.ˣⁱ  This implicative tendency can rightly be cited as a central reason for our distrust of Kinbote’s narration.

Pale Fire hinges upon Kinbote’s construction of a fictive history – the narrator cannot remember the past, and so fabricates one instead.  Nabokov further complicates our understanding of memory and reality in Pale Fire through his use of recurring language, persistent formal tics, and repeated details, all of which work together to cause memory-related glitches in the reader’s own head. For example, Kinbote brings up mirrors or instances of mirroring at least 10 times in Pale Fire.ˣⁱⁱ  We learn that the name “Zembla” translates as “land of resemblers”ˣⁱⁱⁱ and that a famous Zemblan mirror maker with the anagrammatic name “Sudarg of Bokay” once constructed a jewel-encrusted cheval glass for King Charles the Beloved’s grandfather.ˣⁱᵛ  Even the most unobservant reader cannot help but assume that all this talk of mirroring must mean something.  By the end of the novel, however, nothing is explained concretely.  We are left wondering about the significance of mirroring as a literary theme and hypothesizing about other possible examples of mirroring in the text.

It is easy, from this point, to begin to “explain” the book in terms of mirroring: Kinbote alone might be read as a sort of mirror image of Shade, King Charles, Gradus, or Hazel.  Looking elsewhere for mirrors, there are obvious parallels to be drawn between Kinbote and Nabokov himself.  Both were exiled from Communist countries, both taught at small universities (Nabokov at Cornell) in the New England area, and both, at the most basic level, are writers.  This comparison is openly encouraged by Kinbote when he writes, “I may turn up yet, on another campus, as an old, happy, healthy, heterosexual Russian, a writer in exile…”ˣᵛ  Finally, Kinbote might easily be read as a mirror image of us, the readers of Nabokov’s Pale Fire.  On a very literal level, he misreads Shade’s poem egomaniacally, inserting himself into the narrative whenever he gets the chance.  After digesting Pale Fire, it is hard not to think that we are doing the same thing.

The book actively promotes disorientation and paranoia in its readers.  Whenever it seems that a unifying narrative explanation is looming, Kinbote proceeds to complicate things even more.  On page 272, for example, he inadvertently describes the form of the book in which he is a character: “…our poet suggests here that human life is but a series of footnotes to a vast obscure unfinished masterpiece.”ˣᵛⁱ  It seems like this line should have serious consequences in the world of the book, and that it should tell us something important about Kinbote and his narrative voice.  Any conclusions we reach because of quotes like this, however, are ultimately inferred and not necessarily present in the text.

Memory and Authority

Although we have spent much time pointing out Kinbote’s many narrative failures, the fact remains that his is the only narrative voice in Pale Fire.  Even Shade’s poem has been filtered through his head.  Everything we say about him, then, must have originated with him at some point. No matter how hard we try to see through his narration to some hidden “real” world underneath, we will ultimately only come face to face with his own words.  On page 261, Kinbote quotes Franklin Lane and inadvertently describes what we want most in the book:

And if I had passed into that other land, whom would I have sought?...Aristotle! – Ah, there would be a man to talk with!  What satisfaction to see him take, like reins from between his fingers, the long ribbon of man’s life and trace it through the mystifying maze of all the wonderful adventure….The crooked made straight.  The Daedalian plan simplified by a look from above – smeared out as it were by the splotch of some master thumb that made the whole involuted, boggling thing one beautiful straight line.ˣᵛⁱⁱ

Kinbote is completely incapable of “explaining” the events in Pale Fire – he cannot make “the whole involuted, boggling thing one beautiful straight line.”  What he can do and does do, in fact, is show us his own path through the maze.  Kinbote’s own version of “Pale Fire” (and Pale Fire, for that matter) is probably not the one that we would choose (had we been offered the choice), but it is the one we are stuck with.  To be succinct: Kinbote’s narration, even though it comes from a seriously flawed memory, is the basis of all authority in Pale Fire.  By reinventing the past, Kinbote seriously and permanently influences the future.

Pale Fire effectively demonstrates the power of a single narrative voice to alter history forever, and so to gain great authority in the present.  This idea holds great implications for many disciplines outside of literature, especially in those fields that rely heavily on narrative. That said, literature in general and the novel in particular are exceptionally capable of pointing out this detail – more so, I believe, than any other discourse.  Nabokov describes the essential character of the written word when he writes:

We are absurdly accustomed to the miracle of a few written signs being able to contain immortal imagery, involutions of thought, new worlds with live people, speaking, weeping, laughing.  We take it for granted so simply that in a sense, by the very act of brutish routine acceptance, we undo the work of the ages, the history of the gradual elaboration of poetical description and construction, form the treeman to Browning, from the caveman to Keats.  What if we awake one day, all of us, and find ourselves utterly unable to read?  I wish you to gasp not only at what you read but at the miracle of its being readable.ˣᵛⁱⁱⁱ

The very existence of language and the consequent work that it does for us is proof of its ultimate authority.  In the same way that Kinbote controls and restrains any understanding we think we have of Pale Fire, language inherently mitigates our understanding of the so-called “real” world. Ultimately, then, we are only capable of choosing our own path through the maze.

Letter  Editors from the

Dear Northwestern Community, 

We are pleased to present the fifth edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research

Journal (NURJ). As part of Northwesterns distinguished research community, NURJ aims to foster the opportunity for outstanding undergraduate researchers to publish their work and share their findings with the broader Northwestern community and to promote more cohesive communication across academic disciplines. 

In the past year, the NURJ executive board expanded our involvement in the undergraduate research community. This year, not only did we recruit and receive strong submissions from a broader range of academic fields previously unrepresented in our journal (including history and anthropology), but also we expanded our programs to include a quarterly newsletter designed to give Northwestern undergraduates a wider exposure to the exemplary research community on campus. 

The fifth edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal has been made possible by the incredible dedication and hard work of many individuals. We would like to extend our gratitude to all of the authors and contributing writers for taking the time and effort to submit such high-quality work. In addition we would like to extend our deepest thanks to all of our faculty and student reviewers, without whom our editorial review process would be inconceivable. Finally, we would like to thank the staff and executive board of NURJ for their efforts and dedication to producing a high-quality journal. Sincerely,

Danwen Song Editor-in-Chief

title: Economic Stimulus Means More Opportunity, More Research for NU
notes: News feature on American Recovery and Reinvestment Act research funding at Northwestern. The footer of printed page 5 reads "VOLUME 4, MAY 2008" (left over from the previous volume) and is included in the text.
text:
FEATURE

Economic Stimulus Means More Opportunity, More Research for NU JESSICA GOTTESMAN

Despite the economic recession, the influx of Northwestern Universitys proposals for science research is at an all time high. Due to the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) signed by President Obama on February 17th of this year,  opportunities for short-term economy-stimulating research have received a record boost.  Allotting $10 billion to NIH for health research and refurbishing of their facilities, $3 billion to NSF for basic science and engineering, $1 billion to NASA, as well as $1.6 billion to agencies ranging from climate science to nuclear physics, these grants are structured differently from those previously offered. In order to aid in economic recovery, the funds are to be awarded almost immediately instead of in gradual stages, many stipulate that the research must be completed within two years, and all require the researches to report on their progress four times a year instead of annually. Considering the enormous turnout from researchers, most people dont seem to mind navigating a few new requirements. In fact, the scale of the competition poses the greatest challenge to Northwesterns benefiting from the stimulus plan.  Susan Ross, director of Sponsored Research at Northwestern, admits that the success rate for accepted proposals is expected to be low. For the NIHs April Challenge Grant deadline, the agency intended to award 200 proposals, including a small percentage of prior submissions they had on file. More than 200 new proposals were sent out from Northwestern alone, competing against institutions from around the country.  Despite the adversaries, Northwestern is determined to be among the most competitive, and working equally hard on this front is Dr. Holly Falk-Krzesinski, Academic Director for the Office of Research Development. My job is to make sure Northwestern gets more than its fair share, she notes. Weve really encouraged researchers to send in proposals. Beyond the hope of success, however, Dr. Falk-Krzesinski also observes that putting together the proposals are good experiences for the researchers, no matter the result. The efforts have increased cooperation and collaboration among departments at Northwestern as Kellogg, SESP, the Law school, Medill, and others have partnered with schools like Feinberg to create joint projects.  The stimulus for scientific research, while generally considered a positive strategy, has also created a number

FEATURE of problems. As federal agencies scramble to review new projects, the details are often not as thoroughly worked out as they have been for previous grants, leading to confusion on the part of institutions as well as contradictory feedback and guidance from the agencies. Nevertheless, contends Dr. Falk-Krzesinski, the atmosphere remains optimis- tic. Folks at these federal agencies have been incredibly responsive and helpful in working with us, she says, though having to clear up these problems on top of organizing the flurry of new proposals and questions has only added to the number of overtime hours she and others in her office are putting in.  This is all happening incredibly quickly in terms of how government agencies and universities normally work, Ross said over the phone as she dashed home to pack and catch a flight for another meeting. Its put a huge stress on the system. Ross had people working 7 days a week to prepare for the Challenge Grant deadline in April, and with a new NIH deadline approaching and weekly deadlines from various other organizations, theres no end in sight. Thus far, the effort seems to be paying off. Every proposal turned into their office was successfully finalized and submitted by the deadline. Meanwhile, in between teaching both in Evanston and downtown, Dr. Falk-Krzesinski constantly updates her departments website and sends out notification emails through a special listserv. People in her office joke, Were not sure if this has stimulated the economy, but its definitely stimulated more work.  Still, more work doesnt necessarily translate into generating new jobs at Northwestern. Though the staff works overtime, Northwestern has no immediate plans to hire new employees. We have to balance that against the fact that the endowments down and Northwesterns working hard not to lay people off, stresses Dr. Falk-Krzesinski, but she notes that as proposals are accepted, new jobs may be in store for the future. Awarded investigators are expected to apply for supplemental grants to cover lab technicians, pay researchers, fund graduate research, and cover equipment costs. This is good news for high school students and undergraduates as well, who will not only have more opportunities to fund their own research projects, but will be able to find new lab opportunities available to aid researchers.  Dr. Falk-Krzesinski adds with confidence, Northwestern expects to do well. Were committed to the end. Many thanks to Susan Ross and Dr. Holly Falk-Krzesinski for their information and support in creating this article, especially at this busy time.

VOLUME 4, MAY 2008

title: Breast Cancer and Early Development
text:
FEATURE Breast Cancer and Early Development NOEL SLESINGER

They grow up so fast. It seems to be a common sentiment among the older generation, especially as they watch the children in their lives grow up in an age dominated by technology and easily accessible information on almost any topic. However, recent studies have shown that girls are not just growing up faster mentally, but physically as well.  Normally, puberty begins for girls around the age of ten. However, many girls have been showing the first sign of puberty, breast development, at the age of nine, especially girls with a Body Mass Index that falls in the obese range. Dr. Joyce Lee of the University of Michigan reported to BBC News, Previous studies had found that girls who have earlier puberty tend to have higher body mass index, but it was unclear whether puberty led to the weight gain or weight gain led to the earlier onset of pubertyOur study offers evidence that it is the latter. One explanation for this early onset places the hormone leptin, which is produced by fat tissue and triggers puberty, as the culprit. Another fifteen year study by the University of Copenhagen theorizes that exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals is to blame. Both of these studies show, though, that no matter what the cause, the age for entering puberty is changing.  But that leaves the question: Why is one year so important?  The problem is that early puberty has been linked to a number of physical and social problems. Early development has been linked with depression, and girls who enter puberty earlier are more prone to engage in high-risk behavior. Also, girls who developed early have a higher risk of diabetes later in life. One theory is that, because breast tissue has been shown to be sensitive to hormones, it makes it highly resistant to insulin. Furthermore, because girls who are obese tend to have more breast tissue, they are put at a higher risk for diabetes.  Not only do girls who develop early have a higher risk of diabetes, they also have a higher risk of developing breast cancer. Like diabetes, though, hormones may play a part. Estrogen, the hormone that plays a role in breast development and growth by stimulating breast cell division, has been shown to be one of the factors involved in the development of breast cancer. Because it supports the growth of estrogen-responsive tumors, women who have had a higher exposure to estrogen may have a higher risk of developing breast cancer. As girls enter puberty earlier, they are exposed to estrogen for longer periods of time, which may put them at risk for breast cancer later in life.  What has many researchers worried is what this change might mean for the larger population. As Dr. Lise Aksglaede of Copenhagen University Hospital told The New York Times, Changes in development, such as early puberty, might reflect changes in the general health in a population. However, nothing has been proven yet, and, when it comes to breast cancer and other health risks, other factors-- such as environment, health, and geneticscannot be ignored. Research continues to investigate the causes as to why breast development has changed so rapidly as well as the consequences it may entail. While researchers continue to look for answers to these complicated questions, to quote Dr. Askglaede, Probably the majority of these girls will mature without any side effects. The problem is that we do not know.

title: The Skinny on Stress: Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Birth Weight in the Philippines
notes: Printed page 9 is missing from the capture, so the text jumps from the middle of the results to the end of the discussion.
