What is your research topic, in a nutshell? How do once meaningful discourses become distorted with time to become counter-productive, normalizing terms?

What is your research topic, in a nutshell? The 20th century poet that initiated avant-garde writing in Mexico, Manuel Maples Arce, has been largely overlooked in literary history in Spanish and English. His ingenuity deserves recognition—although he may have been more conventional than he thought—including translations of much of his poetry into English for the first time.

How did you come up with your research topic? I have been passionate about the issue of sexual assault on college campuses for a long time, and I knew I wanted to incorporate it largely into my thesis. In my junior year, I did an independent study with Professor Mary Dietz, who later became my thesis advisor, and I became fascinated with radical feminism, particularly with Catharine MacKinnon. The project started as a what would radical feminists, who argued essentially that no sex is truly consensual due to inherent power differentials, think about this issue of sexual assault on college campuses, but particularly the way that we talk about it. What have you been up to since graduation? In August 2015, I began working at the Manhattan District Attorney's Office as a paralegal. I assist with trial preparation on a variety of cases, ranging from misdemeanor drug possession to sexual assault and other felonies. I hope to apply for law school in fall 2016. What is your favorite class at Northwestern? My favorite class, and also one of my most challenging courses, was Feminist Theory with Professor Mary Dietz.

How did you come up with your research topic? I first read Maples Arce in Harris Feinsod’s multidisciplinary (Spanish/English/Comparative Literature) Poetry of History in the Americas class. This innovative class led me to identify Professor Feinsod as my thesis advisor, and he helped me discern this project as feasible, significant, and ideal for my interest in translation. What have you been up to since graduation? I have been living in my hometown of Chicago, spending many weekends in Milwaukee, job hunting, and working part-time online as a proposal editor for a California-based government technical contractor. I was lucky enough to visit SoCal and the Grand Canyon for the first time this summer! What is your favorite class at Northwestern? Perhaps unpredictably, the class I usually say I enjoyed the most was Intro to Metaphysics with Fabrizio Cariani. Our philosophical discussions of existence, time travel, and possible universes entirely captivated my curiosity.

title: LETTER FROM THE EDITORS
text:
LETTER FROM THE EDITORS To the Northwestern Research Community: 

We are pleased to present the sixth edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ). NURJ is part of an increasing effort to involve and recognize undergraduates in cutting-edge research. It provides them with a forum to share their work from the laboratory to the broader community and incorporates the work of student researchers from all academic disciplines.   This year, we proudly feature articles from diverse academic fields within the Northwestern University research community. From International Studies and Psychology to Biology and Slavic Studies, the 2010-2011 Journal is a testament to the fact that research can be performed in a variety of settings. 

While the Journal always strives to spread awareness about undergraduate research, this years Journal seeks to inspire potential researchers as well. The interviews with the Churchill scholars, in addition to the double feature articles, represent the apex of research achievement. We hope that our readers refer to the guide to beginning research at the back of the Journal as a starting point for their own endeavors.

Sincerely, 

Alina Dunbar

title: Navigating the Tangle of Pathology: Community Organization and Family Strength in Watts on the Eve of the 1965 Rebellion
notes: Full title from the contents page; the opening page's text gives only the part after the colon. Henry Binford is named as faculty advisor (Department of History) on the opening page. Includes notes and sources; note numerals are extracted separately from the note text.
text:
Community Organization and Family Strength in Watts on the Eve of the 1965 Rebellion

Colin McGrath DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY

Henry Binford FACULTY ADVISOR DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

On August 11th, 1965, one of the largest urban uprisings in American history broke out in Los Angeles.i Black residents from the Watts district  and  surrounding  areas  looted  local businesses,  burned  buildings,  overturned  cars,  fought police officers, and stoned firemen. The district and its surrounding areas contained a concentrated population of  black  Americans  who  suffered  from  acute  poverty. During  the  rebellion,  reporters  depicted  images  of hoodlums  running  lawless  through  the  streets  of  Los Angeles. All major newspapers termed the conflagration a  riot.  Professional-class  Americans  argued  that  the rebellion erupted in a community where poor leadership and broken homes produced a riot-prone youth. Yet the black community evinced substantive forms of political and social organization at the time of the rebellion. Blacks developed organizational tools to cope with their shared experience of poverty and discrimination. The rebellions pattern  of  property  damage  shows  that  participants targeted the same set of structural injustices. They were integrated  within  an  organized  and  politically  engaged community. Urban violence was the black communitys response  to  political,  social,  and  economic  inequalities the  U.S.s  racialized  political  economy  produced.  For participants,  the  conflagration  offered  the  only  means for expressing outrage; political marginalization denied black  residents  any  other  effective  avenues.ii    But professional-class  Americans  failed  to  seeand  chose to ignorethe political intent of the black community. Contemporaneous  social  science  research  influenced professional-class  perceptions  of  poverty  and  distorted their interpretation of the rebellion. Culture of Poverty, Tangle of Pathology In the 1960s, social scientists in the United States produced a  body  of  research  highlighting  cultural  differences between  poor  and  affluent  Americans.  Researchers among them Oscar Lewis, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, and Kenneth Clarkinvestigated the cultural pathologies of poor communities to explain the production of poverty across  generations.  By  synecdoche,  anthropologist Oscar  Lewis  applied  the  conclusions  from  his  popular ethnography on Latin American poverty to the poverty of black Americans.iii In 1963 he wrote an article, The Culture of Poverty, in which he claimed, The problems we think of as distinctivelyNegro problems also exist in countries where there are no ethnic groups involved.iv He explained that culture, not racial conflict, perpetuated poverty in the U.S. In 1965, psychologist Kenneth Clark published Dark Ghetto and described urban poverty thus: The ghetto develops the sinister power to perpetuate its own  pathology,  to  demand  conformity  to  its  norms.v He coined a term, tangle of pathology, to encapsulate the  debilitating  cultural  he  found  endemic  in  poor communities. Sociologist  and  politician  Daniel  Patrick MoynihanAssistant  Secretary  of  Labor  and  Director of Policy Planning and Research under the Kennedy and Johnson administrationsborrowed Clarks term in his study  The  Negro  Family:  The  Case  for  National  Action, popularly  titled,  The  Moynihan  Report.  The  study explained that the insidious tangle of pathology ensnared black youths. Central to the tangle, he explained, was the weakness  of  the  family  structure.vi  Through  slavery and  subsequent  penury,  black  men  lost  the  masculine traits  necessary  for  raising  successful  families.  Without suitable fathers, children flounder and failvii: they grow up lacking ambition and are unable to successfully raise their own children. Moynihan concluded that the tangle of pathology could perpetuate itself without assistance from  the  white  world.viii  His  reasoning  echoed  that  of Oscar  Lewis:  racial  injustice  could  no  longer  explain inequality  in  the  United  States.  The  ghetto  produced poverty on its own. Government  officials  intended  for  the  Moynihan Report to remain an internal document. But in July 1965 full summaries of the report leaked into the public sphere and fomented a nationwide debate on race, poverty, and the  structure  of  black  families.  When  the  rebellion  in Watts broke out a month later, the Moynihan Report was the primary frame of reference through which Americans interpreted the conditions in Watts and the meaning of the rebellion. As  journalists  and  government  officials  struggled to understand the rebellion, they failed to recognize the rebellions  social  and  political  impetus.  Through  the lens  of  racial  stereotypes  and  literature  on  the  culture of  poverty,  whitesand  some  blacksdeemed  the rebellion  a  meaningless  riot:  it  was  the  product  of pathologies  social  scientists  found  endemic  in  black urban  ghettos.  Journalists  reported  that  community disorganization,  emasculation  and  shiftlessness  of black males, and single-mother households destabilized black  neighborhoods.  A  headline  in  the  Wall  Street Journal  boldly  announced,  Behind  the  Riots:  Family Life  Breakdown  in  Negro  Slums  Sows  Seeds  of  Race Violence. The article argued that the violence was not protesting  any  specific  civil  rights  grievances.  Instead, the  participants  were  primarily  young  hoodlums lashing out against society and authority in general. Such youths, it added, are being bred in the Negro sections of cities across the country by broken homes, illegitimacy, and  other  social  ills.ix  Other  journalism  explicitly referenced  the  Moynihan  Report.  On  August  26th,  the Chicago Tribune proclaimed, Study Traces Negro Riots to Inferior Homes.x Rowland Evans and Robert Novaks column  The  Inside  Report  drew  another  explicit  link between Watts and Moynihan. In a brief summary of the Moynihan  Report,  they  asserted  that  key  White  House figures  feel  that  the  Moynihan  report  might  open  the door to new ideas and avert continuous guerrilla warfare in Negro ghettoes.xi The McCone Commissiona research group that Californias  Governor  Brown  appointed  to  investigate the  rebellionechoed  these  views  in  an  official  report titled,  Violence  in  the  CityAn  End  or  a  Beginning?  xii But  the  commissions  own  records  reveal  a  different image of the community. Their interviews with residents of  Watts  show  that  members  of  the  community  were more  articulate,  organized,  and  perspicacious  than professional-class Americans reported. Coping Mechanisms and Forms of Social Organization in Watts Individuals in Watts took proactive actions to cope with their adverse circumstances. Unemployed black men did not constitute a uniformly weak and depressed segment of society; men found informal yet legal ways to secure an income. Single mothers took proactive steps to organize with one another in order to care for their children and navigate  bureaucratic  mazes  to  access  welfare  money. Youths  in  Watts  formed  political  coalitions  to  combat social  and  economic  injustices  within  the  community. These interlocking actions held Watts together while Los Angeless white-dominated society threatened to break it apart. Because  white  employers  were  reluctant  to  hire blacks,  men  in  Watts  became  informal  entrepreneurs. Their  entrepreneurship  mitigated  the  neighborhoods chronic unemployment. One man named Willie Brown described  himself  as  professionally  unemployed.xiii To  secure  an  income  for  himself  while  assisting  men in  situations  similar  to  his  own,  Brown  established an  informal  employment  and  transportation  service. Individuals from Woodland Hills, a more affluent city in the San Fernando Valley, had provided Brown with a 37- seat bus. He used the bus to transport day laborers from Watts  to  Woodland  Hills  for  work  that  paid  $14  a  day. Each worker paid Brown $2 a day for his service. Young-adults  in  Watts  formed  organizations  to strengthen  their  communitys  bonds  and  ameliorate their living conditions. Students at Jordan High School, a  low-income  school  in  Watts,  founded  one  such organization: the Student Committee for Improvement in  Watts  (SCFIW),  which  had  120  registered  members and 80 active participants.xiv The SCFIW addressed many of the problems of economic exploitation and absentee ownership that the rebellion would later target through violence. The group petitioned against absentee landlords who allowed buildings to deteriorate. Lynda Bryant, the SCFIWs president, inveighed against poor ownership and observed: The people who owned the buildings had left  and  they  didnt  care  about  the  buildings,  orhow they were kept up. The group gathered 2,500 signatures in  opposition  to  property  neglect  and  successfully campaigned to convert the abandoned and deteriorating Villa Maria Hotel into a community cultural center.xv The SCFIW also assisted in a campaign to register voters in opposition to Californias Proposition 14, legislation that would allow landholders to deny property sales to buyers on the basis of race.xvi Two SCFIW members received a grant from UCLAs Industrial Relations Department to publish  a  research  paper  in  the  research  compilation, Hardcore  Unemployment  and  Poverty  in  Los  Angeles.xvii Students  in  Watts  cared  about  their  surroundings  and could successfully mobilize their community to combat sources of exploitation and urban decay.

Voices from Watts Following  the  rebellion,  the  McCone  Commission hired investigators to interview individuals from Watts. Through listening to the black communitys grievances, the commission hoped to ascertain the rebellions causes. Concerns that blacks articulated corresponded with the frustrations that inspired blacks from Watts to engage in social  and  economic  entrepreneurship.  These  concerns also paralleled the injustices participants in the rebellion reacted  to  with  violence.  Frequent  themes  included employers racist hiring patterns, antagonistic community- police relations, white shopkeepers exploitation of black customers, and political marginalization. Blacks from  Watts linked chronic unemployment to  employers  racist  hiring  practices  and  Los  Angeless racialized, segregated industrial geography. At the Avalon Community  Center  near  Watts,  blacks  who  attended  a meeting  with  a  government  investigator  observed  that the  stores  in  the  area  refused  to  hire  minorities,  and especially Negroes.xviii A younger girl stated, When you go  to  look  for  a  job,  they  dont  want  you.xix  The  jobs blacks did get were so marginal that the employers go out  of  business  or  go  bankrupt  before  they  are  able  to pay them. Some employers refused to pay their workers. xx One man recounted having excelled in school only to graduate and not find a job because employers favored whites: I was a better student than them, but they got the jobs. Even if the citys hiring and firing process was legally  fair,  he  observed,  It  doesnt  stop  the  individual from  practicing  discrimination.xxi  Others  noted  that 8 the stable, well-paying jobs were situated far outside of Watts. In  Watts  and  nearby  areas,  police  officers symbolized  the  white  power  structure  that  oppressed black  Americans.  One  resident  stated,  The  people  in Watts call the police the Gestapochildren and adults alike.xxii A woman claimed that the police would request sexual favors. If a woman refused to comply, she would go  to  jail  on  some  trumped-up  charge.  The  police would  hold  unyielding  women  for  24  hours  before releasing them without formal charges.xxiii A young man named Doe participated in the rebellion because he had a  personal  dislike  for  the  police  ever  since  two  white officers  attempted  to  rape  his mother.xxiv  In  a public forum, a speaker linked his anger towards the police with the  problem  of  unemployment  in  Watts.  He  observed, If  two  or  moreboys  are  together,  they  are  always picked up by the police and held for 24 hours. The police would  release  them  without  pressing  any  charges,  but the  youths  would  still  have  a  police  record,  and  when they  apply  for  a  jobthey  are  denied  work.xxv  Watts residents frequently and angrily quoted the Los Angeles Police Departments Chief Parker as saying, Theyre like a bunch of monkeys in a cage. To many blacks, Parkers incautious, inflammatory comment confirmed the police departments distain for the community. In  many  discussions,  blacks  excoriated  white business  ownersmany  of  whom  were  Jewishfor exploiting blacks. A public-forum speaker stated that the food  sold  in  his  neighborhood  was  exorbitantly  priced and of inferior quality: the vegetables, the meat, and the bread were almost always old and barely fit for human consumption. Prices were higher in Watts than in white neighborhoods  where  products  were  of  better  quality. xxvi Multiple  speakers  shared  in  this  frustration.  As  one interviewee  vituperated:  There  were  just  a  bunch  of Jews selling us a second-class merchandise for first-class prices.xxvii Patterns of Destruction The pattern of property damage from the rebellion indicates that participants acted in precise and consistent ways that reflected the attitudes blacks shared throughout the community. Participants burned and looted stores owned by whitesespecially stores notorious for selling inferior goods at exorbitant prices. They spared homes, schools, community centers, black-owned businesses, and white-owned businesses with good reputa- tions. Though  no  leader  organized  the  Watts  rebellion, a  logic  guided  the  pattern  of  property  destruction.  A McCone Commission memorandum reported:

It  was  noted  that  the  burning  was highly  selective.  The  Urban  Leagues, Poverty  Program  Watts  Project, for  example,  was  the  only  unburned building  left  in  the  block.  A  Negro owned  restaurant  was  left  standing and  unlooted  while  a  furniture  store next door was burned to the ground. The memorandum also noted that some white businesses were still operating and had not been bothered because: they treated the people o.k. and did come back and open their stores even after the newspapers and T.V. said this was a race riot.  Further indicating  that the rebellions logic  was  nuanced  enough  to  see  past  simple  racial divisions,  the  memorandum  observed:  Some  Negro businesses  (with  bad  policies  towards  customers)  were attacked.xxviii These  patterns  show  that  the  rebellions participants  shared  their  perceived  injustices  with  the rest  of  the  community.  Lynda  Bryant,  president  of  the SCFIW, illustrated a bond between organized individuals and the rebellions participants when she testified before the McCone Commission. She linked the rebellion to the frigid  business-community  relationship  in  Watts.  As  a student who organized against economic injustice in her community,  she  assailed  local  merchants  for  exploiting their  customers.  In  Watts,  she  explained,  most  of  the clothes  are  real  cheap,  the  material  and  allbut  the prices  are  real  high.  In  her  opinion,  this  was  one  of the  reasons  why  participants  burned  and  looted  stores during  the  rebellion.xxix  Bryant  did  not  participate  in the  conflagration.  She  nonetheless  saw  that  individuals who resorted to violence did so for the same reasons that inspired her involvement with the SCFIW. Conclusion The participants were engaged with the civic and social life of their surrounding community. They razed the businesses that exploited them and they acted deliberately enough to preserve the agencies that supported their community. Their actions stemmed directly from the communitys underrepresentation in Los Angeless political sphere: if civic politics allowed blacks to pressure the city government into policymaking beneficial to the Watts district, they would not have resorted to political violence as a means of expression. Yet the McCone Commission blatantly ignored this evidence in their report on the rebellion. In so doing, they exonerated political leaders whose favoritism and policymaking had facilitated Los Angeless racial inequalities; they sanctioned the Los Angeles Police Departments heavy-handed presence in Watts; and they obviated the need to consider racist attitudes among whites as a cause for the rebellion. When professional-class Americans investigated and reported on the Watts community, they chose to see hoodlums rather than activists and pathology instead of political intent. Echoing the tangle of pathology, the McCone Commission evoked an ominous spiral of failure when explaining the origins of the rebellion. The commission warned that unemployed fathers had compromised the stability of families, thereby producing a riot-prone youth. Even if an unemployed father remained with his family, such a man was not a worthy example to his children. Unable to motivate his children to succeed in school and life, the unemployed parent passed his pathologies on to a younger generation.xxx This interpretation of the rebellion discursively marginalized Los Angeless urban poor. It safeguarded the socioeconomic status of American elites vis-à-vis poor blacks after the rebellion brought a social order into question. But the rebellions pattern of destruction indicates that the violence was political, intentional, and reflected the social and civic awareness of its participants. It was not the passive product of social pathologies among black youths. Individuals who participated in the rebellion responded to the same grievances that formal and informal organizations in Watts worked to ameliorate. Only they did so with a different method: violence. The rebellion was a political tool for breaking down the racialized social and economic forces that marginalized their community and reproduced poverty across generations.

title: Strain Differences in Follicle Development and Gene Expression in Mice
notes: The opening page names Teresa Woodruff as faculty advisor and Lei Lei and Candace Tingen as postdoctoral mentors (Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Feinberg School of Medicine). Printed page 12 carries only Figure 1 and its caption in the text; the figure's tables are not in the text. Section 12 begins with a garbled symbol block.
text:
Strain Differences in Follicle Development and Gene Expression in Mice Jessina Thomas DEPARTMENT OF BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES

Teresa Woodruff FACULTY ADVISOR DEPARTMENT OF OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY FEINBERG SCHOOL OF MEDICINE

Lei Lei POSTDOCTORAL MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY FEINBERG SCHOOL OF MEDICINE

Candace Tingen POSTDOCTORAL MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF OBSTETRICS AND GYNECOLOGY FEINBERG SCHOOL OF MEDICINE

The ovarian follicle, the functional unit of the ovary, consists of an oocyte surrounded by somatic granulosa cells. Women (and mice) are born with a non-renewable follicle reserve, so understanding how an individual follicle begins the process of development during one menstrual cycle is crucial to the progress of fertility research.[1] The mouse serves as an accurate model of human follicle growth and development. It was previously observed that the number of follicles during each developmental stage depended on the strain of the mouse tested.[2] Because the number of follicles differs among strains of mice, we hypothesized that the expression of various genes that control the follicle initiation stages must also differ between mice strains. The gene expression patterns in pre-pubertal CD-1 and C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice ovaries were analyzed to determine if they affected the very first follicle initiation stage. RNA was isolated from ovarian samples (day 12 and 16) gene expression levels of Gdf9, Bmp15, Fshr, Foxl2, Cyp11a, Cyp17, and Amh in the ovary were determined through real-time PCR. The expression levels of the Foxl2, Cyp11a and Cyp17 genes were found to vary between day 12 and 16 in both strains of mice.

Introduction Mice are commonly used as model systems for mammalian research, because they share a high degree of anatomy and physiology with humans, including their reproductive axis. Because women (and mice) are born with a non-renewable number of follicles, understanding how an individual follicle begins the process of development during any given ovulatory cycle is a key element to the progress of oncofertility.[1] CD-1  and  C57BL/6j  x  CBA/Ca  are  two  mouse strains used in our lab for follicle development studies. In our present study, we focused on the pre-pubertal stage of ovarian development in which the ovary has started the early stages of follicular growth (folliculogenesis) in preparation for the first ovulation. Here, we analyzed the difference  in  follicle  development  between  two  strains of mouse, inbred C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca and outbred CD-

1, and have identified key genes that may be important in  the  regulation  of  early  follicle  development  in  both strains and for the model, overall. Materials and Methods Animals Female F1 of hybrids (C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca) and CD- 1 mice were bred in our lab. Mice were maintained in accordance to all required policies. Breeding mice were housed in constant temperature, humidity and photoperiod (12L, 12D) with food and water available ad libitum. Breeders (90-180d, 6-8 weeks old) were fed with a soy-free mouse chow (Harlan 7926) to limit exogenous phytoestrogen intake through food. At the time of delivery (day of birth), eight pups were kept with each female to minimize the possible difference in pup development caused by nutrient availability.

ď€ ď€

Figure 1. The pre-pubertal follicle development in two strains of mice. (A) Histological morphology of day 12 CD-1 mouse ovary. (B) Histological morphology of day 12 C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mouse ovary. (C~F) The morphology of follicle class: (C) primordial follicle, (arrow); (D) primary follicle; (E) two-layer secondary follicle; (F) multi-layered secondary follicle. (Table 1) The number of the follicles at different development stage. (Table 2) The percentage of the different stage follicle in the ovary. (G) The oocyte diameter of the different stage follicle in day 16 mice* shows the difference (P< 0.05 )

RNA isolation and real-time PCR Total RNA was isolated from ovaries (n=4) using a Qiagen mini prep RNA isolation kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) according to a manufacturer protocol. On-column DNAse digestion was performed using an RNase-free DNAse set (Qiagen) to eliminate DNA contamination. 1 µg of RNA of each sample was reverse transcribed with MMV reverse transcriptase (Promega). Real-time PCR was performed to reveal the expression of growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), bone morphogenetic protein 15 (BMP15), follicle stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR), forkhead box L2 (FOXL2), CYP11A, CYP17, and anti-müllerian hormone (AMH). Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) served as an endogenous control.  PCR was performed using Taqman gene expression assay according to manufacturers instructions (Applied Biosystem). Tissue processing and follicle counting Animal ovaries were fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde and dehydrated before paraffin embedding.  Serial sections of 5 µm were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin. The numbers of primordial, primary, two-layer secondary and multi-layered secondary follicles were examined under light- microscope at 120X. The follicle counts and calculations were performed according to a method developed by the lab and used extensively to characterize folliculogenesis.[3] In vivo ovulation (IVO) IVO was induced on postnatal day 21 in CD-1 and C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice. The mice were injected i.p. with 5 IU PMSG and then induced to ovulate with 5 IU hCG after 48 h. Intact cumulus-oocyte complexes (COCs) were collected from the thin walled portion of the oviduct 14 hours after hCG treatment under the dissection microscope. The number of COCs was counted.

Oocyte diameter measurement The diameter of the oocytes of different stage follicles and the oocytes acquired from COCs were measured using SPOT Advanced software. The oocytes only with obvious nucleolus were chosen for diameter measurements.  The maximal distance across the oocyte was recorded as the diameter.

Statistical analysis Comparisons for follicle counts, litter size, number of COCs ovulated, oocyte diameter, hormone level, and gene expression were made between CD-1 and C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice using a t test with the software PRISM. A level of P<0.05 was considered significant. Results Strain differences in follicle development in pre-pubertal mice To examine follicle development in the pre-pubertal ovary, follicle counts were performed across the pre- pubertal period.  All of the follicles were counted and assigned a class (Table 1).  In both day 12 and day 16 ovaries, CD-1 mice had significantly more primordial follicles and total follicles than C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca ovaries.  In order to examine follicle development more closely, the percentage of follicles in a particular stage was calculated (Table 2). The percentage of the developing follicles (multi-layered secondary follicle) was higher in C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice than in CD-1 mice in both day 12 and day 16 ovaries. The oocyte diameters of different stage follicles were measured to examine oocyte development. In CD-1 mice, the oocytes of two-layer secondary and multi-layered secondary follicles had bigger oocytes than those of C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice. Strain differences in oocyte development in gonadotropin primed pre-pubertal mice Oocyte maturation was measured after ovarian hyperstimulation and induced ovulation of follicles in

Figure 2. The oocyte development in hormone primed pre-pubertal mice. (A) The number of COCs collected from two strains of mice. (B) The oocyte diameter of two strain mice.

Figure 3. The expression of early folliculogenesis related genes in day 12 mouse ovary (A) and day 16 mouse ovary (B). Due to insufficient replicates, statistical analysis could not be performed.

the two strains of mice with gonadotropins (Figure 2). Oocyte development was demonstrated by the number of COCs and the diameter of the oocytes of the COCs. Although more COCs were acquired from CD-1 mice than from C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice, no statistical difference was detected. Also, the oocytes from the two strains of mice did not show statistical differences in diameter.  The expression of early folliculogenesis related genes To further explore the mechanisms underlying the differences in follicle development between two strains of mice, genes known to be expressed in early follicles were measured (Figure 3). Foxl2 (forkhead box L2), Amh (anti-müllerian hormone), Gdf9 (growth differentiation factor 9), and Bmp15 (bone morphogenetic protein 15) are important for early stage follicle initiation and development.[4]  Fshr (follicle stimulating hormone receptor) is critical for the developing follicle in that it is the binding site of FSH.[5] Cyp11a encodes the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (P450scc) that catalyzes the first rate-limiting step for the biosynthesis of sex hormones, and Cyp17 plays a critical role in the production of androgens.[6] 14

In this study, we used these genes as markers for functional differentiation of follicular theca cells. In day 12 C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca ovaries, Foxl2, Cyp11a, and Cyp17 were highly expressed (Figure 7). However, in day 16 ovaries, Cyp11a was expressed more in C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca ovaries than in CD-1 mice ovaries.  In both strains, levels of Amh, Fshr, Gdf9, and Bmp15 were not significantly different in day 12 and day 16 ovaries. Discussion In the present study, the regulation of follicle development during the first stage of follicle initiation (folliculogenesis) was examined in two strains of mice. We determined that CD-1 mice have more primordial, secondary, and total follicles after the initiation of folliculogenesis than C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice have. In addition, CD-1 mice have oocytes that are significantly larger than those of C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice.  Even though CD-1 mice have quantitatively more follicles, oocyte development is identical in both strains. By examining the follicle numbers in each strain, we demonstrated the possible relation between follicle development and the fertility of the animal. This permits us to examine genes that are involved in follicle development and not in oocyte health. We hypothesized that since the follicle numbers differ between these two strains, the expression of various genes that control the follicle initiation stages would also differ. Our hypothesis was proven by the results of our experiments.  Higher levels of Foxl2 and Cyp11a were expressed in CD-1 mice than in C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice.  However, the levels of expression of Cyp17 were lower in CD-1 mice than in C57 x CBA mice. It is now crucial to understand how these genes regulate follicle activation.  Importantly, these studies provide the first window into early follicle activation and may be useful to women who need to preserve their reproductive potential at the time of cancer diagnosis.  The genes identified here may serve as important markers of healthy human follicle development in vitro.  From our results, future work involving the relationship between the number of COCs present in a mouse, the size of a mouses litter, and the number of follicles a mouse possesses may be explored.

I also thank Lei Lei and Candace Tingen for their instruction of lab techniques and continuous guidance. Finally, I would like to thank everyone in the Woodruff Lab for their encouragement and instruction during the duration of my research project. References [1] [2]

title: Quest for National Self-Identity: Neoprimitivist Theory and Practice in Russian Art and Literature
notes: Printed under the journal's FEATURE label. The title is from the contents page; the opening page's text lacks it. The opening page names Nina Gourianova, Kasey Evans and Michal Ginsburg alongside the labels FACULTY ADVISOR (Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures), FACULTY MENTOR (Department of English) and FACULTY MENTOR (Comparative Literary Studies Program); the extracted text does not pair names with labels unambiguously. The contributors page says she worked under the guidance of Professor Nina Gourianova and gives her majors as Comparative Literature and Political Science.
text:
Natalia Goncharova, Planting Potatoes, 1909

Irina Dykhne DEPARTMENT OF SLAVIC LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES COMPARATIVE LITERARY STUDIES PROGRAM

FACULTY ADVISOR DEPARTMENT OF SLAVIC LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Kasey Evans

Michal Ginsburg

FACULTY MENTOR DEPARTMENT OF ENGLISH NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Nina Gourianova

FACULTY MENTOR COMPARATIVE LITERARY STUDIES PROGRAM NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY

Introduction In this paper I intend to make a comparative analysis of Velimir Khlebnikovs poems Venus and the Shaman and Stone Woman, Natalia Goncharovas paint- ings Planting Potatoes and Stone Woman, and Mikhail Larionovs painting Jewish Venus. In the first decade of the 20th century, leaders of the emerging Russian avant-garde movement, Mikhail Larionov, Natalia Goncharova, and Velimir Khlebnikov made a conscious and deliberate decision to shake off the tethers of Western European influence2 and create art and poetry that is uniquely Russian. They de- fined this new Russianness as Neoprimitivism. In their quest for a national self-identity, they combined modern literary and visual techniques with primitive subject matter: peasants, soldiers, and mythical figures from Russian history and folklore. Through the platform of Neoprimi- tivsm, they proposed a model of a future that is informed and strengthened by the values and history of a uniquely Russian past. I argue that Larinovs, Goncharovas, and Khlebnikovs representation of the cultural hero as a female figure serves as a proposal for a future oriented toward strong national self-identity, independent of Eurocen- tric influence. This paper will also attempt to explain why the female figure seemed to serve the nationalist objectives of Neoprimitivism by embodying physical and spiritual strength. My argument will proceed in three parts. First, I will briefly outline the development and goals of Neoprimitivism. I will then focus on the representation of the female figure by offering close readings of specific works of art and poetry. In conclusion, I will discuss the stakes of my project.

ism, technological progress would blaze through the past on military tanks as machine conquers nature (Nicholls). Quite in opposition to Italian Futurist doctrine, the Russians drew their inspiration from the narratives of the past. Despite their later development, Russian Futurists asserted their independence from the Italian movement and even claimed that they practiced Futurism before the publication of Marinettis manifesto.4 The two schools of thought were, in fact, quite different and according to Camilla Gray, the name Futurism is almost all that unites the Russian and the Italian movements.5 Russian Futurism was spearheaded by visual artists Mikhail Larinov and his collaborator Natalia Goncharova. Velimir Khlebnikov, Alexei Kruchenykh, Vasily Kamensky, David 1 Burliuk, and Vladimir Mayakovsky led Futurist poetry (Markov, 1992). Like the Italians, Russian Futurists were also interested in nationalism, but did not share the Italians zealous passion for machinery. Instead, they expressed their nationalist objectives by focusing on everyday Russian subject matter, and had a particular interest in child- hood, prehistory, and Russian folklore. In response to the development of Russian Futurism, Marinetti reportedly said that: the Russians are false Futurists, who distort the true meaning of the great religion for the renewal of the world by means of Futurism, (Gray 94). According to Marinetti, the Russians lived in a plusquamperfectum rather than a futurum (Markov 158, 1992). Most Russian Futurists had an equally an- tagonizing attitude toward Marinetti. When Marinetti visited Russia in 1914, Larionov encouraged his fellow Futurists to hurl rotten eggs at the Italian (Markov 150, 1992). By adopting the name, but inverting the philosophy of Italian Futurism, the Russians under- scored their rejection of European influence. Neoprimitivism, the primitivist branch of Russian Futurism, was particularly invested in embracing and exalting Russian cultural history and values. Poet and artist, Aleksandr Shevchenko was the first to use the term in print in his book titled Neo-primitivzm published in 1913.6 Neo-primitivzm describes the value of seeking inspiration and beauty in simple and primitive traditions: Primitive art formsicons, lubki, trays, signboards, fabrics of the East, etc.these are speci- mens of genuine value and painterly beauty,7 declares

Art for life and even more - life for art!

Mikhail Larionov and Natalia Goncharova

Neoprimitivism and the Rejection of the West However paradoxical it may sound, in the history of Russian culture, Neoprimitivism was always linked to Russian Futurism. Russian Futurism, in turn, developed around the same time as Italian Futurism. As outlined by its founder, Filippo Tommasso Marinetti, in his 1909 Futurist Manifesto, Italian Futurism embraced technology, speed, machinery, violence, militarism, and was highly nationalist.3 Enamored by progress, the Italian Futurists rejected the past. For instance, Marinetti claimed that Progressis always right even when it is wrong, because it is movement, life, struggle, hope (Nicholls 99). According to the tenets of Italian Futur-

Shevchenko. Although, technically, the term was not used in print until several years later, the Neoprimitivist style in the visual arts was first introduced to the Russian public by Larionov and Goncharova in December 1909, at the third Golden Fleece exhibition. Some time after this exhibition, Goncharova and Larionov founded the radical Donkey Tails group, which served as a platform for their theories and ideologies (Markov 39, 1992). Primitivism in Futurist poetry developed on the heels of painting, first appearing at the end of 1912, with the publication of the controversial and influential A Slap in the Face of Public Taste, which I will discuss at greater length below (Markov 45, 1992). Even prior to the publication of this manifesto, the Futurist poets adopted the name Hylae: an ancient Greek term borrowed from the Histories of Herodotus, where it described the lands oc- cupied by the Taurii, a Scythian tribe. This name appealed to the poets interest in the primitive, helping to characterize them as poetic savages or the wild men of Russia (Parton 100). An interest in similar ideas facilitated frequent collaboration by Futurist painters and poets. For instance, Goncharova and Larinov illustrated numerous Futurist books including several of Khlebnikovs. Russian Futurists were well aware of Europes contemporaneous interest in the primitive, which functioned as an expression of disenchantment with modernity. But the Russians declared their primitivism as more authentic. The Futurists argued that before it was tamed by the Westernization of Peter the Great, Russian culture was intimately intertwined with Asian tradition (Parton 77). Unlike Picasso on his journeys to Africa or Gauguin during his exploits in Tahiti, because of their cultural ties and close geographic proximity to Asia, the Futurists didnt have to seek out the other, and could look inside themselves for the coveted primitive inspiration. Thus Russias internal otherness made their connection to primitivism more natural and original (Parton 77). In the catalogue preface of her second one-man exhibition in Moscow in 1913, Goncharova declared her rejection of the West because of Russias intimate ties with the East:

I have studied all that the West could give me, but in fact, my country has created everything that derives from the West.  Now  I  shake  the  dust  from  my  feet  and  leave  the West,  considering  its  vulgarizing  significance  trivial  and insignificantmy path is toward the source of all arts, the East.  The  art  of  my  country  is  incomparably  more  pro- found  and  important  than  anything  that  I  know  in  the West.

Goncharova even claimed that Cubism had revealed itself in Russia long before it was invented by the French. Russians had created stacking dolls and kamennaia babasstone sculptures found in the Southern Russian steppes generations before Gauguin or Picasso or any other European decided to incor- porate indigenous inspiration into their work, she argued. By claiming that Europeans were searching for what has existed in Russia for ages, Neoprimitivism offered the Futurists a way to assert independence from Europe and create a uniquely Russian niche in the world of art (Markov 35, 1992). Anthony Parton argues that this deliber- Natalia Goncharova, Stone Woman, 1908 ate separation from Europe made Neoprimitivism a self-consciously Russian school (77). Despite ternal body creating and nourishing her children, was perceived as the source of political authority, as well as fertility (Hubbs 21). When Christian missionaries converted the Slavic people, they could not subdue the pagan cult of the Mother Goddess. Instead, they used the figure of Mary, the Mother of God, as a replacement of Mokosh. While in the West the virginity of Mary was stressed, in the Russian Orthodox tradition it is her role as mother that is most important (Hubbs 100). The following proverb summarizes the attempts of the Christian missionaries to eradicate the worship of Mother Earth: Your first mother is Mary; your second mother is the earth; and your third mother is your own mother (Hubbs 21). Today, the country itself is still referred to as Mother Russia. It is important to recognize that the female is more than just a symbol of fertility. Because of her connection with land and nature, the woman is also associated with physical and spiritual strength. In Russian tradition, just like nature is beyond human control, there is something authentic, almost primal about female strength that resists control by man, civilization, domestication, or machinery. Even linguistically, the words for nature, earth, planet, culture, homeland, strength, freedom, independence, life, and Russia are all female gendered words. Russian Futurists wanted to build national identity by tapping into internal Russian traits and values rather than by relying on external sources such as machinery and technology. The female, and their representation of her as a cultural hero, allowed the Futurists to express these goals. Not only is the woman the mother from whom Russian culture and history emanate, but this image of the woman demonstrates strength and free spiritedness that could defy the pressures of Westernization and facilitate the construction of an independent national identity. The exploration of the various degrees and layers of strength embodied in the female figure unifies the widely ranging Futurist works that focus on the female form. Khlebnikovs 1912 poem, Venus and the Shaman is a playful work in which the female figures strong and willful sprit are represented through the wanton, unbridled sexuality of the goddess Venus.12 Khlebnikov depicts Venus as fully nude, flirtatious, and arrogant calling herself a river of delights. Her explo- sive sexuality overflows bursting forth like spring fever / all in flower with the sultriness of passion gleaming in her eyes. Permeating through her core, Venus sexuality is so innate and deeply embedded in the essence of her being, that it cannot be restrained even by Venus herself. She finds herself in a dilemma because of her inability to contain her sexuality and societys desire to do just that.

Venuss worshipers abandon her because they are unable to control her eroticism. Gradually turning from polytheism, her followers become more conserva- tive and try to civilize the goddess by forcing her to conceal her nudity. They made me cover my forget- me-nots!...Id rather die / than have to sunbathe on the sly, complains a distraught Venus. Now, no one builds statues in her honor, no one sings her praises, her name has been forgotten, and her breasts, which used to con- quer multitudes, are ignored. Desperate and dejected, Venus seeks shelter with the wise Shaman who has spent his life isolated from society and civilization. In her vulnerable state of abandonment, Venus seems to give into the pressures to overcome her nature and accept domestication. She claims that she wants to lead a simple life like the Shaman and get back in touch with the birds and bees / far from the hum of the pressing crowd. Exerting a genuine effort, she seems to grow more modest and self- conscious. She blushes and questions whether it is polite to show up naked in a strange mans house. When the Shaman throws her a fox-fur jacket she does not resist and is actually grateful for the cover. Venus even seems to become more attune to housework as she crossly chastises the Shaman, instructing him to keep his dugout clean and to stop smoking! She also cuts open the carcass of a deer and prepares one of her favorite dishes: Venison a la Venus. But the domestication and transformation of the goddess of love into an irritable housewife is meant hu- morously and satirically. Where did she learn to cook? Olympus? It is a commentary on the process of domestication and suggests that there is something unnatural about external influences forcibly imposing changes on ones character and impulses. Because it is unnatural, Venus transformation is unsustainable and she doesnt revel in the simple life of housewifery too long. A dying swan delivers a message that her people love and miss her and need her to return. Venus quickly decides to leave the Shaman and asks him to forget my breasts. / Put them out of your mind. / Forget my face, my sweet behind. Simple life is not for her. Instantly, Venus reverts back to what she was when she first came to the Shaman: untamed and uncovered sexuality. She strokes his beard and disappears like a sweet mistake. Venuss journey comes full circle and she embrac- es the sexuality that caused her such grief. Though the simplicity of her life with the Shaman may have been tempting, even enjoyable, it was inorganic to her nature. And just like Venus eventually shakes off her domestication because it is alien to who she is, the Futurists proposed that Russians shake off  the foreign influence of the West and embrace their intrinsic connection to the East and the primitive (Goncharova).

Khlebnikovs Stone Woman, written in 1919, is a more somber piece that like Venus and the Shaman functions as a commentary on the spiritual power of the female figure.13 Here, however, the females sexuality is secondary. Instead, it is her connection with nature and eternity that gives the female figure power and allows her to transcend human life and death. Khlebnikov demonstrates the closeness of the female figure to the natural world by selecting an enchanted place, presumably far from civilization, as the home of the Stone Woman. A Scythian stone idol, she has stood lifeless and breathless in the same spot for generations and is condemned to stand here forever more. Her power is eternal and universal, stretching from sky to sky.14 It is comparable only to the power of the nature that surrounds her: The mountains whirl in webs of snow, / unwindings of millennial sounds. The mountains too are bound to stand here eternally and have incomprehensible knowledge. Thus the Stone Woman is surrounded by a grandiose natural landscape and is one with it. An anguished young man disturbs the stillness and fairytale wonder by approaching the Stone Woman, desperate for the idols comforting presence. He weeps for all those who have died in wars and battles. Helpless in the face of death, he feels like a miniscule speck in the spectrum of time beating like a captured butterfly in the meshes of the Milky Way. In contrast to this one humans helpless position, the Stone Womans power is boundless because of her connection to the earth and so she transcends any single mortal life and death. As the man weeps, a motha symbol of naturesuddenly lands on the idol bringing her to life. Her transformation further emphasizes the connection between the Stone Woman, nature, life, and death. The transformative moment imbues the poem with the vitality of life as the Stone Womans eyes flicker and fill with intelligence while she breaks into a frenzied dance. Khlebnikov describes her birth with imagery of fire, but the life-giving moth is unlikely to survive the flickering cherry stain. Furthermore, the Stone Womans turbulent dance sharply contrasts with her disciples mournful cries for the blood filling the Tisza and Vistula rivers. Death and dance are juxtaposed because the female figures connection with nature, land, and earth allow her to transcend the limits imposed on humanity. Like Mother Nature or Mother Russia who is eternal, universal, and all seeing, the Stone Woman is a seer through the Milky Way. She will remain a source of power, comfort, and inspiration for eternity regardless of how many individuals live or die. This work can be read as a commentary on the connection of Russian people. Even as mortal lives end, their sprits are united by their shared history and idols, which allows the cycle of life and death to continue. The Stone Woman is a very different female figure than Venus. While Venus exudes life and sensuality, the Stone Woman is coarse and lifeless. But they share a common spirita sprit that transcends everyday life and cant be tamed or even understood. And it is this strength of spirit upon which the Futurists believed that national strength and identity should be fashioned. Like Khlebnikovs poem, Natalia Goncharovas 1908 painting Stone Woman also depicts the Scythian stone sculpture. But in Goncharovas Stone Woman she strives to bring the extraordinarythe idolinto everyday life by situating the Stone Woman in the role of a nude model. The Stone Woman, though she is inanimate, has a very dynamic role in this piece as she destabilizes several norms by actively redefining her representation. The Stone Woman is not the traditional Western representation of beauty as she is far from the voluptuous, milk-skinned nude. Instead, Goncharova assigns this role to an inanimate, crude, and distinctly primitive stone sculpture, thereby replacing the Western ideal of beauty with the other. Goncharova uses modernist techniques of flattening and figural distortion to emphasize how distant the Stone Woman is from the Western ideal of beauty. The Stone Woman has no neck and instead her smooth oval head is pasted onto her torso. Her facial features are somewhat blurred, with half-closed eyes that appear as thin slits. A long nose runs down the length of her face and meets thin, slightly pursed lips. Willowy arms extend from comparatively broad and muscular shoulders. The same stark contrast is repeated by the tiny feet, which extend from disproportion- ably full thighs. Unlike the typical female nude, this female figure is desexualized although she is naked. Not sprawled on a bed fully exposed, she is, instead, com- pressed in a fetal-like position with legs tucked up to her torso, arms held protectively over her flattened rather than voluptuous chest. In addition to defying what the nude model should look like, the Stone Woman reimagines the role of the model. Next to Stone Woman appear painters brushes, behind her is a canvas with flowers, and in her hands she holds a small tubepossibly a tube of paint. The canvas and painterly tools suggest that she is both model and artist. Thus the Stone Woman refuses to conform to what is proper and expected; instead she takes a very active role in redefining and reinventing. Not only does she defy the traditional representation of beauty, but she reinvents the role of the passive model by actively participating in the act of creating. The Stone Womans refusal to be confined to a certain kind of representation accurately aligns with the goals of the

Futurists, as this is the same active participation they proposed for the construction of a Russian national identity. Unlike Stone Woman, which straddles the lines between the extraordinary and the mundane, in Planting Potatoes, completed around 1909, Goncharova is fully situated in the world of familiar subject matter. The female figure is no longer the divine being of the Stone Woman or the goddess Venus, but is an ordinary peasant working in the fields. By capturing an indefinite moment in the everyday life of the Russian peasant, Goncharova romanticizes hard work and the ordinary, demonstrating her interest in heroizing and mytholo- gizing the mundane. While the works discussed above primarily explored the female figures spiritual strength, in this painting, the womens physical strength is most significant. Although Goncharova has not adopted total abstraction, in the modernist style, she has rejected traditional realism and distorts the human form to emphasize certain elements of the piece. Without the use of modeling and shading, Goncharova depicts the women as flattened and geometric with disproportionately large hands and feet. Their shovels, on the other hand, appear diminutive in contrast to their towering bodies. The scale and strength of the womens physicality demonstrates that they dont lead lives of leisure but have adapted to long hours of strenuous work. Suggesting that these peasant women are intimately tied to the land on which they work, their feet are like thick roots firmly planted into their domestic soil. In the distance appears the paintings only male figure. Smaller and further away, his inclusion again underscores the womens closeness to the land and implies that they are able to wok independently of men. With olive skin tone and dark eyes, the womens sharp, angular facial feature dont appear to be European or even Eastern European. Closer to the the true face of peasant RussiaAsiatic and Scythian, the women represent the Russian other that the Futurists idolized (State 12). Red headscarves, traditionally worn by female peasantry, explicitly stress their Russianness. Notably, Goncharova is not depicting a portrait of specific women at a particular moment in time. This can be inferred because the womens faces lack detail and individualization, their clothes cannot be dated, and their location cannot be ascertained. In creating an ambiguous time and space within the painting, Goncharova intends these laborers to represent all peasant woman hard at work in the fields at all moments of Russian history. Planting Potatoes is particularly compelling because the peasant women arent overly romanti- cized. They are not lovely, sensuous maidens leisurely sprawled on a luscious pasture as their cattle graze nearby. Neither clean nor pretty, their work demands that they toil with shovels, lug heavy bags of potatoes, and soil their coarse, bare feet. Goncharova is not just idolizing the primitive, she is idolizing and heroizing the hard work of the primitive. Greatly valuing labor, Goncharova reportedly said that Everything passesfriendship and love; the only thing that remains is work, (State 10). Strong, independent, and timeless, these female peasants personify a nation built on hard, Russian work. The binaries of the divine and mundane, established by Khelbnikov and Goncahrova, are reconciled in Larionovs Jewish Venus from 1912. By depicting a naked army prostitute confidently prostrated on a bed, Jewish Venus instills the divine qualities of the untamed sexuality and spirit of Venus into a mortal form. This piece also demonstrates Larionovs interest in blur- ring the distinctions of high and low art by portraying classes, races, and ethnicities typically dismissed by the Academy. Like Goncharova, Larionov plays with realistic representation by rendering the prostitute as flattened with large and exaggerated facial features. She is fully nude yet, like Khlebnikovs Venus, she is not ashamed of her nudity nor is she portrayed in a position of victim- ization. She is defiant, boldly staring at the viewer as she shamelessly displays photographs of soldiersher cli- entstriumphantly pasted on the wall behind her. Her collection of client photographs is empowering because it demonstrates that the prostitute is not ashamed of her position in life. On the contrary, she collects mementos to commemorate her conquests. The photographs can also be read as a commentary on the Nemprimitivists stance on technology and modernity. Although photog- raphy was not a particularly new invention at this time, it nonetheless represents technology and innovation. Its inclusion in this work reaffirms that the Futurists were not interested in rejecting modernization but wanted progress to proceed on Russian terms. According to Parton, the prostitutes defiant gaze and the stark pallor of her skin against a bright green wall are direct references to Edouard Manets Olympia (52). But Larionovs Venus is no frail, high-class cour- tesan. She has a peasants physicality with large, strong arms and feet. A peasant prostitute, she could easily spend her days as one of Goncharovas potato planters. Depicting the female with what Larionov perceived as distinctly Jewish features reveals his interest in exploring the ethnological canons of beauty (Parton 52). Larionov studied ethnography and was particularly interested in the themes of racial characteristics. He wanted to uncover the unique features that different ethnic groups use to measure the standards of beauty.

Armed with this alternative beauty vocabulary, Larionov strives to challenge Western ideals of perfection (Parton 97). The rejection of European high art is further asserted by the single red rose that appears on the wall next to the soldiers photographs. Parton suggests that the rose is a reference to the Greek myth of Venus and Adonis (Parton 109). By referencing the classical Venus, Larionov is emphasizing that he is reimagining the ideal. The divine goddess is brought to earth and becomes the earthly and tangible goddess of love (Parton 52). But not only is the divine or academic Venus made obsolete and the West dusted off, but the notions of love, passion, and sensuality are now embodied in a Russian peasant prostitute (Goncharova). Although the female figure appears in several manifestations in the works I have discussed, she main- tains certain core characteristics in every reincarnation. From the Stone Woman to the Jewish Venus, the female figure is strong, empowered, and authentic. She is represented as raw and unrefined, bears who she is proudly, and is in control of how she is perceived. The construction of national identity based on core, unrefined values is an empowering philosophy and opens up research opportunities in a variety of fields. Conclusion The role of the powerful female cultural hero makes Neoprimitivism a rich period of study for feminist and gender critics because it proposes a new model of feminist identity in which the woman is not just an image of fertility, but an image of strength and power. The Futurist philosophy is particularly interesting because they were not making a comparison of the male and female strength. Rather than propose that the female is as strong as a men, the Futurists asserted that the female is strong independently of men. Unfortunately, the empowered role of the woman can also have destabilizing consequences because of the potential tensions between strength/liberated sexuality and fertility/motherhood. In a world where the role of the woman is to be more than a mother, what happens to the sanctity of motherhood? Can the sexually liberated, empowered Jewish Venus also be a strong mother figure? Beyond the role of the female figure, this project has stakes for Art Historians. Russian Futurism was one of the first times that Russia became a leader and innovator in the visual arts (Gray 94). With the founda- tion established by the groundbreaking and progressive innovations of Larionov and Goncharoav, younger Russian artists had a basis upon which to structure their theories. Some of these theories, including Malevich Suprematism, attained more recognition in the West, but the Futurists were instrumental in introducing Russia to the global art conversation. Additionally, this was a unique period in Russian Art History because the visual arts preceded and led literature, as most innovations were first made visually and then replicated in poetry. Typically in the history of Russian culture, this relationship was reversed and literature paved the way for visual developments (Gray 108). Finally, the study of the Futurists quest for national identity can add value to cultural studies. The Futurists wanted Russia to reject dominant world- views and fashion a national identity based on her own culture and values. They were fully invested in figuring out how to be progressive and forward thinking while preserving Russian culture and history. Maintaining cultural independence is a vital and challenging question even todayperhaps more than ever todaybecause of the homogenization of values and ideas fueled by globalization and global communication. The Futurists offer one empowering method of deriving independence by introspectively identifying sources of national strength such as the female was for Russia. Footnotes 1 2
