How did you come to your research topic? I was having a conversation with my supervisor, Dr. Jocelyn Sage Mitchell, during my first days as a freshman. As we were talking, I mentioned my goal to write narratives about Palestinians living in the West Bank. Although it was a plan for the far future, professor Mitchell still suggested applying for the Summer URG grant and recommended several books, 169

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 169

Onyinyechi Jessica Ogwumike— Radical Redress: Black Birth Workers Respond to Maternal Mortality Onyinyechi Jessica Ogwumike (she/they) (Class of 2019) graduated from Northwestern’s Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences with departmental honors in African-American studies. Jessica completed pre-health coursework, and their primary passions include birth and racial justice. At Northwestern, Jessica worked as a Writing Place tutor, organized toward the improvement of the university’s mental health resources and the well-being of Black students, and co-founded an artist collective for creatives of color. They are a labor doula and look forward to serving the Lawndale community as a Northwestern University Public Interest Program (NUPIP) fellow, working as a care manager of Lawndale Christian Health Center. Jessica hopes to go on to develop a birth work practice, using empathy and curious communication to support people and communities as they grow lives that center healing justice and connection.

and witnessing the re-orientation of national conversations that Black birth workers perform via social media. Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? I would like to see future researchers attend to how the conversation surrounding Black maternal mortality post-media sensation has and has not influenced policy change, and the efficacy of such policy for Black birthing populations specifically.

What is your research, in a nutshell? My research responds to predominant depictions of Black maternal life and death by centering Black birthing people and birth workers’ counterrepresentation of Black birth. How did you come to your research topic? I came to a passion for alternative birth storytelling by attending events hosted by Chicago Volunteer Doulas 170

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 170

Samantha Oberman— Evaluating Interactive Social Justice Education: The Relationship between Responsive Fiction and Social Empathy What is your research, in a nutshell?

Samantha Franzblau Oberman (Class of 2019) studied human development and psychological services, gender and sexuality studies, and psychology. During her time at Northwestern, she was a member of WildCHAT, Northwestern’s only student-run mental health hotline, and served on the organization’s executive board for two years. She started and ran a listening workshop to teach Northwestern students how to better support their friends and promote positive mental health on campus, and served as a listener on the hotline. Samantha also worked as a research assistant for Terri Sabol in the Development Early Education Policy (DEEP) Lab, and for Danny M. Cohen in the Unsilence Lab. In the Unsilence Lab, she was a general member for a year, after which she began to serve as a mentor for undergraduate students. She helped to create social justice education programming, including “Tomorrow,” which can be found at www.unsilence.org/tomorrow. Now, Samantha is working at the Noble Academy in Lincoln Park, teaching high school diverse learning students. She is simultaneously getting her master’s in teaching, specializing in special education, from the Relay Graduate School of Education.

My project analyzed two different social justice interactive pedagogies in relation to participants’ social empathy. I studied Tomorrow, a social justice program that guides participants through an interactive story about the barriers to addressing mental health and suicide in high school. Through this story, participants learn about the personal, cultural, and institutional factors that prevent conversation about these topics, and how that silencing hurts students. Through a peer-reviewed Likert-scale measure I compared how going through these program, either facilitated or working through the online program in small groups without facilitation, affected participants’ social empathy. In addition, I interviewed participants to collect qualitative data on their experience of the program and what they learned. Overall, I found promising results on the relationship between social justice education (SJE) and social empathy. I focused my final claims on a call for education designers and teachers to include interactive storytelling in their classrooms; a call for researchers to do more research on the relationship between conceptual knowledge and social empathy to empower our students to be socially aware; lastly, a call for teachers and administrators to be prepared to have these crucial conversations. 171

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 171

How did you come to your research topic? I’ve always been passionate about education and what the main goal of education should be. During my time at Northwestern I spent a lot of time studying social justice and working for a SJE non-profit, which claimed that their programs increased empathy that ultimately led to social action. I was fascinated by the idea that empathy could lead toaction and found a lot of literature supporting that claim. However, I couldn’t find any robust literature on what types of programs or pedagogies increased empathy. There was significant research on what SJE was and what the learning goals of SJE were. However, there was not commensurate research on what programs were achieving these goals. So, I decided to find out myself! I studied what the relationship was between SJE and social empathy and how this differed when engaging in facilitated workshops versus non-facilitated online led workshops. Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? This research project was fundamental in its effort to understand the relationship between social empathy and social justice education. Most importantly, my study was exploratory and designed to look for relationships rather than make causal claims. Future research should take the relationships I found and run true randomized control trials to identify any causal relationships. In my conclusion I hypothesized the nature of these relationships based on participant responses, however the field requires more rigorous experiments. Additionally, this project also discussed education design and implementation. Not only researchers, but teachers, education designers, policy makers, and donors could use this research to inform what types of education should be prioritized. SJE has historically been ignored due to the lack of understanding of its impact. However, now more than ever it is essential that we teach our children to be empathetic and socially aware. My study highlights the importance of this work, and the potential impact it can have.

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 172

Hassan Sayed— Colonial Distortions: A Model of Extraction and Social Fabric Hassan Sayed (Class of 2019) graduated from Northwestern’s Mathematical Studies in the Social Sciences (MMSS) program. In his free time, he composes music. Sayed is currently pursuing a PhD in microeconomics at Princeton University. What is your research, in a nutshell? I design a game-theoretic model that links the extractive facets of colonialism with its disruption of local social orders. How did you come to your research topic? I’ve always read lots about the destructive social impacts of colonialism in my humanities classes and my own personal reading, partially with applications in South Asia. However, nothing in economics was out there that really described these social effects, and I thought that was a problem for economic researchers that wanted to study colonialism in any way. So, I set about trying to create some economic theory that tied together colonial resource extraction and disruption of social fabric. Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? No one in economic theory has done any work that combines colonialism with its social effects — so this 1) exhibits a model for building political economy models on underlying social trends and 2) opens up avenues for structural econometric work that relies on my theoretical model as a primitive. 173

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 173

Jessica Schwalb— “A Man With Many Faces, All Turned in the Same Direction”: Julius Lester on Anti-Semitism, Anti-Blackness, and Black-Jewish Coalitions Jessica Schwalb (Class of 2019) studied history and Spanish, with a focus on civil rights history and the relationship between Ashkenazi Jews and whiteness in the United States. She is interested in how collective memory and historical narrative shape social movements, and how leftist movements form coalitions to fight white supremacy and other forms of oppression. Since graduating, she has accepted a Fulbright research study award to continue her past research about the Palestinian population of Chile.

in American Jewish communities surrounding the end of the famed “Black-Jewish coalition”during the 1950s-1960s, and hoped to interrogate and problematize the popular understanding that Black activists’ antiSemitism was the major cause of that coalition’s rupture. I found Lester’s work and life an unexpected, complex, and illuminating look at the most contentious moments of disagreement about the nature of anti-Semitism and anti-Black racism between Black and Jewish civil rights groups, and believe him to be a surprisingly understudied figure of the Civil Rights movement.

What is your research, in a nutshell?

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading?

I explore the life and writings of Julius Lester, a Black civil rights activist who converted to Judaism, reveal the lack of visibility of Black Jews in the 20th Century and lack of white Jewish willingness to confront racism. My research centers around the underlying assumptions about oppression, power, and identity in major moments of controversy over so-called Jewish racism and Black anti-Semitism, moments that roiled civil rights groups during and after the 1960s and that continue to polarize political parties in the 21st century.

While historians have studied Black-Jewish relations in the 20th century, further inquiry into the racialization of Jews and the relationship between anti-Semitism and anti-Blackness are crucial to understanding the criticism of the Civil Rights movement. Where interracial coalition and solidarity are concerned, there is no shortage of contention — I therefore hope that other scholars will seek out figures whose voices are not often highlighted within dominant historical narratives of Black or Jewish civil rights struggles in order to more deeply contend with the legacy of deep disagreements over the nature of racism in this country.

How did you come to your research topic? I learned about Lester in an African American studies class in the context of a feud he had with James Baldwin. I had long been interested in historical narrative 174

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 174

Jun Kyung You— The Subsumptivist Generalist Position in Ethical AI Research and Its Motivation Jun Kyung You (Class of 2019) graduated from Northwestern with a bachelor’s in philosophy, with honors with distinction. At Northwestern, You was briefly a research assistant with the Jewish Studies Department. You served as an army sergeant in the Korean military partway through his studies, where he translated and edited official documentation and communications.

examined. Consulting philosophers, which to some extent is a process that is already ongoing in some institutions, would allow these commitments to be responsible commitments.

What is your research, in a nutshell? The unabridged version of the thesis is concerned with the motivations, current efforts, and the very possibility of replicating ethical decision-making in artificial agents. How did you come to your research topic? AI suggests a pipe-dream where, in a sufficiently advanced state, a tool could completely “replace” a human agent. I was intrigued by whether our capacity to make decisions in ethical situations could also be replaced true impact. Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? Ethical AI researchers, in the course of suggesting a way to replicate ethical decision-making, make philosophical commitments to their view on what morality consists of. I find that some of these commitments are not well175

97023 Body_176pg_6.7x9.8_R5.indd 175

Isabelle Zinghini— Missing the Point: China, Chineseness, and Rhinoceros Endangerment Where do you see the future direction of this work leading?

Isabelle Zinghini (Class of 2019) double majored in Asian languages and cultures, with a concentration in Chinese, and physics. She took several engineering courses in her last two years of college, and decided to pursue a career in engineering after graduation. She currently uses her physics and Chinese experience as a design engineer in Chicago, for a company with a strong presence in China and Taiwan.

I see several great opportunities for future researchers to build on this. The rhinoceros is not the only animal trafficked to Asia — animals like the pangolin, tiger, and elephant have been poached and illegally traded for their scales, bones, and tusks. These cases, like that of the rhinoceros, warrant the attention of cultural scholars to assess the similarities and differences in their representations of China and Asia. There is also work to be done on representations of the supply side of the rhinoceros horn trade, as little has been done to situate representations of poachers in existing scholarship on Africa.

What is your research, in a nutshell? The rhinoceros is being poached to extinction due to high demand for rhinoceros horn in parts of Asia. My thesis examines the representations of Asia’s (and particularly China’s) role in the endangerment of the rhinoceros, and how those representations fit into larger discourses on China and Asia. How did you come to your research topic? I spent a quarter abroad in South Africa studying public health, during which we visited Kruger Park for a safari. A researcher from Kruger told us that rhinoceros were being poached to near extinction their horns were worth exorbitant amounts in China and Vietnam, even though rhinoceros horns are only made of keratin (the material of our fingernails)! My initial intention was to simply figure out why something made of a material I found commonplace would be worth so much, but as I researched my topic evolved to focus on representations. 176

FROM THE ADVISERS

Dear Readers:

We would like to welcome you to Volume 18 of the Northwestern Undergradu­ ate Research Journal (NURJ). Volume 18, includes the best senior theses selected by seven academic departments and seven feature stories exploring the essence of research and its importance at Northwestern University (N.U.) and globally.

The 2022–2023 issue is the product of a year’s work by the students who lead and contribute to the NURJ, a student-produced annual print publication. In addition to this journal, our students publish new research packages on their website, www.thenurj.com, as well as podcast episodes with research leaders within and outside the Northwestern University community.

Copies of the NURJ are freely available to students at newsstands at major campus locations. Additionally, the NURJ is distributed to N.U. Deans, Depart­ ment Chairs, and Program Chairs as well as to academic, advising, and research offices across campus.

The journal you hold in your hand is a creation by hundreds of minds from N.U., and the pieces included are from some of the brightest voices of under­ graduate research in the nation, all of which would not be possible without continuous funding by the Office of the President and the Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education. LETTER

FROM THE EDITORS

Dear Readers:

We are excited to welcome you to the 18th annual edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ).

NURJ would not be possible without all the incredibly talented researchers and dedicated NURJ staff writers, editors and designers. For our 18th edition journal, our guiding principle was to be courageous and bold, pursuing questions and ideas that challenged our perception of the norm. With this theme, we have carefully selected seven honors senior theses — from Af­ rican American Studies and Asian American Studies, to Theatre and Comparative Literature — to showcase the intersection of nuance, diversity, and excellence within their respective fields. The volume also includes seven feature stories from our NURJ print team staff, who discuss research on a metaphysical level. They pose questions on legally reengineering the planet and investigate why medical schools stress undergraduate research experience.

In addition to this publication, we invite you to explore Northwestern University’s (N.U.’s) archives through the NURJ Archives Special Editions, the first of its kind published last year and housed on www.thenurj.com, and the second of which will come out this fall. We have released quarterly online packages that feature other undergraduate research in the N.U. community. You can also learn more about N.U. and Yale University’s histories of racial (in)justice through the Of Many Strands collaboration, as well as other various collaborations NURJ has conducted.

None of this would be possible without the generous sponsorship and continued guidance from all the support from the Office of the President and Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education. We would specifically like to thank President Michael Schill, for his belief in the NURJ and his ongoing support, as well as Associate Provost Miriam Sherin, for her continued support and guidance for the longstanding future of the NURJ; we are eternally grateful.

We would also like to thank all the incredible faculty, staff, and student researchers at N.U. for their support and trust in the NURJ. Last but not least, we must recognize our outstanding faculty adviseors, Dr. Peter Civetta and Professor Patti Wolter, who continue to go above and beyond in their leadership for our organization, and Tori Saxum, the administrative assistant at the Office of Undergraduate Research. — Jenna Greezaid & Kallista Zhuang

title: “When did the depictions become worse than the reality?”: Black Trauma Porn and The Black Horror Genre in Television and Film
notes: Senior thesis excerpt with abstract. Advisor from "Faculty Adviser" on the opening page. Footnote blocks and pull quotes are moved to paragraph breaks so column text runs on. Includes an appendix of referenced films and television series (printed page 19) and a bibliography whose entries are split across blocks. The contributors section (printed page 116) has a Q&A with the author.
text:
“When did the depictions become worse than the reality?”: Black Trauma Porn and The Black Horror Genre in Television and Film by Karina Karbo-Wright

Department of African American Studies

Faculty Adviser: Barnor Hesse

Abstract The American film industry is inextricably tied to the history of racism in the United States; thus, Black representation in film and T.V. has been a topic of rigorous academic and public debate. Most recently, that debate has circulated around the topic of “Black Trauma Porn” (BTP). Emerging on social media in 2016 during the Black Lives Matter movement, Black thinkers used the phrase “Black Trauma Porn” to articulate the nuanced complexities of the phenomenon, specifically sharing police brutality videos and the production of films and T.V. series with similar themes. Many piec­ es have received extreme backlash, and BTP became loaded with negative connotations, labeling the pieces as exploitative and harmful. However, as the phrase gained popularity, the analysis of these movies and T.V. shows became derivative and uncritical, instigating the need to investigate if the phrase properly articulates what authors were utilizing it for. To interrogate BTP, it is necessary to explain the impact of film on the spectator and engage the history of race in Hollywood in order to conclude that BTP is actually a modernist subgenre of Black horror. This conclusion is supported through an analysis of white versus Black horror as well as a deep-dive into what “trauma” and “porn” mean individually and within this context. Reframing and usurping the phrase BTP provides the beginning to a new framework for analyzing Black historical horror films and answering larger questions about Black representation in film and T.V.

Introduction Unlike everyone else I knew, I did not see Get Out (2017) until two years after its release. At the time, I could not exactly pinpoint why I had no desire to see it. When asked, I would just say that I was not interested, or that even though I loved Key & Peele (2012), I did not think this movie would be my speed. Shortly after, I read the phrase “Black Trauma Porn” on my social media, and I felt an over­ whelming sense of relief. It put a word to the feeling of fear that kept me from the theater and the uneasiness I experienced when I saw videos of police violence. In a way, it served as validation that remedied much of my guilt toward not watching movies that dealt with anti-Blackness. It was not because I did not like Black movies — Jumping the Broom (2011) and Barbershop (2002) were my favorite childhood films — but there was a sense of guardedness that I had learnt from previous experiences of watching unsettling media that kept me from watching certain films. When I saw the phrase BTP, I felt validated and com­ forted in the fact that I would not watch Get Out or any other movie of which I was wary. After this point, any movie or series I saw labeled as BTP became unwatchable to me.

The BTP issue has emerged in tan­ dem with the Black Lives Matter move­ ment, beginning in the early 2010s with the murder of Trayvon Martin in 2012 and the success and notoriety of 12 Years a Slave (2013) shortly afterwards. This is when the conversation began to emerge. However, the first articulation of the term was not until 2016 in a South African ar­ ticle by Nkumane,1 which describes the conflicting impact of consuming videos of white supremacist violence against Black people. The article recognized how these videos force necessary conversations but also incite terror among viewers. This article, along with equally popular articles entitled “Orange is the New Black is Trau­ ma Porn Written for White People” and “Yeah, I’m Finished With The Black Suf­ fering Trauma Porn Of Orange Is The New Black,” was widely circulated across Twit­ ter in the summer of 2016.2 This spurred a mass increase in the use of the term to describe the phenomenon at hand: videos, films, and T.V. shows that depict extreme violence by white civilians or state officials against Black people are disseminated for mass public consumption and/or mass entertainment, which impacts white and Black spectators differently, despite being distributed with the assumption that some amount of pleasure is extrapolated from it by the general viewing public.

1 Nkumane, Z. (2016). No longer will I partake in Black trauma porn. OkayAfrica. 2 Wear Your Voice Magazine 2016; [Very Smart Bros]. (2016). Yeah, I’m Finished With The Black Suffering Trauma Porn Of Orange Is The New Black -- by @inomallday

What followed was a seemingly correlated increase in the visibility of an­ ti-Black police brutality and the creation and popularity of films and T.V. shows that depicted white supremacy and the Black experience, the most notable of these being Get Out. The discourse surrounding this phenomenon focuses on three main concerns with the purpose and effects of depicting violence against Black people in movies and T.V.: the immense violence inflicted on the Black characters within these films and T.V. shows is unnecessar­ ily incessant and an exploitative derivative of real-life Black trauma, the traumatic impact of violent anti-Black depictions on Black spectators, and the pornifica­ tion of these violent depictions by white spectators who are believed to gain some form of pleasure or gratification from the visualizations.3 In other words, these ten­ sions exist around negotiations of violence against Black people and the subsequent Black/non-Black spectatorship of those depictions. This centering of Black specta­ tors is commendable and unprecedented in mainstream film analysis, but it seems that the nuances that contextualize Black story­ telling are not a part of these critiques.

It is always necessary to interrogate the terms which we use to critique our own culture’s creations. In the case here, BTP could be used to further censor and marginalize the already racially gatekept world of film. Black storytelling has im­ mense power and ability to be able to communicate and negotiate matters of cul­ ture and identity. I hope that by exploring this phenomenon, this paper will mediate questions of Black representation and bring awareness to the necessity of intentionality and analysis when forming opinions on Black T.V. and film.

The History of Film and the Horror Genre There have been many historical instances of immense violence which impact entire societies of people, like the Transatlantic Slave Trade, World Wars I and II, The

Holocaust, and the occupation of Pal­ estine; through the collective trauma of these events, the perpetrators and victims are relationally linked together in what Elm et al. calls a “traumatized society.”4 One of the ways by which a traumatized society may cope or heal from the trauma is through cinema, which can give “expres­ sion to trauma and violence for a wounded [community]” through the visualization and actualization it provides.5 As a medium of mediated realistic reenactment,6 film can act as a preserver of traumatic history and can provide catharsis and healing for those within the traumatized society who create and view the film. Film can also aid in individual and collective7 memory re­ tention as well as in cultural preservation, revealing levels of history and memory which, for societies that have experienced trauma through destruction, can be vital in protecting cultural history. However, it can also be used as a tool of suppression or cover to erase and rewrite history for po­ liticized propaganda-like efforts,8 and this is most often seen through an analysis of Hollywood and its relationship with race.

3 Braxton, G. (2021, April 19). Media images of Black Death have a cost, experts say. many viewers are fed up. Los Angeles Times.; Cha­ risma, T. (2021, June 18). Trauma porn and the commercialisation of Black Pain. tmrw.; Giorgis, H. (2021, April 18). Who wants to watch Black pain? The Atlantic.; Muhammad, M. (2019, June 2). Getting off: What black trauma porn is and why we hate it. Medium. 4 Elm, Kabalek, K., & Köhne, J. B. (2014). The horrors of trauma in cinema : violence void visualization. Cambridge Scholars Publishing. 5 Ibid., 4 6 Ibid., 4 7 Ibid., 4 8 Ibid., 4 9 Crouthamel, J. (2016). The Horrors of Trauma in Cinema: Violence Void Visualization. Film & History, 46(2), 86–89. 10 Ibid., 4; Bernardi. (2007). The Persistence of Whiteness : Race and Contemporary Hollywood Cinema. Taylor & Francis.

Elm et al. proposes that the horror genre is one of the best genres for success­ fully encapsulating a historical trauma nar­ rative on film.9 Horror is able to portray the tenacity of the violence experienced in historical trauma while also providing the cinematic tools to unpack that violence within the horror narrative.10 Through the analysis of historical trauma film, I believe that several Contemporary Black stories in film are current iterations of Black horror. In that account of historical trauma films, Elm et al. explains the benefit of using horror to communicate impactful stories of historical trauma.11 As a tool of com­ municating Black history in the present U.S. that is largely sculpted by collective and historical traumas as well as a tool for critiquing and commenting on white hege­ mony through horror genre tropes, these contemporary Black stories in film utilize the genre of horror. In order to character­ ize this thesis, an exploration of the Black and white horror genres will provide the necessary groundwork for my argument.

Horror is a genre of “literature, film, and T.V. that is meant to scare, startle, shock, and even repulse audiences” where the “story and characters are just as import­ ant as mood and atmosphere.”12 Because of the horror story’s ability to “[shock] and [provoke] with its exploration of the un­ known,”13 it is a great tool for cross-genre productions and social impact, including matters of race.14

11 Ibid., 4 12 MasterClass, & Stine, R. L. (2021, September 7). What is horror fiction? learn about the horror genre, plus 7 classic horror novels you should read - 2022. MasterClass. 13 Ibid., 12 14 Curtis. (2008). Dark places : the haunted house in film. Reaktion. 15 Clasen, M. (2021). On the psychology of Horror movies. Psychology Today.; The Psychology of Fear: Concordia University, St. Paul online. CSP Online. (2021, October 21). 16 Jóhann, B. (2020, September 14). A brief history of Hollywood’s racism, sexism, and homophobia. Medium. 17 Ibid., 15; Hess, J. P. (2013, October 23). The psychology of scary movies. Filmmaker IQ. 18 Gormley. (2005). The new-brutality film race and affect in contemporary Hollywood cinema. Intellect; Du Gay et al. 1997 from Erigha. (2015). Race, Gender, Hollywood: Representation in Cultural Production and Digital Media’s Potential for Change. Sociology Com­ pass, 9(1), 78–89.; Erigha. (2019). The Hollywood Jim Crow : the racial politics of the movie industry. New York University Press. 19 Ibid., 18 20 Ibid., 15; Ibid., 17 21 Ibid., 15; Ibid., 17

”

Film can act as a preserver of traumatic history and can provide catharsis and healing for those within the traumatized society who create and view the film.

What can be considered horror is extremely vast because what scares one spectator may not scare another.15 How­ ever, the staple elements of a horror film are the central elements of violence and/ or fear.16 Psychologist Dr. Glenn D. Wal­ ters theorizes three main aspects of horror films that establish the genre and produce audience attraction.17 The first aspect is tension. Created by the techniques of film highlighted in horror — dialogue, sudden perspective changes,18 unsettling shots that are either too quick or very slow,19 sound and music, and lighting — tension comes through suspense, mystery, intrigue, ter­ ror, gore, and shock.20 Often, this is under­ stood to be “universal relevance,” referring to the fears “everyone” has — specifically “the psychology of fear of death and the unknown, or cultural relevance of social issues” — but it may refer to personal rel­ evance as well.21 The final result is that cinema provides us with what Walters calls “unrealism.” This means that despite the validity of the content of the piece, the spectator is still consuming the narrative and is not within it. To enjoy viewing horror films, the spectators must also feel physically and mentally safe in order to de­ tach themselves from the film.22

While horror films, like all films, are deeply influenced by the spectator’s reac­ tion, there are also important impacts felt from the content of these films. As a central part of social life, films have a specific and influential role in shaping what emotions look and sound like;23 horror films have the unique role of defining what is fear and what is fearful. In a study on the so­ cial experience of horror films, Renda ex­ plains, “Scariness is not (only) an attribute of the film content but is said to stem from cognitive factors such as the individual’s empathy with film characters or person­ ally held moral beliefs and expectations.”24 This socially constructed factor of fear is central to horror movies, but the complex genre’s norms also include the engagement with taboos and rupture of boundaries, the unfamiliar penetrating the familiar, the resistance of typical bounds and flow of narrative creations, and the challenging of the rational.25 It is this intentional disrup­ tion aspect of these norms and the horror films’ oscillations between the spectrum of good and evil that crafts what is and is not scary. However, as a genre created and continued by Hollywood, I would like to reframe horror films as the determination and identification of narratives centering on what horrifies white people.

I make this assertion because what is understood as conventional horror was created through white storytelling from popular horror writers like Edgar Allan Poe and pivotal texts like Mary Shelly’s Frankenstein (1818) or Bram Stoker’s Drac­ ula (1897).26 These stories are not only populated largely by white creators but also within the narrative; the stories privilege white experiences, fears, and losses and further bolster them as universal.27 Because Hollywood is a segregated tool of white storytelling, the horror stories present in film and T.V. most often follow those of white individuals; thus, conventional and mainstream horror is about what horrifies white people.

22 Ibid., 15 23 Renda. (2019). Watching “Insidious”--On the Social Construction of Fear. Qualitative Report, 24(7), 1784–. 24 Ibid., 23 25 Ibid., 16; Ibid., 23 26 Ibid., 12 27 Bogle. (2001). Toms, Coons, Mulattoes, Mammies, and Bucks: An Interpretive History of Blacks in American Films, Fourth Edition. Burns & Oates Imprint.; Hill Collins. (2014). Black feminist thought: knowledge, consciousness, and the politics of empowerment (Revised tenth anniversary edition.). Routledge.; Ibid., 16; Nittle, N. K. (2021, March 6). The 5 most common black stereotypes in TV and film. ThoughtCo. The Take (2020) “A History of Black Stereotypes Onscreen” Youtube.

If Black stories in horror films are narratives “about Black experiences and

Black cultural traditions” ... then the

Black horror genre will refer to what horrifies Black people. “

”

For example, in Scream (1996), the fear is centered around the killers’ ability to forcibly enter the house, a space that is supposed to be safe, and their complete control over whether the victim lives or dies, stripping the victim of their agency over their life. Forcibly entering the home can be equated to white community’s fear and consequent disgruntlement with in­ tegration, but the fear stemming from the loss of agency is most terrifying. This claim is supported by the role of white women in the film, who historically have been used to identify what is most fearful. This theme can be tracked through almost all (white) horror films popular in Hollywood, in­ cluding the three listed above — that a loss of white agency, whether through murder, paranormal possessions, or psychological torture, is the real fear. This film is white horror because the story told features spe­ cific circumstances in which only white people lose their sense of agency. If cinema is playing on the fears of white people for conventional white horror, then the ques­ tion remains: what is Black horror?

Because of horror’s ability to “[shock] and [provoke] with its exploration of the unknown,”28 it becomes a ripe place for so­ cial commentary and critique, especially on matters of race.29 This unique engagement of commercial value, peculiar narrative, and fluctuating aesthetic has made horror extremely useful for debating “dilemmas of difference.”30 If Black stories in horror films are narratives “about Black experiences and Black cultural traditions — a Black cultural milieu and history swirling around and impacting Blacks’ lives in America” communicated through the horror genre,31 which conceptualizes the surrounding so­ cial and political worlds through the Black gaze, either actively or passively critiquing white hegemony and centering Black sto­ ries, then the Black horror genre will refer to what horrifies Black people.

28 Ibid., 12 29 Curtis. (2008). Dark places : the haunted house in film. Reaktion. 30 Ibid., 27 31 Ibid., 27 32 Ibid., 27 33 Bellot, G., Cox, R., & Mckinney, D. (2021, November 10). How black horror became America’s most powerful cinematic genre. The New York Times. 34 Breznican, A. (2020, August 3). Black storytellers are using horror to battle hate. Vanity Fair. 14 chilling African American horror novels. UNC Chapel Hill Libraries. (2021, October 28).

In the Black horror genre, Black art­ ists are looking to spark “sociopolitical dis­ courses … through representations about … Blackness” that “‘speaks’ difference” to and interrogates whiteness by reversing white horror’s placement of Blackness as the “Other.”32 Horror has long been in the history of Black storytelling and oral tradi­ tions. Black folklore about ghosts and oth­ er mythologies that stretched the African continent followed enslaved Black people to the Americas; the oral tradition helped craft the origins of the Black culture we know today.33 Memory served as a form of resistance, and these tales began to trans­ form into stories about revolution and freedom. Black cultural productions were working through various newspapers, films, novels, and storytelling that fea­ tured horror or horror aesthetics.34 What Black horror cultural productions have in common is the engagement with the Black experience throughout Black history.

As it exists in tension with the strug­ gle to tell stories about Blackness, Black storytelling must make the link between depicting Black culture within horror and answer the question, “What horrifies

Black people?” The answer is the horrors of Black history. For Black people around the world, because of the immense history of unthinkable violence and the structural positions that continue that violence, there may be nothing more horrifying for Black people than the past.35 From the brutali­ ties of dehumanization to social death and physical mutilation,36 slavery began this cycle of the horrors of Black history. The Black horror genre through time proves that what horrifies Black people are the horrors of Black history. The Black horror genre in film and T.V. as it stands today begins to emerge in conversation through films like Get Out (2017) and Us (2019). The current subgenre is what is being contested in the larger argument of this thesis.

The Black horror genre, then, is able to provide a critique of white hegemony through film and subverts (white) horror norms by setting whiteness in Black his­ tory as the antagonist, as proposed by the theory of historical trauma films.37 The Black horror genre conveys that Black his­ tory is filled with horror, and these films are depicting Black history through Black horror. These issues of the relationship between the horrors of Black history and Black horror genre necessitate the interro­ gation of what is being critiqued with the BTP phenomenon, and what specifically BTP is supposed to explain.

Black Trauma Porn: Current Debates and Positionings The question of Black horror has recently been taken up by critics who complain of BTP. The issue of BTP is the videos, films, and T.V. shows that depict extreme violence by white civilians or state officials against Black people that are then dissemi­ nated for mass public consumption and/or mass entertainment, which impacts both white and Black spectators differently, despite being distributed with the assump­ tion that pleasure is extrapolated from it by the general viewing public.38 It has generated questions about who Black me­ dia is made for.39 Despite existing in films and T.V. shows throughout the twentieth century, the argument around the usage of Black experiences and anti-Black violence was reignited by Jordan Peele’s social thriller, Get Out. The pieces depicting anti-Black violence fit into four thematic categories which reflect the various pe­ riods of time that indicate major events in Black history: slavery, segregation/ Jim Crow, mass incarceration, and police brutality.40 Developed out of those who were opposed to it, BTP was to refer to a negative phenomenon.41 However, even in its first iterations, it was unclear exactly what BTP carried in its meaning. In order to understand if BTP is really describing what it is meant to allude to, I will present the critiques of the films and T.V. shows to which it refers and unpack the words comprising the phrase to decipher if BTP is the best term to describe the phenome­ non at hand.

35 Ibid., 3 36 Patterson, 1982. 37 Ibid., 4 38 Jackson, K. (2019, June 11). ‘when they see us’ and the delicate balance of depicting black trauma. Women’s Media Center. 39 Ibid., 3 40 Ibid., 3 41 Ibid., 1

There are three main critiques of what is being called BTP: the incessant violence against Black characters in these depictions and the visual exploitation of Black trauma, the possible harm these de­ pictions have on Black spectators, and the consumption of these violent depictions by white spectators.42

The first critique about the BTP phe­ nomenon is the belief that the violence depicted in these films and series is unnec­ essary and excessive.43 In a comparison of Little Marvin’s Them and Jordan Peele’s Get Out, author Maryann Erigha says that Get Out gets the depictions of white supremacy right without the violence:

There’s a subtlety with that film, which is why it was so successful … People understood the message without the film having to show physical trauma. But in Them, the message is being lost when you take it to that level of violence. I don’t think you need to see brutalization happening in order to understand the brutality of racism or anti-Blackness.44

Erigha’s sentiment is shared throughout other films and T.V. shows at the center of the critique of BTP.45 Film and T.V. are most often seen as entertainment, so critics believe that this violence holds a different weight when presented as “es­ capist fare” because for Black people, “it’s not entertainment.”46 This critique is what foregrounds the others.

The second critique is that these depictions harm Black spectators.47 The concern is that since the stories reflect real events in Black life, their presentation as entertainment is triggering and traumatic for the Black viewer.48 Author Hannah Giorgis says that Black films invite more speculation around intent than white films, and this will cause Black spectators to consider the impact of the medium in a specific, shared way, especially when it comes to anti-Black violence in horror.49 Thus, “in the case of Them, the sheer inten­ sity and meaninglessness of the cruelty on display lends credence to arguments that Little Marvin didn’t anticipate how the show might affect Black audiences, many of whom view it as a bloodied funhouse mirror of an already-horrifying reality,”50 even though according to Marvin himself, he only thought of Black spectators during the creative process.51 The critique is deep­ er than just creator intent; the concern is that Black people are being reduced sole­ ly to their trauma and pain.52 This then prompts the question of spectatorship and who these films are for: “‘But as a Black horror artist, I have to ask myself, Who would that be for?’”53 This is where the fi­ nal critique rests.

42 Ibid., 3 43 Ibid., 3; Ibid., 38 44 Ibid., 3 45 Films mentioned in writings on Black trauma porn: Two Distant Strangers, Fruitvale Station, Selma, and The Hate U Give, Lovecraft Country, Watchmen, Antebellum, When They See Us 46 Ibid., 3 47 Ibid., 3 48 Ibid., 3 49 Ibid., 3 50 Ibid., 3; dir. Marvin. (2021). “Them.” 51 Braxton, G. (2021, April 10). The violence in Amazon’s ‘them’ left execs ‘shaken.’ does it go too far? Los Angeles Times. 52 Ibid., 3 53 Ibid., 3 54 Ibid., 3

The final critique is that white specta­ tors are granted too much access to depic­ tions of the Black experience and extract some form of pleasure from the violent de­ pictions.54 If the goal is to generate atten­ tion or gain recognition through increased viewership, then instances of Black trauma are being exploited to satisfy that desire.55 Another concern is that Black experiences are exploited for the purpose of educating non-Black people on anti-Blackness and appeasing white guilt at the expense of Black consumers, who will be harmed by seeing their trauma visualized.56 More ne­ fariously, some fear that white audiences, continuing the traditions of lynchings, are either sadistically “getting off” on the de­ pictions of anti-Black violence by living vi­ cariously through the white aggressors on screen, voyeuristically “exploring” Black­ ness, attempting to ease their white guilt, or gratifying their obsession with moni­ toring Blackness.57 While it is relevant and radical to center the experience of the Black spectator and critique that of the white spectators in an otherwise white-centered world, what the BTP perspective fails to examine is the relationship between Black history and its horrors and the importance of witnessing and engaging with that.

I am calling into question the very term and definitions of BTP itself, posing these pieces of media as necessities rather than trauma exploitation. I am concerned with the extent to which the horrors of Black history are being addressed by the critics of BTP and whether some of these critics see these films as developing the Black horror genre. To discuss these ques­ tions, it is necessary to unpack the words which comprise the phrase BTP.

Through an analysis of traumatic film, vicarious trauma, and spectacle hor­ ror, the idea of BTP can be problematized. The term itself does not encapsulate the intended meaning because the utilization of the term does not take into account the analysis of and historical engagement with

Black trauma and traumatic film, and it does not critically engage with the entirety of the Black experience in which vicarious trauma happens, particularly because Black history and Black trauma are inextricably linked. We cannot witness our history without also vicariously experiencing in­ sidious and collective trauma. This means that, in tandem with the understandings of trauma and memory, that Black trauma is Black history. However, Black history is not Black trauma. What is then relevant to the BTP critique is that Black trauma is Black history, and Black history is Black horror – thus Black trauma is Black horror, or what horrifies Black people.

55 Safford, D. (2019). “How to Use Three-Act Structure to Write a Story Readers Can’t Put Down,” The Writing Practice. 56 Ibid., 3 57 Ibid., 3

I propose that it is not BTP and the exploitation of Black trauma taking place, but a new articulation of the Black horror genre – that these films are depicting, in their entirety, what horrifies Black people in Black history. For this analysis, I’d like to rename this new subgenre of the Black horror genre, Black historical horror, to replace BTP as a title. This new interpre­ tation of the Black horror genre capitalizes on the new space for Black art in society and uses the popularity and cultural force of the cinema industry to depict and dis­ seminate the suppressed realities of Black history as a necessary liberatory technique with the contemporary power to unsettle whiteness and white supremacy.

Conclusion There is a significance in being able to provide nuance to Black narratives that are being analyzed without doing so in the public sphere. Throughout this thesis, I have aimed to argue that the BTP argu­ ment is an unnuanced approach to what I have called Black historical horror. I have discussed the basis for where this argu­ ment emerges from, where I believe it sits, and the analysis to support it.

“Black storytelling is an extremely expansive discipline, and to analyze it without nuance is to further subjugate Black narratives.”

The impact of film and T.V. is im­ mense, as is the reality that Black creations no longer exist within a vacuum. From this, it is clear that Black thinkers are trying to conceptualize the benefits and setbacks of this impact on racial conceptualizations of whiteness and Blackness. Because of the current historical positioning in culture allowing more space for Black films and T.V. shows, there is contention over what types of Black stories should be shared. Out of these tensions, I wanted to see what exactly BTP is trying to describe and un­ derstand how that might affect the Black stories being told. In order to do so, this paper explained Hollywood’s history of violence against Black characters through white storytelling in film and T.V. Then, I discussed how this necessitated the de­ velopment of the Black gaze and a distinct Black storytelling in film and T.V. This history provided the necessary background for understanding the role race has played in American cinematic history and fore­ grounded and characterized this phenome­ non. This thesis explained the combination of what is called “historical trauma film”58 and Black film to yield the basis for un­ derstanding BTP to be a new articulation of the Black horror genre: Black historical horror. By dissecting what the white and Black horror genres entail and applying that analysis to the historical trauma film, I positioned the BTP phenomenon as ex­ isting between the storytelling of Black horror genre and the horrors of Black his­ tory. Following this, the paper discussed contentions surrounding the BTP issue and interrogated how these contentions related to the interrogation of the terms “trauma” and “porn.” These examinations proposed the guidelines for rearticulation.

58 Elm, Kabalek, K., & Köhne, J. B. (2014). The horrors of trauma in cinema: violence void visualization. Cambridge Scholars Publishing.

I found it almost ironic that when I set out to do this analysis, I personally agreed with the arguments I worked against. Black storytelling is an extremely expansive dis­ cipline, and to analyze it without nuance is to further subjugate Black narratives. The main conclusion from this thesis is that film is an incredibly powerful tool that has rev­ olutionary power when used to commu­ nicate stories of Blackness. Experiences of the representation of Blackness in film and T.V. and the vicarious trauma that may be experienced when viewing those represen­ tations may vary widely from spectator to spectator. However, whether or not Black critics enjoy or loathe the creation, it is still necessary to analyze the purpose and im­ pact of the film or series’ message and pon­ der the question: if we don’t tell our stories, who will? The BTP debate is negating the tensions between violence against Black people on the screen, white and Black consumption of that violence, and what contemporary Black representation should or should not look like. By labeling pieces of Black film and T.V. as BTP, critics are inflicting unforeseen consequences against Black cinema, which may severely limit progress and continue to erase narratives of the horrors of Black history and Black trauma. By usurping the phrase BTP and developing a new framework for analyzing Black historical horror and questions about Black representation in cinema, this thesis provides the foundational grounds for unearthing new answers for questions of Black representation in contemporary film and T.V.◆

title: Serendipity and Struggle: Reflections on the Social Dynamics of Research
notes: Q&A interview with Bryan Hunter, a chemistry professor who moved from Harvard University to Northwestern (Hunter Lab), about his research on sustainability and catalysis and his path into academia.
text:
Serendipity and Struggle:

Reflections on the Social Dynamics of Research

By Andrew Lu

On the surface, life in a university seems like a straightforward process. Teach. Research. Publish. However, the reality is that the world of aca­ demia is a beautiful mess of hard work, passion, and luck. Professor Bry­ an Hunter recently moved from Harvard University to teach chemistry and continue his research in the Hunter Lab at Northwestern University (N.U.). In this interview, he speaks about his research on sustainability and reflects on his personal journey thus far.

[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

What sort of research does your lab do?

My lab is interested in sustainability and renewable energy. What I do on a day-today basis is to look at important reactions in the world, which are typically [done] through catalysis. You have some material or substance which permits a reaction to happen at a lower barrier, so it’s kineti­ cally more favorable. A lot of these reac­ tions take place at high temperatures and high pressures, such as the Haber–Bosch process. These are inherently inefficient reactions because entropy losses occur in the process of moving to high tempera­ tures and pressures. So, we’re interested in converting these reactions into electro­ chemical reactions that are done at room temperature, with ambient pressure, and often in solution. To do this, you need to develop a new class of catalysts — catalysts that are electro-catalysts. We develop and produce materials and molecules that serve as electro-catalysts for a variety of reactions. Additionally, we’re interested in water splitting, carbon dioxide reduc­ tion, ammonia production, [and] things like that.

Do you see many practical applications for your re­ search?

Yes, we’ve made some major contribu­ tions to water-splitting catalysis. These have been incorporated and integrated into water electrolyzers, which are com­ mercially available — that technology is used. It’s not yet used on a large scale because we don’t have, currently, the de­ mand for a huge amount of clean hydro­ gen. However, I think that there will be demand for it in the future, and making improvements to those technologies now is pertinent and timely.

We’ve patented several things, such as this catalysis for C-H bond activation that has applications in pharmaceuticals and some technology that uses electro­ chemistry in medical settings. We’ve been able to repurpose some of the catalysts that we’ve used for water splitting to generate local pH changes in tissue. Then, we patented this methodology of being able to reshape stiff tissue just by passing an electrical current through it with an appropriate catalyst.

You patent things because you think it’ll be useful in industry. You never know what exactly the impact of your research is going to be. Particularly for fundamen­ tal research in chemistry, [the] majority of people are doing basic research, which is stuff that is one more step removed from real world applications. But you never know.

What was your decision be­ hind pursuing graduate edu­ cation?

I knew I loved research, and I had always had a dream of getting my Ph.D., but it seemed really far off — it seemed like an impossible thing to do. I remember in col­ lege, as an undergraduate, putting myself in that mindset … because of that, I didn’t go directly to graduate school after under­ graduate degree.

I would say up until maybe the sec­ ond semester of my senior year, I wasn’t sure what I was going to do. I then met a recruiter for Teach For America, and he had done the two-year commitment [in] teaching – this guy was just amazing. He really inspired me about the mission of Teach For America and the effect I could have just out of college. So I applied, and I got accepted. I taught chemistry in south­ east Los Angeles for two years. While I was doing that, I obtained a master’s degree in teaching. And then, somewhere in that process, I really thought about what it is that I still wanted to do. I kept getting drawn back to graduate school. So, I used an additional gap year to apply to graduate school, make some connections, do some research, and by the next fall, I was enrolled in the California Institute of Technology working for someone I had always really admired. Taking those years off really did some good for me. I learned a lot about myself.

I think people feel like they have to be 100% a medical school student or 100% a chemistry graduate school student in the future, even as freshmen. It’s okay to explore many career paths and ultimately be sure of what you’re doing. Everyone is different and operates on their own time­ line. There’s nothing wrong with taking longer — there’s nothing wrong with do­ ing something else and then returning to something you’re really passionate about.

Why did you choose N.U.?

N.U. is obviously a fantastic school, and in particular, the Chemistry Department at N.U. is this jewel. It’s remarkable how quickly it has grown to being a top 10 department — and certainly I think a top 5 department — in the country. Some of it’s just that it worked out, timing wise. I was ready to make an arrangement for my next step after Harvard University, and N.U. was hiring during COVID when no­ body else was hiring. They really [wanted] to grow and improve. There’s no place I would’ve gone instead.

So there was a mix of ser­ endipity and hard-work that worked out for you?

A lot of it is serendipity — that’s a good way to put it. A lot of it is somewhat a roll of the dice. So much of it is you’re in the right place at the right time. That’s also a major source of frustration. You can work as hard as someone else, but you don’t get lucky. It’s not like industry, where you get rewarded for doing a good job. Academia is a little different. You need to be exceptional at all times, and even then, you’re just doing your job. You won’t be rewarded.

There are a lot of things out of your control. Most of the things in your control are your attitude and work ethic, and if you can really work on those things, you can set yourself up for success. But, there’s still this aspect of luck. Every part of your life has a luck component.

Were there any challenges moving around a lot, pur­ suing your education, and research?

At the highest level of research, you fol­ low the science. You look at what’s going to stimulate you intellectually, and you make the sacrifice. It’s particularly tough if you’re in a relationship or married or with somebody close … breaking those relationships and putting them on pause is really tough. They call this in academia the two-bodied problem, which is that you ar­ en’t just worried about yourself. You can’t just pick up and leave.

That part is really tough. And being in a new city, especially as a postdoctoral fellow, which are shorter periods of time where you’re doing an intense amount of research — it can be lonely. But I think if you are enjoying what you are doing, that brings a lot of comfort. You know that at the end of the road, you’re going to take a position that’s a permanent position, and you’ll finally get to settle down. That kind of makes that settling down very sweet, because you’ve earned it.

Any advice for undergradu­ ates seeking research?

If there’s not a spot, don’t take things personally and don’t let that discourage you from reaching out to someone else. At the end of the day, this is a profession of people. Research doesn’t do itself. There are personnel-type things that have to come into play.

My advice to undergraduate students is to put yourself out there. Do the leg­ work to show that you’ve actually done some background research and then put it on them. Ask them if there are opportuni­ ties for you to be involved. Get integrated into the culture of the group. Graduate students are your best friends. Get a desk in the lab and do your homework there instead of the library so that you get to be a part of the group. Get the experience of being a part-time researcher, and that’s how you know if that’s the life for you.
