text:
Defeating the Dragon: Epistemic Injustice Towards Asian/ American Women by Olive Liu

Departments of Asian American Studies and Philosophy

Faculty Advisors: Sanford Goldberg and Ji-yeon Yuh

Abstract Epistemic injustice, and testimonial injustice specifically, is a type of dis­ crimination that occurs when a person suffers a credibility deficit because of an identity-based prejudice. This is an issue that affects many marginalized groups and can have larger repercussions on one’s perception of self, loss of resources and opportunities, and continued mistreatment, both epistemically and non-epistemically. My project explores this phenomenon in relation to Asian/American women, which I identify to be an at-risk group for system­ atic, testimonial injustice. Through the course of this thesis, I discuss how stereotypes about Asian/Americans, and Asian/American women in partic­ ular, were created and how these stereotypes negatively impact the perceived credibility of Asian/Americans, both historically and currently. The goal of this is to problematize the dominant images of Asian/American women and to show how this idea is not informed by actual Asian/American women but by dominant and oppressive forces such as white supremacy, patriarchal power, and Western exceptionalism. Furthermore, I argue that testimonial injustice against Asian/American women can reproduce and maintain these negative images and that the discrediting of this group can lead to further, non-epistemic harms like physical and sexual violence. Because of this, how we conceptualize justice for Asian/American women socially and politically is deeply tied to epistemic justice, which serves as a method I discuss for overall resistance to violent powers.

Introduction On Mar. 16, 2021, Robert Aaron Long en­ tered three different spas in Georgia with the intention to kill. His eight victims included six Asian-American women: Xiaojie Tan, Douyou Feng, Soon Chung Park, Hyun Jung Grant, Suncha Kim, and Yong Ae Yue. When interrogated by the police, Long said that his shootings were an attempt to eliminate the “temptations” of his “sexual addiction.”1

Although Long never admitted that his crimes were racially-motivated, it is no mistake that his targets were Asian-operated spas. The perceived connection between Asian/American women and hyper-sexu­ ality is something that has been forged and maintained through long histories of discrim­ inatory laws, American military occupation, and derogatory representations of Asian/ American women in Western media as docile, submissive, and emotionally uncaring.

While violence against Asian/Amer­ ican women is perpetrated in many ways, this project aims to uncover the impacts of epistemic injustice, specifically testimonial injustice.2 My intention is to understand how knowledge production can be discriminatory and how excluding and discrediting certain groups can contribute to continued oppres­ sion and violence.

Section 1: On the Relevance of Epistemic Injustice To understand why epistemic injustice is a relevant topic to Asian/American wom­ en and marginalized groups as a whole, it is necessary to establish definitions and frameworks for how social categories, such as race and gender, are formed. Fol­ lowing scholars like Micheal Omi, Howard Winant, and Judith Butler, I propose that race and gender are categories that are given meaning by a variety of socio-po­ litical forces and will fluctuate depending on the change in these influences. As Omi and Winant write, these social categories can be understood as “concept[s] that [sig­ nify] and [symbolize] social conflicts and interests by referring to different types of human bodies.”3 Similarly, Judith Butler points out in Gender Trouble that gender is not the biological differences in chro­ mosomes, but rather, “the various acts of gender” that “create the idea of gender” by imbuing meaning into certain characteris­ tics.4 In this sense, social categories allow people to not only identify when others are a part of a certain group but to also have expectations for how that individual should act based on dominant perceptions of the entire community.

1 Anna North, “Claims of ‘sexual addiction’ are a distraction in the Atlanta killing”, Vox, March 18, 2021, https://www.vox. com/22336271/atlanta-shooter-sex-addiction-robert-aaron-long 2 A brief note on definitions - Although I use the language of ‘women’ throughout this project, I also include any non-cisgender Asian/Americans that may resonate with this experience but do not identify as women, such as myself. 3 Michael Omi and Howard Winant, Racial Formation in the United States, 3rd Edition. (New York: Routledge, 2014), 110. 4 Judith Butler, Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity, 3rd Edition. (New York: Routledge, 2006), 178 5 Michel Foucault, “Truth and Method,” in The Foucault Reader, ed. Paul Rabinow. (New York: Pantheon, 1984), 72-73

However, one’s understanding of these social categories is not objective. In Truth and Method, Michel Foucault discusses the cycle between power and knowledge, writing that “truth isn’t outside of power, or lacking in power … Each society has its regime of truth.”5 In other words, those in power can produce and circulate knowledge that justi­ fies their dominance while also derogating their inferiors. Such understandings are often institutionalized through education, politics, and other systems, making them difficult to disrupt and question.

This kind of dominance can be seen in the idea of controlling images, which Pa­ tricia Hill Collins introduces in her work, Black Feminist Thought. Controlling images are negative characterizations of minority groups that detract from their humanity, “mak[ing] racism, sexism, poverty, and other forms of injustice appear to be more normal, and inevitable parts of everyday life.”6 In this sense, controlling images often conceal the truth of the histories of oppression certain groups have faced by making their marginalized position seem self-evident. It is important to note that these controlling images will probably not reflect the actual lived experiences of the group they describe. Thus, one may ask why these ideas were formed without in­ terruption, despite the actual violence that they may cause. I believe that these ques­ tions can be answered by explaining the function of epistemic injustice, specifically testimonial injustice.

According to Miranda Fricker in her seminal text, Epistemic Injustice: Power and Ethics of Knowing, testimonial injustice occurs when a speaker “receives a credibility deficit owing to identity prejudice in the hearer.”7 Note that I am focusing on systematic testi­ monial injustice, which occurs when some­ one unjustly discredits their interlocutor, not because of the content or context of their tes­ timony, but because of their social identities like race and gender. Here, one can see how the relationship between knowledge and power is important to testimonial injustice: if one is made to believe that a certain iden­ tity group is inferior, they are likely to grant them less credibility than someone without such an identity. For instance, if someone believes that women are less intelligent than men, they may discredit a woman’s testimo­ ny regardless of its accuracy.

6 Patricia Hill Collins, Black Feminist Thought, 1st Edition. (New York: Routledge, 1990), 69 7 Miranda Fricker, Epistemic Injustice: Power & The Ethics of Knowing. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009), 28 8 Kristie Dotson, “Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing,” Hypatia, Vol. 26, No. 2 (2011): 242 9 Ibid. 10 Ibid., 244

Beyond Fricker’s concept of testimo­ nial injustice, Kristie Dotson points out ad­ ditional kinds of epistemic injustices in her paper titled “Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing.” The first is testimonial quieting, in which “an audience fails to identify a speaker as a knower.”8 She directly links this sort of violence to Hill Collins’ idea of controlling images, as these images detract from their perception as knowers and their level of credibility.9 The second is testimonial smothering, which occurs when a person limits their testimo­ ny if they feel that their listener may not consider their knowledge fairly because of the content of their account or because of prejudices against their identity.10

As a group, Asian/American women are particularly at risk for these different testimonial injustices because of a history of racially gendered violence, harmful stereo­ types, and exclusionary policies. Thus, to un­ derstand how epistemic injustice manifests and affects Asian/American women, I want to provide a brief analysis of three major factors that have influenced dominant con­ ceptions of this group: Orientalism, overseas occupation, and domestic oppression.

Section 2: Camptown Women, Lotus Blossoms, and Dragon Ladies Before delving into the more specific histo­ ries of Asian/American women, I want to introduce the framework of Orientalism, which was first coined by Edward Said to describe the relationship between the West (the Occident) and the East (the Orient). Al­ though Said is writing about the relationship between Europe and the Middle East specif­ ically, the idea of Orientalism can still offer us a useful framework for understanding power and knowledge and how it influenced the identity of Asian/American women. According to Said, the Western conception of the ‘Orient’ or Asia is largely a construc­ tion invented by Europe, which he calls the Occident.11 In essence, the way the Occident understands the Orient is integral to its perception of itself and its superiority, as the Orient defines the West as being an inferior “image, idea, personality, experience.”12 Be­ cause of this, people identified as ‘Orientals’ are perceived as being inherently lesser than their Western counterparts, an idea that un­ dergirds many stereotypes directed towards Asian/American women.

For instance, the Page Act of 1875 (henceforth referred to as the Page Act), while explicitly banning the entry of coerced laborers, convicted felons, and prostitutes from Asia, implicitly prevented the immigra­ tion of Chinese women to the U.S. by gener­ alizing them as sex workers.13 Using language like “lewd and immoral” as justification to deny their entry, the Page Act perpetuated the popular racist sentiment that Chinese women were impure and hyper-sexual.14 The role that testimonial injustice played in the denial of Chinese women from immigrating to the U.S. was also premised on these beliefs. Many women were interrogated in port cit­ ies like San Francisco and turned away for a variety of reasons, such as being unmarried or having a job for which they had no previ­ ous experience.15 Regardless of whether they were sex workers, the testimonies of these women were denied based on racially gen­ dered beliefs against Chinese women.

11 Edward Said, Orientalism, 25th Anniversary Edition. (London: Penguin Books, 1994), 2 12 Ibid., 2 13 Page Act of 1875, 18 Stat. 477, Chap. 141 (1875). https://loveman.sdsu.edu/docs/1875Immigration%20Act.pdf 14 Ibid., Chap. 141 15 David Haekwon Kim, “Asian American Philosophy and Feminism,” in The Oxford Handbook of Feminist Philosophy, ed. Kim Q. Hall and Ásta (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2021) 7 16 Harry Truman, “Statement by the President, Truman on Korea, June 27, 1950,” in Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Harry Truman, 1945-1953, History and Public Policy Program Digital Archive, https://digitalarchive.wilsoncenter.org/docu­ ment/116192.pdf?v=cd0b66b71d6a0412d275a5088a18db5d 17 Katharine H.S. Moon, Sex Among Allies: Military Prostitution in US-Korea Relations. (New York: Columbia University Press, 1997), 28

Having started with my analysis of the Page Act, I now want to move on and explore another point in history in which racially gendered perceptions resulted in the subjugation of Asian/American women: Korean camptowns and camptown women in post-war South Korea. The existence of Asian women serving and being exploited by military troops is not an uncommon phenomenon: during the era of Japanese colonization in Korea and World War II, many Asian women were forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese military. Even after Japan’s withdrawal from Korea after World War II, Korean women continued to work as prostitutes — this time, to fill the camp­ town clubs surrounding the U.S. army bases that had been recently set up after the estab­ lishment of the U.S.-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty in 1954.16

The Korean War also fueled massive growth in Korean sex workers because of wartime poverty, the separation of families which created orphans and widows, and the socio-political consequences of the war.17 Katharine Moon points out that many Ko­ reans sought safety in areas where U.S. forces were stationed and depended heavily on the bases for economic survival. However, the abundance of camptown clubs cannot be simply blamed on the circumstances of the war. Although these factors heavily contrib­ uted to the abuse and exploitation of Korean women, the attitudes that American soldiers had toward these women cannot be ignored. For instance, in her interviews with Amer­ ican G.I.s, Moon reveals that the ideas that men had about Asian women contributed to the popularity of militarized prostitution. One Army chaplain stated that the abun­ dance of sex clubs in Korea was attributed to “the culture” and that prostitution was “a way of life for Asians and that some Asians liked prostitution.”18 Another states:

What the soldiers have read and heard before ever arriving in a foreign country influence[s] prostitution a lot. For example, stories about Korean or Thai women being beautiful, subservient — they’re tall tales, glamorized … U.S. men would fall in lust with Korean women. They were property, things, slaves … Racism, sexism — it’s all there. The men don’t see the women as human beings — they’re disgusting, things to be thrown away … They speak of women in the diminutive.19

Here, one can see how the popularity of certain stereotypes about Asian/Amer­ ican women shaped the violent treatment of many camptown women, using their perceived sexual nature to justify the high engagement of American men with Korean women. When considering how this relates to testimonial injustice, I would argue that the G.I.s’ expectations of and prejudices against Asian women encouraged them to discredit any testimonies of the unethical nature of camptowns or objections to engaging in sex work. One particular example of this is the enforcement of laws and policies attempting to reduce the transmission of venereal dis­ ease (VD). Camptown women were often accused as the source of infection when an American soldier got sick and penalized with little regard to whether or not the accusation was true.20 Conversely, camptown women’s testimonies were often disregarded, as preju­ dices about their social identities and profes­ sion discredited them compared to the G.I.s. In this sense, camptown women suffered from testimonial quieting, as the controlling image of them as a hyper-sexual and morally inferior group negatively impacted the per­ ception of their credibility.

18 Ibid., 36 19 Ibid., 34 20 Na-Young Lee, “Un/forgettable Histories of US Camptown Prostitution in South Korea: Women’s Experiences of Sexual Labor and Government Policies,” Sexualities, Vol. 2018, No. 21 (5-6) (2018): 763, https://doi.org/10.1177/1363460716688683 21 Renee Tajima-Peña, “Lotus Blossoms Don’t Bleed: Images of Asian Women,” in Making Waves: An Anthology of Writing By and About Asian American Women, ed. Asian Women United of California. (Boston: Beacon Press, 1989), 309

I now want to turn towards other stereotypes of Asian/American women depicted in popular media to identify some additional harms Asian/American women might encounter, and how histories like that of camptown women influence ideas of Asian/American women today. For this pa­ per, I will focus on two stereotypes explored by Renee E. Tajima in “Lotus Blossoms Don’t Bleed”: the Lotus Blossom and the Dragon Lady. The former is characterized as “a sexual-romantic object” who is “utter­ ly feminine [and] delicate” and “exist[s] to serve men,” especially white men.21 A popu­ lar example of this is Kim from the musical Miss Saigon, a Vietnamese sex worker who is seemingly ‘saved’ from her profession by an American soldier, Chris. Consistently characterized as virginal and pure, Kim falls in love with Chris, only to commit suicide once she discovers that he has re-married after leaving Vietnam. This reveals that Kim’s character exists only as the object of Chris’ sexual desires, being discarded when she no longer serves her purpose.

While the Lotus Blossom presents an innocent and submissive image of Asian/ American women, the Dragon Lady subverts this idea, placing Asian/American women in a position of sexual dominance. She is char­ acterized by her “excessively dangerous sex­ uality” and “Oriental femininity,” which are weaponized as tools of manipulation.22 Yet, this overt sexuality often masks the emotion­ ally cold and cruel intentions of the Dragon Lady, which are often antagonistic against white and male power. Perhaps one of the most famous examples of this character is O-ren Ishii in Kill Bill Vol. 1. Portrayed by Lucy Liu, O-ren’s cold demeanor juxtaposes the excessive violence she wreaks through­ out the movie, using her femininity as a tool to seize power and seek revenge. This char­ acterization may imply that Asian/American women as lacking fundamental humanity — they are willing to cross moral boundaries and weaponize deeply personal things, such as sex, to get what they want.

Section 3: Epistemic Injustice and its Effects on Asian/ American Women Using both the stereotypes and the history of camptown women that I have previ­ ously explored, I will now sketch out the justifications one may use when commit­ ting an act of testimonial injustice against Asian/American women. The Lotus Blos­ som is perhaps the clearer one to dissect: because they are directly characterized as shy, submissive, and docile, it is easy to see why they may be seen as having low credi­ bility. Their perceived tendency is to defer to their male counterparts, and as a result, they often have things decided for them and not with them, thus being treated more like property rather than actual human beings. On the other end, the Dragon Lady is often perceived to be powerful, and even dom­ inant over men. While this might seem like it awards them an adequate amount of credibility, it is important to note that this power comes from their sexuality and cruelty.23 Because they use immoral means to procure their position over others, their testimony is often seen as untrustworthy or manipulative.

22 Ibid., 309 23 Elyse Pham, “Here’s how pop culture has perpetuated harmful stereotypes of Asian women,” Today, April 1, 2021, https://www. today.com/popculture/here-s-how-pop-culture-has-perpetuated-harmful-stereotypes-asian-t213676

The negative effects of this are also seen when American servicemen justify their involvement with military prosti­ tution by attributing it to the culture of Asian countries. The implication is that Asian women are inherently hyper-sexual, and should be used and treated as such. When camptown women spoke up about the violence that they faced at the hands of G.I.s or club managers, their line of work, gender, race, and class called their integrity and credibility into question.

With this information, I offer this account of what epistemic, and specifically testimonial, injustice looks like for Asian/ American women: Asian/American wom­ en are likely to suffer instances of testimo­ nial injustice when their audience holds a prejudiced idea about them that stems from the controlling images of Asian/ American women as sexual, subservient, untrustworthy, and passive. These stereo­ types directly detract from their status as knowers by undermining their credibility, particularly in situations relating to sex, intimate relationships, and personal harm. Furthermore, Asian/American women, and especially those who are lower-class, immigrants, or in other disadvantaged groups, are at risk of smothering their testimony because the content of it often puts them at risk for violence, either in­ terpersonally or from the state. This often results in epistemic oppression, which Kristie Dotson defines as the “persistent epistemic exclusion that hinders one’s contribution to knowledge production.”24 Because of this consistent exclusion and silencing, the testimonies and experiences of Asian/American women often do not shape the knowledge surrounding them, allowing for the continued epistemic, so­ cial, and political violence against them.

This account can best be thought of through the concept of a positive feedback loop, in which the result of an initial action causes more of that action to occur. With testimonial injustice against Asian/Amer­ ican women, the initial event is often the development of prejudice against them, including traits that take agency away from Asian/American women, such as how the Lotus Blossom trope portrays Asian/ American women as submissive and docile. This may invite people to think about these women in a way that dismisses their needs or experiences in favor of their own.

This leads to an increased potential of acts of testimonial injustice against Asian/ American women, as these views are likely to detract from their credibility as know­ ers. These instances of testimonial injustice will likely confirm the original prejudice, especially because any resistance to the act will usually be suppressed as a consequence of testimonial quieting due to a lack of credibility. This creates a positive feedback loop of holding prejudices, acting on those beliefs, denying any resistance to acts of injustice based on stereotypes, and using one’s interactions to provide further evi­ dence for these negative views. Addition­ ally, Asian/American women may inter­ nalize these negative images, behaving in certain stereotypical ways to avoid further racial violence. This creates another source that confirms the original bias, normaliz­ ing it as an observation of Asian/American women and not as a prejudice. As Collins previously points out, controlling images make racist and sexist perceptions a part of everyday life, and not something to be concerned with.

24 Kristie Dotson, “Conceptualizing Epistemic Oppression,” Social Epistemology, Vol. 28, No. 2 (2014): 115

“

”

Asian/ American women are likely to suffer instances of testimonial injustice when their audience holds a prejudiced idea about them that stems from the controlling images of Asian/ American women as sexual, subservient, untrustworthy, and passive. These stereotypes directly detract from their status as knowers by undermining their credibility, particularly in situations relating to sex, intimate relationships, and personal harm.

When assessing the consequences that come from these acts of testimonial injustice, I have identified two major types of harm: psychological and sexual. Both can be seen in the sexual fetishization of Asian/American women, which is termed ‘yellow fever.’ Fetishists often justify their preference for Asian/American women by citing stereotypes like the Lotus Blossom, arguing that such women are superior because of their submissive personality and hyper-sexual nature. However, in her paper “Why Yellow Fever Isn’t Flattering,” Robin Zheng points out that this kind of fetishization can place a “psychological burden” on its victims by making them feel “depersonalized and homogenized” by reducing their worth to purely their race and gender.25 As further shown in a study by Connie Chan, being a victim of fetishi­ zation can lead Asian/American women to blame themselves instead of seeing how the problem was “external, based upon cul­ tural and societal stereotypes.”26

While it isn’t initially clear how the harms of fetishization can be epistemic, I would argue that people with Asian fe­ tishes are more prone to committing acts of testimonial injustice when speaking to a potential Asian partner. Because racial fetishes often create a homogenized image of a larger group of people, any discrep­ ancies to this image will often be ignored or shut down completely. For example, if someone has an Asian fetish because they believe Asian/American women to be more submissive, they may commit an act of testimonial injustice by discrediting any objection or issue she has with their relationship. This can be especially dan­ gerous in sexual situations. As Sumi K. Cho states:

Asian Pacific American women are at particular risk of being racially and sexually harassed because of the synergism that results when sexualized racial stereotypes combine with racialized gender stereotypes. Model minority traits of passivity and submissiveness are intensified and gendered through the stock portrayal of obedient and servile Asian Pacific women in popular culture. The repeated projection of a compliant and catering Asian feminine nature feeds harasser’s beliefs that Asian Pacific American women will be receptive objects of their advances, make good victims, and will not fight back.27

25 Robin Zheng, “Why Yellow Fever Isn’t Flattering: A Case Against Racial Fetishes,” Journal of the American Philosophical Associa­ tion, Vol. 2, No. 3 (2016): 407 26 Connie Chan, “Asian-American Women: Psychological Responses to Sexual Exploitation & Cultural Stereotypes,” Asian Ameri­ can Psychological Association Journal, Vol. 12, No. 1 (1987): 37 27 Sumi K. Cho, “Asian Pacific American Women and Racialized Sexual Harassment,” in Making More Waves: New Writing by Asian American Women, ed. Elaine H. Kim, Lilia V Villanueva, and Asian Women United of California (Boston: Beacon Press, 1997) 164

Cho’s point about Asian/American women being perceived as sexually recep­ tive is especially important in my analysis of testimonial injustice — because Asian/ American women are constantly charac­ terized as sexually eager and submissive, any testimony they give that resists this image might be regarded as untrue. If an Asian/American woman says no to some­ one’s sexual advances, their denial might be seen as less credible to someone that be­ lieves that all Asian/American women are hyper-sexual. As a result, that person may disregard their refusal and proceed, which often results in sexual violence.

At the same time, this characteriza­ tion of Asian/American women might make them seem less credible when talking about acts of sexual violence against them. For example, there are often narratives about how wearing revealing clothing sig­ nals sexual availability to others. Barring the misogynistic and immoral implications of this, someone’s testimony of their assault might lose credibility because of what they wore. For Asian/American women, their very race and gender signal sexual availability to certain people, which may make their account of their assault less believable. This is visible in how mil­ itary prostitution was permitted in Asia but not in Europe, signaling that the often violent and negative treatment of Asian women was allowed because of how their perceived hyper-sexuality was attributed as inherent to their nature. This normal­ ization of harm against Asian/American women makes it difficult to speak up about sexual violence and demand justice.

On top of this, Asian/American wom­ en often smother their own testimony about sexual assault, not only because of the socie­ tal and cultural stigma but also because their livelihood, things like immigration status and access to resources, might be negatively affected. With a low conviction rate, many women, Asian/American and otherwise, may feel as though the social ostracization and potential trauma are not worth it. This is not to blame victims of sexual assault for not speaking out — rather, it is to point out that our judicial system is built in such a way that excludes the means for justice for spe­ cific groups of people. Thus, Asian/Amer­ ican women face a multi-layered problem: their identity is often understood through sexually violent ways, which places them at risk for things like sexual harassment and assault. However, their identity might also justify this violence by characterizing all Asian/American women as sexually eager or submissive, discrediting their initial re­ fusal of sexual advances and their testimo­ nies of assault.

28 José Medina, The Epistemology of Resistance: Gender and Racial Oppression, Epistemic Injustice, and the Social Imagination. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012), 213 29 Ibid. 30 Ibid., 237 31 Ibid., 200

Section 4: Epistemic Justice: How People Can Do Better Through this analysis, it becomes clear that testimonial injustice can be used as a tool of epistemic, sexual, and psychological harm. Thus, it is important to develop a method of epistemic justice as a form of re­ sistance. In their book, The Epistemology of Resistance,  José Medina proposes the idea of meta-lucidity, which is the awareness of one’s social position and how it relates to the identities, histories, and beliefs of oth­ ers.28 In doing so, one is better equipped to identify the gaps in their knowledge or diagnose certain beliefs as inaccurate or problematic, which will affect how they assign credibility to others in the future. The goal in doing so is to expand and fill the gaps in one’s knowledge by “pursu[ing] interventions and transformations aimed at instilling new attitudes and habits.”29 In other words, it is not enough to become aware of one’s epistemic practices — peo­ ple must work to correct them by directly interacting with the groups that are affect­ ed by their beliefs. This is done through epistemic interactions, particularly in­ teractions that create epistemic friction, which can be understood as “experiencing resistance from significantly different perspectives in social interaction.”30 By attempting to correct one’s own and learn new beliefs, people develop a “kaleidoscop­ ic consciousness that remains forever open to being expanded,” which pushes one to “acknowledge and engage new perspec­ tives” in relation to their own knowledge.31

In terms of how this relates to testi­ monial justice, I argue that practicing this kind of reflection with one’s identity and willingness to change one’s perceptions of others will make people more open to learning about different identities and less motivated to make assumptions about other groups. A kaleidoscopic conscious­ ness can also help someone recognize that some communities have been systemically excluded from contributing to collective epistemic resources, as their accounts might have critiqued and detracted from the authority that racial, gendered, and other social powers have. Because of this, people can assess whether their ideas about others are harmful and question the validi­ ty of such beliefs, making them more open to change when they encounter epistemic friction with them. This can address the prejudices that inform acts of testimonial injustice, as Medina’s model pushes people to question why such beliefs are formed, how they reify current structures of power, and how people can rectify these gaps in their knowledge.

Like epistemic injustice, epistemic justice can also exist in a positive feedback loop. As I explained previously, one’s re­ alization that their perceptions of others are problematic should be followed by attempts to unlearn these beliefs. For in­ stance, in Section 2, I discussed how Ori­ entalism often characterized Asian people as less human than their Western counter­ parts. If a person learns about this history, they should be more critical of the current idea that Chinese people are responsible for COVID-19 because they consume non-traditional animals like bats or dogs. They might realize that the rhetoric that the media uses is prejudiced against Chi­ nese people, which should push them to realize how things like the news reproduce certain racist biases. Thus, when they view news articles like those that characterize Black Lives Matter protestors as violent looters, they will probably be less likely to accept this at face value and instead seek out the experiences of those who were actually a part of these movements. The cause (recognizing one’s own harmful be­ liefs) leads to the effect (trying to learn and repair one’s knowledge about the group they are prejudiced toward), which leads back to the cause, increasing the number of things that one might identify as problem­ atic. Of course, not every individual will undergo such a process when unlearning certain prejudices and stereotypes. The importance of epistemic justice is that it cultivates a certain sense of curiosity about how certain concepts came to be and how others see these ideas and the world.

It is not enough to become aware of one’s epistemic practices — people must work to correct them by directly interacting with the groups that are affected by their beliefs. “

”

Conclusion My intention throughout this thesis has been to illuminate an issue that many people face and to give others the language and tools to identify these types of injustices in their own lives. In doing so, I hope that more people will recognize how their perceptions of Asian/ American women might be harmful, which will encourage them to seek out the stories and histories of these women. By learning about these experiences, I believe people will question and be more critical of the oppressive forces that informed their ini­ tial prejudices, which will hopefully strip these powers of their dominance. This is the ultimate future that epistemic justice can lead us to. The knowledge that one possesses and uses is constantly changing and responding to different influences and experiences in our lives. We should consider it a powerful tool that can push us towards a better world — one in which we are no longer objects of domination, but instead are subjects of positive change.

Acknowledgments Throughout my academic, profession­ al, and personal journeys, I have always believed in the power of community and care. That being said, I am very thankful for the community that came to my sup­ port and guided me with patience and genuine interest in my project. First, my advisors: Professor Goldberg in Philoso­ phy and Professor Yuh in Asian American Studies, who not only took the time to give me thoughtful feedback and insights throughout my writing but also pushed me to recognize the importance and value of my work. Thank you both for listening to my academic ideas and my anxieties and for treating both of them as equally valid and important. I also want to extend my gratitude towards other faculty members in Philosophy and Asian-American Stud­ ies. To Professor Medina, thank you for responding to my emails even on sabbat­ ical and for offering me so much wisdom and guidance on how to approach this topic. To Professor Huang, I am grateful for the time, suggestions, and readings you offered to me and for listening to me ramble even during your lunch breaks. To Professor Mueller and Professor Nguyen, who provided space for me to present my thesis and believed in its worth, even in its beginning stages. Finally, I am so grateful to my friends and partner, who took late- night phone calls, read through my work, helped me with editing, and allowed me to talk their ear off about this project to make sense of it. I couldn’t have done this project without these people, who have repeatedly shown me what community means and how we can care for each other.◆

title: Understanding and Applying Corporate Personhood: A Q&A with Professor Nicolette Bruner
notes: Q&A interview with Nicolette Bruner, Assistant Professor of Instruction at the Center for Legal Studies and the Program in American Studies, about corporate personhood and "Thing People".
text:
Understanding and Applying

Corporate Personhood:

A Q&A with Professor

Nicolette Bruner

By Noah Coyle

Professor Nicolette Bruner is an Assistant Professor of Instruction at the Center for Legal Studies and the Program in American Studies. Her educational background includes both a J.D. and a Ph.D. in English Lan­ guage and Literature from the University of Michigan. Prior to joining Northwestern University’s (N.U.’s) faculty, she was a postdoctoral fel­ low with the Stevanovich Institute on the Formation of Knowledge at the University of Chicago and taught in the Department of English at Western Kentucky University.

Professor Bruner’s research explores how the law shapes the way we (humans) understand and interact with the nonhuman entities and systems around us. She is currently working on the book project “Thing People: Living with Corporations and Other Nonhumans,” which exam­ ines how the legal doctrine of corporate personhood offers a framework for articulating the rights and responsibilities of other nonhuman enti­ ties, including animals, plants, rivers, and robots.

The following is a conversation with Professor Bruner, which touched on Professor Bruner’s unique educational background, the con­ cept of corporate personhood, and “Thing People.”

[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

What initially drew you to law, and how does your back­ ground in English tie in with your legal background? When I went into law school at the University of Michigan, I was hoping to do environmental litigation: I wanted to protect trees. Over the course of law school, I realized a couple of things. One was that I didn’t think litigation was for me, and the other was that a lot of the things that really interested me — particularly what the legal idea of a person is  — were things that I could pursue in a graduate education context.

I graduated from law school, and then that fall went straight into an English Ph.D. program. I chose to continue studying at the University of Michigan because I was able to work under the advisement of another J.D.-Ph.D., Professor Greg Crane, who worked in English. There aren’t that many of us J.D.-Ph.D.s who are in English: it’s more common to find J.D.-Ph.D.s who are legal historians. It was really nice to have somebody who understood the legalese even as he was encouraging me to refine my skills in literature.

My understanding is that your specific research interest is corporate personhood. How did you become interested in this legal principle? I remember watching this documentary before I even started law school called “The Corporation,” which was all about corporate personhood. I came into law school thinking corporate personhood is bad, this is evil, and this makes no sense. I think it stuck in my mind in part because I knew that there had to be a reason why it existed, and I wanted to figure out why that was.

In the spring of my first year of law school, I took an upper-level seminar called “The Concept of a Person.” We talked about a lot of different forms of legal personhood: children, the seas, etc. I got hooked on this robust philosophical debate, as I realized that there was this whole body of writing out there where people were trying to understand what exactly a corporation is — because there’s not a good sense of how it became the way it was — and how we deal with the fact that it is a legal person. Right after finishing that paper, I went off and worked in Amazon on this oil case that involved Chevron-Texaco, where the indigenous inhabitants of the Orientales area had been suing Chevron-Texaco for irresponsible drilling practices. It was actually Texaco that did it, but when Chevron merged with Texaco, Chevron inherited the responsibility even though Chevron hadn’t had anything to do with it. When they bought Texaco, they bought the responsibility as well as the assets. I just found that fascinating, looking at how this works in terms of inheritance in terms of multinational corporate power. I just got hooked, and I’m still hooked.

What is corporate personhood, and how did it come to be? When we say that a corporation is a person, all that we mean from a legal sense is that a corporation has certain rights and certain responsibilities to the other members of the legal community. The way we got to corporate personhood is very, very old. Different scholars will trace different origins, but we can all agree that when William Blackstone was codifying English common law in the late 18th century, he wrote about corporations at the very end of his first volume, which is all about persons. Blackstone explains that we have corporate persons because it’s seen as “for the good of the public” to have certain institutions be able to do things like own land and enter into contracts. For example, with N.U., we have the idea that N.U. can own the land and the buildings upon which it functions. We don’t grant each successive president with authority and ownership over that, because then the properties would be each president’s personal assets. We want to say that the university is something that can own land, and so that is legal personhood.

Originally, the corporate person was only granted by the sovereign to public inter­ est works. In the early republic, you could get a charter from the state legislature to do so, but you had to show that it was for a public purpose. Ironically, the Jacksonians are the ones who are responsible for the modern state of the corporation. They didn’t like the fact that you had to have influence with the legislature to get a charter, so they lobbied to make the status of forming a corporation open to everyone just by filing paperwork. So, we had what’s called general incorporation, in which each state had its own proce­ dure for granting the corporate person, which led to the gradual loosening of the public service requirement.

That’s the origin of corporate personhood. Even the people who argue that we should abolish it will say that they don’t have a problem with a corporation owning its own property or being able to enter into a contract. What they’re actually arguing when they say they want to abolish corporate personhood is that they want the corporate person to have a more narrow set of rights than it now enjoys. I honestly would agree that a corporation has more rights than it can bear, but I don’t think the answer is to abolish corporate personhood because I don’t think that’s practical or feasible. We can use corporate personhood in a way that is more socially just.

Considering “Thing People,” how does corporate personhood offer a framework for articulating the rights and responsibili­ ties of other nonhuman entities? In my earlier career, I was mostly just working on corporate personhood, but I was also interested in Animal Studies. It took me a little while to realize that those weren’t different interests; they were actually part of the same question, which is how we, as humans, relate to entities that aren’t human. Part of the way in which we’ve gotten into the current, distorted state of corporate personhood is that we have expectations of the corporation that it can’t bear. We cannot expect a corporation to feel: to feel guilt, to feel empathy. It’s not built like that, but we give it these rights that in a natural person — which is what the law calls an individual person like you and me — would be balanced by all of these other responsibilities that we know how to bear, given how individual human minds work. When we ask corporations to do these things, we end up in trouble.

My argument is that we need to acknowledge that we are interacting with and ex­ pecting things of nonhumans, who then can sometimes expect things from us in return. I’m not arguing that a dog should have the same set of rights and responsibilities as a human being, a tree, a lizard, or so on. What I’m saying is that we are already expecting things from nonhumans and asking them to do things and interacting with them. I think that if we just clear our minds of the idea that a person has to be a human and that there are only a few ways to be a person, then we can just understand these relationships we already have a lot more clearly, as corporate personhood has already opened up the idea that we can imagine in law a person that’s not a human.

title: The Effects of Power Dynamics in University-Community Partnerships
department: School of Education and Social Policy
notes: Senior thesis excerpt; a case study of the Young People's Race Power and Technology Project (YPRPT). Advisors from "Faculty Advisers" on the opening page, where the department, advisers and abstract are extracted as one block (39.3). Pull quotes are moved to paragraph breaks. Includes an appendix of end-of-year survey questions and a bibliography. The contributors section (printed page 120) has a Q&A with the author.
text:
The Effects of Power Dynamics in University- Community Partnerships by Nina M. Wetoska

School of Education and Social Policy Faculty Advisers: Sepehr Vakil and Terri Sabol Abstract This study will examine the power dynamics between undergraduate students and adult community members, and their effects on mediating these relation­ ships within the realm of university—community partnerships. More specifi­ cally, this paper explores a community engagement program categorized as an out-of-school learning initiative. This means that the partnership is between a university entity and an external organization, or in this case, several communi­ ty organizations. The relationships between undergraduate students and adult community members is an important dimension to investigate because it is vast­ ly understudied and consequential to the outcome of the partnership. Through the analysis of end-of-the-year surveys, Identity Journals, and Team Lead focus group transcripts, the data reveals the significant effects of preexisting content expertise, pre-planning meetings, and resource access. These observations led to my present research question: How do power dynamics mediate relationships between Team Leads (T.L.s) and Undergraduate Collaboratives (U.C.s) within Young People’s Race Power and Technology Project (YPRPT)?

This case study of YPRPT reveals the complexity of undergraduate and com­ munity member relationships within an organization bringing high schoolers, undergraduates (U.C.s), and community partners (T.L.s) together to investigate the impacts that technology has on marginalized groups of color through the cre­ ation of investigative documentaries. Successful interactions occurred when the intrapersonal skills of all facilitators were respected and valued, which was aided by interpersonal skills such as active listening and a shared sense of teamwork and purpose. The most cited interaction event mentioned was the collaborative method of planning sessions. These gave the facilitators time to get to know each other on both a personal and professional level. This gained knowledge then led to a sense of trust, limited due to time but still present and evident, and a division of responsibilities that supported the learning of the participants.

Methodology To understand the relationships between the U.C.s and T.L.s, I examined the surveys and focus group transcripts that were collected after the completion of the 2020–2021 YPRPT cohort in June and July 2021. This data will be complemented by Identity Journals that included reflections upon weekly meetings between U.C. and T.L. personnel, from January to June 2021. YPRPT involved both a program and a research component. With support from a National Science Foundation grant, T.L.s were compensated with $1,350, and U.C.s were compensated with $675, which was distributed at the end of the program. I experienced the YPRPT program as an U.C., which unfortunately barred me from viewing the data of my personal T.L.s due to IRB restrictions, and the research component as a member of the research team, which allowed me convenient access to the data from this population and deep knowledge about the program’s context. The data includes a thorough survey taken at the end of the program by both the T.L.s and U.C.s, which I designed with the help of YPRPT’s Curriculum Team, transcripts from Team Lead focus groups that were conducted in June and July 2021, and Iden­ tity Journals completed at the end of every weekly session throughout the program. The use of YPRPT as a case study is in­ tended to extend current scholarship and address the broader context of undergrad­ uate-community member relationships in university-community partnerships.

I perceive several concerns regard­ ing sample size and anonymity. Since the sample is small — 8 U.C.s and 13 T.L.s — identities can be compromised if not handled carefully. Additionally, this sample is representative of the population in this specific case study, but there is a range of university-community part­ nerships that vary in nature and scale. Despite these limitations, YPRPT remains an important case study to use to explore university-community partnerships. The out-of-school learning initiative currently works with community members and undergraduates and is rapidly growing and adapting as it progresses through its first few years.

“

”

“How do power dynamics mediate relationships between Team Leads (T.L.s) and Undergraduate

Collaboratives (U.C.s) within Young People’s Race Power and Technology Project (YPRPT)?”

Analytic Approach My approach to the analysis of all three sources, particularly the focus group transcripts that offered the most in terms of the amount of content, combined inductive (drawing conclusions from the observations) and deductive (drawing conclusions from one’s logic and previous premises) reasoning. All the analysis and notes on findings regarding the sources were recorded on a Google Docs. I used a spreadsheet to record qualitative data because the data sources were not ex­ tensive or lengthy, so a more complex method such as coding via NVivo could distract from the content of the data. The dual reasoning approach began with the application of inductive reasoning, allow­ ing me to develop a notion about how the individuals experienced the program. Next, deductive reasoning required going into the data a second time, through the lens of inductive reasoning’s findings, to determine whether or not there was any substantive evidence to support the claims. I created a comprehensive codebook in Google Sheets after reading through all three sources of data to be used across all the sources. This comprehensive method main­ tained cohesion and consistency in coding.

Results All names are pseudonymized to protect the individuals’ identities. Team 1’s pseud­ onyms include U.C. 1, T.L. A, and T.L. B; Team 2’s pseudonyms include U.C. 2, T.L. C, and T.L. B.

Undergraduate Collaborators’  Views of Team Leads Data taken from Identity Journals and end-of-the-year surveys illuminated the perception of the T.L.s by the U.C.s. The overall sentiment was satisfaction with the pairings of T.L.s and U.C.s. The U.C.s gave the responses of Great and Excellent to the survey question, “How would you rate your overall experience with your T.L.s?” Three overarching themes included U.C.s’ acknowledgment of T.L.s’ content expertise, imbalance of preparation responsibilities, and mixed experiences with communication.

Firstly, several times in the docu­ ments, the U.C.s spoke about the preexist­ ing knowledge that their respective T.L.s brought to the program. U.C. 1 included the following response in their survey: “My T.L.s were amazing at their jobs of connect­ ing to students, making them feel welcome, and checking up on whether they were engaged. [T.L. B] went above and beyond with helping out with video production/ editing, and I don’t think I could’ve done it without them.” The content expertise came from the prior work experience that T.L. B had with video production and editing. The T.L.’s current job is video producing, meaning they sponsored students who also took part in video production and editing and thus had some awareness coming into the program. Both T.L.s had a connection with their students that created a comfort­ able environment in which the students engaged with the material and each other.

Despite both U.C.s being positive about the skillset and connection with the students that the T.L.s brought, there was an imbalance in workload — elucidating the second theme. U.C. 1 listed several responsibilities that they took on that the T.L.s did not. Though they wrote “which is normally totally cool!”, they continued to write that they felt rushed, which increased pressure on the U.C. even before entering a weekly session. The same U.C. expressed their frustration with the work distribution and responsibilities that mostly fell onto the U.C.s; however, it is unclear whether or not the preparation work was explained or available for the T.L.s to complete. Either way, the imbalance resulted in U.C. 1 feeling tired, which could have adversely affected the U.C.-T.L. relationship. However, U.C. 1 did mention that the T.L.s conducted the communication with the participants and their parents.

The third theme revolves around the myriad of experiences in communi­ cation between the U.C.s and T.L.s. This communication took place outside of pre-planning sessions and weekly sessions. The latter will be discussed in the Collab­ oration Approaches section. As was noted in statements by U.C. 1, over-communi­ cation was caused by an unclear division of roles and program progress. They also noted that overall communication “could have been smoother.” Contrastingly, U.C. 2 proposes that frequent communication helped the team in its production of the documentaries. Additional coordination was required for this U.C. compared to the other seven teams due to the multiple documentaries that this U.C.’s partnership chose to complete. The strength of their communication resulted in more oppor­ tunities for the students in the group to be directly involved in the documentary creation, whether that be in the form of a director, producer, or editor.

Team Leads’  Views of Undergraduate Collaborators Similar to the U.C.s, the T.L.s selected the answer choices of Good and Excellent for the question: How would you rate your overall experience with your team’s U.C.? Across the data of all four T.L.s included in the sample, they most frequently described their U.C.s in terms of personality charac­ teristics and connection as well as access to Northwestern University’s (N.U.’s) resources. An interesting finding was also that T.L.s talked far less about the U.C.s in their Identity Journals than the U.C.s talked about them. They also seldom brought up their U.C. in the focus groups. Additional­ ly, there were several occasions where the experiences of the U.C.s and T.L.s did not align, such as their opinions on the quality of communication.

When describing the U.C.s, T.L.s often resort to personal characteristics to describe their U.C. in contrast with the U.C.s citing the T.L.s’ strengths while commenting on their relationship. The following quote reflects the views of U.C. 1 by one T.L. of Group 1, T.L. B:

My team leader, [U.C. 1], was really good at encouraging [their group] and shining the work that they did. And just giving that boost of confidence … just shout[ing] them out and say[ing], “Man, thank you for contributing your work. Thank you for contributing your piece.” Like [U.C. 1] was really great with that.

Some key descriptors revolve around their connection to the students. The nature of U.C. 1 encouraged participants to open up and thus be more involved in weekly sessions and share more of themselves. Unlike the T.L.s, U.C. 1 did not know the other students before the program, which makes this connection noteworthy. Ab­ sent from T.L. B’s Identity Journals are any mention of the U.C.’s content knowledge. The void is intriguing because the U.C. at­ tended weekly meetings in preparation for the program and continued to attend week­ ly curriculum preparatory meetings run by members of the Curriculum Team. Despite this, the U.C.’s genial attitude was the main takeaway by the T.L.s on their relationship.

On the more logistical side of the program, the T.L.s acknowledged the U.C.s’ access to N.U.’s vast wealth of resources. As students, the U.C.s could obtain materials from N.U. that T.L.s’ did not. T.L. B notes this beneficial access as the following: “[U.C. 1] made sure that our team succeeded by providing resources and equipping students with laptops or by [U.C. 1] utilizing NWU [N.U.’s] equipment to open USB drives.” T.L. B recognizes that the U.C. has the privilege of acquiring equipment from N.U., which was at no cost to the undergraduate. This was instrumental for this team’s students to actively participate in the documenta­ ry—making process.

Facilitators as a Support System While examining the data, the most com­ monly cited theme was the concept of an internal support system. All individuals studied commented on the appreciation they had for the other facilitation team members bringing positive energy to the sessions and taking charge when the individuals were not able to. The findings were not unique to one group but were replicated and described in comparable ways among all of the groups. The follow­ ing two quotes came from Identity Jour­ nals on Week 1 and Week 4 respectively.

U.C. 1: Today was a little overwhelming — first time co-leading was a little nerve wracking … I’m so incredibly grateful for my co-leads in making these 1.5 hours go by smoothly and keeping up the friendly atmosphere.

T.L. A: My alarm rang today for TREE [also known as YPRPT] and in the activities of the day, I did not connect that it was Tuesday for Zoom. I feel that my co—facilitators had to pull my weight. I need to be more attentive.

U.C. 1 felt the support in the form of com­ fort. They did not participate or facilitate any less, but they did lean into and subse­ quently acknowledge the atmosphere and efficient facilitation that the T.L.s provid­ ed. The quote by T.L. A was an occurrence that was cited by three of the four T.L.s. Whether it was forgetting the meeting, having weather and car troubles, or not having a reliable internet connection, none of these T.L.s felt unsupported by their fellow T.L.s and U.C.s. The two other facilitators smoothly ran the meetings and found solutions to issues such as unreliable internet. Facilitators shifted responsibili­ ties based on the abilities, both technolog­ ically and personally, of each individual. Additionally, there were no mentions of the absence of a U.C. or T.L. in any of the data sources, which means they did not recount or mention the absence or disrup­ tion of not having a facilitator present at the meetings.

All individuals studied commented on the appreciation they had for the other facilitation team members bringing positive energy to the sessions and taking charge when the individuals were not able to. “

”

Role and Involvement Concerns Both parties, but primarily the T.L.s, lacked an understanding of their role within the facilitation portion and direct involvement in the participants’ activities. The most thorough and explicit examples come from the T.L. focus group transcripts. A variety of confusion was present, such as the lev­ el of involvement they should have with the documentary creation and curriculum knowledge. The latter was an issue for two reasons: (1) groups that had their sessions early in the week received the curriculum (i.e., task list) on Sundays and thus had lit­ tle time to prepare and (2) the U.C.s had weekly preparation meetings where they went over the activities and objectives of the week, while the only knowledge the T.L.s had was the curriculum that was sent out on Sundays. T.L. C describes the issue of involvement level: “And it was just like ... I always struggle with like, how hands- off we wanted to be? ‘Cause we were pretty hands-off in the beginning and at the end, I was like, ‘Oh, actually this group needs someone who’s like way more hands-on.’” The selected excerpt and remaining re­ sponses show that there was confusion not only when directly interacting with the students, but also when T.L.s and U.C.s went into their Zoom breakout rooms. As noted by T.L. C, there was a learning curve in which teams had to learn what worked best for them and tailor the facilitation plan to the students’ needs. Though the flexibility and adaptability of the facilita­ tion can make the program more suited to the team, one reason that the program was successful was because there was not a set or defined way to interact with the partici­ pants. Neither the U.C.s, who were versed in the curriculum, nor the T.L.s, who were not, received information on the level of involvement they should have had in the documentary process. The lack of concrete directions or suggestions led to a feeling of confusion and disorder.

Discussion and Concluding Thoughts In summary, the YPRPT case study reveals the complexity of undergraduate (U.C.) and community member (T.L.) relationships.

Successful interactions occurred when the intrapersonal skills of all facilitators were respected and valued, and this gained knowledge led to a sense of trust, limited due to time but still present and evident. Unfor­ tunately, academic researchers, including the N.U. students, continue to hold the status of academic superiority and legitimacy; how­ ever, the T.L.s attempted to mitigate these. Through expressing their own preexisting knowledge and expertise as well as a desire to educate the students, T.L.s voiced and emphasized the value of their knowledge.

Program Suggestions Suggestions for YPRPT stem from these findings. Although the capacity of many T.L.s and U.C.s is limited beyond the re­ quirements of the program, implementing a flexible time or avenue for the facilitators to connect and organize sessions would help with the formal and informal relationships. These could also serve as opportunities to mitigate any issues. As noted previously, U.C.s can be overwhelmed by the additional responsibility of logistical planning and cre­ ating necessary materials for the meetings, but do not always feel comfortable voicing their concerns. Finding that balance between program commitments and realistic expecta­ tions pertaining to the facilitators’ capacity is difficult but deserves more attention.

Additionally, the N.U. students had primary access to the resources of N.U. and YPRPT. The relationships that U.C.s built with the YPRPT team due to their time spent interacting and being educated by the team created an imbalance in power. T.L.s were less likely to reach out to YPRPT than U.C.s because T.L.s would often ask the U.C. to connect with the high schoolers as medi­ ators instead. U.C.s also received curriculum training prior to the introduction of the community organizations into the program.

Offering a program tailored to the needs of the T.L.s would create a more cohesive program and mitigate the issues of role un­ derstanding. A training proposal for T.L.s is to make the program open to any local com­ munity members interested in the YPRPT themes. The proposal is a way to recruit them earlier without the pressure to commit too far in advance. After the completion of the sessions, they would decide if they would like to participate in the program. This will help introduce the T.L.s to both YPRPT program managers and the curriculum and mitigate the access imbalance between U.C.s and T.L.s.

Understandably, the capacity was limit­ ed during the second iteration of the program, but as it scales, the team will need to grow to fill the gaps in training and assistance offer­ ings. A suggestion is to pause at the current size and try adjusting the program to resolve issues before scaling any further. One such adjustment would be the curriculum, which can be improved by bringing together YPRPT members, U.C.s, T.L.s, and participants to co—produce the lessons. Once these are creat­ ed, the facilitators would benefit from having all the lessons accessible to them in a Google Drive. This way, they can plan together more than the week before. U.C.s and T.L.s could also educate themselves on the topics before they are expected to instruct the participants which will increase facilitation confidence.

Limitations and Future Directions The use of YPRPT as a case study does not allow for the data to be extrapolated to all university-community partnerships, but it does highlight the complex nature of the undergraduate-community member rela­ tionship. The small sample size of two of the eight teams makes a generalization of the U.C.-T.L. relationships within YPRPT po­ tentially problematic. As the data was collect­ ed before the completion of this thesis, I did not have the opportunity to ask follow-up questions, particularly in the case of T.L. focus groups. Other than simple clarification questions, there are multiple instances where a T.L. used a word related to YPRPT termi­ nology, but it was not clear whether or not it fell into the specific definition. For example, T.L.s used “co-facilitators” and “team leads” throughout their responses. These terms did not pose confusion when in the plu­ ral form, but when they became singular it was more difficult to discern whether the T.L. was referring to their fellow T.L. or the U.C.. This problem arose because T.L.s appeared to be substituting the terms “co-facilitators” and “team leads” for each other throughout responses.

“Knowledge of the length and extent of contact is needed to stimulate and encourage trust-building.”

Future research should aim to test pre-program approaches to craft positive re­ lationships between these parties. The aspect of time spent building these relationships is a worthwhile study. The university-commu­ nity partnerships require time spent outside of one’s primary job or responsibilities. Al­ though YPRPT offered a stipend to under­ graduates and community members, many similar partnerships do not have this benefit. Other than paying participants for their time, programs need to find the most efficient ways to train and build connections between facilitators. Knowledge of the length and extent of contact is needed to stimulate and encourage trust-building. This would ensure that those involved do not need to overex­ tend themselves, but still experience the benefits of having a trustworthy and reliable relationship with their fellow facilitators. ◆
