title: How We Can Ensure Success in STEM: Professor Marcel Vinces
notes: Profile of Professor Marcel Vinces and his work on teaching approaches in introductory biology; the contents page spells the name "Marcelo Vinces". Ends with a reference list.
text:
How We Can Ensure

Success in STEM: Professor Marcel Vinces

By Zaina Karim

In the fall of 2021, 4,204 students at Northwestern University (N.U.) were enrolled in the Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences. A significant portion of these students pursued, and continue to pursue, majors in biological or pre-health-related fields, making participation in an introductory biology class inevitable. For many, starting biology courses at N.U. will be the first experience that they have with a collegiate level of biological sciences, and therefore, hold great importance for a student’s attitude toward success in biology and beyond. With this in mind, it would behoove N.U. students, faculty, and administrators to ask, “What can be done to ensure the optimal outcome of introductory biology classes?” This is exactly what Professor Marcelo Vinces, a Weinberg academic advisor, has worked to answer during his time at and before N.U.. By closely examining and evaluating the teaching and student reception of introductory biology courses, Professor Vinces and his colleagues at Oberlin College were able to pinpoint the distinction between unsuccessful “teacher-centered learning” and constructive “problem/project-based learning.” Many students made the decision not to continue science-related degrees following introductory biology courses, raising questions about what different variations of class structures might lead to more students persisting in STEM fields. Traditionally, biology classes are taught with a lecturer speaking, students quietly taking notes, and then the students taking two midterms and a final. However, when asked about this approach, Vinces emphasized the much more effective learning outcomes of “problem-based learning, where instead of the professor just talking and the students taking notes, students are given problems in the class, often in groups.” This, he said, causes students to “engage more deeply with the material,” and provides the practical foundation needed to retain information and apply knowledge on exams. While problem-based learning is better for students in the long run and leads to improved performance later, it might cause a degree of discomfort in the moment. In looking at students’ perception of their own learning, students felt like they were learning more when being lectured, rather than doing problems and engaging in project/ problem-based learning. Although students who use problem-solving and group skills to acquire information encode knowledge on a deeper level, they often feel uncertain about their own retention because they are not being explicitly told the information. In his research, Vinces worked to identify a way that this initial resistance to problem-based learning, what he described to be a type of “culture shock,” could be remedied. Eventually, with student survey reports and interviews, he was able to identify that through gradual acclimation and realization of the benefits, students grow comfortable with the approach and persist longer in biology and other STEM fields. With continued exposure to practice problems, group work, and opportunities to earn better grades, students will soon become intrinsically motivated to participate in class, work with others, and push themselves to showcase their expertise. One way in which this can be implemented is by giving students rewards for participation, group work, and practice, and then gradually transitioning them to taking part in these activities for their benefit and without reinforcement. It is crucial for N.U. not to neglect this issue. Weinberg advisors such as Professor Vinces experience firsthand the struggle that some students endure with courses such as Introductory Biology. Vinces mentioned that students in separate sections of a single class at N.U. have expressed dissatisfaction with the fact that their peers had instructors offering a higher frequency of graded assessments such as homework and quizzes, as opposed to their own curriculum that relies on midterms and a final examination. He continued by stating that some classrooms exhibit a “climate where students can more easily ask questions.” These disparities can be easily addressed at our school with communication between teachers and a focus on the benefits of demonstrative and problem-based learning. With the addition of the recently acquired grant aimed towards furthering research on various types of learning settings, N.U. can work towards these improvements in Introductory Biology, and all classrooms.

Through gradual acclimation and realization of the benefits, students grow comfortable with the approach and persist longer in biology and other STEM fields.

title: Monstrous Masculinities, Male Angst, and Adolescent Development in the Twilight Saga
notes: The thesis introduction, per the author's Q&A in the contributors section (printed page 115). Advisor from "Faculty Adviser" on the opening page. Footnote blocks and pull quotes are moved to paragraph breaks. Includes a bibliography and a list of works consulted.
text:
Monstrous Masculinities, Male Angst, and Adolescent Development in the Twilight Saga by Juliet Jacques

Department of English Faculty Adviser: Nick Davis

Introduction Over the past two decades, the Twilight series has become a staple of popular culture, with an enormous and dedicated fanbase. The “vampire versus werewolf” or “Edward versus Jacob” debate is almost universally recognizable, especially among fans of 2010s Young Adult (Y.A.) media. However, fans and critics alike miss a crucial element of analysis (or obsession) in Twilight. Inseparable from this study of masculinity is the related issue of ra­ cialization, which is especially salient for werewolf and love interest Jacob Black — Edward’s chief rival in the franchise from both a romantic and species (coded as racial) standpoint.

1 See Melissa Click’s Bitten by Twilight for a comprehensive collection of essays on Twilight’s influence on fandom culture, Holly­ wood teenage idols, and the commodification of literature.

Twilight may at first appear as an un­ usual object of literary analysis. The saga has attracted no lack of criticism, ranging all the way from its depiction of unhealthy teenage relationships to the quality of its writing. However, the series has had a profound impact on the entire Y.A. genre of popular culture. Many scholars cred­ it Twilight as paving the way for other popular franchises such as Fifty Shades of Grey, which originated as Twilight fanfic­ tion, and other teenage romances such as The Hunger Games, which has continued Twilight’s revival of the Y.A. genre’s in­ terest in tropes such as love triangles and strong, independent, teenage heroines.1 It is clear that the series has had an enduring effect on popular culture, cementing it as a cornerstone of Y.A. literature. Due to the immeasurable impact of both the original novels and the multimedia phenomenon they launched, Twilight deserves its own field of scholarship. Millions of readers and viewers have seen and internalized the saga’s surprisingly new themes surround­ ing gender roles and masculinity. Literary analysis of Twilight’s language, character construction, recurring metaphors, and Gothic antecedents can uncover the spe­ cific themes and messaging that have made Twilight such an enduring, influential, and beloved series. Furthermore, it can help us to understand the way that Y.A. literature engages with and reshapes representations of adolescent masculinity.

Analysis of the Current State of Twilight Scholarship The field of Twilight scholarship is quite young, with scholarship beginning around 2010 after the first of the novels were published in 2006 and the first film was released in 2008. Even so, in the decade since the start of the field, there has been enormous growth in scholarship and perspectives surrounding Twilight, with a growing confidence in approaching this series through various modes of literary analysis. Thus far, Twilight scholarship has followed two main avenues: close-reading analyses that examine the language and rhetoric of the texts independently as well as more sociological approaches that think about elements of the series in conversa­ tion with the success and reception of the franchise. The field is, in general, con­ flicted about how much these approaches should overlap or rely on each other. It appears as if the inclination to analyze the Twilight novels as literary texts separately from their corresponding cultural impact only came later in the 2010s. After all, it takes courage to admit to studying this series as literature.

2 It is interesting that many of the first books on Twilight were published by McFarland, including a third book, Wilson’s Seduced by Twilight. The publisher is especially known for its books on popular culture and media.

The first books and essays written on Twilight focus heavily on the sociological and cultural aspects of the series. For ex­ ample, Amy Clarke’s The Twilight Mystique (2010) and Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing Twilight: Critical Essays on What’s at Stake in a Post-Vampire World (2011) explore the overall series through the lens of its recent success.2 The essays in these books are often reflexive in that they think both about how Twilight is influenced by popu­ lar culture norms and stereotypes as well as how it influences them in return. Thus, in these earlier books, it is harder to separate literary analysis from sociological analysis. These articles act almost as primary sourc­ es because they differ so much from the intricate, detailed analyses of language and theme that come later. In fact, early authors such as Benning (2011) acknowledge that they are writing at the very beginning of the field and suggest many potential topics for later authors. These older articles often cover both a sociological analysis of the readers and culture surrounding Twilight as well as more literary elements of the text itself, particularly genre tropes and influ­ ential literary predecessors. However, this seemingly comprehensive approach actu­ ally weakens the literary analysis because scholars are unwilling to look at Twilight’s language and themes for their own merit, separately from the ensuing reception and sociological aspects. To better understand the success and appeal of the series and its legacy in Y.A. fiction, we should also view the textual elements themselves as insight­ ful and intentional.

Indeed, as more articles were writ­ ten and published, the field became more varied and more accommodating of close-reading methodologies. For exam­ ple, Anne Morey’s collection Genre, Recep­ tion, and Adaptation in the ‘Twilight’ Series (2012) looks and reads much differently from earlier collections in its willingness to analyze the literary aspects of the series separately from the sociological. Claudia Bucciferro’s collection The Twilight Saga: Exploring the Global Phenomenon (2014) also demonstrates this growth, though it is no­ table that studies of Twilight remain con­ fined to para-academic publishers and not major university presses. Overall, these later books divide the two types of analysis more than previous collections — a trend that only grows throughout the rest of the decade. Morey’s introduction separates the articles by subject matter: first looking at genre and narrative within Twilight, then turning to the reception of Twilight as a cultural phenomenon, and finally study­ ing adaptation and film. Significantly, Morey emphasizes the importance of studying novels in the romance genre — a well-established practice within literary and cultural studies, especially in the wake of Janice Radway’s foundational text Reading the Romance (1991), but not previously applied to Twilight, at least in print. As with Morey’s, Bucciferro’s book is divided into sections for articles on spe­ cific areas of study, such as fandom and reception, gender in Twilight, and looking beyond the franchise. This last section is particularly interesting, as it recognizes Y.A. novels as their own genre that de­ serves analysis by examining common themes and tropes across a varied section of series and franchises.

3  Examples of this common tendency include Torkelson’s Violence, Agency, and the Women of Twilight (2011), Rocha’s Wife, Mother, Vampire: The Female Role in the Twilight Series (2014), Durham’s Blood, Lust and Love: Interrogating Gender Violence in the Twilight Phenomenon (2011), and similar critiques cited later in this thesis. 4 Ashley Benning’s “How Old are You?” Representations of Age in the Saga (2011) argues that the lack and ineffectiveness of parental figures in Twilight allows Bella the independence to come of age.

Other clear patterns emerge as schol­ arship on Twilight evolves. Early literature focused on critiquing antifeminist and mi­ sogynist aspects of the series, arguing that Bella was forced to submit to a dominant patriarchal culture.3 After this initial ap­ proach, and likely in response to the cul­ tural backlash and hatred for the series, an opposing, postfeminist movement arose, wherein scholars began to look at the ways in which Bella could still represent a progressive, autonomous character. These two reactions formed the basis for the field of scholarship, but authors then quickly moved beyond these “good” and “bad” bi­ naries, and scholarship began to be more detailed, intricate, and creative. Twilight scholarship became more diversified as authors looked beyond the more obvious aspects of the series, such as the portrayal of unhealthy teenage relationships, to take a more nuanced look at gender roles and relationships, albeit with a predominant interest in the female gender. Scholarship also began looking at Twilight as a coming- of-age series or bildungsroman in which Bella finds her place and identity in the world.4 Whereas earlier authors wrote broadly about the series, later authors began filling in the gaps, finding more intricacies and subtleties. For example, Nicole Willms, writing in Bucciferro’s collection, discusses race, masculinity, and rivalry in the series, and Sara Day, as a contributor to Morey’s anthology, argues that Bella’s increasing passivity can be un­ derstood through the lens of what she calls “narrative intimacy” and her weakening relationship with the reader as the series progresses. Both of these articles lay the key groundwork for readings I pursue later in this thesis.

The Limits of Current Approaches to the Study of Gender and Masculinity Within this emerging field of Twilight literary scholarship, one subfield looks at portrayals of gender and masculinity using two common approaches. The first refer­ ences Gothic tropes and historical charac­ teristics in relation to gender and sexuality. For example, Budruweit (2016) argues that Twilight sanitizes Gothic monsters, instead making women’s uncontrolled bodies into the primary sites of the “mon­ strous.” In contrast, Moruzi (2012) gives a postfeminist reading of Bella, arguing that the incorporation of Gothic characteristics intensifies the romance, adding danger and allowing Bella to explore her desires and identity, which can be messy without being monstrous. Moruzi argues that as­ pects of Edward such as self-discipline, in­ experience, and “vegetarianism” (Twilight’s language for vampires who refuse to feed off humans) shift the power dynamics of their relationship, obligating the male part­ ner to the stereotypically feminine task of relentless self-monitoring, and by contrast allowing Bella more control and autonomy.

5 There is a large, in-depth body of literature on this Gothic tradition, especially for Twilight’s 19th century vampiric counterparts as Stoker’s Dracula (1897) and Le Fanu’s Carmilla (1872). Just a few of the essays on this topic include Craft’s “Kiss Me with those Red Lips”: Gender and Inversion in Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1984), Signoretti’s Repossessing the Body – Transgressive Desire in “Carmilla” and “Dracula” (1996), and Schaffer’s “A Wilde Desire Took Me”: The Homoerotic History of Dracula (1994).

Beyond short-changing the texts under review, these Bella-centric approaches to the series lead scholars to ignore masculine characters’ questions and anxieties about their own performance of masculinity and the way male identity relates to the supernatural. “

“

These two examples demonstrate the common elements scholars often de­ fer to when talking about the Gothic in conjunction with Twilight. These generic tropes, whether physical (blood), moral or behavioral (self-control), affective (desire), or specifically sexual (including queerness, or an alleged lack of queerness) can be cat­ egorized as disparate yet closely connected aspects of the Gothic, all of which center the body in some way. Desire for blood and desire for sex always go hand in hand in this tradition: The act of desiring and drinking blood is often erotic, representing other sexual desires, usually those deemed devi­ ant.5 For example, scholars such as Moruzi (2012) and Lindén (2013) argue that the desire for blood is replaced or subordinated by the desire for sex in these more recent, Y.A.-style reinterpretations of vampirism. However, this approach again fails to look at major, masculine characters such as Ed­ ward as individuals who confront other conflicts and wrestle with their own stages of development, separate from their ro­ mantic relationships. Thus, critical lenses such as postfeminism and others that pre­ vail in Twilight scholarship may not do full analytical justice to these characters.

Within this Gothic approach, schol­ ars also look at Twilight in terms of its po­ tential historical influences from 19th-cen­ tury British novels and their often Byronic heroes. Common comparisons in studies such as Nancy Reagin’s Twilight and Histo­ ry (2010) include the love interests from Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Eyre (1847), and Wuthering Heights (1847).6 These texts are often chosen because of overt refer­ ences in the Twilight novels. However, scholarship too often conflates Twilight’s themes and internal dynamics with those of its famous predecessors without paying enough attention to their differences or, once more, thinking more forwardly about masculinity and male characters. In other words, while literary-historical analysis foregrounding 19th-century antecedents of Twilight is an interesting and fruitful approach, there is a gap in that literature connecting these historical perspectives with how Edward thinks of himself, his masculinity, and his quasi-filial relation to his vampire “creator,” Carlisle. In addition, there is a dearth of scholarship that reads Twilight with its more monstrous, Gothic predecessors, an issue that will be discussed more in Chapter 2. Because Bella is the pri­ mary narrator, scholars are more likely to think critically about her actions and moti­ vations while taking Edward’s at face val­ ue, even if he is Twilight’s clearest anchor within the Gothic tradition specifically and perhaps in 19th-century character tropes more broadly.

6 For a variety of articles on this topic, see Parke and Wilson’s Theorizing Twilight (2010), specifically the second part of the col­ lection titled: Once Upon a Twilight: Fairy Tales, Byronic (Anti) Heroes, Post-Feminist Romance, and Growing Up in a Twilight World.

The other common approach to looking at gender and masculinity moves away from literary and cultural paths to argue that characters such as Edward are most interesting for how they embody the characteristics and desires of current soci­ ety. This approach, whether or not it re­ flects the sociological and reception-based tendencies in early Twilight criticism, also considers the way Twilight both influences and is influenced by societal values. For example, Christensen’s article Blood Absti­ nent Vampires and the Women Who Consume Them (2013) argues that these 21st-century vampires represent a desirable Other, an antiseptic epitome of consumer culture in explicit contrast to Gothic messiness. In Twilight, the Cullen family is inhumanly beautiful and perfect: a collective para­ gon, to which other characters, as well as readers, aspire. In Mukherjea’s My Vampire Boyfriend: Postfeminism, “Perfect” Masculini­ ty, and the Contemporary Appeal of Paranor­ mal Romance (2011) she argues that these vampire boyfriends present a “perfect” mix of masculinity, embodying white, old-fash­ ioned, gentlemanly, and protective values without crossing a line into patriarchal creepiness or overtly controlling behavior (in Twilight alone, Bella describes Edward as “perfect” over 30 times). Characters such as Edward also juggle values from multiple eras and classes. This combination allows female characters to perform patriarchal norms of femininity while also gaining freedom from societal values and explor­ ing their own independence. Once again, articles like these omit any focus on mas­ culinity or male angst, instead centering anxieties around postfeminism and how to be feminist. The two examples I have cited, though seemingly very different, get close to the issue of men’s anxiety around mas­ culinity and growth, specifically Edward’s, but never actually address it. Christensen focuses only on the 21st-century aspects of vampires, without thinking about their influences from previous eras. Mukherjea acknowledges that characters like Edward are juggling values from multiple eras but focuses only on how that confusion affects their romantic partners. They argue that Edward and other male characters always portray masculinity “perfectly” without considering how this pressure to perform may affect them internally, even though the original novels clearly indicate that struggle.

Midnight Sun further confirms that there are more elements at play in the series than Ed­ ward’s relationship with Bella.

Beyond short-changing the texts un­ der review, these Bella-centric approaches to the series lead scholars to ignore mas­ culine characters’ questions and anxieties about their own performance of mascu­ linity and the way male identity relates to the supernatural. More broadly, these interpretive angles perpetuate patriarchal assumptions and norms around the in­ fallibility and confidence of cis-heterosex­ ual men. Much of Edward’s inner conflict centers around his own relationship with vampirism, aging, and eternal adolescence, rather than being focused solely on Bella. Distancing our analysis of Edward from Bel­ la’s perspective will reveal his own deep dis­ comfort and insecurity, foregrounding his intense self-scrutiny rather than Bella’s sec­ ond-hand and often idealized observations.

“

”

As a subject of analysis, masculinity regularly receives less focus than women and feminism, with particular gaps around cis, straight, masculine characters. By paying attention to these gaps and studying these types of masculinities, we can gain a better understanding of how these characters internalize and perpetuate toxic patriarchal norms, but also offer alternative masculinities that already exist.

In reality, as a very old vampire, Ed­ ward is navigating both these historical values and current ones. The messiness of these past and present pressures reveals how some forms of masculine and patriar­ chal anxieties have not changed completely for men over this long historical timespan. The past and present often unstably coexist for Edward, although Twilight criticism of­ ten does try to partition the past from the present. We need to look at how maturity is portrayed within an unchanging but eter­ nal vampire body and how Edward views his maturation in relation to both humans, such as Bella, and other vampires, like Carlisle. Edward’s relationship to growth is fraught because his expected character development and societal pressure contrast with his allegedly “perfect,” unchangeable, and impermeable exterior. In other words, as Edward’s life changes and society chang­ es around him, his appearance cannot also change in parallel. The mythology around vampires as unchanging and set in stone both physically and psychologically at the age they are “turned” (when they are bitten) contributes to his general anxiety and insecurity about his inhumanness and inability to change. Because scholarship focuses on Bella’s relationships and char­ acter growth, we are currently missing an understanding of how Edward has his own anxieties around morality and masculinity and how being a vampire not only “freez­ es” his development, but also prompts his constant uneasiness and self-questioning. This pattern within Twilight scholarship also points to a broader gap in masculinity scholarship within the field of gender stud­ ies as a whole, including its engagement with literature. As a subject of analysis, masculinity regularly receives less focus than women and feminism, with particular gaps around cis, straight, masculine char­ acters. By paying attention to these gaps and studying these types of masculinities, we can gain a better understanding of how these characters internalize and perpetuate toxic patriarchal norms, but also offer al­ ternative masculinities that already exist.

To gain a fuller understanding of Ed­ ward and the diverse — and perhaps con­ tradictory — ways masculinity is presented within the series, we need to think of him as an independent and fallible character rather than only as an ideal romantic inter­ est for Bella. This, of course, is inherently difficult because Bella’s voice offers our only direct access to Edward’s headspace until Midnight Sun directly engages his per­ spective. But even before that point, when we consciously step back from Bella’s nar­ ration and cast doubt on her omniscience, the first Twilight novel does offer ways to take stock of Edward’s feelings and conflicts in ways that are not solely about Bella. By decentering Bella, even in the texts she nar­ rates, we can glean suggestive information about Edward’s other relationships, such as the father-son or perhaps creator-creature relationship with Carlisle, whom he often looks to as a role model.

In tandem with this new approach, we need to turn to other, often ignored Gothic aspects to understand Edward as an independent, three-dimensional character. As mentioned earlier, Twilight scholarship always reverts to Gothic vampiric tropes associated with sex and desire. Instead, we should also look at Gothic elements such as the interior versus the exterior, the du­ ality of identity, and the monster within. Midnight Sun’s emphasis on the monstrous Gothic solidifies Twilight’s connections to foundational novels like Dracula, as well as revealing its nods to other kinds of Gothic novels, such as Robert Louis Stevenson’s Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1886) and Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890).

Twilight’s complex masculine love interests and characters are at odds with the traditional heroes of romance novels by even being allowed to grow and change, rather than offering a fantastical, uniform, and “perfect” symbol of masculinity. Twi­ light’s massive, global readership means that the themes and characters within the series have an incalculable influence on fans, pop culture, and the genre of Y.A. fiction. Studying Edward well outside the terms of his romantic relationship with Bella serves not just to help us better un­ derstand his character, but to provide a whole new lens through which to under­ stand all masculine characters in the series.

“Twilight’s complex masculine love interests and characters are at odds with the traditional heroes of romance novels by even being allowed to grow and change, rather than offering a fantastical, uniform, and ‘perfect’ symbol of masculinity.”

Although it is easy to see Edward and Jacob as the pop cultural movement tends to por­ tray them, and which is exacerbated by the films, particularly New Moon and Eclipse, they are so much more than two dimen­ sional, hypersexualized, and idolized love interests.7 As the franchise has emphasized and commercialized the love triangle, the characters themselves are forced into stereotypical roles to portray hegemonic, toxic representations of masculinity. In parallel, the seemingly equal competition and dislike between the werewolves and the vampires is unbalanced and entirely due to the actions of the Cullens. When we take a closer look at the novels, we see a much more complex version of these char­ acters, many of whom do not fit into the masculine tropes that critics often assume the series to be arguing for, as well as a more nuanced portrayal of race.

Ultimately, all the masculine char­ acters in Twilight, both supernatural and human, are part of a complex system of social dynamics, each navigating their own relationship to masculinity and patriarchal norms, and each invites and deserves more attention and investigation than we often are willing to give characters credit for in a seemingly banal, generic teenage romance novel. As Nina Auerbach argues in her foundational book Our Vampires, Ourselves (1995), “every age embraces the vampire it needs” (145).8 Edward is certainly one of the most prominent vampires of this generation and so analyzing his own trials and tribulations with adolescence, matu­ ration, and the performance of masculin­ ity will perhaps help us understand why so many people gravitate toward Twilight, and what about the teenage experience in the 2000s has made it such an influential and beloved series.◆

7 See Cunningham (2012) for a thoughtful analysis of the changes between the novels and their adaptations. Beyond the ways the movies alter the narratives, even the promotional campaigns rewrite the modes and relations of different masculinities as I have outlined them in this project. For example, the hugely prevalent posters advertising the films feature Edward and Jacob looking brooding and dark, with Bella posed in between, directly in the spirit of the patterns Radway set forth but which Meyer compli­ cates. 8 Auerbach is an omnipresent, influential authority in the field of vampire studies. Her detailed and wide-ranging book documents and analyzes literary vampires from the 19th and 20th centuries, using the varied representations of vampires throughout the decades as a lens to study cultural history. This quote in particular is cited ubiquitously in vampire scholarship, and so this thesis would not be complete without following in this tradition.

title: The Center: Where Art and Science Converge
notes: Profile of the Center for Scientific Studies in the Arts, a collaboration between Northwestern and the Art Institute of Chicago, quoting co-director Professor Aggelos Katsaggelos and Dr. Maria Kokkori. The contents page lists it as "The Center: Where Art and Science Convergent".
text:
The Center: Where Art and Science Converge by Maggie Rose Baron

Professor Aggelos Katsaggelos

Dr. Maria Kokkori

In one of the thousands of art muse­ ums around the world, an onlooker stands in front of an oil painting and notices tiny blisters on the surface of the artwork. The surrounding paintings may be affected in a similar way, but to a degree imperceptible to the human eye. In either instance, the study of these damages is vital to the choic­ es that conservation scientists make to protect and restore works of art. So, what causes the bubbles that form beneath the surface of oil paintings?

The Center for Scientific Studies in the Arts (hereafter referred to as “the Cen­ ter”), a collaboration between Northwest­ ern University (N.U.) and the Art Institute of Chicago, tackles these kinds of questions through the incorporation of technologies from a range of fields including materials science, engineering, and chemistry.

Professor Aggelos Katsag­ gelos, co-director of the Center and professor of Elec­ trical and Computer Engineering at N.U., says the Center’s goal is “to serve the cultural heritage and general community … but along the way, [we] es­ tablish scientific methodology that can be of use in many other fields: scientific fields, fields of investigation.”

The Center’s research is object-based, which Senior Scientist and Associate Re­ search Professor Maria Kokkori describes as “an art historical method that centers physical study of a work of art as a primary text.” This kind of research, Kokkori says, “can provide information about the chem­ ical composition … as well as insights into artists techniques, and damages and repairs over an artwork’s lifetime.”

Take the oil painting question. Through the use of X-Ray and fluores­ cence techniques, as well as the chemical analysis of the materials used by artist Georgia O’Keeffe in her oil paintings, re­ searchers determined that the blisters in these paintings are caused by metal soaps that form through chemical reactions in the paint.

The discovery prompted the research­ ers to develop a hand-held tool that can map works of art for these protrusions to determine the conditions that may cause them to change. The project, while inspired by a physical work of art, impacts far more than simply the understanding of soap bubbles on a single O’Keeffe painting.

To serve the cultural heritage and general community … but along the way, [we] establish scientific methodology that can be of use in many other fields: scientific fields, fields of investigation.

”

”

Projects have ranged from the investigation of different painting pigments and techniques to the discovery of ancient Roman writing hidden in bookbinding. With each project, the Center expands the breadth of knowl­ edge in areas of conservation science and develops new technologies and techniques for broader applications.

According to Kokkori, the Center provides training and mentorship in con­ servation science to students and early-ca­ reer researchers in an effort to “lead the next wave of advances” in the field.

The advancements are bolstered by the Center’s collaborative nature. While the scientific techniques, technologies, and expertise are mostly housed within N.U., outside institutions can also tap into these resources to explore their own ques­ tions and projects. According to Katsag­ gelos, the Center aims to “democratize” the technology by giving museums and libraries access to N.U.’s physical instru­ ments as well as the algorithms devel­ oped by Center researchers.

The Center is, quite fittingly, at the center of a range of disciplines. They might seem unconnected in other contexts, but without each and every field included within the institution, the Center’s work would not be possible.

“This field of conservation science and the Center … is a unique contribution to sometimes make the invisible visible,” Kokkori says. “But also to make us think, in a broader, different way, what our knowl­ edge, no matter from which discipline we are coming from, can contribute to expand our knowledge on the study of art.”

Currently, the Center is funded by the Mellon Foundation. However, as that funding draws to a close, the faculty at the Center are working to keep it thriv­ ing long-term. According to Katsaggelos, establishing permanent faculty positions within the Center may be key to its future.

“We can be here for the very long run,” Katsaggelos says. “It’s endless, the number of problems … that one can address.”

The [disciplines] might seem unconnected in other contexts, but without each and every field included within the institution, the Center’s work would not be possible.”

”

title: God, Absurdism, and Law: Suffering and Meaning in the Works of Nietzsche, Dostoevsky, and Camus
notes: Senior thesis excerpt. Advisor from "Faculty Adviser" on the opening page; the contents page gives the department as "Comparative Literature Studies". Footnote blocks and pull quotes are moved to paragraph breaks. Includes a bibliography. The contributors section (printed page 114) has a Q&A with the author.
text:
God, Absurdism, and Law: Suffering and Meaning in the Works of Nietzsche, Dostoevsky, and Camus by Violet Decker

Department of Comparative Literary Studies

Faculty Adviser: Jonas Rosenbrück

Introduction

There are three powers, only three powers on earth, capable of conquering and holding captive forever the conscience of these feeble rebels, for their own happiness — these powers are miracle, mystery, and authority.

— Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov

In “The Grand Inquisitor,” a story told by the character of Ivan Karamazov in The Brothers Karamazov and one of Dosto­ evsky’s most celebrated passages, Christ is reprimanded for his choice to give human beings free will. In turn, says the Inquisitor, humanity is destined to suffer: “Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man will not consent to live and will sooner destroy himself … There is nothing more seductive for man than the freedom of his conscience, but there is nothing more tormenting either” (Dostoevsky 254). Through its transforming characters, religious and judicial themes, and elaborate musings of life and death, Dostoevsky’s novel is an account of both the depths and heights of humanity when faced with an existence of freedom. 77 years later, Albert Camus’ monological novel The Fall draws upon these same themes of freedom, judgment, and faith to also showcase the madness that results from total freedom and the dissonance between the legal system and man’s true nature. Each work calls to find reconciliation between these disparate needs — though we desire feeling as though our lives embodied freedom and had meaning, we require some kind of unifying system to live under, without which we find existence lacking all sense. Ultimately, Dostoevsky points to faith in Christ and practicing active love as the only solution to this paradox. Camus urges an acceptance of the paradox with no finality (“the Absurd”) as fuel to continue man’s instinct towards art and rebellion — a mindset that will best allow for both progress and relief.

Both Dostoevsky and Camus stand in a relationship with one of modernity’s most trenchant thinkers of the links be­ tween suffering, freedom, and meaning: Friedrich Nietzsche. Nietzschean propos­ als, notably the exigency to find meaning in suffering and the will to power, create a foundational claim for our need for limit­ ing systems despite the blatant inadequacy and self-denial found in judicial and reli­ gious frameworks. His assertion that one must undergo personal transformation in order to reach self-fulfillment and meaning further the notion that preconceived sys­ tems limit this search, and it is this notion to which Dostoevsky and Camus both re­ spond in their literary works.

Nietzsche

Freedom and The Three Metamorphoses Nietzsche’s The Three Metamorphoses out­ lines his basis for a meaningful existence — the continual creation of new ideals and ways of life. Nietzsche affirms that this must come from personal experience: “Breaking with the norms of the past is meaningful for us only if we had previ­ ously valued them … Otherwise, we are merely dressing the norms of the past in new clothing” (Gordon).

Central to this transformation is his depiction of three distinct stages of de­ velopment: the camel, the lion, and the child. One begins as the burden-seeking camel, both consciously and unconscious­ ly searching for experiences that give rise to suffering. This asserts existence, while starting the drive to find meaning in suf­ fering, which for Nietzsche is the major intent of life and a bandage for the wounds of total freedom.

1 The Nietzschean concept of “the Great Dragon” is those values and beliefs culturally upheld that are given to us as moral and right, without demanding personal experience to find agreement with them. They serve as temptation of the natural inclination for a guiding framework — but “the rebel resists this temptation by embracing uncertainty” (Illing 34). He recognized that in these pre-existing frameworks that have a hold on morality, law, culture, religion, and science, there does exist something mankind needs in order to survive: a limiting model in which to point our creative, intellectual, and emotional energies. However, without continuing to reflect on and modify these frameworks through personal introspection and experience, they render society and the individual stuck and suffering.

The camel then becomes a lion when a more aggressive, freedom-seeking ethos comes to the forefront. The lion demands victory and becomes its own master: “‘Thou shalt’ is the name of the Great Dragon.1 But the spirit of the lion says ‘I will’” (Nietzsche, 2006, 17). The lion embodies an intent to­ wards freedom, creation, and autonomy that moves beyond the search for suffering.

Finally, the lion becomes a child by reclaiming humility and a childlike sense of wonder that can give rise to new poten­ tialities: “Why must the preying lion still become a child? The child is innocence and forgetting, a new beginning … a first movement” (Nietzsche, 2006, 17). It is nec­ essary, then, to access a childlike spirit in order to free oneself from the chains of ex­ ternal systems and allow for new creation.

Mercy

Mercy remains … the prerogative of the strongest … Whenever a community gains in power and pride, its penal code becomes more lenient, while the moment it is weakened or endangered the harshest methods of the past are revived.

— Friedrich Nietzsche, The Birth of Tragedy and the Genealogy of Morals

It is paramount to note Nietzsche’s rec­ ognition that the law operates in tandem with its nation’s current social and polit­ ical landscape. Because the law operates as a universal system, its treatment of the individual depends not squarely on the accused’s behavior or circumstance, but on a larger framework embodying aspects outside of any individual’s control. The above quote recognizes that the legal sys­ tem asserts dominance over its members in times of strife by minimizing leniency and exercising its domination in full.

In such scenarios, despite the law’s supposed aim of enforcing universal safety and morality for the betterment of society, this notion of separateness and disconnect permeates the courtroom and legal system: the courtroom as separate from the exter­ nal world, the judge as separate from the criminal, and the accused as separate from the accuser. If mercy is given more fre­ quently in times of political and social ease, there is a split between the framework of law and the assertion of universal and hu­ manistic values.

The Will to Power and Morality/ Law/Religion

According to Nietzsche, he who wants to be a creator of good and of evil, must first destroy all values.

— Albert Camus, The Rebel: An Essay on Man in Revolt

The self-exploration and individual per­ spective involved in breaking past “the Great Dragon” is, in essence, the asser­ tion of the self. Those already in power achieved their position through the will, and therefore, it was a solitary act that then makes it impossible to ensure that societal laws can account completely for the good of the universal. This is why Nietzsche stresses the importance of individual re­ flection and rebellion against pre-existing systems. By doing so, one asserts their own will to power, which Nietzsche sees as a major solution to the paradox and distress of freedom.

2 “To behold suffering gives pleasure, but to cause another to suffer affords an even greater pleasure” (Nietzsche, 1956, 198).

This driving force is a major element of both The Brothers Karamazov and The Fall. Dostoevsky’s characters in particular “are engaged in a desperate and unending struggle to disentangle their own image of themselves from the world’s image of them as preliminary to achieving an attitude to themselves independent of the world’s at­ titude” (Jones 100). In both novels, charac­ ters attempt to assert their own existence and dominance by seeking superiority and action both within and against the legal system. The desire both for and against justice is therefore seen as a mere illusion that is fundamentally the will to power. Rebelling against these systems, which affirm the collective but destroy the indi­ vidual, is an assertion of our consciousness and autonomy as individuals.

Suffering and Meaning Nietzsche asserts that we enjoy both experiencing and inflicting suffering,2 for it operates from our will to power. For example, monks suffer through self-denial and thereby gain a prideful kind of pleasure in which they view themselves worthy of judging others for not living by the same asceticism. Through this lens, the powers which Dostoevsky writes could “conquer” people’s consciences are really frameworks that give meaning to suffering. They attempt to impose meaning onto our per­ plexing experience of freedom and pain. In actuality, “what makes people rebel against suffering is not really suffer­ ing itself but the senselessness of suffering” (Nietzsche, 1956, 205). With this in mind, the frameworks (religious, legal, intellectual, and creative) may be consid­ ered a sort of bearable comprehension for meaningless suffering. Nietzsche claims, for example, “the ascetic ideal arises from the protective and curative instinct of a life that is degenerating and yet fighting tooth and nail for its preservation” (Nietzsche, 1956, 256). By accepting religious ideals, one can find a reason to live despite an otherwise miserable or ill existence. Nietzsche also insists that suffering best finds release in mechanical or creative activity. Note how the specific environ­ ments of a prisoner in jail, a criminal in a courtroom, or a novice in a monastery are subdued and involve little movement or mental stimulation. Without any release, one may be more inclined to search for meaning in the framework of legal or religious ideas. Religion and law may then serve as “safety valves” for overwhelming emotion and suffering (Nietzsche, 1956, 276): it places limits on existence to make sense of the body and current circum­ stance. This necessitates living by creation rather than denial: “Nietzsche … belonged to the party which envisioned a society where judges would no longer rule, but where artists/creators would reign” (Du­ vall 551).

Dostoevsky

The Brothers Karamazov and the Characterization of Existential Strivings In The Brothers Karamazov, the character of a cold, loveless, and ultimately murdered father Fyodor Karamazov can be seen as the depths from which his sons attempt to escape. His three sons Dmitri (who chooses to live by instinctual passion and desire), Ivan (who chooses to live solely by rational and intellectual thought), and Alyosha (who follows the path of faith as a novice monk) present three different guiding life frameworks.

3 Nietzsche expressed similar sentiments when speaking of all beliefs and systems we follow: “how can we ever hope to find what we have never looked for? … Our thoughts should grow out of our values with the same necessity as the fruit out of the tree” (Ni­ etzsche, 1956, 150). The ideal path for both Nietzsche and Dostoevsky ought not to be one of ease and following, but the intractable and strong desire to empirically discover our own values, which calls upon the gamut of emotional and practical experience.

Dmitri, the eldest, pursues excesses and pleasures of life. It is notable that he refers to his own self as the “fallen man” (Dostoevsky 107), and similar to what will be examined later in Camus’ The Fall, this references the Bible’s Genesis story of man being relegated from innocent and faithful to disobedient and distanced from God/unity.

Dostoevsky critiques this choice by presenting Dmitri’s arrest for the murder of his father. The impulsive way of life Dmitri has chosen leads to his inevitable downfall, for though it satisfies the self’s desire for pleasure and joy, it neglects the full portrait of life and other people. This results in ostracism and more suffering, and Dostoevsky uses Fyodor’s murder and the legal system to flesh out this realization. Because he has not in fact committed the act, this storyline accomplishes two other distinct aims of Dostoevsky’s work: one, to display the inexorably nonsensical and cru­ el nature of the justice system, and two, to demonstrate through Dmitri’s transforma­ tion — which takes place after the accusal and his time of suffering in the legal system — that the move from disbelief to faith can only be transcended through suffering and must come from personal experience.3

When Dmitri is finally declared guilty, he proclaims, “I swear by God and by his terrible judgment, I am not guilty of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends, have pity on the other woman!” (Dostoevsky 753). It is greatly significant that Dmitri first calls out to God when he learns of his fate, for the novel starts with him living solely for himself. Additionally, he speaks of the others in­ volved in the murder case to show his ex­ istence is now one more aligned with unity than separation.

Dostoevsky’s style often points to the multifaceted aspects of man, sometimes showcasing opposites actually existing more in tandem than typically considered. Phrases such as “the kind of hatred that is only a hair’s breadth from love” and “do you understand that one can kill oneself from a certain kind of ecstasy?” exempli­ fy his point that systems relying on strict rules and judgments, specifically the legal system, cannot possibly accurately account for the complex and contradictory states of human nature (Dostoevsky 114, 115). The act of imprisonment itself can then be concluded to be a type of judgment that re­ stricts man’s character into something that can never reflect the multiple traits and emotions within.

Meanwhile, Dostoevsky’s “furnace of doubt was itself receiving its most memo­ rable fictional expression in the person of Ivan Karamazov” (Jones 25). Ivan, the mid­ dle brother of the family, experiences a tur­ bulent struggle regarding the acceptance of God. He rejects viewing the nature of the world through the lens of faith primarily due to his inability to reconcile the atroci­ ties and suffering of life with an all-loving and all-powerful God. This rational dis­ belief within Ivan makes him a character of metaphysical rebellion.4 He seeks unity between all, similar to people of faith, but has justified a move away from religion be­ cause of it, and instead pursues the avenue of intellectualism and reason. He similarly does not understand the tenets that Christ preached, such as universal love, stating, “I never could understand how it’s possible to love one’s neighbors … occasionally from a distance, but hardly ever up close” (Dosto­ evsky 236). This kind of impersonal focus on the collective as opposed to the unique individual is the same philosophy found in the legal system.

4 This term first appears in Camus’ The Rebel over 70 years later, but distinctly defines a man protesting not against a specific or temporary condition, but against his inescapable condition of living and the whole of creation — a protest against the intrinsic sufferings of existence: “Camus was drawn to figures like Ivan Karamazov because he understood metaphysical revolt as a negation of reality” (Illing 206).

The superiority of any system can only be rightfully known and recognized when one personally rebels against it or experiences its breakdown. “

”

The novel hints that intellectualism leaves much to be desired, which explains Ivan’s lengthy grappling with this subject and eventual descent into madness. He rec­ ognizes the “absurdism” of reality, yet after the arrest of his brother, he cannot find peace in man-made attempts to reconcile this absurdism. Dostoevsky makes a point of characterizing Ivan as a man of youth who revels in this, even stating, “By the age of thirty, I will probably drop the cup [give up on life], even if I haven’t emptied it, and walk away … But until my thirtieth year, I know this for certain, my youth will overcome everything” (Avramenko 230). Though seemingly self-assured, Ivan has not found a guiding principle that he is confident will support him through his life.

Serving as a foil to Ivan’s stark practi­ cal intellectualism, Alyosha is the youngest son who chooses to go in the direction of faith and live in a monastery. In a pivotal scene, he is told by his elder Zosima to at once leave the monastery in order to see and experience more of life:5 “You will have to endure everything before you come back again … You will behold great sorrow, and in this sorrow you will be happy” (Dosto­ evsky 77). He is told that leaving will equip him with the right experiences and suffer­ ing to further unite him with mankind and deepen his faith. It becomes clear through the journeys of each character in the novel that Dostoevsky does not wish for religion to be a dictatorial system like the legal sys­ tem: it is necessary that the universal love he sees as emblematic of Christ is realized on a personal level.

The Necessity of Collapse and Tragedy

Karamazov or Nietzsche only entered the world of death because they wanted to discover the true life. So that by a process of inversion, it is the desperate appeal for order that rings through this insane universe.

— Albert Camus, The Rebel: An Essay on Man in Revolt

Due to Dostoevsky’s notion that personal experience and transformation is necessary to experience Christ, we see each brother undergo a collapse of the previous self and ideology in some way to attain something larger. This is referenced not only through characterization but also through smaller anecdotes and quotations: “Othello’s soul is simply shattered and his whole world view clouded because his ideal is destroyed” (Dostoevsky 380). Destruction is implicat­ ed in the novel as a necessary ingredient to enlightenment and personal connection to universal love. Dmitri’s imprisonment, Ivan’s breakdown, and Alyosha’s encour­ agement to leave the monastery all involve religious experience following a collapse of the ideologies that have carried each brother to adulthood. This also builds on Nietzsche’s encouragement to practice personal rebellious thinking, for the supe­ riority of any system can only be rightfully known and recognized when one per­ sonally rebels against it or experiences its breakdown.6 All characters are forced to undergo a transformative event in order to directly experience this kind of universal love, or Christianity.

5 “The elder sent me to reconcile and unite” (Dostoevsky 196). 6 Grushenka, a young and vivacious woman in the novel, “falls into one of those illnesses that, in Dostoevsky’s works, are at once

“

”

By choosing an imposed collective value system, we sacrifice the individual search for and understanding of truth and meaning.

Camus

Camus and the Absurd While Dostoevsky sees religion as the preferable opposition to law, Camus places religion in the same category as the law: seeking to confine mankind when our very nature resists that at every turn. He renounces this false consolation, turning instead to the only sort of solutions he believes would prevail: “Art and rebellion will only die with the death of the last man on earth” (Camus 1951, 270).

His concept of the Absurd is no more aptly demonstrated than in The Fall, where Camus points out the contradictions and inadequacy of the justice system to account for man’s true nature. The novel, referenc­ ing the Genesis story, demonstrates the crumbling of the illusion of the moral and obedient self; the protagonist Jean-Baptiste Clamence, a retired lawyer, comes to terms with his true nature, which lies at odds with justice.

Once an esteemed lawyer and judge in Paris, Clamence grapples throughout the novel with an event in which he had the opportunity to save a woman from death after witnessing her jump from a bridge, but chose not to. Clamence hides behind a veneer, acting as someone who imposes morality and fairness upon all of society. Yet again, this references the concept dis­ played in The Brothers Karamazov: that by choosing an imposed collective value sys­ tem, we sacrifice the individual search for and understanding of truth and meaning. Our response to the absurd can be total ni­ hilism, extricating oneself through pre-ex­ isting systems, or rebellion and art.

Clamence lives with neither grace nor justice yet acts as though he is enforcing the latter. He kills without directly partak­ ing in the action of killing and embodies the Nietzschean concept of the will to power. The criminal and the judge, much like the rebel or intellectual and the intel­ lectual or religious ascetic, are divided in their aims. One works within a system, and one attempts escape by living by their only personally relatable value: the assertion of their self-consciousness and existence.

the sign of intense spiritual conflict and the harbinger of renewal. After five weeks of suffering, during one of which she is uncon­ scious, she emerges ‘very much changed’” (Paris 129).

7 “When I see a new face, something in me sounds the alarm. ‘Slow! Danger!’ Even when the attraction is strongest, I am on my guard” (Camus, 1956, 11).

Away from the court, Clamence expe­ riences a total lack of unity with, and fear of, people around him.7 He states that he has desired his job in order to feel superior: “If fate had forced me to choose between work at a lathe or a roofer, don’t worry, I’d have chosen the roofs and become ac­ quainted with dizziness. Coalbine, ships’ holds, undergrounds, grottoes, pits were repulsive to me” (Camus 1956, 24). This admittance is noteworthy because Cla­ mence’s job is supposedly one that instills equal treatment and punishment as well as works to maintain a moral and just society, but he himself desires domination. When Clamence does not go after the women, this strengthens his admittance of feeling so comfortable being both literally and metaphorically above others that he does not mind if others are harmed or even killed in the process of getting him there. Further, in order for Clamence to continue acting as the role of judge he depends on a continual supply of others who are to “fall” and be punished: one cannot exist without the other.

The Fall as Legal and Ascetic Critique Clamence is presented as a protagonist who has full awareness of himself and his motives. He contrasts heavily with the character of Ivan, who professes “I made up my mind long ago not to understand” (Dostoevsky 243). Whereas one witnesses at first glance the battle between good and evil in The Fall, the battle appears to be between the devil and God in The Brothers Karamazov.

However, “Clamence seems to speak for Camus in denouncing the religion of Christ as a merciless cult of Judgment, which has made of the cross a kind of judge’s gavel” (Sharpe 155). Clamence has accepted his duplicity and has full self-awareness of the gulf between his true self and the imposed rules and morality his career has him follow. Because of this awareness, he hoists himself to a position in which he sees himself as a rightful judge. He knows, as preached by Zosima in The Brothers Karamazov,8 that he is equal to the criminal. By acknowledging his own du­ plicity and guilt, he makes the move from being a singular to universal figure, and can then by his logic judge others, because he is simultaneously judging himself. It is pre­ cisely this awareness that seems to make a mockery of both the justice system and re­ ligion. Clamence’s reflections allow him to stand outside both systems, asserting that the only truthful and knowable element is his own drive and consciousness.

Conclusion Clamence’s ability to see the totality and duplicity of himself offers a self-knowledge not demonstrated by any character in The Brothers Karamazov.9 He is able to assuage himself of guilt by fully understanding himself. Camus presents this as a possible means to “salvation” (salvation meaning, in this sense, freedom from the awareness of Absurdity).

Zosima claims that “as soon as you sincerely make yourself responsible for everything and for all men, you will see at once that it is really so, and that you are to blame for every one and for all things” (Avramenko 20).10 Clamence does precise­ ly this, and by acknowledging his baseness, he finds personal redemption that allows him to then play the part of a judge. The justice system, however, while claiming to seek unity, separates people from each other, puts guilt only on the trespasser, and locks him away, enforcing an overarching disconnect that gives rise to more univer­ sal suffering and search for meaning. The characterization of Clamence shows his true nature to operate entirely outside of this belief system — he represents an un­ derstanding that human nature is bigger than the systems it finds itself existing under. This proves to be his true salvation. He goes so far as to say that Jesus, too, was not altogether innocent, which is why he accepted his crucifixion.

8 “Make yourself responsible for all the sins of men” (Dostoevsky 320) 9 The only instance that bears resemblance is when Fyodor claims, “It always seems to me, when I go somewhere, that I am lower than everyone else and that they all take me for a buffoon —  so let me indeed play the buffoon, because all of you, to me, are lower and stupider than I am” (Dostoevsky 86). While he does not acknowledge his own duplicity or contradictory nature, he immerses himself in the ‘play,’ giving himself over to the illusory mask of his personality. 10 Recall Fyodor, also, openly admitting his ‘wickedness.’ This self-awareness appeared to absolve him of any shame or self-hatred.

For Camus, artistic creation and the act of rebellion both operate as ideal guid­ ing frameworks for humanity and best solve our desires for structure, meaning, and individual freedom. What Dostoevsky sees as a call to faith, the absurd “anguish of ignorance and indecision” (Dostoevsky 392), is precisely what Camus proposes we embrace in order to reconcile our unan­ swerable questions. And what Dostoevsky would interpret as the “blows of fate [that] are the means by which God manifests his power” (Paris 130), Camus sees as absurd­ ism, which is precisely the space of limbo and puzzlement that acts as a catalyst for rebellion and creation. While Dostoevsky has his characters go through contradic­ tion and suffering to create a new person, in The Fall, there is no certain transfor­ mation other than Clamence accepting an irreconcilable discordance between the truth of the self and the desire for higher value and morality. “After prolonged re­ search on myself,” he says, “I brought out the fundamental duplicity of the human being” (Camus, 1956, 84). It becomes im­ possible, Clamence demonstrates, for us to be accurately embodied in any generalizing system of strong boundaries, for we are contradictory by nature. Absurdism paves the way for a morality that is moreso a “creative action” as opposed to a given set of unchangeable tenets (Bowker 170). Be­ cause of this, it can also work in tandem with new ideas and progress and is not constrained by itself.

Both rebellion and art still operate de­ pendently on a system, which is why they are successful means to assuage the suffer­ ing and chaos found in freedom. “The first thing that a landscape painter does is to square off his canvas” (Camus, 1951, 225): they still represent a need for unity and a coherent system. They provide limitations and order, which relieve us of the burden and perplexity of total expansive freedom. They reflect parts of ourselves back to us, marking our existence and value while supplying us with a sense of unity.

These solutions are a never-ending process. The duality that exists within us can therefore find expression and relief in rebellion and art: art says, “Be like me, the Original Mother, who, constantly creat­ ing, finds satisfaction in the turbulent flux of appearances” (Nietzsche, 1956, 102). In this way, the continual creations of art and rebellion are more pure and accurate manifestations of the self. They seek to be expressions of truth, not implementations of constraints.

The paradox of justice lies in its desire for unity and peace despite its denial of all as intrinsically connected. The characters who reject this interconnectedness are doomed to isolation, anxiety, and despair, but the recognition of this brings enlightenment, peace, and reconciliation. The fixed nature of law and religion can be alleviated and ultimately changed through rebelling in order to experience and understand what these systems lack, and the expression of difficult and complex truths through liter­ ature and art. Without choosing mystery, we choose to avoid full realization of the self. The goal must not be to encourage vi­ olence, generalizations, or limitations, but rather to become Nietzsche’s “child” and challenge the impersonal systems of law and dogmatic religion, opening up new and creative means to handle social conflict while encouraging all to go in the direction of art and rebellion.◆

title: Re-engineering the Planet, Legally
notes: Profile of Dr. Wil Burns, Visiting Professor of Environmental Policy and Culture, and his research on geoengineering under international law. The title and byline are extracted last on the opening page (108.8). Ends with a reference list.
text:
Re-engineering the Planet, Legally By Lynna Deng

In 2015, 196 parties, including the U.S., signed the Paris Agreement, mark­ ing a global commitment to limit global temperatures to 2.0°C above pre-indus­ trial levels. In the seven years since, the parties’ actions toward this commitment have proved deficient as global tem­ peratures continue to soar. Based on the International Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) estimates, in a “business-as-usu­ al” scenario, temperatures are likely to rise to 2.7°C above pre-industrial lev­ els by the end of this century, and, in a worst case scenario, they may even rise 4.4°C. (Hausfather et al., 2020). The IPCC thus reported that simply cutting greenhouse gas emissions is no longer enough – we now must actively remove carbon dioxide from the atmo­ sphere for any chance of fulfilling the Paris Agreement (IPCC, 2021).

This burgeoning field of carbon dioxide removal (CDR), alongside solar radiation management, where sunlight is blocked to decrease global tempera­ tures, has been dubbed “geoengineering.” Increasing scientific interest in geoengi­ neering has created a vast menu of op­ tions, including mechanically capturing atmospheric carbon dioxide (direct air capture), using rocks to react with and trap atmospheric carbon dioxide (min­ eralization), adding certain compounds into the ocean to increase its absorption of carbon dioxide (alkalinity enhance­ ment), and even releasing giant mirrors into space.

The decision of which of these op­ tions to implement and how looms ever closer, but with geoengineering research only beginning, it is a politically, legally, socially, and ethically fraught choice. Herein lies Environmental Policy and Culture Visiting Professor Dr. Wil Burns’ current area of research: navigating geo­ engineering under international law.

As Professor Burns tells it, his career has been a series of “serendipitous” mo­ ments, taking him from studying biology and political science as an undergraduate, to forming an international wildlife law think tank, to working in climate change litigation. Professor Burns recounts the particular serendipitous moment that first introduced him to geoengineering:

“I had been asked to be a visiting scholar at Williams College, and I was flying there to start teaching … international environmental law to undergraduates. I discovered that instead of 16 weeks, which is what I thought the semester was, it was 17 weeks. I said, ‘Yikes, I don’t have a topic for another week.’ I was getting ready to get off the plane, and the guy next to me left his ‘USA Today’ on the seat … There was a small article on climate geoengineering, and I thought, ‘Oh, that’s an interesting topic combining science and technology and law and politics and ethics. I bet by Week 17, I could have a lecture on this for the students.’ And I did.”

At the time, geoengineering was truly in its infancy. “There weren’t many people in geoengineering, full stop, but there was nobody on the social science side,” Profes­ sor Burns says. When he and a colleague at American University founded their research center, the Washington Geoengineering Consortium, in 2013, it was the first working on the social science of geoengineering.

Now, as the field has flourished under the interest of researchers, start-ups, and investors, it has become clear that deploying any geoengineering technique will have a global impact. Yet, with geoengineering only being seriously considered in the past few years, most existing international law doesn’t directly govern the practice. Thus, Professor Burns’ current work seeks to understand how the international laws and customs cur­ rently in place would affect geoengineering’s deployment, as well as what new legislation needs to be enacted to fully regulate it. This stands in stark contrast to many others’ work in international law, including Professor Burns’ former work in in­ ternational wildlife law, where legislation is specifi­ cally aimed at the issue of interest. On comparing the two, Professor Burns says:

“On one hand, [international law for geoengineering is] daunting and frustrating. On the other hand, that’s kind of an interesting role for a lawyer … When it comes to these fields, where they’re relatively new, I think you can play a role in helping to establish that foundation, figuring out how we repurpose some of these laws to fit, or identifying what gaps we have that we’re going to have to fill with more law or more regulatory provisions in the future. And that’s fun to do.”

With such a lengthy list of geoengineering options, there is an equally lengthy list of interna­ tional laws and customs that could apply to each. Professor Burns explains that, when he sifts through the options to select what to research, his choice is a “judgment call.” He clarifies, “You have to … make your own decisions about where you focus based on your in­ terest, your expertise, and whatever criteria you estab­ lish.” For him, those criteria are, “Is [the geoengineering technique] economically vi­ able? Is it relatively low risk? … Might [the public] look at this and say, ‘Yeah, we could live with this’?” Designating these criteria allows some options, such as alkalinity enhancement, to rise to the top for Professor Burns.

You can play a role in helping to establish that foundation, fig­ uring out how we re­ purpose some of these laws to fit, or identify­ ing what gaps we have that we’re going to have to fill with more law or more regulatory provisions in the future.

”

As geoengineering has gained prominence, people outside of academia have begun seeking out Professor Burns’ 15 years of expertise. From briefing congressional representatives and law firms, to speak­ ing with reporters, to consulting for start-up companies, to running a pod­ cast and webinar series, he finds that being a social scientist makes him well equipped to give such explanations and recommendations. “In some ways, [it’s] easier … than having a scientist com­ municate because scientists sometimes just can’t break it down. [Scientists] don’t know what [others] don’t know,” he says.

The aforementioned decision of which geoengineering technologies to use and how relies heavily on this com­ munication. Professor Burns says that, based on a new study from the Univer­ sity of Oxford, the number of people in a given country who report they know about carbon removal “ranges from four or five percent, maybe up to 18% ... But I even question [what people mean] when they say they know about carbon removal; there’s no reason for most people to know about this, right?” (Smith et al., 2023).

Indeed, perhaps most people feel they have no reason to stay informed about geoengineering, but as our un­ willingness to make drastic emission cuts catapults us toward a terrifying future, we all certainly need to. Pro­ fessor Burns’ work in geoengineering research and education thus only grows in urgency and importance.
