title: ABOUT THE CONTRIBUTORS
notes: Contents: "Biographies and Interviews of Thesis Contributors". One page per thesis author (Emily Brooks, Violet Decker, Juliet Jacques, Karina Karbo-Wright, Olive Liu over two pages, Kiana Staples, Nina M. Wetoska), each with name, thesis title and answers on their research topic, how they came to it, future directions and plans after graduation. The opener (printed page 112) lists the names and repeats "ABOUT THE CONTRIBUTORS" twice.
text:
ABOUT

THE CONTRIBUTORS

ABOUT

THE CONTRIBUTORS

Emily Ann Brooks

Violet Decker

Juliet Jacques

Karina Karbo-Wright

Olive Liu

Kiana Staples

Nina M. Wetoska

Emily Brooks Going On Seventeen:

“Type,” the Ingenue, and Teenage Girlhood Onstage

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? The trope or “type” of the ingenue, the expectations it creates for teenage girl­ hood/young womanhood onstage, and the impact of those expectations on theatre artists and audiences.

How did you come to your research topic? As a young female theatre artist often considered for “ingenue” roles, I had found the type limiting and untruthful, and was interested in investigating how to interface with this “type” while telling the kind of stories I wanted to tell. Research, particularly community conversations, soon showed me that my frustrations rep­ resented only a small, shallow portion of the ramifications of ingenue expectations.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I would hope that this work would further push a shift in mindset in the theatre industry toward greater respect and rec­ ognition of each artist as a full, agentive, creative individual, allowed to express the fullness of themselves onstage and unlim­ ited by reductive, untruthful, exclusive notions of what it is to be a young wom­ an. My combined process of traditional academic reading, ensemble discussion, and performance as research could be in­ credibly generative if applied to different, similar, or even the same topic with a dif­ ferent core ensemble of individuals. While I focused on the demographic of teenage girlhood and the “type” of the ingenue, there is much exciting research and cre­ ative work to be done around expectations for other ages, genders, and “types”/cate­ gories of role onstage, and what processes and texts can tell each of our stories with the most truth and positive impact.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I’ll be staying in Chicago to work profes­ sionally as a theatre artist, particularly focused on performance, choreography, and direction. I can’t wait to continue to pursue my passions of healthy artist ex­ periences and meaningful, collaborative, positively impactful storytelling!

Violet Decker God, Absurdism, and Law: Suffering and Meaning in the Works of Nietzsche, Dostoevsky, and Camus

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research seeks to find textual support and connections in specific works of Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, and Fyodor Dostoevsky regarding the purpose and nature of the legal system and religion in society. The thesis seeks to explore, through literary works and the lives of the respective authors, the drives toward strict religious and/or legal beliefs and the larger result of this on both personal development and society at large.

How did you come to your research topic? In my reading of French and Russian lit­ erature through my major of Comparative Literary Studies, I noticed a repetitive theme of the legal system and the common threads of its portrayal in numerous nov­ els. I became interested in exploring this further to seek practical understandings of how these portrayals might guide us in revising relevant legal frameworks, or creating new frameworks that might lead to better personal and societal fulfillment and meaning.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I see much more to dissect regarding the legal system’s portrayal in world literatures and how that, in time, could translate to a greater understanding of some of its pit­ falls and challenges. Because literary works focus so richly on human nature in a way the legal system alone cannot, it brings a new dimension to our under­ standing of judgment and law. Any por­ trayal of character involvement with (or against) the legal system in fictional works in world literature can help enhance these understandings.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I am preparing for an M.F.A. in Creative Nonfiction writing.

Juliet Jacques

Monstrous Masculinities, Male Angst, and Adolescent

Development in the

Twilight Saga

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My thesis is centered around studying representations of masculinity for adoles­ cent characters in the Twilight Saga. This global book series and movie franchise has had an incalculable effect on the genre of Young Adult fiction as a whole. I argue that despite its seeming banality as a romance novel, it is actually doing some­ thing new and important in the way that it portrays teenage boys’ fraught relationship to patriarchal standards of masculinity.

After discussion with my advisor, I submitted the introduction of my thesis to the NURJ. In this, I summarize the field of Twilight scholarship, trace the way that it has evolved over the past decade, and ar­ gue that there is a gap in the study of mas­ culine characters. I argue that this is also representative of a larger trend in literary and gender studies, which tend to focus on feminist studies without a parallel under­ standing of the way that men, especially during adolescent, are also necessarily a part of and affected by patriarchal systems. I then go on to outline my arguments for the three chapters of my thesis and con­ clude with the importance of this research.

How did you come to your research topic? I’ve been a Twilight fan since middle school, but only recently have begun to not be embarrassed about it! I feel strongly about defending seemingly silly romance novels, which because of the way they are marketed towards women, get a hugely dis­ proportional amount of hate and criticism.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I feel that my work on masculine characters in Twilight is only the beginning. I focus on two main primary characters, but I argue that all characters within the series are interacting with masculinity in different and interesting ways, and all would be fruitful objects of analysis. I also think that the frameworks I have developed for thinking about these characters can definitely be applied to other novels in the genre.

Where are you heading to after graduation? University of Wisconsin-Madison Law School with a full scholarship

Karina Karbo-Wright

“When did the depictions become worse than the reality?”: Black Trauma Porn and The Black Horror Genre in Television and Film

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? I am looking at what is meant by “Black Trauma Porn” and if the best phrase to describe the phenomenon is being used specifically in relation to television and film.

How did you come to your research topic? Professor Hesse and I were chatting about research topics and he brought up Black Trauma Porn and asked my opinion on it. When I gave it, which was pretty much a regurgitation of what is online, he asked me if I’d be willing to interrogate it. As a film lover, I thought it was a great idea!

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I would LOVE to continue this work in a graduate study program. In the conclusion of my full thesis, I say that there are other avenues within Black horror and within other Black genres that I could explore. I also proposed the idea of engaing with how colorism and interracial relationships play a role in these films as well. I would love to explore Black horror more. I think that besides the authors mentioned throughout the thesis, there is not a ton work on Black film genres, especially horror, with it’s impact on current con­ ceptualizations compared to other fields in Black studies. I’d love to see how people could expand on these ideas in analysis of other Black genres, Black performance fields, and Black creations.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I currently work at Vivacity Tech PBC as a Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Spe­ cialist, however, I would very much like to continue my study in a Black studies PhD program.

Olive Liu

Defeating the Dragon:

Epistemic Injustice

Towards Asian/ American Women

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? Epistemic injustice, and testimonial injus­ tice specifically, is a type of discrimination that occurs when a person suffers a cred­ ibility deficit because of an identity-based prejudice. This presentation seeks to understand testimonial injustice and its relevance to Asian/American women. Through the course of this project, I explain what prejudices influence acts of testimonial injustice against Asian/Ameri­ can women, tracing both their historical and theoretical roots. I will also discuss the po­ tential effects of testimonial injustice, which consists of two main types of harm: sexual and psychological. Finally, I present the idea of epistemic justice as a counter to epistemic injustice and how it can be practiced.

How did you come to your research topic? In the winter quarter of my junior year, I took a course on the topic of epistemic injustice with my advisor, Sanford Gold­ berg. Throughout this class, I realized that testimonial injustice was something I had experienced for most of my life as an Asian/American femme. There was a huge sense of relief in being to describe this kind of discrimination, and have the tools to combat it in my own life. Because of this, I became interested in how the influencing factors of testimonial injustice towards Asian/American women have been shaped and influenced throughout histories of racially gendered and colonial­ ist violence.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? As it stands, epistemic injustice is a relatively new concept within Philosophy. Yet, for most of the people I spoke with throughout this project, it was something they had experienced frequently. Thus, I think that one of the goals of this project was to provide the language and tools for people to identify and combat this kind of injustice in their own communities. In terms of the future direction of this work, I think that the development of a more specific account of testimonial injustice for different groups would be valuable, especially in thinking about how specific communities can work against and heal from epistemic injustice. Even further, I’m curious to see how epistemic injustice changes depending on the intersections of certain identities, shifting cultural contexts, and modes of communication, like digitally.

Where are you heading to after graduation? Currently, I am working at Chicago Pub­ lic Schools as a NU Public Interest Pro­ gram Fellow. After the program ends, I hope to continue my research by applying to Ph.D. programs in either Philosophy or Ethnic Studies.

Kiana Staples

Unashamed: Exploring A South Korean Female Tattoo

Artist’s Negotiation

Of Identity

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? The role of women in South Korea’s tattoo history and culture, as well as the experi­ ences of South Korean female tattoo artists.

How did you come to your research topic? As a female tattoo collector myself, I wanted to investigate the experiences of women in South Korea’s tattoo scene. I noticed many female tattoo artists in South Korea who were popular, but not a lot of research on them apart from writings on beauty tattooing (such as tattooing semi permanent makeup).

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I am hoping to interview more artists as my Korean proficiency continues to improve. I’m hoping that other researchers in my field will consider the usefulness of ethnographic methods such as oral history to supplement exist­ ing research that focuses on literature or other sources.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I’m currently taking a gap year at home, spending time with my mom, little broth­ er, and cats. I hope to earn a master’s and PhD in my field and eventually become a college professor.

Nina M. Wetoska

The Effects of Power Dynamics in University- Community Partnerships

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? This study looks into the power dynamics between undergraduate students and adult community members and their effects on mediating these relationships within the realm of university-communi­ ty partnerships.

How did you come to your research topic? I participated in the Young People’s Race, Power, and Technology Project (YPRPT) as an Undergraduate Coordinator for the 2020-2021 academic year. I also completed a credit-bearing Research Apprenticeship working with Dr. Sepehr Vakil and the YPRPT Research Team. My experiences led me to choose university-community partnerships as my topic and YPRPT as my case study.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I see the findings of this work and emphasis on the adult community member and undergraduate relationship contributing to future improvements in university-community partnerships. There is so much left to discover in this field, particularly because the town and gown dichotomy continues to hold true, at least to some degree, in many towns where universities reside.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I’m currently working at the Buehler Center for Health Policy and Economics at the Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago.

title: Letter from the Advisers
notes: Signed Dr. Peter Civetta and Patti Wolter, NURJ Faculty Advisers. Says Volume 19 holds senior theses selected by seven departments and nine feature stories.
text:
Letter from the Advisers

Dear readers:

Welcome to Volume 19 of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ). Volume 19 includes the best senior theses selected by seven academic departments and nine feature stories exploring the essence of research and its importance at Northwestern University (N.U.) and globally. This year’s mix celebrates a wide-range of intellectual inquiry at N.U. from some of the nation’s brightest voices in undergraduate research. Open up--or click through--these pages and connect with new developments in fields X-ray crystallography, new insights into social media tools, or new reflections on post-war orchestras and their social impact (and so many more unique topics).

The 2023–2024 issue is the product of a year’s work by the students who lead and contribute to the NURJ, a student-produced annual print publication. In addition to this journal, our students publish new research packages on their website, www.thenurj.com, as well as podcast episodes with research leaders within and outside the Northwestern University community. At the center of this work is their deep commitment to the Northwestern community. “Research” as defined by the NURJ champions the broadest array of disciplines and reflects the efforts and guidance of not just faculty, but the indefatigable work of staff, fellow researchers and more.

The journal you hold in your hand is a creation by hundreds of minds from N.U. and is made possible through the continuous funding by the Office of the President and the Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education. Copies of the NURJ are freely available to students at newsstands at major campus locations. Additionally, the NURJ is distributed to N.U. Deans, Department Chairs, and Program Chairs as well as to academic, advising, and research offices across campus.

We hope you find sparks of inspiration, enjoyment, and wonder as you read this journal. As the founding editor and NURJ adviser for 18 years, the late Professor Allen Taflove, used to sign off: Now, enjoy learning about the marvelous research investigations of Northwestern’s top students!

Best, Dr. Peter Civetta and Patti Wolter NURJ Faculty Advisers

text:
Letter from the Editors

Dear readers:

We are thrilled to welcome you to the 19th volume of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ) and present a diverse array of writing that showcases groundbreaking work. From analyses of authenticity on popular social media app BeReal to the role that social security plays in wellbeing, this issue features a myriad of honors theses that exemplify the intersection of depth, diversity, and academic excellence within their respective disciplines. In addition to the seven senior theses, this volume also includes nine feature stories from our NURJ print staff that highlight both the research and the people behind the innovative breakthroughs at Northwestern.

The theme of Volume 19 centers around cool-toned colors that embody serenity and flow. With round, flowy shapes, we hoped to capture the fluidity and dynamism of this year that was navigated with grace and balance. As we navigate through the changing years, we envisioned the design to showcase the adaptability and growth in our staff, students, and community as a whole. This theme not only aligned with the journey of our team this year, but also reflects the growth mindset we embrace going into the next year.

In addition to our annual print edition, we invite you to explore our Archives Special Edition project and semiannual online packages that highlight research done by the Northwestern community.

NURJ continues to be a testament to the hard work and passion of our brilliant student-re­ searchers and the dedication of our talented writers, editors, and designers. Without our lovely staff, we would not have been able to bring our visions to life. Furthermore, we are eternally grateful for the generous sponsorship and continued support from President Michael Schill and Associate Provost Miriam Sherin. To our phenomenal faculty advisers, Dr. Peter Civetta and Professor Patti Wolter — we are so thankful for their unwavering support and guidance, we could not have done it without them. And lastly, to you, our readers and the entire Northwestern community — thank you for entrusting the NURJ to share student research, for supporting NURJ in person and online.

We hope you enjoy this journal!

— Helen Zhu & Aden Morvice Co-Editors-in-Chief, NURJ 2023-2024

title: The Lasting Legacy of A Divided City: The Berlin Orchestras as a Microcosm for Germany during the Wendezeit
notes: Senior thesis (presented as a condensed thesis). Advisers from "Faculty Advisers" on the opening page: Dr. Isabel von Holt, DAAD Visiting Assistant Professor of German, and Dr. Jesse Rosenberg, Associate Professor of Musicology. The opening page sets the title as "The Lasting Legacy of A Divided City" with the subtitle on separate lines; the contents writes "The Lasting Legacy of a Divided City: ...". Supported by an Undergraduate Research Grant and the Friedman-Kline Foundation. Includes German-language block quotes with English footnote translations, pull quotes and a bibliography. Printed page 8 is mostly a photograph of the Brandenburg Gate behind barbed wire. Footnotes and pull quotes are placed at the nearest paragraph break.
text:
Departments of German and Musicology

The Lasting Legacy of A Divided City The Berlin Orchestras as a Microcosm for Germany during the Wendezeit by Eden Stargardt

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Isabel von Holt, DAAD Visiting Assistant Professor of German Dr. Jesse Rosenberg, Associate Professor of Musicology

Abstract Orchestras are important cultural institutions and as such they are representations of greater socio—political movements. They often act as mirrors of political, social, and cultural landscapes, and reflect the greater values and beliefs within a given time. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the greater themes of Germany during the Wendezeit were reflected in the activities of the orchestras, musical institutions, and concert program­ ming in the orchestras in Berlin and acted as representations of cultural politics during this transitional period. By examining three significant reunification concerts in Berlin between late 1989 and early 1990, I will explain the ways in which the orchestras in Berlin acted as a microcosm for the greater German society. Through these analyses, I will highlight the unequal preservation of cultural institutions in the former East Berlin and the Bundesrepublik and explain the resurgence of the ideals of the French Revolu­ tion and Germany as das Land der Dichter und Denker that is intertwined with it. I will illustrate the connections between the large presence of Beethoven’s music, the idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk, and the influence of figures such as Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, and Karl Friedrich Schinkel on the curated image of the reunification concerts in Berlin. I will also question who controlled the narrative in this period of transition and who the collective audience was after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The research resulting in this thesis was assisted by a grant from the Undergraduate Research Grant Program which is administered by Northwestern University’s Office of Undergraduate Research. However, the conclusions, opinions, and other statements in this publication are the author’s and not necessarily those of the sponsoring institution. This thesis project would not have been possible without the generous funding from the Friedman—Kline Founda­ tion and the immense support of the German Department at Northwestern.

Introduction: The Orchestra as a Center of Culture Orchestras are multifaceted and complex institutions that are greatly influenced by and reflective of greater cultural beliefs and ideals. At their core, orchestras have been described as being “as much about people as they are about music” (Lehman 37). As cultural institutions, orchestras “preserve and promote the musical heritage of past, present, and future composers” (Lehman 37). As performing arts organizations, their primary function is to present per­ formances for live audiences; however, as a social entity, these organizations depend on engagement with audiences and those who support them.

Historically, orchestras have served as symbols of cultural identity — cities, regions, and nations all have unique values, traditions, societal ideals, and achievements that are recognized and embodied in the reputation of their orchestras. The orches­ tra has been considered “one of the great cultural achievements of European civili­ zation” and has served as one of Europe’s most significant cultural exports (Lawson 251), a statement equally true in Germany. The cultural appreciation and importance of classical music have a long—standing history, particularly in Germany, and a sense of identity and self—representation can be observed in the so—called “Germa­ ny’s best;” composers such as Johann Sebas­ tian Bach, Ludwig van Beethoven, and Jo­ hannes Brahms all hold a great significance in the classical music canon (Reucher). The concept of the classical canon and standard orchestral repertoire is already a complex and exclusionary practice when consid­ ering who created the collection of music that is deemed superior, who the audience was, and how these notions intersected with German nationalism. Germany’s dis­ tinctive appreciation for the arts is so cher­ ished that in 2019 it was recognized in the Bundesweites Verzeichnis Immaterielles Kul­ turerbe as an “intangible cultural heritage of humanity” (‘Bundesweites Verzeichnis’).

The drastic political, social, and cul­ tural changes in 20th—century Germany all greatly influenced the direction of musical life in the city of Berlin. The transition from a divided Germany to a reunited nation largely impacted the orchestras within the city, and there was a return to the ideals of the Weimarer Klassik — and therefore the values of the original Ger­ man Unification in 1871.

The orchestras in Berlin are a micro­ cosm of German society during the Wen­ dezeit. In my understanding, viewing the orchestra as a microcosm represents what has been outlined as the “perception of the institution reflecting the social world in miniature that has led to metaphoric conceptualizations of its inner workings to describe and theorize the functioning of different kinds of collectives and social re­ lationships” (Ramnarine 329). Conductor and musician Daniel Barenboim is partic­ ularly aware of the power of the orchestra as a vehicle for social change. He elaborates on this crucial role:

An orchestra is a microcosm of society… Each musician simply opens a window into the soul of the orchestra, which is something unimaginable to an outsider: the soul of the orchestra is a constantly changing original composition being collectively written by all of its members, who can tell its story better than anyone else (Cheah 1).

The idea of something that is “collec­ tive” is particularly interesting to consider. This concept of collectivity introduces the idea of a societal ideal that is inclusive of everyone in a democratic process. Baren­ boim is projecting the idea that everyone’s voice is heard and that the members of the orchestra are empowered and able to share their own stories: this is simply not the reality. It is interesting to compare this far—fetched assumption made by Barenboim to the attitudes present in the Bundesrepublik after the fall of the Wall. Both reunified Germany and Barenboim are trying to project an idealized version of society where everyone is valued and heard. Ironically, Barenboim says that the story of the orchestra can only be told by the members, yet he is the one who is telling the story.

Barenboim speaks not only to the impermanence and complexity of this cultural institution but also to the collab­ oration and emotional expression required to participate as a member of an orchestra. In bringing together such diverse groups of people — both with musicians onstage and the audience members offstage — the orchestra is an excellent example of a cre­ ated community that is a representation of a larger society. Barenboim also describes this unique working and music—mak­ ing environment as something that is “unimaginable to an outsider” and that can only be accurately described by those within the “soul of the orchestra.” Through this description, he introduces the question of who the “insiders” and the “outsiders” are within classical music, without clarifying who is “in” and who is “out.” Through this description, there is a separation and creation of a mythical world that is fabricated, where art is created and is not accessible or penetrable by outsid­ ers. Suddenly, the orchestra becomes an exclusive and secretive community within the larger society, which also undervalues the experience of the audiences and the role of administrative institutions in the workings of the orchestra.

Historical Context: Reunified Germany I am viewing the cultural institution of the orchestra as a microcosm of Berlin. Similarly, I propose to see the divided and reunited Berlin as a representation of a divided and reunited Germany during the Wendezeit — and their larger global implications. Throughout this thesis, I will use the term reunification to describe the re—establishment of Germany as a single sovereign state that was finalized on October 3, 1990, and the term Wendezeit to describe the period between the fall of the Berlin Wall on November 9, 1989, and the official German Reunification in 1990. The primary focus of my research is on the concerts that occur during this period of transition.

Oftentimes, the image of an orchestra that is presented to the public is a curat­ ed, idealized version of reality. Perhaps this has something to do with the fact that this period of transition is not something that is regarded as remarkable, despite its objectively major impact on both German society and the world: “The journey Ger­ many embarked on roughly twenty—five years ago has been a remarkable one. Moreover, it is even more extraordinary because virtually no one seems to dwell on the idea that it is extraordinary in any way” (Lys and Dreyer 5). When considering that this period is not dwelled on as “extraordi­ nary,” it does not mean that this period of transition was not significant, rather that the radical changes were not recognized as profound — despite the reunification representing the beginning of the end of a global political struggle between capitalism and communism. Considering this seems to be the attitude adopted, perhaps this can provide insight into the reality back then. The presence of this mindset that turned away from the difficulties of reuni­ fication (or rather failed to acknowledge their existence) could have significantly impacted the way post—reunification pol­ itics were handled. Although perhaps the resulting actions were intentional and were made to appear as a natural process as a way of over— and unwriting the past of the German Democratic Republic through the decisions made by the Bundesrepublik.

This is not to say that no outward attempt was made for inclusion and pres­ ervation during this transition period; however, it is interesting to note the effec­ tiveness (or lack thereof) of these attempts:

Der grundsätzliche Blickwinkel, unter dem die heutige Diskussion der Integration der DDR—Kultur steht, ergibt sich aus Artikel 35, Absatz 6 des Einigungsvertrages der beiden deutschen Regierungen vom 31. August 1990. Hier wird festgeschrieben, dass die kulturelle Substanz in dem Beitrittsgebiet keinen Schaden nehmen darf1 (Allmendinger 324).

The bigger question is if the presen­ tation of this clause ensured any tangible action towards the equal preservation of both cultural traditions and ideals. It is one thing to propose ideas, and another to fol­ low through with actions.

1 Article 35, Paragraph 6 of the Unification Treaty of the two German governments of August 31, 1990, states that the cultural substance in the acceding territory must not be damaged.

The Berlin Wall was created in 1961 to formally divide East and West Berlin, creating a physical barrier not only between the two political entities, but also between the increasingly opposing viewpoints, ide­ ologies, and ways of life for those living within Germany. When the Wall fell on November 9th, 1989, a formerly divided city was suddenly reunited. Yet, a distinct separation remained between who and what belonged to East and West Germany. There was a visible, public unification that was displayed through public celebrations, concerts, and performances; however, the outward appearance of unity was merely a façade masking the great difficulties of a reunited country that was largely still very divided.

Unlike other regions of Germany, the events after the Wende in Berlin were strikingly unique. This can be attributed largely to the proximity of such radically different political and social identities. Because the city of Berlin was divided, the larger themes and difficulties of reunifica­ tion were brought to the forefront:

On October 30, 1990, precisely at midnight, the flag of a reunited Germany was raised over the Reichstag in Berlin, accompanied by celebratory fireworks across the city. The act signaled the end of one state, the German Democratic Republic (GDR), and the continuation of another, the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG) (Lys and Dreyer 1).

The wording of this statement is par­ ticularly interesting when considering the representation of both former halves of Germany during the period of reunification — there was an “end” of one and a “contin­ uation” of the other. If one state (and with those elements of its culture) is coming to an end while another is continuing to exist, what does this mean for the so—called equal representation and preservation of both cultures that are outlined in the previously discussed “Diskussion der Integration der DDR—Kultur” that was written in German law? The word “end” implies a sense of finality and extinction — what does this say about how the culture in the former East is viewed and remembered? Are the ideals, traditions, and cultural expressions in the Bundesrepublik viewed as superior — and do they therefore remain the dominant voice and cultural standard?

“There was a visible, public unification that was displayed through public celebrations, concerts, and performances; however, the outward appearance of unity was merely a façade masking the great difficulties of a reunited country that was largely still very divided”

When asked if the substance of the orchestral culture had been damaged in the 30 years following the fall of the Wall, the musicologist Arnold Jacobshagen explained the sobering statistics for the fates of the orchestras during and after the Wendezeit:

Zwischen 1992 und 2020 hat sich die Gesamtzahl der Berufsorchester in Deutschland von 168 auf 129 verringert. Zugleich ging die Anzahl der Planstellen um rund 20 Prozent zurück, von 12.159 auf 9.766. Erwartungsgemäß betraf diese Entwicklung den Osten Deutschlands mit einem Rückgang um insgesamt 38 Prozent (von 5.032 auf 3.132 Stellen) in weitaus stärkerem Maße als den Westen, wo innerhalb von fast 30 Jahren lediglich 7 Prozent der Orchesterstellen entfielen2 (Mertens 14).

This statistic — while primarily showing the impact of the reunification on greater Germany — is also reflective of the stark differences in the impact on the former East and West Berlin. The fact that the orchestras in the former East saw a 38 percent reduction, whereas those in the West only saw a 7 percent decrease is remarkable.

Methodology: “Imagined Communities” I primarily draw upon the methodology outlined by Benedict Anderson in his book Imagined Communities, in which he describes a nation as “an imagined political community” (Anderson 6). In my thesis, I use the term imagined or created commu­ nity (which I previously implemented to address orchestras in the introduction) to describe German society during the Wen­ dezeit and to acknowledge the complexity and intangibility of the cultural narrative that is driven by the West. Anderson questions the implications of these com­ munities on the people existing within (or outside) them. I am taking the ideas brought forward in his book and applying them to my concert analysis. In doing so, I will highlight the imagined community created after the fall of the Berlin Wall and will question the narrative that is furthered and the ideals that are presented as being those of a (seemingly) reunified Germany.

In this condensed thesis, I will explain my analysis of one of three reunification concerts that took place in Berlin between November 1989 and January 1990. The analysis of this concert will serve as the basis for better understanding the themes pre­ viously outlined and will begin to answer the posed questions about how the Berlin orchestras are representative of greater German society during the Wendezeit.

2 Between 1992 and 2020, the total number of professional orchestras in Germany decreased from 168 to 129. At the same time, the number of permanent positions fell by around 20 percent, from 12,159 to 9,766. This development affected eastern Germany, which experienced a total decline of 38 percent (from 5,032 to 3,132 positions). The former East was affected to a much greater extent than the West, where only 7 percent of orchestra positions were lost in almost 30 years.

Brotherhood and Freedom: the Leonard Bernstein Concerts In what was one of the most public and globally—recognized musical displays of the German Reunification, Leonard Bernstein led an orchestra consisting of members of the former East and West Germany, as well as members of combat­ ive nations involved in World War II — Great Britain, France, The United States, and The Soviet Union. Two concerts were held in December of 1989 — one for the citizens of the former GDR and the other for those in the West with the most well— known concert taking place in the Konzer­ thaus Berlin in the Gendarmenmarkt. These concerts were broadcast to nearly 20,000 onlookers into the streets of the old West through speakers on the roofs of buildings on Kurfürstendamm (Dennis 1), as well as to hundreds of thousands of people in more than 30 countries around the world (Berlin Celebration Concert). The target audience for this concert appeared to extend beyond those in Berlin, as demonstrated by the numerous forms of media broadcasting and recording this event and the large international audience, which again raises the question of the curation of the image presented to the world about the “true” values of a reunited Germany.

This ad hoc orchestra, which came together for only two days, played Bee­ thoven’s Symphony No. 9 to celebrate the recent fall of the Berlin Wall. Historically, this orchestral work is deeply symbolic of “hope, unity, and fellowship — across bor­ ders and through conflicts” (Johnson and Suchtet). In fact, since 1985 the “Ode an die Freude” section of the last movement, has acted as the official anthem of the European Union because “in the universal language of music, [it] expresses the European ideals of freedom, peace, and solidarity” (‘Euro­ pean Anthem’).

The combination of the many con­ nections back to a time of great German cultural significance (i.e., the emergence of the narrative as das Land der Dichter und Denker) and the highly publicized nature of this event is not coincidental. It seems to project exactly the desired image of a reunited Germany with ties to a specific cultural heritage — but in presenting an orchestrated image to the world that fur­ thers the narrative of the West and over­ writes that of the East, this cannot be an accurate representation of German society because it is exclusionary by nature.

“The highly publicized nature of this event is not coincidental. It seems to project exactly the desired image of a reunited Germany with ties to a specific cultural heritage.”

In these concerts, a large emphasis was placed on the concept of Brüderlich­ keit — not only between East and West Germany but also between the countries with a presence in Berlin after World War II. It was as if this concert symbolized the act of setting aside long—standing tension in celebration of not just the reunification of the German states, but also the global implications that came with it. Leonard Bernstein even famously changed the word Freude to Freiheit in the final movement of the symphony to commemorate this joyous occasion. While the act of changing the text of Friedrich Schiller’s poem is often credited to Bernstein, this gesture has ties to the late 18th Century when the “German rebels appropriated the poem during the French revolutionary era for the use as the text of a political Lied, sung with the word Freiheit replacing Freude” (Dennis 26). In claiming this seemingly small change to the poem as his authentic reaction to the displays of freedom in Berlin (despite the greater implications of this gesture and by ignoring the important connections back to the French Revolution), Bernstein’s decision to claim this revision as his own is quite questionable, as his Western, US— American perspective is overwriting a sig­ nificant and unique German cultural refer­ ence. In presenting an orchestrated image to the world that furthers the narrative of the West and overwrites that of the East, it cannot be an accurate representation of German society if not everyone is included.

The location of the concert in the Gendarmenmarkt — an important historical square with a Konzerthaus designed by the German architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel with a towering statue of Schiller directly in the middle of the plaza — is a crucial element to consider when remembering this historic event. It is no coincidence that Bernstein’s concert takes place di­ rectly behind the famous statue of Schil­ ler — whose poem “Ode an die Freude ‘’ is the basis for the final movement of Bee­ thoven’s Symphony No. 9. Additionally, Schinkel was an architect who was “dafür verantwortlich, Berlin in eine repräsen­ tative Hauptstadt umzugestalten”3 (von Treptow). The aesthetic of Schinkel’s architecture served as the foundation for the literary aesthetic of the Weimarer Klassik with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Schiller as its main representatives (Snodin et al 39). Therefore, on a funda­ mental level, this concert building was not only a part of the movement to make Berlin the center of arts and culture but also part of the inspiration and foundation for one of the most recognizably “German” literary movements. Once again, there is a strong tie back to the ideals and triumphs of 18th and 19th century Germany.

3 Schinkel was an architect who was responsible for transforming Berlin into a representative capital city 4 The idea of a Gesamtkunstwerk can be found in the architectural theory of E.—L. Boullée with the design of Idealstädte, which was supported by the French Revolution

This multidisciplinary event that was broadcast into the streets of Berlin and to the world also has a tangible connection to the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk. This term, meaning “total artwork” describes a work or process in which the combination of different art forms creates a cohesive whole: generally, Gesamtkunstwerke con­ tains elements of music, drama, poetry, architecture, or painting (Mühlenberend 282). Not only does this concert combine artistic elements (such as instrumen­ tal music, choir, poetry, sculpture, and architecture) in a way consistent with a Gesamtkunstwerk, but this very concept has a strong connection with the ideals of the French Revolution and the development of “ideal” cities4 (Mühlenberend 282). In a way, the connection between the Leonard Bernstein concert being a Gesamtkunstwerk and the greater implication of this term strengthens the narrative being created after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Berlin was an ideal city, not only in the sense that an idealized reunified Germany was being projected but also in the idealized possibil­ ity of the reunion of two halves of a city that embodied (and continued to embody) such different political and cultural ideolo­ gies. Berlin is an Idealstadt in the sense that it overcame such difficulties of separation, and yet this centuries—old narrative of deep cultural importance still survived.

The connection between Beethoven’s works and the ideals of the French Revo­ lution mirrors the creation of Germany through the birth of the nation—states and official recognition as a country in 1871. These ideals — Freiheit, Gleichheit, Brüderlichkeit — served as the basis for the emerging political and cultural changes.

The ideals associated with the Weimarer Klassik were primarily shaped and created by Goethe and Schiller, and the ideological basis for the emergence of Weimar Clas­ sicism was the French Revolution and its impact on public life in Germany (Stephan 186). The Schiller statue was unveiled in the Gendarmenmarkt plaza in 1871, which shows just how intertwined the newly established nationhood of Germany and the great Dichter and Denker are. This is particularly relevant because Goethe and Schiller are the poets and thinkers ref­ erenced in the expression of das Volk der Dichter und Denker, and there is a strong connection between Goethe and Schiller and the birth of the German nation states: ”Die Deutschen, die die Goethezeit als die Epoche ihrer Klassik bezeichneten, zei­ gen ein verändertes Klassikverständnis an, das auch im Zusammenhang mit der Herausbildung der modernen Nation­ alstaaten gesehen werden muss”5 (Stephan 233—234). It is essential to recognize the interconnectedness of these important fig­ ures in the history of the development and establishment of Germany as a nation and as das Land der Dichter und Dichter.

It is no coincidence that three of the main proponents of Weimar Classicism — Goethe, Schiller, and Schinkel — and the music of Beethoven all simultaneously occupy the space in the Gendarmenmarkt during this concert, and that this is the image that is chosen to be broadcast for the world to see. The striking ties to German cultural history around 1800 are pres­ ent in the concert venue, and these links significantly impact the reception of the orchestrated ideal conveyed through the Gesamtkunstwerk.

Beethoven and das Land der Dichter und Denker Beethoven’s music is noticeably very pres­ ent post—German reunification — par­ ticularly in the reunification celebration concerts. Nearly every concert contains one (or more) of his works, and there are even greater connections to established cultural traditions that go deeper than the explicit contents of the music. There is an important relationship between the increased presence of Beethoven’s music and the narrative of the ideals of the for­ mer West Germany, as well as in the pull towards an ideal identity of Germany as das Land der Dichter und Denker.

5 The Germans indicate a changed understanding of classicism — one that must be seen in the context of the formation of modern nation states.

“Berlin is an Idealstadt in the sense that it overcame such difficulties of separation, and yet this centuries—old narrative of deep cultural importance still survived.”

Throughout modern German histo­ ry, Beethoven has been synonymous with and representative of the German iden­ tity. His role within German culture has changed throughout the last two centuries; however, what has remained constant is his music being “symbolic of its [the society’s] particular vision of the German future” (Dennis 6). This remains true for the role of Beethoven in the Wendezeit, as his music helped project an idealized soci­ ety within Berlin.

To understand the relevance of Bee­ thoven’s music during the Wendezeit, we must first go back to the point in history when his music became synonymous with the ideals of the French Revolution and became deeply intertwined with and rep­ resentative of German culture. During the celebrations of Germany becoming a country in the late 19th century, Bee­ thoven’s music was used for parades and celebrations (this coincided with the hun­ dredth anniversary of his birth). The use of his music for these occasions set the precedent for the use during the German reunification in 1989, and “the evocations of Beethoven in nineteenth—century Ger­ man political culture — particularly those before unification in 1871 — enhance our understanding of the early development of a German identity based on cultural, and in large part musical, nationalism” (Dennis 5). Bonn is often regarded as Beetho­ ven’s city, being that it is his birthplace and hometown. Beethoven — who is often hailed as not only one of the greatest com­ posers of all time but also as one of the most “German” — is celebrated there frequently through festivals and memorials. Interest­ ingly, Bonn was the capital of the Bundesre­ publik — and this says something about the remembrance culture during the German reunification when reminders of the West were constantly overshadowing all other viewpoints and experiences. There is a clear connection between the program­ ming of Beethoven’s music and what Bonn represents to the Bundesrepublik. This city distances itself from the complicated his­ tory of twentieth—century Germany and reminds the audience (whoever that may be) of the ideals of the (especially West) German people:

Throughout the Cold War, Bonn epitomized the image that West Germany wanted to project to a suspicious world — pleasant, provincial, even a little bit boring … Bonn’s most celebrated son [Ludwig van Beethoven] also suited West Germany’s public image — classless, liberal, international. Since reunification, his significance has grown and grown. In a country where so many cultural icons are tainted by association, Beethoven presents no problems. He has none of Wagner’s baggage. He is a hero Germans can celebrate without apology or shame (Cook 67).

With Beethoven, and therefore Bonn, representing West German ideals, the expression of the cultural formation and heritage of those in the East tends to be overwritten. The subtle programming and pushing of the narrative of the old West seems to work against the established com­ mitment to equally preserving elements of both cultures. This supports the idea that the “imagined community” created after the German Reunification centered on only one group of people and projected an idealized version of society onto the others.

Conclusion: Greater Implications of German Reunification The reunification of Germany led to a return to a specific set of cultural tradi­ tions: i.e., a resurgence of the ideals of the Weimarer Klassik and the implications of the French Revolution on German politics and culture. Many connections to the past can be observed in the celebration concerts during the Wendezeit. In taking a critical look at the preservation of both the former

East and West German cultural identities, an idealized narrative of reunified Berlin was projected onto the Berliners. The idea of “presenting East German identity as a danger to German unity implies that unity can only occur if Eastern identities cease to exist, which suggests that German identity is akin to West German identity” (Clark and Wöfel 144). This reveals a kind of Leitkultur within German society — with proponents of this idea believing that “the so—called German Leitkultur should dominate as the core cultural identity in Germany … that is to say that East German identity should be considered problematic because it does not fit in with their con­ cept of Germanness” (Clark and Wöfel 145). This concept was not only present in greater society but it can also be clearly observed in the idealized and curated image from the orchestras within Berlin at this time.

In the time since the Fall of the Wall, shocking statistics about the unequal impacts on the orchestras in the former East and West have been released — with a striking difference in the loss of orchestras in the former East:

In Zahlen wird der Strukturwandel besonders deutlich: Von 168 Orchestern bei der ersten gesamtdeutschen Erfassung 1992 existieren heute noch 129. 39 Orchester sind durch Fusionen oder Abwicklungen endgültig von der Landkarte verschwunden. Ganz überwiegend im Osten, vereinzelt im Westen. Damit verschwanden auch fast 3000 Musikerstellen6 (Mertens 10).

It is entirely expected that orches­ tra positions and entire orchestras would be lost during the reunification process. However, what is so striking is the dis­ parity between the impact on the former East and West. A vow was made to pre­ serve both cultures equally; however, the reality of the situation protected the values of the West, overshadowing the cultural institutions of the former East. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the majority culture favored the ideas and culture tying back to an ideal of Germany as das Land der Dichter und Denker. As previously mentioned, the strong pull towards these values reflects an effort to reclaim a German identity that has not been entirely soiled by National Socialism. Again, it is simply naïve to attempt to return to this idealized version of society without acknowledgment of the impact of the horrors of the 20th century.

The fall of the Berlin Wall had an impact on more than just the narrow view of what was constituted as “German enough,” and the furthering of a narrative that does not acknowledge this is problematic.

6 Of 168 orchestras existing in 1992, only 129 still exist today. 39 orchestras have disappeared entirely due to mergers or liquida­ tions. Most of these were in the East, with a few in the West. Almost 3,000 musician positions were lost through this process.

“A vow was made to preserve both cultures equally; however, the reality of the situation protected the values of the West, overshadowing the cultural institutions of the former East.”

The orchestra is a microcosm of German society during this period of tran­ sition, and the impact of reunification on the orchestras, as shown through statistical data, intentional concert programming, and curated concerts, mirrors the larger social and political changes occurring not only in Berlin but also throughout

Germany. When considering the effects of the fall of the Berlin Wall, it is essential to question who controlled the narrative, to recognize who the audience was during the Wendezeit and after the official reunifi­ cation, and to examine what impact these decisions had on the people in Berlin. ◆
