title: “Beauty Sickness”: Dr. Renee Engeln on Researching Body Image and Vigilance
notes: Profile of Dr. Renee Engeln, Northwestern professor and Director of the Body and Media (BAM) Lab, author of Beauty Sick, and her research on body image.
text:
“Beauty Sickness”: Dr. Renee Engeln on Researching Body Image and Vigilance

By: Izzy Pareja

Body image, defined as the way in which someone perceives their own body, has become an increasingly popular topic of conversation, especially with the rise of social media and photo editing platforms that make it easy to promote unrealistic appearance standards.

Both historically and currently, women have been especially susceptible to pressures sur­ rounding appearance. Margaret Atwood, award-winning author of The Handmaid’s Tale, attempted to describe the intense relationship women have with their bodies in her 1993 novel The Robber Bride: “. . . pretending you’re unseen, pretending you have a life of your own, that you can wash your feet and comb your hair unconscious of the ever-present watcher peering through the keyhole, peering through the keyhole in your own head, if nowhere else . . . You are your own voyeur.”

With the field of body image research experiencing a growth like never before over the last decade, the idea that Atwood presents, one of a constant, second-nature vigilance extended by women towards their bodies, seems to have gained much empirical support.

Dr. Renee Engeln, a Northwestern professor and Director of the Body and Media (BAM) Lab, is one researcher dedicated to investi­ gating this phenomenon. In her book Beauty Sick: How the Cultural Obsession with Beauty Hurts Girls and Women, she identifies a trend in which “women’s emotional energy gets so bound up with what they see in the mirror that it becomes harder for them to see other aspects of their lives,” which is sustained by “a culture that focuses on women’s appearance over anything else they might do or say or be.” She calls this sensation “beauty sickness,” a term that encapsulates one of the prominent issues at the core of her research.

“In general, what we look at are factors in our culture, broadly, that make it hard to feel okay about your body,” Engeln said while describing her lab’s agenda. “We mostly focus on women, but we also do some work in particular on sexual minorities and body image that is more gender inclusive.”

Her lab’s research goals are highly oriented around those of her research assistants and the relevance of certain topics.

“To some extent, what we’re focusing on at any given time just has to do with what’s going on with students’ research projects, but also just what’s going on in the world that’s interesting,” Engeln said.

While Engeln and her team have managed to contribute various extremely relevant findings to the field of body image research, that doesn’t mean she and other researchers haven’t experienced their fair share of challenges.

“It’s a hard topic to study because a lot of people don’t take it seriously.” Engeln described an experience listening to a methods in psychology podcast episode in which the hosts critiqued a journal article published in the journal Body Image. “The two podcasters, who were both men, said ‘Wait, what journal is this in? Body Image? How could there be a journal called Body Image?’ . . . They just immediately dismissed it.”

Engeln finds this sentiment particularly frustrating, especially since there is ample evidence of damaging appearance-related messages present in every-day life.

“Look at the diet industry, look at the beauty industry, look at rates of eating disorder behavior, and then tell me that body image doesn’t matter.”

Engeln is also concerned with producing research that is more representative of different kinds of bodies and people, especially since the field has historically neglected to do so.

“Early on, a lot of work in this area was about pretty much privileged white women with anorexia,” Engeln said. “That was sort of what people thought of body image struggles.”

Despite its necessity, this effort has presented its own set of obstacles that have been difficult to overcome in a traditional research setting.

“One of the broad challenges we face is how to be more inclusive,” Engeln said. “Both in terms of what we’re studying, who we’re studying, where we’re getting our data, dealing with real limits in terms of the money we have to pay research participants—a very small amount, right—or the access we have to different populations to study.”

Issues surrounding body image have become popular topics for discussion as well, especially on social media platforms like TikTok. The popularity of movements promot­ ing body positivity and mental health maintenance in recent years have also increased conversation surrounding the subject. This, too, comes with its own set of challenges, as Engeln points out.

“There are a lot of well-meaning people who are trying to have a positive impact on body image who are doing things for which there is no empirical support.”

Despite the misinformation circulating through social media apps, stigma against body image as a valid research area, and struggle to implement more inclusive research frameworks, the field continues to grow stronger as researchers gain a deeper under­ standing of how women develop relationships with their bodies. This alone has been a success for researchers like Engeln, who began their work during a time where issues women often experienced with body image were written off as matters of confidence or vanity.

“We do a much better job now,” Engeln said. “Realizing that there’s more going on than that, realizing that body image isn’t just something that happens in you, in your head, but it’s something between you and your culture that is deeply interpersonal.”

title: The Impact of School Security on Student Wellbeing
notes: Senior thesis. Advisers from "Faculty Advisers" on the opening page. The contents writes the title in sentence case and the school as "School of Education and Social Policy". Survey of 97 Northwestern first-year students and 10 follow-up interviews. Appendices: survey protocol (A), interview protocol (B) and a demographics table (Table 1); in the survey protocol the answer options for question 6 follow question 7 because the extraction keeps questions 1-7 in one block. Pull quotes are placed at the nearest paragraph break. Ends with a bibliography.
text:
School of Education & Social Policy

The Impact of School Security on Student Wellbeing by Jacob Geil

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Timothy Dohrer and Dr. Regina Logan

Abstract Over the last decade, public schools have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). Although several studies have examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focus­ ing on quantitative analyses. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences. The present study seeks to fill these gaps by examining the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. A survey was completed by 97 Northwestern first-year students, assessing their high school’s climate with or without a school security presence. Afterward, 10 students were selected for follow-up interviews. The semi-structured interviews con­ sisted of items related to dimensions of school climate and adolescent wellbeing, and all selected interviewees graduated from a high school with a security presence. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different perceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relation­ ship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how a lack of adequate support affects student perception of school climate and student wellbeing.

Introduction Public schools over the last decade have seen a dramatic rise in the use of visible school security measures, including metal detectors, security cameras, and security personnel (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). In response to several high-profile school shootings in the 1990s, federal and state legislation began establishing a security presence in schools that continues to grow.

This has prompted a fierce debate. Supporters argue that a security presence protects against school violence and helps to improve relationships between young people and security personnel. Opponents rebut that security in schools is disruptive and criminalizes student behavior with disproportionate damage done to minority students and students with disabilities.

Several studies have examined the impact of school security on student out­ comes. However, only a few studies have looked at how a security presence impacts school climate and student wellbeing, largely focusing on quantitative analyses. This leaves gaps in what to date has been observed and reported. The lack of more qualitative approaches that offer in-depth descriptions of students’ lived experiences limits the scope of assessments examining school security presences.

School climate plays a critical role in a school’s efforts toward meeting goals and resolving problems, as students ex­ periencing a positive school climate show stronger academic performance and lower rates of absenteeism, truancy, and drop out than that of students experiencing a nega­ tive school climate (Norton, 1984; Payne, 2018). Furthermore, schools have an enor­ mous impact on a student’s development, especially during adolescence, which is an important and complex period of the lifes­ pan, characterized by significant physical, psychological, and social transitions (PRB, 2014). Considering this importance, a thorough understanding of the elements of school climate and the factors that might be negatively impacting perceived school climate is essential to achieving academ­ ic goals, as well as promoting positive emotional and behavioral outcomes for students.

Additionally, this research, in exam­ ining school security through the lens of school climate and student experience, will help to establish a better understanding of how previously researched inequities related to school security and punishment manifest in student experiences and out­ comes, and what their consequences are for students of color. These findings could be informative to educators and adminis­ trators as they contemplate equity-based changes to their school security and school climate procedures.

This study examined the relationship between school security and school climate through the lens of its extended conse­ quences for student wellbeing. Through its methodology, it collected and examined student experiences of stress, safety, fear, and discomfort, assessed how they mani­ fested in anxiety, depression, and other mental health challenges among students, and explored their connection with the se­ curity presence at the student’s high school.

Review of Literature

Violence Within Schools School violence can encompass a mul­ titude of behaviors, including bullying, fighting, verbal threats, weapon posses­ sion, physical aggression, and acts of sexual violence, including harassment and assault (Turanovic & Siennick, 2022). Regardless of its form, school violence has been found to have a traumatic impact on everyone within a school community, most of all students, who are especially vulnerable to many of its consequences, including lone­ liness, low self-esteem, depression, anx­ iety, suicidality, self-harm, and fear (NIJ, 2022). Furthermore, due to the sensitivity of adolescence, experiencing violence in school during this period of development can have long-term effects on a student’s health, such as reactive attachment dis­ order, obesity, diabetes, heavy alcohol or substance use, and other poor health outcomes, in addition to the emotional consequences listed above (Ferrara et al., 2019).

Increase in School Security Presence In an attempt to mitigate threats of school violence, public schools over the last de­ cade have seen a rise in the use of visible school security measures (Tanner-Smith & Fisher, 2015). From 2005-2006, 26.2% of public primary schools and 75.2% of public high schools had a regular security presence. By 2017-2018, these numbers had inflated to 51.4% for public primary schools and 84.3% for public high schools. School Resource Officer (SRO) programs refer to the permanent placement of law enforcement officers within schools, and as a response to increasing rates of school shootings, SRO programs have grown in both size and mission over the last two decades (Ryan et al., 2017). As of 2017- 2018, 36% of public primary schools and 72% of public high schools had armed law enforcement stationed on campus (NCES, 2020). Nonetheless, evidence has shown that a school security presence does not neces­ sarily prevent school-based violence nor lead to increased school safety (Kupchik & Farina, 2016). Although some researchers have reported positive impacts of an SRO presence in schools (Johnson, 2016), based on a report by the National Center for Education Statistics (2022), the 2020-2021 school year saw the highest number of school shootings in two decades, despite a rise in the use of school security.

Impact of School Security on Student Outcomes Several studies have critically examined the impact of a school security presence on students’ academic outcomes and educa­ tional futures, finding that the presence of school security can lead to increased rates of student suspension and arrest (Finn & Servoss, 2014). The consequences of in­ creased suspension, expulsion, and arrest rates of students are severe, as any policy that removes a student who misbehaves from the classroom creates an “educational disruption” that prevents that student from receiving the protective effects of education on misbehavior or crime, there­ by predisposing that student to further misbehavior, disciplinary infractions, or incarceration (Passero, 2022).

Furthermore, researchers have found that race and gender play a large role in the frequency and severity of punishment received in schools (Pentek & Eisenberg, 2018). Research has shown a severe discrep­ ancy in who is punished, how frequently they are punished, to what severity they are punished, and the lasting consequences they might face. Black students, and Black female students in particular, experience dispro­ portionately high suspension and expulsion rates (Morris & Perry, 2017). Considering how law enforcement, other security mea­ sures, and punitive policies have created an avenue for student incarceration, the conse­ quences of these disparities and the implicit bias they affirm are severe.

School Climate School climate refers to the combination of beliefs, attitudes, and values that shape interactions between students, teachers, and administrators (Mitchell et al., 2010). It is the atmosphere and personality of a school, including its norms, values, expectations, and social characteristics (Brookover et al., 1978; Anderson, 1982). School climate has been linked to many student outcomes, such as academic achievement, discipline problems, and rates of absenteeism, truancy, and student dropout (Mitchell et al., 2010; Norton, 1984; Payne, 2018). Furthermore, the per­ ceived quality of school climate has been associated with behavioral and emotional adjustment in adolescents, with a negative perception contributing to declines in aca­ demic performance, self-image, perceived social support, and perceived quality of school life (Kuperminc et al., 1997).

School Security, School Climate, and Adolescent Wellbeing The use of certain visible security mea­ sures has been found to lead to a signifi­ cant decrease in students feeling safe while in school (Perumean-Chaney & Sutton, 2013). Even after controlling for the school’s level of violence, the use of metal detectors, security guards, or locked doors in a school is highly correlated with height­ ened levels of student fear (Gastic, 2011; Bachman et al., 2011). Particularly among students who have previously experienced victimization, research shows that visible security measures may magnify fear, promote distrust, and serve as a reminder of the threat of violence (Bachman et al., 2011). The stress, fear, and discomfort that may result from the use of certain visible security measures all impact dimensions of school climate.

There are five proposed domains of adolescent wellbeing: good health and op­ timum nutrition; connectedness, positive values, and contribution to society; safety and a supportive environment; learn­ ing, competence, education, skills, and employability; and agency and resilience (Ross et al., 2020). These five domains are meant to encompass both subjective and objective constructs of wellbeing, which include personal experiences and individual fulfillment, as well as quality of life indicators, such as material resources and social attributes (Ross et al., 2020). As we consider the impact a school security presence might have on school climate, in­ cluding increased levels of perceived fear, discomfort, or lack of safety, as well as the behavioral and emotional repercussions for a negatively perceived school climate, the extended consequences for student wellbeing are clear.

“Research has shown a severe discrepancy in who is punished, how frequently they are punished, to what severity they are punished, and the lasting consequences they might face.”

Methodology For data collection, this study incorporated a mixed methods approach. I collected quantitative data from a Qualtrics survey, distributed to students at Northwestern

University. These data were then sorted to only include responses from first-year col­ lege students who graduated in the last year from high school. Additionally, I collected qualitative data from interviews conducted with first-year students at Northwestern University who graduated the previous year from a high school with a security presence. “Security presence” was defined as a school’s use of police, security guards, security cameras, metal detectors, or any combination of the four. The quantitative method allowed me to identify potential trends in the relationship between school security and school climate, which I then built upon with personalized and detailed participant perspectives through the quali­ tative method.

Quantitative data was collected first, via the Qualtrics survey. I obtained 97 via­ ble responses to use in my analysis, which provided a sample size of about 5.7% of Northwestern University first-year stu­ dents. From the 2,039-person class of 2026, I subtracted an approximate number of Northwestern first-year students who took a gap year (based on national trends), as well as students who transferred from another university, as these students, despite being in their first year at North­ western, graduated from high school more than one year prior (Northwestern Admis­ sions; Hadden & Kaplan, 2020). See Table 1 for demographic details of the 97 total participants, including race, gender, type of high school attended, how many of the students’ schools had a security presence, and various types of security utilized by the students’ schools.

The survey began with demographic questions, questions about the school from which the student graduated, and questions about the security presence (or lack thereof) in said high school. From there, students were presented with 11 questions assessing school climate and wellbeing. A Likert-type scale ranging from one (Strongly Disagree) to five (Strongly Agree) was used to as­ sess students’ emotional reactions to these prompts, which included themes such as safety and comfort at school, instances of harassment or abuse, and experiences of mental health challenges. At the end of the survey, participants were asked if they were willing to be contacted in the future for an interview. See Appendix A for a full list of survey questions.

The quantitative data were analyzed using linear regressions, frequency tests, and one-way ANOVA tests through the program JASP. These analyses allowed me to identify potential relationships between school security and elements of school cli­ mate that negatively impact student well­ being, such as stress, discomfort, fear, and lack of safety, as well as ensure statistical validity and control for confounds. The trends established through these analyses informed the questions I asked in my in­ terview protocol and were used as support for themes that emerged in the interviews.

“Black students, and Black female students in particular, experience disproportionately high suspension and expulsion rates.”

Interview participants were selected based on their indicated willingness from the survey. I interviewed 10 individuals, which ensured that proper data saturation was reached (Guest et al., 2006), and in­ terviews took place over Zoom, due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Although there were no specific demographic re­ quirements for interviewees, I recruited a target population that was diverse in terms of personal and high school demographics based on the survey responses. The final sample of interviewees was Elizabeth, Alice, Emily, Jack, Elise, Deva, Marianna, Abby, Landon, and Maya. Nine were public school graduates, and one, Elizabeth, was a private school graduate. Alice, Elise, Jack, and Abby are white, Elizabeth is Black, Emily is East Asian, Deva is South Asian, Marianna is Hispanic/Latine, and two stu­ dents were multiracial: Maya is Black and white, and Landon is Hispanic/Latine and white. Alice, Elise, Abby, Elizabeth, Emily, Marianna, and Maya are female-identify­ ing, Jack and Landon are male-identifying, and Deva is non-binary/non-conforming. Among the 10 interviewees, every possible response to the student’s assessment of their school climate on the survey was rep­ resented, ensuring a diverse sample both in terms of student identity, as well as student perception of their school and its security.

The interview protocol consisted of 10 questions and followed a semi-struc­ tured approach. By using semi-structured interviews, I was able to introduce new concepts based on an interviewee’s re­ sponse. The semi-structured interview protocol consisted of original questions, drawn from previously researched mea­ sures of school climate, and informed by trends established via the quantitative sur­ vey (Bernhardt, 1998). It began with ques­ tions regarding the student’s high school and its security presence, including the type of security present, its visibility to stu­ dents, and the systems of support the high school offered in conjunction with the security presence. From there, questions pertained to interactions with and emo­ tional reactions and feelings as they related to the security presence. See Appendix B for a copy of the semi-structured interview protocol.

Qualitative data were organized and analyzed following a grounded theory framework. As a methodology designed to uncover explanatory theories grounded in data, utilizing this framework not only al­ lowed for a potential relationship between a student’s wellbeing and their school’s se­ curity presence to emerge, but also helped create a buffer for the biases that could oth­ erwise influence my interpretation (Chun Tie et al., 2019).

Findings In assessing each student’s impression of their school’s security, the level of school violence experienced or witnessed by the student emerged as a predictor. Students such as Alice, Maya, Deva, and Marianna, who reported the most negative percep­ tions of their school’s security, were also the students who reported experiencing or witnessing the most violence on a reg­ ular basis within their school. This finding stands out, as Maya, Alice, Deva, and Marianna would theoretically have the most to gain from the presence of school security, considering the intention behind security measures is to protect students from the violence that these students were experiencing and witnessing. However, Maya, Alice, Deva, and Marianna spoke of a gap between the intention of the school security, the funding that it required, and the actual effect, or lack thereof, on the school climate and their feelings of safety as a main reason behind their negative perceptions of their school’s security. They witnessed the violence that contributed to the hiring of their school’s security pres­ ence; they experienced the security, took notice of the resources it consumed, and in some cases, experienced harm as a result; and they failed to see its promised changes in either mitigated acts or threats of vio­ lence or positive effects to their wellbeing.

Similarly, the students who had the most positive reactions toward their school’s security, as well as the students who were mostly indifferent toward their school’s security, all reported low levels of violence within their schools and con­ sistent feelings of safety. Two students remarked that their school’s security offi­ cer felt like a member of the school com­ munity. Although there were a number of characteristics of the officer contributing to this perception that these students list­ ed, such as frequent, positive interactions and conversations with students, as well as active involvement in school events, the fact that none of these students had to encounter violence presents an alternative explanation as to why the security presence could exist purely as a community mem­ ber; neither student had to experience the security presence outside of that context. Their interactions could entirely consist of greetings and friendly questions, and the interactions they had to witness only revolved around standard school rules, which both students thought were fair. Furthermore, neither student had to ex­ perience a situation of violence by which to assess the security’s effectiveness at its intended protection, in the way that the students with negative reactions did.

For some students, the type of securi­ ty that was present proved a big distinction in the student’s perception of said security. Different types of security include passive measures, such as cameras, and active mea­ sures, such as bag checks, security guards or paraprofessionals, and SROs or police. When asked about their school security presence, regardless of which types were present within the school, students more often brought up active measures than passive measures. Similarly, when asked about various consequences of the secu­ rity presence, either positive or negative, students more often defaulted toward commenting on security personnel, such as security guards/paraprofessionals or SROs/police. It may be the case that stu­ dents think of passive security measures either differently than active measures or not at all, due to differences in frequency and type of encounter between the two types of measures.

Many students reported having posi­ tive impressions of and relationships with the security guards or paraprofessionals at their school, regardless of their gener­ al reaction toward security. For students who reported negative feelings related to features of the security, such as them be­ ing armed, or to harm committed by the security presence, such as instances of racial profiling and targeting or especially forceful or punitive protocols, the students differentiated between SROs/police and security guards/paraprofessionals when the two contrasted in these features or behaviors. This was amplified when, as it was in many of these cases, the security guard or paraprofessional did not resemble what one might imagine a typical security presence to be, such as one student de­ scribing her school’s paraprofessionals as “old ladies”.

Every male-identifying interviewee reported a positive or neutral percep­ tion of their school security, and only female-identifying and non-binary in­ terviewees reported negative reactions. Additionally, only interviewees of color discussed instances of racism when an­ swering questions about the impact of their school’s security on the school cli­ mate. Thus, it may be the case that cer­ tain kinds of violence are only included in assessments of school security when the assessment is being conducted by stu­ dents of certain identities, emphasizing the need for diverse perspectives on the matter. Furthermore, as only students of certain identities can speak firsthand to the emotional, mental, and physical impact of instances of discrimination or prejudice, it is critical that we include diverse voices in our conversations, if we hope to get a complete picture of the impact of school security.

Several students described witnessing or experiencing acts of racism from their school’s security. These included racial profiling, targeting, microaggressions, and acts of violence against Black and brown students. For these students, all of whom are students of color, these observed and experienced acts of racism shaped the student’s view of and relationship with security, as well as greatly impacted their wellbeing as a student within the school.

When describing their high school experience, many students mentioned the necessity of mental health support, speaking on behalf of both themselves and their peers. However, despite this stated significance of mental health challenges in a student’s experience at and perception of their school, the majority of the students describing mental health challenges faced by themselves or their peers followed those sentiments with reports of inadequate re­ sources and care. Several of the students remarked on how this lack of support amplified their frustration toward their school and its security. They saw the se­ curity presence growing, absorbing more and more of their school’s resources and funding, and they continued experienc­ ing and witnessing violence, all the while seeing students suffer without adequate support. Several students also mentioned that they saw mental health support as key to addressing the violence and conflicts they witnessed or experienced within their school. Especially for the students who saw security measures as punitive, reactionary, and ultimately ineffective, they described mental health support as an opportunity to address school-based conflicts and violence at their source before they turned more severe.

“. . . as only students of certain identites can speak firsthand to the emotional, mental, and physical impact of instances of discrimination or prejudice, it is critical that we include diverse voices in our conversations, if we hope to get a complete picture of the impact of school security.”

Discussion and Analysis As we consider the relationship between security, school climate, and student well­ being, the greatest reported impact from the interviewed students came from the security’s perceived ineffectiveness. The students that encountered regular violence experienced a negative impact on their school climate caused by said violence that had ramifications for their wellbe­ ing. Additionally, when acts of violence disproportionately affected Black and brown students, as was the case in some schools, we see an even greater disruption in the school’s climate for these (Black and brown) students. These disruptions had an emotional and mental toll on these students, as they navigated intense feelings of fear and lack of safety.

With the addition of school security, the impact was amplified. In some cases, this came from acts of violence and racism committed by security officers. However, for many of these students, it came from the security’s perceived ineffectiveness at addressing the violence in the schools: the safety it failed to ensure, the emotion­ al and mental stress it failed to remedy, and the frustration toward the school, its administration, and the security presence that it prompted. Many students explained that they saw security as a failure on their school’s part to protect them from the threats, both internal and external, that they were experiencing. It communicat­ ed a lack of care and support on behalf of the school, regardless of whether this was the school’s intention. Furthermore, these students were already experiencing intense anxiety and fear related to actual and perceived threats to their safety, and this added an additional layer, where these anxieties and fears were not eased, and students now felt as though they could not trust their school to support them. In con­ junction with inadequate systems of men­ tal health support, students described situ­ ations spiraling, feelings of frustration and lack of trust in the school, and a collective hopelessness at the idea of receiving help or support from the school, all of which contributed to a negative perception of the school’s climate and thus, facilitated the negative consequences of a poor percep­ tion of school climate for these students.

“They saw the security presence growing, absorbing more and more of their school’s resources and funding, and they continued experiencing and witnessing violence, all the while seeing students suffer without adequate support.”

For many students, there was a dis­ tinction made between different types of security, particularly security guards or paraprofessionals and SROs or police. This finding is somewhat supported by current research but also presents an opportunity for future research. Some studies differ­ entiate between school security measures through characteristics such as visibility, in­ trusiveness, and rigidity, which aligns with the distinction between active and passive measures found in this study (NCES, 2012; NASP, 2018). However, most research assessing the impact of school security categorizes all security measures within the same definition of security or only focuses on the measures often associated with most people’s conception of school security, such as metal detectors, security guards, and police. There have been few studies examining how different types of security may affect students differently, but based on this study, this could be an area of research worth exploring, particularly for schools that wish to maintain a security presence.

Throughout the study, students of different gender and racial identities de­ scribed varying perceptions and impacts of their school’s security, revealing how students of different identities can have different experiences within the same school climate and, thus, will form unique impressions and bear unique consequences of their school’s security and climate. This is supported by current research, which has found that race and gender play a large role in the frequency and severity of pun­ ishment for subjective infractions in school (Pentek & Eisenberg, 2018; Morris & Per­ ry, 2017), and presents an area for future research. A thorough understanding of the role of intersecting identities in school punishment and discipline is critical for a complete assessment of school security and its impact: on students, their perception of their school’s climate, and their wellbeing.

Conclusion This study attempted to fill in the gaps in current school security literature by exam­ ining the impact of a school security pres­ ence on school climate through the lens of student wellbeing. In this study, student wellbeing was assessed through student experiences with stress, perceived safety, fear, and discomfort, as well as how these emotional outcomes manifested in student experiences with depression, anxiety, and other mental health challenges. Findings of the study included the impact of school violence on a student’s relationship with their school’s security and administration, and its consequences for school climate and student wellbeing; direct impacts of school security on student wellbeing; how different security types elicit different per­ ceptions in students; how student identity impacts the relationship between a student and their school’s security presence; and how lack of adequate support affects student perception of climate and student wellbeing.

Hopefully, these findings will pave the way for future research on the matter, as well as meaningfully contribute to the current literature. As threats and acts of violence within schools continue to affect student learning and wellbeing, and as an unprecedented number of schools resort to security measures and security personnel, it is critical that we continue to study the best ways to support our students, protect them from threats, and promote their long-term wellbeing. Furthermore, it is imperative that we acknowledge that these answers will only emerge once we begin to not only include but center student voices and experiences in this conversation.◆
