title: Finding an Equilibrium in Life: An Interview With a Chemistry Graduate Student
notes: Q&A interview with Luis Sierra Ossa, a first-year Ph.D. student in theoretical chemistry from Cali, Colombia. The byline reads "Hannah Xu"; the masthead lists an editor "Hannah Zu". The question "Could you describe your research?" is doubled in the text layer (block 71.1).
text:
Finding an Equilibrium in Life: An Interview

With a Chemistry Graduate Student

By: Hannah Xu

Luis Sierra Ossa is a first-year Ph.D. student from Cali, Colombia. After completing his B.S. in Chemistry at Universidad del Valle, he began his graduate studies at Northwestern University. He is currently a graduate researcher in The Tempelaar Team, which focuses on exploring quantum and classical theories and developing hybrid models that implement both. [This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

What was your undergraduate education like?

I was born and raised in Colombia, and I went to a public university called Universidad del Valle for my Bachelor’s degree in Chemistry. My undergraduate education was five years long, which is common in Colombia. During the last three years, I did research in a theoretical chemistry group at my undergraduate institution, developing theories on entanglement in low-dimensional systems. This research is what I wrote my undergrad­ uate thesis on. In my last year, I had the incredible opportunity to do research as an international student in the iScholar program at the University of Rochester. In my research group there, I did theoretical chemistry research, using programming to simulate the optical and electrical properties of materials. It went very well, and that opened the doors for me to apply to Ph.D. programs, including the one here at Northwestern. What made you interested in pursuing a Ph.D.? Everyone has a different journey, but for me, it was easy to decide that a Ph.D. was the best option. I have a lot of passion for research, and while I love my country, I wanted to do a Ph.D. somewhere with more opportunities for scientists. I also felt that pursuing a Ph.D. was a challenge that was valuable for my personal development, as it involved moving to a new environment, meeting new people, and learning new things.

How did you identify your research interests?

I knew very early on that I was interested in theoretical chemistry. I remember taking general chemistry my first year with the professor who was my undergraduate thesis mentor. I was amazed not only by how physics can tell you what is happening in chem­ ical processes, but also by the fundamental questions asked when exploring theory in chemistry. I always wanted to understand the fundamental concepts in chemistry, so it felt natural for me to pursue theory.

What was the Ph.D. application process like?

Before applying, I made a long list of all the Ph.D. programs I could be interested in. I looked into each program, and I narrowed the list down to only the nine I applied to. I took this very seriously, as doing a Ph.D. is a major life opportunity. I sent emails to 25twenty-five professors whose research I was interested in, which was important to make a good first impression. Around half of these professors responded, including Prof. Roel Tempelaar at Northwestern. After talking to some of them, I submitted my applications, and I did a few interviews in which I talked about myself and my research, among other things. In the end, I received my decision notifications between December and February. This was simply my experience applying to Ph.D. programs, and it may be slightly different from others’ experiences because I am an international student in theoretical chemistry. Even within chemistry, the interviews can be different if you are an ex­ perimentalist rather than a theorist, and it can also depend on the professor you are interested in working with.

How did you decide between Ph.D. programs?

I was accepted to five schools, but Northwestern stood out to me because of two main reasons: the structure of the program and my research mentor. I like the structure of Northwestern’s graduate program because it places a lot more em­ phasis on research than classes. Northwestern requires graduate students in chemistry to take six classes their first year, but then students are free to dedicate their time fully to research. Some schools emphasize classes more, so students there are required to do more than one year of classes. This can be beneficial for some students because you learn more background from classes before doing research. However, I believe that having more time to do research is important because what you learn through your research is often far more complex than what classes can teach. Apart from the program structure, I also came to Northwestern for Roel Tempelaar, whose research aligns well with my interests.

Could you describe your research? Could you describe your research?

My research is in theoretical chemistry. These two words may seem odd together be­ cause chemistry is largely experimental. What is theoretical chemistry? Essentially, we use mathematical and physical tools to study chemical phenomena. When theoretical insights match experimental results, they provide a fuller explanation of phenomena. For example, the orbital is a very interesting concept that was made by theorists, and orbitals are now used by experimentalists to explain many chemical processes. In my research group, we aim to develop these kinds of tools for everyone in the field to use. My project focuses on mixed quantum-classical dynamics, developing theories to understand what is happening to electrons in materials in the presence of phonons, which are crystal vibrations. We begin with a model, develop theories to understand the model, and then use computer programming to run theoretical simulations. The theoretical results can be compared to lab results, which tells us if our theories provide a plausible explanation for what is observed.

What are your responsibilities as a first-year graduate student at Northwestern?

The first year is challenging in the sense that you need to adjust to a new lifestyle, develop new skills, and manage your time well. There is also a wider variety of responsibilities in the first year, which includes taking classes, doing research, and teaching undergraduate students. During my first year, I am taking two classes each quarter so that I also have time to do research for at least one hour every day, but I will be able to dedicate more time to research once I am done with classes at the end of this year. I will also be a teaching assistant for five quarters during the Ph.D. program. As a teaching assistant, I discuss content with the professor, grade assessments, prepare review sessions, hold of­ fice hours, and am there for students. It is a lot of work sometimes, but I enjoy it because I think the best way to fully understand the depth of a topic is to teach it. Explaining concepts in simpler terms is incredibly beneficial because it is difficult and it requires me to think about them in different ways. Outside of these responsibilities, I try to find an equilibrium in my life through my hobbies.

What do you plan on doing after your Ph.D.?

I don’t know, actually. Anything can change during a Ph.D. I would love to keep work­ ing on research, not necessarily as an assistant professor, but maybe in an institution. But it is also important to be realistic. Academia is hard, even more so for international students. My goal for now is to develop a complete set of skills that enables me to choose whatever path I want after my Ph.D., whether it’s industry, academia, opening a bakery, or anything else. This is why I feel like a Ph.D. is a life opportunity—at the end of the day, it will help me develop strong skills so that I have more options when I need to make a decision.

Do you have any advice for undergraduates who are interested in pursuing a Ph.D.?

Life is too short to not do a Ph.D. Naturally, it’s not for everyone. A Ph.D. opens a lot of doors, but it closes others. The most important thing in a Ph.D. is your research, and making sure that it’s something you love to do. Asking questions about the universe, interpreting your findings … if you’re passionate about these things, a Ph.D. is a very good opportunity to deepen your understanding of your field and discover what you want to do with your life. Discover your signature. It even helps you develop as a person because you constantly approach problems differently, encounter failures, and try to solve them. Nothing is black and white here—everything is colorful. You put yourself completely in your work, and you learn a lot about yourself through your research. Every challenge is beneficial for you, and it helps you develop both your research and your life skills, teaching you how to improve your time management, balance your responsibilities, and find equilibrium in your life.

title: Are People “Real” on BeReal? Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App
notes: Senior thesis. Adviser from "Faculty Adviser" on the opening page; the opening page also names a Second Reader, William Horton, Ph.D. The contents and contributors pages write "Are People “Real” on BeReal?: Perception ...". Supported by an Academic Undergraduate Research Grant. Online survey of 200 U.S. college students (100 BeReal users, 100 non-users). Printed pages 85-96 are an appendix of statistical tables (Tables 1-6 and 1A-8A); table cells are extracted as separate short blocks. The first and last blocks of printed page 97 read "97 97" (a doubled page number). Pull quotes are placed at the nearest paragraph break.
text:
Department of Psychology

Are People “Real” on BeReal?

Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App by Amy Fan

Faculty Adviser: Alissa Chung, Ph.D. Second Reader: William Horton, Ph.D.

Author Note This research was supported by the Academic Undergraduate Research Grant through Northwestern’s Office of Undergraduate Research. Conclusions, opinions, and other statements of the author are not necessarily representative of Northwestern University. This project would not have been possible without the support of my adviser, Dr. Alissa Chung; my senior thesis seminar instructor, Dr. Sandra Waxman; and teaching assis­ tant, Kayla Garner.

Abstract BeReal grew rapidly in popularity throughout 2022. Created as a response to social media platforms where idealized images and higher usage are encouraged, BeReal takes a different approach. Valuing authenticity, BeReal asks users to post a daily front and back-facing picture within a random two-minute time slot and provides a short daily feed of BeReals from friends. In an online survey, U.S. college students 18-23 years old were studied in two groups: BeReal users (n = 100) and non-BeReal users (n =100). Both groups completed questions on perception and usage of different social media platforms and anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and authenticity scales. BeReal users were asked additional questions to observe trends in how people use and perceive BeReal, determine the extent to which BeReal usage moderates the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, and examine whether inauthentic BeReal behaviors are correlated with greater anxiety, self-consciousness, fear of missing out, and inauthenticity. Results show that BeReal usage did not significantly mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out, public self-conscious­ ness, and authenticity. The average user posted 78% of the time, posted late 52% of the time, and retook their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors, with the median accepted late post of 10 hours late and the median accepted number of retakes being three. We also found that the percentage of late posts had a negative public correlation with anxiety, and the percentage of skipped posts had a positive correlation with public self-consciousness. Keywords: BeReal, social media, authentic­ ity, anxiety, public self-consciousness, fear of missing out

Are People “Real” on BeReal? Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App

With over 10 million daily users and 53 million downloads, BeReal claims to be “a new and unique way to discover who your friends really are in their daily life” (BeReal). Created as a response to social media platforms like Instagram, where us­ ers tend to post picture-perfect images on a never-ending feed, BeReal takes a different approach. The app shows a limited daily feed of friends’ BeReals, taking up only a small part of the day.

The overall objective of this app is to “be real.” A BeReal user gets a notification at any point during the day and has two minutes to take a front and back-facing camera picture. If they do not post within that time frame, the delayed time is shown; for example, “10 minutes late” or “8 hours late.” Users are discouraged from posting later when they may be doing something that is more appealing to their audience. Users cannot see their friends’ BeReals for the day until they post one themselves. BeReal does not show the feature of likes or followers but instead has “reacts” where users can respond to a BeReal with a pic­ ture, emoji, or comment. Users can only see friends’ BeReals from that day and not from past days to keep users’ feeds short and up to date. All these aspects combined could potentially eliminate the popularity aspect of other social media platforms, such as comparing numbers of followers, likes, and other interactions. The main goal of the app is for users to see what their friends are up to while mitigating the neg­ ative effects of other social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. Due to the novel popularity of BeReal, there is no current literature studying this platform.

“While the app was designed to promote authenticity by keeping users accountable, actual users were more forgiving with these inauthentic behaviors.”

Given its widespread usage among college students and younger adolescents, looking into how people use and perceive BeReal could reveal unintended negative conse­ quences to using the app and/or show that it is a social media app that connects people in a positive manner.

Existing Authenticity in Social Media Platforms

Before BeReal’s prominence, authen­ ticity on social media platforms was en­ couraged in other ways. For example, on Instagram, users often have a main account and a “finsta” or a “fake Instagram.” The main account is where users post their best pictures for a more general audience, while the finsta is where users post less polished photos, emotional photos, archival photos, funny moments (Kang & Wei, 2020), and unfiltered thoughts to a small group of friends (Huang & Vitak, 2022). Despite this push for authenticity by using Instagram in this manner, young adults and children still may face certain pressures to “perform” on these finstas since there are a set of norms as to what content is posted and how often (Dewar et al., 2019).

Looking even further into the past, blogging in a personal journal or diary form on platforms like MySpace and Tumblr has allowed users to vent and seek feedback on difficult situations or everyday life situations by giving users an online platform where it is appropriate and encouraged to share personal experi­ ences and seek support from a community (Baker et al., 2008). Certain social con­ straints hinder people from bringing these situations up in face-to-face conversations. When comparing bloggers on MySpace to nonbloggers, bloggers’ social integration, reliable alliance, and friendship satisfaction all increased compared to nonbloggers’, suggesting that blogging may have benefits in perceived social support (Baker et al., 2008). Blogging could even be used as a form of self-therapy (Tan et al., 2018).

Despite the push for authenticity in previously existing social media using these two methods, BeReal remains dis­ tinct. BeReal is a photo & caption-based platform with authenticity as a focus throughout the design process. Finstas and blogging on MySpace are features embed­ ded in the larger overall platform. People use Instagram and MySpace for purposes other than finstas and blogging on those respective platforms, so there could still be several other features on the platform that could negatively affect how authentic users are.

“Despite this push for authenticity by using Instagram in this manner, young adults and children still may face certain pressures to ‘perform.’”

Authenticity, despite its nuances, is important to study because past research has shown that authenticity is related to a lower risk of developing social media addiction (Monacis et al., 2021). In addi­ tion, authentic self-expression is associated with greater reported life satisfaction compared to self-idealized self-expression (Bailey et al., 2020).

Self-Presentation & Authenticity

False or adapted self-presentation and inauthenticity in portraying one’s life and emotions is a frequent problem with certain social media platforms (Gil- Or et al., 2015). Even with the measures against false self-presentation and push for showing the true self on BeReal, like the two-minute time limit and the randomized time a user gets a notification to post for the day, there is still an opportunity for inauthenticity through retakes, not post­ ing on time, and not posting at all. If the first photo is bad, the user might retake the photo to get a better angle of themselves. If the user feels like they are not doing some­ thing interesting enough, they could wait to post until later. And there is always the option of not posting at all if they do not want to show themselves for that day.

The number of friends a user has on social media could push users to in­ crease positive self-presentation regardless of whether the user is doing well or not (Kim & Lee, 2011). BeReal shows friend counts in increments after a certain point. For example, if a person has 68 friends on BeReal, it is displayed as 50+ instead of that specific number. It is possible that the relationship between audience and false self-presentation is hindered by the lack of specificity in BeReal of how many friends a person has added. However, there are lim­ itations to studying the effect of this spe­ cific feature due to other factors affecting false self-presentation like the presence of photos (Gil-Or et al., 2015) and the makeup of the audience (Rui, 2013). And it is still possible that those with more friends may still display more false self-presentation behaviors than those with fewer friends on BeReal.

Despite research showing that authentic self-expression can be positive, it is also important to note that there could be moments where authenticity can be negative. For instance, “vague-booking” is defined as when people go on Facebook to post a true but vague message about their current feelings that elicits a response from other users (Astleitner et al., 2023). Vague-booking may mediate the rela­ tionship between personality and mental health and is linked to suicidal ideation (Berryman et al., 2017). It is possible that sometimes going to social media to com­ municate and seek support may not be the best form of action, and it may be better to reach out to personal networks instead.

Social Media & Fear of Missing Out

Past studies suggest that an increase in social media usage is correlated with lower self-esteem (Jan et al., 2017; Hawi & Samaha, 2016). Lower self-esteem is associated with lower life satisfaction (Hawi & Samaha, 2016). A phenomenon where social media users feel left out of specific social events is known as the Fear of Missing Out (FoMO). Studies have shown that the negative impacts of social media sites leading to lower self-esteem are mediated by FoMO (Salim et al., 2017). Higher levels of FoMO were also related to increased social media presence through behaviors like updating their status more often or posting more pictures. BeReal aims to avoid FoMO by showing when users post late as an accountability fea­ ture. That way, people cannot only post their most interesting social interactions because they need to post when prompted to avoid “being late.” However, FoMO may still be prominent since users will likely see if they were left out of a social gathering on BeReal.

Social Media & Psychopathology

Several studies have implicated more time spent on social media as a risk factor for developing an anxiety disorder (Keles et al., 2020; Vannucci et al., 2017). Increased social media use has been linked to depression and anxiety, particularly when there is greater emotional invest­ ment in social media (Woods & Scott, 2016). Since BeReal is designed to take up a relatively short amount of time per day (~10 minutes), it is possible that users who primarily use BeReal and no other social media platforms have a reduced risk of developing psychopathology due to the minimal time spent on the app. In addi­ tion, if users utilize BeReal in an authentic manner, it is possible BeReal use mitigates the relationship between social media use and negative outcomes.

Research Questions

This study will explore the ques­ tions: (1) Does BeReal usage mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out (FoMO), public self-consciousness (PSC), and au­ thenticity? (2) How do people use BeReal, and what do they think BeReal’s intended purpose is compared to other social media apps? (3) Are inauthentic BeReal behaviors such as retakes, posting late, and skipping related to greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and inauthenticity?

Main Hypotheses

My hypothesis is that BeReal use moderates the link between total time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity. Past research has shown a link between total time spent on social media and increasing anxiety, FoMO, and self-consciousness and decreasing self-esteem and authenticity (Monacis et al., 2021). BeReal’s push for authentic use could potentially mitigate these negative outcomes.

In open-ended questions about BeRe­ al, participants are expected to report ben­ efits like functionality (which limits time spent on the app), the encouraged lower friend count, the refreshed daily feed, and the spontaneity of posting. Some disadvan­ tages participants may bring up are FoMO, opportunities for inauthenticity often re­ ferred to as “being fake,” and the random notification during the day being at an inconvenient time. I expect there to be a greater positive attitude toward BeReal compared to other social media platforms.

Those who have more BeReal friends and exhibit more inauthentic behaviors such as greater average number of retakes, posting late, and skipping posts despite seeing the notification on time may have greater anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and less au­ thenticity. Those who have greater anxi­ ety, PSC, and FoMO, and less authenticity may care more about how they look during the two-minute window than remaining authentic, so they may retake their BeReal more often and skip or post late instead of showing what they are doing at the time of notification. A greater percentage of time spent scrolling through feeds may be correlated with higher levels of anxiety and FoMO due to a greater likelihood that a user may see other friends spending time with each other, while a greater percent­ age of time spent interacting with friends’ BeReals may be correlated with greater authenticity and lower FoMO.

Methods

Participants

Undergraduate college students of all genders, races, and ethnicities who are En­ glish speakers (n = 650) aged 18-23 years old across the United States were surveyed about their TikTok, Instagram, and BeRe­ al usage on the research platform Prolific. This screening on Prolific was used to sep­ arate participants into two groups. Group 1 participants (n = 100) did not use BeReal (less than once every two weeks for one month). Group 2 participants (n = 100) did use BeReal (at least once every two weeks for one month). Additional participants for the BeReal survey were sought out from the Northwestern University under­ graduate community due to the low num­ ber of qualifying BeReal users (n = 158). Participants in Group 2 (n = 100) were a mix of Prolific users (n = 75) who were compensated and Northwestern students (n = 25) who were not. Participants were only asked what college they go to in the demographics section since Prolific pro­ vides data on age, race, ethnicity, gender identity, year in school, and region.

Questionnaires

The survey included a question on college attended, questions on general so­ cial media usage across different platforms, questions about their perception of each social media platform (purpose, affect, etc.), questions specific to BeReal, the Gen­ eral Anxiety Disorder-7 Scale (Spitzer et al., 2006), Public Self-Consciousness Scale (Scheier and Carver, 1985), the Fear of Missing Out Scale (Przybylski et al., 2013), and Authenticity Scale (Wood et al., 2008).

General Anxiety Disorder Scale

The General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) was used to measure anxiety in the current state (Spitzer et al., 2006). This short questionnaire utilized a Likert scale of 0-3 (not at all, several days, more than half the days, and nearly every day) with prompts like “Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge” and “Worrying too much about different things.” Scores were calculated by summing the numerical score of each item for a final score. For this study, scores were treated as a continuous variable. A greater score is indicative of greater anx­ iety. Cronbach’s α for the GAD-7 scale in this sample is 0.938 (n = 191). The GAD-7 Scale is widely used in clinical settings and was shown to be reliable and valid (Spitzer et al., 2006).

Public Self-Consciousness Scale

Public Self-Consciousness (PSC) re­ fers to the tendency to think about aspects of self in the matter of public display. Only the PSC Scale from the overall Self-Con­ sciousness Scale (Scheier and Carver, 1985) was utilized as this form of self-conscious­ ness may be particularly relevant to BeReal usage. The seven-item questionnaire gave prompts like “I am concerned with my style of doing things” and “I usually worry about making a good impression,” which are an­ swered on a 0-3 Likert scale (not like me at all, a little like me, somewhat like me, a lot like me). Scores were averaged to obtain an overall score. A higher score is indicative of greater PSC. The PSC Scale was shown to be reliable and valid (Scheier and Carv­ er, 1985). Cronbach’s α for the PSC Scale in this sample is 0.846 (n = 191).

Fearing of Missing Out Scale

The 10-item FoMO Scale was used to measure the degree to which someone fears missing out on social events and uses social media to remain hyper-connected using a 5-point Likert scale (not at all true of me, slightly true of me, moderately true of me, very true of me, and extremely true of me) with prompts like “I get worried when I find out my friends are having fun with­ out me” and “I fear my friends have more rewarding experiences than me.” Each item’s score from 1-5 points was summed to a total score, and an average between all answers provided a final score. A greater score is indicative of a greater fear of miss­ ing out. The FoMO Scale was shown to be reliable and valid (Przybylski et al., 2013). Cronbach’s α for the FoMO Scale in this sample is 0.897 (n = 191).

Authenticity Scale

The 12-item Authenticity Scale mea­ sured authenticity in knowing oneself, expressing emotions in a way that is con­ gruent with values and beliefs, and staying true to personal beliefs despite external influences (Wood et al., 2008). There were four items for each of the three subscales: Self-Alienation (AS), Authentic Living (AL), and Accepting of External Influences (AE). Participants were given prompts like “I feel as if I don’t know myself very well,” “I live in accordance to my values and be­ liefs,” and “I am strongly influenced by the opinions of others,” which were answered on a Likert scale of 1-7 (does not describe me at all to describes me very well). The AS and AE Subscales were reverse-scored. The final authenticity score was the sum of the reverse-scored subscale items and AL Subscale items. In the overall Authenticity Scale and AL Subscale, a greater score was indicative of greater authenticity. For the AS and AE Subscales, a lower score was indicative of greater authenticity. The Au­ thenticity Scale and Subscales were shown to be reliable and valid (Wood et al., 2008). The Authenticity Scale Cronbach’s α is 0.832. The AS Subscale (α = 0.958), AL Subscale (α = 0.855), and AE Subscale (α

= 0.852) were also internally reliable (n =191).

General Social Media Questions

This nine-item section was repeated for every social media platform partic­ ipants indicated they use. Participants were asked which social media platforms they used, percentage breakdowns of the amount of time spent on each platform, how often they used each platform (daily or almost daily, 2-3 times per week, 1 time per week, 1-2 times per month, <1 per month), average amount of time spent per day, how they used each platform (catch up with friends, scroll through feed for en­ tertainment, scroll through feed for news, post about own life, make entertaining content, other) and percentage breakdown of time spent on those options. They were also asked open-ended questions about what they thought the intended purpose of this platform was and whether the benefits outweigh the disadvantages.

BeReal Questions

Group 2 participants (n = 100) who were active users of BeReal (at least once every two weeks for a month) were asked a separate set of questions (28 items). They were asked how many friends they have on BeReal, the percentage of time they post, the percentage of time they are on time when they post, the percentage of time they retake their BeReal before posting, the percentage of time they retake 1, 2, 3, or 4 times, the motivation behind retak­ ing BeReals, what percentage of time they scroll through the feed after they post, the percentage of time they skip the BeReal despite seeing the notification on time, the percentage of time they skip the Be­ Real after seeing the notification late, the percentage of time they interact with their friends’ BeReals, and when they do inter­ act with friends’ BeReals, the percentage of time they utilize face react compared to emoji compared to comment. The last two questions gauged when users thought the latest someone could post and the maxi­ mum number of retakes that they would consider to be socially acceptable to them.

Plan of Analysis

We ran a linear regression to com­ pare total time spent on social media and the four numerical dependent variable scores. BeReal use is expected to moderate the correlation between total time spent on social media and the four DVs, so hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use acted as independent variables and an interaction term between hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use was included in the model. Pearson correlations were run between separate IVs (number of friends, percent of times posted, percentage of late posts, percentage of retakes, average number of retakes per BeReal, percentage of skips despite seeing BeReal on time, per­ centage of skips after seeing notification on time, percentage of time spent scrolling through feed after post, percentage of time they interact with friends’ BeReals) and the four DVs to determine further correla­ tions. Qualitative data was coded for the top five occurrences.

Results

Data Cleaning & Scoring

Participants were removed from the data if they did not meet certain criteria (n = 9). For both the General Survey and the BeReal Survey, those who did not complete the questionnaires about anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity were re­ moved (n = 3). Those who took the BeReal survey and did not post at least twice in the last 30 days were removed (n = 5). Partic­ ipants who had given out-of-range data (e.g., over 24 hours of social media use per day) were also removed (n = 1). 191 par­ ticipants remained: 93 BeReal users and 98 non-BeReal users.

Social Media Usage

Results are based on hours spent on social media per day and on what specific apps are shown (Table 1). On average, par­ ticipants used apps like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube for a greater amount of time. For the BeReal group, the mean time spent on social media was 4.0 hours (SD = 2.3) per day. The BeReal use percentage mean was 4.96 (SD = 5.86), ~12 minutes a day.

TikTok and Instagram percentages were higher for the BeReal group, with a slightly lower YouTube percentage (Table 2). We see that Facebook percentages are low across the board for college students. Many participants thought the intended purpose of Facebook is to connect with friends and family of the older generation or for event invites and notifications.

How social media was used greatly differed depending on the platform. Par­ ticipants generally used BeReal to scroll through their feed or stories to see what people in their network were up to (M = 51.7%, SD = 35.5%) and post or create con­ tent (M = 27.8%, SD = 32.9%). Participants primarily scrolled through their feed for entertainment on TikTok (M = 72.4%, SD = 26.6%)) and YouTube (M = 72.0%, SD = 35.3%), while Instagram was used in a greater variety of ways: scrolling through the feed to keep up with network (M = 36.8%, SD = 27.3%), scrolling through the feed for entertainment (M = 31.0%, SD = 25.8%), and directly interacting with friends (M = 21.9%, SD = 22.6%). Face­ book’s main usage was scrolling through the feed to keep up with their network (M

= 48.4%, SD = 35.6%).

BeReal Results

In the BeReal data set, participants posted a BeReal 78% of the time. Of our 93 participants, 55 provided insight as to why they skipped posts (Table 3). Participants posted late on average 53.8% of the time (SD = 29.3%). The most occurring reasons for posting late were inconvenient times, perceived interest, and apathy (Table 4). Out of our 93 participants, 84 participants provided qualitative data on reasons for posting late. The mean percentage they re­ took their BeReal before posting was 37.5% (SD = 30.8%). When participants retook their BeReal, they tended to retake it only once (M = 74.2%, SD = 24.6%) or twice (M = 19.4%, SD = 18.9%). Most users retook BeReals for unclear photos, appearance of self, and because it did not include desired content (Table 5). Out of our 93 partici­ pants, 90 participants provided qualitative data on reasons for retaking BeReals.

The mean percentage of participants interacting with friends’ BeReals was 56.5% (SD = 38.1%). The methods participants used to interact with friends on BeReal were Face React (M = 60.3%, SD = 37.0%), Comment (M = 19.4%, SD = 25.1%), and Emoji React (M = 12.6%, SD = 25.8%). Face React, or taking a selfie response, was the most popular. The median number of friends users had on BeReal was 47 (SD = 15). In users’ opinion, the mean max hours a user should post late is 11.9 with a me­ dian of 10 hours (SD = 8.8), and the mean max number of retakes a user should take is 3.7 with a median of 3 retakes (SD = 2.6).

Primary Analyses

We ran Pearson correlations be­ tween time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity and found a positive correlation between time on social media and anxiety (Table 6). Cor­ relations between the four scales were all significant. Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all had moderate positive correlations with each other, while anxiety, PDC, and FoMo had moderate negative correlations with authenticity (Table 6).

To test if BeReal use moderated the relationship between total time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity, four linear regression models were run with those four variables as the DVs. Hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use acted as independent vari­ ables, with an interaction term between hours spent on social media per week and BeReal use included in the model. There is no evidence that BeReal use mitigates the relationship between total time spent on social media and the DVs (Table 1A-4A).

Analyses were also run to test the BeReal group and see if authentic vs. in­ authentic BeReal use moderates the rela­ tionship between total time spent on social media and anxiety. Authentic BeReal use was defined as practical reasons for not us­ ing BeReal as intended. If a participant said that they could not take the BeReal on time because they were in the shower or in class, that reasoning would be coded “authentic.” If a participant said they could not take the BeReal because they were doing something boring and would do something more in­ teresting later, then their reason was coded “inauthentic.” Similar reasoning was ap­ plied to reasons for retakes and skipping the BeReal. Authentic usage did not mod­ erate the relationship between total time spent on social media per week and the four DVs (Table 5A-7A).

Secondary Analyses

Percentage of late posts had a positive correlation with the authenticity scores (r

= 0.279, p < 0.003) and a moderate negative correlation with the self-alienation authen­ ticity score (r = -0.429, p < 0.001). In this subscale, the higher the score, the greater self-alienation and decreased authenticity in that aspect. The percentage of late posts also had a slight negative correlation with the GAD-7 anxiety score (r = -0.306, p < 0.003). Percentage of skips had a positive correlation with the PSC score (r = 0.208, p < 0.046). See Table 8A for full results.

Discussion

Summary & Interpretation of Results

In terms of general social media use, we found that apps that have an entertain­ ment aspect, like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, were used for a greater duration. Time spent on BeReal is generally low (Ta­ ble 2). BeReal was mainly used to keep up with people in users’ networks and post or create content that has a greater social or community aspect.

We found that BeReal use does not mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, PSC, FoMO, and authenticity. In addition, out of the four possible correlations between time spent on social media and the four DVs, only time spent on social media and anx­ iety had a significant positive correlation. Descriptive statistics showed that among those who use BeReal, the average user posted 78% of the time. When users post­ ed, they tended to post late 52% of the time and retake their BeReal at least once 37% of the time before posting. It is possible that because users did not always adhere to the intended use of BeReal, no moderating effects were observed, as users only spent 12 minutes on BeReal every day. A shared understanding that it is okay to post late or retake your BeReal despite the counter­ measures built into BeReal shows that it was not being used in the intended way.

“We found that BeReal use does not mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, public self- consciousness (PSC), fear of missing out

(FoMO), and authenticity.”

Anxiety, PSC, and FoMO all had moderately positive correlations with each other, while anxiety, PSC, and FoMO had moderate negative correlations with authenticity. This result showed those with either high anxiety, PSC, or FoMO may have higher scores in the other two variables as well. The percentage of late posts has a positive correlation with the Authenticity Scale and a moderate neg­ ative correlation with the self-alienation authenticity scores, which differed from the hypothesis. We expected that those who exhibited more inauthentic behavior would show lower authenticity scores. Those who posted late may be more likely to be engaging in in-person activities in­ volving others, which suggests authentic living outside of the app. The percentage of late posts also had a negative correla­ tion with anxiety, which could possibly be explained by the idea that those with less anxiety may not be as vigilant about post­ ing on time. If a user cares a lot about how they are seen by the public, then they may have opted to skip BeReal altogether even when they are available to post late, which explains the positive relationship between percentage of skips with PSC score.

Limitations

In the data collection process for au­ thentic usage in retakes, posting late, and skipping, participants were asked for rea­ sons why they retake, post late, and skip, which we coded as authentic or inauthen­ tic. While the number of participants who listed each reason was obtained, data were not collected longitudinally to see the fre­ quency of each reason in specific instances. Although some may have listed authentic or inauthentic reasons, we still do not know how often they are engaging these behav­ iors for authentic or inauthentic reasons and whether some users fall somewhere in the middle in terms of authentic use. More detailed studies on BeReal use with a great­ er sample size are necessary to gain a better understanding of this relationship.

Future Direction

The predicted mitigation effect of BeReal was hypothesized under the as­ sumption that BeReal would largely be used in the intended manner. We found that this was not the case. However, since we collected a great deal of data on how BeReal is used, that can be helpful in cre­ ating and designing further BeReal studies.

The most recent update on BeReal showed a significant change in design. Now, users can post up to three BeReals if they post their first BeReal on time. They likely made this decision because, as this study shows, adherence to BeReal rules is low. However, this does defeat the original purpose of the app, which was for users to show what they are doing at any given time during the day. This new update makes BeReal more of a mix between the original app and Instagram, where you post your highlights. Although some may argue that the new BeReal update is still better than Instagram since users must post on time to unlock the extra posts, there is a possi­ bility that this could lead to more FoMO since BeReal is already an intimate view into one’s life as a daily task. Now, with the added option of posting up to three times a day, there is even greater visibility. Re­ searchers must adapt to these changes to fully understand the relationship between social media and psychopathology. ◆

title: Learning to juggle: Undergraduates balance research with busy lives
notes: Feature on how undergraduates Izzy Mroczek and Ashley Brobbey (named under their photos on the opening page) balance lab research with other commitments. The contents gives the title as "Learning to juggle: undergrads balance research with busy lives".
text:
Learning to juggle: Undergraduates balance research with busy lives by Maggie Rose Baron

Izzy Mroczek Ashley Brobbey

Classes, work, sports, pre-professional organizations, extracurricu­ lars, and volunteer hours. A typical undergraduate Northwestern student is pulled in a thousand different directions, and some find the time to add another item to their plate: research.

“It’s really fascinating to me, because you can ask questions, and answer them,” third-year Izzy Mroczek said of her research. “You’re constantly stim­ ulating a new topic and kind of solving puzzles in ways that really matter.”

Mroczek is a double major in biological sciences and Slavic language and literature. Since June of 2022, she has worked as an undergraduate research assistant in the Shilatifard Lab, an epigenetics cancer lab at Northwestern’s Feinberg School of Medicine.

Research can take many forms for a Northwestern undergraduate, from working in a physical laboratory with scientific experiments, to sifting through archival texts on a computer or in a library. Mroczek’s work is the former: she studies the degradation of a protein that transcribes DNA to RNA, and her specific project is part of the Shilatifard Lab’s overall focus on mutations in transcriptional machinery and how those mutations are linked to cancer.

“You’re really contributing, even if it’s in a small way as an undergrad with a small little project,” Mroczek said. “It still makes a difference, so I find that really cool.”

Commuting to Feinberg, which is located in Chicago, gives Mroczek a different experience than other undergraduate researchers who stay in Evanston.

“It’s kind of harder since I do have to … commute to the city,” Mroczek said. “I don’t have as much freedom with my experiments as I’d like because there’s only so much I can do within the two days.”

Nonetheless, Mroczek said that her lab’s location within Feinberg offers her opportunities she would never have if she did research on the Evanston campus. She has been able to attend seminars, learn about research outside of her own field and get connected to faculty and medical students. Since Mroczek plans to go to medical school after undergrad, these experiences have been invaluable to her.

For students in other fields of research, being part of a lab can offer similar opportunities for mentorship and support.

“They will support you as you do your own projects in their lab,” said Ashley Brobbey, a third-year majoring in psychology and global health stud­ ies who works in the Personality Across Development Lab (PADlab). “They guide you not only in undergraduate but also through graduate, because they are really your mentors and they’re here to help you do your PhD path or your grad school path, whatever it is you want to do with your future.”

The PADlab studies developmental psychology and the psychology of personality, and Brobbey, who started as an undergraduate research assistant in the summer of 2023, specifically studies how the personalities of children are shaped by their environment and their socioeconomic and racial statuses. She was drawn to the PADlab both because of her interest in their research and because of the flexible and supportive environment the lab embodies.

That flexibility is important to Brobbey in part because she has so many other involvements on campus. Brobbey is a member of Northwestern’s cheerleading team and holds positions in Black Formal, Society of Women Engineers, Minority Association of Pre-Med Students and Physicians for Human Rights.

“I like this lab because you can work part time when your schedule is busy,” Brobbey said. “And then come back to full time, or even take a full quarter break from lab until you want to come back.”

Brobbey stressed the importance of having good time management and sticking to a schedule when balancing lab work with the rest of her life.

“I do all of my lab work on Fridays, so I can just go in and just knock it all out, and that way I can focus on the rest of those other commitments.”

Mroczek, who works in her lab around 13 hours a week on top of her classes and involvement in Quest+, Matriculate and Physicians for Human Rights, said she has been lucky that her many commitments have not clashed. Like Brobbey, she emphasized the importance of a consistent schedule. For Mroczek, this means commuting to Feinberg every Monday and Friday, a routine she has been able to keep up throughout her time at the Shilatifard Lab.

While research is a commitment that busy undergraduate students may have to juggle with the rest of their lives, both Brobbey and Mroczek encouraged students who know they want to do research to get involved early, even if that means joining a lab that does not entirely align with their interests.

“The most important thing is to get involved in a lab that will support you and give you the opportunities to grow,” Mroczek said. “If you join a lab where it’s possibly something you’re interested in but maybe not to the fullest extent, but they really do support you and give you a place to grow … I think that’s the biggest thing to look for when looking at research groups to join.”

title: Illustrating Indigeneity: Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022
notes: Senior honors thesis. Advisers from "Faculty Advisers" on the opening page (the contributors page says Sharma is in Art History and Carroll in History). Text includes Chinese characters. Footnotes and pull quotes are placed at the nearest paragraph break; footnotes 20-23 run from printed page 107 onto 108 and are kept together. The first block of printed page 113 reads "113 / 113" (a doubled page number). Ends with a bibliography.
text:
Department of Art History

Illustrating Indigeneity: Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal

Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022 by Grace A. Wu

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Yuthika Sharma and Dr. Peter J. Carroll

Visualizing Empire After decades of battle, the Aisin-Gioro clan from Manchuria officially became the sovereigns of Imperial China after conquering Beijing in 1644, establishing the Qing 清 dynasty. Among the 10 rulers of the dynasty, the Qianlong 乾隆 emperor (r. 1736–95) reigned the second-longest and oversaw China at its geographic peak. During his 60- year tenure, the ruler immersed himself in administrative and artisanal affairs, serving “as conqueror and empire builder, aesthete and sponsor of culture, poet and artist, grand ruler over the world’s largest society.”1 A series of military campaigns from the 1740s to 1790s doubled the geographic size of the Qing empire, extending from Mongolia to Myanmar and Xinjiang to Tai­ wan (Figure 1). This expansion also brought numerous ethnic groups into the empire’s domain. To celebrate this success, the Qianlong emperor instructed his court to create the Huang Qing zhigong tu 皇清職貢圖 [Qing Imperial Illustration of Tributaries], which historian Laura Hostetler describes as a “cultural cartography of empire.”2 The Huang Qing zhigong tu contains image likenesses and textual descriptions of over 300 groups of people within the mid- to late-18th century Qing domain. Upon imperial behest, court artists made several versions, leading to the circulation of ethnographic tropes, including nakedness, animalistic qualities, and ‘uncultured’ mannerisms.

1 Mote, Imperial China, 900-1800, 912. 2 Hostetler and Wu, Qing Imperial Illustrations.

Although the genre of zhigong tu histori­ cally depicts people who paid tribute to the Chinese court, the large number of figures—who did not all pay tribute—in the Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects the scope of the Qing domain. Empire is as much of a visual project as a material one, and the Qing utilized cultural cartography to supplement topographical maps they created. The National Palace Museum’s il­ luminated handscroll version of the Huang Qing zhigong tu, attributed to court artist Xie Sui 謝遂 (hereinafter “Xie Sui scrolls” or “NPM scrolls”), has distinct formal attributes, such as its brilliant illumination (Figure 2). The four Xie Sui scrolls are unique out of surviving editions of the Huang Qing zhigong tu (Appendix A) due to their frequent public display in Tai­ wan’s National Palace Museum (Appendix C). Curators’ decision to regularly exhibit these scrolls highlights their curatorial and educational importance in 21st centu­ ry Taiwan, which I discuss further in the conclusion.

The Qing-Imagined World The genre of zhigong tu 職貢圖 first emerged during the Liang 梁 (502–57) dynasty. Zhi 職 is used in phrases relating to duty and responsibility; gong 貢 is shorthand for gongfu 貢賦, or tribute. Together, zhigong expresses the obligation to respectfully submit, obey, and present things to someone higher in the hierar­ chy. Tu 圖 describes an image, illustration, or map. Zhigong tu, or illustrated tributary documents, is unique from textual docu­ mentation of tribute because it contains the supposed visual likeness of the indi­ vidual or group.

Throughout Chinese history, the imperial court leveraged zhigong tu to celebrate the dynasty’s influence within and outside of its domain. Their high-quality materiality and careful documentation suggest only the highest-ranking officials viewed them, celebrating their political and diplomatic successes. The earliest-known zhigong tu, Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court (c. sixth century), depicts full-length portraits of the actual ambassadors who paid tribute to the Chinese court (Figure 3). Despite the envoys’ formalized stiff poses, each of the over two dozen illustrated figures ex­ hibits individualized characters with emo­ tions and personalities. An accompanying textual description of their respective polity details its topography, customs, re­ lationship with the Liang, and the tributes presented to the court.3

3 Zheng, “Tribute Bearers to the Liang Court,” 36. 4 Zhigong manifested in three types of relationships: “from tributary states to the Qing empire, from regional governments to the court, and from individual officials above a certain rank to the emperor.” The Qing tributary system was complex and flexible to changing conditions. In this thesis, I focus on the foreign relations aspect of this system. Ko, The Social Life of Inkstones, 45.

“Despite the claims of faithful representation, the provincial and court artists inevitably generalized millions of people into 300 male-female paradigmatic types.”

Zhigong tu supplemented chaogong tixi 朝貢體系 [the tributary system].4 With rudimentary origins during the Han 漢 dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE), the Chinese tributary system reinforced imperial suzerainty by organizing people by their perceived civility. The frequency of tribute paid to the center vaguely determined the groups’ positionality.5 The Qing codified the tributary system, conducting foreign relations through this “abstract creed of loy­ alty.”6 Although not all polities interpreted the practice of zhigong as demonstrating loyalty to the Chinese emperor, the Qing perceived their submission as such; the in­ clusion of European countries in the Huang Qing zhigong tu serves as a prime example of this difference in understanding.

The Qing viewed the tributary system as a method for foreigners and ethnic mi­ norities to gravitate towards the court out of admiration of the political, military, and cultural supremacy of the Chinese state. As a visual reflection of these beliefs, the Huang Qing zhigong tu exhibits the dynas­ ty’s narrative of its superiority within and beyond its borders. Content evolved from individu­ alized portraiture to ethnographic repre­ sentations that delineated the dress and habits of the other 12 centuries after the first known zhigong tu’s creation. Instead of documenting male ambassadors who physically were at court, the Huang Qing zhigong tu depicts male-female stock pairs who lived far from the imperial center. This shift to male-female pairs reflects an attempt to know ‘all’ people of a group. As the distance widens between the Qing court and their subjects, the illustrations in the Huang Qing zhigong tu become more exaggerated and archetypal. Terminologies in the Huang Qing zhigong tu also emerged to convey ideas of cultural difference and inferiority, such as referring to Indigenous Taiwanese as fan 番. Though its meaning is nuanced, fan translated as “savage” or “barbarian.”7 The Qing’s usage of fan enables its superiority by accentuating Taiwanese’s relative and cultural distance from the inner court.

The handscroll versions of Huang Qing zhigong tu offers a unique viewing experience for the audience. The viewer would first lay the scroll flat on a table; then, they would unroll about a shoul­ der-width section of the tributary scroll to simultaneously view one to three entries. To progress further along the handscroll, the viewer would roll the right roller end while unrolling the left, bringing more figures into his gaze. This interactive na­ ture of a constant progression brings the viewer on a journey throughout the Qing domain without leaving Beijing.

Creation and Layout of the Huang Qing zhigong tu In 1751, the Qianlong emperor issued edicts to governor-generals within the empire detailing the imperial ethnographic and encyclopedic project that later became known as the Huang Qing zhigong tu:

My dynasty has united the vast expanses. Of all various peoples from within and beyond [neiwai miaoyi 內外 苗夷] our domains, there are none who have not sincerely turned toward Us and been transformed. As for their clothing, caps, appearance, and bearing, each has its differences. Now although we have likenesses from several places, they are not yet uniform and complete. Gather together the several models that we now have, and deliver them to each of the gov­ ernors and governors-general near the borders. Order them to take the Miao, Yao, Li, and Zhuang within their jurisdictions, as well as the myriad Yi and Fan beyond, and according to these examples copy their appearance, bearing, clothing, and ornaments, make illustrations and send them to the Grand Council for classification and arrangement for presentation and inspection.8

Incumbent government officers across China mobilized upon receiving this decree. As the governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang, Karjišan 喀爾吉 善 quickly instructed his subordinates to create detailed visual likenesses of “all various peoples” with whom they crossed paths with, such as during trade.9 Other Fujian provincial officials sent the sketches to Karjišan’s office, where workers created final drawings. After an official envoy approved them upon detailed inspection, workers decorated the compiled album for presentation to the Qianlong emperor.10 To accompany the drawings sent to Bei­ jing in 1752, provincial officials included a written addendum presenting the illus­ trations to the emperor, describing the people’s clothing, accessories, facial char­ acteristics, culture, preferences, and geo­ graphic jurisdiction. The Grand Council in Beijing received and finished compiling the submissions from across the empire in

1758; the Council then likely presented the drawings to the emperor for inspection before handing them to court artists.11 This process of creating and approving the illustrated likenesses at different levels of the government reflects how deeply the Qing administration involved itself in every step of the Huang Qing zhigong tu’s creation.

The Qianlong emperor personally appointed a master court painter to work on each of the four scrolls: Ding Guan­ peng 丁觀鵬, Jin Tingbiao 金廷標, Yao Wenhan 姚文瀚, and Cheng Liang 程梁, respectively.12 As part of their roles, these painters analyzed the provincial albums and finalized the colored likenesses. To fulfill the Qianlong emperor’s wish to have his empire recorded for posterity, other court artists—including Xie Sui—triplicat­ ed each scroll and created a polished album folio of each figure (Appendix A).13

Each of the NPM handscrolls is roughly one-foot tall, and their lengths vary from 46- to almost 60-feet long.14 The expressive title of each scroll written on the orange frontispiece celebrates the power of the Qing court through its col­ lection of tributary subjects (Appendix B). Poems appear at the beginning and end of each scroll, praising the prosperity of the multi-ethnic Qing-ruled society and claim­ ing the information in the scrolls—spe­ cifically the illustrations—as accurate and trustworthy.15 Despite the claims of faith­ ful representation, the provincial and court artists inevitably generalized millions of people into 300 male-female paradigmatic types. However, the Qianlong emperor’s approval signals these drawings were good enough for the Qing’s self-admiration. Hundreds of vertical sections, with varying widths between six- and 12-inch­ es, lie between the bookend colophon poems. Each section, or entry, depicts a group of people associated with a foreign polity or Qing administrative region. In the upper register of the scroll, text in the Qing’s official languages, Chinese and Manchu, identifies the group and describes their social customs. Sometimes the text explicitly mentions tribute being made to the Qing court, which would have been performed by ambassadors or carefully se­ lected representatives.

Illustrated figures that correspond to the text occupy the lower register. In al­ most all the entries, an archetypal male and female pair in generalized local dress rep­ resents the group. The figures are roughly five- to six-inches tall and interact with a quotidian object, local crop, or animal mentioned in the text. Some figures stand erect, and others contort their bodies while engaged in an activity or turn away from the viewer. The figures seemingly float on the paper with no painted background; clearly, the focus of the object is on people’s visual likeness, dress, and other local cus­ toms. In a compendium of over 300 entries and 100,000 words,16 the diversity of dress, pose, and color visually displays the cultur­ al heterogeneity and geographic span of the Qing empire. The Qianlong emperor then viewed the final product, claiming all of these subjects in his domain by stamping important personal seals onto the scroll.

Taiwan in the Huang Qing zhigong tu: A Case Study From the founding of the Qing dynasty in the seventeenth century until the early 19th century, Taiwan had “an uprising each three years, a rebellion every five” largely due to both Ming loyalists attempting to subvert the Qing dynasty and inter-ethnic conflicts between Han Chinese settlers and Indigenous Taiwanese communities.18 In 1684, the Qing annexed Taiwan into Fujian Province—naming it “Taiwan Prefecture”—in hopes of directly combatting future threats emerging from the island (Figure 4).

“The entries’ text and image mutually reinforce Qing notions of savagery yet sometimes diverge on their extent, creating conflicting portrayals of fan.”

Documents like the Huang Qing zhi­ gong tu demonstrate the Qing continued to view Taiwan as liminal and savage a centu­ ry after the annexation through their ter­ minology, text, and illustrations. Although fan became a general term for unaccultur­ ated people, three specific subdivisions of fan became closely associated with Taiwan: shoufan 熟番, guihua shengfan 歸化生番, and shengfan 生番. The terms sheng 生 and shou 熟 literally translate to “raw” and “cooked,” respectively, with connotations of “wild” and “tame” or “unacculturated” and “acculturated.”19A third term, guihua shengfan 歸化生番 [naturalized raw fan], or huafan 化番 for short, refers to a middle designation where wild fan affirm their al­ legiance to the Qing court through tribute and taxes. The representation of the sub­ divisions fan in the Xie Sui scrolls demon­ strates tension between the arguments that the Taiwanese aboriginals can become assimilated into Chinese society but also have less developed ways of living, such as a reliance on hunting and eating raw food.

In the second NPM scroll, 13 Tai­ wanese male-female pairs appear in the Fujian Province section, and their titles all contain the “fan” label.20 The entries’ order is organized by a perceived decline in cul­ tural refinement; there are eight shoufan followed by three huafan and two shengfan (Appendix D). Savagery is most visually apparent through the male figure’s pose, dress, and facial expression while the fe­ male figures are more passive, have fairer skin, and dressed more modestly than their male companion.21 The details in the text and illustrations complement and refer­ ence one another, though some differences are apparent upon closer inspection.

By 1747, Qing records included 299 aboriginal villages by name. The consol­ idation of the almost-300 villages into 13 male-female pairs in the Xie Sui scrolls is a deliberate one; the title of each entry sug­ gests that the information generalizes the living practices of the fan living in a partic­ ular Qing administrative region (Appendix D).22 The Huang Qing zhigong tu reflects an ethnographic framework by documenting Taiwanese society through specific cate­ gories—such as housing, food, costume, marriages, burials, and tools—though the depth of detail varies depending on the Qing’s familiarity with that group.23 This structure, organization, and emphasis re­ flect Qing administrative and cultural log­ ics rather than how the Taiwanese identi­ fied themselves.

The seventh Taiwanese entry doc­ uments the shoufan of Dehua and other communities in Danshui Subprefecture in northwest Taiwan (Figure 5). These shou­ fan are among the most modestly dressed, and their upright pose and direct gaze fur­ ther connotes their civility and humanity. An excerpt of the accompanying text de­ scribes the terrain and people:

Their lands are very swampy be­ cause they are close to the ocean. They therefore use thatch or wooden boards to make their dwellings. They eat mil­ let together with a mixture of fish and shrimp prepared in a spicy broth. Both men and women wear short upper gar­ ments bound at the waist with a strip of cloth. They work hard at farming and they also fish and hunt. They play flutes and zithers made of bamboo for enter­ tainment in their spare time.24

The text portrays the shoufan as adaptable and resourceful, with the con­ junction “therefore” to explain the logic of using construction materials suitable for the swampy environment. The sho­ ufan also utilize local natural resources, catching fish and shrimp from the ocean to sustain themselves. Reflecting their shou [“cooked”] and acculturated nature, their food involves cooking with fire. The text also notes that these fan have gustatory re­ finement: they add spices to this dish and mix different flavors and textures together in their food.

The pair’s illustrated costume departs from the text. Instead of wearing “short upper garments bound at the waist,” both figures wear embroidered and woven cloth shirts that loosely extend beyond their hips and cover their arms. Though the text does not mention leg garments, the pair wears long flowy skirts that cover the entirety of their legs. This length of skirt would be highly impractical while farming and fishing in swampy surroundings; this dis­ connect shows the artist’s creative liberty in rendering costumes without seriously contemplating the textual description. The man holds a bamboo flute in his hands and eagerly offers it in the direction of his female companion, who gazes to her right towards the next entry while hold­ ing a hoe and basket. The text notes that the shoufan sustain themselves through farming, fishing, and hunting, but the artist only included agricultural tools. The deliberate exclusion of weaponry elevates the shoufan’s perceived civility through their non-threatening appearance. Thus, the textual description and illustrations work together to portray this group as hardworking, yet also engaging in cultural entertainment during their spare time.

The second case study pair, the huafan in Zhuluo County (Figure 6) have customs that situate them in the Qing imaginary as unacculturated fan. The figures’ concentric bracelets and leg wrappings highlight their exoticness and distance from the Manchu Qing. A portion of the accompanying text documents their living habits:

They dwell in mountainous earth­ en caves. Their dress and diet are similar to those of Shanzhumao and other com­ munities. They are not well versed in farming, only raising sweet potatoes and taro in cracks in the rock. They use bow and arrow to hunt river deer for food. Their feet are like chicken claws, allowing them to climb steep surfaces as if they were flat. They annually submit a head tax of more than 30 silver taels.25

In contrast to the more resourceful shoufan who build their residences, the text says the huafan live in “earthen caves” in the mountains. The huafan’s practice of growing food “in cracks in the rock” fur­ ther signals the group’s liminal position between developed civilization and the wilderness placing themselves on a lower register in the Qing imagination.

In the bottom half of the entry, the man and woman face one another, stand­ ing upright. They both wear sleeved deer­ skin jackets and patterned woven skirts with fabric belts. The man holds a barbed spear in his right hand, and he carries a bow, quiver, and basket filled with flowers on his back. The text does not discuss hunting spears; the addition of this weap­ on in the image depicts these people as potentially threatening. The combination of collected flowers and weaponry simulta­ neously asserts the huafan as primitive yet potentially hostile. In line with the text, the male figure has long, claw-like nails on his feet. In contrast, the female figure has nor­ mal-length toenails, and she displays the group’s craftsmanship by holding a beaded circle and wearing a beaded necklace. This artistic insistence of expressing savagery through the male figure while simultane­ ously refining the female reflects the Qing perception of wild fan and Chinese values of the demure woman. This visual repre­ sentation demonstrates the nuanced Qing understanding of fan as having the poten­ tial to assimilate into Chinese society yet perpetually far from civilization.

The last Taiwanese entry in the sec­ ond scroll, the shengfan of Youwunai and other wild communities in Danshui (Fig­ ure 7), contains the most-nude figures out of the 13 pairs. In Chinese visual culture, women are rarely portrayed bare-chested; the Qing perceived these people to be so savage that the artist broke cultural norms to illustrate an exposed female chest. The accompanying text purportedly reports the shengfan’s untamed living habits:

The Shengfan live in the moun­ tains. Men and women both bare their bodies. Some wear deerskins or use leaves for clothing. They eat raw food. Their nature is strong and fierce. They kill for a living. In winter when the grass and streams dry up they shoot deer. They can climb tall trees and run as if they are flying.26

The text’s tone differs greatly from the shoufan and huafan in the scrolls. The mentions of mountains, nakedness, un­ cooked food, and physical agility support the claim that the shengfan’s “nature is strong and fierce.” The “bare…bodies” of both male and female shengfan accentuate their separation from civilization. Though “some” shengfan wear clothing, deerskin and foliage are closer to nature than woven fabric. The ambiguity of the type of “raw food” the shengfan “kill” and eat contributes to a feeling of distance and unfamiliarity. Lastly, the text associates the shengfan with animals, describing their running “as if they are flying”; this detail works with the phrase “they kill for a living” to create an image of a group of fierce and threatening people.

“People residing in the 21st century, myself included, boldly “write back” to the Qing empire that its view of Taiwanese fan does not have the last say in our collective history and understanding of Taiwan’s original peoples.”

Both the male and female figures wear deerskin cloaks that cover their shoulders and upper backs, exposing their torso. A contradiction between artistic expression and the textual description is the female’s fabric skirt despite its noninclusion in the text; the artist attempted to give some level of civility to the female through a woven skirt rather than a full animal hide cos­ tume. The male wears a deerskin skirt, and he raises a downwards-facing barbed spear with his right hand and holds a sheathed sword-like object in his left. He raises his right foot as if he is about to spear an an­ imal. The exaggerated lines on his face, limbs, and chest accentuate his grotesque­ ness and muscular strength. Compared to her fierce male companion, the female’s gaze is blank. Her pose suggests she cau­ tiously walks in the presence of her fero­ cious companion. These shengfan are the only Taiwanese fan who have a “raw” diet, and this detail’s artistic exclusion is glaring because sheng literally translates to “raw.” Working with—yet sometimes departing from—the text, the artist created a literal image of Indigenous Taiwanese who are wild and hostile.

Throughout the three case studies of Taiwanese fan, image and text collaborate to create a supposed authoritative record of those who are refined versus barbaric. The representations of savagery are most explicit through the males’ costumes, asso­ ciation with weaponry, corporal pose, and grotesque facial features. The males’ cloth­ ing encapsulates the progression of barba­ rism from tame fan to wild fan: the shoufan of Danshui wears layers of woven textiles, the huafan of Zhuluo dons a deerskin jack­ et and a woven patterned skirt, and the shengfan of Danshui is the least-clothed in his deerskin costume. The male figures’ object-interactions become increasingly threatening, from the shoufan presenting a musical instrument to the huafan carrying weapons to the shengfan actively spearing an unspecified target. All three men have untied, freely flowing hair in sharp contrast to the braided Manchu queue hairstyles required in the empire, highlighting their cultural distance from the Qing. None of the Taiwanese figures wear hats nor shoes, further indicating their primitiveness. The diet of these three groups literally reflects the categories of “cooked” fan and “raw” fan: the acculturated “cooked” fan makes broth for himself, and the wild “raw” fan eats raw food. The entries’ text and image mutually reinforce Qing notions of savage­ ry yet sometimes diverge on their extent, creating conflicting portrayals of fan. The Huang Qing zhigong tu emphasizes this framework of tiered savagery through the Taiwanese entries’ visual representations, reflecting Taiwan’s liminal position in the Qing empire.

The Twenty-first Century Afterlife of Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu Chinese settler-colonialism of Taiwan continued to grow through the Qing era and into the present; people of aboriginal descent comprise 2.28% of present-day Taiwan’s 23-million population.27 Despite their small proportion in society, Indige­ nous Taiwanese have been the subject of growing public interest in recent decades. This increased respect towards and signif­ icance of Indigenous culture and history stems from a desire to distinguish Taiwan­ ese identity and nationality from China, including the modern-day Communist state and the Chinese imperial past. Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu resided in the imperial Qing collection upon its completion in the eighteenth cen­ tury.28 After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, portions of the imperial collections formed the collection of the newly estab­ lished, state-operated Palace Museum in Beijing. To safeguard the museum’s most culturally valuable objects from military threats—from the Japanese in the 1930s and from the Chinese Communists in the 1940s—the Chinese Nationalist govern­ ment evacuated thousands of crates filled with these objects around the country and then to Taiwan, respectively. Alongside the Nationalist government’s retreat to Taiwan, these select portions of the Qing imperial collections found their new home in the National Palace Museum in Taipei’s Shilin District in 1965. Today, the museum is internationally acclaimed for its extensive collection of imperial Chinese artifacts, and the Xie Sui scrolls serve as strong visual references for postcolonial discussions of Taiwanese Indigeneity.

In the early 2000s, aboriginal national legislator Kung Wen-chi 孔文吉 urged the NPM to develop more programming rele­ vant to Taiwan’s Indigenous communities; the public echoed his sentiment, as former NPM Director Wu Mi-cha 吳密察 said in an interview.29 Wu Mi-cha elaborated on the museum’s best efforts to meet pub­ lic interest, saying, “it is difficult to make interesting exhibitions” that highlight ab­ original Taiwanese society from the muse­ um’s Qing archives because the collection contains mostly text manuscripts.30 Thus, the exhibitions discussing Taiwanese Indi­ geneity often incorporate the second Xie

Sui scroll due to its visual representations of aboriginal Taiwanese figures.

Wu Mi-cha noted a crucial step in facilitating present-day people’s compre­ hension of Qing archives: clarifying Qing terminology.31 “Fan” carries a derogatory connotation in modern-day Taiwanese society, and the 2022 exhibition What is “Fandz”? Taiwanese Indigenous Peoples in Historical Documents of the Qing Empire32 not only gave museumgoers an opportunity to understand the Taiwanese aboriginals’ liminal positionality in the Qing empire, but also encouraged them to recenter Indigenous perspectives in imperialist archives through “write back” exercises.33 The Xie Sui scrolls served as an education­ al tool, providing visual references for each Qing-imagined category of fan: shoufan (tame fan), guihua shengfan (wild fan who pay taxes), and shengfan (wild fan).

Museum staff utilized the Taiwanese figures in several aspects of the exhibi­ tion to not only highlight the association between the Qing-imagined savage and Taiwanese fan, but also call attention to the imperial prejudice and ethnographic oversimplification within the displayed documents. The main decal in the 2022 exhibition hall (Figure 8) features some of Xie Sui’s aboriginal figures—including the male-female shengfan from Danshui (Figure 7)—transposed on a Qing map of Taiwan. The original figures in the Huang Qing zhigong tu sit on a blank background, so giving them an illustrated backdrop modifies their meaning. This addition affirms Indigenous presence in Taiwan; they inhabited real spaces on the island and did not aimlessly float in ethnographic documents.

To accompany the Fandz exhibition, the curatorial staff created a website titled “Nixie Qingdiguo 逆寫清帝國” [“Write back the Qing Empire”] (Figure 9). Nixie 逆寫 [“write back”] encourages the public to share new interpretations of Xie Sui’s fan figures through postcolonial interven­ tions, such as summoning collective mem­ ory and rejecting the language of the colo­ nizer.34 This method draws upon the work of several British, Indian, African, and ab­ original Taiwanese postcolonial theorists, which encourage the reconstruction of the (historically marginalized) subject through embracing Indigenous theory and replac­ ing imperialist terminologies and ste­ reotyped motifs.35 The website currently features seven “write back” pieces by high school and graduate students in Taiwan, along with an aboriginal author. These short historical fiction essays draw inspi­ ration from Xie Sui’s Taiwanese figures, offering imagined interactions between the Indigenous Taiwanese and the Qing scribes who recorded their likenesses.36 The first-person narratives include: diary entries of a court painter in Beijing during the production of the Huang Qing zhigong tu, the dog accompanying the shoufan of Dadu witnessing a Qing official command his subordinates to sketch the dog’s owner, and an aboriginal individual criticizing the Qing’s failure to depict her culture’s shawl correctly. This last essay, written by a stu­ dent of one of Taiwan’s best all-girls high schools, calls attention to the ambiguous state of the images’ accuracy as Qing impe­ rial preconceptions of Manchu superiority hung over the project.
