Public engagement with “write back” also extends to this thesis: in this academ­ ic project, I chose to consider the Xie Sui scrolls in not only their historical context, but also of the present. I critically studied the textual description and formal repre­ sentation of three paradigmatic Taiwanese fan types in Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu, noting discrepancies and how they visually assert the Qing-imagined savageness of Taiwanese aboriginals. While understand­ ing Qing imperialist ideologies shines valuable light on why the Taiwanese rep­ resentations take the form they do, study­ ing them without considering their pres­ ent-day impact can perpetuate or diminish the weight of these harmful narratives. Thus, this conclusion embraces the post­ colonial “write back” methodology by also analyzing how people in the present-day think about these objects, emancipating the scrolls from solely holding historical significance. People residing in the 21st century, myself included, boldly “write back” to the Qing empire that its view of Taiwanese fan does not have the last say in our collective history and understanding of Taiwan’s original peoples. ◆

title: Hypercapnia and Immune Suppression with Dr. Peter Sporn
notes: Feature on Dr. Peter Sporn's research (Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Feinberg) on hypercapnia, immune suppression and the ZFHX3 gene.
text:
Hypercapnia and Immune

Suppression with

Dr. Peter Sporn

By: Avery Morawa

Hypercapnia, an excess concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood­ stream, is often used as a marker of adverse outcomes in clinical practice for patients with advanced lung disease such as COPD, asthma, acute lung injury, or cystic fibrosis. At this stage, patients often succumb to infection, but the association between contagion and hypercapnia wasn’t clear. Peter Sporn, a professor at the Feinberg School of Medicine, began to wonder if hypercapnia plays a causal role rather than an associative role in the infection rates of patients with advanced respiratory complications. This problem is extremely pertinent to clinical care: investigating the relationship between these two factors could potentially change the way that medical care systems approach the treatment of lung disease.

Through the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine at Fein­ berg, Sporn and his research team began exposing cells in an in vitro envi­ ronment to high levels of CO2 to model hypercapnia. They found that excess CO2 concentration inhibited a number of phages important to host defense and innate immunity as well as inhibiting cytokine secretion, phagocytosis, and respiratory burst, which all play a role in defending the body from mi­ croorganisms. Hypercapnia was shown to have suppressive effects on both cell groups and the total organism as mice in hypercapnia in the study died more quickly and had a higher mortality rate, but this left Sporn with more questions. Hypercapnia certainly played a causal role in developing an infec­ tion, but would it make infection worse?

Sporn and his group performed a genetic screen on drosophila fly genes in order to identify genes whose expression was required for CO2 mediated immunosuppression. Although the drosophila genetic code is primitive in comparison to mammalian heredity, there are various mammalian homo­ logues and genes related to the drosophila genes that have similar effects on the organism and its cells. ZFH2, a gene that encodes transcription factors for cellular development and hypercapnic immune response in drosophila, was identified and the group developed flies with ZFH2 knockout. Flies with the knockout gene were protected from the immunosuppressive effects of hypercapnia, so the group looked to the homologue ZFHX3 gene in mice to investigate the impact of this conserved gene on mammals. However, the study was presented with an interesting problem: due to its role in mamma­ lian cellular development, this gene was an embryonic lethal mutation. In order to create mice with the knockout phenotype, the knockout could only be present in the myeloid cell line to prevent embryonic death.

The treatments and results indicated that the ZFHX3 gene was central to hypercapnic immunosuppression. Mice with the ZFHX3 myeloid defi­ ciency were reported to have had less lung injury, reduced burn, and partial protection against hypercapnic suppression, establishing ZFHX3 as the first known mammalian mediator of hypercapnic immune suppression.

Sporn’s research group will conduct further research on the molecular mechanisms by which hypercapnia signals through ZFHX3 to impact im­ mune function. They have begun searching for potential CO2 sensors or receptors that signal to ZFHX3 or incite cellular pathways that interact with the gene. Once these receptors or pathways are identified, research can be conducted on their role in various cell types present in the lungs and this can guide the development of a treatment for hypercapnia induced immunosup­ pression. “If there are ways to interrupt hypercapnia’s suppressive effects, we can reduce the patients’ resistance to infection or improve their outcomes if they are infected,” Sporn noted, hoping to see a future where his impactful work can save lives.

title: Nanotechnology & Medicine with Dr. Katie Gesmundo
notes: Q&A interview with Professor Katie Gesmundo, who teaches chemistry at Northwestern, on her graduate research with Joseph DeSimone at UNC (nanoparticles, microneedle patches) and her path into academia. Edited for clarity and brevity.
text:
Nanotechnology & Medicine with

Dr. Katie Gesmundo

By: Caroline Guerra

[This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.] Interviewer: Could you tell me about your research in graduate school? Professor Gesmundo: I did research in graduate school at the University of North Carolina (UNC), and I worked for Professor Joseph DeSimone. One of the projects that I started reading a lot about was nanoparticles for cancer therapeutic delivery, which was one of the things I was really interested in his research group. Joe’s research group was very interdisciplinary. We had people from the chemistry department, the school of pharmacy, biology, NC State’s College of Engineering, and a couple of empty Ph.D. students. It was a really wide range of people. I believe the lab had 65 members at the time I joined, so it was really big. However, I was the only analytical chemist in the lab at that time, so I was concerned when I started reading about the project and the work that he was doing on it that I would end up being kind of a go-to analyst to solve problems for other people’s projects. So, even though I was really interested in the oncology group, I was a little hesitant to join without having a project I could truly own myself.

I ended up starting a new type of project for the group, which was really a cool avenue. Joe was interested in delivering nanoparticles in different ways, not just through traditional oral systemic delivery, but using the technology his lab was really good at to deliver drugs transdermally, or through the skin. Hearing about this project and wanting to have something that was my own niche, I was really interested in it. We also discussed at the time if the project could have a cancer application, which was very much possi­ ble, so I started working on that. I worked on creating microstructures using the same technology that we use to create nanoparticles, and adapting the platform for a larger particulate shape was a little bit of an engineering challenge that was really fun. We started loading chemotherapeutics into the microparticles once we actually had proof of concept. As much as I was passionate about that project, it had a lot of hurdles to get it to pass a mouse-modeled type of avenue. So we ended up doing an even more fundamental study of trying to figure out what types of molecules we could deliver with these micro­ particles that went through the skin.

My thesis turned out to be a lot of fundamental studies of loading larger and larg­ er therapeutic surrogates into microparticles and looking at how they would be trans­ formed through the skin barrier using mostly mice models. We looked at small molecules of fluorophores, protein therapeutics, and nanoparticles, which are kind of packaged into these microparticles. I guess the main conclusion of my research is that it was possible to deliver all of these things with our technology. The microparticles are part of a field called microneedle patches, and so after showing proof of concept from small molecules to nano particulates, we could really get this type of technology working to deliver drugs to the body.

Interviewer: Have you seen your research on microneedle patches be used practically or commercially?

Professor Gesmundo: Yeah, there are a few labs that have advanced them quite a bit further than what we were doing at the time when I was working on this research. We were working on a very specific application of microneedle patches. We were looking for something that could be completely soluble, so our approach was like thinking of a Band-Aid with a bunch of spikes, but the spikes were so short that they entered your skin without touching your pain receptors. Our vision was using water to dissolve the backing; there would be no waste, ultimately kind of contained in a Band-Aid-like packaging, and we were thinking that this would be something that could be really useful for self-administration. You wouldn’t need medical professionals to do that. There’s an advertisement for a flu vaccine with an absurdly small needle, which is technically a microneedle technology. It is just one that would require a nurse or some medical professional to actually still administer. There are some products on the market that have needles involved in them that are in clinical trials right now. I don’t think any of them have really met that need of completely soluble that I was working on, but there are definitely pieces of this technology that exist today.

Interviewer: How did you decide to pursue graduate school? Professor Gesmundo: So, I went to college to be a high school teacher, and I picked a university that had a really great college of education. I envisioned myself teaching high school chemistry and physics, so I picked that specialization when I went into college. Picking that specialization was really useful because it put me in chemistry courses over things like biology courses in my first year of school, so I could take some of the more advanced chemistry courses earlier in my degree, and that’s how I realized that I really liked chemistry.

I started doing undergraduate research with the professor who taught me or­ ganic chemistry. He was taking students, and he wasn’t necessarily scared away by the fact that I was not a chemistry major. I really thank him for that. I was very, very lucky that he took a chance on letting somebody do some research over the course of my first three years. I really did like teaching, but I spent more of my time doing research than I did probably any other extracurricular activity. When I was a junior in college, finishing up my third year of research, he asked me if I had considered graduate school. I said no, I’m not really considering that, I’m thinking of going into teaching. He basically said, I don’t think you should turn down the option to try to learn more about chemistry; you really like this, and I had to agree with him. I really did. He talked to me about what it meant to be a professor in chemistry and what types of teaching opportunities I would have if I was more committed to teaching than I was to high schoolers. There was an avenue for me to learn more about chem­ istry but still keep teaching in my future career. I thought that was really powerful.

At that point, after three years in college, I added a major in chemistry, which is a little bit nuts. But it was possible to finish my degree since I started taking upper-level chemistry courses out of curiosity. After I applied to graduate school and was accepted, I did some visit weekends, and I got really excited about this option. I took a chance on graduate school once I was accepted to UNC, which was pretty much my dream school.

Interviewer: From my understanding, your organic chemistry professor served as a mentor to you; having someone who can encourage you and inspire you is very valuable.

Professor Gesmundo: I really cannot thank those professors enough. You can’t really oversell how important it is to have someone in your corner when you’re thinking about what to do with the rest of your life. One of the things that I love about working here is that I do get to have conversations with a lot of people about what their future might look like. I know how valuable a professor was for my personal experience, so I really don’t take it lightly when I talk to people about what they want to do. I think it’s one of the joys of being a faculty. I am pretty grateful that I have the opportunity to do for somebody else what was so powerful for me.

Interviewer: What are some valuable lessons you have learned along your journey in academia?

Professor Gesmundo: That’s a hard question. The first thing I learned about academia was when I was sitting as an undergraduate thinking about what it meant to be a chem­ istry professor. I had one thing in mind of what it looked like to be a chemistry professor, and it turns out that there are a lot of different ways to work in higher education as a chemist. I went to a small liberal arts college, so the role of a professor is to teach undergraduate courses and do undergraduate research. Occasionally you go to present your work or publish a few papers. That’s not what my role is now. At Northwestern, which is considered a research one university, R1 faculty members and their research labs are mostly populated by graduate students and postdocs. A majority of their publica­ tions don’t involve undergraduates. I really wanted to work with undergraduates; that’s something that was important to me. I didn’t really see how I would fit in a big school if I wanted to work with undergraduates. My role as a teaching faculty member at North­ western is a little bit different than both of those. What I am expected to do for most of my job is instruct undergraduate courses, but I also work with graduate student TAs. I also work with the larger curriculum committees to kind of map out what it means to be a chemistry major at Northwestern. I teach chemistry courses like the freshman seminar, which helps me understand what it means for a Weinberg College first-year student to feel prepared to keep going through the rest of their journey. That type of role is really unique. I didn’t know about that role when I went to graduate school.

My first teaching job was at Ohio State, which is quite a large university. Part of my role in that teaching job was to work with graduate students and help them learn to be good teaching assistants. I absolutely loved that part of my job. I really love working with graduate students, and I have a unique background in teaching and pedagogy that a lot of people didn’t have. I love sharing that knowledge and helping graduate students learn about a job like mine because I didn’t know about it at all.

When I was looking for a job in the Chicago area, I was really attracted to North­ western because it would allow me to instruct undergraduates and keep working with graduate students. Those were the two things that I found I was most passionate about in my career, so my first lesson is that academia is not one size fits all. There are a lot of different roles that you can have. Exploring what those roles look like and what types of jobs are available is something that I would recommend to anyone who might want to work at a university. There are more options than I ever thought when I was an undergraduate.

I’ll do one more lesson. One thing that is really important when you’re working at a university is to keep everyone’s identities in mind when approaching your work with them. All of the different populations of people that I work with have unique needs. They are individuals that come to the table with different motivations. I try really hard to keep policies that keep my students in mind, but no policy is completely custom­ ized to an individual. Allowing yourself to recognize everyone’s individual differences, concerns, and needs in the moment is really important when working at this level. It’s something that I spend a lot of time thinking about, and I really think that all students benefit when you not only consider their status as a student, but you also consider them as an individual. Keeping that in mind when advising students or organizing courses is really important to me.

title: The Health Identities of Northwestern Students with Chronic Physical Health Conditions
notes: Senior thesis. Advisers from "Faculty Advisers" on the opening page. Interview study of Northwestern undergraduates with chronic physical illnesses. Includes an appendix with the interview guide (printed pages 132-134) and a bibliography. Footnotes and pull quotes are placed at the nearest paragraph break.
text:
Department of Sociology

The Health Identities of Northwestern Students with Chronic Physical Health Conditions by Sierra Erdman-Luntz

Faculty Advisers: Dr. Bruce Carruthers and Dr. Steven Epstein

Introduction “How do Northwestern undergraduate students with chronic physical conditions inte­ grate their health status into their identities?”

I interviewed Northwestern undergraduates who have been physically ill for the past six or more months to understand how they have or have not integrated their health status into their identities.1 In this sense, “identity” refers to a part of someone’s sense of self that they either disclose or choose not to disclose in different settings. My interview guide covered a wide array of situations, from intimate, private conversations between friends or family to very public settings such as at work, on medical forms, in govern­ mental surveys, and so on.

Part of making an accessible world is first studying how disabled individuals and communities understand themselves and relate to society. However, there is a gap in the literature regarding the intersection of disability studies and identity formation when it comes to ill young adults. Identities are impactful and important: they help dictate who is excluded or included in a group, help build a sense of community and alliance, and help people publicly express their internal experiences. Since the 1980s, the queer community has experienced a proliferation of labeling, including the reclamation of some words and the rejection of others, which sociologists have studied to better understand the queer community and its needs on a social policy level. My study aims to do parallel work within disabled spaces.

1 Note: 6+ months of illnesses is an accepted distinction between acute and chronic illnesses in the medical community.

Literature Review My study investigates how Northwestern undergraduate students with long-term illness(es) form an identity around their health and how they think about, express, and label their health during that process. There is an abundance of sociological research on identity formation, and many studies empirically apply this theory to chronically ill communities. My study specifically aims to understand the unique experiences of young adults in college.

Identity Formation

Psychologist and psycho-analyst Erik Erikson popularized identity formation as a social science subcategory in the mid- to-late 20th century. Heavily influenced by Freudian thought, Erikson developed a “psychosocial construct of identity for­ mation” (Herman 2011) that he labeled the theory of ego (Erikson 1950). This theory proposed that young adulthood was a time of self-reflection and individualization where young adults either developed a unique, individual identity or failed to do so and then struggled to become full adults.

Even before Erikson, Charles Cooley was the first to specifically discuss identity formation in the context of sociol­ ogy (1902). He proposed the looking-glass self theory, which argued that individuals create a sense of self and identity by con­ sidering how they are perceived by others and by society writ large. In other words, people use how they think others think about themselves to determine how they view themselves.

George Herbert Mead and Charles W. Morris furthered sociological thought with their symbolic interactionism theory (1934). Symbolic interactionism proposed that conversations, interactions, and expe­ riences with other people informed how someone built their identity and how they viewed themselves. Thus, it constructed the individual from a sociological per­ spective by studying “how the individual internalizes the self and its roles from in­ teractions with others” (Brekus 2020).

Erving Goffman added to identity formation theory by coining the term “social identities,” which suggested that an individual’s identities might change based on social context (1959). Goffman specif­ ically employed a drama allegory to relate different social contexts to different acts in a play. Just like actors might change their behavior or comportment for different scenes, people might act differently and even think about themselves differently depending on their current social context.

Anthony Giddens critically built upon identity formation by conceptualizing it as a reflexive process between the individual and their social environment. He argued that society shifted from low to high with the advent of mass-mediated communica­ tion via the internet, late-stage capitalism, and globalization. As a result, identity for­ mation became both active and political: individuals taking up or refusing certain identities shifted larger social institutions’ perception of those identities, which could influence social processes such as individ­ uals’ future identification, social relations between people with different identities, politics, and so on (Giddens 1991). In re­ sponse to their changing worlds, individu­ als increasingly and repeatedly reconstruct their identities to match their environment and create a stable life story.

Most studies that consider identity formation theory’s specific application to physical health conditions are interviews and surveys that researched how respon­ dents felt their illness impacted their life or how they manage their illness in academic, medical, personal, and other settings. The most influential thinker on this topic is Michael Bury (1982; 1911), whose early work on chronic illness as “biographical disruption” provided the foundations for an identity-based approach within med­ ical sociology. Biographical disruption is the idea that becoming chronically ill is so life-changing that it can alter or disrupt the ill individual’s other identities and sense of self.

Sociological interrogation of Bury’s theories can be found in recent studies, like the Oris et al. study that investigated how chronically ill adults had or had not integrated their illness into their identities, using four potential stages: engulfment, rejection, acceptance, and enrichment (2018). The study did not ask how labels inform or intersect with the four stages. However, the four stages have been em­ ployed in other studies, such as one on how youth handled their Type 1 Diabetes diagnoses (Raymaekers 2019).

A few leading studies consider illness identity formation specifically in the con­ text of young adulthood. Ceri Wilson and Jennifer Stock’s research noted that phys­ ically ill young adults reported experienc­ ing a mixture of emotions related to their health, including personal empowerment, depression, anxiety, and “being different” (2019). Spencer et al. studied the experi­ ence of chronically ill college students, in particular how each participant felt their illness impacted their daily life, how they explained their illnesses to both them­ selves and to their peers, and how they tried to manage their health alongside all of the other pressures of university (2021). My study aims to build upon this body of knowledge.

Motivation The motivation behind this project is threefold: sociological, current relevance, and personal. On the sociological level, outlined above in the literature review, there are few studies that specifically con­ sider young adults with long-term illness and how their health might impact their identity, making my research topic both interesting and significant.

Secondly, this topic is timely and increasingly relevant in the context of COVID-19, the looming threat of another pandemic, climate change, and other so­ cial health hazards that disproportionately impact and create chronically ill people. These social and medical catastrophes pushed conversations about disability and disabled people to the forefront of national discourse, albeit temporarily. One conver­ sation focused on how hospitals should triage COVID-19 patients when they had limited ventilators: disabled people were often the first to be deprioritized (Chen and McNamara 2020). Another discussed who should qualify to receive a COVID-19 vaccine in the first few waves of distribu­ tion: people with very specific diagnosed conditions were prioritized, but many other disabled people were not. Largely missing from both of these conversations were the voices of disabled people. Thus, re­ search on how this population understands their health and how they choose to frame it in different engagements with society is incredibly pressing and necessary. I believe my research will positively impact the so­ ciological and chronically ill communities.

Finally, my interest in this topic is also deeply personal. As a person with chronic physical health conditions, my own experience reflects a roughly linear trajectory from engulfment to enrich­ ment. Throughout my thesis, I was aware that my personal experiences might skew my interpretation of data collected in the interviews, mistakenly and erroneously pushing my data closer to my hypotheses. I implemented a couple of mechanisms in place to counteract my bias. First, I was aware enough of my bias to be able to name and recognize it, making it easier to identi­ fy moments where my assumptions might have overridden the data directly collected through the interviews. Second, I worked with two faculty members and a cohort of other seniors writing theses whose feed­ back and review helped me identify and counterbalance my biases. Third, I was a competitive debater in high school and now coach debate, so I have ample practice divorcing my personal feelings and attach­ ments to my professional work. Further­ more, I believe my personal experience with my research material also benefited my project: I strategically and succinctly self-disclosed my health status at times during interviews, allowing me to relate to respondents on a level that encouraged more fruitful and lush answers.

Methods I collected data through one-time, semi-structured interviews with a small sample size of Northwestern students. I was primarily interested in the thought processes and experiences that shaped and influenced each participant’s health identi­ ty, so my study was qualitative rather than quantitative.

My interview guide started with a short introduction about myself and my study, a reminder that participants can skip questions or stop the interview at any time, and a couple of easier, get-to- know-you questions to build rapport, such as their major at Northwestern and their favorite place to study. The main body of my interview had two distinct parts.2 The first phase included a series of closed-end­ ed statements adapted from the survey in Oris et al’s study. I asked respondents to rank each statement on a Likert scale from one to five (one meaning strongly disagree, three neither disagree nor agree, and five strongly agree).3 Like the Oris et al. study, each statement corresponded to a different stage of identity development: engulfment, rejection, acceptance, and enrichment. Af­ ter the interview, I tallied how many points a respondent accrued in each of the four categories, placing them into the category in which they had the most points. I spe­ cifically compared a participant’s average score in each category during this process (raw score divided by number of questions for that stage) because each category had a different number of questions.

2 Note: please find a complete copy of the interview guide in appendix one. 3 Oris, L., Luyckx, K., Rassart, J. et al. Illness Identity in Adults with a Chronic Illness. J Clin Psychol Med Settings 25, 429–440 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10880-018-9552-0

The interview’s second phase consist­ ed of open-ended questions to understand the thought processes and experiences that influenced and shaped the participant’s responses to phase one. The open-end­ ed questions started with their internal health identity, progressed to more private expressions of their health identity, and ended on more public displays. While I could not guarantee my participants told me the truth, I made it clear throughout the interview that participants were free to skip questions if they found them too pri­ vate and also tried to read the participants’ body language. If they seemed too uncom­ fortable with a line of questioning, I would switch to a different topic that would hope­ fully make them feel more comfortable and more likely to tell me their truth.

For recruitment, AccessibleNU shared my study via email with all North­ western students currently receiving ac­ ademic accommodations who might be eligible for my study, which helped me reach students on campus who held other marginalized identities. Although my sam­ ple size was still too small to make defin­ itive statements or generalizations about how holding other marginalized identities might impact someone’s health identity, I identified a few preliminary trends.

Interviews lasted anywhere from 30 minutes to two hours, with most inter­ views falling between 40 and 60 minutes. On average, I spoke for 10% of the inter­ view time and the interviewee spoke for 90% of the time. I interviewed 13 people for my study.

Initial Empirical Analysis As an inductive study, its purpose was to identify key emergent themes in how Northwestern students with long-term health conditions understood and labeled their health. Thus, analysis throughout the data collection period was critical because it informed how I guided future interviews to gather data relevant to the emerging themes. My intended sample size was 10-20 participants, so I conducted my first round of preliminary analysis after the first 4 interviews. I uploaded the transcripts to ATLAS.ti, a software for analyzing and coding qualitative data. It was advantageous because I could input my codes and easily apply them to quotes, search all transcripts by codes or key­ words, and highlight critical passages for later review. It also provided small-scale quantitative data, such as how often I used each code, that helped me quickly identify patterns.

My analysis section had two parts that corresponded with the interview’s two parts. First, I turned to the data collected in the interview’s statement section. I tallied the participant’s points in each category and then computed each category’s aver­ age score: average scores above three in any category indicated that the participant identified with that stage of identity forma­ tion, and scores below three denoted a lack of identification with the respective stage. Scores close to three indicated ambivalence while scores notably higher or lower than three indicated a stronger feeling.

Second, I analyzed the respondents’ answers to the open-ended questions, tak­ ing note of patterns and creating relevant codes in my codebook. The first major codes I imputed into ATLAS.ti were still the four health identity integration phases from the Oris et al. study: engulfment (coded 76 times), rejection (34), acceptance (218), and enrichment (66). As I started coding and potential themes emerged, I then added other codes: accommodations and school (85), interactions with others (72), managing health/treatment/coping mechanisms (88), interactions with med­ ical institutes (48), explicit mentions of label preferences (74), explicit or implicit mentions of perceived illness validity (55), and mentions of illness’s visibility or in­ viibility (58).

See Appendix II for details about each participant.

Findings The analysis revealed some of the shared experiences of Northwestern students with chronic physical health conditions. It supported the theory of four stages of health integration but complicated my hypothesis that students would prog­ ress linearly through the stages. While participants did report a roughly linear progression in terms of how they thought about and mentally understood their health, their actual health symptoms did not always improve linearly. As a result, some participants reported being mentally in the acceptance or enrichment stages while also scoring highly in the engulfment stage due to their burdensome daily symptoms.

It is noteworthy but not surprising that none of my participants scored in the “rejection” stage as their primary catego­ ry: students who were actively rejecting their health conditions were least likely to self-select to participate in a study explic­ itly about their health status. Most partic­ ipants scored primarily in the acceptance stage, which would explain their willing­ ness and comfort in participating in an interview about their health. Participants mentally and physically in the engulfment stages tended to be diagnosed the lon­ gest, suggesting that time since diagnosis increased their comfortability in talking about their health despite their persistent and pronounced challenges. Supporting my secondary hypothesis, I did find a cor­ relation between the participants’ mental integration stage and their preferred labels. Finally, I also identified other emergent themes, social identities, and experiences that directly influenced participants’ health identities and can inform future research.

Four Stages & Linear(ish) Progression

My findings support the validity of the four stages of identity integration: par­ ticipants who scored highly in engulfment spoke about feeling overwhelmed by their health during the open-ended questions, participants in acceptance affirmed their peace with their illness, and so on. Par­ ticipants who scored highly in the engulf­ ment stage most often reported a lack of social support and all-encompassing daily symptoms:

On feeling engulfed as a child: I was so used to pain…so all of that was going on for years and…my dad refused to take me to a doctor and my dad is a doctor, but he couldn’t fathom the idea of something being wrong with his kid…so he did not take me to a doctor, even when I literally couldn’t move my hands very much for years…it finally got really, really bad and then my dad agreed to take me. (Participant 4)

“While participants did report a roughly linear progression in terms of how they thought about and mentally understood their health, their actual health symptoms did not always improve linearly.”

As explained above, none of my par­ ticipants scored highest in the rejection stage, which makes sense given that peo­ ple rejecting their health probably would not self-select to participate in a study on chronic illness. On the other end of the spectrum, people who scored highly in the acceptance or enrichment categories talked about their health and its impact on their life in less emotionally charged or negative ways, often citing more manageable daily symptoms, coping mechanisms that en­ abled them to continue living their lives, and a strong support system:

I can deal with the pain…I’ve learned to just get through it…If I don’t eat in a very specific way then it’s GI symptoms [that impact her life the most] but I have learned the way to manage it. So most of the time I’m good, but that’s only through very specific decisions. (Participant 1, acceptance = 4)

I have ill days, like one to two days a month now, which is great. It used to be much more than that where I, physically, I’m stuck in bed, physically ill, cannot walk….I have gotten much better, thankfully. (Participant 6, acceptance = 4.6)

I’m definitely better now at setting boundaries and listening to myself… my friends now and my two roommates, they know everything and they’re always so respectful and my boyfriend is really understanding. He helps me a lot and my family, of course, is very understanding. (Participant 5, enrichment = 3.7)

Participants who scored highly spe­ cifically in the enrichment stage often identified one or more ways that their life was improved or positively impacted by their health:

I’ve had a lot of positive [medical interactions], like such a positive impact that they had in my life and how supportive medical professionals were really inspired me to want to do something in healthcare. (Participant 1, enrichment = 3.6)

I make [TikTok] videos because I

[think] a lot of content on chronic illness and autoimmune disease is really negative on social media. (Participant 5, enrichment = 3.7)

I specifically work with a lot of disabled populations now because I love it and I’m really passionate about it, and it’s something that I do so much advocacy work for…I am able to empathize so much with their situation. (Participant 6, enrichment = 4.9)

Participants in the acceptance and enrichment stages also spoke about their lived experiences, acting as a social re­ minder that anyone can become disabled at any time or point in their life:

Prior to developing [gastroparesis], I was an otherwise able-bodied person. I am sort of proof of the really uncomfortable truth, that able- bodied people don’t like to listen and hear, that you can become disabled at any time. You can develop a chronic illness at any time…The scary thing is that there’s still a lot of people who have this internalized ableism. (Participant 9, acceptance = 3.8)

It’s this idea of like, trying to be like “Hey, no, [disability] can happen to young people. Young people can have non- sports related injuries. Or non-sports related, like physical health problems. (Participant 12, enrichment = 3.3)

I like to inform people that I used to know not be this disabled, and it just happened all of a sudden. And that can happen for anybody. You know, I also like to remind people that COVID has caused so many illnesses for people who were completely healthy before they got COVID. You know, just as a warning? (Participant 8, acceptance = 4.4)

Suggesting an approximately linear progression through the health identity stages, participants in the engulfment stage reported working towards acceptance and participants in acceptance or enrichment often retroactively reported starting in a place of engulfment:

I feel like the past three years have been consumed by dealing with these sorts of issues. I feel like I’ve just tried to find ways to adjust and not make that the center of my life, even though it takes up a lot of time and energy. (Participant 7, acceptance = 3.8)

I would never have used the word… ”disability” when I was that young, right?... I was in middle school, I would pretty much just be like, “Oh, I have joint issues.” Like, that was kind of the extent of it. (Participant 10, acceptance = 4.2)

I don’t see it as a moral failing of myself [that] I can’t get a job right now. Or that I’ve had to take time off of school. Like I don’t. When I was younger, I used to definitely feel that way about myself. But by now I’ve been able to…hear like, you know, disability, acceptance and awareness. (Participant 8, acceptance = 4.4)

“I don’t see it as a moral failing of myself [that] I can’t get a job right now.

Or that I’ve had to take time off school.

Like I don’t.When

I was younger, I used to definitely feel that way about myself. But by now

I’ve been able to…hear like, you know, disability, acceptance and awareness.”

While my data supports a linear pro­ gression in terms of mental models around participants’ health identities, I also discov­ ered two different iterations of the engulf­ ment stage that complicated my results. One iteration was the mental engulfment depicted in the above analysis. The second was physical rather than mental engulfment. Participants who were physically engulfed had such severe daily symptoms that they scored highly in the engulfment stage. Still, they also scored highly in the acceptance or enrichment stage as they more accurately reflected their current mental model:

I love Northwestern other than accessibility issues and dorm lifestyle. I like Northwestern and I really do, I like my teachers, my friends, I love the area. And I love what I’m learning. I would like to continue progress… I’ve enjoyed [college]. But it definitely got harder, the more that my collection of illnesses hit me. And it was harder to keep up with assignments… It was hard to stay awake because of the physical effects of my illness, like I couldn’t…. I was struggling to do schoolwork.

I was you know, I’ve been getting extensions all the time… I was getting accommodations. Unfortunately, it wasn’t as many as I probably needed… I was still struggling with my migraines all the time, which made it so I couldn’t read. I couldn’t walk around the house. (Participant 8, engulfment = 3.75, acceptance = 4.4)

Thus, my data supports the four- stage theory of identity formation, com­ plicated slightly by the two different forms of engulfment. This formation process also proved to be approximately linear, encour­ aged by factors such as manageable daily symptoms and a strong social support net­ work. I will next analyze how label prefer­ ence intersects and reflects a participant’s current stage of identity formation.

Discussion Aside from its small size, a few other factors potentially made my sample more biased and less representative. First is self-selection bias. My participants con­ centrated more on the acceptance and enrichment end of the identity formation spectrum, and none identified with “rejec­ tion” as their primary stage. Second, my main recruitment method for this study was an informational email sent from AccessibleNU to students who currently receive accommodations due to a physical illness they have experienced over the past 6 or more months. Thus, my recruitment methods themselves limited my potential participants to people who have already disclosed their health conditions to the school and their professors.

“Identifying, labeling, and proving social problems and barriers faced by marginalized populations such as the disabled community is a critical first step to creating institutional and social policy that would make both Northwestern’s campus and the rest of the world a more accessible and safer place.”

As an inductive study, it created more questions than answers, such as the poten­ tial relationship between perceived visibil­ ity and feelings of validity. Hopefully, larg­ er and more resourced studies in the future can help fill some of the gaps in my study. It would be helpful to more actively recruit participants who are less confident in their health, more recently ill, and who hold other marginalized identities to under­ stand how those variables impact one’s un­ derstanding of their health and their health identity. It would also be advantageous to conduct studies with larger sample sizes that might be generalizable and to examine how populations other than young adults in prestigious academic environments re­ flect or do not reflect the themes identified in this study. My study underscores the im­ portance of researching disabled people to gain knowledge about their thoughts and social engagements. Identifying, labeling, and proving social problems and barriers faced by marginalized populations such as the disabled community is a critical first step to creating institutional and social pol­ icy that would make both Northwestern’s campus and the rest of the world a more accessible and safer place. ◆

title: InterConnention: Overlap in Env Sci and EPS Majors at Northwestern
notes: Feature comparing Northwestern's environmental science and Earth and planetary science majors. The opening page misprints "InterConnention"; the contents has "InterConnection". The contents gives page 138; the feature is on printed pages 136-137.
text:
InterConnention:

Overlap in Env Sci and EPS Majors at Northwestern

By: Gabrielle Walthour

The living and the dead. The environment and the Earth. Two sides of the same coin. At Northwestern, environmental science “prepares students to address one of soci­ ety’s greatest challenges: preservation and stewardship of the natural world”1 and Earth and planetary science is the study of “ the past, present, and future of the Earth and other planets [and helps] scientists address fundamental scientific questions important for un­ derstanding the Earth and society’s connection to it.”2 Both are majors at Northwestern.

Although they both deal with the environment, fundamental distinctions lead to major differences in curriculums. Within the environmental science program, there are two pathways: science and policy. The science track is interdisciplinary and students can choose to focus on sciences like biology and chemistry. The policy track is more eco­ nomics-focused which can be misleading. Within the environmental science major, it is expected that students take two environmental policy classes, but for students more interested in policy, Weinberg offers an environmental policy and culture adjunct major and minor.

The Earth and planetary major also has different concentrations: Earth materials, geochemistry, seismology, geology, climate/paleoclimate, geophysics & planetary, and geobiology. Students must take courses from at least four of the seven subdisciplines leading to interdisciplinary work. A plus is that the general requirements for the two majors are mostly similar so first-year students have the whole freshman year to decide which major they want to pursue.

Even though there are fundamental differences between the two majors there is much collaboration between the two departments. For example, there is much collabo­ ration between the leadership in both departments, and multiple teachers are affiliated or related faculty with both programs. Also, it is not uncommon to learn about topics pertaining to one major in a class for the other, because they are related topics, both involving the environment.

While there are major differences in the curriculum at Northwestern, the two ma­ jors are close to each other regarding careers and the future. Both majors can lead to jobs in industry, government, or academic work. There is even overlap with students major­ ing in Earth and planetary science getting a higher degree in environmental science. The interdisciplinary work that students do for both majors can lead to similar job work, but it is important to note that each major’s coursework prepares students for certain jobs differently.

1 Northwestern Environmental Science website: https://envsci.northwestern.edu/about/ 2 Northwestern Earth and Planetary Science website: https://www.earth.northwestern.edu/about/

title: Shattering the Finance Ceiling & Breaking Boundaries: Fintech’s Female Frontier
notes: Profile of Whitney Chen, a sophomore in economics researching leadership and negotiation at the Kellogg School of Management and General Manager of Northwestern University Fintech (NUFT), on women in quantitative finance. Answers edited for clarity and brevity. The contents gives page 140; the feature is on printed pages 138-139.
text:
Shattering the Finance Ceiling & Breaking Boundaries:

Fintech’s Female Frontier

By: Rebecca Chen & Ellen Liu

In the bustling world of quantitative finance, the clinking of numbers and the whirlwind of algorithms form the backdrop of high-stakes deci­ sion-making, yet diversity remains a crucial but often elusive goal. How­ ever, individuals like Whitney Chen, a sophomore majoring in economics, are challenging the status quo with fer­ vor and innovation. At Northwestern University, her impact extends far beyond her academic pursuits.

Within the Kellogg School of Management, Chen is research­ ing leadership and organizational behavior, striving to uncover effec­ tive strategies for navigating complex dynamics in quantitative finance. “My research centers on understanding how leaders can negotiate with stakeholders to enact meaningful change within their organizations,” she explains. Through meticu­ lous study and analysis, Chen explores the intricate interplay between power dynamics, communication strategies, and organizational structures. Her work not only sheds light on the nuanced art of negotiation but also offers valuable insights into fostering trans­ formative change within modern workplaces and organizations, with a particular focus on empowering women in finance.

Chen’s research has far-reaching implications for the finance industry. By eluci­ dating the intricacies of negotiation dynamics, she offers actionable insights and strat­ egies to navigate challenging organizational landscapes, particularly in terms of gender inequality, and drive positive change. Through her research, Chen’s focus on female empowerment within quantitative finance highlights the pressing need for diversity and inclusivity in traditionally male-dominated fields.

The most rewarding aspect of Chen’s research journey lies in its potential to affect real-world change. “The fact that the insights that I uncover in my research have the possibility of making an impact is what is most rewarding for me” she reflects.

Northwestern University Fintech (NUFT) aims to prepare students for competitive industry roles in quantita­ tive analysis and research, training their members in quantitative analysis and research skills while exposing members to a top-tier pre-professional environment. As the General Manager of NUFT, Chen has focused on taking initiative to increase female participation in a traditionally male-dominated space.

“One of the challenges we faced was the lack of representation,” she explained. “Women often felt sidelined or intimidated, leading to a significant gender disparity in club participation.”

In response to this challenge, Chen took decisive action by spearheading a series of initiatives within NUFT. From the start, her goal was clear: to empower and educate women interested in Fintech, fostering an environment conducive to their growth and success. “We wanted to shatter the glass ceiling one initiative at a time,” Chen emphasized during our inter­ view. Her words resonated with a sense of purpose; with each endeavor, Chen is steadfast in her previous commitment, paving the way for a more inclusive future.

When asked what event was most effective in promoting female involve­ ment, Chen replied “Definitely the series of training workshops and networking events tailored specifically to the needs of women in Fintech, such as inviting women who are already leaders in the field to speak about their experiences.” According to Chen, “this provided mentorship and con­ nections that extended beyond the event, which is immensely helpful in navigating and thriving in a male-dominated field like finance.”

“Representation matters,” Chen stressed, “and by showing success stories of women in finance [through panel dis­ cussions and networking events], we can inspire others to follow suit, forming the next generation of female leaders.” She further emphasized, “Right now, diversity and inclusion are major missions of tech culture.” As a result, Chen’s commitment to promoting diversity and inclusion mir­ rors the evolving landscape of the tech and finance industry.

Chen, in recognizing the vital sig­ nificance of outreach and recruitment, took proactive steps to increase NUFT’s exposure to women interested in the field. By having NUFT participate in events like Women in Computing, and actively engaging with attendees, Chen not only shares the club’s mission but also creates a welcoming environment, encouraging women to explore opportunities within the club.

“Recruiting more women into the club was very important to me,” Chen explained. “It is not just about increasing numbers or meeting a quota. For me and many others, it is about fostering a sense of belonging and creating a space where women feel empowered to pursue their passions in Fintech.”

The impact of Chen’s initiatives has been visible, as there has been a significant increase in female membership and partic­ ipation in executive roles within NUFT. “Seeing more women actively engaged and making their voices heard has been incred­ ibly rewarding. There is still so much work to be done in terms of fostering diversity and inclusion within the finance industry,” Chen remarked. “But we are just getting started.”

[Answers have been edited for clarity and brevity]

title: About the Contributors
notes: Contents lists it as "Contributors: Biographies and Interviews of Thesis Contributors" at page 136; it is on printed pages 140-147. One page each for Eden Stargardt, Jacob Geil, Michael Richards, Rebecca C. Wu, Amy Fan, Grace A. Wu and Sierra Erdman-Luntz: thesis title, photo and short Q&A on their research topic, how they came to it, future directions and post-graduation plans.
text:
About the Contributors

Eden Stargardt

Jacob Geil Michael Richards

Rebecca C. Wu

Amy Fan Grace A. Wu Sierra Erdman-Luntz

Eden Stargardt

The Lasting Legacy of a Divided City: The Berlin Orchestras as a Microcosm for Germany during the Wendezeit

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? Orchestras are important cultural institu­ tions and as such they are representations of greater socio-political movements. They often act as mirrors of political, social, and cultural landscapes, and reflect the greater values and beliefs within a given time. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the greater themes of Germany during the Wendezeit were reflected in the activities of the orchestras, musical institutions, and concert program­ ming in the orchestras in Berlin and acted as representations of cultural politics during this transitional period. By examining three significant reunification concerts that oc­ curred in Berlin between late 1989 and early 1990, my research explains the ways in which the orchestras in Berlin acted as a microcosm for the greater German society. Through these analyses, I highlight the unequal preservation of cultural institutions in the former East Berlin and the Bundesrepublik and will explain the resurgence of the ideals of the French Revolution and Germany as das Land der Dichter und Denker that is in­ tertwined with it. I illustrate the connections between the large presence of Beethoven’s music, the idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk, and the influence of figures such as Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Friedrich Schiller, and

Karl Friedrich Schinkel on the curated image of the reunification concerts in Berlin. I also question who controlled the narrative in this period of transition and who the collective audience is after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

How did you come to your research topic? I came to my research topic after taking Professor von Holt’s class entitled Berlin and the Culture of Democracy. I was looking for a way to combine my two areas of study (German and music performance) and want­ ed to create a project to culminate my time at Northwestern. In her class, we learned about the impact of the German Reunification on other artforms (i.e., popular music, dance, film), but I noticed that there was not wide­ ly-available literature explaining the impact on classical music and the orchestras. I trav­ eled to Berlin on a Summer research grant and discovered that the materials existed but had not been translated into English. This discovery served as the basis for my project.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I will be continuing my studies at Northwest­ ern this fall and will be starting a graduate degree in music performance at the Bienen School of Music.

Jacob Geil

The Impact of School Security on Student Wellbeing

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research is on the impact of school secu­ rity on student wellbeing. It examined how attending school alongside a security pres­ ence affects school climate, and its extended consequences for student wellbeing, includ­ ing student experiences of stress, safety, fear, and discomfort, and how they manifested in anxiety, depression, and other mental health challenges.

How did you come to your research topic? I attended a high school with a large and very visible security presence, including armed police officers, metal detectors, cameras, and weekly drug tests. Assuming this was typical, I did not question this security pres­ ence while a high school student. However, after getting to Northwestern and learning that not all high schools operate like this, I began wondering how this sort of regular exposure to intense security measures might have been affecting mine and my peers’ day- to-day experience as students, as well as the learning environment my school was trying to foster. This inspired my research topic.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I am excited to see how this research con­ tinues to develop. I believe there are many future directions for this research to take, including a broader sample size; incorpo­ rating students of various age groups and periods of development; further research into the role of identity and intersectionality in this relationship; and further research into the kinds of support that are most effective for students and how to make this support accessible to schools.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I will be working as a Higher Education An­ alyst with Huron Consulting Group in New York City.

Michael Richards

Structural Characterization via X-Ray Crystallography of III-Nitrides for APDs

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? Using a piece of equipment to determine the structural (physical) properties of a particu­ lar type of semiconductor using x-rays and subsequent analysis. This seminconductor family (III-Nitrides) is very good for optical applications in the UV region and is capable of high sensitivity, provided we minimize defects during growth.

How did you come to your research topic? I found my lab, CQD, after taking EE223 with Prof. Razeghi my sophomore year. I began exploring III-Nitrides there and began my journey with structural characterization using the XRD there. Since then, I have also explored the electrical and optical properties and got more involved in the APD device fabrication.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? Semiconductor photodiodes are undoubt­ edly the future of optics and detection. In the UV region in particular, which is what III-Nitrides are good for, is huge for a lot of sensitive-detection applications, which now include the quick and accurate detection of pathogens and viruses like COVID-19. These devices start with a better understand­ ing of the materials they are made of so that higher quality devices can be made - and this requires further research using characteriza­ tion tech like XRD.

Where are you heading to after graduation? After graduating in 2024 with my BS & MS in electrical engineering, I plan to go to law school and pursue a career in patent law.

Rebecca C. Wu

Baby got Bac: Associations Between Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Infant Gut Microbiota in Cebu, Phillipines

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research involves looking at the effects of maternal prenatal stress on the composition and diversity of the infant gut microbiome and infant health outcomes.

How did you come to your research topic? I became interested in the human gut micro­ biota after joining Dr. Katie Amato’s lab at the end of my freshman year. As a former pre-med, I was interested in how health inequities manifested through stress-based pathways, and the microbiota is at the center of stress and physiology, which led naturally to my research topic

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I think there is still a lot to be done with lon­ gitudinal work on the relationship between maternal stress and child health outcomes beyond infancy. I am specifically interested in investigating immune and inflammatory measures of health in the first few years of life, as these are closely related to the micro­ biota. Other research in biological anthro­ pology and related fields has investigated this as a result of climate change and through the measurement of cognitive development.

Amy Fan

Are People “Real” on BeReal?: Perception and Authenticity in Utilization of Social Media App

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research study focuses on how college students use the social media app BeReal. Be­ Real claims to be “A new and unique way to discover who your friends really are in their daily life” (BeReal). Created as a response to social media platforms like Instagram where users tend to post picture perfect images on a never-ending feed with ads, BeReal takes a different approach. As an app designed to value authenticity from its users with a limit­ ed daily feed of BeReals from friends, it takes up a minimal part of a user’s day. The main goal of the app is to provide a platform for users to stay in touch with their social circle while reducing inauthenticity. I studied how college students use the social media app BeReal compared to other social media apps and whether BeReal is effective at promot­ ing authenticity and reducing negative links often related to social media usage. Looking into how people use and perceive BeReal could reveal unintended negative conse­ quences to using the app or determine that it is indeed a social media app that connects people in an authentic, positive manner. This study explored the questions (1) does BeReal usage mitigate the link between time spent on social media and anxiety, fear of missing out, public self-consciousness, and authen­ ticity (2) how do people use BeReal and what do they think BeReal’s intended purpose is compared to other social media apps, (3) do inauthentic BeReal behaviors such as retakes, posting late, and skipping posts correlate with greater anxiety, public self-conscious­ ness, and fear of missing out and vice versa?

How did you come to your research topic? Watching BeReal grow in popularity, I saw an opportunity to investigate if the design of BeReal allowed users to act more authentically on the app. Through research, my friends and fellow peers who use the app would become more knowledgeable about the technology we are engaging in every day and be able to make informed decisions based on the results.

Where are you heading to after graduation? After spending a gap year working as a medical assistant, I hope to attend medical school to become an OB/GYN, contributing to the community through primary care and patient outcomes research.

Grace A. Wu

Illustrating Indigeneity: Xie Sui’s Huang Qing zhigong tu and the critical reevaluation of its depictions of aboriginal Taiwanese peoples, 1751–1775 and 2006–2022

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research centers around an eigh­ teenth-century Qing illuminated handscroll that contains written and illustrated ethno­ graphic descriptions of different groups of people in the Qing empire. I explore how “fan 番,” or those who are “barbaric” or “savage,” is expressed in the thirteen depic­ tions of aboriginal Taiwanese male-female pairs, in addition to notions of savagery versus imperial and cultural superiority. I also bring this object into the present and analyze not only how twenty-first century Taiwanese curators have thought about and exhibited this handscroll in the National Palace Museum in Taiwan, but also how the public has engaged with this object through a postcolonial lens.

How did you come to your research topic? I knew I wanted to write an art history senior honors thesis about Taiwan, so I connected with Professors Yuthika Sharma (Art History) and Peter J. Carroll (History) to brainstorm ideas. Professor Carroll mentioned seeing one of these scrolls at the National Palace Museum years ago, and it immediately piqued my interest because of its themes of imperialism, construction of race/Otherness, and inclusion of Indige­ nous Taiwanese communities. The National Palace Museum’s 2022 special exhibition of the scroll was also on view during this time, which made me realize I could also inves­ tigate the contemporary attitudes toward this manuscript and compare/contrast them with eighteenth-century Qing perspectives.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? While the ethnographic depictions in the handscroll are unique for their brilliant illumination and frequent public display, other versions of the same content exist in other media, such as woodblock-printed books and illuminated albums. Some of the books were destroyed in conflict, but a book is currently in the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., and some illuminated album folios are in the Bibliothèque natio­ nale de France in Paris, France. No scholar has yet written in English how these man­ uscripts left China or what non-Manchu people thought about its contents, which would be an exciting future direction of inquiry.

Sierra Erdman-Luntz

The Health Identities of Northwestern Students with Chronic Physical Health Conditions

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research considers how college students with long-term illnesses integrate their health status into their personal identities.

How did you come to your research topic? While I have been sick since I was 16, it took years for me to identify as chronically ill and disabled, and I only recently started advocacy work for my conditions. I was curious how other students in similar positions to mine navigated being sick as a young adult.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? There are so many aspects of identity and circumstance that might influence one’s health integration journey that I was unable to explore in my study due to time and sam­ ple size constraints. Future researchers could look at how class, age at diagnosis, gender identity, type of diagnosis, geographic loca­ tion, sexuality, and race could impact how someone does or does not integrate their health into their identity. My full thesis also considered how labeling theory intersects with identity development, which is current­ ly a large gap in the literature.

Where are you heading to after graduation? A few years gap and then law school.
