text:
LETTER FROM THE ADVISERS

Dear Readers,

We would like to welcome you to the Volume 17 of the Northwestern Undergraduate

Research Journal (NURJ). This 2021-2022 issue is the product of a year’s work by the students who lead and contribute to the NURJ, a student-produced annual print publication funded by the Office of the President and the Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education. This year marks our first as advisors for the NURJ following in the footsteps of the late Professor Allen Taflove, who was with the NURJ for its first

18 years. We have seen incredible work done this year, all of it in Taflove’s honor, and celebrate the students who have made this publication possible, particularly the Editors- in-Chief Shreya Sriram and Jenna Greenzaid.

This past year has been the first that students have been able to work together again in person, and the creations by the NURJ, including this journal, has been a product of coming together again. In addition to this journal, our students were able to create an outstanding online package by interviewing student researchers in person, continue to make new episodes on the NURJ Talks Podcast, and find new ways for student researchers to share their work and experiences across campus.

The NURJ staff continues to grow, expanding to 70 members, all of who study a wide variety of subjects. The convergence of different backgrounds has allowed the

NURJ to continue to grow and prosper by creating a more collaborative, creative, and passionate community where new ideas are welcomed. We have been lucky to see these new ideas come to life and become staple parts of the work this organization puts together, from this print edition to the Archives project, interactive online publications, and everything in between.

As you continue through this Volume 17 journal, you’ll find the intersection of excellent research and excellent media, all done by and for Northwestern students.

Best, Dr. Peter Civetta and Patti Wolter

NURJ Faculty Advisors

title: LETTER FROM THE EDITORS
notes: Signed by the Editors-in-Chief.
text:
LETTER FROM THE EDITORS

Dear Readers,

The NURJ is grateful to have crossed paths with all the incredibly talented researchers that have contributed to this new edition. As we started the 2021-2022 academic year, we redefined what expansion meant for the journal. Whereas previous editions sought to include the entire spectrum of scholarship at Northwestern University, this year we curated the edition you hold in your hands with more care, concern, and critical analysis. We present a careful selection of 11 honors senior theses, all contributing important discoveries and revelations to their respective fields. This volume also includes eight feature stories that reflect the diversity of research at Northwestern, including a very special ninth. This feature is an interview with outgoing Northwestern President Morton Schapiro, an inaugural piece in what we hope to instill as an everlasting tradition to honor our founder and late faculty adviser, Professor Allen Taflove (1949-2021).

The NURJ has continued supporting student engagement with research on Northwestern’s campus through our Online volumes, NURJ Talks, our very own podcast, and our recent string of in-person research presentations. These talks are by various Northwestern professors and faculty who offer their insights into the current landscape of research in their fields and advice for the thriving research community here. As always, we collaborated with those organizations and departments who offer ever- fruitful inspiration and partnerships, such as the Office of Undergraduate Research’s EXPO, the Chicago Area Undergraduate Research Symposium, and the University Archives. We encourage you to visit our website (thenurj.com) and view all the amazing student work those projects highlight.

None of this would be possible without the generous sponsorship and continued guidance from President Morton Schapiro and Associate Provost Miriam Sherin, for which we are eternally grateful for. We would also like to thank Dean Sarah Pritchard, Dr. Peter Civetta, Dr. Megan Wood, Liz Hamilton, Chris Diaz, and numerous other faculty, staff, and student researchers at Northwestern University for all their support. Last but not least, we must recognize our wonderful new faculty advisors, Dr. Peter Civetta and Professor Patti Wolter, who stepped into the role with courage and faith for our dreams. Their expertise and time is one of the most valuable gifts we’ve received since our inception, and we want to extend our deepest gratitude to them for their unwavering belief in us. Although Shreya will be graduating this Spring 2022, Jenna will return as Editor-in-Chief alongside Kallista Zhuang, a duo more than capable of continuing the NURJ’s excellence.

Sincerely, Jenna Greenzaid and Shreya Sriram Editors-in-Chief

title: Taflove’s VIPs: Q&A with Northwestern President Morton Schapiro
notes: Interview with outgoing Northwestern President Morton Schapiro by the Editors-in-Chief, introduced as the first of an annual "Taflove’s VIPs" feature honoring late faculty adviser Allen Taflove. Title as given in the contents; the opening page prints "Taflove’s VIPs:" over "Q&A with Northwestern President Morton Schapiro". The introduction's drop cap "M" is a separate block (8.14).
text:
Taflove’s VIPs:

Q&A with Northwestern President

Morton Schapiro by Editors-in-Chief Jenna Greenzaid and Shreya Sriram

A note from the NURJ:

Our late faculty adviser, Professor Allen Taflove, had a list of faculty names whom he fondly referred to as his “VIPs.” These were members of the Northwestern University community who were hand-picked to receive a special copy of the NURJ’s annual Print Edition. As a dedication to Professor Taflove, we have created “Taflove’s VIPs” — a place for us to talk with some of our fellow exceptional Wildcats, both on and off the initial list. We hope to establish this as an annual feature, such that Professor Taflove’s vision and dedication can be eternally celebrated.

To commence this tradition, we thought it only fitting to present a special sit-down with Northwestern professor, economist, and departing president of 13 years, Morton Schapiro.

Morton Schapiro has been the president of Northwestern University for the past 13 years and has taught graduate and undergraduate students for 43 consecutive years. He is an economist, a professor, and a self-proclaimed life-long reader. At Northwestern, Schapiro dedicated himself to furthering the liberal arts education and fostering a collaborative environment for all parts of the Northwestern community, including undergraduate research. Considering the perfect alignment of that goal with our driving mission, we were especially excited to speak with Schapiro, a long-time supporter of the NURJ. In this interview, we gained insight into his beliefs on the role that research plays at Northwestern and what he has learned from his years here.

Editor’s Note: The following interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

NURJ: What were some of your main goals that you were hoping to achieve when you first became president?

Schapiro: When I took the job 13 years ago, I was thinking, “Well, I love the focus of the liberal arts college, but I also love the vitality of the research university. Let me see if I can try to bring them together as much as I could.” And that’s what I’ve tried to do for 13 years.

N: Best of both worlds.

S: In a lot of ways, it is.

N: Since we are a research insti- tution, and independent research in and of itself is more geared towards graduate students and professionals, what role do you think undergraduates have in continuing and furthering that mission?

S: I came from the mentality with 20 years at Williams [College] that undergraduates are research partners. I’ve also co-authored a lot of articles, including [some] here with undergraduates. I think that, at Northwestern, we do a very good job providing

[research] opportunities for everyone, not just for sponsored research. If you’re in the humanistic social sciences, you don’t usually get sponsored research, which is why we’ve had this enormous expansion of research funds for faculty to sign up for the summer, and undergrads to, hopefully, co-author articles. That happens a lot here now, and I’m really proud of that and to have a small role in that.

N: For books that you’ve written both with other professors and on your own, what does that writing process look like? Is there research involved on an individual level and a collaborative level?

S: The first book we [Morton Schapiro and Saul Morrison] did, we were just getting to know each other, so what we wrote didn’t flow the way the last two have. I have had fabulous co-authors in economics journals and articles — David Figlio is a brilliant economist, and he and I have written a series of articles. … It’s a little different having been a president for 22 years. A lot of presidents kind of move on from that faculty role, and they don’t teach and publish. I came into the business because I love to teach and publish, and I never gave it up.

N: This is a bit out there — but do you see any potential collaboration between Northwestern’s research community and our thriving athlet- ics program? Or any way that students could meld the two and their interest in them?

S: At a place like Northwestern, we’re not all that compartmentalized. You know, we have a great music school, but it’s not a conservatory where the musicians are separated from everyone else. We don’t just have our journalists doing journalism; they’re doing everything else too. It’s one of the things I like about Northwestern — we pursue excellence in every regard, but we don’t compartmentalize fields of study the way some schools do.

N: As a student, I’ve been thinking a lot about my intellectual curiosity and how I’m going to be able to satisfy that once I leave my education. You’re in a similar spot where you’re leaving academia behind, so how do you think you’re going to keep your intellectual curiosity thriving?

S: I always say when people ask me, “What do you hope you have instilled in your undergraduates at graduation?” that I hope they have quantitative skills because that’s really important, and I hope they have the aesthetic sensibilities developed. I hope they have a real respect for diversity and inclusion and an understanding of what that means. I hope they have the tools to educate themselves for a lifetime, which they get at a place like Northwestern, but most importantly, the humility to know how little they know. It’s called commencement; it’s not called the ending — it’s the beginning of your intellectual journey. I think about how much more I know, not just in my field of economics, but in everything over the years by reading and listening. I’m hoping that I get a little smarter, a little better educated as I get older — there’s a long way to go.

N: Lifelong learning.

S: Yeah. Lifelong learning is exactly what it’s about. ◆

Visit thenurj.com to see Morton Schapiro’s current book recommendations and hear exclusive interview moments.

title: Black-Owned Small Businesses in Englewood, Chicago: Documenting the Effects of COVID-19 and the Black Lives Matter Movement in 2020
department: School of Education and Social Policy & Department of Statistics
notes: Senior thesis (mixed methods). Faculty advisers named on the opening page; the contents labels it "Social Policy and Statistics". Tables 1-3 and Appendix B are extracted cell by cell; Appendix A is the interview protocol, with list numbers in blocks of their own. Pull quotes on printed pages 17-18 repeat text from the body. Bibliography entries are split across blocks mid-entry.
text:
Black-Owned Small Businesses in Englewood, Chicago:

Documenting the Effects of COVID-19 and the Black Lives Matter Movement in 2020 by Sophie Boorstein

School of Education and Social Policy

& Department of Statistics Faculty Advisers: Prof. Jonathan Guryan, Ph.D., Prof. Reuel Rogers, Ph.D., & Prof. Elizabeth Tipton, Ph.D.

Background

The year 2020 was characterized by insurmountable losses for communities around the world. Amid the global COVID-19 pandemic and the largest recession since the mid-20th century in the U.S., the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement rose to a global scale and brought the epidemic of police brutality to the public eye. All aforementioned events in the United States disproportionately impacted Black communities, amplifying pre-existing racial health, income, and social disparities.

News media reported that Black- owned businesses were severely financially impacted by 2020’s crisis events. From

February to April 2020, the number of all active business owners in the United States dropped by 22%. During the same period, the number of active Black business owners dropped 41% (Leatherby, 2020). When BLM protests erupted in all 50 American states in response to George Floyd’s murder and the unjust murders of countless other Black victims, a minority of protesters, including individuals not associated with the protests, looted local businesses in several cities across the country.

Englewood, a neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, was identified as one of the areas severely damaged by looting and the COVID-19 pandemic (Bayne,

2020). The area of Englewood, for the purposes of this paper, contains two adjacent neighborhoods: West Englewood and Englewood. Of Englewood’s 75,000 residents, approximately 90% are Black (“Household Income in Englewood,” 2020). The median household income in Englewood is $28,000, which is half of Chicago’s overall median household income, and at least 30% of its residents live below the poverty line. According to Englewood activists’ testimonies, COVID-19 restrictions and looting activity exacerbated many hardships that Englewood community members already faced.

Yet, policy responses inadequately addressed Black-owned businesses’ heightened vulnerability in 2020. The federal government attempted to remedy the effects of the recession on all small businesses through the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), a $669 billion loan program from the Small Business Administration (SBA). However, structural characteristics of the PPP disadvantaged Black-owned small businesses’ access to loans (Abramson, 2020; Selvam, 2020). Even prior to the contingencies and concerns exacerbated by COVID-19, Black- owned small businesses were at higher risk of financial hardship compared to white- owned small businesses. Although 32% of Chicago residents are Black, in 2017, Chicago had only 1,875 Black-owned businesses, comprising only 3.7% of all Chicago businesses (Marotti & Elejalde-Ruiz, 2020). Systemic racism in financial institutions, which have become systems that maintain white supremacy, is one cause of racial financial inequities. Historically, non-white business owners have had disproportionately low access to bank credit, and lower-income, minority neighborhoods have suffered from lower lending rates than higher-income, white neighborhoods (Blanchard et al., 2008). Due to racial disparities in credit access, the majority of small businesses in Chicago that have fewer than two weeks of cash reserves are in majority-Black neighborhoods (Leatherby, 2020).

Historical crisis events reveal potential direct and indirect effects of the 2020 crises on Black-owned small businesses in Englewood. After the riots in Ferguson, Missouri, following the 2014 murder of Michael Brown, businesses in Ferguson suffered up to 50% in profit losses, regardless of whether they were physically damaged (Hackman, 2014). Literature has documented indirect damages of riots during the Civil Rights Movement, and the effects were particularly significant for Black-owned properties because the majority of cities’ Black populations resided in riot-affected areas. Further, economic recessions disproportionately affect minority and low-income communities due to predatory lending and low cash reserves among family units and local businesses (Williams et al., 2013).

Despite the significant challenges that Black business owners face, scholars have found that Black-owned business development is an effective strategy to create job opportunities in urban areas, and Black business owners exhibit higher political activity and a stronger commitment to community development than white business owners. Black-owned small businesses can politically and financially support their community amid crisis events, as Black-identifying businesspeople have leadership abilities that can influence local political institutions and strengthen human capital in disadvantaged neighborhoods (Ferleger & Lavallee, 2018).

To better understand how Black- owned businesses can succeed and positively impact their communities, the present research aims to understand the effects of combined 2020 crisis events on Chicago’s minority-owned small businesses, using Englewood as a case study. The work builds upon topics covered by scholars examining natural disasters, riots, and recessions, which have to date significantly impacted low-income and non- white communities like Englewood. Using a mixed-methods approach, I address the research question: how were Black-owned businesses in Englewood economically impacted by COVID-19 and the BLM movement in the spring and summer of 2020? More specifically, I examine two secondary research questions:

1. How was Englewood economically impacted according to foot traffic data records? 2. How was Englewood economically impacted according to business owners’ accounts?

Methods

Quantitative Methods For quantitative analyses, I employed mobile phone data from SafeGraph, Inc., a commercial entity that offered free datasets in 2020 to aid scholarly research on the COVID-19 pandemic. SafeGraph’s compiled mobility datasets used ano- nymized cell phone location records and governmental open data to capture weekly population movements at the census block group (CBG) level. Two datasets provided foot traffic data on visitations to respective points of interest (POI), defined as locations at which a consumer spends money or time.

Quantitative analyses focused on two events of interest in Chicago: (1) the Illinois stay-at-home order declared on March 21, 2020, and (2) the murder of George Floyd on May 25, 2020. I aimed to determine if there existed significant differences in business visitation following the two events of interest between (1) majority-Black Chicago neighborhoods as compared to majority-non-Black Chicago neighborhoods and (2) Englewood as compared to other majority-Black Chicago neighborhoods. Because majority-Black neighborhoods have higher rates of Black business ownership, examining foot traffic on the CBG-level provided information on foot traffic at Black-owned businesses, and demographic variables served as a proxy to examine the research questions (Frey, 2018; Safegraph, 2020). A difference in difference analysis with two

Before analyses began, significant data cleaning occurred. I added a total of 218,343 new data points with unique week and POI combinations to include visit counts of zero. I then assigned POI to Chicago neighborhoods, or Chicago Community Areas (CCA), through their CBG identification. I matched each data- point with demographic variables corresponding to its CCA, using data from the City of Chicago and a Tract to Community Area Equivalency File (Chicago Data Guy, n.d.; Community Snapshots Raw Data). Finally, for each data point, I added the average COVID-19 positivity rate by week for each neighborhood.

I used Gower’s distance calculations to establish comparison groups. I first created a dissimilarity matrix to analyze dissimilarity between the 77 Chicago neighborhoods, including all 14 variables in the final dataset.1 I used R’s Partition Around Medoids algo- rithm for clustering. The silhouette plots indicated that two clusters were ideal, with an average silhouette width of 0.2, as shown in Figure 1. Cluster 1 contained 49 neighborhoods while Cluster 2 contained 28 neighborhoods. Appendix B displays the average characteristics for Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 neighborhoods. After establishing comparison groups, I assessed the parallel trends assumption using a sandwich estimator of linear regression with the two outcome variables. Qualitative Methods Qualitative data and quantitative data were collected separately, but the two methods took place simultaneously and informed each other. I chose one-on-one interviews for the qualitative methodology due to their potential to yield contextualized findings on business owners’ perceptions of the policy and events, supplementing the quantitative data that offered aggre- gate insights into foot traffic patterns and indicated potential policy and event effects on transactions.

There were three primary methods for recruitment: contacting business owners directly, referrals from participants, and referrals from local organizations. There were a total of eight participants, seven of whom identify as Black and/or African American and own a small business in Englewood. I additionally interviewed the manager of a non-profit cafe, owned and run by an executive board with a majority of members who identify as Black or African American. I would like to address the specific limitations, risks, and biases in the project. Some participants may have been coping with the psychological costs from the 2020 crises, and they may have experienced discomfort during interviews when asked to reflect on personal experiences. Further, differences between the participants and myself existed on the levels of race, age, religion, socioeconomic status, education, and overall social location, or some combination of them. Due to my positionality as a white woman, participants may have been reluctant to reveal vulnerability during interviews. Concerns or discomfort from participants were considered seriously, and throughout the research, it was imperative that I elevated participants’ voices, centering their experiences rather than my own perceptions. Engaging with the data with high awareness of the strengths and limits of my subjectivity was my highest priority in this process.

Results

Quantitative Results Covariate balance and parallel trend tests maintained that difference in differences was an appropriate tool for the research question. The subsequent analyses assessing the influence of Event 1, the stay-at- home order, on foot traffic found that businesses in neighborhoods with higher proportions of Black residents experienced a smaller decline in visitors and visits per week after the stay-at-home order was enforced than did businesses in neighborhoods with lower proportions of Black residents. This finding is visualized in the sharper decrease in the line representing majority-non-Black neighborhoods in Figure 2. This was true when comparing (1) neighborhoods indexed as 0-33% Black with neighborhoods indexed as 66-100% Black, (2) neighborhoods 33-66% Black with neighborhoods 66-100% Black, and (3) neighborhoods in Cluster 1 with those in Cluster 2. The higher foot traffic in majority-Black neighborhoods after the stay-at- home order may seem to contradict news media reports that Black businesses have been influenced most negatively by the pandemic. However, essential workers traveling to their workplace within majority-Black neighborhoods could explain the statistically significant higher visitor counts. There are a disproportionate number of Black workers who work in “essential industries” and who are less likely to work from their own homes as an alternative to in-person work during the pandemic (Gould & Wilson, 2020).

Meanwhile, there was no significant difference in visit or visitor count in Englewood as compared to other majority-Black neighborhoods or other neighborhoods in Cluster 2. This finding suggests that the impact of the stay-at-home order on foot traffic was similar in Englewood as in other majority-Black neighborhoods. During interviews, Englewood small business owners reported that customer visitation dropped significantly in the spring and summer of 2020, confirming that business visitation declined in Englewood. Furthermore, participants’ descriptions of decreased business visitation and the effects of these drops on profit are likely consistent with the experiences of business owners in other majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.

Analyses for Event 2, the murder of George Floyd, showed that after May 25, 2020, majority-Black neighborhoods experienced a smaller increase in visit count and visitor count as compared to majority-non-Black neighborhoods. This was true when comparing (1) neighborhoods 0-33% Black with neighborhoods 66-100% Black and (2) neighborhoods in Cluster 1 with those in Cluster 2. Figure 3 shows that business visitation increased disproportionately in majority-non-Black neighborhoods as compared to majority-Black neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, and that total visitor counts in neighborhoods indexed as 0-33% Black rises at a higher rate around and after May 25, 2020, as compared to neighborhoods indexed as 33- 66% Black. The significant findings align with analyses 6 and 9, and Table 3 displays the point estimates and significance levels.

While foot traffic increased disproportionately in majority-non-Black neighborhoods after George Floyd’s murder on May 25, 2020, there were no differences in visit or visitor count in Englewood as

Thus, Englewood is statistically similar to other majority-Black neighborhoods in terms of business visitation after the murder of George Floyd. Business owners in the present study’s sample explained that generally few protests occur in Englewood: “I think a lot of times protests come from groups that have a little bit more than what we have. We’re more in survival mode than we are in changing mode.” News media also confirms that thousands of individuals rallied in majority-non-Black Chicago neighborhoods to protest for causes associated with the BLM movement. Because quantitative data indicates that Englewood is comparable to other majority-Black neighborhoods after May 25, 2020, it can be reasonably concluded that the increase in total visit counts and visitor counts in majority-non-Black neighborhoods relative to majority-Black neighborhoods can be attributed to higher protest activity in majority-non-Black neighborhoods.

Qualitative Results Although quantitative data indicates a disproportionate decline in business visitation in Chicago’s majority-non-Black neighborhoods, interviews show that the majority of businesses in the Englewood sample experienced declines in business visitation after the March 2020 stay-at-home order, which participants attributed to customer fear of contracting COVID-19. At the time of the interviews, the majority of participants said that visitation was at 50-60% of the pre-pandemic volume. In fact, COVID-19 exacerbated the challenges of acquiring and retaining customers among the participants sam- pled. Customer health concerns about the virus were likely amplified by poor public health infrastructure and high COVID-19 positivity rates in Englewood compared to other neighborhoods in Chicago (“COVID-19 Community Mobility Report,” 2020). Participant 7 stated that before the pandemic, most of his customers lived in majority-white, north-side Chicago neighborhoods. After the stay-at-home order, Participant 7 noticed that these customers “haven’t been calling.” Participants said that even prior to COVID-19, “acquiring a customer was much harder than in a different neighborhood” in Chicago due to public perception of Englewood as dangerous, and customers from outside of the neighborhood were less likely to patronize businesses in Englewood.

COVID-19 precautions also increased business costs and decreased revenue through modes other than business visitation. For

Visitor Count Pre- and Post-May 25 example, Participant 3 stopped making food for delivery services like DoorDash due to “problems where delivery people didn’t want to wear masks.” Sanitation supplies to address COVID-19 were costly, and shortages early in the pandemic contributed to high expenditures on the sanitation supplies. Participant 5 explained, “Say you made about five or six hundred dollars for the week. Now, you have to take $100 of that just for sanitation. That’s not including your lights, your gas, your product.” The majority of participants were forced to balance cost and revenue streams by decreasing the number of days their business was in operation, lowering service prices, or let- ting go of employees. It is important to note that business success after the stay-at-home order varied by industry; the funeral home and hardware store had higher customer visitation than before 2020. However, such improved business performance was due at least in part to implications of the stay- at-home order, including increases in bike riding and home repairs. And, even with unharmed revenue streams, the COVID-19 pandemic affected these businesses’ interactions with customers due to mask mandates and storefront capacity limits. Participant 2, whose profit was not affected by the stay- at-home order, recounted his concern with employee and customer health: “We talked with employees about the importance of not only keeping them safe and healthy, but also keeping the public safe. And that we were concerned about them as our staff. We were concerned about their family.”

All participants’ businesses were at least partially re-opened by June 2021 after the initial economic shock from COVID-19 restrictions. However, Participant 5 explained that just after her business re-opened in June, looting occurred in Englewood. She said, “It was very heartbreaking for that damage of all breaking in and stealing stuff and destroying stuff. It was really tough. Especially mixed in with this pandemic.” The two participants whose storefronts experienced looting damage assumed additional financial obligations for repairs. Participant 5’s costs amounted to over $25,000, with

90% of products and “countless” pieces of equipment stolen. Looters broke Participant 3’s doors and windows in an attempt to steal the ATM machine. Business owners who did not experience direct effects of looting reckoned with the destruction of their community. Participant 4 explained that looters “burnt down a lot of stores and bust out windows around the Englewood area.” Participant 3 told me that she “watched someone’s business being destroyed for eight hours” and that at the liquor store across the street from her business, looters took “about $6 or $7 million worth of alcohol.”

While participants stayed in their businesses as long as possible, sometimes the entire night, many returned home to sleep, at which point the looting occurred. Unpro- tected and vulnerable to the physical damage of their storefronts, the consequences of looting in Englewood amid pre-existing financial hardship represent the racial and socioeconomic discrimination inhibiting the success of Black-owned small businesses.

Physical damage from looting associated with the BLM movement after the murder of George Floyd negatively affected participants’ businesses and emotional well-being, but participants reported some positive consequences of the BLM movement itself, which helped counteract the negative effects of the pandemic. After losing customers in majority-white neighborhoods, Participant 7 began posting ad- vertisement flyers in the Englewood area to attract new customers. Now, the majority of Participant 7’s customers live in Englewood, and he has a higher proportion of Black customers. He said, “Ever since COVID, a lot of Black people have been trying to look for a Black computer repairman.” BLM affected Black customers’ patronization of Black-owned businesses, demonstrating intra-community asset-building. Therefore, participants revealed BLM as an avenue to bolster economic capital in addition to political capital.

As expected from the accounts of decreased profit and increased costs, participants in the sample demonstrated considerable financial need in 2020. Some business owners in Englewood, explained Participant 4, were not “able to pay the landlord their rent” due to “losing their business” in 2020. Participant 3 explained that what she needed most right now was “financial aid,” and half of the participants reported using out-of-pocket or personal funds to support their businesses in this “time of need.” Additionally, rather than discussing expansion or business strategy, most participants explained that their most important “business goal for 2020” was “to stay open.” This data indicates that positive effects of the BLM movement on patronization of Black-owned businesses did not remedy the financial crises that participants faced in 2020. Ultimately, Englewood’s Black-owned businesses faced immense socioeconomic and emotional hardship throughout the crisis events in 2020.

Discussion Numerous circumstances in 2020 interacted to affect the experiences of Black-identifying business owners in Englewood. In sum, their experiences, hardships, and perspectives are not quantifiable. While the effect of the stay-at-home order was more statistically significant in majority-non-Black neighborhoods, business owners in Englewood reported significant economic dam-

” ages from COVID-19. Statistical analyses suggested that participants’ descriptions of decreased business visitation and the effects of these drops on profit are consistent with the experiences of business owners in other majority-Black neighborhoods in Chicago.

After the murder of George Floyd, foot traffic increased disproportionately in majority-white neighborhoods, reflecting participants’ accounts of low protest activity, at least in part due to political and economic disinvestment in majority-Black neighborhoods like Englewood. At the same time, interviews revealed that looting activity after the murder of George Floyd injured Englewood’s physical storefronts and further inhibited financial security for participants in the sample. Clearly, political protests — and police presence — are more salient in Chicago’s majority-non-Black neighborhoods, while majority-Black neighborhoods like Englewood are deprived of the political infrastructure to manage or prevent looting.

Although some business owners experienced increased patronage from customers in Englewood due to increased awareness of BLM — and one participant noticed that Englewood residents displayed an increased propensity for patronizing his business because it is Black-owned — the movement was an insufficient force for substantially increasing business visitation at Black-owned businesses in Englewood. Customers from majority-white neighborhoods stopped using another participant’s services due to COVID-19 safety concerns. This aligns with some media accounts that support for Black-owned businesses because of the 2020 BLM movement most benefited majority-white, north-side neighborhoods. Future research and media reports should clarify the effects of the BLM movement on patronization by delineating interactions among Black customers, white customers, businesses in majority-white neighborhoods, and businesses in majority-non-white neighborhoods.

The present discussion is limited due to the range of businesses represented in the study. This is especially true in analyses of looting effects; according to participants, liquor stores and corner stores were frequently looted, but they were not included in the sample due to outreach constraints. I interviewed only two business owners among the dozens of looted stores in Englewood. Additionally, a limitation to the quantitative methods is my ability to differentiate between protest foot traffic and business visitation foot traffic due to the inaccuracy of SafeGraph geospatial data. However, the mixed-methods nature of this research remedies some potential limitations in that interview findings on protest activity and business visitation suggest that the quantitative results are accurate.

Fortunately, scholars will likely continue to document the impacts of 2020’s crisis events on small businesses in Chicago. However, the effects of these crises will last for decades to come, especially in minority and low-income communities, as has been observed after recessions in the 20th century and after Civil Rights-Era riots (Collins & Margo, 2007; Williams et al., 2013). While this paper demonstrates that business owners’ experiences amid crises are highly complex, it also forms a foundation on which researchers can examine the potentially enduring damages of 2020 crises in majority-Black and low-income communities in Chicago. Equally as important, the research provides information for future policy- making so that, as Participant 8 expressed, policymakers, NGOs, and private firms can “take action and be held accountable to bring resources to the Englewood community.” ◆

title: KHOA PHAN HOWARD ON PURSUING RESEARCH AND GRADUATE SCHOOL IN THE SOCIAL SCIENCES
notes: Q&A with Khoa Phan Howard, a second-year Ph.D. student in Sociology at Northwestern. The contents gives the title as "Khoa Phan on Pursuing Research and Graduate School in the Social Sciences".
text:
Q & A Q & A Q & A

KHOA PHAN HOWARD ON PURSUING RESEARCH AND

GRADUATE SCHOOL IN THE

SOCIAL SCIENCES by Catherine Campusano and Prerita Pandya

Khoa Phan Howard is a second-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Sociology at Northwestern University. He is also a Gender and Sexuality Studies Mellon Fellow in the Department of Gender and Sexuality Studies and a Fellow in the Center for Legal Studies. His current research focuses on how social institutions can shape the space of intimate relationships.

We were able to sit down with Khoa to gain insight into the experiences of conducting research and securing funding and mentorship in the social sciences at both the undergraduate and graduate levels through his own experiences.

[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

Could you tell us a bit about yourself? I went to college down the street at the University of Chicago, and I graduated in 2019. I majored in English and sociology. My current research interests include looking at intimate relationships. I study institutional structures and how they are shaped, as well as how people make sense of them within and beyond these institutions.

When did you get involved in research as an undergraduate student? My first exposure to research happened during the summer between my first and second years of school. I got a job as a research assistant for a sociology professor. The job was in Vietnam and I’m Vietnamese, so the stars kind of aligned there. That project was a very foundational experience for me in terms of exposing me to the subject of sociology and the day-to-day work of doing research, and it was the starting point for my research path towards sociology.

What was your experience in finding your first research assistantship position? My case was unique and I therefore wouldn’t generalize my case, but overall, I do not think it was very difficult for me to acquire the job. I coincidentally met this professor when I was in Vietnam the summer before. I was interning at a newspaper, and the professor contacted the newspaper to access their resources. I became connected to the professor through the editor-in-chief. Generally, though, you are most likely not going to get the first research job you apply to. However, I think if you are persistent about applying, you can probably get a position to do research somewhere.

Why did you decide to attend graduate school, and what is something you think undergraduate students should know when considering pursuing graduate school? When I went to college, I had no idea about academia or doing a Ph.D. and that specific pathway, so that research assistantship position was my introduction to this whole field. I liked being in the field, interviewing people, observing, and then analyzing that data. I find all these steps of the research process very enjoyable. One of the biggest constraints about graduate school that I feel should be more transparent is that for a good five to seven years of your 20s, you’re not making that much money while your friends … start very lucrative careers. Investment-wise, it’s almost like a sacrifice. I think this is one of the many points of consideration that students should think very carefully about if they are considering going to grad school.

What was your experience like applying for graduate school? One resource I got was from my professors themselves, the ones who I asked for letters of recommendation from. Professors in the department who I had not noticed before gave me recommendations on places to apply to, their reputations, etc. I applied for fewer graduate schools than I think the average sociology applicant would aim for due to geographical constraints with my partner. Something I really had to consider was that I would be spending at least five to seven years in this one place. I think this is another important point of consideration for students if they’re going down the Ph.D. route.

Why did you decide to attend Northwestern University? Northwestern was an overall good fit for me in terms of the topics in which I am interested. Also, the stellar reputation of Northwestern appears to be true, specifically for the Sociology Department; the community is collegial, the support system is good, and the stipend is good, compared to other schools. It ended up being a good choice and a good fit for me.

What was your experience like trying to secure funding for research during graduate school? One thing I have come to realize is that it is much easier to get undergraduate funding than graduate funding. In graduate school, it seems as if everyone is applying for funding. Applying for funding sources inevitably becomes a part of your academic career. The process taught me a lot about how to write a strong research proposal and summarize everything I want to study into a few pages.

What has your experience conducting research as a graduate student been like so far, and what have you learned about graduate-level research in the social sciences from it? I am in my second year and have been mainly doing research more on my own. I think most people in the social sciences conduct research on their own. There are also people who express interest in working in a specific lab and aligning their theses/papers to that lab’s research. Additionally, some people become research assistants for professors, and the process becomes more involved when you are a graduate student. I think a friend of mine is even doing manuscript preparation for one of her professor’s books. It might be specific to sociology or maybe the social sciences in general, but this is how I see research assistantships happening in graduate school.

Do you feel there is a difference in securing research funding, say in comparison to STEM majors? I think in the humanities and social sciences, research is much more individualistic in that you do your own project. On the other hand, as STEM majors, you’re usually working under an existing research lab. From there, the student can pursue a specific line of research within whatever resources are available in the lab.

Are there any other similarities or differences you noted in your experiences with research as an undergraduate compared to as a graduate student? In graduate school, there is often an idea of mentorship. It’s a relationship with two people involved and is based on how you are communicating and asking for mentorship from the mentor. I think as an undergraduate, there is more hand-holding. For example, I could be analyzing a set of quotes, and my adviser would nudge me towards a more pre- cise way to analyze something. In graduate school, the adviser would not really prompt you like that. You figure it out yourself. The advisers may give suggestions, but you are also crafting your own identity and mindset as a scholar.

Do you have any advice for current undergraduate students trying to pursue research in the realm of the social sciences? I think research is, especially in the social sciences, a rewarding process. It is an opportunity to explore and learn something new about the world and understand how the social world works by using the tools that you have learned about in classes. You are creating new knowledge. It is a rewarding process, but it is also a difficult one. There are other dimensions of the experience of graduate school that are not just research: grant-writing, learning how to network and how to navigate reaching out and getting mentorship from other scholars in the field, or going to talks. All of these attributes of graduate school could also be done during your undergraduate education as a precursor for graduate school, and you could potentially start building some skills that can help you in the long run when it comes to succeeding in graduate school. Even if you do not want to go to graduate school, college is a very cool opportunity to learn new things, and so, if it means pursuing a project just to learn something that you are interested in, I definitely suggest going for it. ◆

title: Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement
notes: Senior thesis. The opening page prints the full title as "The Green Dream: Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement" (the main title and subtitle are separate blocks there); the title recorded is the subtitle as given in the contents and contributor page. Faculty adviser named on the opening page. Footnotes are placed after each page's body text. Bibliography entries are split across blocks mid-entry, and their extracted order does not always follow the printed columns.
text:
The Green Dream:

Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement by Keerti Gopal

Department of American Studies Faculty Adviser: Prof. Chloe Thurston, Ph.D.

Introduction

On Nov. 13, 2018, a group called the Sunrise Movement (hereafter referred to as “Sunrise”) made national headlines for taking over Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office, staging a sit-in to demand immediate federal action to address the climate crisis. The sit-in was led by 200 teenagers and young adults wearing matching black and yellow t-shirts and holding signs with slogans like “12 years”1 and “we have a right to good jobs and a livable future.” Singing, chant- ing, and giving speeches, they were soon joined by newly elected Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who would later co-introduce the Green New Deal resolution — a proposed set of guidelines for federal action to combat the climate crisis while tackling economic inequality. The resolution posits that it is the federal government’s duty to “achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions through a fair and just transition for all communities and workers” by investing in infrastructure, creating “millions of good, high-wage jobs” in clean energy industries, and focusing on the communities that will bear the brunt of devastation from climate change: poor, Indigenous, Black and brown communities, young people, and unhoused populations, among others.2

“The green dream or whatever they call it, nobody knows what that is,” said Pelosi in 2019, responding to the resolution’s

1 This number refers to a special report published in 2018 by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) that stated if global warming is worsened by any more than 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2030, the planet will experience climate devastation past the point of repair. 2 Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, “Text - H.Res.109 - 116th Congress (2019–2020): Recognizing the Duty of the Federal Government to Create a Green New Deal.” Congress.gov. February 12, 2019. Accessed March 02, 2021. https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-resolution/109/text.

introduction.3 Pelosi’s words set a tone for establishment backlash labeling the Green New Deal as too radical or unrealistic,4 but over the next two years, the Green New Deal became a fixture in national Democratic politics; it infiltrated local, state, and federal elections and legislation, getting adopted by 16 presidential candidates and appearing in national headlines and debate stages. Meanwhile, Sunrise grew to operate as a key player in the national mobilization around climate justice.5

In this project, I explore Sunrise’s communication strategies and operations,6 focusing on the organization’s tactics around framing from its founding in 2016 through 2020. Through 21 semi-structured interviews with young people currently involved with Sunrise, I explore how the young (defined as under 35) organizers who make up the group conceptualize and disseminate their strategic messaging. Looking at these interviews alongside selected social media outputs and drawing from existing social movement research in the fields of sociology, political science, and media studies, I argue that Sunrise’s strategy of using movement rhetoric and outsider framing to work within the electoral process provides an example of how organizations can bridge the gap between movements and electoral politics to mobilize young people to take civic action. I also argue that the exploration of Sunrise’s framing and social media communication illustrates the possibility that the United States (U.S.) is in the process of an economic and political paradigm shift, characterized by a renewed understanding of who has a stake in the political process.

Bridging the Youth Movement-Electoral Divide In recent years, it has been well documented that young people in the U.S. are less involved in formal politics than older people. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 18–29-year-olds are consistently the least reliable voting bloc in the U.S.,7 and a 2017 study found that trends of low youth participation extended to other political activities like writing to representatives, attending town halls and public legislative meetings, and campaigning or working for political parties.8 A 2000 survey by Heather Bastedo found that young people were less likely than any other age group to express interest in traditional politics, follow political news, or participate as a member in an advocacy organization, but the young people in this study were not apathetic; instead of voting, subjects identified protest and community volunteering

3 Tina Nguyen, “Nancy Pelosi Isn’t Exactly Rushing to Endorse A.O.C.’s ‘Green Dream,’” Vanity Fair, Vanity Fair, 7 Feb. 2019, www.vanityfair.com/news/2019/02/nancy-pelosi-alexandria-ocasio-cortez-new-green-deal. 4 Michael Grunwald et al. “The Trouble With the ‘Green New Deal’.” POLITICO Magazine, 15 Jan. 2019, www.politico.com/magazine/story/2019/01/15/the-trouble-with-the-green-new-deal-223977. 5 Ruairí Arrieta-Kenna, Jeremy B. White, Sam Sutton and Carly Sitrin, and Bill Mahoney and Josh Gerstein, “The Sunrise Movement Actually Changed the Democratic Conversation. So What Do You Do For a Sequel?” POLITICO Magazine, June 16, 2019. Accessed November 11, 2020. https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2019/06/16/sunrise-movement-boot-camp-227109. 6 Sunrise Movement is an organization that engages in a wide range of tactics, including significant in-person direct actions like protests, rallies, sit-ins, marches, birddogging, and more. These actions are relevant to this project and some will be touched upon, but the focus of this project is on communications strategy, and will not cover the organization’s strategy around direct actions in great depth. 7 U.S. Census Bureau, “Behind the 2018 U.S. Midterm Election Turnout,” The United States Census Bureau, 16 July 2019, www. census.gov/library/stories/2019/04/behind-2018-united-states-midterm-election-turnout.html. 8 Heather Bastedo, “Not ‘One of Us’: Understanding How Non-Engaged Youth Feel about Politics and Political Leadership,” Journal of Youth Studies, vol. 18, no. 5, 2014, pp. 649–665., doi:10.1080/13676261.2014.992309, p. 656.

as their preferred methods of social and political engagement.9 These findings are in line with the consensus among social movement scholars that young people have been critical to the operational success of U.S. social movements over the past half-century, even while exhibiting low levels of interaction in formalized politics.10 In other words, there has been a youth participation gap: young people are heavily involved in social movements while exhibiting less consistent involvement in more traditional electoral politics.

The 2020 elections, however, saw a significant increase in youth electoral engagement and participation, following a trend of increased politicization in the nation as a whole. In fact, the 2020 presidential election garnered the highest voter turnout in over a century at 66.3%, followed closely only by the

1908 election of William Howard Taft with 65.7%.11 Youth engagement, in particular, rose as well, estimated to be as much as 55% according to Tuft’s CIRCLE institute, compared to the previous high of 50% in 2008.12 This rise in overall electoral engagement seems to suggest a broader shift in public behavior, but given the history of young people’s disinterest particularly in formalized politics, the proliferation of youth electoral organizing is especially notable.

Anjali Mitra, an 18-year-old and one of Sunrise’s middle/high school organizing leads, described this rise in youth electoral organizing by referencing the passion and energy she’s seen from her peers, namely middle and high schoolers throughout the country working with Sunrise and other groups to lead phone banks, canvasses, and endorsement processes for local candidates, despite many of them being too young to vote themselves. Mitra said:

Middle and high schoolers, even though they can’t vote, understand that this moment in history is still a moment that people need to step up because policies that they can’t vote on will still affect them. And honestly, because of that, they have more of a moral authority,13 if you will, to speak out to fight for what they believe in because if the people in power won’t do it for them and the people who vote won’t do it for them, who will?14

Mitra went on to note that involvement from young people who cannot vote in

9 Bastedo, “Not ‘One of Us.’” 10 Jennifer Earl, Thomas V. Maher, and Thomas Elliott, “Youth, Activism, and Social Movements,” Sociology Compass 11, no. 4 (2017): |PAGE|, doi:10.1111/soc4.12465. 11 Kevin Schaul, Kate Rabinowitz, “2020 Turnout Is the Highest in over a Century,” The Washington Post, December 08, 2020, accessed February 21, 2021. https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/elections/voter-turnout/. 12 Circle at Tufts, November 25, 2020, accessed February 21, 2021. https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/election-week-2020. 13 The concept of “moral authority” that Mitra cites here is a central tenet of Sunrise messaging. Although there are different definitions of the term, Sunrise generally uses “moral authority” to make an argument that young people are of particular importance to conversations on climate change and labor rights, as the younger generations will be both most impacted by the crisis and are arguably least to blame, having not been alive for the rise of fossil fuel industry and not in power during decades of climate denial and inaction. 14 Anjali Mitra (Sunrise Movement), in discussion with the author, December 2020.

Sunrise demands that those in political power listen to young people, or step aside. “ ” direct actions (protests, rallies, etc.) and other efforts that utilize movement tactics for electoral aims signals what she believes is a necessary re-evaluation of what it means to be an engaged citizen:

That kind of belief in the power of people power and direct action to get things done on the political level is something that a lot of adults don’t always remember. I think a lot of adults are like, “Oh, I voted, my job is done.” And that is not true. That is the bare minimum, maybe not even. And middle and high schoolers are showing that direct action and showing up for what you believe in is more powerful than just dropping your ballot in a box.15

Mitra’s testimony invokes an expanding definition of civic engagement that em- bodies the blurring of the line between movement and electoral involvement by cementing a narrative of elections being part of a larger process that includes movement activities like protest and direct action. Her words situate Sunrise as a prime example16 of an organization that bridges the youth participation gap.

Sunrise’s theory of change calls for both “people power” (an active base of public support) and “political power” (enthusiastic involvement from public officials) as essential components of winning progress,17 demonstrating a narrative framing that brings outsider energy — the energy of a social movement — into formalized politics and questioning existing ideas of who has power in political processes and what political participation can look like. By combining movement rhetoric with political aims, Sunrise asserts that although politicians do not often seem to have the best interests of the youth (roughly defined as Gen Z and younger millennials) in mind, they should. Sunrise demands that those in political power listen to young people, or step aside.

Framing in the Sunrise Movement For Sunrise and other organizations like it, a crucial aspect of building both people power and political power is telling a convincing story, or in other words, political framing. In the social movement scholarship in the fields of sociology, political science, and communication and media studies, a frame is a way of looking at information.18 Framing describes the way that movement actors, like organizations or leaders, attempt to publicly explain the problems they are working to solve and the solutions that they propose. There is a prevalent idea in social psychology that people live in a perceived world, meaning that they respond to external events based on their built perceptions of what is happening around them. This suggests that, for social movements, framing has potential for real-world impact; if people’s perceptions shape their responses, then influencing those perceptions is a task with great potential power.19

Benford and Snow’s seminal 1988 sociological scholarship on social movement framing provides a blueprint for social movement organizations (SMOs) looking to develop effective framing. The authors write that frames for collective actions are “intended to mobilize potential adherents

15 Mitra. 16 Other examples of organizations that focused on youth voter outreach include, on the left, March for Our Lives, Dream Defend- ers, Youth Democratic Socialists of America, and Next Gen America, and on the right, Turning Point USA and Young Americans for Freedom. 17 Sunrise Movement, “Sunrise 101: Our Culture,” 2019. 18 Ibid., 118. 19 Jacquelien Van Stekelenburg and Bert Klandermans, “The Social Psychology of Protest.” Current Sociology 61, no. 5–6 (2013): 886–905. doi:10.1177/0011392113479314.

and constituents, to garner bystander support, and to demobilize antagonists.”20 In other words, when SMOs strategize around framing, they are looking to inspire participation amongst people who are aligned with their cause, convert neutrals into supporters, and disempower those who disagree with their cause from action. According to Benford and Snow, there are three main stages for this kind of frame: diagnostic framing, or the identification and description of a problem; prognostic framing, or the proposal of a solution; and motivational framing, or the rationale for action.21

Sunrise’s framing falls clearly into Benford and Snow’s three stages. First, they diagnose the problem: the climate crisis is here, and we have (now) less than 10 years before our habitat is damaged beyond repair, but the fossil fuel execu- tives and corrupt politicians who brought about this crisis continue to enact their decades-long strategy of blocking action in protection of their profits. Meanwhile, the dominance of neoliberalism over the past several decades has cemented economic and racial hierarchies that ensure that poor communities of color are most immediately in danger of the devastating impacts of climate change.22

Next, the prognosis: we need the federal government to lead a complete transition away from fossil fuels, invest in green housing and infrastructure, concentrate aid to frontline communities, and enact a jobs guarantee to ensure good union jobs for any American in need during this transition. These changes need to be enacted immediately and comprehensively, and the cost of these investments is nothing compared to the devastating economic and societal dangers of allowing the climate crisis to continue unchecked.23

In order to achieve such a comprehensive transformation in society, we need to change the cultural understanding of what is politically possible and what needs to be accomplished in order to combat climate change. This calls for a paradigm shift — one that will prioritize people over profits and advocate for dignity, justice, equality, and the common good. Achieving such a shift will require a combination of people power (in the streets) and political power (in government).24 This is where Sunrise’s motivational framing comes in: young people must join the movement and take action because time is running out, and there is no path to winning a Green

20 Robert D. Benford and David A. Snow, “Framing Processes and Social Movements: An Overview and Assessment,” Annual Review of Sociology 26, no. 1 (2000): p. 614, doi:10.1146/annurev.soc.26.1.611. 21 Benford and Snow, p. 615–617. 22 Sunrise Movement. “Sunrise 101: Our Culture.” 2019. 23 Ibid. 24 Ibid.

“Middle and high schoolers are showing that direct action ... is more powerful than just dropping your ballot in a box.”

New Deal without building credible power through mass mobilization, both in the streets and at the phone banks and polls.

Digital Dimensions: Disseminating the Frame Sunrise’s use of contemporary social media platforms — particularly Instagram, Twitter, and sometimes TikTok — has been essential in the organization’s dissemination of its messaging, exemplifying how digital tools create a more decentralized and participatory information society. This paves a way for new voices to be included in political idea generation and illustrates how the bounds of what constitutes a political stakeholder are being expanded.

At the time of this writing, Sunrise uses Twitter and Instagram, along with (to a lesser degree) TikTok and (even more decreasingly) Facebook, to disseminate its framing and communicate with the public.25 Sunrise also engages with more traditional media sources — members li- aise with the press and place op-eds and letters-to-the-editor in mainstream news sources — but a significant portion of the organization’s recruitment and communication efforts occur over social media platforms. “I think a lot of Sunrise’s success has been in … changing dominant cultural narratives around climate justice topics,” Sunrise’s Oregon-based video network lead Allyson Woodward said, discussing the way that the Green New Deal rhetoric has infiltrated mainstream media and politics. “I do think that we could not have done it without digital organizing,” she added, suggesting that social media was a key element of the organization’s strategy.

She went on to explain that the digital dimension of Sunrise’s strategy is about gaining narrative power:

How do we destroy the climate versus jobs narrative, and how do we get our own to be dominant, which is this idea of tying good jobs to climate action? We do that through effective organizing … but it can’t happen unless we are pulling organizing into smart digital campaigns that further our narrative.

Woodward went on to argue that in the current information landscape, social media platforms like Instagram and Twitter are essential to ensuring that people see an SMO’s organizing. “Digital comm[unica- tions] are the tools to gain cultural power,” she summarized.26 And this cultural power can manifest through the infiltration of mainstream narratives and rhetoric in both media and legislative spheres.

Digital Framing in Action: #YoungAndNaive Sunrise’s strategic use of digital communications as a tool for building power and infiltrating mainstream media discourse was emblemized when videos27 of Pennsylvania gubernatorial candidate Scott Wagner (who lost to Democrat Tom Wolf) calling Sunrise activist Rose Strauss “young and naive” went viral. Sunrise used Twitter in conjunction with traditional media outlets to cap- italize on the moment — which could otherwise have been seen as a blow to the movement’s credibility — and start a conversation about the moral authority of young people, claiming that the younger generation has a unique perspective on

25 Sunrise uses a range of digital communications including email newsletters and text banking campaigns, but for the sake of clarity and focus this project will only discuss their use of social media. 26 Allyson Woodward (Sunrise Movement), in discussion with the author, December 2020. 27 Scott Wagner Callously Dismisses Voter As “Young And Naive” For Caring About Climate Change. July 19, 2018. Accessed February 27, 2021. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tC4VRRiEKO0.

the future and challenging the prevailing notion that young people should be kept out of political ideation due to a lack of knowledge or experience.28

The story began when, during a Q&A at a campaign event, Sunrise member Rose Strauss stood to ask Wagner a question.

“My name is Rose,” she began. “I’m 18, and I’m really concerned about the future of our country. Two-thirds of Pennsylva- nians think that climate change is an issue that needs to be addressed, but you’ve said that climate change is a result of people’s body heat and are refusing to take action on the issue. Does this have anything to do with the $200,000 that you have taken from the fossil fuel industry?”

Wagner paused for less than a full second before responding.

“Rose, I appreciate you being here,” he said. “And you’re 18 years old. You know, you’re a little young and naive. Let’s talk about something else.” Wagner turned away from Strauss and looked at the rest of the people at the event, many of whom were clapping and cheering, before continuing, “Are we here to elect a governor, or are we here to elect a scientist?” Multiple videos of the exchange began to circulate online — mostly on Twitter and YouTube — starting some buzz about the candidate’s attitude.29

This was an opportunity for Sunrise to take hold of the narrative, and the organization did just that. Sunrise took to Twitter, starting the hashtag “#youngandnaive” in order to weaponize Wagner’s words against him and elevate its own platform.

As the hashtag began gaining attention, Sunrise turned to traditional media. In an op-ed for Teen Vogue, Rose Strauss described the exchange as “one of the most embarrassing and frustrating moments of [her] life,” saying she felt “belittled” and “insignificant.”30 She then went on to reclaim and repurpose the candidate’s words. “If being ‘young and naive’ means I expect my politicians to reject contributions from the fossil fuel CEOs and lobbyists most responsible for burning our planet, then call me young and naive,” she wrote, addressing her response to Wagner and “all politicians like him.”31 By turning Wagner’s words against him, Strauss questioned the notion that her youth was a weakness and instead painted Wagner to be a symbol of the establishment — old and out of touch.

By reframing the narrative around Wagner’s words, Sunrise pushed back at the idea that an 18-year-old should keep her nose out of politics and instead asserted that being “young and naive” was a designation of moral authority: to be young and naive was to be uncorrupted by money and the fossil fuel industry, to be clear-eyed and strong. This narrative resonated in both traditional and participatory information spaces; the exchange was covered by local and national publications including the Philly Voice, The Guardian, and The New York Times, and the hashtag was used by organizations and public figures like NextGen America, 350 Action, Now This, and Al Gore. Democratic lieutenant governor candidate John Fetterman even adopted Wagner’s words

28 Rose Strauss, “A Candidate for Pennsylvania Governor Called Me ‘Young and Naive’.” Teen Vogue. July 25, 2018. Accessed March 02, 2021. https://www.teenvogue.com/story/pennsylvania-gubernatorial-candidate-scott-wagner-called-me-young-naive. 29 Dan Levin, “A Politician Called Her ‘Young and Naïve.’ Now She’s Striking Back.,” The New York Times, July 25, 2018, accessed April 30, 2021, https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/25/us/young-and-naive-rose-strauss.html. 30 Rose Strauss, “A Candidate for Pennsylvania Governor Called Me ‘Young and Naive’,” Teen Vogue, July 25, 2018. Accessed March 04, 2021, https://www.teenvogue.com/story/pennsylvania-gubernatorial-candidate-scott-wagner-called-me-young-naive. 31 Ibid.

for a campaign t-shirt.32 The spreading of the video — and the enthusiasm about Strauss and Sunrise’s response — suggests that Sunrise’s framing strategy was effective at infiltrating public consciousness.

In this instance, social media allowed Sunrise to send a clear message. A 2018 New York Times article featuring an interview with Strauss introduced the exchange by noting that “it quickly went viral on social media,” using this as a justification for its newsworthiness. Here, successful framing on Twitter (a participatory platform) gave Sunrise clout in the traditional media realm, providing them with access to a massive platform like The New York Times. And there, in turn, Strauss — representing Sunrise — was able to use that platform to publicize the movement, urging young people like her to “join a movement, not an isolated or singular thing. March- ing, demonstrating is great, but we need sustained action to really turn the tide.”33

That Sunrise was able to begin spreading this story on Twitter, get noticed by press, public figures, and political actors, and then successfully transition to traditional media sources, shows how participatory media platforms can influence political discourse by giving voices that might ordinarily be discounted — like Strauss’ — the opportunity for greater reach. On Twitter, politicians, activists, and unofficial actors are using the same platform; participatory social media disrupts the previously entrenched dynamics of who has access to spheres of political idea-generation and persuasive messaging.

Participatory technologies also influence the ease with which the public consumes movement messaging. Although viral activism, sometimes known as “slacktivism” and defined as showing support for a social cause on social media alone, is often criticized for being low effort and lacking substance,34 Sunrise’s strategy exemplifies a different dimension of digital organizing. For Sunrise, the battle does not end with the virality of #youngandnaive, it begins there: social media is a vehicle for framing, which seeks to reach young people in order to politicize and, subsequently, mobilize.

The Impact of Sunrise’s Reframing: A People’s Politics Video network lead Allyson Woodward noted that in her mind, the proliferation of the Green New Deal into mainstream Democratic politics indicates a significant shift in political ideology and a transition around where political power is held:

Sunrise, in two years, has smashed the climate versus jobs narrative among Democrats. We’re still working on it for culture as a whole, but when Joe Biden gets up on stage to accept the presidential nomination and he’s like, “we’re going to create millions of good jobs — clean union jobs — while addressing climate change,” he’s basically parroting a Sunrise talking point. And so, we didn’t get the candidate we wanted, right, we got Joe Biden.35 But our cultural narratives have gained so much power in our society that he can’t ignore them because they are that powerful. Politics is a game of power, not of persuasion.

32 John L. Micek | Jmicek@pennlive.com, “‘Young and Naive’: GOP Governor Candidate Wagner’s Viral Video Moment Is a T-shirt,” Pennlive, July 24, 2018, accessed March 04, 2021, https://www.pennlive.com/capitol-notebook/2018/07/young_and_na- ive_thatd_look_gre.html. 33 Levin, 2018. 34 Nojin Kwak et al., “Perceptions of Social Media for Politics: Testing the Slacktivism Hypothesis,” Human Communication Research 44, no. 2 (2018): doi:10.1093/hcr/hqx008. 35 Sunrise endorsed Sen. Bernie Sanders in the Democratic Primary and did not endorse any candidate in the general, although the organization did do significant phone banking and voter outreach for Biden’s campaign.

And our narrative gained so much power that Joe Biden has to parrot it, even in his most important speeches, because he knows he can’t ignore it.36

What Woodward describes here is a victory of framing. The Green New Deal rhetoric went from being derided by mainstream Democrats as a “dream” to being invoked by the party’s presidential nominee himself. In fact, on Earth Day 2020, Speaker Pelosi — who, as previously mentioned, once publicly derided the Green New Deal as “the green dream or whatever” — tweeted from the @TeamPelosi handle, “Together, we will create millions of good-paying green jobs as we #BuildBackBetter and modernize our infrastructure.”37 This phrasing of “creat[ing] millions of good-paying green jobs” is almost exactly the same as the words in Sunrise’s mission statement38 and clearly emulates the Green New Deal resolution’s framework.39 The fact that Pelosi, who previously saw the Green New Deal as a pipe dream, now sees its rhetoric as politically viable enough to warrant its use suggests that the narrative paradigm shift that Sunrise seeks — changing the landscape of formal politics to be a more participatory movement space — is indeed in motion.

Sunrise is just one example of how this potential paradigm shift is manifesting in robust social movement engagement and translating to electoral spheres. This shift is further evidenced in the recent influx of progressive politicians who cut their political teeth organizing with movements outside the system, not amongst the establishment. One example is Rep. Ocasio-Cortez, who in the past three years has rocketed to political superstardom and got her start through movement participation in the #NoDAPL movement at Standing Rock. Another example is Cori Bush, the Missouri congresswoman who ran her campaign on her experience as a Black Lives Matter organizer in Ferguson after the murder of Michael Brown.

The resurgence of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020 after the murders of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and many others sparked what was estimated to be the largest protests in U.S. history, with 15–26 million demonstrators in June alone,40 and it continues to fuel significant shifts in public opinion and a deepening and widening public understanding of the realities of racism and police violence.41 During the COVID-19 pandemic, we

“

”

As more people enter into political processes ... the realm of possibility expands until everyone sees themselves in their representatives, organizers, and changemakers.

have seen expansions in mutual-aid and union-related activism across the country.42 Young people have stepped up in monumental ways to speak out against gun violence, organizers have called nationally for an overhaul of the immigration system, and activist calls for reparations for Black Americans have begun to turn into real legislative progress.43 And youth climate activism, globally, is on the rise.44

Sunrise is part of this moment where shifting conceptions of what is politically possible abound. Its framing strategies and digital practices, along with its outsider infiltration of formalized electoral politics, provide an example of how progressive organizations can (and are) bridging the gap between youth movement energy and electoral action, while also illustrating the prevalence of shifting paradigms for economic and political thought and suggesting that maybe it is time for the establishment of a new common sense. For young people, Sunrise provides a blueprint for building political power and taking control of their country’s narrative. Reflecting on the way her involvement with Sunrise has impacted her personally, Woodward summed it up.

“Before Sunrise, I felt like I was screaming into the void and that I didn’t really have any impact or effect on larger world events or the political process, and I didn’t even see a pathway into how to get that,” she said. “I feel now that I understand how to shape [the] larger public understanding of issues, and that I can’t do it alone, but I also am connected with other people, and as a collective, we can, like, to- tally shift the dominant cultural narratives if we choose to.”45

Perhaps this is the true impact of framing: it provides people who have been left out of the political process and have had no faith in their ability to impact politics or their government’s interest in working for them with a new understanding of their own power and a new motivation to fight. As more people enter into political processes, staking their claim on the establishment, the realm of possibility expands until everyone sees themselves in their representatives, organizers, and changemakers. Ultimately, the paradigm shift becomes this: the realization of true democracy, where the power lies with the people. ◆
