title: Discussing the Politics of Climate Change with NU-Q Student Researcher Natasha Das
notes: Profile of NU-Q undergraduate Natasha Das and her senior thesis, The Politics of Climate Change, with quotations from the thesis set as margin notes (the arrow blocks).
text:
Discussing the Politics of

Climate Change with NU-Q Student Researcher

Natasha Das by Rachel Chiu and Grace Lee

Having grown up in New Delhi, India, Natasha Das — an undergraduate student and researcher at Northwestern University in Qatar (NU-Q) — has always had a particular interest in environmental research. She recalls her personal experience with air pollution in New Delhi: “The smog in New Delhi is so thick that when you get off the airplane and you walk into the airport, … your eyes will burn from the pungent smoke.” Given the severity of pollution in her city, Natasha notes that her school experience was marked by numerous projects designed to teach students about environmental sustainability. In high school, however, Natasha began to realize that “there was this huge disconnect between all the science and what we’re being taught versus how much people actually ended up doing.”

Combining this observation with her passion for communications studies, Natasha began delving into the connection between human behavior and climate change. At NU-Q, she began to get involved in researching the politics of climate change, the topic on which her senior thesis focuses. We were able to sit down with Natasha to learn about her research and gain more insight into her thoughts regarding climate change and environmental policies. We feature key points from her thesis, The Politics of Climate Change (as seen by the quotations an- notated in the margins throughout this piece), along with parts of our conversation to bring together her thoughts regarding human action, or the lack thereof, in environmental sustainability.

“ ”

[F]or decades, there has existed a dichotomy between scientific consensus and human action.

In her thesis, Natasha discusses the necessity of increasing climate ambition. When asked about what this specifically entails, she brings in her experience working in public relations to expand upon the idea:

Companies will say something to seem like they’re very environmentally friendly — say, ‘we’ve done x, y, z initiatives.’ And I’ll be able to sell it to you that this company is doing so much for the environment. … But the truth is: I’m making you believe that because we’re persuasive enough. This is what we’ve been trained to do. The question you should be asking is: Why has this company only done x, y, and z, and why isn’t it more?

With this, Natasha calls for action on all different levels — from the government all the way to the local level. She believes in the power of collective action, envisioning a collaboration in which individuals, neighborhoods, and schools can work with small and big businesses to eventually reach higher levels of policy change. She explains:

It’s really difficult for those policies on top to change very quickly at the level that we need it to, so I think our best hope right now is with local communities. … [W]e can set really high goals for ourselves [and] then for … our neighborhood to meet certain goals, and I think that’s really achievable as well.

Natasha’s vision for bottom-up, collective action may seem idyllic to some, as it is often the case that people are rather apathetic to environmental issues. She acknowledges, “Unless you live in a place like New Delhi, where there’s just smog hitting you all the time, environmental issues are not necessarily straight up in your face for you to care about it every day — like in Doha, [the capital of Qatar,] there’s so many times when I just forget.”

In her thesis, Natasha addresses some key factors that contribute to the “underwhelming amount of action” in response to climate change. Lack of belief in the science behind climate change, pre-existing cultural influences that skew scientific rea- soning, and the prioritization of capitalistic success over environmental sustainability are all factors that

“To stand a fighting chance against climate change, we need to ‘significantly increase our climate ambition’ and contribute towards this problem more substantially (Cantellano, 2020).”

←

“[T]o get organizations to act in an environmentally friendly manner, there needs to be a bigger role taken by governments or by local communities taking initiative to be climate friendly.”

←

“Climate change’s very nature makes it difficult for people to be concerned because it is invisible, seems distant, and its effects are not palpable enough to cause action.”

← contextualize human inaction against climate change. Natasha stresses that these factors, along with the seemingly intangible nature of climate change, make it difficult for people to feel immediately concerned.

Despite the multitude of factors that discourage concrete action, Natasha believes that there is a way to get people to be more invested and involved in the very real issue of climate change. This belief stems from a personal anecdote from her high school days in Doha. She shares, “I remember I was just so frus- trated. … The focus in all these clubs [in my school] would be to raise money for the cause, [but] we don’t really know where all the money is going and exactly how it works.” Natasha began to wonder what would happen if the problem became more personal for the students: “I just thought, … What if we just focused on our own community and made it better?”

With this thought, Natasha began initiating programs at her school that focused more on local sustainability and community-based changes, and the effects were immediate. “People immediately got more engaged,” she reflects, “and within two years, the school became drastically more sustainable because people felt like they could relate to what was going on, and suddenly, environmental issues seemed more than just these theories that were floating in the air.”

Having seen firsthand the impact of creating a more personal, common goal for people to work towards, Natasha stresses the importance of inspiring community-based action. “Human relations are something that’s important to all of us, regardless of where we’re from,” Natasha states. She expands upon this by saying that given the value that people tend to place on human relationships and how they are perceived by others, phenomena like the collective action theory and the free-rider problem are “not very applicable to local communities, where people know each other and relationships are stronger.” Cooperation and willing- ness to take action become stronger once the stakes become more personal: “So if we could somehow tap into that [aspect of human behavior] to create goals and policies, … I think that could be a good solution.”

“Environmental action requires collective action, which occurs when individuals successfully cooperate in pursuit of one common goal despite their diverging self-interests.”

�

“People are more likely to engage in a local collective action program because it helps them feel [like] a part of the community and triggers emotions such as benevolence and conformity. … Within the community, people want to be seen in a positive light and there is a reputation to be gained on a smaller scale.”

�

We ended our conversation with Natasha by asking her if there is one thing she would change, if given the power, about the discourse regarding climate change. Natasha answers, “The thing that I would fix is the way that we’re talking about the problem.” Especially as a communications major, Natasha is greatly interested in the way in which the problem is framed:

From what I’ve seen in most environmentally themed movies or communication pieces, they try to make it sound like if you don’t do something, then the world is going to end. And usually, they’re not very clear on what that thing is, and the focus is more on the ‘world end’ thing. That kind of fear freezes people and makes them unable to do something.

Instead of framing climate change as a ‘doomsday-es- que’ phenomenon and instilling fear in people’s minds, Natasha believes in inspiring a collective approach towards a positive reward. “I think the focus has to be more on we should all do x, y, and z, and then something good will happen,” she explains. Inspired by “the hope and all the positive literature that’s out there about local communities doing something [together],” she envisions a future in which a collection of small efforts eventually leads to macro-level, systemic change. She concludes, “I don’t know how quickly it can happen, but I’m hopeful that [it will].” ◆

title: The Impact of Climate Change on Energy Poverty: Evidence from the European Union, 2004–2019
notes: Senior thesis with abstract. Faculty advisers named on the opening page. Tables 1-6 in the appendix are extracted cell by cell (the bottom rows of Table 1 come first in the text layer). Equation (2) and the paragraph after it (50.6, 50.7, 51.1), whose symbols are garbled in the text layer, are read from the page image.
text:
The Impact of Climate Change on Energy Poverty:

Evidence from the European Union, 2004–2019 by Ginny Ip

Department of Economics Faculty Advisers: Prof. Mar Reguant, Ph.D.

& Prof. Jeffrey Lewis, Ph.D.

Abstract Energy poverty can be understood as the inability or difficulty of a household to meet their basic energy needs. While the condition is already widespread across Europe, it will likely worsen in the near future, as average temperatures increase due to climate change and there becomes a greater need for heating and/or cooling. The present study addresses the gap in research in this area by using Eurostat data on energy poverty and changes in heating degree-days (HDD) and cooling degree-days (CDD) across the 28 European Union (EU) Member States from 2004–2019. These metrics are then used to create a composite indicator of energy poverty based on a household’s inability to keep warm, pay utility bills on time, and the presence of damp, leakage, or rot in the home. The results indicate that an increase in the number of days in which air conditioning is needed to be comfortable significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of temporal and macroeconomic trends shows that energy poverty is severely unevenly distributed across the Member States and that both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities. Thus, policy implications include increasing general awareness of the phenomenon and implementing country-specific policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate, especially in Southern and Eastern European EU countries.

I. Introduction and Background Awareness of energy poverty has been rapidly growing in recent years and is increasingly being recognized as a critical social policy issue. Importantly, energy poverty not only affects those living in the poorest countries without any access to power but also those in some of the wealthiest countries in the world. While the term “energy poverty” does not have a universal definition, it is generally understood as a distinct form of poverty associated with households who have a hard time meeting their basic energy needs or spend a very high proportion of their income to do so. For example, the United Kingdom officially declares a household energy-poor if it “needs to spend more than 10 per cent of its income on fuel to maintain a satisfactory heating regime” (DTI, 2007). However, this definition of energy poverty may be overly simplistic, as the causes of energy poverty are often multidimensional, stemming from a combination of low household incomes, high energy expenditures, and energy inefficient buildings and appliances (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2016).

As a result, energy poverty is not only a development issue but also involves public health, environmental, and national security issues, as its prevalence is often associated with adverse consequences ranging from respiratory and cardiac illnesses, exacerbated mental health problems, increased air pollution, and higher levels of social unrest and instability (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2016; Yumkella & Bazilian, 2015). Additionally, energy poverty often coincides with food poverty, as energy-poor, income-constrained households are forced to choose between prioritizing their energy needs or food needs (Omic, 2019). Thus, addressing energy poverty has the potential to bring many benefits, including healthier citizens, a healthier environment, improved social security, and higher levels of economic productivity overall.

Energy Poverty & Climate Change Recent decades have seen increasing average temperatures and extreme temperature days due to the onset of climate change. For instance, a group of climate scientists found that each of six European heat waves since 2010 was significantly more likely and intense because of climate change (Schiermeier, 2019). This may elicit an increase in household energy demand, particularly for cooling purposes, causing a positive feedback loop that further perpetuates climate change and puts a strain on existing energy services (Jessel et al., 2019). However, most of the current literature on household energy to date have not sufficiently considered climate change and its impact on vulnerable populations (Jessel et al., 2019).

Moreover, subsequent global efforts to undertake an energy transition, which involves moving away from conventional sources of energy such as oil and gas and “towards a more sustainable energy system characterised by universal access to energy services … and security and reliability of supply from efficient, low-carbon sources,” are also having a significant impact on household energy bills (Bridge et al., 2013). McGee and Greiner (2019) have found that attempts to address climate change through subsidies and other in- centives for carbon mitigation, including transitioning away from fossil fuels, have disproportionately increased the percentage of household income spent on energy by marginalized groups. Bouzarovski & Herrero (2017) would agree, arguing that European energy transitions in particular have deepened existing regional inequalities and energy poverty.

Acknowledging this gap, the present study uses panel data to examine how changing average temperatures as a result of global climate change have impacted energy poverty levels in European Union (EU) Member States over the last few decades. The principal finding is that an increase in the number of CDD significantly increases the share of energy-poor households, but there is no significant association with HDD. Moreover, energy poverty is indeed very unevenly distributed across the Member States, and both climate change and the ongoing energy transition will likely exacerbate these inequalities.

Energy Poverty in the EU I focused on the EU for three reasons. First, an estimated 30 million people were living in energy poverty as of 2019, with the highest rates in Southern and Central-Eastern European countries (Omic, 2019). Many countries are still suffering the repercussions of the economic crisis of 2008/9, with high unemployment and inequality rates having serious consequences on the living conditions of EU citizens (Kyprianou et al., 2019). Second, there is a high degree of geographic, social, and economic variation across the Member States, which means that climate change will likely have very different effects on energy poverty levels across the EU. Bouzarovski and Herrero (2017) note that the “classic economic development distinction between the core and periphery also holds true in the case of energy poverty,” where the Southern and Eastern European countries are simultaneously milder in climate and poorer compared to the frigid but wealthy Northern countries. At the same time, the EU Member States share both a common currency and an interconnected power grid, which makes it easier to compare and control for trends in energy costs and prices. This unique combination is particularly useful in understanding the macro-scale spatial patterns of energy poverty and how they relate to wider economic and geographic disparities within the EU, an area that is also currently under-researched (Petrakos et al., 2011). Finally, the Eurostat provides a rich body of publicly available, highly reliable data on energy poverty that is currently un- matched in other regions of the world.

II. Data & Descriptive Statistics The main data source was the EU Energy Poverty Observatory (EPOV), launched in 2018 by the European Commission with the goal of better monitoring and addressing energy poverty across member countries (EU Energy Poverty Observatory, 2019). It recognizes the multidimensional nature of energy poverty and thus includes a portfolio of indicators that I used collectively. Specifically, I combined three primary indicators to create an Energy Poverty Index using the following formula:

(1) EP = 0.4 · % W + 0.4 · % A + 0.2 · % HP

EP – Energy Poverty

W – Warm A – Arrears H – Housing Problems

The variables warm, arrears, and housing problems measure the population percentages of people who reported (1) not being able to keep their homes adequately warm, (2) having trouble paying their utility bills on time, and (3) the presence of damp, rot, or a leaking roof in the home, respectively.1 This approach is based on Bouzarovski & Herrero’s (2017) energy poverty index and previously developed efforts to capture the multidimensional nature of energy poverty. However, while Bouzarovski & Herrero’s index gives warm a weight of 0.5 and gives arrears and housing problems a weight of 0.25 each, I gave the same weight to warm and arrears and gave housing problems a lower weight. This was because the latter is not necessarily a direct indicator of energy poverty, while the former two are. For instance, a household might have a leaking roof but have no problem meeting its energy needs. Likewise, a household might have a perfectly functioning home but can barely afford to pay the heating bills in the winter. Additionally, I did not weigh warm higher than arrears because the former does not take into account the inability of households to keep cool in the summer, which is highly relevant in the context of a predominantly warming climate, while the latter keeps track of late payment in energy bills pertaining to both heating and cooling.

Other secondary indicators that were included as controls are household electricity prices and household gas prices, both of which include taxes and levies and are measured in cents per kilowatt hour (ct/kWh); the percentage of the population living in an area with intermediate urbanisation; the percentage of the population who are paying tenure market rent; and the percentage of the population with access to air conditioning and heating in the home, respectively.

The other main dataset that tracks historical temperature patterns was supplied by the Eurostat (the Statistical Office of the

European Union). The annual data series covers the Member States of the EU and the EU aggregated from 1975 to 2019, except Cyprus, which only has data from 1978 to 2019. The two variables of interest were Heating Degree Days (HDD) and Cooling Degree Days (CDD). HDD measures the difference between the daily mean outdoor temperature (Ti) and 15°C, below which a building is assumed to need heating; CDD measures the difference between Ti and 24°C, above which a building is assumed to need cooling. Both estimates are based on daily observations from approximately 3,000 weather stations across Europe, which are then added up to make yearly °C temperature sums (Eurostat, 2019).

To control for differences in macroeconomic conditions across the EU countries, two additional datasets from the World Bank and World Inequality Data- base were included.

The former dataset includes information on national GDP per capita (in thousands of U.S. dollars) and the unemployment rate from 1960 to 2019, while the latter captures income inequality by measuring the bottom 50% share of total national income from 2004–2019.

A few weaknesses in the data sources need to be acknowledged. First, while most studies have used household-level microdata in their analysis of energy poverty, I used individual Member States as the unit of analysis, which means that the maximum yearly sample size is 28.2 Nevertheless, this approach is in line with the objective of the analysis to uncover patterns across Member States as a whole. I also supplemented my macroanalysis with a case study on Spanish

Second, the EPOV energy poverty indicators are based on the consensual-based European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) survey microdata that rely on households’ self-reported assessments, which has received some criticism in the literature (Thomson et al., 2020). However, it is difficult to think of other ways to go about gathering the more qualitative data, such as a household’s inability to keep warm, that are not completely exempt of methodological problems either. Further, the EPOV has included a methodology guidebook on their website which details the measures they took to ensure full compliance with Eurostat rules (Thomson et al., 2020). Finally, since the main EPOV energy poverty indicators only cover the period from 2004–2019, the regression analysis was limited to this time period, even though there is temperature and macro data dating back to the 1970s. Data for the percentage of the population with access to heating and cooling were only available for the year 2007, which means that these two variables are time-invariant. For this reason, they were omitted from the regression models where fixed-effects were added.3

Table 1 presents summary statistics for the main variables used in the analysis. The table shows that the mean percentage of arrears, warm, and housing problems are 10.82%, 12.27%, and 16.89%, respectively (see Appendix). Those variables taken in combination, according to equation (1), find that the mean energy poverty is approximately 12.5% across all EU countries. Also, it is interesting to note that while more than 90% of the population are equipped with heating, only roughly

10% of the population are equipped with air conditioning, a problem which will be magnified with climate change and increasingly hot summers.

As an initial exploration of the differences in climate and characteristics of energy poverty across the EU, Table 2 reports average CDD and HDD statistics, the population percentage unable to keep warm, and energy poverty index by country. The means confirm the paradox involving EU members in the Mediterranean Basin: even though winters are milder in Southern Member States such as Cyprus, Portugal, and Greece, households in these countries consistently report higher percentages of people who are unable to stay warm in their home (Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017). This phenomenon is shown more clearly in Figures 2A and 2B, where the number of HDD is highest in the Scandinavian and Northern European countries and lowest in the Southern and Eastern European countries, yet the opposite is true for the percentage of households unable to keep warm.

Additionally, one can see that energy poverty levels are by far the highest in previously socialist states such as Bulgaria, Lat- via, and Lithuania. This can be attributed to the legacies of the centrally planned economy, including poor thermal insulation of the housing stock and historically low energy prices (Fig. 1; Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017). When these countries transitioned to a market economy in the 1990s, energy tar- iffs increased without accompanying social welfare and energy-efficiency mechanisms, which further exacerbated the problem (Bouzarovski & Herrero, 2017).

Table 3 presents the correlation matrix for central macroeconomic indicators and energy poverty. As expected, GDP per capita is highly inversely related to both energy poverty and unemployment, meaning that richer Member States tend to have lower rates of both unemployment and energy poverty-related issues. Also, richer societies tend to have a more equal distribution of income, with a higher share of GDP going to the bottom 50% of the population. Subsequently, a country’s level of income inequality seems to be a huge predictor of energy poverty prevalence — the two are highly inversely related with a correlation coefficient of -0.511.

In plotting average yearly unemployment rates and energy poverty in 2004– 2019 (Fig. 3), there is also strong evidence for unemployment as a main driver of energy poverty. In line with the literature, the spike in unemployment following the 2008/9 economic recession drastically increased energy poverty prevalence in Europe, especially in Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece, and Spain (the PIIGS countries; Halkos & Gkampoura, 2021). The gradual drop in unemployment rate after peak- ing at over 11% in 2013 is accompanied by a similar drop in energy poverty rates, suggesting that the two go hand-in-hand. However, it seems that after the dramatic spike in energy poverty rate from 6% in 2004 to 9% in 2005, energy poverty rate did not decrease along with the unemployment rate in the years preceding the recession, suggesting that other factors might be causing energy poverty to be sticky.

III. Empirical Model I used a country-level approach and regressed the energy poverty index on cooling or heating degree days, macroeconomic factors, and other relevant controls. The general model was:

(2) yst = β0 + β1x(t-1)s + β2z2007s + β3x(t-1)z2007s +

Mst + Hst + βs + βt + βst The dependent variable, yst, denotes the energy poverty index as calculated by (1) in Member State s and year t. In some specifications, I also broke down the index into its component parts and used either inability to keep warm or arrears on utility bills as the dependent variable. x(t-1)s is the independent variable of interest, either HDD or CDD. I took degree days data from the year before under the assumption that respondents are thinking of their ability to pay bills or comfort experienced in the months leading to the survey, which could span the previous year. z2007j is either the fraction of the population with heating when the independent variable is HDD or the fraction of the population with air conditioning when the independent variable is CDD. Similarly, xt-1z2007s is the interaction term between either HDD and heating or CDD and air conditioning. Mst includes a vector of macroeconomic controls, including the bottom 50% share of total national income (income inequality), real GDP per capita, and unemployment rate. Hst is a vector of housing characteristics, including dwelling type and urbanisation level. The vectors γs and νt are country and year fixed effects, respectively. The former controls for unobservable variables that vary across countries but not over time, such as national energy resources and welfare policies, while the latter controls for unobservable variables that vary across time but not countries, such as oil shocks and global recessions.

Some specifications also include country-specific linear time trends, which allow trends over time to differ across countries. This is owing to the huge variation in development stage and economic and political climate across different Member States. For instance, we might expect a steeper decline in those unable to keep their houses warm for poorer Member States compared to richer ones because there is more potential for technological progress in poorer countries.

As I discuss later, not all of these controls are included in each specification. My preferred specification includes both country and year fixed effects but not time trends. This is because time trends absorb too much of the variation in the dependent variables, leading to imprecise estimates of the coefficients. For all of my models, I used robust standard errors that are clustered by country in order to eliminate the possibility of heteroscedasticity, and I assigned weights to countries based on their total population.

IV. Results The main results for HDD and CDD on energy poverty are presented in Tables 4 and 5, respectively. I provide four specifications to highlight the role played by the control variables and fixed effects. In the first column, neither interactions nor fixed effects are included in the regressions. The second column adds country fixed effects, and the third column has both country and year effects. The last column adds country-specific linear time trends.

The results show that the number of HDD is not statistically associated with energy poverty but that the number of CDD is consistently positively associated with energy poverty. The CDD coefficients are statistically significant below the 5% level in every specification presented in Table 5, except for specification 2. In my preferred specification, which includes both country and year effects (column 3), the results imply that for every 100 °C sum increase in CDD per year (which has a range of 0 to 812 °C/yr), mean energy poverty is expected to increase by an estimated 1.383%, all other factors held constant. This result is statistically significant at the 1% level.

Additionally, the increasing importance of household air conditioning is high- lighted in Table 5. In column 1, the aircon coefficient implies that a 1% increase in the share of the population with air conditioning leads to an estimated 0.132% reduction in energy poverty incidence. Moreover, the interaction term between CDD and aircon in column 3 suggests that for any given number of CDD, a 1% increase in household air conditioning reduces energy poverty by a further 0.056%. Both results are statistically significant at the 1% level. However, the results for heating seem to be less robust. Table 4 predicts that a 1% increase in the share of population with heating reduces energy poverty by 0.103% (column 1), but once fixed effects are added, the interaction term between HDD and heating is no longer significant (column 3).

As expected, controlling for country and year effects has a large impact on estimated degree day effects. These fixed effects control for unobserved differences across the Member States and across time. Without these controls, the estimated climate effect is biased upward; the HDD coefficients drop from positive to negative (albeit insignificantly), and the CDD coefficient drops from 2.414 (column 1) to 1.383 when both fixed effects are included (column 3). However, when country-specific time trends are added (column 4), the coefficients become imprecise, as they absorb too much of the variation in the dependent variable, which is reinforced by the extremely high adjusted R-squared value of 0.982 in both tables. With regard to the macroeconomic control variables, the results show that many of them are significantly associated with energy poverty (column 1) but have insignificant effects once fixed effects are added (column 3). Nevertheless, three variables in particular stand out: household gas prices and the unemployment rate are consistently positively associated with energy poverty, especially for CDD, and GDP per capita is significantly negatively associated with energy poverty.

The main results using the preferred specification (both country and time fixed effects but no linear time trends) are presented in Table 6. I also include the results when the composite energy poverty index is broken down into its components, with inability to keep warm (column 1) and arrears on utility bills (columns 2 and 3) as the dependent variables, respectively. The regression tables showing the results of the four different specifications for warm and arrears can be found in Tables 4, 5, and 6 in the Appendix.

The results in Table 6 are mostly robust across the three dependent variables. The exception is the negative association between HDD and both the inability to keep warm and arrears on utility bills (columns 1 and 2), which is significant at the 10% level. This seems counterintuitive, since an increase in the number of cold days should make it harder to stay warm, not easier. Additionally, the interaction term between HDD and heating is positively associated with both warm and arrears and is significant at the 5% level. Again, this is counterintuitive, as it suggests that conditioning on HDD, an increase in the share of households with access to heating actually increases their difficulty of keeping warm and paying their utility bills on time. It is possible that the Mediterranean Paradox is behind some of these counterintuitive estimates, but it is also likely that some important explanatory variables are missing from the model and are therefore limiting our ability to see the full picture.

The fact that the presence of damp, leakage, or rot is significantly associated with warm and arrears only when HDD, and not CDD, is concerned highlights the importance of the energy efficiency of the home during the cold winter months. Additionally, the larger association with warm than with arrears (where

V. Conclusion This paper has sought to investigate the link between the climate crisis and energy poverty in the EU against a backdrop of existing regional spatial inequalities and the ongoing energy transition. My theoretical approach has identified some of the key dimensions that link climate change and energy poverty: the need to position increasing average temperatures and its effect on overall energy poverty within the context of existing patterns of uneven geographic and economic conditions, while keeping in mind the important role that renewable energy policies play in exacerbating existing or creating new disparities. The empirical model has involved regressing degree-days temperature data on a multidimensional energy poverty indicator and a vector of controls over time and states to (1) uncover the aggre- gate effect of a warming climate on energy poverty incidence and (2) understand the complex macro-scale spatial patterns of energy poverty and how they relate to wider disparities within the EU.

In relation to the first aim of the study, a cross-country and time series analysis of Eurostat data showed that higher average temperatures and more frequent heat waves have increased the overall share of energy-poor households across all EU Member States and that this trend will likely continue in the absence of targeted policy intervention.

Addressing the second aim of the study, the results support the findings of previous studies by showing that there is a clear regional and economic division between the Northern and Southern EU countries that is similarly reflected in terms of an energy divide. In the colder but well-off North, income inequality and unemployment rates are lower, a higher percentage of the population have access to heating and air conditioning, and as a result, energy poverty rates are much lower. On the other hand, the warmer but poorer South experiences a much higher rate of energy poverty and population percentage that is unable to keep warm in the winter; this is in part due to the legacies of socialism, the 2008/9 economic recession, and the low efficiency and quality of the housing stock.

The results do not indicate that the ongoing energy transition is having any

significant effect on energy poverty levels in the EU as a whole, but there is reason to suggest that they have or will have important impacts on regional inequalities for individual Member States, given the speed and direction in which the EU is moving in this arena. This highlights a need for more research into how specific renewable energy policies and projects are impacting energy poverty and overall welfare levels in individual EU countries. This also shows a general necessity to acknowledge the energy poverty risks associated with a long-term transition towards a decarbonised future and the necessary steps needed to overcome them.

Nevertheless, this paper serves as a starting point in examining the relationship between climate change and energy poverty at the regional level. Further analysis could be done in other contexts, especially those in the global South that will be hardest hit by climate change, to inform a wider range of policy and development projects. To this end, there is a need for greater general awareness of the phenomenon of energy poverty at both the national and international levels, as well as recognition of the importance of implementing policies that directly address energy poverty in the context of a changing climate. ◆

title: Reformulating Korean Anti-American Literature: Feminist resistance against double colonialism in 중국인거리 (Junggugingeori)
notes: Senior thesis with abstract and trigger warning. Faculty adviser named on the opening page. Quotations from the novella are given in Korean followed by the author's English translation; Korean words garbled in the text layer (66.2, 66.3, 68.1, and the Korean bibliography entries 72.5, 72.6, 72.12) are read from the page image.
text:
Reformulating Korean Anti-American Literature: Feminist resistance against double colonialism in 중국인거리 (Junggugingeori)

by Hanbyul-Jenny Kang

Department of Comparative Literary Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Evan Mwangi, Ph.D.

Abstract Under the double oppression of the U.S.’ neocolonial occupation and the South Korean state’s neo-Confucian patriarchy, Korean women experience an alienation from their own bodies, becoming objects of sexual production. Although this is an issue that is written about passionately within the banmi, or anti-American literary genre, it is an issue that is often categorized under the greater narrative of national liberation from U.S. forces. This male-centered utilization of female suffering is unfortunately also a part of South Korea’s double colonialism.

Oh Jung-Hee’s Junggugingeori, a novella that delivers its anti-American criticism indirectly through metaphors and juxtaposition, is uninterested in metaphorizing the female experience to merely become a pawn in the drive towards a male-centered decolonization. Instead, Junggugingeori simultaneously criticizes the U.S. and the South Korean state through the depiction of female characters’ suffering and resistance against the double oppression of patriarchy and neocolonialism, partaking in the banmi literary movement without offering the female experience up for male exploitation.

The purpose of this project is to examine how Junggugingeori portrays its protag- onists’ individual bodily resistance to double colonialism. I propose that Oh portrays resistance against the joint forces of patriarchy and U.S. neocolonial oppression through the juxtaposition of the narrator’s witnessing of the sexualized violence that the adult women in her life are forced to suffer with her own private and seemingly unrelated physical resistance against her body.

Trigger warning: The following thesis includes mentions of violence against women, including homicide.

Introduction Although the use of women’s narratives has been crucial to anti-American, or banmi, literature in South Korea, these narratives are often subsumed under the greater cause of a nationalist, male-centered anti-American resistance and liberation from U.S. neocolonialism.1 As feminist writer Cho Hye-jong criticizes of anti-American literature that exists up to 1987, female characters and their experiences are often used as means to progress a narrative, unable to participate as important figures in Korean political history (15). Within an androcentric view of banmi movements, the violence inflicted on Korean women merely becomes an allegory for the occupied Korean state, and female characters act as props to expose and criticize the U.S., not as individuals who can resist or even imagine a new feminist future in their own right (Kim 178). Though the banmi movement sought to present itself as an emancipatory nationalism opposing the deep-seated role of the U.S. military in developing the South Korean nation-state and the South Korean government’s sub- servience to the U.S., it was still tied to a heteropatriarchal idea of freedom that required the sacrifice of women. As a result, it reproduced the state’s gendered nationalism and failed to envision freedom as a project that would liberate all Koreans, not just Korean men. This failure was a result of a deficit in intersectional approaches to anti-imperialist resistance against the U.S.2 This thesis seeks to tackle the specific double colonization of heterosexual, cisgender, and able-bodied Korean women within banmi-moonhak, or anti-American literature, to highlight how feminist banmi texts portray women’s resistance to double colonialism. In addition, it illustrates possibilities of freedom beyond the patriarchal

1 To clarify why I use “neocolonialism” to describe the U.S, I offer Kwame Nkrumah’s definition of it in conjunction with Bruce Cumings’ analysis of the U.S. occupation. Nkrumah argues that the neocolonized state is independent in theory but economically and politically controlled externally in practice (3); for example, the colonizer may be “helping” the establishment of a new government or funding a defense structure in the neocolonized state. The U.S. military has formally occupied southern Korea since 1945, installing systems to organize Korea as a politically friendly place to the U.S., rather than for Korean independence (Cumings 135–6). The U.S.’ occupation in Korea, from its beginnings and beyond, has been ingrained in the goal to strengthen the U.S.’ position in the Cold War whilst posing the outward appearance of aid, just as Nkrumah describes of neocolonial powers. This is why I characterize the U.S.’ presence in South Korea as a form of neocolonialism, not just as an occupation or a hegemony. 2 This framework of considering multiple and overlapping forms of oppression was coined as “intersectionality” by Kimberlé Crenshaw. The term has roots in Black feminism and highlights how women of color experience the joint oppressions of various logics of oppression, especially racism and sexism. The term is an important foundation that I have laid underneath my emphasis on this double colonial experience of the South Korean woman. If we are to untangle the ways “systems of power work within and beyond identity claims alone,” this doubly colonial experience is an overlapping oppression that necessitates an intersectional lens, a “dynamic form of matrix thinking” (Schalk 8).

“

”

[In anti-American literature,] female characters and their experiences are often used as means to progress a narrative, unable to participate as important figures in Korean political history.

imagination of decolonization.3 Though the term double colonialism deceptively suggests that there are only two modes of oppression at play, I use the term double colonialism to emphasize the intertwining oppressions of Korean patriarchy and U.S. neocolonialism in the 20th century post-Korean War context, rather than render elements such as race, sexuality, disability, gender beyond the binary, class, religion, and so many more sources of oppression as invisible or unimportant (Choi and Kim 3).4

Two state projects are key to understanding the double colonization of South Korean women. First, in the years following the Korean War, the South Korean state invested in strengthening the patriarchal structure. National policy focused on stripping women of wartime bread-winning roles and reinstating them as sexual producers and home-makers to create workers for the new nation (S. Moon 2). Second, the Korean government legally endorsed official sex workers to work for U.S. G.I.s, establishing an otherwise illegal prostitution industry for the U.S. military (K. Moon 29-39). These measures created a legal system in which Korean women’s bodies could be utilized for the pleasure of men, both Korean and American.

I reformulate the male-centered, nationalistic understanding of South Korean anti-American resistance by presenting how Oh Jung-hee’s 중국인거리

(Junggugingeori or “Chinatown”), published in 1979, portrays a young girl’s bodily resistance against the female destiny of sexual labor, serving the patriarchal state, and the U.S. neocolonial occupants’ collaborative nation-building goals. Junggugingeori is a bildungsroman novella written from the perspective of a young girl, about 10 years old, whose family moves to junggugingeori, or Chinatown, in the direct aftermath of the Korean War — the late 1950s. The narrator’s family settles in Chinatown, a neighbourhood of misfits who do not belong to the nationalist canon of who is and can become a Korean citizen: poor Koreans, sex workers for the nearby U.S. military base, and Chinese immigrants. A statue of U.S. military general Douglas MacArthur looms over Chinatown, as if to represent the U.S.’ constant watchful eye over South Korea. In this unfamiliar place, the young narrator’s childhood slips away as she attempts to reclaim her body by resisting what she witnesses as the fate of adult female bodies.

Finding a Space to Re- belong: Resistance and Protest Through the Body

The juxtaposition of feigned nonchalance and the body divulging resistance In Junggugingeori, the adult female characters, Mother and Maegi, represent to the young narrator the existing models of

3 The term “double colonialism” was coined by Petersen and Rutherford to describe the state of women living in colonised or post-colonial places suffering simultaneously from colonisation and patriarchy. The term has been conceptualised by many other authors: for example, as “double oppression” by bell hooks, and subaltern women of colonised states by Gayatri Spivak. 4 We must acknowledge the fundamentally flawed assumptions we make if we proceed with an understanding that there are only two genders, or that all women exist in the same way. The female body’s biologically-based distinction from male bodies, a heteronormative and binary-based division, is the fundamental defining piece that ties the Korean woman to double colonialism. This limited category of one kind of “woman,” for all its limitations, is useful here as the double oppression I speak of is situated within the physicality of a cisgender, heterosexual woman’s body. Moreover, Kafer emphasizes that compulsory able-bodiedness intertwines with compulsory heterosexuality when we discuss “women who are physically capable of bearing children and working outside of the home” (84). Though within the scope of this essay I have not made sufficient room for considerations of disabled women’s bodily resistance, it is important to consider the manifold possibilities of bodily resistance that open up to us when we think beyond the limitations of compulsory able-bodiedness (Kafer 85).

womanhood that a girl may aspire to be in South Korea. The narrator’s mother fulfills her role as a sexual reproducer, endlessly giving birth to children, and Maegi, a young woman renting a room in the narrator’s friend Chi Ok’s home, fulfills her role in the larger national system that utilizes women to satisfy U.S. military soldiers through sexual labor (K. Moon 152). The narrator frequently describes her mother and Maegi in death-like, death-imitating, or death-desiring states, weathered and exhausted by their unbelonging to their own bodies. In these states, as Spivak says, the subaltern woman cannot speak. Even if and when she speaks, she cannot offer herself in a way in which she is heard. What results is, as the narrator describes of her mother and Maegi, a shell of a human being, unable to resist and deadened.

The narrator interprets her mother and Maegi’s lifeless lives as a future that will irrefutably be hers. The narrator attempts to resist this by resisting the site of oppression: her own body. Her resistance, materializing as an aversion to and a rejection of the maturation of her own body into an adult female’s sexually reproductive one, reads as her resentment of her body as the root cause of her pre-determined fate. Rather than allow the process of sexual labor to alienate her from her own body, the narrator rejects her body first, disallowing any external force from having the power to alienate her from herself. The narrator masks her resistance against her own body as growing pains, separated from her observations of the bodily labor her mother and Maegi perform. Even the scenes in which the narrator observes the ways in which her mother and Maegi’s lives are marked by their existence as sexual objects only last a few sentences at most, often reported in conjunction with surrounding sounds or movements to further downplay their significance. The narrator moves on quickly from such moments and offers the reader only her most unemotional and detached observations. This uninterested attitude seems to reduce the women even further to the physical function of their female bodies — specifically, the body’s sexual and reproductive potential. However, the narrator’s nonchalant facade is inter- rupted as Oh chooses to juxtapose scenes in which the narrator witnesses the violence of sexual labor with scenes in which the narrator is rejecting her own body. In placing the narrator’s verbal nonchalance alongside her visceral non-verbal reactions to witnessing her mother and Maegi’s lives of endless sexual labor, Oh ensures that the reader senses the narrator’s apathy is an effort to separate herself from her own inevitable female future of losing her body to the structures of society. These sequential but dissociated scenes may be read together as such to unveil how they complement and inform each other.

The final scene of the novella, when the narrator’s mother gives birth to her eighth child, is one such instance in which the juxtaposition of two scenes unveils the narrator’s resistance against the double colonization of the female body. Even though the narrator hears her mother screaming from labor, she proceeds about her day in a seemingly unrelated manner:

안방에서는 어머니가 산고의 비명을 지르고 있었으나 나는 이층으로 올라갔다. 그리고 숨바꼭질을 할 때처럼 몰래 벽장 속으로 숨어 들어갔다. 한낮이어도 벽장 속은 한 점의 빛도 들이지 않아 어두웠다. 나는 차라리 죽여줘라고 부르짖는 어머니의 비명과 언제부터인가 울리기 시작한 종소리를 들으며 죽음과도 같은 낮잠에 빠져들어 갔다.

In the bedroom, mother was screaming of labor, but I headed to the second floor. And like when playing hide- and-seek, secretly hid into the closet. Though it was the middle of the day, the closet was dark as it didn’t let in a single spot of light. I listened to my mother’s screaming cries that she would rather be dead alongside the sound of bells that had begun ringing at some point, and slipped into a death-like nap (63).

To establish the narrator’s facade, Oh uses a juxtaposition of the scenes in which the narrator witnesses the physical laboring of her mother, allowing for a distance between the narrator’s indifferent reaction in the moment of her witnessing and her actual anxiety about the scene. Though the narrator refuses to explicitly connect her mother’s desperate cries with her own desire to hide in a dark closet, the juxtaposition of the two scenes suggests to the reader that the narrator is profoundly troubled by the implications of her mother’s pain for the future of her own maturing female body. The narrator hears her mother’s screams, “but” heads to the second floor — the short, one-word transition portrays the narrator as seemingly untouched by her mother’s pain as she is able to leave the scene without so much as a momentary hesitation. In the Korean text, there is not even one word that allows for this transition. Whilst in English, a transitional word “but” is needed to indicate the fact that the narrator is leaving despite her mother’s screams, in Korean, this “but” is incorporated into the phrase “있었으나,” in which the first two characters, “있었” is the ending phrase necessarily attached behind verbs (“비명을 지르고”) to indicate something is happening, whilst the last two characters, “으나,” indicate the despite-what-is-happening-ness to the phrase. In other words, the English “but” can be reduced to the latter two characters

“으나,” diminishing the significance of her mother’s screams even more in the Korean reading. The attitude of the narrator, or the attitude she attempts to portray, seems to be ‘my mother was screaming, but, no bother, I went upstairs.’ Considering that there are words in Korean such as “하지만” or “그러 나” that translate to the English “but,” Oh’s choice to structurally reduce the narrator’s judgement to a connecting-end-word is a choice that attempts to mirror the narrator’s desire to pretend to, or attempt to, reduce the impact that her mother’s screams has on her, as well as the narrator’s desire to move on quickly from the reality of her mother’s pain during childbirth.

Additionally, whilst the narrator hears her mother screaming about how she would rather be dead than give birth, the narrator “slips” into a “death-like” nap. The verb “slip” indicates the almost weightlessness of the narrator’s mind as she falls away into sleep. The reader senses that though the narrator attempts to maintain nonchalance in her thoughts, she removes herself physically from the reality of her mother’s labor — both the specific labor of pregnancy

[T]he narrator’s protesting of her own private body by trying to make herself unseeable or hidden can be a protest of the state’s violence on the woman’s body. “

” her mother is experiencing in the moment, as well as the more general gendered labor of birth her mother endures long-term. Despite the narrator’s efforts, the negative connotation of “death” in her “death-like” nap interrupts her composed front. “Death- like” is a striking descriptor of the deep and uninterrupted nap the narrator has at this moment due to her indifference to her mother’s pain. However, given how the narrator makes herself as invisible as possible by entering a dark closet and reducing herself in size to fit into the space, it seems that the use of “death-like” as a descriptor hints at the narrator’s desire to disappear or hide her female body so that it is not seen. Though the narrator’s careful nonchalance in the thoughts that she reveals to the reader may suggest otherwise, her actions reflect that she is affected by her mother’s pain. By juxtaposing scenes in which the narrator is dully describing the pain of her mother with the narrator’s unease towards her own body, the author suggests that the narrator’s resentment of her own female body may be triggered by the pain of her mother’s gendered labor and the narrator’s understanding of how, eventually, she too will lose autonomy over her own body.

This is further demonstrated in the next paragraph when the narrator wakes to find that her mother has lived but that the birth was not successful. At this moment, the narrator calls out for her mother from inside the closet. Then, the narrator realizes that she has menstruated for the first time:

어두운 벽장 속에서 나는 이해할 수 없는 절망감과 막막함으로 어머니를 불렀다.

그리고 옷속에 손을 넣어 거미줄처럼 온몸을 끈끈하게 죄고 있는 후덥덥한 열기를, 그 열기의 정체를 찾아내었다.

초조였다.

Inside the dark closet, I called for Mother with a sense of hopelessness and suffocating loss that I could not understand. I put my hand inside my clothes, and found the source of the humid, stuffy heat, a heat that was closing tightly around my entire body like a spider web.

It was my menarche. (64)

This scene confirms the suspicion that the narrator is more moved by hearing the cries of her mother than she wants to reveal. Although throughout the novella the narrator repeats that her mother will die from this eighth pregnancy, the narrator wakes to find her mother has lived, but the baby has not. Despite the baby’s death, the narrator’s hopelessness and loss seems to come not from mourning the baby, her sibling, but from the narrator’s release of her overwhelming emotions. Given how earlier in the novella the narrator attempts to resist the growth of her breasts by wrapping them tightly with ripped cloth5 and also how she expresses her sympathy with the animality of a woman’s life when she realizes that her mother is pregnant for the eighth time, this final scene in the novella highlights the narrator’s frustration at her failure to prevent the inevitable maturation of her female body, which will eventually be reduced to its animalistic sexual function.6 Her menstruation is a sign that she is physically able to become pregnant

5 This technique of wrapping her breasts is suggested to the narrator by her grandmother, a character who succeeds in avoiding sexualized gendered labor. This harkens to Katrak’s idea of how women may use tactics known only by women to resist or protest the domination of their body. Authors show female resistance through “tactics that are often part of a woman’s way of knowing and acting” (7–8). 6 The narrator’s recognition of the specifically animalistic nature of the woman’s body can be read as part of the postcolonial critique of the animalization of colored bodies, and specifically, female bodies. In “Postcolonial Critique in a Multispecies World,” Neel Ahuja describes how Black scholars such as W.E.B. DuBois, Ngugi wa Thiong’o, and Frantz Fanon have criticized this animalization as it is a means through which the colonizer legitimizes its domination of the colored person’s body (Ahuja 557). Specifically and to inherit this animalistic, child-bearing labor of the Korean woman. This moment is characterized by both the stuffiness of the heat and the stuffiness of the feeling of loss. I translated “막막함” to a “suffocating loss,” but “막막함” is ineffable in English, as it is a specific feeling of a stuffy, suffocating-ness that fills one with an inability to think or move forward. It is a state of feeling lost, but lost in stuffiness. Oh’s emphasis on the stuffiness of this moment portrays how the narrator is, after a novella of attempting to hide her emotions, feeling overwhelmingly lost and stuffed with an angst for her physical maturation into a woman’s body and what that signifies for her future.

The narrator, in seeing her mother in labor, understands the way she will be disconnected from her own matured body when it is exploited as a site of labor for patriarchal nation-building. Oh insinuates that the narrator understands the domination of the female body through gendered labor, leading her to both mentally and physically disassociate herself from her mother’s pain as well as from the maturation of her own body: her protest of her inevitable fate. As her mother’s constant pregnancies and childbirths fundamentally fulfill the state’s goals of strengthening itself through a stronger and larger population, the narrator’s protesting of her own private body by trying to make herself unseeable or hidden can be a protest of the state’s violence on the woman’s body. If the maturation of the narrator’s body is in line with the state’s nation-building goals, then the narrator’s protest of her own maturation is simultaneously a protest of the state. Hence, the body is revealed as a site that experiences the dominance of state violence on an intimate level but also finds a way to try to protest this larger oppression on an individual scale.

Bedbugs and the female body; resisting the American contaminant Oh expands on how the female body is exploited by revealing how women’s sexual labor for the U.S. military undermines female bodily autonomy but also how the body can, again, be a site of protest. Maegi, a young woman who rents a spare room in the narrator’s friend’s home, connects the town directly with the U.S.’ presence and is a visible reminder of their occupation in South Korea. Though it is never specified what Maegi does for a living, given the narrator’s descriptions of her, the reader is led to as- sume that Maegi is a sex worker for the U.S. military. In the scene preceding the murder of Maegi by a U.S. G.I., the narrator is seen fighting bedbugs in her sleep. Woken by a sound, the narrator realizes that Maegi’s U.S. G.I. cohabitant has killed her by throwing her off their second-floor apartment:

옅은 잠 속에서 손톱을 세워 긁적이며 빈대와 싸우던 나는 둔탁하고 메마른 소리에 눈을 떴다 […]

잠시 후 요란한 사이렌을 울리며 미군 지프가 달려왔다. 겹겹이 진을 친 사람들이 순식간에 양쪽으로 갈라졌다. 헤드라이트의 쏟아질 듯 밝은 불빛 속에 매기 언니가 반듯이 누워 있었다. 염색한, 길고 숱 많은 머리털이 흩어져 후광처럼 얼굴을 감싸고 있었다. 위에서 던져 버렸다는군.

In a shallow sleep, I was fighting bed bugs by scratching myself with poised nails, when a blunt and parched sound woke me […]

in the case of the female body, bell hooks has argued that the animalization of the Black woman into a sexualised object is deeply connected to preserving the racial order (hooks 62). In the context of Junggugingeori, the female body is subjected to an animalization not only through the sex industry created by and for the U.S. military, it is also subjected to an animalization via the South Korean state. Not only is the female body diminished to a lower racial order than the U.S. colonizer, it is rendered further non-human, thus even further subaltern, by its own state.

Moments later, a U.S. military jeep rushed over, ringing its boisterous siren. The layers of people who had set up camp immediately divided into two. In the middle of the headlights, so bright as if the light could spill, Maegi lay neatly. Her dyed, long, voluminous hair was scattered, framing her face like a backlight. They say she was thrown from above (53).

In this scene, Oh highlights the detrimental effects of the parasitical U.S. military on women’s bodies. Maegi is viewed solely as a body by the U.S. military. Not only does she labor as a sex worker for U.S. G.I.s, she also has a child with a U.S. G.I., lives with another U.S. G.I., and is finally murdered by the G.I. with whom she lives, Gum-doong-ee.7 Her body is exploited, from the beginning of the narrative to the end, by the men who represent and enforce U.S. governance in South Korea. When Maegi is murdered by Gum-doong-ee, a military jeep comes in to shelter, protect, and rescue him, rather than express care for Maegi or attend to her tragic death. The way the Military Police (MP) covers Gum-doong-ee’s naked body with a U.S. military uniform reveals a gesture of unity between the military men, leaving behind the death of Maegi for the community to deal with. The U.S. G.I.’s body is posed as one that is more important than the body of Maegi’s – in direct contrast between the care given to Gum-doong-ee’s nakedness and Maegi’s death. In this scene, no words are exchanged between the Americans and the Koreans. Within just six sentences, the jeep rushes into the scene, shining a head- light on the scene of the murder, and leaves. In fact, it is the military jeep that first shines a light on who is dead, a light so bright that it seems to spill out of the jeep, placing the murder of Maegi in plain sight. Nevertheless, the U.S. troops are able to leave the scene with no consequences. Maegi’s death reveals how, at the hands of the U.S. military, women are completely alienated from their bodies, even losing the autonomy to live or die — a power that the U.S. military is capable of controlling with impunity.

By juxtaposing the narrator fighting bedbugs, a pest, with Maegi’s death, the author suggests that the bedbugs can be seen as a metaphor for the U.S. military, casting the latter as a parasite that plagues the town.8 Hence, the narrator’s fight is representative of the narrator’s protest against the U.S. military’s parasitic exploitation of the female body. Although bedbugs are difficult to see with the naked eye, they infiltrate the intimate space of rest that the bed symbolizes, causing distress, discomfort, and sometimes even pain with their bloodsucking bites. Like bedbugs, the parasitic presence of U.S. troops in South Korea infiltrates the intimate space that is the woman’s body, as U.S. G.I.s literally get in bed with female sex workers. Here, the bed is the very site of the nexus of the invasion of the female body. The harmful consequences of the U.S. presence is thus revealed through the physical experience of the body, much like the physical experience of bedbugs’ bites on the body.9

7 Considering that Gum-doong-ee is a Black U.S. G.I., there certainly seems to be a racialization of the bad American as Black. ‘Gum-doong-ee’ literally translates in English to something along the lines of “Black-ie”, highlighting that indeed, there is an emphasis on his Blackness, revealing the author’s racial bias in her use of a Black person as the only American the reader encounters in a novella that criticizes the U.S. Perhaps writing the bad American as Black was one way Oh thought she could write about the U.S. critically with less backlash from both government and U.S. censorship. 8 This delegation of the “pest” as the U.S. instead of the Korean people is a reversal of the way non-Western people, such as Black people or Native Americans have been named “pests” by white colonizers. Usually, this reduction of people to a vermin being allows for a justification of their elimination, or the control of them (Mavhunga 152-153). In the author’s flipping of this tradition, she uses the tradition of colonizers against them. 9 The comparison of the U.S. military to a parasite may not just be an astute metaphor. Coincidentally, even after Korea eliminated

The metaphor of the U.S. military as a parasite reveals the connection between the dehumanizing fate of women in Korea to the narrator’s physical protest against this loss of bodily autonomy. The fact that the narrator fights bedbugs off her own body during her sleep suggests again to the reader that despite the narrator’s seeming lack of concern for Maegi’s depressed state or her eventual death, in reality, the narrator is deeply affected by it. Her lack of concern is an attempt to distance herself from the woman’s fate of sexual labor, just as she tries to do when her mother gives birth. Most of the narrator’s descriptions of Maegi are of her during the daytime when she is off work, when she is lifeless and dull, lying all day completely under her covers and never once speaking to the narrator. Though the narrator’s interactions with Maegi are limited as such, in the narrator’s sleep, a subconscious state, she fights the bedbugs that represent the U.S. military and their exploitation of sex workers, a phenomenon she sees through Maegi’s life. She imagines that she is fighting the bedbugs “with poised nails” in an attacking position rather than in a limp and unconscious drowsiness, revealing that even in her sleep, the narrator is actively attempting to ward the bugs away. That the bedbugs attack the body in its most vulnerable state, in the dark, during sleep, reveals why even in her sleep, the narrator must maintain an attacking position, wary of the domination of her body. If the bedbugs represent the U.S. military, Oh is underlining the intimate and pervasive violence of the U.S. military, leaving the female body unable to rest alone, even in sleep.

Conclusion I conceive of feminist resistance within the Korean context as one that takes shapes in clusters due to the fragmented nature of women’s positionality within a doubly oppressive environment. In resisting an oppressive system, Junggugingeori’s narrator uses the tools with which she is left to resist through her individual body, even against her own body. Change happens whether or not external viewers believe in it or are disappointed in it, as “resistance is effective in that it produces a new reality, a new condition from which to resist” (Tuck and Yang 13). Maria Lugones argues similarly for small-scale and non-public resistance: resistance, often “expressing itself infra-politically,” is not the end or goal of political struggle, but rather the beginning (746). These scholars show the multiplici- ty of resistance within systems that do not accommodate ‘others,’ underlining the ways in which we must challenge the notion that resistance is limited to the dramatic, public, and visible domains. Though the lonely resistance of Junggugingeori’s narrator may feel merely like a pyrrhic victory, we can become witnesses to the narrator’s seemingly invisible resistance if we make a “commitment to the problem of bedbugs, the pest has seemed to return to Korea through the U.S. A 2008 study on the re-emergence of bedbugs in South Korea examined how after two decades of no reports of bedbugs, a woman who had arrived to Korea from New Jersey, USA brought back the pest into Seoul. See: Lee, In-Yong et al. “Reemergence of the bedbug Cimex lectularius in Seoul, Korea.”

“The feminist anti-American resistance portrayed in Junggugingeori extends beyond literature and its history to the non-literary politics of today’s South Korea.” interpret [her] experience ‘against the grain of power’” (Cruz, 2010, 7).

Importantly, the feminist anti-American resistance portrayed in Junggugingeori extends beyond literature and its history to the non-literary politics of today’s South Korea. This paper highlights the neglected radical feminist resistance within anti-American literature to emphasize that the integration of women in anti-imperialist political spaces in South Korea has already been imagined and articulated. Though this paper focuses on just one text in one country in one short snippet of time, I have written with the hope of transnational and multiracial coalitions of resistance in mind. In bridging together Gayatri Spivak, Ketu Katrak, Cindy Cruz, etc. with feminist resistance in Korean literature, I underscore how the oppressions women face follow similar patterns, surfacing in familiar logics. Accordingly, to imagine that the individual resistances revealed in Junggugingeori are only Korean would be a shortcoming. As I have attempted to show through a diversity of sources, these methods of resistance have sustained women of all kinds in varying oppressive situations. We must read the resistance of women against imperialism as a legacy of work that must continue as the problems of double colonialism continue, whether in their original or newfan- gled forms. Although my essay highlights a double colonialism that predates the wealthy, globalized, technology-driven, COVID-fighting, K-Pop making, so-called “first-world” nation that South Korea is today, the problems outlined within the text have remained painfully with Korean women. For example, the double colonialism, previously geographically contained within South Korea in my two texts, has extended abroad, whether it be through the direct international marriages between U.S.

G.I.s and former South Korean sex workers or through the diaspora of Korean women who have immigrated to the U.S. Both groups of Korean women have been and continue to be subjected to the intersecting oppressions of racialization, sexualization, familial expectations, etc., rooted in the double colonialism that originated within the neo-Confucian patriarchy and U.S. neocolonialism and its camptowns. It is also important to think about the ways in which Korean women have learned to oppress others and each other, born out of the mentality of patriarchy and of being colonized. Thus, although the resistance of Junggugingeori’s narrator may not necessarily need to be rep- licated exactly today, these literatures and their characters allow us Korean women to belong to a long genealogy, whether imagined into life through literature or written into history through literature, of resisting women. Indeed, Junggugingeori, written and published during a time in which the South Korean state and the occupying U.S. rendered any potential anti-Americanism as a threat, is, in and of itself, a resistance against double colonialism.

In writing this paper, I hope to have produced a small portion of knowledge, courage, and a feeling of persistent legacy that contributes to the history of Korean feminist resistance against imperialism. However, as Korean women, we are not alone in this resistance. As we continue to form coalitions with others who are forging their own paths of decolonial resistance, the resistance work we do will flourish in the end. Together, from all our different corners in the world, we are imagining, building, and living a decolonial futurity that dreams of the emancipation of all peoples. Eventually, I believe that the systems that oppress us will collapse under our collective work. ◆
