title: The Office of Undergraduate Research: The Student Researcher’s Ideal One-Stop Shop
notes: Feature on Northwestern's Office of Undergraduate Research, with OUR advisor Diamond Jones and Circumnavigator Travel Grant winner Vivica E. Lewis. Title as given in the contents; the opening page prints it in capitals. The first paragraph's drop cap "A" is a separate block (73.1).
text:
THE OFFICE OF UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH

THE STUDENT RESEARCHER’S

IDEAL ONE-STOP SHOP by Stephanie Kim and Peirong She

As one of the most prestigious research institutions in the United States, Northwestern University (NU) is known to attract many students interested in conducting some form of research during their undergraduate careers. Whether it takes place in laboratories, dance studios, libraries, or online, student research life is notably vibrant on the NU campus.

Among the many support systems in place to assist students in their pursuits, the Office of Undergraduate Research (OUR) is the first stop that students should visit as they begin their research journeys. Simply from their weekly newsletters and numerous video series, one can tell that the OUR is nothing like the stereotypical college office that any prospective student may imagine, but is instead an inviting place filled with spirited and passionate advisors committed to helping students in any way possible to achieve their research dreams.

One of the most prominent questions that surrounded the return to campus this year was how different things would be as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. Concerns about COVID-19 have dictated many changes to the way in which people live their lives, and it is no surprise that the world of research has been affected as well. For the past two years, COVID-19 restrictions have prevented students from pursuing research exactly according to plan, especially in disciplines that require travel or in-person experimentation.

We had the pleasure of speaking to Outreach Coordinator and OUR Advisor Dia- mond Jones, who also happens to be a recent graduate of NU. Regarding the effects that COVID-19 has had on student research, Jones says that the OUR has made tremendous efforts to mitigate as many COVID-19 related issues as possible.

Most grants that the OUR provides now have COVID-19 stipulations, meaning that students must demonstrate a plan to continue their proposed research amidst anything unexpected that may hinder their original ideas. The benefit of this additional policy is that it allows students to think ahead so that “even if their perfect project can’t come to fruition, they’re still not barred from using [the OUR’s] systems and money and making their dreams come true.”

The hybrid nature of a post-COVID-19 world also makes the components and logistics of research such as advising appointments even more accessible and flexible. Drop-in office hours and advising sessions can be held both in-person and on Zoom; thus, if anything, COVID-19 has improved this aspect of advising.

But how has research funding changed because of the pandemic? A common concern among many departments is that there is a strain in the supply of funds that they are able to give out, causing the funding of student projects to be more conservative. Although this is indeed a critical issue, the OUR is committed to finding other ways to financially support students for their research endeavors, namely by linking them to other available resources.

Having been a student in the same position up until just last year, Jones completely understands students’ anxiety about research during the pandemic. However, she assures students that the OUR is constantly in contact with various offices to keep students updated on NU’s COVID-19 policies. “For every student who is worried about whether they will be able to work at a lab or if [the lab will] be open, I can definitively say that, based on NU’s guidelines, they are prioritizing keeping labs open for students who are trying to get involved with that research,” she says.

The main role of the OUR in any situation is to be the bridge between students and any other departments that students may not know to reach out to. It is a useful stepping stone to find out specific information that each student may need access to based on their individual needs.

Although it may seem daunting at first, there is a lot to gain from simple, 30–45-minute advising appointments, and once a student is paired with an advisor, they are there for the student during every step of the process. “A lot of students think, ‘If I don’t have something concrete, they can’t help me with anything,’ and ‘If I don’t hit X milestone, I can’t go on to the next,’ [but the research process] is really not linear,” Jones says of the perspective that many NU students seem to hold. She adds, “Not a lot of students realize that we can offer various avenues of support, no matter where you are in your journey.”

Perhaps even more daunting are the application processes for the many forms of financial support that the OUR offers for students pursuing research in all varieties of fields. Although many students are under the impression that applying for and receiving grants is

“The main role of the OUR in any situation is to be the bridge between students and any other departments.” incredibly competitive and difficult, Jones wishes to clarify that each research topic is so unique and personalized that there really is no way to compare them against each other.

Vivica E. Lewis, the winner of the 2022 Circumnavigator Travel Grant, began her research journey in the winter quarter of her freshman year with the Undergraduate Research Assistant Program (URAP), which she says turned out to be a valuable learning experience. She had no prior experience with research and “knew absolutely nothing about research,” but the OUR was very accessible for her. As a freshman, she appreciated their newsletters, classroom presentations, and warm welcomes to every student.

It was not until the beginning of her third year that Lewis returned to research. At first, she was not sure if research was right for her. But after meeting with advisors to develop her research proposal, she realized that research was still one of her passions. She also wanted to be part of the solution of breaking down the various barriers to entering research and make research as a whole a more inclusive field. While crafting her research project with the support of her advisors, she created a project that integrated her personal and professional values about doing ethical research, working with communities and allowing them to tell their stories and incorporating inclusive, accessible language. She hopes she can serve as one example of a researcher who stays true to herself and makes the changes she wants to see in the field of research.

For Lewis, the greatest resource at the OUR was the help of the advisors. She appreciated the weekly meeting with her advisor Dr. Peter Civetta. He was very flexible throughout the process, and he went as far as giving Lewis feedback at 9 a.m. meetings for drafts that he received at 2 a.m. Although Lewis was unfamiliar with research, Dr. Civetta never made her feel embarrassed or less than capable throughout the entire process of writing her research grant. Therefore, Lewis hopes more students from diverse backgrounds will become involved in research. Specifically, she hopes more students from diverse backgrounds can take on the researcher role, and believes every student with any interest in research should get involved, knowing that the OUR has their back with each step. ◆

title: Revolutionary Women: Literary Performativity, Classical Pseudonyms, and the Public Sphere in the Correspondence of Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren
notes: Senior thesis. Faculty adviser named on the opening page; the opening section is headed "Remember the Ladies?". Verse quotations from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar are extracted line by line.
text:
Revolutionary Women:

Literary Performativity, Classical Pseudonyms, and the Public Sphere in the Correspondence of Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren by Lauren Katz

Department of English Faculty Adviser: Prof. Kelly Wisecup, Ph.D.

Remember the Ladies?

Adams and Warren began a long-time epistolary correspondence in 1773, becoming the two Revolutionary-era women with the most abundant surviving record of writing.1 Through their epistolary correspondence, Adams and Warren engaged in a nuanced dialogue and literary performance in which they experimented with ways that women could carve a space for their voices in the public sphere, ultimately reimagining what constituted the public sphere, and even femininity, altogether. These women capitalized on the circumstances of war and America’s transitioning identity as a new republic in order to reimagine the relationship between the classical and the modern, the Stoical and the sentimental, the public and the private, the national and the domestic, and the masculine and the feminine. Adams’s and Warren’s epistolary correspondence in the late 18th century marks their tandem efforts to complicate these binaries and examine their deep-seeded interrelations in an attempt to actualize their historical and literary voices.

In order to understand the ways in which Adams and Warren challenge conventional perceptions of the public sphere and femininity, it is important to first identify a major constraint that perpetuated these conventions: the ideology of republican motherhood. Republican motherhood was an 18th-century attitude that intended to reinforce the separation between the women’s domestic sphere and the men’s

1 Edith B. Gelles, “Bonds of Friendship: The Correspondence of Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren,” Proceedings of the Massachusetts Historical Society 108 (1996): 35–71, JSTOR http://www.jstor.org/stable/25081114 (Accessed May 2, 2020), 36.

public sphere. However, this ideology also conversely brought about an “integration of domestic and political behavior,” since it required women to possess a dedication to “the service of civic virtue.”2 Republican motherhood extended a woman’s obligations to educating male citizens, such as their sons, in the ways of republican virtue, which consequently prompted a ground- breaking question: If women were able to counsel men on behaviors and virtues that were allegedly “masculine,” how different could men and women truly be?3 Thus, republican motherhood gave women access to “the language of patriotism,” which in turn provided women with a means to justify their involvement in the previously deemed “masculine” worlds of public politics and authorship.4

In addition to republican motherhood, performativity was also an essential element of women’s epistolary authorship as well as letter writing’s mobility between the public and private spheres in the late 18th century. While letters were often publicly performed in a social setting, their performative potential was most influential in the private creation of a literary pseudo-public sphere.5 The epistolary experience was unique in that it required reciprocity and was distinguished by the

“desire to incorporate a specific reader response within the world of the narrative.”6 There was a sense of intimate, collective world building between the correspon- dents that was further heightened by epistolary language, as such language relied on “absence” and on “make-believe” in order to hold a personal conversation with an addressee who was physically elsewhere.7 Such literary performativity began to manifest itself in late 17th-century En- gland and ultimately 18th-century America in the form of Roman allusions and pseudonyms.8 American leaders assumed these classical cognomens, simultaneously

2 Linda Kerber, “The Republican Mother: Women and the Enlightenment-An American Perspective.” American Quarterly 28, no. 2 (1976): 187–205. JSTOR, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2712349 (Accessed May 5, 2020), 3. 3 Vietto, Women and Authorship, 50. 4 Philip Hicks, “The Roman Matron in Britain: Female Political influence and Republican Response, ca. 1750-1800,” The Journal of Modern History 77, no. 1 (2005): 35–69, JSTOR, https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/429428 (Accessed May 5, 2020), 7. 5 A “literary pseudo-public sphere” is the creation of an alternate public sphere in epistolary letters through private, performative world-building. This sphere only exists intimately between the people that are narrating such a world in their correspondence. A “literary public sphere” is more directly connected to the actual public sphere, denoting works that are in circulation among public literary culture. 6 Altman, Epistolarity, 91. 7 Ibid., 140. 8 Eran Shalev, “Ancient Masks, American Fathers: Classical Pseudonyms During the American Revolution and Early Republic.” Journal of the Early Republic 23, no. 2 (2003): 151–72, JSTOR, http://www.jstor.com/stable/3125034 (Accessed September 7, 2020), 154.

“

”

These women capitalized on the circumstances of war and America’s transitioning identity as a new republic in order to reimagine the relationship between the classical and the modern, the Stoical and the sentimental, the public and the private, the national and the domestic, and the masculine and the feminine.

aligning themselves with Warner’s republican “negativity” and initiating a parallel between the fall of the Roman Republic and the American Revolution. However, it was not only men who were capable of employing these Roman pseudonyms, as women possessed the tradition of “female worthies,” which consisted of a “catalog of illustrious women” that contemporary women could pull from to substantiate their progressive gender agendas.9 American women particularly were influenced by George Ballard’s books, Memoirs of Several Ladies of Great Britain (1752) and Biographi- um Faemineum (1766), which held memoirs of women being “celebrated for their writings or skill in the learned languages, arts, and sciences.”10 Ballard’s books used “the catalog of exemplary women as evidence of women’s capability” in order to fight for their improved education.11 Furthermore, women specifically favored pulling from a catalogue of Roman matrons over the Spar- tans or Amazons because the Roman matron “constituted a relatively safe, unthreatening exemplar, with fewer unwelcome connotations,” while “at the same time, she could promote daring political acts committed in the name of the greater good.”12

On Aug. 27, 1775, Adams chose to sign her letter to Warren under the Roman matron pseudonym “Portia,” employing literary performativity as a means to activate her own epistolary public sphere. Warren subsequently returned the favor, tailoring her response to “the world of the narrative” by signing her following letter under the Roman matron pseudonym “Marcia.” Adams’s and Warren’s epistolary correspondence under these classical pseudonyms spanned the course of around five years, with Warren’s last letter under “Marcia” occurring in 1779 and Adams’s last letter under “Portia” happening soon after in 1780. This thesis will focus on a selection of these women’s earlier Roman pseudonym letters from 1775–1777. I chose this time frame because it also cor- responds with the start of the American Revolution, a time in which both Adams and Warren were continually separated from their husbands, causing them to rely more heavily on their epistolary exchange with each other for conversation, political news, and moral support. Additionally, the American Revolution was a period in which America’s wartime narrative provided easy access to the employment of antiquity by most directly paralleling the fall of the Roman Republic.13 Not only have I chosen to focus on a section of Adams’s and Warren’s correspondence that re- volves around the presence, or purposeful lack thereof, of Roman matron pen names, but I have also chosen letters that use classical and neoclassical references, which add a multi-dimensional complexity to their engagements with antiquity. Furthermore, while the use of Roman matrons and classical antiquity has primarily appealed to and been studied by historians, my thesis seeks to fill a scholarly gap by using history solely as a means to contextualize a primarily literary analysis of Adams’s and Warren’s

While Adams and Warren were both concerned with the same end goal of figuring out how to best carve a space for women’s historical and literary voices, such as their own, their letters as Portia and Marcia revealed the intricacies of their conversation, as both women chose to experiment with different approaches. Adams experimented with using literary performativity as a means to circumvent Stoical republicanism altogether, creating her own epistolary pseudo-public sphere in which women could occupy public positions of power. Warren, however, recuperated the sentimental in order to reframe virtue and patriotism as particularly feminine and to modernize performativity so that she could achieve self-actualization as a playwright and historian through the private epistolary sphere.

Abigail Adams: Creating a Literary, Pseudo-Public Sphere Adams employs literary performativity not only to envision herself as occupying roles that had traditionally corresponded with republicanism, masculinity, and the public sphere, but she does so in a way that allows her to circumvent the Stoical narrative of a modest and selfless entrance into public service. By creating her own literary, pseudo-public sphere, Adams could bypass the tenets of Stoical republicanism and thus more directly and unabashedly insert her voice into the public canon. Engaging in a performance of any kind requires the process of world building, which includes establishing the rules of the world by setting up the permissions. In Adams’s epistolary correspondence with Warren, she uses the pen name Portia to establish that she is employing literary performativity and to communicate a sense of theatrical and literary permission. Adams uses her Roman matron signature to signal that, in her epistolary world, she is capable of linguistically moving between classical and contemporary roles, an action that I will term “body hopping.” By comparing Adams’s April 10, 1776, letter to John Adams with her April 13, 1776, letter to Warren — two letters in which Adams quotes the same passage in Shakespeare’s The Tragedy of Julius Caesar — I will illu- minate exactly what makes Adams’s and Warren’s female-female correspondence invaluable. Adams pens letters to her husband on April 7 and April 10, 1776, that chronicle the funeral of General Warren, or Dr. Joseph Warren, an esteemed patriot who died in the Battle of Bunker Hill and became known as the first martyr of the American Revolution.14 She also notes that there was “an oration by Mr. Morton” in which Warren’s death was used to incite a recommitment to the patriot cause, as the “heroic virtues of the disceased” and “the noble cause to which he fell a Martir” was very fresh in “the minds of the Audience.”15 Adams uses a simile, re- marking “the Dead Body like that of Caesars before their Eyes,” and then transcribes an abridged version of Mark Antony’s soliloquy from Act III Scene I of Shakespeare’s play, The Tragedy of Julius Caesar, in order to depict General Warren’s wounds:

Like dumb mouths did ope their ruby lips,

And beg the voice and utterance of a Tongue.

Woe to the Hands that shed this costly blood;

A curse shall light upon their line;

Domestick fury, and firce civil Strife

Shall cumber all the parts of Britton (all emphasis in the quote is mine).16

By explicitly mentioning Caesar in her letter to John Adams, Adams contextualizes the quote within Shakespeare’s play. In The Tragedy of Julius Caesar, Brutus and Cassius are worried by Caesar’s love of power and his ambition to “turn the republic into a dictatorship.”17 As a result, they, along with some other conspira- tors, assassinate Caesar by stabbing him to death in order to “save Rome from tyranny.”18 While Joseph Warren and Caesar represent opposite agendas, the former for liberation and the latter for despotism, both become significant cata- lysts that garner public support for their respective causes in death. In order to illustrate this parallel, Adams talks about Morton’s eulogy directly prior to this quote in order to assign Mark Antony’s speech to Morton, consequently adapt- ing Mark Antony’s statement of “Shall cumber all parts of Italy” to “Shall cumber all parts of Britton.”19 In fact, Morton’s eulogy contains several parallels in both vocabulary and imagery to this quote. For instance, similar to how Mark Antony’s quote uses a simile to transform Caesar’s wounds into lips for his dead body to speak, Morton revitalizes the voice of the deceased General Warren when he proclaims, “Ought we not to listen to the Voice of our slaughtered Brethren, who are now proclaiming aloud to their Country.”20 Additionally, Mark Antony exclaims, “Woe to the Hands that shed this

Adams’s letter to Warren distances the passage from its Shakespearean origins, as she does not put quotes around the passage, whereas she does use quotation marks in her letter to John Adams. Furthermore, the additional lines from Mark Antony’s soliloquy that she chooses to include in her letter to Warren add the first-person pronouns “me” and “I,” which make the language appear to fall under her penmanship and represent her perspective. Through claiming Shakespeare’s language as her own, Adams is able to carry out a literary performance as the orator at Warren’s funeral, a role that women did not have access to in the 18th century. Not only does Adams transform into an orator, but her audience accordingly shifts from her correspondent, Warren, to the American people. By assuming this role, Adams is rewriting history, transporting herself into the public sphere to publicly eulogize and memorialize one of the most forced-conviction-from-the-other-he-stole-assent/ (April 5, 2021). 21 “Addressing Both Understanding and Passions — From the One He Forced Conviction from the Other He Stole Assent.” 22 Adams to Warren, 13 April 1776. 23 Ibid. Unlike the Shakespearean context of Mark Antony speaking these lines to Caesar with no one else on stage, in this new context of Adams as the orator of this quote, she is speaking to the public about how “brave a Man” Joseph Warren was, asserting her loyalty to the General and, ultimately, to the patriotic cause.

However, Adams does not stop there. She uses the Roman roots of the quote to body hop into the classical role of an orator, granting herself another position of masculine, public power. Adams explicitly takes on a prophetic tone with the lines “Woe to [the] hand that shed this costly Blood/Over thy Wounds now do I prophesy,” but the following parenthetical crucially reveals the source of Adams’s oracular power. The simile of “dumb mouths” with “Ruby lips” refers to Warren’s bleeding wounds, portraying these wounds as wanting to speak but being unable to do so. Warren’s wounded body “beg[s] the voice and utterance of a Tongue,” or a spokesperson to speak on his behalf. Thus, by framing this quote as her own speech, Adams subsequently positions herself as the metaphorical “mouth” of Joseph Warren, engaging in a clever form of literary ventriloquism that gives her the utmost level of contemporary and classical authority in her epistolary public sphere. As a modern orator and a classical oracle figure who is authorized by Warren, Adams places a curse of “Domestick fury and firce civil Strife” on Britain on his behalf. Adams merges and blurs the private and public spheres while simultaneously blurring temporality by body hopping between contemporary and classical roles.

Through such temporal dualism, Adams can imagine herself as occupying traditionally masculine, public positions of power in both the past and the present; this literary performance ultimately allows Adams to envision a world in which women, just like men, have a historical pool of canonized female public leaders to emulate.

Mercy Otis Warren: Becoming a Sentimental, Epistolary Playwright and Historian On one hand, it might appear that Warren uses her epistolary correspondence not to craft an alternate persona for herself but to rather reaffirm her already existing public authorship, using letters as “the testing ground for different models of historical explanation, narrative technique, and character sketches.”24 Warren’s corre- spondents thoroughly admire her skill in “mental portraiture,”25 and John Adams describes her responsibility to “delineate Caracters” as one belonging to a “faithfull Historian,” since “the public is so interested in public Characters” that “it becomes the Duty of every good Citizen who happens to be acquainted with them to communicate his Knowledge.”26 However, on the other hand, Warren’s choice to identify under her public roles as a playwright and historian in her private, epistolary correspondence to Adams accentuates that there was something different that letter-writing under these personas supplied her with. When viewed from such a lens, Warren uses letter writing to better actualize her roles as a playwright and historian because she is free to carry out her own sentimen-

Warren’s most prominent public plays, The Adulateur (1772), The Defeat (1773), and The Group (1775), as well as her book, History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution (1805), reflect on and recount the American Revolution through numerous allusions to Roman antiquity.27 For instance, in The Adulateur, Warren names the revolutionary leaders and pa- triots Brutus, Cassius, Junius, Portius, and Marcus, who are “well-known and adored heroes of the Roman Republic,” in order to promote the revolutionary message of expelling tyranny and restoring liberty.28 This apparent dichotomy between the classical Stoicism of Warren’s published works and the modern sentimentalism of her epistolary correspondence with Adams becomes more decipherable when thinking about the demographic that is represented in her public works: men. In all three of these plays, every single character is a man, as Warren uses “a cluster of Roman republican heroes,” who are all men, to embody public leaders in the American Revolution, who are also all men.29 Similarly, in Warren’s History, she only creates literary portraits of public male figures, such as her sections on the “character of Mr. Hutchinson” and the “characters of Samuel Adams and John Hancock.”30 In the public sphere, unlike in the epistolary sphere, Warren cannot renounce the traditionally male-dominated use of exemplar theory. Her public roles as a playwright and historian are constrained by the public sphere’s perpetuation of its inextricable link to republican Stoicism, patriotism, virtue, and masculinity.31 Consequently, Warren’s public works adhere to this same classical, Stoical language of the masculine public sphere. Nevertheless, Warren’s private epistolary correspondence with Adams enables her to modernize virtue in the form of sentimentalism and ironically actualize her public roles by playwriting and history chronicling about contemporary females for a female companion.

In her letters with Adams, Warren first uses her new sentimental, epistolary perspective as a playwright and historian in order to bring to the forefront the possibility that history’s classical models may not be appropriate paragons for the present. Warren explicitly narrates an epistolary tonal shift that mirrors the philosophical transition from Stoicism to sentimentalism when she says, “I must speedily descend from the Altitudes of Heroism, and talk in the simple stile of the Manufacturer and the Humbler Language of the Domestic Dame: who seeketh Wool and Flax and Worketh Willingly with her hands.”32 Warren associates the “Altitudes

Notably, Warren refrains from creating a character portrait but rather uses the description of the “Altitudes of Heroism” to represent Stoicism as an intangible, lofty, and glorified public ideal that she wants to leave in the past.

Warren then alternatively uses her new epistolary role as a playwright and historian to give voice to modern, female characters, such as the private “Domestic Dame,” treating the real world as her metaphorical stage. Warren uses language that evokes vertical movement with the words “descend” and “Altitudes,” building off of the spatial dichotomy that she establishes in her October 1776 letter between “sub- lime qualities” and “Terest[r]ial” bonds, in order to position the character of the “Domestic Dame” as a foil to republican Stoicism and antiquity. Warren highlights how this persona requires a “descent” away from past Roman fantasies and towards a pragmatic contemporaneity grounded in private domesticity and sentimentalism. Furthermore, Warren updates this modern, female classification of the “Domestic Dame” to reflect the present revolutionary circumstances, as these women’s roles in the late 18th century changed in response to men’s shifting roles. Warren reveals that this domestic classification is no longer distinct from the role of “the Manufacturer,” since a housewife “seeketh Wool and Flax” and also “Worketh Willingly with her hands.” Since men were now “Wading in the Field of Blood,” women needed to enter the public sphere as manufacturers in order to secure necessary materials for their families.33 Warren states that the manufacturers from Braintree, Adams’s estate, are led by “one of the Amphyctionic Ladies, to whom the Females of the united states, must in the Future Look up for the Example of Industry and oeconimy” (all emphasis in the quote is mine).34 The word “Amphyctionic” refers to the Amphictyonic League, a system of governance in ancient Greece in which “an association of town- states linked together to form a cultural and political union.”35 While Warren uses classical vocabulary, which might initially appear to contradict her shift from classical Stoicism to contemporary sentimentalism, she substitutes the word “League” with “Ladies,” modernizing the language to create a new contemporary portrait of a group of female leaders rather than an ancient council of men. Instead of fixating on the past, Warren updates this classical term to reflect a present classification of women, showing how female manufacturers were in an influential position to spur on a new, modern lineage of female exemplars.

Thus, not only is Warren able to use her epistolary roles as a playwright and historian to overturn exemplar history, but just like with patriotism and virtue, Warren detaches this methodology from its republican, Stoical, and masculine roots, repurposing it to highlight a female historical canon. Warren even explicitly uses the word “Example,” not to focus on imitating virtues from the past and observing masculine historical paradigms, but rather to pose a new virtuous example that is grounded both in the present and in women. Finally, instead of using the words “Look up” to continue the vertical, spatial visualization of Stoical, Roman matrons as

an antiquated ideal to which women should aspire, she replaces this ideal with the future-oriented exemplar of the modern, female manufacturer. Therefore, while Adams’s letters strategically employ epistolary performativity, Warren’s letters acknowledge Adams’s literary world-building but do not rhetorically position Warren as occupying the role of a performer. Warren complicates the idea of literary performativity by assuming the persona of a playwright and historian, two roles consistent with her actual roles in the public sphere, rather than embodying a character that is located outside of her own sense of self. By situating the roles of a playwright and historian, occupations inherently tied to the public sphere, within the private epistolary sphere, Warren creates a space for herself to criticize self-abnegation and classical allusions. The epistolary sphere ironically allows Warren to fully actualize her identity as a playwright and historian, opening her eyes to these public roles’ potential to capture the nuanced and constantly evolving classifications of modern-day women. Through her epistolary correspondence with Adams, Warrens taps into her new historical and literary voices, paving the way for a modernized use of the exemplar theory of history that originates with the female paragons of the present rather than the Roman matrons of the past. Warren’s repositioning of the traditionally public genres of plays and histories as private, domestic, and epistolary genres suggests that Warren might be starting to create a new role of authorship for herself entirely — that of the modern biographer.36

Conclusion As I argued in my introduction, just because scholars have remembered the “Remember the Ladies” letter, it does not mean that we have properly remembered and understood the literary legacies of historical women like Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren. Examining Adams’s and Warren’s 18th-century epistolary correspondence as “Portia” and “Marcia” through a literary perspective has served to complicate historical scholarship by challenging the binary correlations between women and the private sphere and men and the public sphere. Through her creation of a literary, pseudo-public sphere, Adams transitions away from historical parallels between antiquity and contemporaneity, instead constructing her own alternate reality as a means for her to envision a world that is parallel to the one in which she lived — in which she, as a woman, has access to public positions of political power. Warren ac- tualizes her individual, sentimental voice, allowing her to use epistolary writing to re-envision a public sphere in which she can use her identity as a playwright and historian to create literary characteriza- tions of contemporary women. Adams and Warren differed on exactly how to carve out spaces for their historical and literary voices, as Adams employs republican Stoicism and classical literary performativity, while Warren employs sentimentalism and a novel, modern adaptation of literary performativity. Nevertheless, both women ultimately rewrote the classical models of republican Stoicism and the exemplar theory of history. Adams’s letters to Warren radically pushed the limits of epistolary writing by envisioning an alternate version of the public sphere, reimagining the history of the American Revolution entirely in order to grant women access to the public sphere as well as public positions of authority. Warren’s letters to Adams created an alternate, female-oriented literary lens to interpolate into the historical documentation of the American Revolution. I personally find hope in how these two women, who lived within a re- strictive and republican society, were able to use epistolary writing as a tool to bridge the literal spatial gap between them and to figure out imaginative ways in which they could bridge the public-propagated gap between the private and public spheres. Through complicating the relationship between private and public spheres of influence, Adams and Warren explore the interconnected relationship between what it means and should mean to have a public voice as a woman in late 18th-century America. ◆

title: Op-Ed: The Burgeoning Academic Field of Existential Risk
notes: Opinion essay on existential-risk research, with footnoted sources and a bar chart (Figure 1) of academic paper counts by topic. The first word's drop cap "T" is a separate block (89.3).
text:
Op-Ed: The Burgeoning Academic Field of Existential Risk by Manuel De Leon

The field of existential risk has grown rapidly in the last few years, with new research organizations sprouting up all over the world. This work focuses on maintaining humanity’s long-term potential by reducing the probability of catastrophic threats, such as extreme climate change, nuclear winter, engineered pandemics, and unaligned artificial intelligence. While often disregarded by academics as fanciful or overly apocalyptic, a brief glance at the literature shows that the risks we face in the next century are worth further consideration. While the topic has not yet been widely discussed at Northwestern University (NU), beginning steps have been taken towards researching existential risk, and further initiative will hopefully be taken in the future to bring this important subject to the forefront of research.

An existential risk is a risk that threatens the destruction of humanity’s long-term potential.1 While mostly discussed in the context of extinction, this could also include an unrecoverable collapse or dystopia. The stakes of such a catastrophe are literally astronomical,2 not only harming the 7.8 billion people living now, but also foreclosing the flourishing of all future generations. With so much at stake, thinkers in the discipline believe that even small reductions in the probability of existential risk would generate massive expected value. This research has been undergirded by a philosophy of longtermism,3 which argues that if one wants to do the most good, they should focus on long time scales, perhaps thousands or millions of years into the future. Even if one only examines impacts to people alive today, there seems to be a common-sense case4 for existential risk reduction. For instance, some in the field argue that the risk of human extinction over the next century is around one in six,5 which could have major implications within our lifetimes.

While pressing, many of these concerns are severely neglected in research when compared with other, perhaps less threatening concerns (Fig. 1).

This lack of attention stems from an intuition that existential risks are far-fetched. For instance, in the words of NU Economics Professor Scott

1 Ord, T. (2020). Chapter 2: Existential Risk. In The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity (pp. 37–37). Bloomsbury Publishing.

2 Bostrom, N. (2013, February). Existential Risk prevention as Global priority. Global Policy Volume 4 . Issue 1. Retrieved February 2022 from https://www.existential-risk.org/concept.pdf

3 MacAskill, W. (2020). What We owe the Future. YouTube. Retrieved February 2022, from https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vCpFsvYI-7Y.

4 Wiblin, R., & Harris, K. (2021, October 7). Carl Shulman on the common-sense case for existential risk work and its practical implications. 80,000 Hours. Retrieved February

24, 2022, from https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/carl-shulman-common-sense-case-existential-risks/

5 Ord, T. (2020). Chapter 6: The Risk Landscape. In The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity (pp. 167). Bloomsbury

Publishing.

Ogawa, “Most of them are overblown. … I think this idea of all life going out is preposterous.”6 Once we look more closely, though, it may be the case that this skepticality is the work of cognitive biases. For instance, one must be wary of the availability heuristic, a mental shortcut that assumes something is important only if it can be readily recalled. Since there have not been any catastrophes of this magnitude, these risks are not salient to politicians and the public.7 Similarly, when the numbers become too large, people become numb to the effect of saving lives, causing decision-makers to treat existential risks in a similar way to problems that are less severe by many orders of magnitude.8

Fortunately, there are some strides being made at NU to address these risks. For instance, in collaboration with Underwriters Laboratories, the University has recently created the Center for Advancing Safety of Machine Intelligence9 in order to lower the risk posed by emerging technologies. While progress has been granular, I am optimistic about NU’s position in existential risk research and hope that more academics will use their cross-disciplinary skills to preserve the long-term future. ◆

title: The Role of Habit in Kafka’s “The Burrow” and Proust’s Swann’s Way
notes: Senior thesis. Faculty adviser named on the opening page. Bibliography lines garbled in the text layer (98.4-98.10) are read from the page image.
text:
The Role of Habit in Kafka’s “The Burrow” and Proust’s Swann’s Way by Nikol Kralimarkova

Department of Comparative Literary Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Samuel Weber, Ph.D.

Introduction

Across numerous fields of life, from psychology through philosophy to literature, habitude has been studied and reimagined for centuries. Psychologically, a habit is an energy-efficient behavioral response to any repetitive context, a preservative drive across living creatures, from humans to animals. The term is synonymous with automaticity, suggesting the learned exe- cution of the behavior without involving higher mental processes (Wood and Rünger 291). Normally, habit functions in parallel with a goal system, and the frequency of repetition infers the inten- tionality of a given behavior (Wood and Rünger 289). Towards the end of the 19th century, habit was explored as a pattern across species and cultures. William James, considered the father of American psychology, famously studies habit in The Principles of Psychology (1890), noting that living creatures are first and foremost seen as “bundles of habits” (James). James also describes distinctions of habit as either an innate tendency or instinct, or, if resulting from education, “an act of reason” (James). Further, external factors are shown to affect the balance between habit and goal-oriented behavior, with stress and distraction suppressing decision making and promoting reliance on habit (Wood and Dennis 301). Although habit is often regarded as a psychological term regarding common and necessary behavior in living beings, humans especially, it also remains a complex phenomenon, often problema- tized across the fields. James identifies the limitation of studying habit externally and as an objective, observable process despite the mental aspect remaining covert: “It thus appears that habit covers a very large part of life, and one engaged in studying the objective manifestations of mind is bound at the very outset to define clearly just what its limits are” (James). While psychology ends where the limits of the mind are set, literature can dilute these boundaries in fiction and offer a more disturbing account of habit. Two examples of that tendency of literature, also the critical objects of my analysis, are Franz Kafka’s short story “The Burrow” and Marcel Proust’s first of seven volumes of In Search of Lost Time, Swann’s Way.

Kafka and Proust both belong to the modernist literary movement of the late 19th to early 20th century. Although often regarded separately due to their different linguistic traditions, German and French respectively, both writers’ styles can be characterized with their rejection of traditional literary forms, experimenting with language and narration and di- recting literature towards the subjective experience of reality. With the rise of the bourgeoisie and the separation of private space — as sensory and habitual space — from the public, the theme of interiority and the interior grew too, inevitably followed by the importance of habit(-building). This inward focus on habitude and its implications can be traced in the two selected texts, making them key literary and fictional case studies of the phenomenon. The narrator in “The Burrow,” for instance, presumably a mole-like creature, is situated in the confined space of the burrow he inhabits, obsessively aim- ing to fortify it against external enemies through continual digging and inspection.

The story’s peculiar animal first-person narrative lacks continuous introspec- tion and portrays the subordination of habit to anxiety and the impossibility of forceful habituation in the absence of a feeling of safety. The visual landscape is limited, further suggesting the mole-like identity of the narrator, since moles are blind. However, the auditory scene is disrupted by the uncanny presence of an unidentifiable sound, which sends him on compulsive digging missions despite the planned calculations he attempts and always disrupts. The descriptive and discontinuous nature of the first-person narrative further questions the perspective of the narrator as external to himself, as he reports habitual actions without being able to reflect on them (Türk 152). The discontinuity in conscious memory due to the effects of habit is also illustrated in Swann’s Way, the first volume of Proust’s novel, in which the narrator Marcel is still a child preoccupied with the feeling of abandonment when his mother does not kiss him goodnight during a dinner with their friend Swann. The negative experience initially creates, similarly to “The Burrow,” discontinuity in the first-person narration (Türk 148). Although all seven volumes are in the first person, the second section of Swann’s Way, “Swann in Love,” describing Swann’s problematic romantic relationship with Odette, is ex- clusively in the third person and disrupts the narrator’s habitual mode. Swann, “the

“ ”

While psychology ends where the limits of the mind are set, literature can dilute these boundaries in fiction and offer a more disturbing account of habit.

unconscious author of [the narrator’s] sufferings,” and his role in the narrator’s development thus push the boy to overcome, or at least substitute, the habit of his mother’s past presence (Proust 756). In this light, habit is transformed from a potentially painful and anxious experience into a productive temporal medium upon which the narrator’s imaginative, isolated impressions of his familiar surroundings can be created. To study the role of habit in both texts, I will first briefly explore how its spatial dimension relates to the narratives and will then progress into temporal analysis of habit as repetition and discontinuity (of the narrative) in the modes of anxiety or positive imagination as a form of escapism.

(Subjective Experience of the) Spatial Dimension of Habit The familiar physical space of the narrators in “The Burrow” and Swann’s Way makes up the habitual landscape, but to position oneself in space, sensory input from the environment is key. Thus, the perception of (the self in) the landscape and its stability need to be characterized in order to introduce disruptions that problematize the effects of habit. For the narrator in “The Burrow,” the burrow is what he proclaims as his “own house,” but the origin and location of the place, as well as its exact relation to the narrator, remain unclear (Kafka 163). The German title of the short story is “Der Bau,” which only means “building” since the article only indicates the gender of the noun and is not necessarily a definite article. The phrase does not point to a specific building or burrow (because a building is normally to be found above the ground) to refer to as the narrator’s home. Apart from the numerous chambers he builds and modifies ceaselessly, the auditory cues — rather their absence — shape the narrator’s habitat: “The best thing about my burrow is the silence; of course this is deceptive, at any time the silence can suddenly be shattered, … but at present, it is still there” (Kafka 164). Even though the narrator somewhat eagerly recognizes the impermanence of the silence of the burrow, he praises that negative state of the burrow as ultimate and assumes it as the baseline habitual environment. Nevertheless, even in the opening pages of the story, the narrator continues to describe his environment rather carelessly: “I can hear nothing but the occasional rustling of some lesser creature … otherwise everything is quiet’’ (Kafka 164). Although the described uncertain “rustling” does not provide any certainty about the nature of the sound or creature, it appears that the silence is not at all absolute, and the narrator’s reaffirmation that “everything” is quiet is already refuted by his previous report. Despite his controversial statements, the narrator still discerns intruding sounds from his desired regular, quiet, auditory landscape that would maintain his peace. It appears that the narrator is already trying to impose a certain vision of what the burrow

[H]abit is transformed from a potentially painful and anxious experience into a productive temporal medium. “

” should feel and sound like, and the contra- dictions he presents germinate his sense of insecurity and anxiety.1

Similarly, the narrator in Swann’s Way has a well-defined scenery of his room, which is disturbed by the colorful magic lantern that is placed on top of his lamp to entertain him in his mother’s absence: “But my sorrows were only increased, because this change of lighting destroyed, as nothing else could have done, the customary impression I had formed of my room” (Proust 145). It becomes more obvious through Proust’s narrator that the customary landscape is a subjective impression, rather than a mere physical quality, of the place. Before the magic lantern, Marcel would habitually be sitting in his room in ag- ony, far from his mother, facing “the torture of having to go to bed in [the room]” (Proust 145). In this case, the stable “customary” scenery is where anxiety nests. The narrator’s initial encounter with the magic lantern is overwhelming because of the abrupt change of scenery, which resembles the Burrowman’s response to the change of sound. Be it a state of sound or light, the constancy of subjective perception, or habituation, is only realized when confronted with change, such as a foreign sound or color. However, unlike the narrator in “The Burrow,” Marcel is upset by habit, and its invasive destruction by the magic lantern only offers him an alternative form of escapist habitude. Knowing how the characters position themselves in their space makes possible the exploration of the various temporal effects of habit in the occurrence of disruptions of the context’s stability.

Temporality of Habit in Kafka Once habit is formed, the habitual response to the given contextual cues occurs without making a decision to perform it, indicating that a mental representation of the habitual response is taking place as soon as the cues are perceived (Wood and Rünger 292). This mechanism of habitual response suggests immediate reaction upon presentation of a cue, such as the Burrowman’s uncontrollably repetitive springing into action. As the abnormal reaction overrides the imagined order and comfort, the narrator phases into a state of thoughtless, already automized, habit:

[U]sually after I have been startled out of my sleep, it seems that the current distribution of provisions is completely wrong, that it can lead to great dangers, and that immediately, in all haste, without regard for sleepiness and fatigue, the situation must be corrected; then I hurry, then I fly, then I have no time for calculations, I … arbitrarily seize whatever lands between my teeth, dragging, carrying, moaning, groaning, stumbling, and any random change in the present situation, which seems to me so extremely dangerous, it the only thing that will satisfy me (Kafka 166).

This passage is one of the many re- peating episodes of senseless, perhaps compulsive, behavior of the narrator when presented with a danger — even a potential one. The frequency of “usually” indicates that an unidentified reason startles him out of his sleep habitually, and his thoughtless actions are a reflex — an instinctive unconscious response. If there is a real threat, then strangely, his actions do not produce truly self-preser- vatory behavior, such as fight-or-flight, but rather a stagnating repetitive circu- lar pattern. The fact that the situation is repetitive and the narrator still does not have a learned, and therefore more structured, response indicates the ab-

1 In Freudian terms, anxiety defines what is considered dangerous, especially based on occurrence in the past and the anticipated repetition in the future (Türk 145).

sence of true habituation and feeling of comfort and only a spontaneous desire for such.

These observations are further supported by the first-person narrative in the passage. While Stahman claims that the first-person narrative is self-reflective in the story, another scholar suggests that the first person does not serve this role well because the overall descriptive nature of the narrative, with the observable actions of the mole (“then I hurry, then I fly”), would normally be associated with a third person narrative (Stahman 20) (Türk 152). However, the narration creates distance between the subject and his own actions through the first person, demonstrating a conscious break between his behavior and his conscious judgement. According to J.M. Coetzee, the iterative, habitual, present tense drives the narrator’s existence in the burrow entirely with only short glimpses of realization beyond habit (Türk 152). However, while a repeated, self-made, goal-oriented decision can automate one’s response to the same cue, the narrator in “The Burrow” is subordinate to another force that dictates his behavior — an antag- onist of habit. The estrangement between the narrator and the narrative becomes most obvious later on when he is asleep: “I remain here in deep sleep. I must have slept for a long time, roused only from the last sleep that already dissolves of its own accord; this sleep must be very light, for a hardly audible hissing wakes me” (Kafka 177). This passage is central to the story because of the paradoxical individual sentences and their discontinuity, which signify the quality of the narrative and the narrator’s relation to his existence in the burrow. The first sentence is an impossible statement. If the narrator is asleep, he is unconscious and therefore cannot report his current state. The following sentence then intro- duces an abrupt grammatical and semantic break from the previous statement. That same sentence is internally contradictory because of the cause of the narrator’s waking, for which the narrator initially blames his naturally fading sleep, and then ascribes it to the indefinite hissing2 sound, which raises the question of whether the hissing was already present upon his waking. The passage, through the gaps of narration and absurd conclusions of causality, illuminates the narrator’s impossibility of protecting himself and his sleep from the external noise or of imposing control, comfort, and therefore habit over his being in the burrow. Failing to habituate to the burrow, the narrator exhibits the habit3 of anxiety.

The narrator’s logic of how to detect the hissing again further reiterates the claim that the narrator does not feel safe in the burrow but wants to force habit onto himself: “I had to feel completely at home again in order to hear it; it is, so to speak, only audible to the ear of the homeowner who is truly exercising his authority” (Kafka 177). Here, the mole-like creature tries to impose on himself to feel at home and get into the habit of being home — but, if he truly feels at home, then he wouldn’t stay alert. His ear would be familiarized with the noises, and his attention might not even recognize the noise because of habit. It is when he feels not at home in his familiar living space that he steps out of habit and can register differences in his

2 Benjamin studies Kafka’s animals and suggests that an animal/beast could serve as a representation of Kafka’s deteriorating beast- like symptoms of tuberculosis (Türk 153). This might explain why the mole believes there is an animal and not anything else that might be making its way to his burrow, just like Kafka would be afraid of the “beast” taking over his body. 3 Habit, in this more lay, colloquial sense, doesn’t imply the psychological term in the introduction. Habit of anxiety is used in the sense of the vicious circle of anxiety and the repetitive anxiety attacks observed in “The Burrow.” space. The uncanny experience of his (lack of) authority upon realizing that the noise has been there for a long time without him realizing points to the conflicting dynamics that drive the narrator’s existence. On one hand, he desperately wants to cling to the inexistent constancy of the burrow and habituate, but on the other, his inability to control it (and himself) traps him in the habitual role of anxiety’s puppet. A further question to ask then would be: Can the intermittent hissing sound be a projection of his own anxiety, creeping in when he’s most vulnerable and least aware,4 as when he is asleep?

Temporality of Habit in Proust In Swann’s Way, habit and projections beyond it could look quite different. Proust’s narrator realizes early on that the habits his mother created for him — for example, reading stories to him without including the love scenes — altered his experience of the world, but only after he is left alone in his room. Having his mother around him created “the gaps which this habit made in [his] knowledge” (Proust 719). These gaps in knowledge could also indicate the gaps of his awareness, which is an effect of habit. Thus, the discontinuity of the narrator’s awareness in Swann’s Way, unlike the discontinuous narration in “The Burrow,” is imposed not by anxiety but by the mother figure. The separation from his mother, though, shapes the new setting to which the narrator needs to accustom himself, including the consequent separation anxiety: “Tomorrow night I should again be the victim of anguish and Mamma would not stay by my side. But when these storms of anguish grew calm I could no longer realise their existence” (Proust 756). The serial repetition of the narrator’s pain pathologizes the habitual cues to which he responds. As Freud says, “Anxiety is a mechanism that forms to compensate the helplessness of the anthropologically weak infant. … A danger-situation is a scene, in which a situation of helplessness — which is traumatic — is expected” (Türk 145). The continuous disruption of the old habit of having his mother around him becomes the new traumatic habit of being alone. Then, the reason for calming down is not specified, but it is evident that habituation to the traumatic stimulus occurs eventually and the narrator becomes unconscious of its existence, “no longer realizing” it. The introduction of the magic lantern to his troubled existence then produces a positive, imaginative effect on his perception:

[U]nsleeping, far from my mother and grandmother, my bedroom became the fixed point on which melancholy and anxious thoughts were centered. Someone has had the happy idea of giving me, to distract me on evenings when I seemed abnormally wretched, a magic lantern … in the manner of the master-builders and glass-painters of gothic days it substituted for the opaqueness of my walls an impalpable iridescence, supernatural phenomena of many colours, in which legends were depicted, as on a shifting and transitory window (Proust 145).

The magic lantern, the main disturbance of the narrator’s static yet anxious habitat, changes the scenery of the room and dis- tracts him by opening up the space to new imagery “as a window.” The magic lantern is indeed detrimental to providing stability of the narrator’s room and thus acts against habit, which in Marcel’s case, is a path to (habitual) escapism. The transience of the magic lantern breaks habit apart and offers ever-changing fragments to the

4 One is unconscious when asleep and in a way, that’s similar to being (partially) unconscious to your environment when habituated.

imagination. The habitual coexistence of the traumatic separation with the happy sensory impressions creates a complex web around the narrator’s memories of his early life in Combray, which fixates him on the isolated painful memories (Türk 148). However, the repetition and fragmen- tation of instants open the imaginative possibilities for the narrator in the form of artistic manifestations, the culmination of which is revealed in Time Regained, the last volume of In Search of Time Lost.

These imaginative possibilities can only exist upon the basis of habit whose elements can be used to recreate alternative visions of reality. A scene that beautifully depicts the realized potential of habit’s matter in transcending it, or at least substitut- ing it, is Marcel’s waking: “It is true, when morning drew near, I would long have settled the brief uncertainty of my waking dream, I would know in what room I was actually lying, would have reconstructed it round about me in the darkness … as an architect … , working upon an original” (Proust 3403). Just like in “The Burrow,” the narrator is situated just at the twilight of consciousness upon waking. It is the familiarity of the room to which he is accus- tomed that allows him to gain control over the space, like an architect, and reconstruct it in his mind’s eye in an instant — what the Burrowman never accomplishes. Marcel is able to perform this exciting waking exercise because he has already learned to manipulate the habitual and overcome the traumatic, at least temporarily, with the magic lantern. Instead of having the “master builders and glass painters” project their lantern’s images onto his habitual setting, he can now be the creative master himself, reshaping and decorating habitude. These mental skills later open up the narrator’s experience of the intermittencies of habit, the break from routine, and the emergence of involuntary memory, such as the most celebrated madeleine-tasting episode.

Habit in literature can teach us much, now even more than ever before. Literary giants Kafka and Proust both bring the theme of habit forward in “The Burrow” and Swann’s Way, as well as in the rest of the progression of In Search of Lost Time, that the scope of this paper could not include. They illustrate habit as either a driving force of anxiety or a productive medium for memory and imagination. As Kafka’s peculiar creature illuminates the darkest burrows of anxiety-driven life, his lack of reflexivity and pathological habits allow us to step away from the order of our routine and wonder — wonder not only about the nature of the Burrowman but also translate his existence to any other “Bau” that any of us could be inhabiting. Then, diminutively viewing Marcel’s traumatized childhood narrative, we are still drawn to experience his developing world of impressions, considered a defense mechanism or simply a beautiful, poetic way to master escapism. Experiencing these alternative, fictional realities of habit, we can hone what we already know from psychology and translate it to the human psyche and our own lives. The direction of this project naturally adapted to the current unprecedented reality and reimagined the significance of the discourse I wanted to join, bringing science and literature closer together to elucidate the powers of habit and promote more mindfulness among us, “bundles of habits” (James). ◆

THE FIRST

HOMOSEXUALS:

AN EXPOSITION OF

QUEERNESS IN ART by Morgan Willison

“

When you think about queerness and you think about Islamic art, there [are] two biases and cultural barriers you immediately encounter: … [the] belief that the Islamic art tradition is aniconic,” or lacks figural representation, and the idea that “the Islamic world, especially today, is associated with being a place that is un- accepting of queer people.” This is what College Fellow (2021–22) and Assistant Professor (Fall 2022–) of Art History Thadeus Dowad explained to me when we sat down to discuss an upcoming exhibition that he is working on: a collaborative exhibit of global representations of queerness in art. These assumptions, I would later learn, are wholly incorrect.

The show, titled “The First Homosexuals,” focuses on the time period immediately after the word ‘homosexual’ was coined in European sexological terms (approximately 1860–1950). The show takes a broad definition of homosexuality and queerness, examining “self-portraiture, self-presentation, and the ways in which queer desires figure even in abstract art,” in addition to more traditional paintings, sculptures, photographs, and drawings of same-sex couples.

Professor Dowad was still in the process of choosing the pieces that he wanted to highlight for this exhibition — in fact, he was putting together the final list the day we spoke. He was able to show me a few of the pieces he was considering, which is when I truly learned the extent of my mis- conceptions. I had gone into this interview curious about how queerness could exist in a culture that condemns figural representations. There’s a myth of a lack of represen- tational art, as Dowad explained:

[It] presumes that all of Islam is reducible to text, and it’s just not true. The Islamic world, both historically and today, is an incredibly rich, contradictory space, so there’s tons of figural representation — not only in my particular area of specialty, in this Eastern Mediterranean [region], but all over the Islamic world.

One of approximately 20 curators from all across the world for this exhibit, Dowad, compared to others, has a vast amount of area to cover, quite literally. He is in charge of assembling a collection of queer works from a large part of the Islamic world during this time period, namely the Middle East and North Africa, including Iran. In contrast, there is another curator solely in charge of Poland.

Dowad is excited about the scope of his responsibilities, though. “One of the reasons I’m really excited about this show,” he told me, “is because the period we’re working on here, the 1860s to the first half of the 20th century, is … the most under-researched, unattended sub-field of queerness in Islamic art.” Not only that, but this century is also “a period of serious crisis in [the Islamic world] because it’s being actively colonized at this time.”

A major factor of the colonization effort and colonial establishment in these regions was building art schools to teach European methods of depiction to the artists in this region. Whereas earlier Islamic art took the form of manuscript or wall painting, this period’s art is more commonly found on canvas and more traditional Western forms of the fine arts. The effect of these art schools is that “the kind of art that gets produced is highly disciplined by the colonial context, and those colonial contexts are deeply, deeply homophobic.”

In contrast to popular perception, earlier generations of Islamic art were rich with depictions of queer desire and same- sex attractions. In this period, however, explicit queerness was met with backlash or was highly sexualized. Orientalist art, as it is typically categorized, “has overt queer themes, but always in a very denigratory way. … Artists in this period are having to fight back against [homophobic] stigma against their region,” resulting in significantly less “overt depiction of queerness in Islamic art … so [that] it doesn’t cater to these imposed stereotypes by colonial powers.” Dowad noted, “queerness in Islamic art, in this period especially, is not happening in a vacuum but is happening in a global and colonial context.” Dowad also stressed, “An important takeaway here is that when you think about queerness in Islamic art, it’s not a single thing. … What queerness is, and even what Islamic art is, changes based on your geography [and] your period in history.”

The international nature of this study is what really makes it special. “There’s never been a show like this,” Dowad told me. The show is planned to be split into themes, rather than geographic regions, allowing for artworks from all different cultures to be shown side by side.

In addition to choosing pieces from his region within this time period, Professor Dowad is also tasked with writing an essay to accompany the exhibit: “The hope for the catalog [of essays written by the curators] is that it will be a little bit like a textbook, because there’s no existing study like this.” When asked what it is like to be working on an exhibit that is truly the first of its kind, Dowad responded, “It’s exciting. It’s daunting. But my hope is that this will be the first stab trying to say something meaning- ful and comprehensive” about queerness and the themes of the time period.

The First Homosexuals opens at Wrightwood 659 in Chicago on Oct. 1, 2022. ◆
