Long Distance Nationalism:

Indian Americans and Hindutva by Akash Palani

Department of Political Science Faculty Adviser: Prof. Julie Lee Merseth, Ph.D.

Abstract What explains Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism? Following the election of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2014, Hindutva, or Hindu nationalism, has become a potent political force in India. In the Indian diaspora, particularly in the United States, the past decade has seen an increase in public activity related to Hindu nationalism. From the World Hindu Congress in Chicago to President Trump and Prime Minister Modi’s massive joint rally in Texas to demonstrations against Hindu nationalist citizenship laws in India, Indian Americans are now more vocal than ever about politics in India. This study employs regression analysis to identify key predictors of Hindu nationalism among Indian Americans. Religious identity and behavior, Islamophobia, and certain benchmarks of assimilation emerge as statistically significant. Little empirical work has been conducted on the subject of Hindu nationalism in the United States, especially after the ascendance of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2014. As one of the first surveys of Indian Americans focused on Hindu nationalism, this work evaluates the existing theoretical explanations for the phenomenon and helps set the agenda for future research. Furthermore, this study puts forth a method for quantitatively measuring attitudes towards Hindu nationalism: the index of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Section I. Introduction What explains Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism? And, what are the roles of religious behavior and assimilation in the emergence of these attitudes? Hindu nationalism and its ideological foundation, Hindutva, have become a powerful political force in India in the past decade. With the election of Prime Minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2014, the movement became the dominant strain in Indian politics, reified by the BJP’s landslide wins in the 2019 parliamentary elections. Hindu nationalism itself has roots in colonialism and confrontations with globalization, and it is therefore unsurprising that the vast Indian diaspora has a complex, varied relationship with the movement and Indian politics more generally.

Indian Americans who profess some form of support for Hindu nationalism are participating in the nationalism of a nation in which they have not resided for some time, or even never resided. Especially given the relatively recent entry of Hindu nationalism into the Indian political mainstream and the general rise of right- wing political movements globally, Indian Americans’ attitudes towards Hindutva are a puzzling phenomenon. Few studies have been published looking into this phenomenon in the past decade, during which Hindu nationalism has come to dominate national politics in India. By conducting this research now, I hope to capture some of the effects that this change in Indian politics may have had on Indian Americans’ attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. I use regression analysis of original survey data as the main methodological tool of this research. The findings of this study provide an empirical evaluation of existing theories in the past decade’s new political context. They also help direct urgently needed future research regarding the processes through which Indian Americans form attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.

Section II. Literature Review and Hypotheses To identify key predictors of Hindu nationalism among Indian Americans, I develop a framework that considers religious participation, identity, Islamophobia, and assimilation. The attitudes of many Indian Americans towards Hindu nationalism can best be characterized as “tacit acceptance” (Kurien 2007, 238). To be sure, there are those who are avowed Hindu nationalists, committed to the goals of Hindutva. Both ardent nationalists and quiet supporters are of interest to this study. In the following pages, I present a theoretical framework for how many Indian Americans are exposed to the ideas of Hindu nationalism and how they develop attitudes towards the movement.

Religious Identity, Behavior, and Attitudes Identification with and participation in American Hinduism is likely related to approval of Hindu nationalism. Hinduism in the United States is far more ecumenical and Sanskritic than the vast diversity of Hindu practice found in India (Kurien 2007). These characteristics, while seemingly incongruent with Hinduism in India, are quite similar to the version of Hinduism espoused by the Hindu nationalist movement. Kurien describes “popular” and “official” aspects of American Hinduism

(2007), with popular Hinduism referring to the daily devotional lives of American Hindus and official Hinduism referring to the version of Hinduism crafted by large umbrella organizations. Some of these umbrella organizations, such as the Vishwa Hindu Parishad of America (VHPA), have explicit ties to the Hindu nationalist movement in India (Rajagopal 2000, 479). Many others are not explicitly linked to Hindutva but espouse values and a version of Hinduism that bears stark similarities to those of the Hindu nationalist movement (Rajagopal 2000). While these two facets of American Hinduism, popular and official, may appear disconnected, they interact to shape Hinduism in the United States to be reflective of Hindutva ideology.

The relationship between American Hindu umbrella organizations and Hindu nationalism is clear. Perhaps the most prominent example is the VHPA. A direct offshoot of the Hindu nationalist Vishwa Hindu Parishad, VHPA — founded in 1970 — is one of the oldest Hindu umbrella organizations in the United States and has chapters in 15 U.S. states (Rajagopal 2000, 473; VHPA 2020). VHPA publishes literature promoting a “Hindu way of life,” in addition to organizing religious lectures, seminars, and service projects in India. The organization projects an image of cultural authenticity and leverages this image to shape the American public understanding of Hinduism “almost entirely along the grain of Hindutva thought” (Mathew and Prashad 2000, 526). The influence of Hindutva is clear in the literature published by the VHPA. One recent blog post about unrest in Delhi discusses Hindus being “brutally killed” and portrays Muslims involved in the unrest as organized, militant anti-Hindus (VHPA 2020). The post neglects to mention the 35 Muslims killed during the unrest (Pasha 2020), offering a prime example of the VHPA’s Hindu nationalist slant.

The VHPA is not the only umbrella organization that promotes Hindutva-informed Hinduism in the United States. The Hindu American Foundation, founded in 2004, is not explicitly aligned with any political movement and instead pur- ports to educate the American public about Hinduism and ensure that Hindus are accurately represented in public discourse (Hindu American Foundation 2021). Still, its founding president and other staff have been directly involved with the VHPA (Rao 2003). Other major American Hindu umbrella organizations include the Hindu Students Council, the Infinity Foundation, and more; see Kurien 2007 for a detailed discussion. Many of these umbrella organizations share two key similarities: they seemingly exist to promote awareness of Hinduism and Hindu culture in the United States, but their messaging is also closely aligned with Hindu nationalist ideas. Participation in these organizations is

“

”

Many of these umbrella organizations share two key similarities: they seemingly exist to promote awareness of Hinduism and Hindu culture in the United States, but their messaging is also closely aligned with Hindu nationalist ideas.

almost definitely related to higher levels of support for Hindu nationalism, but most Indian Americans are not active members. The key takeaway is that American Hindu umbrella organizations have a major role in shaping American understanding of Hinduism with a distinctly Hindutva slant.

Next, I turn to the interaction between Hindu umbrella organizations and “popular” American Hinduism, or the ways in which American Hindus practice their religion in their daily lives. Through her extensive ethnographic fieldwork, Kurien finds that worshipping at temples, attending meetings of local Hindu associations, and practicing Hindu rituals at home are the primary ways through which a large number of American Hindus practice their religion (2007). These seem to be strictly religious practices. However, the connection between these seemingly private practices and the aforementioned Hindu umbrella organizations is intimate and far-reaching. Rajagopal writes, “They [VHPA] form a network of contacts and affiliations with other Indian religious and social organizations in the U.S., and often their own members may occupy prominent positions in these other organizations. Thus, its influence extends well beyond its enrollment.” Taken together, the synthesis between official and popular Hinduism in the U.S. makes Indian Americans who participate in organized Hinduism more likely to be exposed to Hindu nationalist ideas and, in turn, more likely to express higher levels of support for these ideas.

As a crucial tenet of Hindutva thought, Islamophobia must also be considered. From the 2000 riots in Gujarat to state violence in Kashmir, Islamophobic policy and action have been a prominent feature of Hindutva praxis. The 2016 National Asian American Survey found that Indian

Americans tend to be more Islamphobic than the nation as a whole (Ramakrishnan et al. 2016). Kapur arrived at the same finding in 2010. In fieldwork conducted with Indian American lobbyists, Therwath found “streaks of virulent Islamophobia” and argued that Islamphobia unites disparate professional Indian American lobbyists to advocate for Islamophobic U.S. foreign policy (2007). After the 2000 riots in Gujarat, Nussbaum found that Indian Americans played a significant role in financing right-wing Hindu nationalist violence during the riots and outlined a number of networks through which Hindu nationalists in the U.S. offer material support to their extremist counterparts in India (2003). There is overwhelming evidence that harboring Islamophobic attitudes is associated with higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Assimilation Assimilation is both a process and an outcome. The temporal dimension of assimilation, both within and across immigrant generations, is quite important. To measure assimilation, I draw from the sociological literature on the subject, with socioeconomic status, intermarriage, linguistic patterns, and spatial dispersion as key factors in assessing assimilation (Waters and Jimenez 2007). I adapt these factors in my own measures of Indian American assimilation, discussed further in the methodology section of this paper.

In the U.S., Asian Americans as a whole are confronted with an ambiguous racial positionality. Masuoka and Junn’s prism model of the contemporary American racial hierarchy offers a useful framework for understanding this ambiguity. They posit that while Asian Americans’ proximity to whiteness is higher than other minority groups, their relationship to “Americanness” is still fraught. Their position in the periphery of the in-group of American society leads them to draw stricter boundaries on American national identity than their counterparts in the core (white Americans), especially on characteristics that are more accessible to Asian Americans (Masuoka and Junn 2013).

I argue that this strict enforcement of boundaries represents a desire, at least in some Indian Americans, to assert their belonging in the United States. Multiculturalism in the U.S. demands that immigrants construct an ethnic identity for public performance (Walzer 1999). For many Indian Americans, Hindu nationalism and the neat, strictly defined version of Hinduism espoused by its adherents offers a convenient identity for those Indian Americans seeking to assimilate into U.S. society. Rajagopal expands on this approach, arguing that the development of an ecumenical Hindu American identity provides a way for Indians to navigate their ambiguous position in the polarized racial hierarchy of the United States. He writes, “For Indian [Americans], to be ‘Hindu’ is to bask in Orientalist visions of an ancient civilization and so compensate at the present time for its bygone glories while muting the stigma of racism” (Rajagopal 2000, 472-473). Mathew and Prashad describe this turn to Hindu identity as an “ontological reversal of racism” (2000). When confronted with racism and white supremacy, some Indian Americans assert the superiority of their own perceived Aryan identity in response (Mathew and Prashad 2000). They argue that Indian American support for Hindutva is as much a response to racism in the United States as it is an expression of affinity for the Hindu Right in India.

Based on the preceding theoretical discussion, the following hypotheses are formulated and tested by this study: 1. Indian Americans who self-identify as Hindu are more likely to express higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Hinduism in the U.S. is characterized by many of the Sanskritic, ritual-focused aspects emphasized by Hindutva’s con- ception of the religion. Self-identification as Hindu by Indian Americans may therefore be related to more agreement with Hindutva broadly. 2. Higher levels of participation in religious organizations are more likely to be related to higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Participation in Hindu religious organizations reinforces perceptions of Hinduism that are closely aligned with Hindu nationalist ideas. In turn, Indian Americans who participate in such organizations are more likely to support Hindu nationalism more broadly. 3. Negative perceptions of Islam are more likely to be related to higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Hindu nationalist policy and activity are deeply Islamophobic. Indian Americans who express negative attitudes towards Islam will be more likely to agree with Hindutva ideology. 4. Higher scores on assimilation benchmarks are more likely to be related to higher levels of Hindu nationalist sentiment.

Highly assimilated Indian Americans express support for Hindu nationalist ideas as a consequence of their assimilation into American society. Confronted with an ambiguous racial positionality, they will be more likely to use the cohesive definition of Hindu offered by Hindutva to construct an identity for themselves.

Section III. Research Design The dataset for this research was constructed from an original survey of Indian Americans. Using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analysis, I tested the hypotheses presented in the previous section to identify statistically significant predictors of Hindu nationalist sentiment (HNS) in Indian Americans.

Survey and Data Collection I developed an original survey instrument to collect data for this project. The survey was hosted on Qualtrics1 and fielded by Bovitz, Inc., in the time frame of February 20, 2021, to March 1, 2021. A non-random sample of 256 Indian Americans was selected for data collection. To construct the sample, Bovitz sent the survey to respondents in its panel who self-identified as Indian American. As an additional check, a screener was included at the beginning of the survey to ensure that respondents identified as Indian American. The surveyed sample was not perfectly representative of the population of all Indian Americans, but I found a reasonable degree of consistency with national characteristics.2

Dependent Variable: Hindu Nationalist Sentiment The dependent variable in this study was the level of support for Hindu nationalism. This was a difficult concept to measure, especially in the context of the Indian diaspora. I adapted an approach from researchers at Lokniti, an Indian public opinion research center (Kumar et al. 2018), to develop an index of Hindu nationalist sentiment among Indian Americans. This approach casted a wide net, assessing attitudes towards a variety of ideas, politics, and policies that can be classified as Hindu nationalist. Respondents were asked to indicate whether they strongly agree, somewhat agree, neither agree nor disagree, somewhat disagree, or strongly disagree with the following six statements:

1. India is the homeland and holy land for all Hindus. 2. All Hindus should adhere to a certain set of rituals and practices. 3. Prime Minister Modi and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) are taking India in the right direction. 4. The demolition of the Babri Masjid was justified. 5. The 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act is good for India. 6. Hinduism is the one true path to enlightenment. Statement 1 addresses one of the core ideological tenets of Hindu nationalism. The movement views India as both home- and holy-land for Hindus only, an idea which it uses to assert both the indigeneity of Hindus and the non-indigeneity of Muslims, Christians, and others. This forms the basis of the exclusionary politics of Hindutva. Statements 2 and 6 address the degree to which respondents agree with Hindutva’s definition of Hinduism. While there is vast diversity found in the practice of Hinduism across India and the Indian diaspora, the Hindu nationalists’ idea of Hindu practice is more narrow, emphasizing a specific set of rules and rituals that Hindus must follow. Statement 3 addresses attitudes towards Prime Minister Modi and the BJP. The current Indian regime, in power since 2014, represents a major increase in political power for Hindu nationalists. Modi and the BJP have vigorously pursued Hindu nationalist rhetoric and politics, making attitudes towards Modi and the BJP an important

1 Access provided by Northwestern University Weinberg College of Arts & Sciences 2 See Table 2 for sample characteristics and discussion of external validity measure of Hindu nationalist sentiment. Finally, Statements 4 and 5 address key events that function as litmus tests for HNS. The demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya is widely perceived as a landmark event in the history of Hindu nationalism. A long-standing Muslim place of worship was destroyed by militant Hindu nationalists who asserted that the masjid was located on the site of the Hindu god Rama’s birthplace (Buchetta 2000). Ayodhya re-entered the spotlight in 2020, with Prime Minister Modi breaking ground on a Hindu temple on the site of the demolished mosque (Gettleman and Kumar 2020). The 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) introduced changes to India’s definition of citizenship that was exclusionary of Muslims and was thus considered a landmark victory for Hindu nationalist politics. The CAA sparked widespread, sometimes violent protests throughout India and the Indian diaspora (Tandon 2020), making it a useful litmus test for HNS.

Using these statements, I constructed an index of Hindu nationalist sentiment for each respondent. Responses to each statement were assigned a weight on a scale from 1 to 5, with 1 corresponding with strong disagreement, 3 corresponding with neutrality, and 5 corresponding with strong agreement. These statement weights were then averaged to assign an HNS index score to each respondent. Thus, higher scores on the index reflected stronger agreement with Hindu nationalism.

Independent Variables The independent variables in this study were categorized into three sets: religion, assimilation, and demographic controls. Four variables were included in the religion set: religious identity, participation in Hindu organizations, Islamophobia towards Muslims in the United States, and

Islamophobia towards Muslims in India. Religious identity was measured by a cate- gorical variable constructed from a survey question in which respondents were asked to report their religious identity from a set of options or to report an identity not included in the options. To measure the level of participation in organized American Hinduism, I constructed an index. Respondents were asked to report the frequency with which they participated in the five major types of organizations identified by Kurien in 2007: local associations, temples, internet forums, student organizations, and umbrella organizations. As an additional measure of participation, I adapted questions from the 2016 National Asian American Survey (Ramakrishnan et al. 2016) regarding leadership positions in religious organizations and attending temples for reasons other than worship. In all, the following seven statements were presented to respondents.

1. Attend a local Hindu organization meeting (Balavihar, satsang, etc.). 2. Pray at a temple. 3. Participate in Hindu internet forums. 4. Engage in Hindu identity-based activism/advocacy. 5. Participate in a Hindu student organization. 6. Serve in a leadership position in a religious organization. 7. Visit a temple with people for reasons other than worship. For each statement, participants were asked to report the frequency with which they participated in each activity (Daily, Weekly, A few times per month, Monthly, A few times per year, Never). A weight from 1-6 was assigned to each response, with 1 corresponding with never, 2 with a few times per year, 3 with a few times per month, and so on. As I discussed above, there was a great degree of interaction between different types of organizations, and in this study, I was interested in assessing the relationship between overall level of participation in organized American Hinduism rather than the impact of specific organization types. To capture this, I computed the mean of each participant’s response to each of the seven statements and assigned that mean as an index of participation. To measure Islamophobia, participants were asked to indicate the degree to which they thought Muslims were a threat to the United States and to India.

I relied on Waters and Jimenez’s framework for assessing immigrant assimilation. According to their review of the sociological literature, key metrics of assimilation include socioeconomic status, residential segregation, intermarriage, and English language acquisition (2005). The most widely used measure of residential segregation was the index of dissimilarity, D (U.S. Census Bureau 2016).3 I adopted the idea of capturing dissimilarity as a measure of residential segregation. Each respondent was asked to report approximately how much of their neighborhood is Indian and/or Indian American. I also constructed variables measuring perceptions of inter- and intra-generational socioeconomic mobility, English language acquisition, and interra- cial/inter-ethnic relationships.

To operationalize confrontations with ambiguous racial positionality, I included perceptions of discrimination as an additional measure of assimilation based on Vijay Prashad’s work (2000). There are a variety of scales used to measure perceptions of discimination (see Williams 2016). I used a common scale for everyday discrimination put forth by Williams et al. (1997) and computed an index of discrimination for each respondent using a similar methodology to those outlined for other indices in this study. Lower scores indicated more frequent perceptions of discrimination.

I also included a set of controls. Hindu nationalist imagery and messaging is dominated by masculinity. Banerjee termed the image of India projected by Hindu nationalists a “masculinized vision of a nation” (2006). I included gender as a control factor to account for the possible effects that the masculinity of Hindu nationalism may have had. I included another control for the immigrant generation, constructed from questions on self, parent, and grandparent nativity. Finally, I included a control for U.S. political ideology. The exclusionary stance that Hindu nationalists take towards minorities, especially Muslims, is incompat- ible with American liberal ideology (Hetherington and Weiler 2010), so self-identified liberals may be less supportive of Hindu nationalism on the whole. Furthermore, the closeness of Prime Minister Modi and President Trump may have led conservative

3 See White 1986 for details on how the index of dissimilarity is computed.

Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism, therefore, vary significantly and are not heavily skewed in favor of or against the movement. “

”

Indian Americans to view Hindu nationalism more favorably. The results of the 2020 Indian American Attitudes Survey showed that there may not have been a significant consistency between their attitudes towards U.S. and Indian politics (Badrinathan et al. 2020). So, while there is some empirical ambiguity about the relationship between U.S. political ideology and Hindu nationalist attitudes, the strength of the theoretical relationship justifies the inclusion of this control. Finally, I included a control for North vs. South Indian origin, as the BJP’s electoral performance in North India is generally much stronger than in South India.

Regression analysis Table 1 summarizes the OLS regression models used in this study. This iterative approach to model building in multivariate regression analysis allows for the demonstration of relationships that persist even in the presence of additional factors, an indicator of a strong correlation. With a quite limited body of work on the subject, this large-N correl- ative approach yields insights into more population-level trends than have been previously identified. Therefore, while the results of regression analysis do not imply causality, the identification of significant predictors of Hindu nationalist sentiment allows for an empirical test of existing hypotheses and helps set the tone for future research.

Section IV. Results and Implications Below, I present a discussion of my findings from the regression analysis and an examina- tion of descriptive statistics. For full regression output, see Appendix B. For detailed variable characteristics, see Appendix C.

Descriptive statistics The key dependent variable in this study is the index of HNS. HNS is computed on a scale from 1 to 5, with higher values in-

S Figure 1. Distribution of Hindu Nationalist Sentiment Index dicating higher levels of support for Hindu nationalist ideas. An index score of 1 indicates strong disagreement, 3 indicates neutrality, and 5 indicates strong agreement.

Figure 1 represents the distribution of the HNS index. The mean index score was 3.09 with a variance of 0.95. Therefore, while the average respondent could accurately be classified as expressing “tacit approval” for Hindu nationalism as discussed above, there is significant variation in the sample. A slightly greater number of respondents indicated less than neutral attitudes towards Hindu nationalism than those indicating positive attitudes, but the split is fairly even. Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism, therefore, vary significantly and are not heavily skewed in favor of or against the movement.

Evaluating Hypotheses

Religious Identity, Behavior, and Attitudes I find strong evidence in support of Hypothesis 1, leading me to conclude that Indian Americans who self identify as Hindu are more likely to express positive attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. It is worth noting that the self-identified Hindu group had the highest coefficient magnitude of any predictor and that no other religious identities had a significant relationship with attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.

Figure 2 is a box plot depicting the HNS index broken down by religious identity. This plot underscores the extent to which self-identification as Hindu affects attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. Not only is the mean response for the Hindu group quite a bit more positive than other

S Figure 2. Hindu Nationalist Sentiment by Religious Identity

Assimilation variables Assimilation variables

Controls groups, but the entire distribution also skews more positive compared to any other group. It would be reasonable to expect that, for instance, Indian American Muslims would be less likely to support Hindu nationalism due to the movement’s explicit Islamophobia. While the descriptive statistics shown in Figure 2 do offer some evidence for this expectation — Muslims are the group with the most generally negative attitudes towards Hindu nationalism — no religious identity other than Hindu emerged as statistically significant in regression analysis. With only Hindu identity emerging as significant, the evidence suggests that the characteristics of Hinduism in the United States, not of other religious identities, are one of the key mechanisms at play.

Hypothesis 2 is also supported by the results of regression analysis. Increased overall levels of participation in Hindu organizations in the United States make Indian Americans more likely to express agreement with Hindu nationalist ideas. This confirmation of Hypothesis 2 offers an important complement to Hypothesis 1. There is clear evidence that American Hindus’ acceptance of Hindu nationalist ideas is not a result of some endogenous feature of Hinduism as a religion. Rather, the evidence suggests that Hindu umbrella organizations in the U.S. have developed a Hindutva-oriented outlook on the Hindu religion and identity through multiple processes. From the organized Hindu Right’s efforts to promote Hindu nationalism through the VHPA to immigrant selection through the U.S. immigration system, numerous factors unrelated to Hindu the- ology have shaped official American Hinduism to be accepting of Hindu nationalist ideas. Confirmation that Indian Americans’ participation in and identification with Hinduism increases their likelihood of expressing agreement with Hindu nationalism demonstrates the extent of the influence that official American Hindu organizations have in day-to-day life for Indian American Hindus. This synthesis of popular and official Hinduism, then, offers a strong explanation for Indian American attitudes towards Hindu nationalism.

Finally, I find compelling evidence in support of Hypothesis 3, which states that Islamophobic attitudes are associated with higher levels of HNS. Negative perceptions of Muslims in India and in the U.S. both emerged as significant predictors of stronger HNS. Earlier in this paper, I cit- ed the Modi regime’s passage of the 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act as an example of Hindu nationalism’s fundamental Islamophobia. The COVID-19 pandemic offers another recent illustration. Many of India’s television news channels harbor a heavy pro-BJP slant. As the deadly coronavirus spread through India, TV anchors scapegoated Muslims, referring to them with epithets ranging from “virus villains” to “human [COVID-19] bombs” (Yasir 2020).

S Figure 3. Hindu Nationalist Sentiment by Immigrant Generation

Given the virulent Islamophobia present in Hindutva ideology, rhetoric, and praxis, it is not particularly surprising that Indian Americans who harbor Islamophobic attitudes are more likely to support Hindu nationalist ideas. Somewhat troubling, though, is the fact that negative perceptions of Muslims both in India and in the U.S. are associated with higher HNS. I discuss Islamophobia in the American context in more detail in the final part of this section.

Assimilation Perceived loss of socioeconomic status, intermarriage, and English language proficiency did not emerge as statistically significant. Therefore, I refrain from drawing definitive conclusions regarding the direction of the relationship between assimilation and HNS. Still, two components of assimilation — perceptions of discrimination and residential segregation — do hold statistical significance. Higher levels of both of these measures are associated with greater support for Hindu nationalism.

The positive relationship between higher levels of discrimination and higher levels of support for Hindu nationalism lends support to Mathew and Prashad’s proposed “reverse racism” mechanism (2000). Taken alone, it would be an over- reach to argue that perceptions of discrimination alone are sufficient to draw conclusions about assimilation more broadly. Still, the significance of perceived discrimination deserves a nuanced discussion. Experiences of discrimination may serve to remind many Indian Americans of their ambiguous position in the racialized hierarchy of U.S. society, thereby creating a desire for belonging. As I explained earlier, Hindutva’s Hinduism offers this feeling of belonging by crafting a version of Hinduism that is compatible with, or even desired by, American society. Thus, Indian Americans who experience higher levels of discrimination may be drawn to Hindu nationalism as a way to grapple with desires for belonging in American society.

Especially in the context of rising anti-Asian racism in the United States, this finding is particularly important. In April 2021, a white mass shooter in Indianapolis killed eight workers at a FedEx facility, four of whom were Sikh Indian Americans (Mervosh et al. 2021). While the motive of the shooter remains under investigation, he is reported to have accessed white supremacist websites (Contreras 2021). Combined with the general climate of anti-Asian sentiment in the U.S., it is likely that Indian Americans have perceived higher levels of discrimination during this recent wave of violent acts and rhetoric. Some of these individuals, including those who have not previously supported Hindu nationalism, may turn to the movement to find a sense of belonging in an American society that has increasingly alienated them.

While residential segregation is one of the benchmarks of immigrant assimilation

“The Hindu Right ... has both effectively shaped public perceptions of Hinduism and influenced the day-to-day religious lives of American Hindus in favor of its religious- nationalist agenda.” outlined by Waters and Jimenez (2005), I refrain from arguing that the association found between higher concentrations of Indian Americans in an individual’s neighborhood and higher levels of support for Hindu nationalism provides sufficient evidence to reject Hypothesis 4. This is especially true given the moderate effect of segregation and the disappearance of statistical significance in the most robust model. Still, some interesting implications emerge. Immigrants living in areas with higher ethnic concentrations are more likely to be exposed to ethnic community organizations and media, thereby lowering the cost of the political mobilization for these residents (Ramakrishnan 2005). For Indian Americans, living in areas with higher concentrations of co-ethnics may lead to greater exposure to Hindu nationalist ideas through Hindu organizations.

More generally, I do not form any definitive conclusions regarding the nature or direction of the relationship between assimilation and support for Hindu nationalism. At the same time, I do not conclude a truly null relationship. Issues with how assimilation was operationalized in the quantitative portion of this study may be an explanation for the mostly null results I found. As both a process and an outcome, the temporal dimension of assimilation is important when assessing its effects. Capturing variation over time and between generations of immigrants within a single survey is difficult.

Implications The findings of this research hold numerous implications regarding the future of Hindu nationalism in the U.S. and the study of Indian American political attitudes and behavior. In this study, I have shown how the Hindu Right, op- erating through organizations of official Hinduism in the U.S., has both effectively shaped public perceptions of Hinduism and influenced the day-to-day religious’s lives of American Hindus in favor of its religious-nationalist agenda. Hindu nationalism will likely continue to be an important component of Indian American politics, and it is reasonable to expect that it will become increasingly popular in Indian American communities.

Even in this study’s sample, in which native-born Indian Americans were over- represented (see Table 2), there is significant, well-distributed variation in attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. Therefore, it is unlikely that Indian Americans will simply “age out” of affinity for Hindutva as the native-born population grows and matures. Immigrant generation was not a significant predictor of HNS in the regression analysis. Figure 3, which shows HNS index scores broken down by immigrant generation, further underscores how the strategies employed by the Hindu Right are effective regardless of nativity or immigrant generation.

S Figure 4. Hindu Nationalist Sentiment by Political Ideology

Although neither a perfectly representative nor truly random sample, this sample still generally aligns with national Indian American population characteristics on a number of parameters. Notably, foreign born Indian Americans are underrepresented, with 69% of the population being foreign born and only 47% being foreign born in the surveyed sample. This holds important implications for the interpretation of regression results presented in this section — and will be discussed further in the next sections. While median income appears to be slightly lower in the sample, respondents were asked to self-report income based on predetermined categories. Combined with respondents’ potential disinclination to accurately report income and the lack of more granular data, the lower median income present in the sample should not be taken as a serious issue for external validity. Educational attainment and age distributions in the sample broadly align with national characteristics with minor deviations. Taken as a rough proxy for Indian American political attitudes, the consistency of sample and population partisanship characteristics on this measure is a positive indicator of the external validity of this study. With the exception of nativity, which will be discussed later, most of this sample’s characteristics suggest that this study holds a strong degree of external validity, though the results are clearly not perfectly generalizable.

In short, demographics alone fail to explain Indian American support for Hindu nationalism. This failure, coupled with the evidence I have presented regarding the efficacy of Hindu nationalist strategies in the U.S., makes it clear that Hindu nationalism will likely continue to be a persistent force in the Indian American community.

For critics of Hindu nationalism, the intuitive response to this study may be to advocate for heightened policing and scru- tiny of American Hindus and American Hindu organizations writ large. Recent U.S. history demonstrates that this would be a disastrously misguided impulse. In the aftermath of the September 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center, the U.S. un- dertook unprecedented mass policing and surveilance of Muslim Americans, leading to significant, long-term negative consequences for those involved (see Quinlan 2015 for a case study of NYPD surveilance and its negative consequences of Muslim New Yorkers). This should not be replicat- ed. The consequences of Islamophobia are present even in the regression analysis presented above, with higher levels of Islamophobia being associated with more positive attitudes towards Hindu nationalism. Continued research into this phenomenon, further challenges to the racist and Orientalist foundations of Hindutva, and community-based organizing will prove far more productive for those interested in engaging critically with Hindu nationalism.

From Indian Americans’ financing of early-2000s Hindu nationalist violence in Gujarat (Nussbaum 2003) to Hindu nationalists’ successful campaign against a 2021 Chicago City Council resolution condemning the Indian regime’s nationalist violence (Husain and Byrne 2021), harboring HNS holds real-world ramifications for politics at all levels. If Indian Americans’

Hindu nationalist support is to persist, so too will its real-world consequences. Indian Americans are widely understood to be a generally Democratic voting bloc. Although they overwhelmingly favored President Joe Biden in the 2020 U.S. presidential election, a growing minority of Indian Americans have been voicing support for more conservative Republicans (Gjetlen 2020; Sirohi 2020).

At some level, this is very surprising, especially given the closeness of Modi and Trump. However, should there indeed prove to be a broader rightward shift in the voting behavior of Indian Americans in the coming years, the results of this study may offer some insight. Immigrant community organizations, including religious organizations, are important vehicles for political mobilization (Wong 2006, 119). The influence of the Hindu Right on American Hindu religious organizations, then, may be related to changing Indian American voter behavior. At the same time, partisanship and political ideology did not emerge as significant predictors of HNS in the regression analysis presented above.

Figure 4 shows a more detailed breakdown of HNS by political ideology. It appears that conservatives and even mod- erates lean more in favor of Hindu nationalism than liberals do. However, given the lack of statistical significance underneath this relationship, the question of the effect of political ideology on HNS remains unan- swered. The relationship between support for Hindu nationalism, political ideology, and voting behavior presents an urgent line of inquiry with immediate implications.

Section V. Conclusion There are a number of limitations to this study that should be discussed. The index of Hindu nationalism I construct as the dependent variable is unique in a number of ways. Few have constructed such an index for measuring sentiment in India, and this study is the first to construct such an index in the diasporic context. My construction of an index for Hindu nationalism is an important caveat for the interpretation of findings presented above. I emphasized capturing the wide set of ideas and political phenomena that can be classified as “Hindu nationalist.” Further research should look to refine measures of this concept and should also consider developing measures for sentiment intensity. While I capture variability, I was not able to capture how strongly Hindu nationalist sentiment is held among Indian Americans. Assessing knowledge of Hindu nationalism would be a useful place to begin measuring the strength of that sentiment. Understanding how strongly Indian Americans hold Hindu nationalist beliefs would enable researchers to unpack what makes a committed Hindu nationalist.

From Table 2, it is clear that foreign-born Indian Americans are underrepresented in the sample I used. The explanations for HNS I put forth in this study are robust in that they persist even when controlling for immigrant generation. However, it is highly likely that factors such as organizational participation and discrimination operate differently on different generations. For instance, second-generation immigrants may have quite different motivations for participating in Hindu religious organizations than their first-generation counterparts (parental insistence, for example). However, given the underrepresentation of first-generation immigrants in the sample, I am unable to quantify these differences, and future studies should look to sampling techniques that allow for better representation in this regard.

Caste and Hindu nationalism are inextricably linked. Indeed, many argue that caste and Hinduism itself are fundamentally related (Ambedkar 1936). I have discussed how Hindu nationalist ideology relies on a narrow set of Vedic, Sanskritic, and upper-caste rituals and practices in its pur- portedly universal definition of Hindu-ness. With upper-caste rituals playing such a crucial role in the very definition of Hindu nationalism, it is only reasonable to expect that attitudes towards caste factor into Hindu nationalist attitude formation. Caste is far from a relic of Indian history. It continues to play a major role in the lives of those living in India and in the diaspora. In 2020, a wave of caste-based discimination alle- gations swept through Silicon Valley (Rai 2020), providing just one example of caste’s relevance in the Indian American context. I included two questions about caste identity and the salience of caste identity in the survey instrument, but these data were ultimately excluded from the main dataset due to significant concerns over data quality and response bias. Undoubtedly, caste must play a prominent role in future attempts to explain attitudes towards Hindu nationalism, and the experience of this research shows the major methodological hurdles that exist for such an endeavor.

Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for future investigations of the relationship between Indian Americans and Hindutva. With little large-N empirical work conducted on this subject since 2014, or even at all, this study marks one of the first large-scale tests of existing theories about diasporic attitude formation regarding Hindu nationalism. By examining religious identity, attitudes, and behavior, as well as assimilation, I have conducted a wide — although not comprehensive — analysis of different factors that may be related to Indian American HNS. Building an understanding of this phenomenon not only advances academic understanding of the subject but also helps mitigate its more harmful effects. ◆

Appendices

Appendix A: Definitions of Key Terms Hindu nationalism — A political, social, and religious movement that aims to build a Hindu Rashtra (lit. “Hindu nation”) in India.

Hindutva — Literally “Hinduness,” Hindutva forms the ideological basis for the Hindu nationalist movement. Hindutva’s defines “Hindus” as the people for whom India is both homeland and holy land, emphasizing indigeneity through connection to the land and Aryan ancestry.

HNS — Throughout this study, the abbreviation HNS is used to refer to “Hindu Nationalist Sentiment,” a measure of the level of approval or disapproval an individual holds towards Hindu nationalism.

RSS — Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (lit. “National Volunteer Organization”). The civil society arm of the Hindu nationalist movement, the RSS works to promote Hindu values and Hindutva.

Sangh Parivar — An umbrella term referring to the collection of organizations spawned by and/or affiliated with the RSS.

BJP — Bharatiya Janata Party. The political arm of the Hindu nationalist movement, the BJP pursues a Hindu nationalist agenda and is the ruling party of India as of April 2021. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is the Parliamentary Chairperson of the BJP.

VHP — Vishwa Hindu Parishad (lit. “World Hindu Council”). The religious arm of the Hindu nationalist movement, the VHP works to “organise, consolidate, and serve Hindu society” (VHP 2020).

VHPA — Vishwa Hindu Parishad of America. An offshoot of the VHP, VHPA shapes the public image of Hinduism in the U.S., promotes what it considers Hindu values, and engages in various service projects in the U.S. and in India.

CAA — Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019. A controversial piece of legislation passed by the Indian Parliament in December 2019, the CAA makes various changes to Indian citizenship rules, notably excluding certain persecuted Muslims from Muslim-majority countries.

Immigrant Generation — First-generation immigrant is defined as a foreign born individual who has immigrated to the U.S. Second-generation immigrant is defined as a native born individual with at least one foreign born parent, and third-generation immigrant is defined as a native born individual with native born parents and at least one foreign born grandparent (Rumbaut 2006).

title: Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our Everyday Lives
notes: Senior thesis with abstract, based on interviews with Northwestern acting faculty, students and alumni. Faculty adviser named on the opening page ("Prof. Gail Shapiro, MFA"). The conclusion's last two paragraphs (132.30-132.31) are extracted after the bibliography on the same page and are placed before it here.
text:
Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our Everyday Lives by Nolan Fizoires Robinson II

Department of Theatre Faculty Adviser: Prof. Gail Shapiro, MFA

Abstract The following paper seeks to explore and discover how the tools and resources that actors gain throughout their training are applicable to vocations outside of just performing and in the process of everyday life. By conducting interviews with current Northwestern students, current and former Northwestern acting professors, as well as Northwestern alumni who are at the pinnacle of their fields in both the entertainment industry and professions outside of this particular industry, I use anecdotes and qualitative applications to dive into the substance, and not just the form, of acting — in short, this paper will share how techniques and skills related to the entertainment industry are crucial to more than just the actor. Furthermore, I argue that being an actor is akin to being a scientist and that the process an actor undergoes in preparing to play a role is a process one should try to implement in their own walk of life.

I. Introduction

“I like to say that if medical professionals get it right, we live longer and healthier lives. If economists get it right, we enjoy higher material standards of living. But without the arts — literature, dance, music, the visual arts, cinema, etc. — life loses its meaning. The arts inspire us, inform us, and help us understand differences. Nothing else comes close.”

— Northwestern University President Morton O. Schapiro

The impetus of this project began to grow from several places throughout my time at Northwestern University, the first of which was a class I registered for in the winter of my junior year: “Economics and the Humanities: Understanding Choice in the Past, Present, and Future.” The course — offered in the College of Arts and Sciences and taught by Morton O. Schapiro, American economist and University President, and Gary Saul Morson, American literary critic and internationally renowned scholar of Slavic studies — required its students to engage in conversations among various disciplines.

Throughout the quarter, I grew in the knowledge that in order to understand the world as I wish to and to connect with those around me, I must be willing to engage in conversations that encourage me to switch points of view and examine questions in perspectives and disciplines different from my own. This prospect fas- cinated me, as it pertained to my studies as an actor. I related this understanding of the world and attitude towards interactions to an essay written by Yale Professor Elinor Fuchs, “EF’s Visit to a Small Planet: Some Questions to Ask a Play,” that provides actors with the tools to analyze and understand the world of a play when discovering it for the first time, as well as what the play itself demands of the actor. She states:

The play asks us to focus upon a total awareness, to bring our attention and curiosity without the censorship of selective interpretation, “good taste,” or “correct form.” Before making judgments, we must ask questions. This is the deepest meaning of the idea, often repeated but little understood, that the study of art shows us how to live.1

This idea of “selective interpretation,” as Fuchs shares, can be akin to the refusal to integrate ideas other than our own in coming to the conclusions that we do in argu- ments — that, essentially, no other world exists but the one we have grown accus- tomed to through our studies, upbringing, and ways of living. The scholarship taken from my humanities class shares the same logic as that of Fuchs’: through breaking out of uncertainty, we cannot focus solely on what we already know, as this keeps us from asking questions — questions that “are intended to light up some of the dark matter in dramatic worlds,” or the worlds in which we live every day.2

As acting is a very specialized path, its power in connecting human beings to the world, to each other, and to their own humanity is seldom understood by those who are not in the craft and sometimes even forgotten by those who have received training, like me. Given this understanding, I followed my impulse to dive deeper into what an acting education truly teaches. The interviews integrated into this paper are conversations I have had with actors, writers, producers, doctors, managers,

1 Fuchs, EF’s Visit to a Small Planet (Some Questions to Ask a Play). 2 Ibid.

financial advisors, etc., who have all studied or taught acting at Northwestern University and discovered how their training has appeared throughout their daily lives. I hope to be in constant communication with the reader through the material that follows, and I hope readers will be able to discover themselves within this work and within these people.

II. Exploring What Acting Is

“We believe to study theatre is to seek to understand what it means to be human.”

— Lookingglass Theatre Founding Ensemble Member and Northwestern Head of Acting David Catlin

The process I developed in conducting this research first required me to step outside of what I already know about the art of acting. As this paper analyzes the tools of an actor, what they know, and how this work and knowledge continue to be present even outside of acting, I began to try to unlearn this craft as if I were discovering it for the first time. I desired for anyone reading this to do the same — to discover, or rediscover, the power and magic behind what acting is. With this, it became crucial that I presented this work for both the seasoned actor and one who has no idea what it is that actors actually do and learn, other than performing and how to perform. So, in examining the factors that propelled me into wanting to pursue acting professionally, the starting point of this thesis naturally gravitated towards acting teachers themselves and what they believe they are teaching their students from the study of acting.

The role of an acting teacher is to, obviously, teach acting. However, just as a mathematics professor strives to teach their students how to analyze the mathematical complexities that surround human beings in everyday life or how political science does more than just encourage students to understand politics and explains through analytical frameworks why political actions are conducted, acting, too, contains more than what many may believe it does. One of the teachers to whom I had the pleasure of speaking is an Emeritus Professor of Acting at Northwestern University, David Downs. Downs was an acting professor from 1973 to 2000 and, during his tenure, taught actors who would go on to become world-renowned artists, including David Schwimmer, Greg Berlanti, Harry Lennix, and Dennis O’Hare. To begin our conversation, I asked him to break down what his job was as an acting teacher, as this profession can have several meanings attached to it. He explained that there was always an impulse in him to be an acting teacher. The paths that “[spun] around in his life” included being an actor and writer, but teaching was the thing that he wanted to do the most. He credited Alvina Krause, former Northwestern University acting professor and the driving force behind the acting sequence still continued today at the university, for contributing to that choice:

“

”

“As acting is a very specialized path, its power in connecting human beings to the world, to each other, and to their own humanity is seldom understood by those who are not in the craft and sometimes even forgotten by those who have received training.”

I met [Alvina Krause] during her career in the 30s, 40s, and 50s, and early 60s. And suddenly, what she believed that acting was, and theater was, hit my heart deeper than anything else that I had done, even all the acting experiences that I’d had. And that’s what I wanted to teach and the reason why was just what you’ve articulated: that beyond the skills that are needed for a certain kind of profession, there was something that the art of theater and the art of acting dealt with [and] developed in people that was profoundly about what it means to be a human being in a culture, in a society. And teaching that in a liberal arts education environment, made great sense. I wouldn’t have wanted to teach in a professional studio in the city, where what acting is is much more specific than what I just described.3

An aspect of training that all actors experience is approaching the question “who am I?” In the process of being able to accurately portray the life of another person in a piece, it is of the utmost importance to know, to the greatest depths, who this person is. “Who am I?” encompasses all of the questions that we ask ourselves every day: who am I? How do I see myself? How does the world see me? How does my family see me? What do I want? How do I get it? How do I feel if I do or do not get it? The processes we use in discovering who we are as individuals are no different from the processes that trained actors use in discovering who they are within the worlds they inhabit. Acting, in a way, is a mode in which those who practice it are able to understand a person made real through the words of a playwright. While we maneuver through this process every single day of our lives, in one of my conversations with Tom Swift, an alumnus, it was fascinating to see just how the “who am I?” comes up in practice and how he uses it in his daily work life.

Swift is a graduate of Northwestern University’s School of Speech,4 where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in theatre. He completed his studies under the instruction of David Downs. He is the co-founder of the Financial Avengers, a financial planning and investment management firm based in Oakland, CA, and has worked in this position for over 20 years. As of today, the Financial Avengers manage over $300 million in client assets. In our email interaction before our interview, Swift mentioned that without his training and background in acting, he would not have succeeded and that all he ever does and will ever do is framed by his acting degree and theatre education. This relates to Downs’ philosophy stated earlier about instilling acting into his students’ lives so that it may become a central part of who they are as educated human beings. Swift said this in relation to Downs’ point:

The work that we do with clients is literally based entirely on acting. So when we do financial planning, everyone thinks, “Oh it’s, you know, all this detailed shit,” and it is — I mean … you know, there’s mathematics and economics, and economics is incredibly fascinating and the numbers don’t lie. But it’s, you know, only ever about how people operate around money, how people operate around finance, how people operate in the world, how people operate relative to their relationship, how people operate based

3 Downs, David Downs Conversation. 4 Northwestern University’s current School of Communication was named the School of Speech from 1921 to 2002. A significant portion of the people I have spoken with attended or taught at the university before it was renamed. The school was renamed to reflect its ever growing catalog of academics, including: Communication Sciences & Disorders, Digital Media, and Health Communication, for example.

on, you know, what their parents told them they could and couldn’t do, what their parents made them, you know, become. Their fears are steeped in all of those human relationships and if you don’t untangle that, then you’ll never fundamentally create a financial plan that addresses their actual needs.5

Part of what Swift is describing lies in the “who am I?” How people operate around money is akin to how characters operate in the environments of their pieces. Questions such as “why does a character act this way towards their partner?” and “why do they think certain ideas about themselves and about the world?” all relate directly to questions about why a person may act the way that they do around money. The accompanying answers lie in the actors discovering their relationship to all the factors that make up their lives, and Swift’s comment argues that the aforementioned questions are continuously present even outside the art of acting.

III. Words, Subtext & Naturalism

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue,

And those who love it will eat its fruit.” -Proverbs 18:21

Words create the universe of a play — they breathe life. They build the foundations of civilizations and the flow of thoughts from one character to another. These words move the actors through a story and create images for both themselves and the audience to follow. To use this manifestation of power means to create.

With this, it is important to understand the unspoken words that actors are trained to understand in their studies, also known as the subtext. Defined by the Oxford Dictionary, subtext is the “hidden meaning or theme in a piece of writing or conversation.”6 Subtext, as per the definition, is the meaning that lies behind the mask that explicit words inherently put over themselves — they are what someone means to say but decides not to. One of the most prolific writers known for allowing actors the opportunity to dig into the meaning lying behind the words is Anton Chekhov. Throughout his career, Chekhov used a naturalistic view of the world in his writing. In a 2002 piece from The Atlantic, journalist Philip Hensher said this about his writing:

His stories, like life, have no beginnings, middles, or ends; they do not deal in crises and happy endings; they are simply glimpses of ordinary lives in their untidiness and irresolution.7

Having been a practicing physician before he became a writer, and drawing from his scientific training, Chekhov believed early on that literature should show life as it is. As a materialist, he believed that in exploring and creating new artistic worlds, he must employ the “concept of scientific objectivity in all of his writing” in order to “depict life as it actually is.”8

The challenge, though, that Chekhov faced throughout his quest of crafting his writing to depict life as it is — and where we may now cue the actors — came from needing to express life “as it ought to be, while avoiding being overtly judgemental

5 Swift. 6 “Subtext.” 7 Hensher, “Incomparable Naturalism: Only an Artificer of the Highest Skill Could Have Produced so Seamless an Illusion of Reality.” 8 Borny, Interpreting Chekhov.

or polemical.”9 This then encouraged him to integrate subtext in the characters’ speech.

Among the various ideas I discussed with Broadway actress Kate Baldwin, subtext was one of them. A graduate from Northwestern’s School of Speech, Kate Baldwin is a renowned actress noted for her work in musical theatre. Having made her Broadway debut in 2000 with the production of The Full Monty, she was featured in several shows following that, including Big Fish, the 2009 revival of Finian’s Rainbow, and the 2017 revival of Hello, Dolly!, the last two of which garnered her Tony Award nominations.

I asked her, “What have you learned about subtext, and how do you think the knowledge that not everything is seen as face value has shown up in your life?” Baldwin replied:

Hmm, that’s — mm-hmm — yeah.10 I find — I don’t know if you have experienced this too, but I find even with a close close friend, if they’re not an actor, I have to ask them three times how they are to get the truth. The first answer is always, “I’m fine.” Are you, though? You know, I mean like. Actually, a friend of mine talked about a phrase that he heard that was called “COVID good.” “How are you?” “Oh, I’m COVID good.”(laughs) Which is different from just, like, regular good. I mean, just as an observant human, you can see a person — their body can, like, revolt when they lie, you know? So you say, “Hey, how are you?” and they go, “Fine.” And then look to the side and you’re like, “You’re not fine; you just lied and your eyes are going — you’re darting to the left,” you know.11

This technique is all the more fascinating when it comes to discovering how all of these ideas continue to appear within another profession: clinical psychology. I had the privilege of speaking with Nina Uziel-Miller, a School of Speech class of ‘92 graduate who studied under Dawn Mora. Working primarily in private practice, Uziel-Miller currently has offices in Chicago and Evanston, IL. She is a faculty member at Northwestern’s Feinberg Medical School and has, for a number of years, taught a class in which she worked with students in navi- gating the transition to the medical profession, addressing topics like work-life balance and inequities in medicine and helping them understand themselves and their goals as they move into working with patients:12

You know, it reminds me of this incident with a woman and her husband, where she was just carrying on about apples he had bought, you know, and, and I said, “You know, I don’t think we’re talking about the apples. I don’t think it’s the apples that matter,” right? And so, being able to sort of hone in on that and articulate it is probably informed by my work as an actor.13

All of these ideas in regard to subtext connect to the theme of a TEDx Presentation by Ann Woodworth — kindly directed to me by Ms. Baldwin — titled “Acting for Your Life.” In it, Woodworth shares that social science studies indicate that “86% of what we communicate … is non-verbal.”14 She goes on to say that of the 14% remaining, 7% is the tone of voice, and only 7% is content. Just as Uziel-Miller was able to

9 Borny. 10 I wish one could hear the inflection she gave of this line. Read as if the subtext is “Oh boy, do I know how this has shown up in my life.” 11 Baldwin, Kate Baldwin Conversation. 12 As of the COVID-19 pandemic, and as of our interview, this class has been discontinued. Per Uziel-Miller, struggles ensued with figuring out how to conduct the class virtually, but “hopefully it will get replaced with something similar and maybe even better.” 13 Uziel-Miller. 14 Woodworth, “Acting for Your Life: Ann Woodworth at TEDxEducationCity.” deduce that her patient’s story about apples was truly not about apples, this awareness of subtext requires an understanding of what these statistics share. Human beings rarely ever say what they mean directly; what we truly mean lies in how we say it and how we show it — through our actions. Actors are keenly aware of this, for discovering words and how human beings present them are part of what they are trained to know.

IV. Acting as a Science For quite some time, I have related what actors do in their training and performance to what physicists learn in their own studies. In order for the following to make sense, it is necessary to understand that the process of performance and human life is the process of motion and that life is in constant motion: past with the present and the future, one person to another, etc. When a play begins, the plot does not end until the last line, and even then, the piece’s contents are still in constant motion with the audience. Theatre, in this sense, is always moving. Isaac Newton’s third law of motion states that:

For every action (force) in nature, there is an equal and opposite reaction. In other words, if object A exerts a force on object B, then Object B also exerts an equal and opposite force on object A.15

This idea can also be illustrated through a Newton’s cradle, which Northwestern University acting teacher Henry Godinez mentioned he has on his desk because it is the “simplest way to demonstrate what acting is.”16

I cannot remember the specific name of this particular acting game, but it was what allowed me to first discover this idea of Newton’s law of motion in motion. About five or so actors stand on the stage next to each other, spreading from stage left to stage right. The furthest stage left person begins with a slight sound, the tiniest idea of what a laugh could be, and once they find it they turn to the next actor and “pass the laugh” to them. The second actor must

15 “Newton’s Third Law.” 16 Godinez, Henry Godinez Interview. 17 Palermo, “How Does Newton’s Cradle Work?”

“[T]he process of performance and human life is the process of motion. [L]ife is in constant motion: past with the present and the future, one person to another, etc.” “

” then match the same level of “force” being exerted onto them, and once they have successfully emulated this, they then increase that “force” and exert it on the next person, and so on, until this one little bit of a sound explodes into the loudest idea of what a laugh can sound like. This same exercise can be explored through crying as well.

Furthermore, I got to speak about listening with the wonderful Kathryn Hahn. Another Northwestern University alum and world-renowned actress, Hahn has been recognized for her roles in the films We’re the Millers, Step Brothers, Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, and Bad Moms. She is also known for her television work in Parks and Recreation and the new Disney Plus series WandaVision. When I asked her if she could recall any moments of her life in which the techniques she had learned in her classes have helped her outside of performing, she said that at the top for her would have to be the idea of stillness:

I had always had an impulse. It took me a long time to find stillness on stage and the power of stillness. … I have a very buzzy interior life, and I always felt like I had to be doing something rather than just being, and when I first found the power of just standing on stage and listening, I remember that being a very profound moment. … I feel that when you are authentically listening, onstage, and receiving and listening with all of your whole self, whether it’s on stage or on camera, that’s where the most magic is happening, even if the words are not yours. If you’re listening with your whole self, that’s where the most connection happens. And so, if you’re listening with your whole self, in your real life, you know, that’s where the deep — real deep — connection can happen as well.18

Hahn’s point about connecting with others, being still, and listening with one’s entire being relates to a tool that actors, throughout their training, are expected to understand and grow in: empathy. Per the Oxford dictionary, empathy is “the ability to understand and share the feelings of another.”19 Empathy can only happen through active listening, and listening happens when actors observe Newton’s third law of motion — exerting force on each other, constantly moving and being moved. Uziel-Miller spoke on this crucial idea in acting and how it relates to her profession as a psychologist:

I think to be a really good actor, you need to have the desire and the ability to understand other perspectives, right? You play roles of people that you at face value might not get, they’re not like you, they’re different, and you have to figure out how to play them in a way that is true and honest, and respectful of that person. I think that’s something that I was able to explore as an acting student. And certainly applies to my work. I can feel compassion for a serial killer, which, you know, might be

18 Hahn, Kathryn Hahn Conversation. 19 “Empathy.”

“[T]here is a true science to what acting is. Acting is a process of discovery, research, and observation that can then be repeated.” stretching it a tiny bit, but I’m always interested in like, what is it that made this, you know. Nobody wakes up in the morning thinking, “How can I do bad things and hurt people?”

As illustrated through my conversations, there is a true science to what acting is. Acting is a process of discovery, research, and observation that can then be repeated. No analysis of these ideas has been truer to what science is.

V. Conclusion When speaking to my acting teacher, who also served as my thesis advisor, about this research, she asked me to dig deeper into why I chose this particular subject — why am I exploring these questions and these ideas? From studying under her, I have learned that all actions have intentions, that I had intention behind this action — researching these ideas and writing this thesis — and that I needed to discover more of that. Truth- fully, I chose this topic out of annoyance and anger. Very often, in approaching the world as an artist, I often receive verbal or non-verbal responses of “why acting?” In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, I also asked myself this question. There was a part of me that felt selfish in exploring this art when I could be investing my time in what — at that moment — I had thought to be more “important” career paths. Needing to consistently justify to the world and to myself (albeit less frequently) that my studies and training as an actor carried with it just as much merit as other professions made me tired and also made me question, “Why is this profession viewed as it is?”

This thought made me think of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, pictured below:

This pyramid is a motivational theory in psychology that comprises a five-tier model of human needs in order of their importance to a human being. Basic needs must be met in order to reach the self-fulfillment needs. These basic needs are those close to the bottom of the pyramid: physiological needs, such as food, water, shelter, etc. The self-fulfillment needs are closer to the top, involving the achieving of one’s full potential and including creative needs.

One theory that I have developed throughout this research relates to why some believe the study of acting needs to be justified: it just is not important enough. I argue that society is in a constant state of physiological and safety needs, especially during this pandemic. When one is starv- ing, everything that they do and everything they strive for becomes about finding food. They care about nothing else, and as long as it never truly becomes fulfilled, we never reach the top, where creativity lies. Once we as a society, hopefully after this pandemic, remember the pyramid has five tiers, we can remember that in order to be fulfilled as human beings, all of these needs must be met.

On the other hand, through this project, I found myself doing the very thing that I said I hated doing when explaining to others my career in acting: justifying it. In many ways, this paper was a justification for why acting is important and why it is more than what many think it is. It allows us to observe, to discover, to connect, to

20 McLeod, “Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.” feel, to research, to investigate, and to understand. I hope that through this thesis, one will be able to open their mind up to a world they may know nothing about, explore this environment and this walk of life, and try to learn something from it. In the last moments of most of my interviews, I asked if acting can make us better humans.

As one continues on in their daily lives, I hope this project has instilled in them an understanding that there is much to learn from what an actor knows and that it can be found if they find stillness, connect to the world, and observe the environment around them. ◆
