title: LAUREN OH ON THE NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES LAB
notes: Q&A with senior Lauren Oh about her work in a Northwestern neurodevelopmental disabilities lab. Printed page 132 (section 133) is a full-page photograph with no text. The contents gives the title as "Lauren Oh on the Neurodevelopmental Disabilities Lab".
text:
LAUREN OH

ON THE NEURODEVELOPMENTAL

DISABILITIES LAB by Joy Zhao

Lauren Oh is a senior majoring in communication sciences and disorders and minoring in Spanish. She works at Northwestern University’s Neurodevelopmental Disabilities Lab, which researches language and other cognitive abilities associated with autism, Fragile X syndrome, and other related conditions. The lab also investigates genetic, environmental, and neural features associated with the aforementioned conditions.

[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

Q&A Q&A

What made you interested in communication sciences and disorders (CSD)? I had always been interested in languages and linguistics, and then I took a class and realized how interesting it was to see those areas being applied clinically. The speech therapy component was particularly intriguing because I had always wanted to become a doctor and work with children. Seeing how this was possible within a different field piqued my interest in exploring CSD. I’ve also always been passionate about helping people and working with young kids, and I thought that this field would be a wonderful way for me to pursue all my interests.

How did you get involved in the lab? I reached out via email before my junior year, and I filled out a brief application. Afterward, I did a quick interview with one of the graduate students working at the lab. The interview process was relatively informal. It was more of an opportunity for me to tell her about the interests I have and for her to tell me more about the lab’s work.

Why did you decide to choose this lab over others? A lot of the other labs in which I was interested were not taking undergraduate students because the COVID-19 pandemic limited their openings. I was particularly interested in this lab because it focuses a lot on the intersection between autism and language, a subject that I am curious about.

How long have you been in the lab, and what is your role there? I have been working at the lab for the past one and a half years. I work as an undergraduate research assistant. Some of my main responsibilities include transcribing and processing recordings of the participants in the research studies. Other undergraduates first type out everything that is being said. Then, I tag each sentence, formally known as an utterance, with a label to categorize them into different types of speech. I also work on cleaning up the utterances so that there is no audio interference and the sample is clean for data processing.

What does the typical day look like in terms of doing that work? My work is done on a weekly basis. I work for five hours on my own time, and I receive credit for independent study.

How has your work been impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic? Normally, all members of the lab would do their work in the lab. Since the pandemic, all work has been remote, and all meetings have been held via Zoom.

What has been the most rewarding part of your research experience? Listening to different interviews has been interesting. A lot of times, the interviews are full of casual chatting or life stories, so I have enjoyed this aspect. Working in a lab has also helped me see how much work goes into setting up reliable, well thought- out studies. Seeing how many people have to process the data and all of the different steps involved have enriched my experience in reading research, as well. I felt like I could not relate to the readings before, but now I can visually see some of the research protocols and methods that papers talk about and appreciate the complexity of the process.

Has working alongside graduate students enriched your undergraduate career or understanding of the field in any way?

Yes, the graduate students have provided a lot of opportunities for us to read papers together and learn from them. They also set up really cool events such as clinical case conferences and Q&A sessions for us to ask them any questions that we might have. They have been really great mentors and passed down a lot of the knowledge and wisdom that they have.

What kind of enrichment opportunities does the lab provide for undergraduate students? One main enrichment is the journal club. Undergraduate students meet with graduate students to discuss a few research papers related to the lab’s work or read research papers published by the lab so that we know exactly what we are working on and how the data we obtain is used to make discoveries about autism and language.

What challenges have you encountered along the way? One of the main challenges that I have encountered is time management. Since we do not have set hours to work at the lab, it has sometimes been difficult to carve out the necessary time each week to transcribe the data, especially when I am busier due to schoolwork.

What is something about neurodevelopmental disabilities that you wish more people knew about? I want people to know that there are so many genetic and environmental factors that influence these conditions and that these conditions are just really complex.

Has this experience given you any insight into what you might want to do in the future? Definitely! I wasn’t really sure about what I wanted to do in the future, but working in the lab has convinced me that I want to go to graduate school and eventually work as a speech-language pathologist. The graduate students have been really encourag- ing. I have also really enjoyed the work that I have been doing, which made me feel more confident about my decision to attend graduate school. ◆

What skills have you gained through doing research? One key skill I have gained is proficiency with Praat, which is a computer software package for speech analysis. I believe that this is a software that I will be using often in the future, so I am glad that I got to familiarize myself with how it works now. Another skill I have gained is being more proficient in navi- gating dense scholarly materials. I gained many helpful tips from the graduate students. Being able to connect academic readings with the work that I see and do in the lab has also made the process more enjoyable and manageable.

Do you have any advice for undergraduates who want to get involved in research? I think my biggest tip is to be proactive. For a while, I was not really sure how I was supposed to get involved in research. I then realized that I had to start looking and reaching out to different labs. Another piece of advice I have is for people to take their time to find a lab. Since there are so many great opportunities at Northwestern, it’s really important to read about each lab’s projects and chat with the people working there to find a lab that matches your interests.

title: The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary Indian Women Authors and the Subversion of the Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment
notes: Senior thesis with trigger warning. Faculty adviser named on the opening page. The opening page prints "Contemporary Indian Women Authors"; the contents and contributor page have "Woman Authors". The faculty-adviser line and the title are extracted as one block (137.5). Appendix A reprints Kirun Kapur's poem "Steubenville Ghazal" and Appendix B Meena Kandasamy's poem "A cunning stunt"; their headings are extracted at the end of their pages and placed first here. Footnotes quote the Hindi originals.
text:
by Tara Shirvaikar

Department of Comparative Literary Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Laura Brueck, Ph.D. The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary Indian Women Authors and the Subversion of the Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment

Introduction

In Indian society, the social divides of caste, class, gender, and urban/rural groups fall along the same fault lines as linguistic divides. These linguistic divides largely fall into two categories: the elite and the vernacular. Language — both elite and vernacular — is always actively changing; the manner in which it is wielded defines it as much as the language itself. A primary example of elite language is the authoritative discourse found in places of heteropatriarchal dominance: education, state government, medical facilities, and even traditional marriages and households in India where literature shows agency and identity usually being wrested from the woman. In contrast, those not traditionally given power/authority in society

— lower castes, lower classes, women, and the rural populations — find themselves unable or unwilling to represent themselves with the elite languages and ideologies made available to them. Thus, they are driven to make themselves heard through a vernacular language instead (Gupta et al., 812). Though the vernacular is traditionally thought of as culturally substandard — in large part because any subjectivity not sanctioned by the societal elite is considered illegitimate — it nevertheless has become a way for voices in these margins to make themselves heard (Lemke 5). The vernacular emphasizes the everyday lived and spoken language of the masses and margins; it is “consistently anti-hierarchical and anti-exclusionary”

(Lemke 5). This thesis will further narrow this definition of vernacular to one of politically gendered identity. This gendered vernacular centralizes female subjectivity through the self-expression of embodied experience and the self-affirmation of the politics of womanhood and resistance. Working through a lens of feminist agency, the vernaculars analyzed in this thesis deconstruct and reappropriate the central social concept of female shame.

In English Heart, Hindi Heartland, Rashmi Sadana posits that “literature reflects and represents, but it is also produced and con- sumed under particular social and political conditions” (Sadana 27). Through examining these particular social and political conditions, this thesis will analyze the work of contemporary Indian women writers, all of whom explicitly engage with the gendered politics of language and the overlaps of (and distances between) their vernacular and the elite. We will consider an array of gendered vernaculars: tribal languages translated to Bengali and then to English, Tamil translated to English, Hindi translated to English, and then finally original works in both English and Hindi. All of the authors discussed in this thesis have deconstructed elite linguistic structures in some way — some by repopulating these structures with their own lived experience and others by communicating through an embodied vernacular instead. Through undercutting and mocking the ostensible cultural and sociopolitical authority denoted by elite languages like Sanskrit and English, these authors’ feminized vernacularization1 of the elite language critiques the language’s role in sustaining heteropatriarchal authority and colonial power structures, all while working to subvert these forms of dominance.

Further, Meenakshi Thapan points out that “oppression, in its psychological form, is then an experience of a disjunc- tion between a woman’s body image and the male constructions of it” (Thapan and Nehru Memorial Museum and Library 19). Essentially, female internalizations of the patriarchal constructions of the female body then inform their own understanding of their body, agency, and sexuality. The heteropatriarchal authority is not external but is an oppressive force that actually exerts its power from within the woman through social expectation. In India specifically, the discourse of shame is intricately tied with womanhood and honor; shame is the internalized punishment for transgressing moral codes imposed and policed by the dominant male social, cultural, and political ideology. As such, women are forced to define their identity within these purely male discourses of shame and purity/honor (Viswanath 318). Thus, this thesis locates shame within the framework of heteropatriarchal power and understands that these authors are part of the movement to challenge its political and social existence/validity.

1 The particularity and singularity of these literary texts work to ground this essay in a hyper-contextualized space, thus avoiding any harmful false generalities; as such, the feminine, female experience, woman’s body, or Indian feminisms discussed will always be that in literature.

Trigger warning: The following thesis includes mentions of violence against women, including forced abortion, sexual assault, and rape.

I. Revealing English Linguistic Oppression: “Draupadi” (1981) and “Neela Scarf” (2014) The original story of Draupadi from the Hindu epic The Mahabharata illustrates the type of female representation and patriarchal control that these writers are fighting to subvert. Indian epics and religious texts were partially responsible for the sanskri- tization of norms and cultural values that are a primary source of violence towards women even today. By creating female characters who are forced to uphold realistically impossible standards of purity, devotion, and compliance, violence is perpetrated in multiple ways. First, holding the female body to these heteropatriarchal standards snuffs out any possibility for female subjectivity because now the woman is forced to be the site upon which social and national ideology and politics are carried out. Second, by worshipping women as shakti, or goddess, society is able to justify putting them on a pedestal and then judge and punish them harshly when they fail to meet these standards of perfection. Thus, these works established — and continue to establish — unreasonable social expectations for the female body.

In The Mahabharata, Draupadi2 is forced to marry five brothers by her mother-in-law after a misunderstanding. After one of the brothers stakes everything — including his wealth, power, and finally, Draupadi — in a gambling game to a jeal- ous king and loses, the king demands that all of the brother’s possessions, including Draupadi, appear before him. The king tries to humiliate Draupadi further by publicly disrobing her in the court, but the

Hindu god Krishna responds to Draupadi’s desperate pleas, intervenes, and blesses her with a never-ending sari. Now, no matter how much the king pulls her sari off, Draupadi’s honor is preserved (“The Story of Draupadi”). This story sets the tone for the expectation of the treatment of a female body and character; Draupadi is never given any choice in husband, home, or fate, and as a character, she is given no emotional or sexual subjectivity/desire. Using Draupadi as an introduction to discuss the nexus of elite language, religious and cultural authority and the conventions of appropriate/pure womanhood, Mahasweta Devi reimagines Draupadi through a feminist lens in her story “Draupadi.”

Mahasweta Devi, a prominent Bengali author and tribal activist, wrote “Draupadi” originally in Bengali and a tribal dialect (Swaminathan). Later translated to English with a foreword written by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Draupadi” is situated against the Naxalite movement, the Bangladesh Liberation War in 1971, and the Hindu epic The Mahabharata. Written in the style of a military report about the ap- prehension of tribal rebels, the short story is about Draupadi (Dopdi) Mehjen, a fight- er who, along with her erstwhile husband Dulna, murders the wealthy landlord in the area to gain access to and democratize the well water during a seasonal drought. She is then apprehended by Officer Senanayak who demands that she be raped by his officers so he can break her resistive silence and find out more information about the rebel uprisings that the military is there to quell.

Dopdi Mehjen brings English closer to a lived language, not just a language of colonial and state domination. When Draupadi is captured and raped by multiple

2 In Hinduism, she is praised as one of the panchakanya (“five virgins”), archetypes of female chastity whose names are believed to dispel sin when recited. She regained her virginity each year after bearing her five husbands’ children (Bhattacharya).

men, she is described like a wounded wolf, with raw animalistic power — she rips the clothes they give her to cover up her wounded body with her teeth and pours the water they give her to clean her wounds on the ground. By refusing the narrative of shame placed upon women’s bodies, Dopdi retools the language of rape, refusing the silence that often excuses that violent behavior, and as an ultimate subversion of power, she refuses to cover herself in the clothes they give her.

Dopdi finally goes to meet Officer Senanayak, unclothed, and Senanayak’s theoretical knowledge of the tribals col- lides with the reality of a wounded tribal woman, turning the tables, and leaving him afraid and ashamed:

The object of your search, Dopdi Mejhen. You asked them to make me up, don’t you want to see how they made me? Draupadi wipes the blood on her palm and says in a voice that is as terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp as her ululation, “What’s the use of clothes? You can strip me, but how can you clothe me again? Are you a man? … There isn’t a man here that I should be ashamed. I will not let you put my cloth on me. What more can you do? Come on, counter me – come on, counter me.” Draupadi pushes Senanayak with her two mangled breasts, and for the first time Senanayak is afraid to stand before an unarmed target, terribly afraid (Spivak and Devi 402).

This is the most powerful moment in the story where Dopdi has the last word, and Officer Senanayak is reduced to silence. Dopdi refuses to be shamed into being dominated by masculine subjectivity and instead asserts her own. She places blame on Senanayak and mocks him by referring to herself as “the object of [his] search.” The italicization and repetition of “counter” foregrounds Dopdi’s vernacularization of the word officially used by the army, “encounter.” A technical, passive term that obscures the actual violence that the army does to bodies, “encounter” is an example of exactly the way in which English is used to dominate a subjugated population through, in this instance, rape or sexual assault. Dopdi actively challenges this, and then by mirroring his violence with her body, she reverses the semiotics of shame and thrusts it back into the face of Senanayak. She refuses to be covered by that language and instead names the violence inscribed on her body, her land, and her people; she turns the verb from passive to active. “Draupadi” draws attention to the feminine vernacular of Dopdi and contrasts it with the masculine violence of English. Initially, the reader sees the officer’s desire to dominate or conquer the subaltern by dominating her linguistic meaning, and the story ends with Dopdi’s

By creating female characters who are forced to uphold realistically impossible standards of purity, devotion and compliance, violence is perpetrated in multiple ways. “

” refusal to succumb to violence at both a bodily level (indicated by her refusal to cover up) and a linguistic level (by sub- verting “encounter” with “counter”). Though she is unclothed in a camp of men, she subverts the physicality of her body from weakness and vulnerability to power by calling into question the masculinity and humanity of Senanayak’s actions and making him come face to face — literally — with his actions and the consequences of his theory of “knowledge” dominance through her appropriation of English. Describing her presence and power as “terrifying, sky splitting, and sharp as her ululation,” Devi is once more calling into mind the tribal connection to land and tight community as well as reminding the reader that the female power and naturalistic vernacular upon which Dopdi draws comes from there. Dopdi daring Senanayak to “counter” her is to dare him to counter all of those reserves of power and is her taking his agency into her own self. He is unable to even question her presence and assert his power because she is reappropriating his English as her vernacular and recreating her body as a space for feminine resistance by using it to assert her socio-political subjectivity. Thus, the link between the vernacularization of language and a woman’s embodied experience is made clear: she refuses both with her words and with her body to submit to the violent appropriation that both the English language and a rape/ assault demand from her, and her refusal and reimagination of that conventional script causes fear.

Whereas English plays an active, mil- itaristic role in “Draupadi” to perpetuate physical violence, the medicalized English in the Hindi-language short story “Neela Scarf” highlights a different form of physical and emotional violence grounded in female isolation. Applauded for its unfiltered look into the female mind, “Neela Scarf” by Anu Singh Chaudhary is a collection of short stories published in 2014 that depicts female narratives across different classes and geographies in India (Fazili). The eponymous- ly-named short story is centered around the protagonist’s refusal to submit to the formalized heteropatriarchal violence and clinical isolation that English represents, so she revolts by only communicating through her embodied experiences. The story is centered around a newly married couple, Shambhavi and Amitesh, and the breakdown of their trust in each other and eventually their relationship. Three months into their marriage, Shambhavi gets pregnant, and Amitesh, claiming that he is not ready, forces her to get an abortion even though she wants to keep the unborn baby. After the abortion procedure, Shambhavi retreats from the marriage both mentally and emotionally. The second time she gets pregnant three years later, Amitesh wants to keep it, but there are pregnancy complications because of the previous abortion, and she must un- dergo another abortive procedure and loses her fallopian tubes in the process. After she recovers, she decides she needs a break from her strained, barely standing marriage and pursues an opportunity for a fellowship abroad. The story ends with Shambhavi not knowing whether she will return.

Although no words are written in Roman script, there are many English words integrated into the Hindi prose in Devanagari script. Categorized by frequency, English medical and physical language is the most common, followed by the language of money and business,3 and then the language of technology and departure.4 Since the medical language is the most common, this thesis will focus on analyzing that, starting with how both Amitesh and Shambhavi refer to the abortion. It is clear that one is able to note a greater level of comfort and intimacy denoted here through the use of Hindi versus English. Whenever Amitesh refers to abortion, he calls it an “अबॉर्शन” (the English word “abortion” written in Devanagari), while Shambhavi refers to it as “उसके विदा हो जाने की दुआ माँगे” (praying for its departure;5 Choudhary 107). When Amitesh uses “abortion” in English, he distances himself from the child and any emotional complications that would be associated with its loss. The constitution of the fetus’s body is negated; Amitesh’s dismissal of the baby’s body through the medicalized language becomes a “key locus for … [his] exercise of power” (Berg and Bowker 533).

However, in Shambhavi’s vernacular construction, she is already giving the child some subjectivity by wondering whether it will take some action (in this case, depart).

The third-person descriptions of her visits to the hospital are saturated with clinical English words6 such as “pregnancy kit,” “bleeding,” “ultrasound,” and “sanitary napkin” (Choudhary). Further, the diagnosis of Shambavi’s Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is again indicative of the cold, medical Western vocabulary of scientific diagnosis and clinical procedure. This clinical English disavows the embodied experience she is going through; no thought is given to offering emotional, personal support for having gone through an abortion or for living life with OCD. Instead, in a form of epistemic violence, her own life is articulated to her in a foreign, formalized English.7 She is categorized and “configured” with English words of procedure and diagnosis (Berg and Bowker 514). Once her mental and physical “disorder[s]” are named, she is cast aside by both her husband and Western medical procedure.

Then, when she does not behave as her husband expects and begins retreating from the marriage because of the forced abortion, Amitesh uses English words

3 Examples in “Neela Scarf” include “Ecommerce,” “loan,” “bank balance,” “venture,” “company,” etc. 4 Examples in “Neela Scarf” include “photos,” “click,” “folder,” “cellphone,” “attachments,” “space,” “airport,” “trolley,” “checkin,” etc. 5 All translations, unless otherwise noted, are my own. 6 The rest of the formalized English medical words are “operation theatre,” “general anesthesia,” “stretcher,” “checkup,” “operation,” “monitor,” “fallopian tube rupture,” and “embryo.” 7 Michel Foucault, a prominent 20th century French philosopher whose theories primarily address the relationship between power and knowledge, brings up a similar distinction of the physical and the metaphysical in his book, “The Birth of the Clinic.” He discusses the distinction between physical “tissue” and the human/emotional “self.” Later critics have noted how this distinction between the purely physical and the metaphysical is the foundation for the power that medicalized language has to hide the true violence done to a human being. By saying the violence is done to a “cell” or a purely physical part, the medical language drains the moral value and outrage that would be present if the same violence were done to a “self” (Allen 212).

“She no longer has any need for her own body and subjectivity to be validated — and governed — by the specter of heteronormativity, embodied ignorance, and apathy.” once again to describe her silence and push her further away. Describing Shambhavi, he says, “Formal. Curt. Ceremonious. Si- lent. Amitesh did not want to believe it”8 (Chaudhary 104). The concept of negative space plays a large role in showcasing the growing distance between the two people and also the helplessness that Shambhavi later becomes ashamed of. The auditory manifestation of this negative space is the silence present in their relationship, the physical manifestation of the space is her empty womb, and emotionally, it represents the lack of space she is allowed to take up in her and Amitesh’s marriage and home. Notably, the only way in which she is able to escape her feeling of helplessness and betrayal to her child is by leaving the space that Amitesh occupies, and she drives this point home by leaving the blue scarf she bought to impress him on one of their first dates back in the airport when she departs. She no longer has any need for her own body and subjectivity to be validated — and governed — by the specter of heteronormativity, embodied ignorance, and apathy.

However, instead of accepting the de- humanization and isolation that follows the procedural dialects of English, she rejects this language and thus refuses to obfuscate her unborn child through the medicalized English language. Instead, Shambhavi’s articulation of her state of mind and heart is through a specific discourse of the body. When she does speak or emote, it is either through embodied emotion (for example, her teary eyes) or through vernacular language that calls into being the body of her absent baby. Most of Shambhavi’s dialogue is assumed to happen off the page or is made up of curt sentences traded with Amitesh. However, here she is given the opportunity to verbalize the baby’s life into the world for the first time. Shambhavi’s longest dialogue by far is with her doctor, who tells her she is pregnant. She replies, “I know. And I also know that by this time, the heart of the child must have started to form, and the brain as well. I know that her eyelashes must have started forming, and she may too have a twist in both elbows”9 (Chaudhary 108). By listing its body parts, she characterizes the physical space and shape the baby inhabits in her womb and also the negative space that will be left when it is gone. Unlike Amitesh, who wishes to remain clinically abstracted and detached from the fetus, Shambhavi refuses to use the word “abortion” throughout the whole story. She only ever asks forgiveness from the unborn child and prays that it stays well after it “departs.” For everyone else, focusing on the humanness of the unborn body is a problem, but she insists on verbalizing it and their connection into reality.

II. Rejecting Sanskritized Shame: “Mitro Marjani” (1967) and “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” (2017) Supported by culturally and religiously fundamental stories such as “Draupadi,” the notion of the ideal woman as chaste, pure of body and mind, and loyal to the patriarch became the popular one. Even in contemporary literature, we see an expectation of the woman to behave this way, as well as a justification of violence towards the woman if she does not. The characterization of Mi-

8 “फ़ॉर्मल। कर्ट। औपचारिक। ख़ामोश। अमितेश मानना नहीं चाहता था।” 9 “जानती हूँ। और ये भी जानती हूँ कि इस वक़्त तक बच्चे का दिल भी बनने लगा होगा, दिमाग़ भी। जानती हूँ कि उसकी पलकें बनने लगी होंगी, दोनों कुहनियों में अबतक मोड़ भी आ गया होगा शायद।” tro in “Mitro Marjani” allows the reader to explore shame as a social discourse as well as its deconstruction by Mitro both in her articulation of her body and in her physical uncovering of it. Building upon Mitro’s exploration of her femininity, Meena Kandasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” further explores the gendered language of sexuality through the protagonist’s radical rejection of her husband’s violent representation of female sexuality.

In 1967, Krishna Sobti — one of the leading female Hindi authors of the twentieth century — wrote “Mitro Marjani,” arguably her most famous work. In it, she depicts a family drama centered on the defiant daughter-in-law of a middle-class Punjabi family. The middle daughter-in- law, Sumitravanti (whose nickname is Mitro), is the most outspoken of all the daughters-in-law, constantly facing threats of violence from Sardarilal (her husband), harsh reprimands from Dhanvanti (the matriarch), and scorn from Suhag (the first daughter-in-law) for her improper behavior. The most controversial aspect of “Mitro Marjani” is the fact that the dialogue is imbued with such potent female subjectivity. At various points in the novella, Mitro speaks freely about her sexual desire and her body. After a family argument about Mitro’s behavior, she speaks to the first daughter-in-law, Suhag, mocking her husband: “Banwari [the eldest son, Suhag’s husband] says — Mitro, your body is all honey, pure honey! I tell the rascal — in this milk and honey of mine, there writhe the serpents of your own desires!”10 (Sobti trans. Yadav 17). Then after taking all of her clothes off, Mitro asks Suhag, “‘Tell me the truth, Jethani, does any other woman have breasts like these?’ Rage blazed through Suhag”11 (Sobti trans. Yadav 18). First, it is pointedly cruel of Mitro to talk about her sexual power over Suhag’s husband with Suhag. With Suhag representing the “ideal” daughter-in-law, Mitro posits herself as superior to Suhag and thus positions herself above the expectations of the household. Through the repetition of “honey,” the reader gets the sense that Mitro is reveling in her own body. Mitro is intimately aware of her body, of the physical space it takes up, and of its powerful capabilities as a sexed body; she dismisses Suhag’s normativity as simple hypocrisy.

Even while Mitro is unapologetically cele- brating the female body, she still emphasizes that the male eye is more sinful than the female body. In recognizing that and thus taking power away from the male gaze, she begins to reassert her own subjectivity. By discussing her body parts, bodily

10 “मित्रो, तेरी देह क्या निरा शीरा है-शी-रा ! उस नास-होने से कहती हूँ... -अरे, इसी शीरे में तेरी जान को डंक मारते सर्पों की फौजें पलती हैं !” (Sobti). 11 “मँझली लेटी-लेटी उठ बैठी । हाथों से छातियाँ ढँक मग्न हो कहा-सच कहना, जिठानी सुहागवन्ती, क्या ऐसी छातियाँ किसी और की भी हैं ?...सुहाग का तन-बदन फुँकने लगा ।” (Sobti).

“

”

Mitro is empowering herself because she is creating a space where she does not have to suppress her subjectivity and submit to sanskritized notions of purity and honor.

processes such as menstruation, and sexual innuendos, Mitro reclaims the female body for herself. She does not let the family — or any other authority — dictate what she wears, how she acts, and what she says. By not suppressing these thoughts and by verbalizing this body-centric, sexualized discourse, Mitro is empowering herself because she is creating a space where she does not have to suppress her subjectivity and submit to sanskritized notions of purity and honor.

One of the most remarkable parts of Sobti’s novella is how she constructs the clash between the patriarchal gaze and Mitro’s sexuality. In the novella, Mitro not only lays claim to her own body but also turns an accusatory eye towards Sardarilal’s body and sexuality. Her deliberate and continual provocations of Sardarilal spring from her unfulfilled sexuality. She says, “The dullard! Had [he] any manhood, [he] would have either licked me all over with relish or torn me apart like a lion” (Sobti trans. Yadav 16-7). Sobti problematizes the phallocentric view of sexuality by showing Mitro taking control of the sexual dynamic between the two; though her takeover is steeped in stereotypical images of manhood, hypermasculinity, and male sexuality, she nonetheless is able to turn a reverse gaze to Sardarilal and his supposed authority over her body. He, in turn, is thrown off guard because the sex is not on his terms. In response, Sardarilal becomes physically abusive whenever Mitro misbehaves. This violence is another manifestation of his own male insecurity due to Mitro now controlling the narrative and discourse of shame within the novel, as well as his inability to verbalize his problem with her objectification of him (Hoque). Incredibly, Mitro is able to dominate the subjectivity within their relationship through her embodied language and fully reappropriate her body through language of desire.

Written exactly half a century after “Mitro Marjani,” Meena Kandasamy’s English novel “When I Hit You: Or, a Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” also reveals the dynamics of a heteropatriarchal household. Similar to Mitro, this unnamed protagonist finds power in the verbaliza- tion of her body and subjectivity, with one key difference being that in Kandasamy’s novel, the protagonist’s husband uses that same female sexuality to abuse and shame her in a far more violent and explicit way than Mitro’s husband ever does. Set during the first couple of months of an increasingly manipulative and abusive marriage, the unnamed female protagonist details the burgeoning emotional, physical, and sexual violence she faces. Although the protagonist falls in love with a passionate Marxist professor in a whirlwind romance, she quickly realizes after their marriage how abusive and controlling he really is. Initially forcing her to give him her email and social media passwords, he eventually controls her internet time, clothing, job prospects, phone time with family, and every single other aspect of her life until the only respite she has left is her writing.

As the relationship gets increasingly violent, the protagonist’s husband uses specifically female sexed language to harm her because he feels threatened. Female sexuality has a negative, insatiable, and dangerous connotation because, like other independent female functions (i.e., menstruation, childbirth), it cannot be controlled by the man. Thus, it provides a significant threat to the level of control the husband wants to have over the protagonist (Viswanath 315). In an effort to “control” her, he constantly shames her for being a dirty, sexually loose woman. After getting mad that his provocations are no longer garnering a reaction from her, he rapes her so she can “prove it to [him] that [she is] not thinking of another man.” Over her screams, he continues, “You are a whore. This is what whores do. … How many men took you from behind? How many? … Fucking cheap whore” (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 102). In the whole passage, “bitch” is repeated twice, “whore” is repeated seven times, and “cunt” three times. The sheer onslaught of slurs that are meant to demolish the female spirit and to disrespect and violate the female body is significant. The husband twists the gendered language of women’s bodies in order to inflict pain and bring shame to his wife. The narrator later writes:

The coarseness of my husband’s insults makes me cringe. I’m ashamed that language allows a man to insult a woman in an infinite number of ways. … Every part of my body is a word spat out in disgust. My cunt, sequestered and quarantined, is nothing but a spittoon for his insults. Once, this language … was a secret place of pleasure (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 106).

Kandasamy reveals language to be gendered, steeped in heteropatriarchal ideology, and predetermined towards favoring the man. The narrator recalls parts of her body as if she is dismembered but also to preserve them by verbalizing them. The final body part — the cunt — is forced into submission, as if a wild animal, to take whatever the man chooses to throw at it. The image of a “spittoon” used in the quote is exacting here: the female body is dismembered and then, in turn, made into the passive receptacle for those very body parts as they are turned into insults that are hurled back at the woman.

However, the protagonist in

Kandasamy’s “When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife” is able to further reappropriate English as her own vernacular. Since the protagonist is an author by trade, this novel also discusses her shifting relationship with English, Tamil, language in general, and writing as a form of resistance and self-preservation. While an authoritative abuse of English (emerging from colonialism) is one form of perpetuated heteropatriarchal violence against women, another far older form is using the cultural discourse of female ownership under the guise of a familial bond. Where before, the protagonist was violat- ed physically by her husband and by English, she now uses English as a vernacular form of self-expression and preservation. As her husband slowly erases all semblance of autonomy from her life, including the ability to write without incurring violence, the protagonist starts writing these letters to imaginary lovers and herself as a form of private rebellion: “Each of my letters, I de- lete after I have finished typing them. Every line I have written to you is a thought- crime, a crime that does not leave a trail of evidence, a crime that is not even a crime” (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 67). The repetition of the word “crime” four times highlights the simple absurdity and desperation of a situation where writing letters would be considered an act so offensive as to be labelled a crime. The only crime is that the protagonist is daring to retain some sense of identity and subjectivity through the act of writing these love letters. Here, she is rebelliously reoccupying the English space with which she was so intimate before her marriage turned it against her. In one of her letters, she writes:

I imbue the word kiss with the idea of clandestine; I smuggle the thought of me into the word caress. You can never dislodge me from each of the words I’ve meticulously occupied. … English makes me a lover, a beloved, a poet. Tamil makes me a word huntress, it makes me a love goddess (Kandasamy, When I Hit You 60).

In regaining a semblance of power through a repossession of both of her vernaculars — English and Tamil — she begins to feel empowered once more. English becomes a space with reciprocal love and physical affection, a concept so foreign to her that she feels she must “smuggle” herself back into the word “caress.” Tamil goes one step beyond the English docility and makes her a warrior; she feels so uplifted by being able to communicate her desires and thoughts through her own vernacular that she secures in herself the subjectivity that her husband is trying to snuff out.

III. Concluding Thoughts As women writers begin to understand how our language shapes thought, they can then begin to push back and repopulate our uses of the language — their vernaculars — with their own agency/ identities instead of mirroring the male subjectivity which social discourse tends to follow. This is exactly what Mahasweta Devi and Gayatri Spivak, Anu Singh Chaudhary, Krishna Sobti, and Meena Kandasamy are able to accomplish with their produced literature. Whether in English, Hindi, a tribal language, or the language of the body, this vernacular creates space for the female subjectivity to exist and be heard in contemporary literature and society. Looking ahead, in her book of essays “My Friend, My Enemy,” Ismat Chughtai, one of India’s most foundational feminist writers in the twentieth century, writes about her wish for women in India to achieve true equality in name, in reality, and in language, stating that “the heroine of the future will be neither heartless nor op- pressed. She will be only a woman, and instead of giving her the title of ahramen [Satan] and yazdaan [God], writers will bless her with the title of woman. And then the process of construction will begin” (Chughtai and Naqvi). ◆

As women writers begin to understand how our language shapes thought, they can then begin to push back and repopulate our uses of the language

— their vernaculars — with their own agency/ identities instead of mirroring the male subjectivity which social discourse tends to follow. “

title: Exoneration of American Violence: The Cultural Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During the War in Vietnam
notes: Senior thesis, presented as an introduction and one chapter ("We Could Never Forget") on Vietnamese-American narratives. Opens with three epigraphs (Tim O'Brien, William Westmoreland, Viet Thanh Nguyen). Faculty adviser named on the opening page. The pull quote at the top of printed page 159 repeats a passage of the conclusion.
text:
Exoneration of American Violence:

The Cultural Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During the War in Vietnam by Saidie Stone

Department of International Studies

Faculty Adviser: Prof. Lauren Stokes, Ph.D.

“I know what happened that day. I know how it happened. I know why. It was the sunlight. It was the wickedness that soaks into your blood and slowly heats up and begins to boil. Frustration, partly. Rage, partly. The enemy was invisible. They were ghosts. … But it went beyond that. Something more mysterious. The smell of incense, maybe. The unknown, the unknowable. The blank faces. The overwhelming otherness. This is not to justify what occurred on March 16, 1968, for in my view such justifications are both futile and outrageous. Rather, it’s to bear witness to the mystery of evil. Twenty-five years ago, as a terrified young PFC, I too could taste the sunlight. I could smell the sin. I could feel the butchery sizzling like grease just under my eyeballs.”

— Tim O’Brien, In the Lake of the Woods

“Well, the Oriental … doesn’t put the same high price on life as does the Westerner. Life is plentiful, life is cheap in the Orient. And as the philosophy of the Orient expresses it, life is not important.”

— General William Westmoreland, Hearts and Minds

“The Vietnamese people and Vietnamese Americans have voices. It’s simply that Americans as a whole tend not to hear them.”

— Viet Thanh Nguyen, “Anger in the Asian American Novel”

Introduction

It is Strange How War Never Ends For Those Involved.1

On March 16, 1968, American soldiers carried out a search-and-destroy operation in the Son My village of South Vietnam.2 Quang Ngai province, called Pinkville by American GIs, had a “reputation as a Viet Cong hotspot.”3 The village includes the hamlets of My Lai, My Khe, Tu Cung, and Co Luy; each hamlet includes several sub-hamlets. Though the province was supposed to be an “enemy bastion … American forces encountered no organized resistance on the morning of March 16th, either in My Lai 4 or My Khe 4.”4 US troops killed an estimated 567 Vietnamese civilians.5 Though the massacre did not occur entirely in either My Lai or My Lai 4, the atrocity is known as the My Lai Massacre.

The troops at My Lai 4 belonged to Charlie Company, led by Lt. William Calley. Calley was ultimately the only person convicted for his involvement in the massacre. Lt. Calley’s conviction was received with bipartisan backlash.6 People opposed to the verdict believed either that the military was using Calley as a scapegoat or that he had done nothing wrong. President Nixon felt justified in pardoning Calley because of the outcry. He shared “the opinion of many Americans” that My Lai was “an aberration, unrepresentative of our country.”7

However, Nick Turse argues in his book Kill Anything That Moves that the My Lai Massacre was not an aberration but “part of a consistent pattern of criminality resulting from policies set at the top.”8 In order to reframe it as an anomaly, the military and the Pentagon focused their investigations only on the killings at My Lai 4 and the subsequent cover-up of those killings; they did not investigate the killings at My Khe 4. According to Turse, the “killings of civilians … were widespread, routine, and directly attributable to U.S. command policies.”9 While there were codes of conduct that were supposed to protect noncomba- tants, they mostly functioned to give the military deniability, since actual conduct differed greatly from what was on paper.10 Officials were desperate to reach the so- called ‘crossover point,’ which was when they killed more guerilla fighters than the Viet Cong could recruit; that goal, along with the military’s intentional indoctrina- tion of racism against Vietnamese people, led to the ‘mere-gook rule,’ or MGR, which held that Vietnamese people were less than human. Success was measured by the number of Vietnamese killed-in-action, and “the mere-gook rule promised that any dead Vietnamese would do.”11

Turse’s point that the military used racism as a tool to instill in soldiers the ability to kill readily and ruthlessly connects to two concepts that Mimi Thi Nguyen

1 Spike Lee, Da Five Bloods (Netflix, 2020). 2 The intent of search-and-destroy missions was to clear a given area of all guerilla fighters. The term became synonymous with “systematic destruction,” since soldiers were given liberty to “’shoot anything that moves.’” Nick Turse, Kill Anything That Moves: The Real American War in Vietnam (New York: Picador, 2013), 51–53. 3 Howard Jones, My Lai: Vietnam, 1968, and the Descent into Darkness, Pivotal Moments in American History (New York, NY: Oxford University Press, 2017), 23. 4 Jones. My Lai, 27–96. 5 Jones, My Lai, 212. 6 Jones, My Lai, 291. 7 Jones, My Lai, 339. 8 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 230. 9 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 22. 10 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 53–5. 11 Turse, Kill Anything That Moves, 50–1; 28–9.

employs in The Gift of Freedom. Nguyen’s work studies how America’s promise to deliver freedom to populations around the world, often through war and violence, inevitably and inescapably colonizes the subjects of that freedom by imposing on them an unpayable debt. Nguyen deploys the Vietnamese refugee as a double target of the gift of freedom: the first time through war and the second time through refuge. Two ideas Nguyen employs are necropower and Foucault’s economy of biopower. The former is “the idea that some deaths don’t matter,” and the latter views racism as “the politics of disposability.”12 To learn to kill without hesitancy is to learn that certain people are disposable.

In the following chapter of my thesis, I examine the work of Vietnamese-American writers about the war and their experiences as immigrants in the United States. I use Mimi Thi Nguyen’s book The Gift of Freedom: War, Debt, and Other Refugee Passages to frame my close readings of Viet Thanh Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and Qui Nguyen’s Vietgone. Many Vietnamese victims of the massacre at My Lai are not living and are therefore unable to share their side of the story. Given this reason, I examine works by Vietnamese-Americans for their perspective of American involvement in Vietnam and the Vietnamese refugee experience.

Before I begin my analysis, I would like to first address how I choose to reference the war, since the name itself has inescap- able implications. Both the ‘Vietnam War,’ the term Americans use, and the ‘American War,’ the term many Vietnamese use, over- simplify the conflict. For example, Laotians and Cambodians lost their lives in massive numbers due to U.S. efforts to bomb North Vietnamese supply chains in those countries — meaning bloodshed from the conflict spilled over borders rather than staying confined to Vietnam.13 For these reasons, among others, in his book Nothing Ever Dies, Viet Thanh Nguyen refers to the conflict as “the war.” He argues, “to deny it a name … clears a space for reimagining and remem- bering the war differently. Denying this war its name also acknowledges what everyone who has lived through a war already knows: their war needs no name, for it is always simply the war.”14 Renny Christopher argues that calling the war “Vietnam” erases “all distinctions between enemy and ally and among Vietnamese individuals,” con- flating the country with “war and evil,” and is another way of victimizing U.S. soldiers by placing blame on the amalgamation of country and war itself. To challenge typical connotations associated with the name ‘the Vietnam War,’ I will instead use the term ‘the war in Vietnam,’ or simply ‘the war.’

Chapter: We Could Never Forget

We have been the subjects of that experiment they call, with a straight face, the Cold War. What a joke, given how hot the war has been for us.15

Biopower, Necropower, and PTSD American stories about the war do not depict Vietnamese people or their experiences accurately or empathetically. Whether Vietnamese people are stereotypical supporting characters or extra bodies to be blown up in the background, their lack of

12 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 89. 13 Viet Thanh Nguyen, Nothing Ever Dies: Vietnam and the Memory of War (Cambridge, Massachusetts: Harvard University Press, 2016), 6–7. Approximately 400,000 people in Laos and 700,000 in Cambodia were killed by U.S. bombs during the Vietnam War. 14 Nguyen, Nothing Ever Dies, 8. 15 Viet Thanh Nguyen, The Sympathizer (New York: Grove Press, 2015), 239; 344–345.

humanity and complexity suggests that they are ‘other,’ ‘alien,’ and less than white Americans. This attitude seeps into and shapes cultural narratives about the war and Vietnamese refugees. I will perform close readings of excerpts from Viet Thanh Nguyen’s The Sympathizer and Qui Nguyen’s Vietgone, using Mimi Thi Nguyen’s reading of trauma as a tool of neoliberal war-making as a framework for my analysis in order to understand how these works counteract cultural narratives that dehumanize Vietnamese people and humanize and center perpetrators of violence.

Mimi Thi Nguyen, like Nick Turse, also critiques the erasure of systemic violence from the American consciousness. She examines how the idea of trauma op- erates differently on American veterans than on Vietnamese refugees in ways that ultimately absolve not only the soldiers who committed the violence but American war-making itself. Put simply, she argues that American veterans can be divorced from their trauma, which reinforces their humanity by highlighting their mental and emotional pain. However, refugees are defined by their trauma and limited to the category of ‘displaced person,’ a permanent status which they must perpetually work to overcome but can never overcome. As Nguyen states, “to be given freedom is a process of becoming without being.”16

Foregrounding Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in American veterans reframes American violence against racial others, transforming perpetrators of brutality into victims of “unimaginable pain.”17 The victimization of perpetrators humanizes them by using their pain and suffering as proof of their humanity.18 In addition, their victimhood eclipses the people toward whom they committed violence and obscures the effects of the violence inflicted on their victims. Finally, the emphasis on their pain “rescue[s] liberal empire[s] from the criminality of its wartime conduct” by framing American violence against racial others (in this case, Vietnamese civilians) as an aberration rather than a fundamental tool of American foreign policy.19 Because of the harmful psychological consequences soldiers experience after perpetrating violence, liberal war is able to claim that such violence is an anomaly. In fact, “public disclosures about cruelties committed by U.S. military forces — including the My Lai massacre … were hugely influential in the diagnosis’s codification.”20 The diagnosis of PTSD, regarded as a psychological abnormality, makes such violence seem aberrant and atypical. Using Nguyen’s understanding, it is no surprise that the My Lai Massacre is turned from “insensible destruction wrought by a supremacist empire” to “a regrettable failure to discern between the good racial subject and the bad one” and “an accident, the unfortunate symptom of soldier’s unbearable experiences.”21

In contrast, under liberal empires, the refugee cannot be separated from their trauma. The refugee becomes not only a person who is traumatized but also a

16 Mimi Thi Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom: War, Debt, and Other Refugee Passages, Next Wave: New Directions in Women’s Studies (USA: Duke University Press, 2012), 18. 17 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 116. 18 As Fassin and Rechtman say in their book Empire of Trauma, “these men should therefore be considered war victims, broken by what they had witnessed and by what they themselves had done.” Didier Fassin and Richard Rechtman, The Empire of Trauma: An Inquiry into the Condition of Victimhood, trans. Rachel Gomme (United States: Princeton University Press, 2009), 91. 19 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 113. 20 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 113. 21 Nguyen, Gift of Freedom, 173.

displaced person who responds to violence ‘abnormally’ and is defined by their ar- rested potentiality. Refugees are divorced from the situations that traumatized them (i.e., political repression or war). Trauma comes to signify abnormality and failure in refugees, rather than the experiences that harmed them. Unlike veterans, refugees are burdened with the necessity of reacting to violence ‘correctly’ or ‘normally’; without a response that is deemed as such, they are seen as deficient or incapacitated.

If the American military uses racism as a weapon to engender in its soldiers the capacity to kill Vietnamese without hesitation, then PTSD absolves the system of American war-making of blame after the war ends. In other words, biopower and necropower operate both during and after the war. During the war, they enable and encourage the perpetration of violence; after, they give way to exoneration over accountability.

The Sympathizer The end of the war is near, and a little Vietnamese boy is “crowned with a Yan- kees cap … and airlifted into the heavens, his ultimate destination being [an American soldier’s] family in St. Louis, where he would be given a golden retriever and the nickname Danny Boy.”22 This quote frames the refugee’s passage from the distant nation of Vietnam to America as an act of salvation. The young boy’s passing to America is depicted as a spiritually purifying journey. “Danny Boy’s” method of travel via helicopter is an act of sanc- tification; it takes him “to the heavens.”23 The destination — in this case, St. Louis — and the gifts that await him there are wholesome and thoroughly American. His new American family welcomes “Danny Boy” with open arms, a baseball cap — a reference to America’s favorite pastime — and the most idyllic pet possible: a golden retriever. After his salvation and his picturesque homecoming, Danny Boy’s life is full of possibility.

Danny Boy’s tale comes from a story within a story, satirizing America’s refugee parable. Danny Boy is a character in The Hamlet, a fictional Hollywood blockbuster in Viet Thanh Nguyen’s novel The Sympathizer. The film parodies many aspects of American cinema and American ideology. Danny Boy’s narrative illustrates not the genuine refugee experience but rather a mocking critique of America’s idealistic understanding of what it has to offer the disadvantaged racial ‘other.’ For Mimi Thi Nguyen, America’s gift of freedom is “composed of pipe dreams, bogus concepts, and moral luck as well as violence at its origin.”24 By juxtaposing Danny Boy’s story with The Sympathizer’s main plot, Viet Thanh Nguyen exposes the refugee parable and shows that it is in fact what Mimi Thi Nguyen says it is: a “pipe dream,”

22 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157. 23 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 157. 24 Nguyen, The Gift of Freedom, 24–5.

“

”

America’s involvement in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engenders in him a deep sense of powerlessness.

“bogus,” and born from violence. Instead of following a young child whose Vietnamese identity and experience of the war are eas- ily and effectively erased by a picturesque American welcome, the novel follows adult men who take active roles in the war and are destroyed by it.

The Sympathizer follows an unnamed North Vietnamese mole — referred to as the Sympathizer — working for a South Vietnamese general who relocates to America after the Communists take over Vietnam. The book begins days before the fall of Saigon. Though the Communists take the capital by the third chapter, the struggle over Vietnam continues for the rest of the book. The war is technically over, but it hasn’t ended strategically or emotionally for any of the Vietnamese characters. Specifically, Bon, one of the narrator’s closest friends and a true be- liever in democracy and South Vietnam, suffers a great loss just before their escape to America. The Sympathizer uses his close relationship with an Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) general to get spaces for Bon, his wife Linh, and his child Duc on a plane to America, but Linh and Duc are shot and killed as they run across the tarmac towards the plane that will take them out of Vietnam.

Bon’s story juxtaposes and undermines the refugee parable represented by Danny Boy. Bon and the Sympathizer are not ‘purified’ or ‘fixed’ by their passage to America. In contrast to Danny Boy’s passage — his salvation — after Linh and Duc are killed on the tarmac, Bon and the Sympathizer bring their bodies onto the plane. Their passage is far from purifying or healing. Bon literally carries his family’s bodies with him to America, and he is unable to leave his pain behind. Leaving their bodies is not an option: the Sympathizer takes Linh’s body and runs onto the plane without discussion. There is no question that both he and Bon will bear this pain; there is no possibility that their passage to America will heal Bon’s heartbreak.

Once in America, Bon’s loss and his experiences in the war cannot be smoothed over or forgotten. In fact, he regrets leaving Vietnam at all, and not only because Linh and Duc were killed. Fighting for his country gave him a sense of purpose that he was willing to give up in order to save his family, but he ends up losing both. To him, life in America is not a life worth living. Their apartment in Los Angeles is “a jail cell,” rather than an idyllic new home; the Americans are their rescuers, but Bon says, “they just didn’t tell us that they’d cut off our balls and cut out our tongues along the way … If we were real men, we wouldn’t have let them do that.”25 America offers Bon neither freedom nor possibility. His escape to America not only costs him his identity as a father and a husband but also his identity as a man. Bon’s anger over his lost masculinity is indicative of his lost autonomy and control. America’s involvement in Vietnam and its ‘rescue’ of South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers engenders in him a deep sense of powerlessness.

Bon’s decision to return to Vietnam underscores America’s inability to heal him. He volunteers to take part in an operation to go back to Vietnam in an attempt to overthrow the Communist government. The operation is widely acknowledged to be a suicide mission by characters in the novel. However, Bon would rather die in Vietnam than live in America. His faith in democracy has disappeared, as has his commitment to any kind of cause. Bon tells an anticommunist admiral in Thailand, “I

25 Nguyen, The Sympathizer, 223.

don’t give a damn about saving anybody, including myself. I just want to kill communists.”26 Bon no longer values his life or anyone else’s life.

Bon’s experience of coming to and living in America differs greatly from Danny Boy’s. In The Hamlet, Danny Boy leaves behind an older brother who died and a sister who was sexually assaulted by the Viet Cong and subsequently disappeared from the movie. Neither the death of his brother nor leaving behind his sister impacts Danny Boy’s quixotic salvation. His potential pain and regret for leaving them behind is never even suggested by the movie’s finale. Instead, a new life with an American family offers a simple, neat, and happy ending.

Nguyen’s novel also works against the narrative propensity to center experiences of the war around those of Americans. Though implicated, Americans are not held directly responsible for any of the main characters’ suffering. Bon’s wife and child are shot by either the North Vietnamese Army or South Vietnamese soldiers (neither is confirmed). However, Bon’s loss is just one example of intra-community violence. The protagonist’s other close friend, Man, was a Communist double agent working in the South Vietnamese Army up until the Communists took over. The day Saigon falls, Communist planes drop Napalm bombs on Man and his South Vietnamese unit. The bomb permanently disfigures him; as a result, he distances himself from his wife and children who are disgusted by and terrified of him. The Sympathizer, who is half-Vietnamese and identifies as Vietnamese (though other characters torment him for his biraciality), kills two other Vietnamese men. Additionally, the Sympathizer claims responsibility for tor- turing a Communist agent nicknamed the Watchman, and in another torture scene, South Vietnamese soldiers rape a female Vietnamese communist during an inter- rogation.27 Nguyen argues that this is how Vietnamese can “reclaim [their] subjectivity” because they “aren’t just victims, but victimizers as well.”28 He speaks about the actual rape of Vietnamese women and the metaphorical rape of Vietnam when he says that he “wanted to show that this was something that wasn’t simply happening in terms of what the West was doing to Vietnam but what the Vietnamese were doing to themselves.”29

Though the story works against the dominant American-centric narratives about the war, the novel remains very

” critical of American involvement in Vietnam. Nguyen does not only blame the American military for violence against the Vietnamese; war is one tool of America’s contemporary empire, but it is not the only tool. There are multiple passages throughout the book that stress the cultural and political significance of The Hamlet, not as ‘just’ a movie but as a weapon of American culture. One passage laments that sometimes art becomes “more real than the real” because the film will continue to have cultural power when the war is reduced to “a paragraph in a schoolbook students won’t even bother to read.”30 While many scholars have argued for the essential role textbooks play in the cultivation and spread of national ideology, Nguyen suggests that Hollywood is more influential.

Hollywood’s ideological and cultural power are intrinsically linked to violence and exploitation in Nguyen’s novel. The Sympathizer often uses violent words and metaphors involving weapons to describe the film’s ideological rule in that the military-industrial complex and Hollywood both contribute to “the obliteration of natives.”31 He describes Hollywood as “relentlessly assaulting the mental defenses of audiences” and being “the launcher of the intercontinental ballistic missile of Amer- icanization,” which ultimately succeeds in the “lobotomization and pickpocketing of the world’s audiences.”32 Nguyen creates an association between America’s military power and its cultural power. The language itself (e.g., the phrases “relentlessly assaulting” and “obliteration”) is violent and aggressive. All of these metaphors carry unmistakable threats of destruction and equate the destructive power of the military and Hollywood.

This overt connection between American culture and exploitation points out the essentiality of violence as a tool for American power abroad. In other words, violence is not an abnormality or an exception, but rather an innate part of American war-making and American cultural dominance worldwide. Exceptional violence “is normalized as a part of the cost of the continuous government of human freedom” — an unfortunate and inevitable consequence — when in fact America “acts murderously” and “evades indictment for doing so.”33

The Hamlet also satirizes Hollywood’s “Vietnam War” movie tropes, including its inaccurate, shallow, and stereotypical portrayals of Vietnamese people. Even though The Hamlet contains speaking roles for Vietnamese characters, it denies them full humanity and cultural and ethnic specificity. The Auteur, the director of the Movie, adds Binh (nicknamed Benny by the Americans), his sister Mai, and their little brother (whose real name is never mentioned and who is nicknamed Danny Boy by the Americans). None of the Vietnamese characters are played by Vietnamese actors; instead, they are played by a Korean-American actor, a Chinese-British actress, and a Filipino actor.34 The actors’ inaccurate ethnicities and their characters’ American nicknames erase anything iden- tifiably Vietnamese about Binh, Mai, and Danny Boy. The fact that these characters are Vietnamese is ultimately not as important as the fact that they are non-white

people protected by white people.35 Their ethnicity and culture does not matter; the film is not about them.

These Vietnamese characters are vio- lently exploited in order to add intrigue to a story about white Americans. Each of their plotlines reinforces that the film is, as the Sympathizer calls it, “an epic about white men saving good yellow people from bad yellow people.”36 Binh’s extended, grue- some death scene underlines the brutality and viciousness of the Viet Cong while his body is brutalized and tortured. Mai’s sexual assault, also perpetrated by Communist soldiers and shown in detail on screen, functions as shock value and justification for the annihilation of the Viet Cong.37 Danny Boy’s rescue establishes America’s benevolence and superiority over this war-ravaged ‘other’ country. Nguyen is clear and unequivocal in his determination that American media — specifically Hollywood — is an essential and powerful tool of American power and ideology.38

Conclusion Vietnamese-American sources regarding the war clearly counter the racist tropes of American narratives by reclaiming agency, individuality, and pain, while also recen- tering Vietnamese experiences and perspectives. The Sympathizer and Vietgone also work against America’s refugee parable, which depicts refugee passage to America as a spiritual rebirth. Furthermore, The Sympathizer criticizes Hollywood not only for the violence against and exploitation of Vietnamese people within its films but also for its powerful and destructive role as a weapon of American power.

The racism that the U.S. military inoculated in its troops during the war in Vietnam is not contained within the specific time and place of war. Mimi Thi Nguyen’s analysis shows how PTSD is used to forgive systemic American violence after wars end. That is one manifestation of racism, and outright violence is another. Anti-Asian violence and sentiment has a long history in the U.S., not beginning or ending with involvement in Vietnam.
