title: WHAT WORK GOES INTO FRAMING THE NEXT GENERATION’S SCIENCE EDUCATION? A LOOK INTO OLIVIA MASSE’S URAP EXPERIENCE
notes: Feature on sophomore Olivia Masse's Undergraduate Research Assistant Program work with Professor Jennifer Richards (School of Education and Social Policy) on science education. The contents gives the title as "What work goes into framing the next generation’s science education?: A look into Olivia Masse’s URAP experience". The drop cap "W" is a separate block (165.2).
text:
WHAT WORK GOES INTO FRAMING THE NEXT GENERATION’S SCIENCE EDUCATION? A LOOK INTO OLIVIA MASSE’S URAP EXPERIENCE by Kallista Zhuang

Within the traditional U.S. public education system, students take multiple science classes over the course of a K–12 education. Whether they enjoyed these science lessons or not, they most likely had some gripes with what was taught or how it was taught, given that standard instruction does not necessarily align with every student’s preferred mode of learning. In other words, the classroom is a place of learning and engagement, but not every classroom can achieve such with their current education strategies.

Professor Jennifer Richards at Northwestern University’s School of Education and Social Policy (SESP) researches science education, or how science is taught in K–12 school systems, in order to create respon- sive classroom environments and understand the relationship between teacher practice and learning.

Professor Richards’ research is incredibly interesting, and the ability to research educator strategies grants her the unique vantage point of exploring what education equity can look like. At least, that is what drew Olivia Masse, a Northwestern University sophomore majoring in neurosci- ence and minoring in Native American and Indigenous Studies (NAIS), to participate in Professor Richards’ research.

Through the Undergraduate Research Assistant Program (URAP) at Northwestern University, Olivia was able to receive funding while participating in a unique, hybrid research experience. During the first half of the summer, Masse worked remotely, reading up on relevant literature and familiarizing herself with research techniques of the field. In the second half, she worked in-person with middle school science teachers and students, transcribing and analyzing interviews.

Masse specifically examined the implementation of the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) on eighth grade science teachers in California and its effect on improving the alignment between instruction and assessment, as she was “interested in seeing the other side of science education.” Middle school teachers were the focus since the respective school district was in the process of implementing NGSS.

NGSS integrates many values within their standards, such as depth over breadth, importance of student collaboration, and assessments that reinforce knowledge. These values, however, need not be applied in the same manner — Masse states that “NGSS also acknowledges that one size does not fit all and that it is important to consider diverse backgrounds and flexi- bility.” Such principles have resonated with Masse, who believes that more of these ideas should be emphasized in science education. Doing so would ultimately lead to a greater foundation in future science learning of younger students.

After spending the summer researching the implementation of new strategies within science education, Masse believes that NGSS was able to enhance science education through novel strategies. For example, assessments would be used as an educator tool to reinforce knowledge, rather than simply measure it. NGSS also incorporates much student collaboration into the curriculum. With better strategies that work with the students rather than against them, NGSS better prepares students who are considering a future in science.

Now, after their research proposal was accepted for the annual National Association for Research in Science Teaching conference, Richards’ lab and Masse will go to Vancouver in March to present their research. From remote literature searches to the in-person evaluation of implementation of NGSS to presenting at a research conference, Olivia has experienced many different sides of research through URAP — even working on the hammocks by the lakefill with her mentor when the weather was warm enough! ◆

title: Radical Caring: A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in the Asian American Communities
notes: Senior thesis (ethnography of frontline workers at Asian American gender-violence organizations; names are pseudonyms). Faculty adviser named on the opening page. Title as given on the contributor page; on the opening page the main title and subtitle are separate blocks. The labels of Chart 1 (printed page 172) are transcribed from the image (173.6-173.13).
text:
Radical Caring:

A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in the Asian American Communities by Chloe Wong

Department of Anthropology Faculty Adviser: Prof. Shalini Shankar, Ph.D.

Introduction

“It wasn’t just a career choice coming to the Asian Women’s Services Center. I am also a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, so I had been working on my own healing journey in my personal life for a number of years. When the Center’s Children’s Advocate job came up, I was at the crossroads of thinking about my career but also thinking about my own personal journey of healing. Having this job come up that seemed to blend together my desire to put out energy outwards instead of just focusing on inner healing for myself — this was really crucial. I think that the combination of having experience working with children, especially children of immigrant families, and really loving that, and then also my own experience of being a survivor and wanting to advocate for families who experienced that themselves. I think those two things came together in this job for me.”1

I spoke to Sun Hee on a bright and early Saturday morning in October 2020. I received her contact information via Diana, one of her colleagues and one of my other interlocutors. I reached out to Sun Hee via email for a Zoom meeting. We originally planned for late September, but Sun Hee had work conflicts. This was a common phenomenon with many of the frontline workers that I spoke to, as well as my colleagues at my internship site during summer 2020. Meetings with staff members could be rescheduled. Meetings with clients could not be delayed and should be prioritized.

Sun Hee was born and raised in South Korea until her family moved to the Midwest when she was an adolescent. She studied art history and religion as an

1 All names and organizations in this paper (Sun Hee, Diana, Asian Women’s Services Center) are pseudonyms to protect the identities of my interlocutors.

undergraduate and began working with children in a variety of capacities after graduation — tutor, admissions counselor, ESL teacher — until she joined the Asian Women’s Services Center in April 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.2 I asked her whether she had a defining experience that sparked her interest in helping survivors of gender violence. With little hesitation, she shared her identity as a survivor and her motivations for joining the Center, a non-profit organization that aims to eradicate gender-based violence for women and children across Asian American communities. Sun Hee’s perspective was especially valuable for understanding the role of the frontline worker because she drew strength from her past experiences of violence. While she was working, she put energy outwards to provide direct services and advocacy to other immigrant children and families. She found kinship with others of similar identities on her personal journey and became determined to serve them as a way of healing herself. Her story demonstrates the resilience and strength of frontline workers in gender-based violence and how they actively serve and survive.

This paper centers the stories and lived experiences of Asian American frontline workers in order to develop the concept of radical caring in eradicating gender-based violence. Sharmila Rudrappa (2004) coined the term “radical caring” as an amalgamation of individual and organizational motivations to care for survivors.3 Direct service professionals do the incredibly hard and emotionally draining work of serving survivors of gender violence day after day. They often make very little pay, work at organizations in dire need of continued funding, and receive very little recognition for their work. Despite this, they continue working. I hypothesized that their sense of responsibility was connected to serving survivors of similar racial identities.

This research asks the following questions: 1) How do frontline workers view their work in relation to their racial and ethnic identities?; 2) How can radical caring, professionalization of empathy, and Asian American Critical Race Theory (AsianCrit) be used as frameworks to understand the labor of frontline workers?; and 3) What is the role of frontline workers in responding to, preventing, and working towards eradicating gender-based violence? Through the

2 At the time of writing, the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic is an ongoing pandemic of a contagious disease. 3 Rudrappa, S. (2004). Radical Caring in an Ethnic Shelter. Gender and Society, 18(5): 588–609. DOI: 10.1177/0891243204268131

“

”

Direct service professionals do the incredibly hard and emotionally draining work of serving survivors of gender violence day after day. They often make very little pay, work at organizations in dire need of continued funding, and receive very little recognition for their work. Despite this, they continue working.

lens of AsianCrit, I argue that the work of women and non-binary individuals within domestic violence and multi-service organizations continues to demonstrate radical caring and the professionalization of empathy. In this paper, I build this argument by reviewing relevant literature and offering ethnographic discussion and analysis. In claiming the sovereignty of caring for their own ethnic communities, Asian American frontline workers build emotional and physical refuges.

Literature Review Gender-based violence (GBV) is defined by the United Nations High Commission- er for Refugees (UNHCR) as:

an umbrella term for any harmful act that is perpetrated against a person’s will and that is based on socially ascribed (i.e., gender) differences between males and females. It includes acts that inflict physical, sexual or mental harm or suffering, threats of such acts, coercion, and other deprivation of liberty. These acts can occur in public or in private.4

GBV includes any type of violence that stems from gender identity or presentation, including violence against men and violence experienced by gender non-con- forming people, who are especially vulnerable due to the marginalization of their gender identity. I discuss eradicating GBV as the long-term goal in the anti-violence movement. Eradicating, eliminating, or ending GBV refers to the complete abolition and removal of all forms of gender violence. This language is adapted from the mission and vision statements of domestic violence agencies both involved in and peripheral to this research. Many international, national, and local organizations typically use prevention or interventions to characterize their work as stopping violence before it occurs. While these efforts are crucial, the ultimate goal should remain as ending all forms of gender violence and transforming the conditions that justify, engender, and perpetuate gender violence into conditions of safety for all people.

Anthropologists have historically examined violence and conflict in relation to warfare, cultural ethos, conflicts over material resources, or cultural rituals.5 Acts of GBV, such as domestic violence, were not deeply discussed or theorized in the canon. Such issues were not thought or understood to also exist within the United States. This foreshadows our following conversations about the role of culture in perpetuating

4 Inter-Agency Field Manual on Reproductive Health in Humanitarian Settings: 2010 Revision for Field Review (2010). Inter-Agency Working Group on Reproductive Health in Crises, 8. Gender-based Violence; Geneva, Switzerland. Available from: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK305160/ 5 Wies, J.R. and Haldane, H.J. (Eds.) (2011). Anthropology on the Front Lines of Gender-Based Violence. Nashville, TN: Vanderbilt University Press.

GBV is an issue of human rights, public health, and social justice that is inextricably linked to interlocked systems of oppression: imperialism, cisheteropatriarchy, racism, and capitalism. “

” assumptions regarding GBV. A noteworthy vacuum in anthropological work was the lack of connection to macrostructures that maintain and reinforce inequalities and violence. GBV is an issue of human rights, public health, and social justice that is inextricably linked to interlocked systems of oppression: imperialism, cisheteropatriarchy, racism, and capitalism.6 This is not to say that one of these components is the root of all gender violence, but GBV has been used as a tool of each system of oppression to enact violence.

It is crucial to ground this research in Critical Race Theory (CRT), specifically AsianCrit. AsianCrit explores the complex racialization of people of Asian descent in the United States, specifically the legacy of state-sanctioned violence and marginalization of Asian American perspectives in both institutional policies and informal social practices.7 I would like to highlight one of the seven tenets of AsianCrit:

Story, Theory, and Praxis is the idea that counter stories, theoretical frameworks, research, and practice are intertwined elements in the analysis of Asian American experiences and in advocacy efforts for Asian American communities. This tenet recognizes the work of Asian American scholars whose work should inform theory and practice.

Story, Theory, and Praxis emphasizes the importance of counter stories and centering in the margins. The stories of frontline workers are pivotal in informing responses to gender violence, which has already been established as a prevalent issue. Therefore, the thoughts of frontline workers add authentic representation to survivor needs.

Methodology

Feminist Ethnography and Fieldwork In this section, I provide my intellectual genealogy of utilizing feminist ethnography. Feminist ethnography grounded in CRT was employed to guide data collection and analysis for this project. Christa Craven and Dána-Ain Davis (2011) define feminist ethnography as “a project committed to documenting lived experience as it is impacted by gender, race, class, sexuality, and other aspects of participants’ lives.”8 The aim of feminist ethnography is not to presume an egalitarian relationship between research and research subjects, but to acknowledge the power dynamics at play.9 Anthropologists should be continuously interrogating their role in meeting the needs of their female and non-binary subjects. My interlocutors were generous with their time and knowledge because they believed that I was doing impactful work simply by listening to them and bringing visibility to GBV in immigrant communities through my academic research. I argue for the use of feminist ethnography because this approach can broaden our understanding of the conditions that lead to violence and map the intersections between race, ethnicity, gender, and justice.

Ethnographic Fieldwork (Participant

Can There Be a Feminist Ethnography? Women & Performance: A Journal of Feminist Theory, 5: 7–27. https://doi-org.turing.library.northwestern.edu/10.1080/07407709008571138

Observation) Participant observation involves the day- to-day aspects of people’s activities, rituals, and interactions to uncover their culture.10 While participant observation is a common component of qualitative research and ethnographic fieldwork, I resist the premise of the “self” and the “other.” In early ethnog- raphies, the “self” has historically been the detached, privileged anthropologist who is merely present to examine the peculiarities and deviations of the “other.” Given my salient identities and personal history with GBV, I questioned the prevailing dichotomy between “self” and “other.” Instead, I was focused on being an active participant who was reflexive of my own coexistence within the same context.

My ethnographic account begins with a brief history of the South Asian Support Center and continues with a description of my involvement and the shelter environment. The South Asian Support Center is located in Uptown Chicago, a north side lakeshore neighborhood home to “Asia on Argyle,” and has a concentration of Chinese, Vietnamese, Cambodian, Laotian, and Thai businesses and residents. In the 1970s, the women’s anti-violence movements gave rise to community-organizing institutions, including domestic violence shelters.11 In the United States, many Asian American women spearheaded specific organizational responses to domestic violence in the 1980s after questioning their own communities’ lack of access to mainstream programs.12 In 1989, the South

Asian Support Center was founded by five Asian women, who were established activists and professionals within Chicagoland. They became increasingly aware of domestic violence cases within the South Asian community. Although the Center was initially dedicated to serving South Asian women, the clientele eventually expanded to all immigrant communities.

I began my virtual internship in June, dedicating four days a week for six weeks to build, develop, and execute an evaluation. I was invited to work once a week from the shelter to support understaffed shelter services. Despite the 8 a.m. shift on Saturday mornings, I was eager to contribute however I could at the shelter. The shelter had just reopened and staff members followed strict COVID-safe guidelines. My primary responsibilities, in addition to my intern tasks, were to ensure the well-being of residents, meet their daily living needs, and maintain a comfortable and safe communal living environment. Staff members and my direct supervi- sor were aware of my intent as a researcher to ask questions and collect information.

My positionality as a researcher blurred with my roles as an intern and colleague. I did not interview any clients in a thesis researcher capacity, yet all of my interactions with clients created greater empathy and emotion for their stories. I experienced vicarious trauma as I spent countless hours researching gender violence and poring over transcripts of clients’ and staff members’ interviews. I was fear- ful of the physical environment outside of

10 McGrath, C. & Rudman, D.L. (2019). Using Participant Observation to Enable Critical Understandings of Disability in Later Life: An Illustration Conducted with Older Adults with Low Vision. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 18. https://doi. org/10.1177/1609406919891292 11 Kim, M. (2005). The Community Engagement Continuum: Outreach, Mobilization, Organizing, and Accountability to Address Violence against Women in Asian and Pacific Islander Communities. Asian Pacific Institute on Gender-Based Violence. https://s3.amazonaws.com/gbv-wp-uploads/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/18233908/Community-Engagement-Continuum-Report-2010.pdf 12 Kim, M. (2010). Innovative Strategies to Address Domestic Violence in Asian and Pacific Islander Communities: Examining Themes, Models, and Interventions. Asian Pacific Institute on Gender-Based Violence. https://s3.amazonaws.com/gbv-wp-uploads/ wp-content/uploads/2017/07/20193227/Innovative-Strategies-Rpt-2010.pdf my apartment and scared of alleyways and men who could emerge from the shadows at any time. My participant observation informed my reflexivity as an anthropologist and reinforced the importance of lived experiences. I also became acutely aware of the limits of compassion and the exhaus- tion of professional care, which influenced my empathy for frontline workers. In the later sections of analysis, I will discuss how the specific limits are reflected in the professional experiences of frontline workers.

Interview Process From August to December 2020, I conducted 14 semi-structured, key informant interviews with frontline workers.13 Purposeful sampling was used to recruit female or non-binary identifying frontline workers within Asian-serving agencies in Chicagoland.14 My co-workers at the South Asian Support Center connected me to other staff members within this small but mighty community. At the end of each interview, I used snowball sampling to recruit additional participants. Once interviewees had a sense of my questions, they would introduce me to their co-workers if my interviewees thought that they would be a good fit.

Interviews ranged from thirty to eighty minutes, depending on the inter- viewee. Due to the ongoing pandemic, all interviews were conducted virtually via phone or Zoom to follow COVID-safe research protocols. A pre-designed interview guide with 15 questions was used to frame the direction of the interview. Follow-up questions and tangents offered additional insights to our conversations. I took notes during all interviews, and interviews were audio-recorded. After all interviews were conducted, they were transcribed. The transcripts were analyzed in NVivo, a qualitative research software, through inductive coding and relationship building. Emerging themes existed on various scales and were then categorized into the socio-ecological framework.

Enacting Radical Care The themes discerned from the qualitative analysis will be discussed on the individual level. I employ the socio-ecological framework to highlight how the work of frontline workers is crucial and interconnected on these levels for combating GBV. The integrated socio-ecological framework for violence prevention by the World Health Organization (WHO) views GBV as the outcome of interactions at the four levels.15 This provides a holis- tic approach to understanding the needs of survivors and contextualizes the range of factors affecting the lives of women and non-binary people of color. Locating Frontline Workers. I define frontline workers as direct service professionals who “comfort, advocate for, and assist victims and survivors of gender-based violence.”16 They are the “actors who provide care and support to survivors of violence: from volunteer-run domestic violence shelters or community-based organizations to the increasingly professionalized service providers giving psychosocial,

13 Cossham, A. and Johanson, G. (2018). The Benefits and Limitations of Using Key Informants in Library and Information Studies Research. Information Research, 24(3). http://informationr.net/ir/24-3/rails/rails1805.html 14 Purposeful sampling refers to the technique in qualitative research of identifying and selecting individuals who are especially knowledgeable or experienced with the subject of interest (Palinkas et al. 2016). 15 World Health Organization (2012). Understanding and Addressing Violence Against Women. Retrieved from http://apps.who. int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/77432/WHO_RHR_12.36_eng.pdf;jsessionid=E7B0B9B497AC762621D13A24632CAC40?sequence=1 16 Wies and Haldane 2011 therapeutic and legal aid.”17 Within this ethnography, frontline workers range from shelter advocates and counselors to program supervisors and directors. I focus on the roles that are derived from and exist within community organizations rather than public service roles (e.g., police officers), which intrinsically reproduce systems of violence and oppression. Within my research, I focus on the frontline workers of five total organizations — three multi-service organizations (Arab American Family Association, Pan-Asian Health Center, Korean Community Center) and two domestic violence (DV) agencies (Asian Women’s Services Center, South Asian Support Center).

Individual Level The first level identifies the life histories of frontline workers to understand their motivations and hopes for their work. As previously stated, they are often the first line of help in efforts to respond to GBV.

Their life histories shape their everyday work with clients because their labor often helps them make sense of their personal experiences and of the injustices that are peripheral in their lives.When examining participants’ objects of regret, we found that 24% had regrets of career choices, 23% had regrets of education, 21% expressed regrets in their marriage or romantic relationships, 17% regretted parenting or relationships with their children, 9% had regrets relating to other family members, 9% had regrets concerning friendships, 7% regretted financial issues, 6% regretted some personal character trait, and 3% had other regrets not included in our coding scheme. Table 4 displays the instances and frequencies of the different objects of regret. Shared Immigrant Identities. Many workers shared immigrant identities and/or ethnic experiences with the clients that they were serving. Munira grew up in Pakistan and came to Chicago to pursue a college educa-

◆Chart 1. Adapted Socio-Ecological Framework for Violence Prevention tion, eventually receiving a master’s degree in counseling. She explained why she initially became interested in counseling:

Growing up in a very collectivistic culture, you hear a lot about things like, “Oh you know you’re a woman, you should be acting in a certain way” or “If a man beats you, it’s okay.” I’ve heard it and seen it to be very normalized, and it has always bothered me. I have seen the manifestations of domestic violence in my relatives. Two of these girls were actually my nieces, but they were around the same age as me. I could not understand. … I saw them after so many years. They used to be very upbeat and friendly, very jolly. After all these years, I was quite shocked, like, “What the hell happened to you, not only physically but emotionally?” I saw some nervous tics.

Although we were on a Zoom call, Munira had an urgent tone and was clearly indignant at the violence inflicted against women within her family and community. Her own training in mental health and counseling informed her understanding of how domestic violence manifests in South Asian communities. She was especially sensitive to how other members of her community responded to unhappy relationships and how her female relatives became increasingly depressed throughout the years. This motivated her to further understand the psychology of humans. I hypothesize that this may have also influenced her immigration to the United States for higher education. She was physically escaping from the culture of neglect and pain in Pakistan but found greater strength from her cultural identity at her workplace in the U.S. She directs these emotions toward assisting survivors of gender violence at the South Asian Support Center because her family members could very well be in the position of these same clients.

Anthropological scholarship has historically theorized culture in a myriad of ways. Culture refers to the values, attitudes, and behaviors that determine definitions and descriptions of norms within distinct societies. Within GBV literature, culture is often scapegoated as the primary influence of violence. It undeniably plays an important role in how such societities “view, perceive, and process sexual acts as well as sexual violence.”18 However, “culture-blaming” is an incorrect narrative that does not accurately reflect the power dynamics at play.

First, “culture-blaming” designates a perceived dichotomy between “traditional” and “modern” cultures. “Traditional” cultures, such as immigrant communities within the United States, have not fully understood the notions of modern, civi- lized culture. Therefore, it is argued that gender violence continues to occur within these communities; however, this is an oversimplified argument that overlooks social, political, and economic inequalities. Modern societies and cultures are located, both physically and imaginarily, within First World nations, many of which are former colonizers or current neo-colonizers. Reckoning with the historical implications of oppression is crucial in doing the work of radical caring. First-Generation Immigrants. Of my 14 interlocutors, seven of them — Soo Jin, Hong, Sharon, Shaima, Sun Hee, Hye Jin, and Munira — were first-generation immigrants who immigrated from Asia. By first-generation, I refer to individuals who were born to one or both parents

18 Kalra, G. and Bhugra, D. (2013). Sexual Violence Against Women: Understanding Cross-Cultural Intersections. Indian Journal of Psychiatry, 55(3): 244–249. DOI: 10.4103/0019-5545.117139 in a country outside of the U.S. and later immigrated to the U.S. for various reasons. Studies on the ethnic identity development of first-generation immigrants in educational settings19 have ascertained that students who have left the comfort of homes seek affirmation of their ethnicity and have a strong relationship between ethnic identity development and self-es- teem. I believe that my interlocutors seek similar affirmations through their current and ongoing work. By serving their cultural and ethnic communities in the U.S., they can continue to remain connected to their parent cultures despite being situated in the dominant white American culture.

Hong was born in Vietnam and came to the United States when she was 7 or 8 years old with her then-17-year-old aunt as a refugee. She recalls leaving Vietnam in the 1980s as “boat people’’ and going to refugee camps before finally arriving in the U.S. This was a formative experience for her that led to her pursuit of roles that could give back to her community. She went on to receive a bachelor’s degree in fine arts and a master’s degree in expressive art therapy. Hong is currently the Group Programs Manager at the Pan-Asian Health Center, as well as an art therapist. Her leadership role in the Behavioral Health Program includes facilitating group programs focused on developing and practicing skills in the community, supervising the caseloads of clinicians and case managers, and supporting advocacy work as needed. Almost 20 years ago, she reached out to the Director of Mental Health at the time with a desire to do art therapy for the community. Since then, she has built many relationships with individual and group clients. Hong describes how she was able to learn how to process her emotions, memories, and experiences through art therapy:

My beliefs in the process of nonverbal expression or communication mean that expressive art is not just visual art but writing and poetry; it could be music or video; it could be any form of expression a person may have to express or explore themselves, or communicate with another person or be a part of a community …

Certainly my own experience with doing art and writing for myself since I was younger and seeing the power of that. The process of working with clay and this particular process triggered a memory that I was really surprised by and just seeing how powerful that process is because I do a lot of work in understanding myself and my experiences. Firsthand I see the power of that, and it’s kind of endless with infinite possibilities.

Expressive art was an important part of her journey in understanding her own

19 Acar, E., Yigit, M.F., and Aslan, D. (2016). Ethnic Identity Development in Schools among First Generation Immigrants in the United States. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(4): 105–110. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1088508

“Frontline workers are critical in comprehensive, intersectional responses of preventing, eliminating, and ending GBV for all communities.” experiences. She comments that this is especially impactful for people who do not speak English or have a high education level. Given that most of her clientele is Vietnamese and she tries to build long-term relationships with clients, I hypothesize that her role as a facilitator is crucial in also maintaining her sense of self and identity.

Conclusion This research began out of my curiosities about the perspectives of female frontline workers of color within the work of combating GBV. My conversations with my 14 interlocutors — Amina, Diana, Farah, Hong, Hye Jin, Jang Mi, Jasmin, Jennifer, Keerthi, Munira, Shaima, Sharon, Soo Jin, and Sun Hee — demonstrate the complex interactions between personal, social, and professional factors that translate in their radical caring for their ethnic communities.

I have the utmost respect for the care, compassion, and labor of frontline workers in addressing and preventing GBV, often at the expense of personal trauma to themselves. In the process of combatting state and interpersonal violence, however, their stories and labor also become marginalized and co-opted through the professionalization of the anti-violence movement. Furthermore, their roles are often made invisible by the overwhelmingly white feminist anti-domestic violence movement. My research speaks to highlighting their unique positionality as counselors, therapists, lawyers, organizers, survivors, workers, students, and advocates who approach their work as women of color with marginalized identities.

While feminist anthropologists have adopted dual roles as scholar-activists on the frontlines, Asian American feminist voices remain crucial in articulating the political connectedness of their own everyday experiences.20 In the tradition of fugitive anthropology, gendered violence should also be researched and represented from the bodily experiences of Black, brown, and Indigenous women, as well as queer women of color.21 These research works restore the agency of women’s space and physical selves, even in academic spaces.

I propose that frontline workers deserve a central, integral position in the conversation of preventing and eradicating GBV, particularly in ethnographic investments of care work. The trauma-informed, culturally relevant radical care of frontline workers aims to promote the survival of their communities through their small, daily acts of labor. In the directions of decolonial feminism, deep coalitions should be formed with the providers of care as central to the movement.22 Frontline workers are critical in comprehensive, intersectional responses of preventing, eliminating, and ending GBV for all communities. ◆

title: 2021 Research Award Winners
notes: Profiles of the 2022 Office of Undergraduate Research Expo award winners: Elana Charlson and Yola Mzizi (Best Expo Poster Presentation, "Talking About Race in the Sociocultural Moment: Emerging Adults’ Critical Consciousness and Racial Identity in Context") and Kade Kelley (Best Overall Oral Presentation, "Novel Mechanisms in Nuclear Receptor Gene Regulation"). Title as given in the contents; the opening page is headed "2022 Research Exposition Award Winners". The poster award heading spans two facing pages (printed 178-179), whose lines are interleaved here in reading order.
text:
2022

Research

Exposition

Award Winners

Office of Undergraduate Research Expo Awards Northwestern University’s annual Undergraduate Research and Arts Exposition (Expo), sponsored by the Office of Undergraduate Research, is the largest student conference on campus and focuses on original research and creative work by Northwestern’s undergraduates across all disciplines.

The $500 Best Expo Poster Presentation Award was presented to Elana Charlson and Yola Mzizi for their project entitled “Talking About Race in the Sociocultural Mo­ ment: Emerging Adults’ Critical Consciousness and Racial Identity in Context.”

The $500 Best Overall Expo Oral Presentation Award was presented to Kade Kelley for his presentation entitled “Novel Mechanisms in Nuclear Receptor Gene Regulation.”

Best Expo Poster Presentation at the Northwestern Undergraduate

Research and Arts Exposition

Award Recipients

Talking About Race in the Sociocultural Moment: Emerging

Adults’ Critical Consciousness and Racial Identity in Context

Elana Charlson

Elana is a rising senior studying Psychology and Global Health Studies. During her sophomore year, Elana joined the Development of Identities in Cultural Environments (DICE) Lab, with Dr. Onnie Rogers. Through her research and extracurricular involvement in Peer Health Ex­ change and the Undergraduate Psychology Association, she has become interested in studying how human development is shaped by the broader social context.

At the undergrad research expo, Elana and her partner Yola Mzizi presented their findings from a research project in the DICE Lab, which was led by Dr. Ursula Moffitt. The objective of this project was to examine how emerging adults made meaning around their racial identities in a sociopolitical context marked by inequity. To explore this question, they used the lens of critical consciousness, which suggests that recognizing social inequity contributes to a strong racial identity and can prompt individuals to take action against injustice. The varying degrees to which white and BIPOC college students critically engaged in conversations about race were shaped by their positionality within the system of racism.

Yola Mzizi

Yola Mzizi is a rising senior from Durban, South Africa, majoring in journalism and sociology and minoring in global health studies. During her undergraduate career, Mzizi has participated in the Kaplan Humanities Scholar’s Programme, the Undergraduate Research Assistant Programme (URAP) and she currently holds the position of  creative director for STITCH Magazine, and is a writer at The Daily Northwestern. Mzizi’s interests in cultural and political reporting, whereby, she hopes to elucidate complex concepts and issues for the public in order to inspire social justice action, has motivated her research experience.

Mzizi joined the Development of Identities in Cultural Environments (DICE) lab, a social psychology lab under the leadership of Dr. Onnie Rogers, in January of 2021 as a research assistant and member of the URAP cohort. In the lab, Mzizi worked with post-doctoral fellow Dr. Ursula Moffitt and fellow research assistant Elana Charlson. Mzizi, Moffitt and Charlson’s work hoped to understand how racial identity development in a time marked by racial violence and political po­ larisation occurred. Mzizi and her co-researchers were interested in how young people gain critical consciousness and how this enables them to better resist and challenge the systems of racial inequity. In their project titled “Talking About Race in the Sociocultural Moment: Emerging Adults’ Critical Consciousness and Racial Identity in Context,” Mzizi and her co-researchers found that in order to actively resist systemic racism, one needs to have developed a strong racial identity which allows them to see their racial identity as inextricably tied to the larger socio-political context. This was particularly imperative for young white people, who, as their data showed, saw race as something other people had, and racism as individual acts they could sympathise with, rather than seeing how their racial identity is implicated in the systems of inequity we see today.

Best Overall Oral Presentation Award Recipient at the Northwestern Undergraduate Research and Arts Exposition

Novel Mechanisms in Nuclear Receptor Gene Regulation

Kade Kelley

Kade Kelley is a third-year student from Falmouth, Maine majoring in biological sci­ ences and chemistry. In addition to research, he is also involved on campus as a Peer Advisor for incoming first-year students and as a Peer-Guided Study Group Facilita­ tor for Organic Chemistry through the Office of Academic Support and Learning Advancement (ASLA). Kade first got involved with research in Spring 2021 when he joined the Radhakrishnan Lab ahead of working over the summer on a Northwestern Undergraduate Research Grant. Since then, his work has focused on the screening and computational docking of small molecules in proteins and the experimental assessment of these interactions.

Kade’s expo project focused on a protein implicated in Parkinson’s disease, Nurr1. Nurr1 is a nuclear receptor (NR) — a protein that responds to environmental signals, modulating gene expression through binding small molecule ligands. Unlike other NRs, however, Nurr1 is an “orphan” NR, lacking the typical ligand-binding pocket. Instead of binding Nurr1, Kade’s project explores the hypothesis that ligands can bind a different protein, a coactivator, in order to control NR activation and gene expres­ sion. Although more work is needed to characterize the effect of ligand-binding on the coactivator-nuclear receptor interaction, current results propose a likely group of lipid ligands and their binding configurations to the coactivator protein. Since orphan NR mechanisms have yet to be discovered, and such proteins have vital roles in cellular metabolism, development, and homeostasis, the research could hold potential implica­ tions for other maladies, too.

title: ABOUT THE CONTRIBUTORS
notes: Opener listing the eleven thesis contributors (an unnumbered page; the contents gives page 180), then one page per contributor with their thesis title and answers to four questions about their research and plans after graduation.
text:
ABOUT THE CONTRIBUTORS

CONTRIBUTORS

Sophie Boorstein

Keerti Gopal

Ginny Ip Hanbyul-Jenny Kang

Lauren Katz Nikol Kralimarkova

Akash Palani Nolan Fizoires Robinson II

Tara Shirvaikar

Saidie Stone

Chloe Wong

Sophie Boorstein Black-Owned Small Businesses in Englewood, Chicago: Documenting the Effects of COVID-19 and the Black Lives Matter Movement in 2020

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

To better understand the obstacles minority business owners face and how they are working to overcome them, my research aims to document the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement on Black-owned small businesses in Englewood, Chicago. The research employs a mixed-methods approach by examining foot-traffic data across Chicago Community Areas and gaining perspective from Englewood’s Black-identifying small business owners in one-on-one interviews.

How did you come to your research topic?

When considering topics for my senior thesis prior to 2020, I took interest in examining the impacts of crisis events, particularly natural disasters, on minority communities. When COVID-19 became a global pandemic and a simultaneous crisis of police brutality emerged at the forefront with the BLM movement, I rewrote my thesis proposal. I hoped that research on contemporaneous crises would enhance scholarly understanding of minority communities’ needs amid crises, which to date are under-documented. I was eager to leverage my background in both social policy and statistical analyses to examine these topics with a mixed-method approach, as well as apply skills from my certificate with the Kellogg School of Management to analyze business operations.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

Research on the effects of COVID-19 and the BLM movement will undoubtedly continue for decades to come, but it is my hope that academics will prioritize examining minority communities’ experiences in 2020. Researchers can specifically build on the present research to examine policy solutions based on the obstacles documented in this paper: looting, intra- community asset building, police response, and inter-community business visitation. Because economic disparities are rooted in systematic racism, the recovery of Black-owned small businesses from the COVID-19 and BLM protests is of paramount importance in supporting the global movement to eliminate racism. As one participant in the research expressed, it is my hope that the present research will not “just be a study,” and it can be used as a basis for future policy research and recommendations.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be working as an Associate Consultant at EY-Parthenon. I completed an internship at the firm in summer 2020 and look forward to continuing my education on business operations.

Keerti Gopal

Framing and Youth Participation in the Sunrise Movement

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

I studied the Sunrise Movement’s (Sunrise) use of narrative framing tactics in digital media to encourage youth electoral engagement, arguing that the group provides an example of how organizations can bridge the youth movement-electoral politics divide through a framing that brings outsider, movement mentality into insider, formal politics.

How did you come to your research topic?

I started researching Sunrise in 2019 through a project on youth motivation for activism, and I joined the organization myself the same year. Through my experience at the organization, I started growing curious about the dissonance I saw between narratives of youth political apathy and the high levels of electoral engagement I saw in my peers at Sunrise. I formulated this project to look at that gap and soon found Sunrise’s narrative framing to be incredibly intriguing, leading to the eventual focus of the project.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

Since I focused my study on Sunrise alone, it would be interesting for further research to look at additional case studies to see if similar patterns emerge. As digital communication tactics are constantly evolving, their use in movement and electoral politics has not yet been thoroughly studied. There is much left to discover with regard to how digital tactics (like social media) are used and what impacts they might have.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

This year, I will be going to Taiwan for a Fulbright-National Geographic Storytelling fellowship to continue my research on youth climate change activism in a different context.

Ginny Ip

The Impact of Climate Change on Energy Poverty: Evidence from the European Union, 2004–2019

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

My research uses historical climate data to explore the potential impacts of climate change on the proportion of EU households who find it difficult to meet their basic energy needs. As average temperatures rise and both the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events increase due to the onset of climate change, there will be a greater need for heating and cooling. In the absence of drastic policy changes, how will this affect the share of energy poor households?

How did you come to your research topic?

During the last two years of my undergraduate career, I worked as a research assistant for Professor Reguant, an energy economist. Our work investigated the distributional impacts of real-time electricity pricing in Spain as opposed to a fixed rate. What we found was that real-time pricing can often be regressive, meaning that it disproportionately places a bigger burden on low-income households. This made me wonder how this might change against a backdrop of climate change, not only in Spain but across Europe and the rest of the world.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

My work only serves as a starting point in examining the relationship between climate change and energy poverty at the regional level. Future researchers can build on my work by conducting further analysis in other contexts, especially those in the global south that will be hardest hit by climate change. Additionally, climate change is an ongoing process. This means that as the world continues to change and more data becomes available, it is important to update these findings to inform more accurate and reliable policies and development projects.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be heading to Boston after graduation and starting my career at Charles River Associates as an economic consultant in the energy industry.

Hanbyul- Jenny Kang

Reformulating Korean Anti-American Literature: Feminist resistance against double colonialism in 중국인거리 (Junggugingeori)

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

My research is about feminist resistance against the double colonialism of U.S. imperialism and South Korean patriarchy in anti-American literatures of South Korea.

How did you come to your research topic?

In 20th century Korea, literature has often been a tool of resistance (for example, against Japanese colonization). However, I found that there has not been as much research focusing on anti-American literature in the 1970s and 1980s in South Korea, particularly within Anglophone scholarship. As such, I was drawn to researching literary manifestations of resistance against the U.S. military occupation in South Korea. During this research, I found that anti-American resistance within Korea has been very male- centered. So, I decided to focus on female authors who wrote anti-U.S. novels from a feminist perspective.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

I believe that we must continue to connect and analyze together the various resistance literatures produced in the numerous countries that have experienced the U.S.’ occupations, interventions, wars, coups, etc. As a Korean person, I wish to draw connections between the Korean literary resistance movement against the U.S.’ militarization and war in Korea with those of other countries around the world. Although there is a lot I still have not read, I hope that researchers may continue to study the commonalities and differences between anti- American literary movements in order to read patterns about the sort of impact the U.S. has had through its foreign policies, not just through an American light, but through local and indigenous eyes.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be working in an immigration law firm in Chicago as I apply to PhD programs.

Lauren Katz

Revolutionary Women: Literary Performativity, Classical Pseudonyms, and the Public Sphere in the Correspondence of Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

In my thesis, I examine the epistolary correspondence between Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren from 1775–1777. During this time, these women engaged in a nuanced dialogue and literary performance in which they reimagine the relationship between the classical and the modern, the Stoical and the sentimental, the public and the private, the national and the domestic, and the masculine and the feminine as a means to actualize their historical and literary voices.

How did you come to your research topic?

During the spring of my sophomore year at Northwestern, I took an English course entitled “Visionary Women and the American Colonies.” I was struck by a line in the first section of Caroline Wigginton’s journal, Transatlantic Feminisms in the Age of Revolutions: “In a moment when America was boldly pronouncing its rejection of British tyranny, Adams called for the end of tyranny of men over women.” I loved the idea that Adams was strategically repurposing America’s fight for her own use, which ultimately led me to her lesser-known performative correspondence with Warren under the respective Roman matron pseudonyms “Portia” and “Marcia.”

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

With my thesis, I want to show future researchers that they can shine a light on historically marginalized groups, such as women, by examining mediums that have not traditionally been regarded as “high-end literature.” I also want to encourage researchers to work to question and challenge simple binaries that trivialize the complexity of human nature/thought, especially when exploring historically marginalized groups. I believe that it is important to work against the stereotypical models into which women are collapsed and the reproduced narratives that pin women against one another. Furthermore, the concept of repurposing an intended limitation as a medium for discovery and ultimately defiance is so powerful and can definitely be applied to other topics throughout our past and present- day history. In terms of opportunities to expand upon the insights made in my thesis, my work on Warren unveiled a whole new avenue of research concerning her potentially new role as a modern biographer that I hope others research further.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be working in New York City as a Client Experience Associate at Broadway Plus.

Nikol Kralimarkova

The Role of Habit in Kafka’s “The Burrow” and Proust’s Swann’s Way

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

The topic of my senior thesis was habit as a psychological and perceptual phenomenon and its role in two major texts, namely Franz Kafka’s short story The Burrow and Marcel Proust’s Swann’s Way. I studied habit and its spatiotemporal dimensions that shape the two narrators’ realities and their respective thoughts and/or behaviors. More concretely, I explored both the constructive and destructive effects of habit or its absence, such as the creative possibilities to recreate and paint over one’s reality as well as the anxieties that could arise if a habit is disturbed.

How did you come to your research topic?

I had been studying Kafka in a couple of Comparative Literary Studies courses and Proust, I immediately fell in love with. Given my diverse background, speaking five languages, two of which French and German, I fell for the intersection between two distinct literary worlds. Still immersed in times of a pandemic and lockdowns, I was strongly drawn by a recurring theme in many of Kafka’s short stories and Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, specifically habit, something that all of us faced in its essence in the past two years. The familiarity of the theme of habit and the literary mastery of the authors and texts on which I focused convinced me to pursue this research topic whilst fighting COVID-19 myself.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

There is a lot more that literature can teach us about the effects of habit and its absence, especially in the times in which we have been living, where we are more isolated and constrained than the previous generation(s) have ever been. Through such literary pieces, we can (re)gain consciousness about the processes of habituation that drive us a majority of the time. Academically speaking, Kafka’s creatures could also be studied individually, as well as Proust’s narrator in the progression of all volumes of In Search of Lost Time to construct more detailed case studies of the habitual existence of the narrators in their literary worlds.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be heading to medical school. I’m currently residing in my home country, Bulgaria, and am applying to medical schools in the U.K., where my family and best friends live.

Akash Palani

Long Distance Nationalism: Indian Americans and Hindutva

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

In the context of Hindu nationalism’s entry into the Indian political mainstream during the past decade, my research seeks to identify the mechanisms through which the Indian diaspora, particularly Indian Americans, form their attitudes towards the movement. Public expressions of Hindu nationalism have become increasingly frequent in the United States, from the World Hindu Congress in Chicago to the prevalence of Hindutva- aligned campus groups. Many Indian Americans may have lived outside of India for decades or may even have been born and raised outside India altogether. This presents a fascinating puzzle: how do they form such attitudes?

How did you come to your research topic?

I came to my research topic through studying Indian history and Asian American activism. The literature on these subjects was compelling, and I saw from my own experiences the need for the questions I put forth to be addressed.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

There is a serious dearth of literature on this subject in American academia, especially in recent years. Future researchers should look to connect the work I put forth with studies of immigration, political polarization both domestic and foreign, and transnational political activism.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be working in Chicago after graduation, with plans to pursue graduate work in political science in the near future.

Nolan Fizoires Robinson II

Transcending the Stage: Exploring the Applicability of an Actor’s Training to Other Vocations and Our Everyday Lives

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

My research topic explores how the tools an acting education and training gives its students are not conducive to just acting, but they can also be used in a variety of professions that lie outside of the theatrical arts and teach us all about the fundamentals of being human.

How did you come to your research topic?

I came to my research topic due to the COVID-19 pandemic. After a year of being unable to perform, I really had to reflect on why my education and training as an actor was crucial to the landscape in which we were and currently are. The arts were suffering and many Americans thought this industry was expendable, but I knew there existed a power inside this art that I needed to unlock — that acting, in its essence, is less about being on a stage and more about being present and human.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

I hope this work allows other actors to discover what their art does for them and how it connects them to their own humanity and others to theirs. Maybe future researchers can dive deeper into the psychological implications of acting and the psyche of an actor, as it takes a certain level of psychological dedication in order to efficiently do one’s job as an actor. It would be interesting to see data on what it does to our brains/the brains of those on stage with us and discover how artificial emotions that an actor creates relate to the moments in which we may actually feel those emotions in real life (fear, anger, sadness, joy, etc.)

Where are you heading to after graduation?

After graduation I am heading to New York to start/complete work on Broadway! I hope to have a bi-coastal career, working in both New York and Los Angeles as an actor and writer.

Tara Shirvaikar

The Rise of the Female Vernacular: Contemporary Indian Woman Authors and the Subversion of the Heteropatriarchal Linguistic Establishment

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

I researched how vernacular could be used to dislocate shame as the place where female sexuality resides, in contemporary Indian literature.

How did you come to your research topic?

I wanted to learn more about how feminism located itself within Indian literature and, more than that, what role language (both elite and vernacular) played in the formation of the female social body and female sexuality. With the guidance of my thesis adviser, I used a lot of older, fundamental feminist works published in India for my senior paper in the CLS department and decided to focus on contemporary literature for my senior thesis.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

There is so much more contextualizing work to be done — locating the female body in literature within different regional, linguistic, class, and caste attributes would be the next step.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I am headed to the Bay Area to work as a hardware engineer at Intel.

Saidie Stone

Exoneration of American Violence: The Cultural Legacy of American Atrocity Against Civilians During the War in Vietnam

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

I examined the representation of American violence against civilians during the war in Vietnam from three different categories of sources: American veteran narratives, Vietnamese-American narratives, and high school American history textbooks.

How did you come to your research topic?

In the fall of 2019, I took Dilemmas of American Power with Medill Professor Peter Slevin. During the week we spent on the war in Vietnam, we learned about the My Lai Massacre of 1968, during which American civilians killed 500 Vietnamese civilians, including elderly people, women, children, and babies.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

Ideally, researchers and educators will read my work and understand the necessity for incorporating more Vietnamese sources and perspectives into high school and collegiate curriculum.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

Chicago!

Chloe Wong

Radical Caring: A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in the Asian American Communities

In a nutshell, what is your research topic?

My research topic is on the role of Asian- identifying, female or non-binary identifying direct service professionals (hereby referred to as frontline workers) in preventing gender-based violence in Asian American communities. By incorporating their salient identities and life histories, they actively serve survivors on individual, relationship, community, and societal levels.

How did you come to your research topic?

I was interested in the topic of gender-based violence because of my personal experiences of the topic. I was further inspired by my internship experiences in Vietnam and Chicago in conducting research and working with survivors.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field?

Anthropological perspectives in gender-based violence are crucial in centering the voices of frontline workers and building a decolonial praxis that restores the agency of survivors. Future researchers can continue allocating resources towards similar works in various communities of urban settings, as well as exploring options of transformative justice.

Where are you heading to after graduation?

I will be participating in the Management Rotational Program in McMaster-Carr.

Join the NURJ

The NURJ welcomes new staff members all year round. We look for people who are passionate about learning more about academic research, writing, and journalism. We offer many opportunities to explore areas such as review and editing, conducting interviews, designing the print and online publications, and helping with publicity.

Submit to the NURJ

Research papers and abstracts must be the author’s own independent work that was performed while they were an undergraduate at Northwestern University or NU- Qatar. The project may be one that the undergraduate pursued with the guidance of a mentor. The NURJ accepts research papers from all fields of study, including the life and physical sciences, social sciences, applied sciences, and the humanities.

Visit thenurj.com to learn more!

The staff of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal would like to express our appreciation for all those who recognize and contribute to our endeavors. Without their support, we would be unable to produce this edition of the Journal.

We would like to thank Michael Schill, President of Northwestern University, along with Provost Kathleen Hagerty and Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education Miriam Sherin for their generous patronage. We are especially appreciative of our faculty advisers, Peter Civetta, the director of the Office of Undergraduate Research in the Office of the Provost, and Patti Wolter, Helen Gurley Brown Magazine Professor and Charles Deering McCormick Distinguished Clinical Professor. Their direction and guidance has allowed us to create the best version of the Journal as possible.

The late Professor Allen Taflove, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at N.U., founded NURJ 20 years ago. Prof. Taflove guided scores of NURJ journalists and researchers in the pursuit of scholastic excellence, and NURJ would not be the success it is today without acknowledging his guidance, wisdom, generosity and legacy.

Join the NURJ The NURJ welcomes new staff members all year round. We look for people who are passionate about learning more about academic research, writing and journalism. We offer many opportunities to explore areas such as review and editing, conducting interviews, designing the print and online publications and helping with publicity.

Submit to the NURJ Research papers and abstracts must be the author’s own independent work that was performed while they were an undergraduate at Northwestern University or NU-Qatar. The project may be one that the undergraduate pursued with the guidance of a mentor. text:
Letter from the Advisors

Dear readers:

Welcome to Volume 20 of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ). At a time when university research funding is facing challenges, NURJ offers this celebration of the essence of research with 10 NURJ-written feature stories as well as seven best senior theses selected by their respective academic departments. This year’s mix celebrates a wide sampling of the range of research at Northwestern, from the historical implications of water pollution on economic systems to the expression of grief in theatre and more.

The 2024–2025 issue is the product of a year’s work by the students who lead and contribute to the NURJ, a student-produced annual print publication. In addition to this journal, our students publish new research packages on www.thenurj.com as well as an archives project that delves into the history of Northwestern. At the center of this work is their deep commitment to the Northwestern community. “Research,” as defined by the NURJ, champions the broadest array of disciplines and reflects the efforts and guidance of not just faculty, but the indefatigable work of staff, fellow researchers and more.

The journal you hold in your hand is a creation by hundreds of minds from NU and is made possible through the continuous funding by the Office of the President and the Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education. Copies of the NURJ are freely available to students at newsstands at major campus locations. Additionally, the NURJ is distributed to NU Deans, Department Chairs, and Program Chairs as well as to academic, advising, and research offices across campus.

We hope this journal brings you inspiration, enjoyment and an appreciation of the breadth and depth of intellectual inquiry at Northwestern University.

As the late Professor Allen Taflove, founding editor and NURJ advisor, used to sign off: Now, enjoy learning about the marvelous research investigations of Northwestern’s top students!

Best, Dr. Peter Civetta and Prof. Patti Wolter NURJ Faculty Advisors

Letter from the Editors

Dear readers:

We are thrilled to welcome you to the 20th volume of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal (NURJ) and present a diverse array of writing that showcases groundbreaking work.

From the effects of merit scholarships on saving for college to the historical underpinnings of war, this issue features a myriad of honors theses that exemplify the intersection of depth, diversity, and academic excellence within their respective disciplines. In addition to the seven senior theses, this volume also includes 10 feature stories from our NURJ print staff that highlight both the research and the people behind the innovative breakthroughs at Northwestern.

The theme of volume 20 centers around warm-toned colors that embody innovation and creativity. The focal point of the cover is a lightbulb, meant to reflect the ingenuity of the pieces that compose this edition. Furthermore, the lightbulb represents the intellectual risk-taking and academic curiosity that each author engaged in to produce impactful research. This theme not only aligned with the journey of our team this year, but also reflects the growth mindset we embrace going into the next year.

In addition to our annual print edition, we invite you to explore our Archives Special Edition project and semiannual online packages that highlight research done by the Northwestern community. This year, we also spearheaded the addition of New York Times-inspired crossword on our website, drawing clues from our published pieces to engage readers in a new way.

NURJ continues to be a testament to the hard work and passion of our brilliant student- researchers and the dedication of our talented writers, editors, and designers. Without our lovely staff, we would not have been able to bring our visions to life. Furthermore, we are eternally grateful for the generous sponsorship and continued support from President Michael Schill and Associate Provost Miriam Sherin. To our phenomenal faculty advisors, Dr. Peter

Civetta and Professor Patti Wolter — we are so thankful for their unwavering support and guidance, we could not have done it without them. And lastly, to you, our readers and the entire Northwestern community — thank you for entrusting the NURJ to share student research, for supporting NURJ in person and online.

We hope you enjoy this journal!

Helen Zhu & Mychaela Mathews
