title: Exploring the Complex History of Reproductive Health: Insights from Dr. Rodriguez
notes: Profile of Dr. Sarah Rodriguez, professor of global health and medical historian.
text:
Exploring the Complex History of Reproductive Health: Insights from Dr. Rodriguez

By: Avery Morawa

The work of Dr. Sarah Rodriguez - a professor of global health, the Co-Director of Undergraduate Studies, and a medical historian - is a testament to curiosity, critical inquiry, and persistence. With an undergraduate background in history and American studies, her academic journey began with a fascination for understanding how society navigates complex issues. This culminated in an honors thesis focused on the history of medicine and reproductive health. This laid the foundation for a career spent uncovering stories that illuminate the intersection between medical ethics and social history.

Researching the Past to Inform the Present

For Dr. Rodriguez, research is more than a search for an answer — it’s a process of exploration that often raises new and unexpected questions along the way. “You can go in with one question and leave with another,” she explains, emphasizing the importance of maintaining an open mind and remaining inquisitive. The process of her work often involves diving into archives, medical journals, court records, and historical newspapers to search for the threads that connect medical practices to broader social and political contexts. “Historical research is looking at ‘stuff’,” she describes. Dr. Rodriguez’s research on maternal mortality is particularly striking. “Counting maternal deaths is difficult,” she notes, describing the challenges of obtaining reliable numerical data. It’s difficult to evaluate exactly how many deaths in or near childbirth are caused by maternal inflictions versus other factors, making this quantitative data burdensome to work with. Instead, her work examines how states and organizations — ranging from individual nations to the World Health Organization — have historically responded to maternal death rates and what those responses reveal about societal values. Changes to law code, establishment of supportive programs such as the Department of Maternal Health, and the creation of private companies such as the Rockefeller foundation are all changes that Rodriguez seeks to investigate and reflect upon. One persistent theme uncovered by her work is the historical prioritization of infant health over maternal health. Dr. Rodriguez attributes such to systemic sexism. Maternal and child health are heavily linked: trends in maternal mortality often follow on the heels of trends in infant mortality. However, despite their codependence, Rodriguez points to historical patterns in which women’s health becomes a priority only when it’s seen as essential to the well-being of children or to addressing population concerns. Confronting this pattern may help develop more effective treatments, better data, and greater equity in healthcare in the future.

The Intersection of Medicine, Ethics, and History

Dr. Rodriguez’s knowledge extends beyond medical history and into the ethical dimensions of medical practices. In her book The Love Surgeon: A Story of Trust, Harm, and the Limits of Medical Regulation (2020), she dives into the controversial career and operations of a physician whose surgical procedures sparked public outcry due to a lack of informed consent. Through court documents, medical files, and interviews, Dr. Rodriguez explores questions about accountability in medicine, the responsibility of physicians to regulate their peers, and societal conditions present during medical ethics dilemmas. Her findings reveal that this physician’s actions were not inherently isolated or malicious, rather they were reflective of broader systemic and social issues within medical practice at the time. “This wasn’t normative behavior, but it wasn’t an outlier either,” Dr. Rodriguez explains, highlighting the importance of understanding historical context to address challenges in medical ethics and regulation.

Reflections on Research and Its Impact

Research is as much about the process as the findings according to Rodriguez. “You need to be open to change and thinking about things differently,” she says, emphasizing the importance of recognizing gaps in knowledge and adapting the research to evolving questions. Whether exploring the evolution of maternal health policies or the ethics of surgical practices, her work is a reminder of the complexities that shape medicine today and the ongoing need to question, learn, and advocate for change. Through her meticulous research and thoughtful analysis, Dr. Rodriguez continues to illuminate the ways history informs present-day discussions on reproductive health.

title: The Effect of Merit Scholarships on Saving for College
department: Departments of Economics and Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences
notes: Senior thesis. Faculty adviser (printed "Dr. Scott Ogawa") named on the opening page. Appendix Tables 1-9 are extracted cell by cell; Figures 1-4B (printed pages 62-65) are plots of merit aid and savings by state with no transcribable text beyond their captions.
text:
The Effect of Merit Scholarships on Saving for College

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Scott Ogawa

Departments of Economics and Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences by Emilya Ershtein

Abstract State merit-based scholarships are a large source of funding for many college students, and the effects of this aid on families, students, and states’ economies is a topic of continued interest and research. There are 22 states with merit aid programs, and because eligibility includes graduating from an in-state high school, students and parents in some states can depend on this aid while others cannot. I use this variation, documented by the InforeED State Financial Aid Dataset, together with survey data on people’s decisions to save for college, provided by the National Financial Capability Survey, to assess the effect of merit aid programs on college savings. I find mixed evidence, some suggesting that living in a state with a merit aid program meaningfully decreases the likelihood of saving for college, and some suggesting that it has no effect. I assess whether the scholarships change the amount parents save using the College Savings Plan Network data on 529 accounts. My results are inconclusive, and I propose redoing my analysis with the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential dataset. My analysis is limited by the fact that data sets containing both a measure of college savings and the state of residence are difficult to obtain and/or to use because of the structure of the available data. The purpose of this paper is, in addition to quantifying the effect of scholarships on savings, to describe the potential data sources, limitations, and possible strategies, to inform future related work.

Introduction Government funding for college has the following direct effects: pushing students slightly below the margin of affording college to attend college, reducing families’ financial burden, reducing students’ financial burden, increasing student charges (increasing tuition or decreasing institutional aid), and replacing other forms of financial aid. The manner in which the funding is distributed between these areas is not, however, decided by the government. Instead, it is determined by the interaction of choices made by students, parents, universities, and various loan and scholarship providers. Theory has helped make predictions and guide the decisions of state and federal governments. But the unpredictability of preferences about college and the complexity of factors playing into funding for college make it difficult to know how exactly government funds are distributed.

In this paper, I focus on the effects of aid on family savings for college. I look at one type of government funding for college: merit-based scholarships given to undergraduate students. I use merit scholarships administered by U.S. states because eligibility for merit aid is determined by residence, and states in various regions of the country have adopted these programs. As a result, outcomes can be compared across states and over time, providing a plausible identification strategy for the treatment effect of government-funded merit-based aid.

The size of the effect on savings is relevant for several reasons. First, it is an interesting behavioral question. Do parents carefully optimize the amount they put into college savings, changing their behavior as they learn more about their child’s scholarship possibilities? Or do they go by some default idea of how much they should save, or by a worst-case scenario savings scheme? It can also be a question about information and certainty about future scholarships. Do parents know enough about merit aid programs and feel that the programs are stable and certain enough to depend on?

My question also relates to the tradeoff between benefiting colleges and helping families faced by any government funding for education. If families reduce their savings for college, and are thus expecting to pay less, this would counteract tuition increases, especially because the reduction in savings has already happened at the time that colleges set their tuition. However, if families do not reduce their savings due to uncertainty about receiving the merit aid, colleges are likely able to demand higher charges from parents.

Another reason to study this question relates to the common criticism that merit aid programs benefit wealthier families. Families that have college savings funds are often more wealthy and can afford college more easily to begin with, so a finding that aid reduces savings could confirm that criticism. The extent to which merit aid decreases savings would help clarify how much the funding is helping to reduce the burden on families who would have paid for college regardless, as opposed to making it affordable for more students.

The theory that merit aid would affect savings is simple: when parents anticipate lower future costs, they save less. It is possible that a parent would not change their saving behavior because of uncertainty about their child’s future qualification for the scholarship; however, one reason to believe that parents can reliably predict eligibility for the scholarship is that the GPA/ SAT requirements for these scholarships tend to be fairly low, so it may be clear early on whether a student will qualify. For example, for the Louisiana TOPS scholarship, which covers full tuition, a 2.5 GPA and approximately a 1000/1600 SAT or 20 ACT score are required. A 2.5 GPA is achievable with half B’s and half C’s, which is generally a very low standard for public schools in the United States. A 1000 SAT score and a 20 ACT score correspond to getting approximately half of the questions correct. The Georgia HOPE scholarship, which covers full tuition, requires a 3.0 GPA (B average). New Mexico, covering full tuition, has no requirements aside from successfully graduating. (See Table 1 for eligibility requirements of all states.) However, it is still possible that parents don’t change their savings decisions due to behavioral explanations, lack of information, or correct expectations. For example, they could correctly expect future tuition increases, lack of eligibility for need-based aid in these states, or lack of availability of other scholarships.

1 These statistics come from National Center for Education Statistics’s National Postsecondary Student Aid Study. 2 These statistics come from the Education Data Initiative.

The Status of Merit Aid Programs in the U.S. State scholarships constitute a fairly large portion of funding for U.S. college students. In 2023, 23% of students received state grants, as compared to 40% receiving federal grants, and 28% receiving institutional grants. The average state grant was $3,500, average federal grant was $4,300, and average institutional grant was $9,900.1 The average cost of in-state tuition was $9,700 and out-of-state was $27,000.2 Students received an average of around $5,000 in scholarships, with low-income students receiving more federal and state aid because much of the aid is based on demonstrated need.

Between 1991 and 2006, 27 states implemented merit aid programs, and five of them have been terminated at some point since. These programs give scholarships to seniors graduating in the state who meet certain merit criteria. The largest program is the Georgia HOPE Scholarship, followed by Tennessee HOPE and Louisiana TOPS. The first one was the Arkansas Academic Challenge Scholarship in 1991, Georgia HOPE in 1993, 12 others starting in the 1990s, and eight starting in the 2000s. The stated goals include reducing families’ and students’ financial burden, as well as increasing the number of students who attend college. Nine states have programs classified as strong by Sjoquist and Winters (2014), a classification that I borrow in this paper, which identifies large participation rates and large average awards. I add Arkansas into the strong category as they expanded in 2011, a year outside of the range that Sjoquist and Winters studied. Each program has specific eligibility requirements, but the requirement shared

“The theory that merit aid would affect savings is simple: when parents anticipate lower future costs, they save less.” by all programs is being a resident of that state at the time of graduation. Programs differ slightly in their merit criteria, but not drastically. They differ in funding amounts, number of students affected, and some have other miscellaneous rules. Table 1 gives a summary of the characteristics of each state’s program.

Literature Review One of the most common criticisms of merit aid programs is that they do not increase college access because they target students who would attend college regardless. Consequently, there are several papers assessing average effects on college enrollment and college completion. Various papers in the literature find con- tradictory results for the average effect on college enrollment, with more recent literature generally finding smaller effects.

Cornwell, Mustard, and Sridar (2006) estimated that between 1988 and 1997, the Georgia HOPE Scholarship increased college enrollment by 5.9%. This corre- sponds to 15% of HOPE recipients being people who would not have gone to a college in Georgia otherwise. These per- centages refer to increase in enrollment in Georgia, so some of the effect may be coming from students choosing to stay in Georgia instead of going out of state, and may not be reflecting enrollment of students who would have not gone to college otherwise. Dynarski (2004) estimated that merit aid programs in Georgia, Arkansas,

Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina had an average effect on in-state enrollment of 5%. Binder and Genderton (2004) find an enrollment effect of 6% in New Mexico.

A comprehensive analysis conducted by Sjoquist and Winters (2014) uses data from 25 states, and distinguishes between weak and strong programs. It finds no effects on college enrollment as well as no effects on college completion. Most recently, Chakabarti, Nober, and Klaauw (2023) use the most granular data yet and find no effect on propensity of attending college or of degree attainment, in the general population as well as among low-income and racial minority groups.

Scott-Clayton and Zafar (2019) find that marginal recipients of the West Virginia merit scholarship have higher incomes, and are more likely to complete graduate degrees. Despite finding no effect on their enrollment in college, it appears that the scholarship decreased the time it took to complete the degree, and improved life outcomes. Cornwell and Mustard (2006) find that Georgia HOPE increased the portion of high ability students choosing to go to in-state colleges, and increased selectivity in universities.

To the best of my knowledge, there have been few attempts to examine which sources of funding the scholarships replace, and none have examined the effect on savings. Chakabarti et al. (2023) find an average effect of about -$1,000 on student

“One of the most common criticisms of merit aid programs is that they do not increase college access, as they target students who would attend college regardless.” loan originations. Long (2004) finds that the Georgia HOPE Scholarship allowed universities to increase student charges by increasing tuition, increasing room and board fees, and reducing institutional scholarships.

There is also an array of past literature looking at other unintended effects of statewide merit aid programs for college, some of which counteract some of the goals of the programs. For example, researchers have investigated if grade inflation occurred in high schools, counteracting the intended impact of improving student achievement to qualify for the scholarship. Sjoquist and Winters (2015) give evidence that merit aid scholarships have diverted students away from STEM majors, but were unable to identify the mechanism behind this trend. Cornwell and Mustard (2007) showed evidence that car regis- trations in richer counties increased as a result of HOPE, suggesting that HOPE was helping families be less burdened by college costs, allowing them to spend on other consumption goods.

Data Close to half of states, varied in demo- graphics and geography, give merit aid, which presents the opportunity to use the other half as a control group to identify the effect of merit aid on savings. The timeline of the implementation of these programs seems also to have the potential for using a difference in difference approach, but unfortunately most of the strong merit aid programs were implemented in the 1990s, and pre-2001 data on college savings is scarce. As a result, the core of my analysis uses cross-sectional data to compare

3 Note: they exclude New Hampshire and Rhode Island, nine years for Nevada, 10 years for Delaware, and one year for South Dakota, because data was not obtainable. They do not add the New Mexico merit aid money, which I manually added in from state reports.

levels of savings between states, with a set of control variables meant to mitigate omitted variable bias. I include a graphical comparison of the change over time of savings in Arkansas, the only state which has a big jump in merit aid, with other states.

I compile two main data sets for my analysis. The variables contained in each are summarized in Table 2. The 529 dataset is at the state-year level, using assets in each state’s 529 program (tax-advantaged college savings account) as a measure of college savings. The saved dummy dataset, with observations at the individual level, uses people’s answers to the question: “Are you setting aside any money for your children’s college education?” as the measure of savings. To measure merit aid, I use the InformED State Financial Aid Dataset, which was compiled by researchers looking through state financial aid reports and contacting higher education officials.3 As a result, I have detailed data on the merit aid distributed in each state. The limitations of my project, which I discuss in detail below, primarily lie with the savings data.

The saved dummy dataset contains individual level observations taken during 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2021. For each individual, the National Financial Capability Survey (NFCS) tells whether they saved for college in addition to their state of residence, income group, education level, number of children, race, household ownership, and age group. I choose these control variables following Korankye and Kalenkoski (2021) who show a significant relationship between these demographic characteristics and savings. I match this data with the amount of merit aid given per student in the respondent’s state of residence. I also add, to both data sets, a dummy for being in a state with a strong merit aid program.

The NFCS gives a binary response of whether parents saved, but it does not give a measure of how much they saved. The best measure I could use of how much they saved was data on the amount of assets in each state’s 529 program, but there are other potential sources for this. Table 3 describes potential sources and their limitations.

The 529 data set covers 2001-2021 and contains how much money is in each state’s 529 programs per resident under 20, and how much merit aid was given out that year per student. I combine data on 529 assets from the College Savings Plan Network with Census data on children under 20 to calculate the savings per child. I combine total merit aid given (InformED) with number of students enrolled in post secondary institutions multiplied by the proportion that are undergraduates4 (National Center for Education Statistics) to get merit aid per student. I combine this with FRED data on median income and World Population Review data on percentage of adults with high school and bachelor’s degrees, which serve as control variables.

Table 3 contains several sources I was not able to use. The Survey of Consumer Finances in particular could potentially be the ideal source for this project, as it contains household level data on the amount of college savings as well as state of residence, 1983–2022. However, demographic characteristics such as state of residence are not included in the publicly available dataset, and I was not able to get authorization for confidential data in the timeline of this project. I believe it is very feasible in future

4 The portion of undergraduates is not available by state, so I use the U.S. percentage each year for all states.

work to use this source to assess the effect of merit aid on savings. The Edward Jones 529 Account Survey, SavingforCollege Survey, and the College Savings Foundation also collect data from individuals about their college savings. They do not make any data publicly available, and I was not able to reach the owners, but these surveys likely also contain both data on savings and on state of residence.

529 Data The College Savings Plan Network (CSPN) works with state sponsored 529 programs to compile data on the total amount of assets and number of accounts in each 529 plan. Every 529 plan is administered by a state, and some states have multiple 529 plans. The data is provided on the CSPN website in separate PDF files for each year/quarter. The New York Fed compiles data on total assets, aggregating over states’ multiple plans into a CSV file, and this is what I use.

There are two types of 529 accounts: prepaid and savings. About 95% of 529 assets are in savings plans, and the other 5% are in prepaid plans. Prepaid plans allow you to prepay tuition, locking in current lower tuition rates for attending the participating universities in the future. Typically, participating universities include all in-state universities. If a child ends up not going to a participating university, funds can typically be transferred to other uses. Prepaid plans do not pay interest, and money must be used to pay tuition or fees. These plans have declined over the years; 22 states used to offer prepaid plans, which has decreased to nine in 2023.

The 529 savings plans, on the other hand, allow account holders to choose from a range of investment portfolio options. Money in a savings plan may be used to pay for room and board expenses in addition to tuition and fees. Incentives for putting college savings into a 529 savings account include federal tax exemptions and state tax benefits, described further in Table 4. There are also disincentives from putting savings that may not be used for educational expenses into 529 accounts. If money in either a savings or prepaid plan is used for nonqualified expenses, it incurs taxes and a 10% penalty.

The first issue with the CSPN data is that it is not available for 1991–2000, the years when some of the largest merit aid programs started, so it is not possible to use difference in difference methods. For the years covered, 2001–present, there is not a lot of variation or jumps in merit aid. I searched merit aid data from 2001– present for jumps (See Figure 1), and the only large jump is Arkansas, which jumped from about 1,000 students receiving $8,500 in their merit aid to about 35,000 students receiving $3,000.

However, data directly from 529 programs on savings prior to 2000 likely exists. Different states started their 529 programs at different times, and many states started these programs several years before a merit aid program, so if this data were obtained it might be possible to do a difference in difference analysis. Unfortunately, however, the rapidity of the uptake of these 529 programs is influenced by many different factors in different states, and so it is unclear if even this analysis would be possible.

The second issue for both panel and cross-sectional analysis is that most programs accept out-of-state account openers. As a result, the state of the 529 program doesn’t correspond perfectly to merit aid eligibility. There is still reason to believe that this data may be fairly representative of states’ residents for certain states. First- ly, 6 states (New Jersey, South Dakota, Florida, South Carolina, West Virginia, Louisiana) do not allow out of state residents to enroll in their program. Second, online sources like Morningstar, which give advice regarding choosing a 529 plan, typically suggest choosing the home state’s 529 program if that state provides tax benefits (39 states), so it is possible that many states’ residents primarily use their home 529. Even if a state’s residents use their own 529 program, the issue remains that the data could overestimate residents’ 529 savings due to out-of-state account holders. The 529 programs offer differing investment portfolio options as well as differing fee structures, making some more desirable, depending on people’s circumstances. One way to get around this issue is to exclude the states that have non-neg- ligible out of state investment. It seems as though there are a handful of states which attract the majority of out-of-state inves- tors. Morningstar provides ratings of the 529 programs, and rates only two to three of them as Gold level. Online advisory sources typically recommend one of several programs including Virginia, Maine, Nevada, and Utah. In my analysis, I exclude

“Incentives for putting college savings into a 529 savings account include federal tax exemptions and state tax benefits.” these states and make the assumption that the remaining states have no out-of-state investment. However, I do not have definitive evidence in support of this assumption, and the results of the regressions using the 529 data is very contingent.

The CSPN data is desirable for answering other questions that exploit variation among states as well; for example, Heim and Winecoff (2023) explore how state specific incentives affect people’s decisions to invest in a college savings account, but they need to assume that all 529 accounts come from in-state residents. Addressing the issue of resident/non-resident accounts could be useful for improving research on a number of topics.

Regression Specification I run several regressions with different specifications. The first set of regressions uses the NFCS survey data with the binary outcome of whether or not respondents saved for college. I run both linear probability models and logit regressions to check that the regression specification does not alter my results, and I report the linear probability results as my main results. There are various ways to measure the largeness of a merit aid program, and I use average merit aid per student and recipients as a percentage of all undergraduate students. Additionally, I use a dummy for having a strong-classified merit aid program as the input variables, because savings decisions may not be sensitive to fluctuations in the exact amounts, but may instead respond to the general knowledge that a strong merit aid program exists.

To interpret these regressions, I assume that the measure of merit aid and all controls have a linear relationship with the probability of saving. I run several ver- sions of the following regressions, where

Ms is one of the three measures of merit aid for state s:

The education control is unavailable for 2009 and 2012, so for regressions including those years,

While I control for demographic characteristics of individuals, a concern I have is that I am not able to control for policy trends. It could be the case that states with merit aid programs may also be more likely to have certain other policies that encourage or discourage savings, and this could be an important omitted variable. Unfortunately, it is difficult to identify which policies affect savings incentives, and I was not able to control for state policies. States with merit aid vary in predominant political party over time, and it is unclear whether merit aid policies are connected to specific political affilia- tions. For the purpose of my regression, I assume that merit aid programs did not

The next set of regressions use state level data on average 529 savings per child 2015-2020 as the outcome variable, and the three different measures of merit aid as input variables of interest. I assume that there is a linear relationship between merit aid and average 529 savings per child; that the only factors correlated with both are median income of the state, percent of adults with a high school degree, and that these also have a linear relationship with college savings. To relate this to general savings, I assume that some fixed percent of college savings goes into 529 accounts, and that this does not vary across states. I run the regression where Ss is savings in state s, Ms is merit aid, HSs is percent of adults with a high school degree, Bs is percent with a bachelor’s degree, and ϵs is an exogenous error term.

In addition to averaging the 2015- 2020 529 assets, I run the regression pool- ing all years, and including state and year fixed effects.

I choose to average over the years 2015-2020 for regression (3) because it is not clear if there is meaningful variation in merit aid in each state across time. There appears to be fluctuations around a base level (see Figure 1), so I decided to simply compare the levels of saving across states for recent years. I averaged over several years to abstract away from chance variation in any particular year. I include regression (4) as well to test if the fluctuations in merit aid do have a meaningful impact on savings decisions. Regression (4) includes state fixed effects as well as year fixed effects, so β1 should capture the effect of the fluctuations in merit aid. I include data for years 2010–2020, starting in 2010, because some 529 programs only started in the 2000s, and the variation in their initial uptake is difficult to understand and account for. The problem of endogeneity is again a concern with the difficulty of controlling for state policies.

Lastly, I graphically compare the trend of Arkansas to other states before and after it expanded its merit aid program in 2011.

Results

NFCS Data Results for regression 1 are shown in Table 4. I find small negative effects of living in a state with more merit aid per student on the probability of saving, in the pooled regressions as well as the individual year regressions for 2012 and 2015. These regressions suggest that giving an average of $1,000 in merit aid (which is approximately what the strong programs do) decreases the probability of parents saving for college by 2-7%. The coefficients are not completely consistent across regressions; the 2021, 2018, and 2009 regressions do not have statistically significant coefficients, suggesting that either the relationship is changing over time, or there are confounding variables changing over time which I am not accounting for. The coefficients are, in particular, less negative in regressions without the education control variable, suggesting that education is an important factor and regressions excluding it are less trustworthy.

Notably, that doesn’t account for the discrepancy between the 2015, 2018, and 2021 regressions. Using the percent of students with aid or the strong program dummy as the measure of merit aid also yields significant negative effects in the pooled regressions, and the 2015 and 2012 regressions, but no significant results for 2009, 2021, and 2018. The former four regressions suggest that a 10% increase in aid recipients causes around a 1% decrease in likelihood of savings. Living in a state with a strong merit aid program is associated with a 1–3% decrease in the probability of saving. All analogous logit regressions agree in coefficient sign and significance with the OLS results. See appendix A for logit results.

529 Data Table 2 summarizes the results for regressions 3–4. There are no statistically significant coefficients on the merit aid variables. However, the coefficient for median income is negative in four out of the six regressions, and the coefficient on percent of college graduates is negative in two out of six, which is very unexpected. Because the NFCS data demonstrates that people with more education and higher income typically save more, I believe the issue is that the assets in each state’s 529 account are not truly representative of the college savings of parents in that state. It is likely the case that there are a lot of out- of-state 529 accounts.

Arkansas Program Expansion In 2011, the Arkansas Academic Challenge Scholarship expanded significantly, going from funding around 1,000 incoming students per year to 30,000. The scholarship currently gives $1,000 the first year, $4,000 the second the third, and $5,000 for the fourth year. Figure 3 shows that

Arkansas is the only state to have a big jump in the amount of merit aid given out per child during the time period for which college savings data is available.

The trajectories of states’ savings measures over time are shown in Figures 2 and 3. The red lines represent strong program states, the black line is Arkansas, and the gray are all others. There is a lot of heterogeneity in the trends of states in both 529 savings and percent of people who save for college. For the percentage of parents saving, neither merit aid states nor non-merit aid states seem to have a common trend. It is unclear whether Arkansas’ trend is more like one or the other. In 529 assets, merit aid states have less overall growth 2007–present than non-merit aid states. Arkansas saw one of the smallest growth rates throughout, with no visible changes after 2011. The case of Arkansas does not give any evidence that merit aid affected college savings.

Conclusion I primarily assessed whether merit aid programs decreased the probability of parents saving for college. The National Financial Capability Survey provided the most reliable source of publicly available data on savings, and formed the core of my analysis. While results from regressions across different years had different results, the majority had statistically significant negative coefficients, and I conclude that merit aid programs likely do decrease the likelihood of parents saving by around 1–3%. $1,000 of merit aid per student decreases the probability of saving by 2–7% and a 10% increase in merit aid recipients decreases the probability of saving by around 1%. While I control for many demographic variables in my regression, there are endogeneity concerns with potential policy omitted variables.

My results tell us about the likelihood that a parent will save, but it remains unclear whether parents who do save decrease the amount that they save when they expect to benefit from a merit aid program. I attempted to assess this using 529 data, but the results appear to be unreliable. The fundamental issue with 529 data is that many people hold accounts in states they do not reside in, and thus the assets in a certain state’s 529 program does not necessarily correspond to merit aid availability. For further work, the Survey of Consumer Finances confidential data could be a good alternative way to assess this question. ◆

title: Comprehension and Misinformation: An Interview with Dr. David N. Rapp
notes: Q&A interview with Dr. David N. Rapp, Walter Dill Scott Professor of Education in Psychology and the School of Education and Social Policy.
text:
Comprehension and Misinformation:

An Interview with Dr. David N. Rapp

By Katie Fu

Dr. David N. Rapp, the Walter Dill Scott Professor of Education in the Department of Psychology and the School of Education and Social Policy, focuses his research on examining memory, language, and the cognitive mechanisms associated with learning. Dr. Rapp received his Masters in Psychology from New York University (NYU), a PhD from Stony Brook University, and completed a post- doc in Classics and Psychology at Tufts University. In the following interview, Dr. Rapp discusses his research in cognitive psychology, its limitations, and the importance of an interdisciplinary view.

[This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.]

Interviewer: Could you tell me about your research in graduate school and what sparked your interest in cognitive psychology?

Professor Rapp: In graduate school, I was very interested in how people understand stories, so I started doing work on reading comprehension and inferencing. I focused on how people understand the themes of a text, how they take away ideas from what the authors are trying to say, and how they add information to what’s left out of the text. A lot of my early work was in memory and language in people’s experiences with fictional stories. Then, I became interested in nonfic- tion and focused on how we can help people not only become better readers with different kinds of materials, but also better at discourse experiences that involve conversation, such as watching videos and movies. While there are many people studying what happens when what you know is wrong but a text tells you the right thing, I became interested in the opposite: what happens when what you know is correct, but the text tells you the wrong thing?

When I was going for a master’s at NYU, I worked with a researcher who studied implicit memory tests, which focus on what people remember when they are not aware that they are being tested. I thought it was really interesting that you could design studies to understand how people are thinking and what they are remembering. She was amazing and it really got me excited about this being a career because the kind of research she’s doing contributes to theoretical understanding. I could see the ways in which it could be applied and that got me excited about cognition.

Interviewer: What are some valuable lessons you learned along your journey in academia?

Professor Rapp: The most valuable lesson I learned was trying many things because you don’t just want to find out what you are interested in, but also want

6969 to figure out what you might not like. When I was an undergraduate, I worked in a lab where I did research but did not like it, and I’m glad I did because it helped me figure out that that’s not something I want to do as a career. It would have been disappointing if, after four years of undergraduate, I went to graduate school to do that work and only figured out I did not enjoy it after all that had happened. So, you want to try many different things and get a lot of experience to see what areas you will be interested in; maybe research is exactly what you want to do, but you need to figure out what kind. Another lesson I learned was treating everyone respectfully because it is not only important and something we should care about, but also some of the best ideas have come from talking to people who aren’t even in psychology. Talking to authors, cartoonists, students, families, teachers, and all different kinds of people who have interesting ideas and intuitions about thinking has been very informative for me to think about what could become projects that help make the world better.

Interviewer: What insights has your research provided about the way people learn from different types of media?

Professor Rapp: Yeah, there’s a lot. Our research has really helped demonstrate that when people are exposed to inaccurate information, even if they know it’s wrong, it could still impact their thoughts and behavior. For a while people thought, well, it doesn’t matter if I already know what’s correct and someone tells me the wrong thing. Our research actually shows it can be influential, which is bad. Some of our research has also described ways in which you can help people become more evaluative, which has been great in terms of talking with teachers in schools to think about how you would build media literacy experiences. It’s also been important in discussing with authors how to write material to help people really understand the world or in talking to journalists trying to help people change their minds when they have to refute an idea that’s already out there. I’m really proud that the work has had theoretical implications and think that there’s still a lot to do so there will be more applications.

Interviewer: What are the challenges of studying the processes involved in understanding and how does this relate to the consequences of being exposed to inaccurate information?

Professor Rapp: You can’t see the things that people are doing. They can tell you what they think they’ve done and you can assess their comprehension, but to really know what they are doing, you need to come up with sophisticated techniques or use expensive technological tools like eye tracking. Getting a sense of both what people do and where they do it is what my lab focuses on. Because we want to understand how the mind works when you can’t see it, we have to ask a lot of questions through introspection interviews. We use a lot of different methods, such as surveys, experiments, and eye tracking, and hope they will all converge on our understanding to help us get a better idea of where people see inaccurate information, how they deal with it, and if there are ways for us to address these experiences. We try to understand from multiple directions what’s going on and maybe, from that, we can build better experiences for people.

Interviewer: How does the interdisciplinary view contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms associated with reading and comprehension?

Professor Rapp: There are psychologists who are studying this information, but we also have to collaborate with linguistic researchers, educational researchers, teachers, and journalists, because they’re all going to have a different set of experiences and a different set of investments in understanding that space. And if we can all come together and understand things from each other’s perspectives, that will allow us to build better models and better accounts. I’m part of the Cognitive Science program here at Northwestern and that’s really what they do at their heart. People from across different units on campus come together, talk about ideas, and share methodologies, because if only one person and one method is used to study an issue, you’re not going to get as rich of an understanding as with multiple people with multiple methods. By bringing computer scientists, anthro- pologists, educational psychologists, learning scientists, and music theorists in to discuss, then you will get a better chance since the folks who are having the biggest impact tend to have multiple disciplines behind the work they’re doing.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to the undergraduate students at Northwestern?

Professor Rapp: You should do research as an undergrad because Northwestern has amazing resources and faculty so you can gain more experience. You might find that it is not something you want to do, but you might also find that it is something that’s really exciting. I only figured it out because I did a lot of research in undergrad and in grad school that helped me figure out what I liked and what I didn’t like. I’m still learning what kind of things I want to do, so doing research is really important. I’m always excited to hear that there are so many Northwestern undergraduates doing research but I also think that more of them should do it because it is so important.

title: The Protect of Total War and the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, 1944-1945
notes: Senior thesis. The opening page prints the title as "The Protect of Total War..."; the contents page and the contributors page print "The Project of Total War...". Faculty adviser (printed "Dr. Ken Alder") named on the opening page. Appendices reproduce Wallace Kirkland's Life magazine photographs (Figures 1-6) with captions. The bibliography is divided into primary sources, secondary sources, archives and consulted sources.
text:
The Protect of Total War and the Minnesota Starvation

Experiment, 1944-1945

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Ken Alder

Department of History by Aimee Flanigan

Abstract When the United States (U.S.) entered World War II in 1942, 12,000 men refused uniformed service through the draft. These conscientious objectors (C.O.s) were, however, willing to perform alternative service. This project focuses on the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, which was conducted between 1944 and 1945 at the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and used C.O.s as volunteer human subjects. In conducting the experiment, the doctors (led by Ancel Keys) and subjects hoped to understand the biological and psychological effects of starvation and illuminate best practices to nourish the starving populations of Europe after World War II. In order to accomplish these aims, the 36 C.O.s under- went a control period of three months, a systematic semistarvation of six months, and a rehabilitation period of three months. This project integrates the Minnesota Experiment with the social and political landscapes of an America engaged in total war, bridging a gap between scholarship that discusses the experiment as a micro- history and broader scholarships of World War II that mention it only in passing. It does so by demonstrating and analyzing the parallels between specific groups in the experiment and specific groups in the military, showing how the character of total war became part of an experiment that was defined by its separation from combat and military institutions. In demonstrating these parallels and contextualizing the experiment in the climate of total war, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment emerges as both extraordinary and unprecedented while also deeply ordinary in the context of its own time.

Introduction Everyone agreed that the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene was an odd place. Due to the lab’s unassuming entrance at Gate 27 of the university’s football stadium, most people passed by without a second glance. When 36 C.O.s reported to the lab in the winter of 1944, most could not find the entrance and walked the perimeter of the stadium, or looked aimlessly around the parking lot, before finding Gate 27. Gate 27 was deeply significant, however, to the small group of people who worked at, lived in, and visited the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene. The lab comprised a maze of tunnels located beneath the stadium. Alongside these tunnels were offices, exam rooms, and a staggering collection of laboratory equipment.1 On Saturday afternoons, the noise of fans enjoying the football game above the researchers’ heads became an ambient rumble. With its exposed pipes, drab walls, summer and winter drafts, and inconspicuous entrance, the lab was certainly utilitarian.2 Suffice it to say that decor was not a priority for the lab’s founder, Dr. Ancel Benjamin Keys.

Keys led a team of physicians who designed and conducted the Minnesota Starvation Experiment. The 36 men who arrived in 1944 were human subjects, all of them draft-age men who had declared themselves to be C.O.s and had agreed to an alternative form of wartime service: systematic starvation in the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene at the University of Minnesota. The C.O.s volunteered for the chance to be of service and to tangibly help others. The experiment, sponsored by the

1 Henry Blackburn, If It Isn’t Fun: A Memior from a Different Sort of Medical Life (Wordpress, 2000), https://henryblackburn. wordpress.com/stories/professional-memoirs/if-it-isnt-fun-volume-i/. 2 “Medicine: The Fat of the Land,” Time, January 13, 1961, https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,828721,00.html. 3 “Arsenal of Democracy,” Fireside Chat, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/node/209416.

U.S. government, mimicked the meager diets starving Europeans suffered as a result of World War II. To study how they could most effectively be rehabilitated, the 36 C.O.s were starved together. They were then divided into four groups of nine and revived by different diets of proteins and vitamins.

Scholars have portrayed the Minnesota Starvation Experiment as an extraordinary experiment. Indeed it was, insofar as nothing quite like it has been attempted before or since. Perhaps for this very reason, scholars have largely neglected to place the Minnesota Starvation Experiment within the broader social and cultural landscape of wartime America. Rather, scholars have either touched on the experiment as a piece of evidence or have examined it in isolation. This thesis bridges this gap, integrating the Minnesota Starvation Experiment into the American story of World War II. In illustrating how the experiment took on the character of total war, this thesis ana- lyzes parallels between the experiment and wartime America to emphasize the degree to which total war permeated American society.

Central to the understanding of the project of total war is World War II’s consumption of American society. When President Roosevelt announced U.S. entry into the war on Dec. 9, 1941, he made it clear to the American public that “we are now in this war… Every single man, woman, and child is a partner in the most tremendous undertaking of our American history.”3 World War II was an era of collective commitment and absolutes that effectively rallied the country. Resources and factories were used to manufacture guns, trucks, tanks, and aircraft engines rather than Fords, Cadillacs, and Chevro- lets.4 Author Mark P. Parillo wrote that “No war before or since touched so many Americans and so many aspects and facets of their lives.”5 From Pearl Harbor until Victory in Europe Day, Americans dedicated themselves, their time, and their money to the war effort.

The 11,996 men who declared themselves C.O.s stood out from this intense and collective mobilization: they were the men who refused noncombatant, uniformed military roles but were willing to contribute to the country’s war effort through alternative forms of service. This group, of which the Minnesota men were a part, made up the Civilian Public Service (CPS).6 In 1942, the CPS allowed these C.O.s to participate as human subjects in a variety of government-sponsored medical experiments that reflected the conditions soldiers might have faced in combat.

Although the Minnesota Starvation Experiment was part of a broader network of human medical experiments that used C.O.s as human subjects, it stood out from these other ventures. The Starvation Experiment’s duration—one year living at the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene—was much longer than other experiments in which C.O.s participated. Furthermore, every day of the experiment required significant personal effort on the part of its human subjects. Indeed, while many of the other experiments that utilized C.O.s were strictly biological, the Starvation Experiment depended not only on the C.O.s’ willingness to sacrifice their

bodies but also on their mental and emotional willingness to dedicate themselves to the experiment. They would be required to take draining tests of intelligence, to honestly report private information such as their dreams and psychological changes to the experiment’s doctors, and to remain on the strict experimental diet as those around them continued eating as normal. The men would be faced with countless choices every day that would test their self-sacrifice and dedication to the experiment. Because of this dynamic, the C.O.s became active participants, partners, and drivers of the Starvation Experiment. They continuously committed themselves to the experiment and to each other in a way that C.O.s engaged in other medical experiments did not.

As this thesis will show, the experiment partook of the character of American wartime. Its execution hinged upon the lead doctors’ ambitious goals and expansive moral license during a period of total warfare and human suffering. The experiment likewise depended on the willingness of the C.O.s to voluntarily subject themselves to intense hardship and medical risk for a prolonged period of time to serve a larger humanitarian purpose. Finally, the risks the C.O.s took captured the public’s attention in ways that can only be understood in light of contemporary reports from Europe, where a five-year war against fascism had wrought unheard-of devastation.

This thesis argues that the Starvation Experiment, though unique in many aspects, also contained deep parallels that connected it to the experience of American military leadership and goals, which drafted all able-bodied young men as combatants and enlisted the entire nation at home in the project of total war. These parallels include the mixes of voluntarism and com- pulsion, war-fighting and peace-planning, and individual initiative and group cohe- sion that existed in the larger experience of World War II and in the microcosm of the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene and the Starvation Experiment.

The Doctors and the Direction of the Experiment The condition of total war influenced the events of the Minnesota Starvation Experiment in that, throughout the experiment, the doctors’ actions, priorities, and concerns mirrored those of American military officers engaged in World War II. Like their officer counterparts, those involved in the experiment established and operated in an environment with a strict hierarchy, with Ancel Keys at the top, followed by the rest of his doctors, staff, and finally, the C.O.s. Similarly to officers, Keys and his team had a complicated and dynamic relationship with the men beneath them in this hierarchy. Their relationship mirrored that between officers and the enlisted men under them, both of which were at times characterized by tension and a constant separation of the two groups. The doctors noticed that the subjects had, over time, developed a “tremendous in-group” identity that excluded the doctors and staff.7 Similarly, when enlisted men bonded with

In a sense, command is the loneliest job in the world.”9

Furthermore, the doctors of the Starvation Experiment were concerned with the morale of the C.O.s, reflecting similar battlefield concerns of those commanding enlisted men. In 1943, the Special Search Division published its first issue of What the Soldier Thinks, which compiled the results of numerous surveys of soldiers conducted between 1942 and 1943. The motivation behind the project, according to the Special Search Division, was “to probe underlying factors affecting morale” as the Army expanded with America’s entry into the War and the ensuing Draft.10 Clearly, the military considered the morale of its soldiers important and devoted resources to assessing it. Similarly, in the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene, Keys was so concerned about morale that he took action: On May 26, he organized a “relief meal.” The men chose the foods they wanted for this one glorious break from the semistarvation diet. Though Keys restricted the quantity of each food in order to maintain the experiment’s integrity, the relief meal was still by far the most food the C.O.s had seen since the start of the experiment.11 The strategy was effective, and the C.O.s’ mood noticeably improved as the men enjoyed the meal. Reluctant to conclude the meal and return to semistarvation, many of the men consumed the peel of an orange that had been part of it. Keys, who had metic- ulously measured and recorded the specific caloric content of each food item in the meal, was furious when he found out this unmeasured consumption of calories he had not predicted.12

Finally, Keys and his team had to adapt to changing and unforeseen circumstances to keep the experiment running and on schedule, just like officers in the military. As the doctors embarked on their unprecedented experiment, various conditions forced them, over time, to alter their conception of the experiment and its purpose, the ways in which they related to the subjects and interacted with them, and their own understanding of nutrition’s effects on the human body. While it was not easy to overcome the difficulties that arose beneath the university’s football stadium between 1944 and 1945, the doctors ultimately managed to bring the experiment to completion in accordance with their original schedule.

Experiment echoed the social solidarities and individual sacrifices of the battlefield. The C.O.s of the Starvation Experiment suffered in their bodies, just like combatants in the theaters of World War II. Both groups shared analogous motivations for the larger purpose of their mission, whether it involved combat or human experimentation. For both, comradeship, defined by historian Gerald H. Linderman as friends’ “love, loyalty, and devotion to one another,” was a fundamental aspect of how the groups conceptualized themselves and the challenges in front of them, even as this bond developed and changed.13 For example, the distinct and painful semistarvation phase strengthened the C.O.’s group mentality. As the weeks passed, they drew upon each other and their group identity for comfort, echoing a coping strategy of soldiers in combat. Surrounded by well-fed doctors and staff, the C.O.s’ only reassurance was the 35 other men living and working beside them under the football stadium who felt the same. Late in the semistarvation phase, one subject remembered that “we all felt like we were in this together…”14 On the battlefield, meanwhile, soldiers similarly sought comfort from others in their unit when faced with the challenges of combat. One soldier described how, after months of combat, he sought emotional support from his com- panions: “The only comfort I received was the knowledge I was not alone in this.”15 For both the C.O.s and soldiers, their group members were the only people who intimately understood how they felt.

Finally, the impact of the experiment even after the men left Minneapolis showed continuing similarities between soldiers battling the Axis powers and the C.O.s battling starvation. Both groups experienced difficulty adjusting to life without the group solidarity and the all-consuming nature of their projects, be it combat or semistarvation. Finally, the legacy of the comradeship lingered in both the subjects’ and soldiers’ recollections of their wartime experiences. One soldier remarked on the force of comradeship, remembering that “we would march in step for us, sing for us, excel for us, endure for us, and… suffer and die for us. For each other.”16 One subject echoed these words when he described how he came to feel about the Starvation Experiment in the months and years following its end. He wrote that “it was for us as much as for them—the name- less them—those who might benefit from the experiment’s findings. It was for all of us—not just the guinea pigs, but the staff and everyone closely involved. It had given us something to believe worthy of our best efforts.”17 The C.O.s’ understanding of the experiment and its legacies of suffering and comradeship paralleled that of American soldiers. Despite their differing stances on war and pacifism, the wartime experiences of both groups were similar in ways that left a lasting impression on the participants.

The similarities in the C.O.s and drafted soldiers’ experiences, despite their different views of war, showed how both violent fighting and pacifist wishes for

Conclusion With the conclusion of the Starvation Experiment on Oct. 20, 1945, the Minneapolis C.O.s spread out across the country and entered an array of careers. When 19 of the men gathered in 1998, all of them had college degrees, and six had PhDs. Among the group, six were college professors, four were teachers, and two were ministers. There was also an architect, a lawyer, an engineer, and a social worker.18

The former subjects all carried reminders of the experiment with them long after they left the Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene. Even 50 years later, the men perfectly recalled their exact body weights throughout the three phases of the Minnesota Experiment. Their weights had dictated their lives for almost a year, and they never forgot them. Many were staunchly against food waste, insisting that their children and grandchildren finish every bite on their plates.19 Some subjects also fixated on providing others with the plenty they had been deprived of during the experiment. Subject Lester Glick, for example, developed an obsession with cinnamon rolls during the experiment that never quite went away. Every Sunday for 20 years, he baked around 400 cinnamon rolls and distributed them to his congregation.20

Finally, although some men fell out of touch, others met lifelong friends through the Starvation Experiment. Towards the end of their lives, many of the

C.O.s reconnected through reunions and personal outreach. When researchers Leah Kalm and Richard Semba interviewed 18 of the men in 2005 as part of an oral history for the Library of Congress, the records of which form an important source base for this project, the former subjects referred to one another as friends. Their excitement at hearing which C.O. was being interviewed next is palpable in the recordings of their conversations. They often asked Kalm and Semba to pass on messages or greetings to the man next on the researchers’ list. In 2005, the C.O.s all felt that the experiment was a major life event. They unanimously agreed that they thought the Starvation Experiment was ethical and that they would volunteer again.21

As for Keys and his team, they worked tirelessly to publish The Biology of Human Starvation in 1950. The work went on to deeply impact science, specifically in the sciences of nutrition and eating disorders. The Starvation Experiment remains the only exploration of the biological and psychological effects of prolonged semistarvation, making it part of the bedrock of these fields. The experiment proved that the psychological symptoms of starvation are so significant that they are often impossible to distinguish from the symptoms of the eating disorder itself. As a result, doctors learned to treat patients for starvation before treating the eating disorder.22

Interestingly, the field of bioethics has also been notably silent on the experiment, suggesting an area for further exploration and analysis. Bioethicists Zohar Lederman and Teck Chuan Voo note that “the [Minnesota Starvation Experiment] seemingly has no mention in the bioethics literature.”23 Indeed, as bioethics has shifted to an explicit condemnation of unethical human experiments, especially after World War II, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment seems to have largely been left out of such discussions. Perhaps this is because the experiment prompts scholars to grapple with complex issues such as volunteerism, social and group pressure and consent, and conflict between the principles of beneficence and individual autonomy.

The Starvation Experiment is also challenging in its subversion of the villain-victim narrative bioethics often uses to discuss human experimentation, in which doctors and researchers uneth- ically impose their will and risky science on a vulnerable population. This is not to say that the villain-victim narrative does not have its place in bioethics and history more generally—cases like the Nazi and Japanese experiments on prisoners of war during World War II, the Tuskegee Syph- ilis Experiment, and the Willowbrook Experiments can and should be analyzed via this binary.24 This view does not—and never has—fit the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, however. The C.O.s who faced the challenges of semistarvation held complicated and changing relationships with the laboratory’s doctors and staff, but ultimately shared their dedication to the experiment. In many ways, they actively cultivated a partnership with one another.

The context of the experiment within a time of total war makes these tensions even more nuanced. For example, the Starvation Experiment exemplified changes to the bioethical principle of beneficence, defined as the obligation of a physician to act for the benefit of the patient. In know- ingly placing the C.O.s of the Starvation Experiment in such physical, mental, and emotional distress, the doctors threatened to contravene this principle. For a nation horrified by Nazi atrocities and mobilized to fight a just war, everyone, including the medical establishment, doctors, and C.O.s, was expected to contribute to an unprecedented degree. Military historian and professor Hew Strachan wrote that World War II was a period in which “the ends justified the means.”25 In such a context, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment became necessary, regardless of the sacrifice of beneficence it required. The difficult choices made by the C.O.s of the Starvation Experiment—to declare their conscientious objection, participate in the experiment, and to repeatedly commit to it—reflected the difficult choices made by many of their enlisted peers and even other Americans, all of whom took various actions and made

25 Hew Strachan, “Essay and Reflection: On Total War and Modern War,” The International History Review 22, no. 2 (June, 2000): 359, http://www.jstor.org/stable/40108371.

life choices within the unique context of a total war environment. They engaged in and endured circumstances that may not have been permissible or accepted in times of peace and stability.

The most famous human experiments and those most readily discussed by the field of bioethics lack the nuance that is foundational to the Minnesota Experiment. For a field like bioethics, which has been shaped so heavily and reactively by atrocities and makes lessons out of cau- tionary tales, the Starvation Experiment hovers uncomfortably in the gray area.

This analysis shows that, while the Starvation Experiment was an endeavor defined by its use of C.O.s and its separation from military institutions and combat, it was a part of the U.S. war machine all the same. Somewhat ironically, the group of men who declared themselves C.O.s, entered the CPS, and volunteered for the Starvation Experiment in the end participated in wartime activities that deeply paralleled that of their enlisted counterparts. The Starvation Experiment shows how a particular group of Americans, set apart by their pacifist principles, engaged with the war effort and, in their own way, sacrificed for the project of total war. Just like so many stories that emerge from war, the story of the Minnesota Starvation Experiment is one that is intrinsically human, full of difficult sacrifices, and situated in its own history and complexities. ◆

title: From Blades to Breakthroughs: Palmy Lamsam’s Journey from Figure Skating to Research
notes: Profile of Thita "Palmy" Lamsam, a former competitive figure skater and Northwestern Marriage and Family Therapy student.
text:
From Blades to Breakthroughs:

Palmy Lamsam’s Journey from Figure Skating to Research

By Evan Hostetler

Seven-year-old Thita “Palmy” Lamsam rushes past the bustling shops of the Imperial World Samrong in February of 2007, her excitement growing with each hurried step towards the ice rink that sat in the middle of hustling crowds. With a gift for her friend Vanessa wrapped tightly in her hands, Palmy was ready to do something she had never done before, despite her longing to do so: skate. Influenced by Disney movies, like the Ice Princess, that showed the beauty and artistry of the sport, Palmy had been waiting for the chance to experience it herself, and she was finally able to at Vanessa’s birthday party. After strapping on her skates and taking her first few wobbly and unsteady strides, Palmy fell in love with the magical feeling of being on the ice. The afternoon passed in a blur of youthful joy and revelry, and that day, a little girl went home with a newfound passion.

From that moment on, Palmy was hooked on the sport of figure skating and would find any opportunity to explore it. She would beg her parents to take her to the rink on the weekends, and if they wouldn’t, she would create her own rink at home, coating her wooden floors with baby powder and “skating” countless hours away with her older sister, Rada. Whether it was her persistent pleading or multiple fiascos with baby powder, her parents eventually relented and enrolled her in recreational skating lessons on the weekends. With each glide, spin, and stumble, Palmy’s talent for the sport deepened quite quickly, and it was clear she was meant to shine on stages bigger and brighter than her living room rink.

As Palmy grew in age, her commitment and passion to the sport grew as well. When she turned eight years old, her recreational coach pushed her to find other coaches that could foster and grow her talent even more, and she and her parents did just that. As she transitioned to her new coaches, she went from skating one or two times a week to three or four times a week.

When she turned nine a year later, her schedule changed again, shifting to five or six practices a week for two hours each day. Eventually, when Palmy reached her peak at about 15 years old, she was practicing six days a week for three hours on the ice, and an additional two hours were spent doing some sort of conditioning (working out at the gym with a personal trainer, taking a dance class, etc.).

This hard work and busy schedule would eventually pay off. Due to her confidence on the ice and immense artistry, Palmy was able to win the Thai National Championship five times. Each time she was able to skate at these championships, Palmy was grateful—grateful that she was skating on home ice, grateful that her body still allowed her to skate (considering she won her last Championship at 20 years old), and grateful she got to compete in the sport she loved so dearly.

Despite her love for the sport, Palmy still yearned to learn about the world around her—not just the best technique to do a double axel or the proper posi- tioning needed to do a flying camel spin. She wanted to understand the reason behind successful coach and skater relationships, as well as the physics behind a double axel or flying camel spin.

To Palmy, it became perfectly clear that she would have to make certain sacrifices in order to strike a balance between her life on the ice and her life in the classroom. She couldn’t complete the International Baccalaureate Diploma at her high school because she consistently missed class for skating competi- tions, so she had to settle for a regular high school diploma. When she was applying to colleges, despite the myriad of opportunities that called out to her at more rigorous institutions, she compromised by attending Michigan State University. This was so she could balance the increased academic workload that came with being a college student with her meticulous skating schedule, especially considering the fact that MSU offered strong student athlete support.

One day, Palmy realized that if she wanted to progress any further in skating, she would have to choose between her skating or academic career. Therefore, she decided that she would take a gap year from her studies, spending all 365 days as a professional athlete. She wanted to understand what her life would be like if she treated figure skating as her full time job in an attempt to discover if it should be the endeavor she dedicated the rest of her life to.

During this gap year, she increased her training regimen ten fold and pushed her body to its limits. Every day was a test of endurance, discipline, and passion—early mornings at the rink, grueling conditioning sessions, and hours spent perfecting the smallest details of her routines. Yet, as the months passed, Palmy began to reflect on what truly fulfilled her, and she realized it was not a life focused solely on skating. Palmy missed the intellectual challenges she had put on hold and found herself looking for some academic outlet.

Around this time, Palmy received a letter from Northwestern University’s Marriage and Family Therapy Program. From her time at Michigan State, she had developed a deep interest in psychology, particularly in the social threads that connect the millions of relationships humans form each day. When she discovered the therapy program at Northwestern, she thought it would be the perfect outlet to continue her academic studies, and sure enough, she was accepted! That day, Palmy decided that she would no longer sacrifice her future in academics for a future in figure skating; she would no longer settle when it came to the pursuit of her interest in psychology. In February 2023, she retired from the sport of figure skating entirely, ready to take advantage of the plethora of opportunities Northwestern had to offer.

Although she no longer had to dedicate hours and hours to her jam-packed figure skating schedule, Palmy still found many ways to keep busy, fitting right in with the hustle and bustle of Northwestern’s campus. She has become quite involved with the Thai Student Association and has given back to the community through multiple service organizations. She is connected with Professors like Claudia Haase, helping out in her research lab and assistant teaching for her classes.

However, her involvement as a Student Therapist at Northwestern’s Family Institute has played a major role in defining her experience at Northwestern, as it helped her discover her own special research topic. In this position, she has had the opportunity to talk to families whose loved ones have been incarcerated, and she has seen the first hand effect this has had, not just on their relationships, but on their mentality as well. Right now, there is very little psychological research that focuses on how to help families in this position. Therefore, she has decided to write a research paper on the psychological and emotional impact of incarceration on relationship dynamics, with a particular focus on how people in relationships navigate the challenges of separation and what kinds of treatment or support might help them do so. Right now, she is in the literature review stage, trying to understand all the current research that has already been done on the subject.

Although Palmy doesn’t compete on the ice anymore, the characteristics she developed as a figure skater continue to shape her approach to research. For one, she uses the time management skills she developed while balancing her hectic life as a figure skater. Palmy is involved in every corner of Northwestern’s campus, yet, she is able to perfectly manage and complete all of her activities, largely due to this experience. Further, she developed a fine-tuned attention to detail from years of perfecting every jump, spin, and glide—she uses this skill everyday in her research. Whether she’s analyzing data, reviewing psychological theories, or fine-tuning her writing, Palmy approaches each task with the same precision she once applied to her routines, ensuring that every detail is up to her standards. Finally, her ability to perform and exceed under pressure has served her immensely, especially as a student at Northwestern. Just as she once thrived under the scrutiny of judges and the intensity of competition, Palmy now excels in high-stakes academic settings—whether it’s presenting her research, engaging in deep, trauma-heavy therapy sessions, or meeting tight deadlines.

Despite the fact that, most days, you’ll find Palmy in an academic or clinical setting, remnants of the former skater within her are expressed a couple times a week at the local ice rink. There, she lets her inner artist flourish, using the skills and tricks developed over the past 18 years of her life. Moreover, Palmy has now added another, instructional aspect to this passion of hers, creating social media videos to share her knowledge and experience when it comes to figure skating.

When that little, seven-year-old girl stepped on the ice for the first time at her friend’s birthday party, she had no idea she would climb the ranks and become one of the best figure skaters in Thailand. Moreover, she probably didn’t expect to transition from the sport all together, becoming a researcher at one of the best institutions in the world. Her journey from a young girl mesmerized by the magic of skating to a dedicated researcher at Northwestern University is a testament to her resilience, adaptability, and passion for learning. Though her skates may be retired, her drive for excellence remains as strong as ever, propelling her forward as she carves a new path—one that is just as meaningful and rewarding as the one she left behind.
