text:
Early Childhood Shocks in Ghana: Evidence on Physical Health and Cognitive Development

Faculty Adviser: Dr. Christopher Udry

Department of Economics by Ila Gupta

Abstract While global economic growth rises, international poverty also continues to increase. From 2022-2023, the population living below the international poverty line increased by 4%, now estimated at 31.4% of the global population. Indeed, poverty is multidimensional, and the multilateral allocation of resources is continuously reevaluated at the household-level. Founded around this guiding principle, alongside modern development theory on poverty traps (Duflo’s “poor but neoclassical”), it is hypothesized that the regular occurrence of economic shocks—e.g. natural disasters, global pandemics, and political, ethnic, and religious conflicts— keep poor households poor by forcing such households to respond by reducing caloric intake, limiting cognitive development and long-term health. We find that short- and long-term effects differ with respect to these outcomes. In particular, significant short-term decreases in nutritional status are found, prominently guided by age-effects, as well as significantly lower assessed cognitive ability. While some long-term differences are reported with regard to physical activities of daily life, more studies must be done in this area to confirm relevance and results.

Introduction Poor and nonpoor households are subject to exogenous shocks. However, for households that experience high frequencies of shocks, or for those with few resources to bounce back, shocks may have significant impacts on short- and long-term outcomes. Moreover, economic shocks have the ability to affect household welfare, especially for vulnerable populations— perhaps exemplified by the COVID-19 pandemic, recent hyperinflation, and the globally disproportionate distribution of natural disasters.1 With comprehensive socio-economic surveys to offer multidimensional insight on household welfare, we can measure the effects of shocks to inform policy which supports household resilience and long-term development outcomes.

Within the context of protecting and supporting human capital formation in poor populations, we consider the consequences of early childhood shocks in Ghana. Rapid biological and cognitive growth occurs during early childhood and adolescence; thus, deficiencies in nutrition or limited socialization, for example, may have long-lasting consequences on cognitive development and educational attainment. Even more so, the reallocation of household resources necessitated by unanticipated economic shocks may have consequences on investments in nutrition, health care, or education. This paper focuses on the effect of early childhood shocks on short- and long-term physical health and youth cognitive development. It is moti- vated by the limited economic evidence we have about early childhood circumstances on both short- and long-term outcomes,

1 Contreras, I., Oseni, G., Palacios-Lopez, A., & Banerjee, R, Household Surveys During Multiple Crises, Modifying Questionnaires to Assess the Impact of Shocks, The World Bank, 2013. 2 Yale Economic Growth Center, “ISSER-Northwestern-Yale Long Term Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey (GSPS),” New Haven Connecticut, 2024.

the gap in our literature pertaining to West African youth populations, and the current lack of infrastructure to assist households with economic recovery.

Accordingly, we examine a cross-sectional panel from the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey, which comprehensively follows over 5,000 households across all 10 regions of Ghana. The survey is particularly well-suited to addressing early life impacts on long-term outcomes because, unlike most short-term panel surveys, GSPS collects consistent and extensive survey data across multiple rounds (2009-10, 2013-14, and 2017-18), and rather than dropping individuals from the panel who leave the study area between these rounds (potentially biasing our understanding of who benefits from and who bears the costs of development), GSPS aims to account for household attri- tion. GSPS has been administered by the Economic Growth Center (EGC) at Yale University and the Institute of Statistical, Social, and Economic Research (ISSER) at the University of Ghana, Legion from 2009-2018.2 Since the Ghana cluster is a relatively novel dataset which comprehensively accounts for individuals across surveys, it introduces a new empirical agenda in producing estimations with less bias. The expansiveness of the survey also offers an opportunity to study associations between household shocks and their outcomes within a multidimensional context. Lastly, Ghana has made significant progress in recent years to invest in economic and policy development; thus, producing evidence in support of those efforts supports ongoing policy action.

In the sections to follow, we will (i) cover a brief overview of Ghana with regard to its political and economic environment, (ii) consider surrounding literature on economic shocks and poverty traps, (iii) situate this study within its theoretical foundations, (iv) frame the empirical approach, (v) describe and detail the data as it pertains to variable specification and panel construction, (vi) present results, and (vii) conclude with provisions for further research.

Background The distribution of industrial and agricultural sectors, the prevalence of economic shocks, and the wealth distribution in Ghana are prominently guided by geography. Ghana lives in the northwest region of the African continent bordering Togo, Côte d’Ivoire, and Burkina Faso, with the south-most regions of Ghana bordering the Atlantic Ocean. Its total population is 33.5 million,3 of which approximately 16.3% is concentrated in Greater Accra4,5 consistently the most densely populated and urbanized region relative to those surrounding.

In recent years, political systems in Ghana have made significant developments towards a democratic multi-party system, consistently ranking as “one of the top three African countries for freedom of speech and press”6. However, with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and hyperinflation on international markets, Ghana is currently undergoing debt restructuring via an IMF program. While the economic climate in Ghana gradually stabilizes, the immediate implications of

the international economic crises have largely impacted the most vulnerable

In October 2019, UNICEF reported at least 1 in 3 children under the age of 5 (over 200 million) as undernourished or overweight globally, but in Ghana, malnutrition is far more prominent.8 With almost 1 in 5 children under the age of five stunted and 1 in 10 children under 10 considered underweight, poor diets and inadequate food systems put Ghanaian children at high risk of “poor brain development, weak learning, low immunity, increased infections and, in many cases, death.”910Malnutrition is ultimately significantly disproportionately distributed amongst poor youth and communities that suffer climate-related natural disasters.

7 ibid. 8 UNICEF, “Poor Diets Damaging Children’s Health Worldwide, Warns UNICEF,” October 16, 2019. 9 ibid. 10 World Health Organization, “Prevalence of malnutrition,” The Global Health Observatory: Nutrition Indicators. 11 Cas, A.G., et al, “The Impact of Parental Death on Child Well-Being,” 2014.

Literature Review

Applied Models: Difference-in-Difference Approach Studies examining the impacts of economic shocks vary widely in the shock types and outcomes measured. One of the most frequently applied econometric approaches exploits the occurrence of a national shock via natural experiment (i.e. natural disaster, war), often offering a large sample size, fixed time effects, and stronger reliance on the exogeneity of a shock.

Cas et al. (2014) take the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami as a framework for exploit- ing an unanticipated shock: parental death in Indonesian households.11 Their specification measures the wellbeing of the same individuals before and after the tsunami, via child fixed effects, to estimate the effect of parental death on children’s wellbeing. Differences are averaged between children who lost one or both parents and children whose parents both survived. Cas et al. find significant differences in wellbeing due to the shock, with variation between

“...poor diets and inadequate food systems put Ghanaian children at high risk of ‘poor brain development, weak learning, low immunity, increased infections and, in many cases, death.’”

Figure 3. Underweight prevalence among children under 5 years of age (% weight-for-age <-2 SD), survey-based estimates (WHO, 2017)10

short- and long-term allocation of expen- diture and time on education and labor. In general, short-term impacts are less pronounced than long-term impacts for children who lost one or both parents.

Frankenberg and Thomas (2017) examine early life shocks on human capital formation through the lenses of in-utero shocks, prenatal nutrition, national financial shocks, and natural disasters.12 Covering an array of shock types, their work demonstrates the complexity in isolating shock effects on human capital development and wellbeing in both short- and long-run analyses and across shock types. Nonetheless, following a similar econometric DiD specification using child fixed effects, Frankenberg and Thomas isolate the effects of the 1998 financial crisis and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Frankenberg and Thomas conclude that households respond to shocks multilaterally to mitigate shock effects on younger generations; households choose either to expend all resources possible in order to avoid falling into poverty traps or to rationally reallocate resources on a micro-level to best recover from shocks. As we examine the effects of early childhood shocks in Ghana, we consider cross-sectional panel data to similarly achieve child fixed effects and to account for differences in short- and long-term outcomes.

Studies on Sub-Saharan Africa With regard to early-life shocks, the literature on sub-Saharan Africa, particularly West Africa, has been limited. Recent

12 Frankenberg, Elizabeth & Thomas, Duncan, “Human Capital and Shocks: Evidence on Education, Health and Nutrition.” Duke University. March 2017. 13 Kämpfen, Fabrice et al, “The effects of negative economic shocks at birth on adolescents’ cognitive outcomes and educational attainment in Malawi,” SSM - population health, vol. 18 101085, 7 Apr. 2022. 14 Agamile, P., & Lawson, D., Rainfall shocks and children’s school attendance: evidence from Uganda. Oxford Development Studies, 49(3), 291–309. 2021 15 Prominent studies have also considered data from Tanzania, Mozambique, South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Madagascar, and Kenya, among others. 16 Alderman, Harold, et al., “Long Term Consequences of Early Childhood Malnutrition,” 2006.

studies from sub-Saharan Africa have, nonetheless, drawn connections between early life shocks and cognitive and educational outcomes. Contributing to this literature, Kampfen, et. al. (2022) study the effect of shocks at birth on adolescent cognitive outcomes in Malawi,13 Agamile, et. al. examine the impact of heavy rainfall on school attendance in Uganda (2021)14, and others15 have been carried out to quantify the consequences of economic shocks among African populations. However, few such studies integrate members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), which this work attempts to improve.

Regarding the current literature on sub-Saharan Africa, Alderman, et. al. (2006) offer findings on long-term effects of early childhood malnutrition, examining associations between preschool malnutrition on subsequent human capital formation in rural Zimbabwe. The study uses a maternal fixed effects-instrumental variables (MFE-IV) estimator to account for endogenous differences between households16; the researchers can then use representations of civil war and drought shocks to compare preschool nutritional status across siblings, precisely isolating shock effects. Alderman, et. al. find that improvements in height-for-age in pre- schoolers are directly related to adolescent height, onset of education, and educational attainment. More precisely, they estimate: if the median height of a preschool child was equal to that of the median child in a developed country, by adolescence, she would be 3.4 centimeters taller, complete an additional 0.85 grades of schooling, and would have commenced school six months earlier.17

As such, the development literature on economic shocks is vast, though limited study on Ghana has been completed in this area. The advent of the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey and the public availability of its first three surveys introduces a truly unique opportunity to examine the effects of community-level shocks on welfare and resource allocations.

Theoretical Foundations The literature discusses two distinct interpretations of poverty. The first is that those in poverty are exactly like those who are not: the poor have the same abilities and capacities for rational decision-making as the nonpoor—their position within cyclical poverty is attributed to external adversities. The second is that, while the poor and nonpoor may face similar objective functions, poverty changes the set of options and constraints that individuals face, affecting individual behavior.18 Modern development economics largely rests on the second view, reframing empirical structures to account for market ineffi- ciencies in a neoclassical environment.

Although we proceed with this relatively novel paradigm, it is important to situate contemporary theory within its foundations, first examining poverty as singularly determined by external adversities. In this case, the decision-making agent is considered “poor but rational,”

17 ibid. 18 Ghatak, Maitreesh,“Theories of Poverty Traps and Anti-Poverty Policies,” The World Bank Economic Review, 29: S77–105, 2015. 19 UNICEF, “Poor Diets Damaging Children’s Health Worldwide,” 2019. 20 Abler, David G., and Vasant A. Sukhatme, “The ‘Efficient but Poor’ Hypothesis,” Review of Agricultural Economics 28, no. 3: 338–43, 2006. 21 Duflo, Esther, Poor but Rational? In Understanding Poverty (367), Oxford University Press, 2006.

a term coined by Ted Schultz with the publication of Transforming Traditional Agriculture (1975), and developed concurrently with Sir Arthur Lewis’ work on surplus labor market transfers.19 In the mid-20th century, it was widely accepted that the marginal product of labor in agriculture was zero such that labor transfers between agricultural and industrial sectors would not impact agricultural production in developing countries. Prior—distinctly biased—beliefs also held that markets in developing countries did not respond to economic incentives.20 Schultz’s central thesis argued against these beliefs—the extreme poor are “efficient but poor”— efficient in their rational decision-making and poor due to “friction-driven” market conditions. In other words, the poor rationally optimize resources, even when facing extreme constraints; the phenomenon of cyclical poverty must then be attributed to the inequity and inefficiency of the market, not of the individual. As clarified by Duflo (2006), “efficient but poor” describes the fact that “the poor certainly have bad lives, but there is nothing special about them; they just do the best they can under the difficult circumstances in which life has placed them and their fields are as productive as possible—they just cannot be very productive.”21

As empirical evidence has grown in the field, particularly through natural experiments and RCTs, recent reevalua- tion of the “poor but rational” theory fails to adequately account for observations of inefficient resource allocation among the extreme poor, making way for a second view of poverty. This second view suggests that while the poor face similar objective functions to the nonpoor, poverty changes the set of constraints that individuals face. Such constraints refer to behavioral, self-reinforcing choices which are encountered as a result of circumstances. For example, a poor household may allocate resources counter to rational expectations, resulting in a market failure: “poor but neoclassical (but not necessarily efficient)” as coined by Duflo (2006).22 Further, facing extreme scarcity on a daily basis, a household must make subsistence-oriented decisions that serve present and near-future needs while limiting investment in future payoffs as we might expect. Hence, this view of poverty is considered “scarcity-driven.”23

Furthermore, there exists a broad range of empirical and theoretical evidence that links household shocks to poverty traps.24 Take, for instance, the nutrition-wage hypothesis: a household with very low income will struggle to obtain adequate nutrition, and in turn, be

22 Duflo, E., Poor but Rational? In Understanding Poverty (367–78), 2006. 23 Ghatak, M, “Theories of Poverty Traps”, 2015. 24 Frankenberg, E., et al., “Human Capital Shocks,” 2017. 25 see: Figure 4 26 Udry, Chris, “Poverty Traps in Nigeria,” ECON 327: Economic Development in Africa, (class lecture, Northwestern University, June 9, 2023).

unable to attain higher wages due to low energy, poor health, and/or detriments in other faculties.2526

Poverty is multidimensional, and accordingly, shocks require a multidimensional response and resource reallocation. Stemming from Schultz’s “poor but rational,” we expect households to efficiently reallocate resources following an economic shock diluting long-term consequences; however, it would perhaps be ignorant to overlook alternate internal constraints at play. We proceed with such theoretical foundations at the forefront of the empirical agenda to follow.

Econometric Approach The econometric approach laid out by Frankenberg and Thomas (2018) identifies three primary concerns from the theoretical framework to guide the structure of the proposed models: (i) it is difficult to identify shocks that are unanticipated and uncorrelated with individual and household choices, hence, to isolate the effect of shocks, we find ways to account for endogeneity; (ii) estimations regarding resource allocation in anticipation or response to shocks are not generalizable as households may differ significantly and multilaterally; (iii) the short- and long-run

“While the poor face similar objective functions to the nonpoor, poverty changes the set of constraints that individuals face.”

Poverty

Nutritional Status

Productivity and Wages impact of shocks may differ as a result of such variation in household responses to. Failure to address any one of these primary concerns poses a threat to the validity of our estimators and the inferences that we draw from them.

We rely on the econometric approaches outlined by Frankenberg and Thomas on the 1998 Indonesian Financial Crisis (2017)27, a two-period model by Alderman, et. al. on early childhood circumstances in Zimbabwe (2006)28, and estimations by Cas, et. al. (2014) on the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami29, alongside theoretical frameworks of this body of literature.30 We proceed with a two-period model that accounts for individual and household variant and invariant effects, as well as a vector-valued variable for shocks (to account for multiple shocks experienced by the household within a given period). It is hypothesized that shocks will reduce early childhood nutrition in Period 1 and reduce physical health and cognitive development in Period 2; however, individual and household characteristics are likely stronger determinants of long-term outcomes which may consequently dilute shock-effects in Period 2. Accordingly, we begin with:

where Wit represents a weight-to-age outcome in Period 1, dependent on, Sit, the occurrence of a community-level shock in Wave 1; Xit and Xi, represent individual and household time variant and time-invariant effects. As we proceed, alternation constructions of Sit are tested: (i) the occurrence of at least one

27 Frankenberg, E., et al., “Human Capital and Shocks,” 2017. 28 Alderman, H., et al., “Long Term Consequences,” 2006. 29 Cas, A. G., et al., “The Impact of Parental Death,” 2014. 30 see: Appendix, Econometric Approach 31 Yale Economic Growth Center, “ISSER-Northwestern-Yale Long Term Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey,” 2024.

community-level shock in Wave 1, (ii) the frequency of community-level shocks in Wave 1, (iii) shock frequency categories (e.g. few shocks, being 0-4 shocks), and (iv) occurrence of at least one shock by type: agricultural, town, or crop price.

For Period 2, we measure physical health and cognitive development outcomes by instrumenting the occurrence of a community-level shock for weight-for- height. Assuming that community-level shocks are exogenous, we can then estimate the effect of nutritional status through Wit.

Outcomes of interest with regard to physical health include weight-for-height over time and the ability to perform activities of daily living (e.g. carry heavy loads, bathe without assistance). Regarding cognitive development, we consider scores from the Raven’s Pattern Cognitive Assessment. These outcome variables are detailed in the data description to follow, alongside the specifications for individual and household-level controls.

Data

Description and Panel Construction We conduct a cross-sectional study relying on the first three waves of the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey, directed from 2009-2018 by the Economic Growth Center (EGC) at Yale University and the Institute of Statistical, Social, and Economic Research (ISSER) at the University of Ghana, Legon.31 The survey is nationally representative of all 10 regions of Ghana, each of which was surveyed by

Wit = β0 + β1Sit + β2Xit + β3Xi + ϵit

Ait = β0 + β1Wit + β2Xit + β3Xi + ϵit randomly selected enumeration areas (EA) proportional to regional population density, with 15 household observations from each EA. In all, GSPS accounts for 19,167 participants within 5,009 households across 334 EAs. Individuals are matched by a combination of the variable FPrimary, which uniquely identifies datasets across waves, and by hhmid, uniquely identifying individuals across surveys. At this stage, we have 54,251 observations and 30 variables pertaining to individual and household characteristics. Age of the sample is then restricted to or under the age of 15, or born after 1994, in Period 1.

This study included survey sections from both the main and community surveys. From the main survey, we have background and household information, physical metrics, and details on children’s health, cognitive function, and fundamental English and math skills. Correlate sections from Waves 2 and 3 are appended. From the Rural Community Survey, we have sections on town events, agricultural shocks, and crop sales. As shocks are surveyed at the community-level, each shock specification is matched to many individuals by EA. From the Urban Community Survey, we have town events and crop sale shocks. Shocks are reported by annual count from 2006-2009.

Variable Construction For short- and long-run effects, we examine physical metrics, activities of daily living, and health in the last two weeks. We construct a weight-for-height measure, setting a lower-bound of minimum premature weight and height32 to account for measurement error. Since physical health outcomes are considered in Period 2, we focus on activities of daily living in

32 Mayo Clinic. “Premature Birth - Symptoms and Causes.” Mayo Clinic. April 14, 2021. 33 see: Appendix, Figures 7-9 the long-run as an indication of general physical wellbeing. In particular, two questions guide our analysis: (1) If [Name] had to carry a heavy load (e.g. size 34 Bucket of water) without any help for 20 meters, could he/she do it?, and (2) If [Name] had to bathe him/herself without any help, could he/ she do it? A respondent may answer: (i) easily, (ii) with difficulty, and (iii) not at all. The responses are coded in a dummy which takes a zero value if the respondent selected “with difficulty” or “not at all” to either question, or a value of one if “easily” is selected for both.

Pertaining to community-level surveys, sections on shocks are reformatted such that we have one observation per shock-type, per EA. In the process of reshaping and cleaning, we accumulatively dropped 791 observations. The shocks reported in the surveys are expansive.33 With respect to town events, the question- naire surveys ethnic/tribal conflicts, religious conflicts, demonstrations, and police brutality, among other shocks. Agricultural shocks (surveyed only in rural-identified EAs) include insects, rodents, animals, or epidemic/disease affecting crops, heavy rainfall, and little rainfall. Lastly, crop sale shocks detail unit prices of six trading crops: cassava, maize, plantain, cocoyam, yam, and millet. Since shocks are surveyed at the community-level, we further specify town events such that those included are relevant at the household-level. To be clear, property damage, murder, or rape, for example, likely have concentrated household-level impacts; when reported at the community-level, shock frequency is overestimated for unaffected households. Hence, we keep the following: ethnic/ tribal conflict, religious conflict, violent demonstrations/strikes, and disease epi- demics affecting people.

Following the above data description, we proceed with four distinct characteriza- tions of shocks in our analysis. First, a shock dummy takes a zero value if an individual encountered no shocks from 2006-2009 or a value of one if an individual encountered at least one shock (town, agricultural, or crop price). Second, a shock count/frequency variable which sums the total number of shocks encountered. Third, we construct categorical shock frequency dummy variables: few shocks for a shock count of 0-4 (i.e. approx. one shock annually), some shocks for 5-16, many shocks for 17-32, and lots of shocks for 33 or more. Last, we construct dummies for shock types: at least one town shock, at least one agricultural shock, and at least one crop shock.

The time-invariant covariates include gender, year of birth (fixed-effects), nationality (e.g. Ghanaian, ECOWAS, other), ethnicity, religion (e.g. Catholic and Muslim), region (e.g. Western, Central, Greater Accra, Volta, Eastern, Ashanti, Brong Ahafo, Northern, Upper East or Upper West), urban (versus rural), relationship to the household head (e.g. child, grandchild), and parents’ highest education level (e.g. none, primary, secondary, or tertiary). Time-variant covariates include household size and parents’ work classifications.

Sample Individual and Household Characteristics Our preliminary analysis checks for significant differences in mean individual-level and household-level characteristics between the “shock” sample and “shock-free” sample. Notably, the sample sizes are unequal with 4,647 observations

34 see: Appendix, Table 1 35 see: Appendix, Table 2 encountering at least one shock from 2006-2009 and 437 observations shock- free. Significant differences appear in nationality and relationship to household heads.34 While all of the shock-free samples are of Ghanaian nationality by birth, there is slight variation across nationalities in the shock sample. Also, approximately 5% more of the shock-free sample is an “other” to the household head (e.g. other relative, non-relative, or house-help) younger than 15 years old, compared to the shock sample.

Difference-in-mean tests by shock/ shock-free show that samples differ significantly on their region, ethnicity, and religion distributions, as well as by parents’ education and work, and household size.35 Western, Central, Eastern, Northern, Upper East, and Upper West are more likely to encounter shocks on average. While Catholic-identifying households are almost 10% less likely to encounter economic shocks, Muslim-identifying households are 13% more likely to do so. As anticipated, fathers’ education is higher on average for the shock-free sample, and there are significantly more working professionals going shock-free; however, unexpectedly, mothers’ education and labor behave in the opposite direction. Last, urban households are both far less likely (49.1% less) to encounter shocks and are significantly smaller on average.

Results

Wave 1 Analyses: Short-Run Effects on Nutritional Status For analyses on the first period, our sample includes 4,766 observations. By construction, our weight-for-height metric is a ratio of the child’s weight (kg) to height

(cm), with a minimum value of 0.04375, a maximum of 0.875, a mean of 0.290, and a standard deviation of 0.096.

We first measure the effect of community-level shocks on weight-for-height, by our (1) shock-dummy regressor, then by (2) shock count. Under both specifications, we find statistically significant, negative estimators for the effect of shocks on weight-for-height. The results, shown in Table 3 (see: Appendix): (1), estimate that the occurrence of at least one community-level shock during a four-year period (2006-2009) lowers weight-for-height in the same period by 0.03 points, significant at the 0.1% level. Even more so, (2) estimates that for every shock an individual encoun- ters at the community level, weight-for- height is expected to decrease by approximately 0.00018 points, also significant at the 0.1% level. Given each specification, we also note very strong age effects inversely related to weight-for-height, as captured by fixed birth-year effects. In comparison to those living in the Upper West region, all region estimates—aside from Greater Accra, Brong Ahafo, and Volta—are negative and statistically significant at (at least) the 5% level. Note, living in the Volta region has a positive statistically significant effect on weight-for-height. Accordingly, urban households have significantly positive effects on weight-for-height; in (1), being urban increases weight-for-height by approximately 0.00814 points, and in (2) by 0.0132 points, both significant at the 0.1% level. Ethnicity and religion have some predictive power with regard to weight- for-height; being a Catholic-identifying household increases weight-for-height by an estimated 0.00625 points. With regard to the father’s work, which significantly

36 see: Appendix, Table 2 differed between the samples,36 we note significant negative effects on weight-for- height given the father’s employment in skilled labor.

Proceeding with a similar econometric specification, results in Table 4 (see: Appendix) measure the effect of shock frequency, constructed as a categorical variable, on weight-for-height. Covariate estimators and significance remain relatively the same as seen in Table 3; however, it is important to note that the only categorical shock variable of statistical significance in this construction is a few shocks (0-4), with an estimated increase in weight-for-height by 0.0217 points compared to encountering lots of shocks. Moreover, if an individual’s community experiences less than 5 shocks 2006-2009, weight-for-height is an estimated 0.0217 points stronger than if 33 or more shocks are experienced.

Results in Table 5 (see: Appendix) proceed with a similar specification, regressing shock type dummy variables on weight-for-height. While age, regional, and ethnicity effects largely remain the same, the predictive power of “urban” diminishes. We can attribute this to the agricultural shock dummy specification; since agriculture shocks are only surveyed in the Rural Community Survey, the inclusion of the agricultural-specific dummy accounts for the shift in predictive power of being an urban household. Categorical shock estimators are significant here: the occurrence of at least one agricultural shock has an estimated negative effect on weight- for-height of -0.0122 points; at least one town shock decreases weight-for-height by approximately 0.00825 points, and at least one crop sale shock decreases weight- for-height by 0.0125 points.

Wave 1-3 Analysis: Long-Run Physical Health Outcomes The Ghana cluster offers a broad range of physical health metrics that target early childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Since the age of our sample in Wave 1 is relatively young (all under the age of 15), we consider the ability to perform activities of daily living, as opposed to measures for health in the past two weeks, as these survey questions account best for overall physical wellbeing and are likely to represent longer-term health trends.

For this analysis, we conduct an instrumental variable (IV) regression, instrumenting shock count for weight- for-height. Results of three regressions are included in Table 6 (p. 27), the first measuring ability to perform daily activities in the first wave, the second measuring this ability in the second wave and controlling for the first, and the third measuring this ability in the third wave, controlling for the two preceding.

We note three interesting results. First, though the instrument is weak in Wave 1 and Wave 3, we do capture a significant estimator (at the 1% level) for weight-for-height on physical health outcomes in Wave 2. This suggests that a Wave 1 shock does indeed have an impact in the medium-long-run, though this effect is diluted in Wave 3. Second, estimates on gender gain statistical significance on Wave 2 and Wave 3 outcomes. Being female has a significant negative effect on the ability to easily carry heavy loads or bathe without assistance, and this effect seems to get stronger and larger over time. Third, age effects remain strong and directly related to physical health outcomes in Wave 1, remain significant for older children in Wave 2, and are largely insignificant in Wave 3.

Wave 1-3 Analysis: Long-Run Cognitive Development Outcomes Using the Children’s Module (Section 9) to examine cognitive development and related measures of early human capital development, we estimate cognitive ability using scores from the Raven’s Pattern Cognitive Assessment. The assessment is administered by 12 questions which require visual inductive reasoning skills, and each question answered correctly contributes 1 point to the total score (12). Incorrect answers are given 0 points.

The econometric structure applied here directly follows from that previous. We instrument shock count for weight- for-height to measure the effect on cognitive skill. In this case, two regressions are conducted: the first measures cognitive functioning in Wave 1, dependent on Wave 1 weight-for-height; the second measures cognitive functioning in Wave 2, dependent on Wave 1 weight-for-height and Wave 1 cognitive functioning score.

Notably, we again find that gender effects are strong and statistically significant such that female respondents score approximately 0.41 points less than male respondents in Wave 1 and 0.49 points less in Wave 2. With respect to nutrition status effects instrumented by frequency of exogenous shocks, effects in Wave 1 are very strong and significant, estimating for a 0.1 point increase in weight-for-height, respondents score approximately 4.509 points higher. The effects in Wave 2 are far smaller and insignificant, suggesting that shock-related nutritional deficiencies have a strong short-term cognitive impact but do not carry in the long-run.

Conclusion The study of household economic shocks offers one of many lenses through which we can consider constraints and resource allocations of poor households. As such, modern development theory and empirical approaches, as well as the expansiveness of GSPS encourage deeper examinations of economic shocks as one correlates to poverty traps in Ghana.

The prevalence of shocks—town events, agricultural, and crop price shocks—is ubiquitous in our sample and has significant and strong effects on short-term nutritional status for children under the age of 15. In particular, we find that frequency of shocks and weight-for- height outcomes are negatively correlated, whereas exposure to few community-level shocks has a significantly positive effect on weight-for-height compared to those exposed to lots of shocks (more than 32 shocks in a 4-year period). When measuring shock effects by type, we find that all shock types have significant negative effects on weight-for-height; however, agricultural shock-effects are the strongest of the three. Results suggest that the occurrence of community-level shocks leads households to restrict investment in nutrition through reduction of caloric intake. Economic shocks trigger such resource reallocations, at the cost of the nutritional needs of young children.

When translating these short-term findings on nutritional status to long-term outcomes of physical well-being and cognitive development, we find significance when instrumenting exogenous shock frequencies for weight-for-height. Notably, stronger weight-for-height in the first period significantly increases the likelihood that an individual will be able to carry out activities of daily life with ease; those activities being (i) carrying heavy loads and (ii) bathing without assistance. Similarly, with regard to the Raven’s Pattern Cognitive Assessment, we find that there are significant short-term effects on cognitive functioning, however, these effects are diminished in the second period. It is reassuring to see long-term effects diminish, suggesting that household responses over time do help individuals recover from shocks.

Though much ground was covered in the involved data and analyses, there is much room to clarify these findings. First, while our sample size is large, one limitation was encountering missing physical health metrics (e.g. height and weight) from certain waves, inconsistent at the individual-level. One amendment to this issue may be to construct estimations for those missing values based on those provided, ultimately vastly expanding the sample and perhaps better accounting for outliers. Second, it is encouraged that continued research using GSPS attempts to examine shock-effects using a difference-in-difference or regression disconti- nuity approach; perhaps selecting a policy that addresses agricultural subsidies or government insurance on property damage could offer a framework by which we can tamper the endogeneity issue.

In all, we conclude significant effects of shocks on short-term nutrition status and long-term physical health.While there is far more to be considered in the expansion of this work, the findings encourage policy action with regard to household-level recovery provisions and access to nutrition in Ghana and elsewhere, and continued study in this area can develop further evidence for doing so. ◆

Appendices

Econometric Approach: Specifications from Literature Review

Applied by Frankenberg and Thomas on the 1998 Indonesian Financial Crisis, the paper constructs a short-term analysis, measuring weight-for-height as a proxy for nutritional status and health inputs (e.g. caloric intake), as well as a long-run analysis, measuring height-for-age to account for overall health.

This framework has been applied across the literature pertaining to shocks and poverty traps. Notably, studying short and long-term consequences of early childhood malnutrition in Zimbabwe, Alderman, et. al. (2006), similarly apply a two-period model. In Period 1, covariates of individual and household characteristics are regressed on a height-for-age outcome variable to estimate the impact of baseline characteristics on nutritional status. In Period 2, height-for-age, individual, and household characteristic covariates are regressed on performance metrics (e.g. educational attainment, academic performance).

H1k = Z1 Z1k + η1k

A1k = H1 H1k + Z2 Z2k + η2k where Z1 and Z1k represent covariate vectors on individual and household characteristics, and η1k and η2k contain errors representing three components: time-invariant household characteristics (e.g. characteristics shared by all children within a given household determined by parents’ tastes and preferences), time-invariant child-specific characteristics (e.g. genetics), and any additional noise. By denoting two periods for short- and long-term effects, this empirical structure accounts account for differences between the two outcomes, and also attempts to capture the true effects of early life nutritional circumstances.

Indeed, issues arise both with the econometric assumption, E (H1k v2k) = 0, under ordinary least squares, and likely correlation between the errors, η1k and η2k. For example, suppose that as a result of stunted growth due to early childhood malnutrition, mothers invest more in their children’s physical health and education as they age in order to minimize those effects. One possible solution for this econometric problem is including sibling fixed effects helps to minimize the likelihood that these assumptions are violated in the least squares.

Parallel to this framework, Cas, et. al. (2014) estimate short- and long-term effects of early childhood shocks on well-being using evidence from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami on Indonesian households. They propose a similar model which attempts to estimate the extent to which accu- mulation of human capital is affected by the death of a parent during the tsunami by the following empirical strategy:

Yit = α + β1 Dit + β2 Xit + β3 Xi + εit where outcomes Yit, for child i at time t, are determined by occurrence of parental death—mother, father, or both—Dit, and both time-varying, Xit, and time-invariant, Xi, child and family characteristics. Note, however, that an estimation issue exists where, if a household invests differently in child human capital in anticipation of the tsunami, the assumption that the error is uncorrelated to parental death is violated. In efforts to mitigate this issue, Cas, et. al. also provide an estimation strategy with a child-specific fixed effect:

Yit = α + β1 Dit + β2 Xit + μi + φit the fixed effect, μi, is included to absorb all time-invariant characteristics of the parent and child which affect the outcome.
