title: About the Contributors
notes: Q&A with the seven thesis authors (Darran Shen, Charlotte Cagliostro, Emilya Ershtein, Aimee Flanigan, Ila Gupta, Maelea Tan, Jeffrey A. Popell): research topic, how they came to it, future directions and post-graduation plans.
text:
About the Contributors

Darran Shen Charlotte Cagliostro

Emilya Ershtein Aimee Flanigan

Ila Gupta Maelea Tan Jeffrey A. Popell

Darran Shen Urban Currents: Upstream Pollution and its Impacts on Intercity Populations Along the Mississippi River

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? I take a look at how river pollution emitted by cities along the Mississippi River affected population levels from 1870-1920. I argue that large quantities of upstream pollution increased mortality rates and/or turned the river into a dis-amenity, which led people downstream of pollution of move away. I measure this effect by modeling the historic concentration of pollution across the length of the Mississippi River at the county level. I also take a look at how contemporary water filtration and chlorination technologies (in addition to new insights in bacteriology) affected the effect of upstream pollution on downstream populations.

How did you come to your research topic? I was thinking about potential senior thesis ideas and I was inspired by two research papers in economic history. Ruixue Jia’s “The Legacies of Forced Freedom: China’s Treaty Ports” looked at differential growth of treaty port cities and non-treaty port cities along China’s coast and the Yangtze River. Heblich et al.’s “East-Side Story: Historical Pollution and Persistent Neighborhood Sorting” had me thinking about the population sorting effects of industrial pollution.

Combining the two, I began thinking about how river pollution may have impacted populations. I’m also a history and economics double major, so I was excited to combine the two. I was really inspired by Hanlon’s economic history class.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? Given more time and access to historical records (specifically local or state-level records), one could analyze the effects of pollution at a more precise level than my existing county-level observations and also look at the differential effects of pollution between inland communities and communities on the river. There are additional opportunities to refine my model of upstream pollution for accuracy, perhaps by drawing from hydrology research. Most examples of detailed hydrology research were focused either on a small geographic area or a single period in time, making it hard. Many of the states in the north like Minnesota and Michigan also tended to care more about the environment and pollution, so their historical records on this issue are better.

One extension of this research may analyze the relationship between upstream pollution and population sorting (i.e., changing income, property values, and literacy in downstream communities), which would also be an interesting application for a hedonic pricing model or externality analysis. Another extension lies in investigating the differential mortality rates of smaller industrial towns, which often lagged behind in implementing modern public health mechanisms (Leonard et al. 2012), and larger communities on the Mississippi that did implement water quality improvements.

Where are you heading to after graduation? Working for Microsoft as a product manager in Seattle.

Charlotte Cagliostro Revisiting the Agentic- Communal Framework: A Conjoint Analysis Approach to Understanding Bias Against Female Leaders in the Workplace

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? Put most generally, my thesis examined how gender stereotypes affect leadership perception. More specifically, I assessed how agency and communality expectations affect the probability of male and female candidates being selected as leaders.

How did you come to your research topic? I worked in the Advancing Teams, Leaders, & Systems Lab during Spring 2022 as an Independent Study course. The main course project was an independent research project, and I chose to examine women in leadership. This investigation gave me a foundational understanding of the stereotypes at play and the methods used by researchers to study them. From this experience, I was inspired to conduct my own experiment to contribute novel findings. Since the topic had been studied extensively before, I decided to use an innovative methodology (conjoint analysis).

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? There is so much more work that ought to be conducted to understand intersec- tionality. While I was able to consider race and gender in my full, extended thesis, I could not discuss it in my journal submis- sion, but there is such limited research in the field to understand the intersections between race and gender in a leadership context.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I have been working in the Psychology Department at Northwestern as the Participant Pool Coordinator for just about two months now. I plan to pursue a PhD in social psychology in a couple years so that I can continue this research.

Emilya Ershtein The Effect of Merit Scholarships on Saving for College

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? The Effect of Merit Aid on College Savings

How did you come to your research topic? I attended a seminar about merit aid scholarships in the US. It left me with unanswered questions, such as this one.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? In general we don’t know whether the merit aid programs are good or justified. What I looked at is one piece of the puz- zle of its effects. Future researchers and policymakers can use this to answer have the question: is implementing broad merit-based tuition reductions/waivers for college a good idea?

Where are you heading to after graduation? Federal Reserve Bank of New York

Aimee Flanigan The Project of Total War and the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, 1944-1945

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research topic is the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, a human experiment conducted at the University of Minnesota’s Laboratory of Physiological Hygiene between 1944 and 1945. Using 36 conscientious objectors as volunteer human subjects, the doctors systematically starved the men to understand the physical and psychological effects of starvation. They then rehabilitated them on different diets to determine how best nourish the starving populations of Europe. I analyze parallels between the doctors who ran the experiment and military officers as well as between the human subjects and their enlisted counterparts to show how the character of total war permeated the Starvation Experiment.

How did you come to your research topic? I found out about the Minnesota Starvation Experiment through a podcast I listened to. I found the story incredibly fascinating and could not believe that I had never known about it before. As I talked to more friends, peers, and professors, I realized that many people had never heard of it! This compelled me to focus on the experiment as my thesis topic. I wanted to learn more, and I wanted to tell others about this extraordinary undertaking. This topic also marries my interest in both history and health, and finally allows me to engage with a history driven by the fascinating people and historical period at its center.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? There is still so much to write about the Minnesota Starvation Experiment. I could have written so many theses on this topic, and there are so many areas open to interesting and valuable analysis. There is surprisingly little written about the experiment, so there is ample room for more works and discussions.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I am beginning a Masters in Public Health at Feinberg and am moving to Chicago.

Ila Gupta Early Childhood Shocks in Ghana: Evidence on Physical Health and Cognitive Development

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? My research studies effects of early childhood shocks in Ghana on short- and long-run physical health and cognitive development. It considers a wide range of shocks (town-related, agricultural, etc.) and estimates their effect on weight-for-height, physical wellbeing indicators, and cognition indicators. We find significant effects.

How did you come to your research topic? I worked at the Global Poverty Research Lab (GPRL) in the later half of my undergrad at Northwestern. While at GPRL, I primarily worked with the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey (GSPS)--cleaning the most recently collected survey data. Already having an interest in development economics (stemming from the first papers I read and the courses I eventually took at Northwestern), I knew I wanted to contribute to this area when approaching my thesis. Since GSPS was so expansive, and I had become so familiar with it, I thought it’d be a great starting point. From there, my interests in health-topic overlaps in economics and studies on early childhood helped shape my research topic.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? There’s plenty left to discover in this field. Though results may not be shocking, their significance and power have the ability to influence policy in not only developing countries, but in poor populations globally (i.e. everywhere). I see this work expanding to better understand the impacts of specific shocks--comparing the effects of town events such as violent/peaceful demonstrations, police brutality, etc. to agricultural shocks- -to better inform the kinds of investments governments can make to protect the affected populations. There are so many directions researchers could continue to build on this: selecting other countries/regions/populations to study, (again) getting deeper into the effects of specific household economic shocks, conducting “natural experiment” studies which support nutrition compensation, for example, for affected populations (and seeing if this changes results), and on.

Where are you heading to after graduation? I begin work at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago as a Research Assistant in Community Development and Regional Economics next week. This is a 2-year position. From there, I’m thinking graduate studies in economics.

Maelea Tan Grief Unmasked

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? I researched Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’ stages of grief and how they manifest in individuals, creating 8 masks to embody and represent these different stages.

How did you come to your research topic? I experienced a lot of loss and grief during my time as an undergraduate student. I arrived at this research topic because there was a lack of artistic experiences to process grief that I resonated with. Thus, I decided to create my own art in hopes that my work would be able to speak to those grieving like I was.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? In the future, I hope to see artistic expressions/processings of grief being made more accessible to those experiencing loss, so they know they’re not alone.

Where are you heading to after graduation? Northwestern University’s MS in Leadership in Creative Enterprises program.

Jeffrey A. Popell The Effect of Copyright Term Extension on Creative Productivity

In a nutshell, what is your research topic? One philosophical justification for copyright protection is that it promotes greater productivity than otherwise. Research seems to show that this is the case. However, it’s less clear that the extreme extensions we’ve seen in recent years have had the same effect. The goal of my research was to determine whether such extensions in fact promote greater productivity or not.

How did you come to your research topic? I’ve long thought modern copyright law was overly restrictive, and wanted to look at the data to see whether that’s actually the case or not.

Where do you see the future direction of this work leading? How might future researchers build on your work, or what is left to discover in this field? I think my methodology was sound, but unfortunately, none of the pairs I looked at had parallel pre-trends, a precondition for the experimental design I used. Future study might try the same thing with other pairs of jurisdictions, to find results on this question.

Where are you heading to after graduation? Still figuring that out.
